papers.title: UniRoad: Unifying Road Representations Across Cities and Tasks
affiliations: Department of Electronic Engineering, Tsinghua University
College of Computer Science, Chongqing University
papers.abstract: Learning generalizable road representations is essential for urban computing, yet remains challenging due to heterogeneous urban signals, city-specific road characteristics, and diverse downstream tasks. Existing methods often encode multi-source information jointly, causing functional, structural, and mobility semantics to be entangled in a single representation space. We propose UniRoad, a unified multi-view framework for cross-city road representation learning. UniRoad decomposes road semantics into three complementary views: an LLM-based profile view that captures functional semantics from road attributes and POI contexts, a prototype-based structure view that learns transferable structural roles from local topology, and a trajectory-informed mobility view that models travel patterns from road sequences. UniRoad further introduces confidence-guided fusion to adaptively integrate these views according to their reliability. Extensive experiments on four cities and four downstream tasks demonstrate that UniRoad consistently outperforms strong baselines and achieves robust cross-city transferability. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/csjiezhao/UniRoad.

papers.title: CoST: Semantic-Aware Urban Understanding via Spatial-Temporal Alignment
affiliations: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
papers.abstract: Geospatial representation learning from satellite imagery is a fundamental problem for large-scale urban analysis and real-world applications. Despite recent advances, current methods struggle with cross-region generalization and semantic interpretability due to their reliance on region-specific auxiliary data and the neglect of semantic alignment within multi-temporal urban imagery. Therefore, we present CoST, a novel Contrastive-based Spatial-Temporal framework that aligns spatial context with multi-temporal semantics to extract universal geographic regularities shared across regions. Specifically, CoST explicitly models spatial correlations to capture transferable geographic structures and exploits multi-year urban change semantics to align learned representations with high-level geo-semantics. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoST consistently achieves superior performance across various downstream tasks and in unseen scenario, yielding an average relative gain of 8.7% over the strongest competing methods across eight city-indicator settings. The code is available in this repo (https://github.com/Arandinglv/CoST).

papers.title: CRAFT: Cross-Region Adaptive Federated Transfer Learning for Urban Spatiotemporal Prediction
papers.abstract: Urban spatiotemporal prediction is crucial for smart city management, yet fragmented data across administrative boundaries significantly impedes effective model training. To overcome data limitations and leverage knowledge from data-rich regions while preserving data privacy, federated transfer learning has emerged as a promising approach for cross-regional urban prediction tasks. However, traditional learning methods encounter the dual challenge: (1) intra-regional knowledge acquisition difficulties due to missing boundaries that weaken spatiotemporal dependencies and cause data sparsity; and (2) cross-regional knowledge transfer bias, where distribution differences between source and target regions trigger negative transfer and reduce model robustness. To address these issues, we propose CRAFT: a novel federated transfer learning framework that integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) for urban spatiotemporal prediction. Leveraging LLMs' powerful semantic understanding and contextual reasoning abilities, CRAFT captures complex spatiotemporal dependencies and uncovers latent regional connections from heterogeneous data sources, thus alleviating boundary-induced data sparsity. Additionally, to address inter-regional data heterogeneity, we employ a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with parameter decoupling, which excels at handling diverse data distributions while minimizing federated communication costs. Experimental results on real-world datasets from multiple cities demonstrate the effectiveness of CRAFT in cross-regional federated transfer learning. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/Jasonxx4/CRAFT.

papers.title: BPR-Net: Bin-Resolved Temporal Responses for Frequency-Aware Prototype Routing in Spatiotemporal Forecasting
affiliations: Graduate School of Data Science, Chonnam National University
papers.abstract: Spatiotemporal forecasting requires modeling temporal dynamics and spatial dependencies across multiple spatial units. Existing approaches construct spatial relations from graph structures, latent representations, or attention weights. This work uses frequency-bin-level temporal responses in the prototype routing cost before spatial-unit-level aggregation. We propose BPR-Net (Bin-aware Prototype Routing Network), a frequency-bin-aware prototype routing model for spatiotemporal forecasting. BPR-Net explicitly represents frequency-bin-level temporal responses before they are aggregated into spatial-unit-level representations and uses them for prototype-based spatial relation learning. Specifically, BPR-Net represents each spatial unit through bin-resolved temporal responses, incorporates them into the prototype routing cost via Bin-Prototype Affinity, and modulates the routed representation using a spectral signature. Experiments on nine datasets across mobile traffic, air quality, taxi flow, and traffic sensor domains show that BPR-Net achieves the best result in 26 out of 28 dataset–metric settings against 19 baselines. Additional analyses show that BPR-Net achieves low forecasting error with short inference time in the reported efficiency settings and maintains low forecasting errors for spatial units with different spectral properties.

papers.title: STAAR: Spatio-Temporal Attention over Adaptive Regions for Traffic Forecasting
affiliations: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)
papers.abstract: Accurate traffic forecasting is essential for Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS). Attention-based Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks (STGNNs) have been widely adopted to capture long-range spatial dependencies, but their node-level attention incurs quadratic complexity and limits scalability in large-scale traffic networks. Although sparse and hierarchical attention mechanisms reduce this cost by restricting node pairs, they still rely on node-level modeling. Through empirical analysis on a 2,352-node benchmark, we find that removing node-level attention from representative baselines does not consistently degrade performance, suggesting that its additional predictive benefit may be marginal in large-scale settings. In contrast, region-level attention appears useful for modeling traffic propagation, which is also consistent with classical traffic engineering models that represent traffic dynamics over aggregated spatial units. Motivated by these observations, we propose STAAR, a Spatio-Temporal Attention over Adaptive Regions framework that dynamically constructs soft traffic regions and models dependencies among them. Specifically, adaptive region assignment assigns each node to multiple regions with normalized weights, while spatio-temporal attention captures time-lagged dependencies by flattening region tokens across time steps into a unified sequence. Extensive experiments on large-scale traffic benchmarks demonstrate that our model achieves competitive accuracy with substantial efficiency gains, reducing training time by 3.5×–29× and inference time by 2.8×–28× compared with existing attention-based STGNNs. The source code of STAAR is publicly available at https://github.com/kaist-dmlab/STAAR.

papers.title: CPTIF: Continuous-Time Perception Traffic Forecasting based on Spatio-Temporal Graph Learning
papers.abstract: Intelligent transportation systems (ITS) increasingly deploy roadside units (RSUs) equipped with sensors for environmental perception. Each RSU captures the surrounding traffic scene as a stream of point clouds, whose volume varies with vehicle density, mutual occlusion, and scene geometry. Since downstream tasks such as object detection, tracking, and cooperative perception depend on these streams, accurately predicting future perception volume is necessary for proactive resource provisioning in real-time ITS applications. However, this volume cannot be reliably determined from conventional traffic variables alone, as the same number of vehicles can produce substantially different amounts of point cloud data under different sensing conditions. Moreover, the perception influence between road sections shifts continuously as vehicles move and alter occlusion conditions, and vehicle arrivals introduce time-varying propagation delays that a fixed road-topology graph cannot capture. To address these challenges, we propose CPTIF, a continuous-time spatiotemporal forecasting framework that models each RSU as a node on a dynamic graph with adaptive edge weights fusing learnable structural priors and state-dependent dynamic relations. Temporal evolution and spatial propagation are unified through a cascaded neural controlled differential equation architecture, where discrete observations are first interpolated into continuous control paths and latent states evolve along these paths, enabling prediction at arbitrary future timestamps without retraining. We construct a perception traffic forecasting benchmark by coupling SUMO-driven traffic simulation with CARLA-rendered sensor perception across five topologically distinct maps. Experiments demonstrate that CPTIF outperforms representative baselines in prediction accuracy and multi-step stability.

papers.title: Region-Guided Slow-Fast Graph ODEs for Traffic Flow Forecasting
papers.abstract: Traffic flow forecasting requires modeling rapidly changing local fluctuations and slowly evolving regional trends. Existing Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (Neural ODE)-based traffic forecasting models usually evolve states at a single spatial granularity, which may entangle node-level volatility with macroscopic evolution and lead to over-smoothed peak predictions under volatile traffic conditions. To capture such mixed-scale dynamics, we propose Hierarchical Slow-Fast Spatial-Temporal Graph ODE (HSF-STGODE), a region-guided slow-fast continuous framework for traffic flow forecasting. HSF-STGODE decomposes traffic evolution into two coupled continuous processes: a Fast Graph ODE modeling node-level short-term fluctuations on the sensor graph, and a Slow Graph ODE capturing region-level trends on a learnable latent region graph. The two processes are connected through bottom-up aggregation and top-down guidance, enabling regional trends to provide stable context for fine-grained node evolution. To further model lagged propagation and irregular local variations, we incorporate a delay-aware pattern module, a flow-consistency regularizer, and a dual-gated fusion mechanism for scale-specific multi-period initialization. Experiments on four widely used PeMS benchmarks show HSF-STGODE achieves the best or tied-best RMSE across all datasets, with strong MAPE performance and competitive MAE results against representative and strong baselines. These results suggest region-guided slow-fast continuous modeling is particularly effective in reducing large forecasting deviations for traffic flow forecasting. Code is available at https://github.com/KYasmaine/HSF-STGODE.

papers.title: RiskTraf: Risk-Extrapolated Residual Learning for Multi-Variate Traffic Flow Prediction
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
papers.abstract: Traffic sensors commonly record flow, speed, and occupancy, but standard traffic flow forecasting benchmarks and models rarely exploit all three raw measurements reliably. Although speed and occupancy provide sensor-native traffic-state information beyond flow alone, existing releases often omit these variables, replace them with proxies, or contain logically inconsistent records. Moreover, direct empirical risk minimization over three-variable inputs may exploit regime-dependent shortcuts, as the relationships among flow, speed, and occupancy vary substantially between free-flow and congested states. We introduce PEMSB-3V , a public benchmark suite that preserves raw flow, speed, and occupancy measurements from PeMS detectors for flow prediction. We also propose RiskTraf , a model-agnostic risk-extrapolated residual plug-in. For each trained spatio-temporal backbone, RiskTraf freezes the selected checkpoint and learns a lightweight zero-start residual head from historical speed and occupancy. The residual head constructs ordered traffic-risk environments and optimizes horizon-wise flow corrections with a risk extrapolation objective, thereby mitigating regime-specific shortcut correlations without modifying the backbone. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RiskTraf consistently improves diverse forecasting backbones and outperforms debiasing and distribution-shift adaptation methods. Our code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/Guangyu4/RiskTraf.

papers.title: The Prism of Interest: Refracting User Needs in Session-Based Recommendation
affiliations: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: Session-based Recommendation (SBR) aims to predict users' next interaction based on short-term anonymous behavior sequences. Yet accurately modeling the dynamic switching and hierarchical dependency of user intent remains a critical challenge. Existing methods typically treat intents as parallel signals thus ignoring the dynamic shift in the dominant decision-making pattern layer within a session. However, we argue that the dominant decision-making pattern shifts across hierarchical intent layers over time, and treating these layers as static or independent inevitably causes mismodeling. To address these issues, we propose a P yramid R outing for I ntent S equence M odeling framework ( PRISM ), which constructs an intent pyramid to parse user decision-making processes. Specifically, we first devise a Hierarchical Vector Quantization module to progressively compress actions into theme and goals. We then employ a Multi-Intent Routing Network to model the cross-layer dependency and information propagation among different intent layers. Finally, to adapt to the dynamic shifting of decision dominance, we design a Mixture of Intent Module that adaptively weights the prediction distributions from different layers, and introduce a Goal-Aware Contrastive Regularizer to ensure the consistency of hierarchical intent representations. Experimental results on three real-world datasets exhibit that PRISM achieves state-of-the-art performance.

papers.title: MAPLE: Mamba-Based Adaptive Prototype Learning for Intent Disentanglement in Sequential Recommendation
papers.abstract: Sequential recommender systems struggle to simultaneously capture persistent long-term preferences and volatile short-term intentions, while existing dual-stream architectures are computationally inefficient when handling long sequences and suffer from feature entanglement between the two interest streams. To address these issues, we propose a Mamba-based Adaptive Prototype LEarning and cross-intent contrastive alignment framework (MAPLE). MAPLE employs Mamba as the long-term encoder; its selective state space mechanism selectively retains important historical signals across the entire interaction sequence, making it well-suited for capturing stable long-term interest features with linear computational complexity. Meanwhile, the GRU-based short-term encoder focuses on a local tail window to model recent preference shifts. To decouple these two interest streams, we maintain a set of global semantic prototypes for each interest type and extract soft proxies as personalized semantic anchors through attention-weighted aggregation, thereby leveraging global intent consensus to enrich individual user representations. These proxies are further applied as contrastive anchors in a novel cross-intent InfoNCE loss, which treats proxies of the complementary intent stream as cross-intent contrastive anchors to promote semantic differentiation between long and short-term representations. Finally, we introduce an asymmetric dynamic gated fusion module that prioritizes long-term features as the main component and incorporates short-term features as the auxiliary component for next-item prediction. Experiments on four real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate that MAPLE achieves highly competitive performance, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art models on rank-aware metrics.

papers.title: DART: Residual Trust and Tail-Aware Dual-View Alignment for Sequential Recommendation
papers.abstract: Sequential recommender systems commonly learn item representations from interaction data. This paradigm works well for frequent items, but becomes unreliable for long-tail items whose ID embeddings receive limited updates. Offline semantic embeddings derived from large language models provide useful item-side knowledge beyond interaction logs. They can therefore compensate for the insufficient interaction supervision of long-tail items. However, directly optimizing such semantic priors for recommendation may distort their original semantic structure. Moreover, semantic information should not be injected uniformly across all items, since head items are already well supported by interactions while long-tail items require semantic compensation more urgently. In this paper, we propose DART, a constrained semantic enhancement framework that couples Residual Trust Semantic Adaptation with Tail-Aware Dual-View Alignment for sequential recommendation. DART treats offline LLM-derived item embeddings as frozen semantic anchors and injects collaborative signals through a trust-region-constrained residual pathway. This design allows item representations to absorb useful collaborative information while limiting semantic drift. To further improve long-tail recommendation, DART introduces a tail-aware dual-view alignment mechanism that concentrates cross-view transfer on long-tail items instead of aligning all items uniformly. Experiments on three public benchmarks show that DART achieves strong overall performance and consistent gains in long-tail settings. Further ablation and representation analyses verify the effectiveness of residual-trust adaptation and tail-aware semantic transfer.

papers.title: LSF-SR: Latent Semantic Fusion for Sequential Recommendation via Flow-based Conditional Variational Autoencoders
affiliations: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
papers.abstract: Sequential recommendation aims to predict users' future interests from their historical interactions. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) capture rich item semantics, existing methods often struggle to align collaborative signals with textual semantic knowledge. As a result, the learned item representations fail to capture the complementary strengths of both signals, leading to suboptimal recommendation quality. To address this limitation, we propose L atent S emantic F usion for S equential R ecommendation via Flow-based Conditional Variational Autoencoders ( LSF-SR ), a novel framework that uses a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) with Normalizing Flows to fuse item ID embeddings and LLM-generated semantic signals. At the core of LSF-SR is a conditional fusion module augmented with planar or radial flows. This module learns a flexible latent space that encourages items with similar semantic profiles to cluster together within the latent manifold. Through extensive experiments on five public benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that LSF-SR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving gains of up to 12.98% and 14.13% in Recall@20 and NDCG@20, respectively.

papers.title: CaLR: Context-Aware Latent Reasoning for Sequential Recommendation
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: Sequential recommendation aims to model users’ evolving preferences from their historical interactions. Recent latent reasoning methods improve sequential recommenders by extending inferencetime computation in continuous representation space, refining user representations without generating explicit reasoning text. However, existing methods mainly reason over the encoded history itself and make limited use of contextual feedback from users’ recent interactions. Such feedback, especially positive and negative signals in the latest session, can not only complement the long-term user representation but also provide directional guidance for latent reasoning by indicating which preference patterns should be strengthened or suppressed. In this paper, we propose Context-Aware Latent Reasoning (CaLR), a model-agnostic framework that grounds latent reasoning in session-level context. From the input perspective, CaLR selects informative positive and negative items from users’ recent sessions as reasoning anchors. From the architecture perspective, it injects these anchors into each reasoning step through a Cross-Attention-based module. From the optimization perspective, it introduces Process Supervision Loss (PSL) to supervise intermediate reasoning states according to anchor feedback polarity. Experiments on two real-world public benchmarks show that CaLR consistently improves multiple sequential recommendation backbones and outperforms strong latent reasoning baselines. Ablation and further analyses verify the effectiveness of each component in CaLR. Moreover, a seven-day online A/B test on Kuaishou Lite demonstrates its effectiveness in real-world industrial deployment. Our code is available at https://github.com/Ak4ne-windsky/CaLR.

papers.title: Building Sequential Recommendation Models upon Thermoelastic Spectral Operators
papers.abstract: Sequential recommendation aims to predict the next item a user will interact with from behavioral history. Frequency-domain methods emerge as a promising approach to capture different behavioral patterns by decomposing user sequences into frequency components with various filters. However, existing spectral filters mainly emphasize or suppress frequency components, without explicitly modeling how preference signals evolve in the spectral domain. To overcome this limitation, we propose TelaRec , a novel physics-inspired sequential recommendation model built upon the Thermoelastic Spectral Operator (TSO). TSO treats user behavior sequences as preference fields and models their evolution through heat conduction and elastic wave propagation, where heat conduction extracts stable preferences and elastic wave propagation captures short-term interests. Derived from partial differential equations, TSO enables analytical spectral operations beyond conventional static or adaptive filtering. We further introduce User-aware Frequency Calibration (UFC) to adjust the propagation scale of each frequency mode according to the current user's spectral response for personalized spectral evolution. Experiments on six benchmark datasets demonstrate that TelaRec achieves competitive recommendation performance and high computational efficiency. Our source code is available at https://github.com/TBI805/TelaRec.

papers.title: Closing the Long-Short View Gap in Sequential Recommendation without Cached History
papers.abstract: Sequential recommenders are typically trained on long user histories to capture rich behavioral signals, yet serving with training-length sequences is often impractical due to real-time efficiency constraints. Directly using only recent behaviors leads to a severe performance drop. To bridge this gap, existing approaches compress user histories into persistent per-user states, storing and retrieving them at inference time; while effective, they impose non-trivial infrastructure overhead and offer little remedy in cold-start scenarios. In this paper, we empirically identify two structural flaws rooted in geometric properties and dataset sparsity, and propose a novel two-stage framework to close the long-short-view performance gap. Specifically, in the first stage, we replace the commonly used dot-product with angular similarity scoring and leverage a modified softmax to counter prefix position bias. In the second stage, we fine-tune only bias and LayerNorm components—universal to standard sequential backbones—for further improvement. Both stages are guided by carefully designed learning objectives. Extensive experiments on two representative backbones across three public datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

papers.title: GOD: Enhancing Generalization via Deep Grafting for Sequential Recommendation
affiliations: Pohang University of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Sequential recommenders often struggle with sparse and noisy histories, limiting generalization to unseen interactions. Knowledge distillation mitigates this by transferring dense supervision from a teacher to a student. However, most distillation methods run teacher and student independently, then match student outputs or representations to the teacher. Such supervision entangles student-component effects, blurring whether weak generalization stems from unreliable embeddings, overfitted encoding, or co-adaptation to sparse histories. In this paper, we propose G raft- O riented D istillation ( GOD ), a component-level distillation framework for improved generalization through grafting. Grafting denotes replacing selected frozen-teacher components with trainable student counterparts to build hybrid source models. GOD uses these hybrid models to evaluate student embeddings with the teacher encoder and the student encoder with teacher embeddings, providing component-level feedback. At inference, GOD uses only the student, incurring no additional cost. Across three real-world datasets, GOD outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by up to 13.92%.

papers.title: Code-as-Auditor: Executable Compliance Reasoning via Regulation-to-Code
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted for compliance and legal reasoning tasks, yet their outputs often lack explicit grounding in legal logic and evidence. We present Code-as-Auditor, an LLM-based framework that extends the model’s reasoning capability toward structured and evidence-grounded compliance assessment. The framework translates regulatory information into (1) formalized checklists and executable decision trees, encoding regulations and conditions as interpretable code structures. During inference, each checklist item is (2) dynamically expanded into factual and counterfactual questions, guiding the model to reason over case-specific evidence and potential violations. This process establishes a reasoning pipeline that proceeds from evidence identification, through rule application, to final decision-making, while a self-verification loop ensures logical consistency and traceability of outcomes. Experiments on privacy and data protection scenarios demonstrate that Code-as-Auditor delivers more accurate and evidence-backed evaluations, enabling automated compliance regulation checking grounded in explicit regulatory criteria.

papers.title: Bridging Intuition and Logic: A Dual-Memory Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Narrative Reasoning
affiliations: Logistics University of People's Armed Police Force
papers.abstract: Narrative reasoning is defined as predicting future events from narrative context, requiring an understanding of event evolution and implicit causality. Current memory-augmented approaches follow two separate paradigms: episodic-memory retrieval, which leverages past analogies but often leads to logical hallucination due to surface-level similarity, and semantic-memory retrieval using Event-centric Knowledge Graphs (EKGs), which ensures logical consistency but suffers from sparsity in open-world settings. Inspired by the Complementary Learning Systems (CLS) theory in cognitive science, we propose a Dual-Memory Neuro-Symbolic Framework (DMNeS), which synergizes episodic intuition and semantic verification for logically reliable narrative reasoning. Specifically, the Episodic Intuition Reasoner generates intuitive predictions based on retrieved analogous episodes. To mitigate potential logical hallucination, these predictions are then validated by the Semantic Logic Verifier using causal-temporal evidence retrieved from an EKG. When an otherwise consistent candidate lacks an explicit EKG path due to sparsity, Abductive Reflection prompts the LLM to hypothesize a latent bridge event and connecting relations, and re-verifies the resulting chain under occurrence and temporal constraints. Finally, the Dynamic Memory Evolution module consolidates both memories, strengthening their interplay. As a fine-tuning-free inference framework, DMNeS achieves a 5.7 percentage-point average gain over the strongest baseline and improves LLM backbones by 7.5--9.7 percentage points across three benchmarks.

papers.title: FISolver: Data-Driven Discovery of First Integrals via Backward Generation and Guided Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: The discovery of first integrals is of profound scientific significance for understanding physical conservation laws in dynamical systems. However, existing symbolic computation systems and Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with this task due to the scarcity of high-quality training data and the reliance on mathematical intuition for finding solutions. This paper introduces FISolver , an LLM-based solver designed to bridge this gap. First, we propose a novel “Backward Generation” algorithm that systematically constructs large-scale datasets of (differential equations, first integrals) pairs by deriving equations from sampled integrals, effectively overcoming the data scarcity bottleneck. Second, we perform supervised fine-tuning on a compact mathematical model and further enhance its capabilities using reinforcement learning with a Levenshtein Distance-based shaped reward function. Additionally, we introduce data synthesis and blending techniques that enable effective adaptation to specific hard instances with sparse examples. Experiments demonstrate that FISolver , with significantly lower computational cost, substantially outperforms larger mathematical LLMs and commercial solvers like Mathematica on complex benchmarks, establishing a new data-driven paradigm for automated mathematical discovery.

papers.title: Steering Large Language Models toward Cross-Cultural Value Alignment via Activation Engineering
affiliations: Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly shape human decision-making as conversational assistants and act on human behalf as autonomous agents, making the cultural values they encode consequential across both settings. Yet ensuring that these systems reflect the values of diverse cultural groups remains an open challenge, as existing alignment approaches offer limited ability to precisely control cultural value orientations on demand. In this work, we investigate cultural value representations in LLM activation space through the lens of Hofstede's six-dimensional framework. We first demonstrate that contrastive activation steering reliably controls individual cultural value dimensions, significantly and consistently outperforming prompt-based steering across two models and two independent evaluation protocols. We then show that cultural value dimensions are not geometrically independent: positively correlated value vectors mutually amplify each other's effects at the cost of response coherence, while negatively correlated vectors attenuate each other through directional cancellation. These interference patterns impose a fundamental constraint on naive multi-dimensional steering. Motivated by this geometric analysis, we propose a selective projection decoupling method that removes inter-dimension interference prior to joint injection and fits steering coefficients to country-level Hofstede profiles. Evaluated on Brazil, China, and the United States, our method achieves consistent improvements in alignment accuracy, direction hits, and cultural similarity across both Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and Ministral-8B-Instruct models, demonstrating that steered models are not only more culturally accurate but achieve high cultural similarity to their intended target profiles.

papers.title: FLoRE: A Formal Language Benchmark for Robustness and Effectiveness Evaluation of LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), especially recent reasoning-oriented models trained with reinforcement learning, achieve near-saturating accuracy on many reasoning benchmarks. However, it remains unclear whether these models truly reason over semantic structure or rely on superficial symbol patterns and familiar language forms. This issue is increasingly critical in the agent era, where reasoning systems must remain reliable under changing representations. We introduce FLoRE, a controllable evaluation benchmark for diagnosing LLM reasoning robustness and effectiveness using formal languages. By isolating reasoning from world knowledge, formal languages enable direct evaluation of structural reasoning with machine-verifiable ground truth. We defines two tasks: Formal Language Recognition and Grammar Induction and construct 25.5k data instances. Evaluating diverse reasoning and non-reasoning LLMs, we identify two universal failure modes. First, models exhibit severe symbol-binding fragility: changing symbolic representations while preserving semantics causes large drops on positive instances but increases accuracy on negative instances, revealing a strong default rejection bias under unfamiliar symbols. Second, many reasoning-oriented local LLMs show negation non-termination during grammar induction, failing to terminate reasoning on negative instances and instead exhausting large portions of the context window. Our results show that current LLM reasoning remains strongly dependent on surface symbol priors and lacks robust semantic invariance and termination stability. FLoRE provides a unified framework for systematically evaluating these properties in controllable formal-language settings. Code and data files are available at https://github.com/HoganZinger/FLoRE

papers.title: Efficient LLM Benchmark Evaluation with Bayesian Item Response and Routed Subspace Selection
affiliations: School of Artificial Intelligence, Nanjing University
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) are evaluated on increasingly large and diverse benchmark suites, running an LLM on the entire benchmark incurs substantial costs. We study efficient LLM evaluation, where the goal is to accurately estimate full-benchmark performance by adaptively querying only a small subset of prompts. The key challenge is that selected prompts should be informative for the target model while remaining representative of diverse response patterns in the benchmark. To address this, we adopt a posterior-aware Bayesian perspective: historical response data are used to characterize complex prompt--model behaviors, and the resulting posterior information guides adaptive prompt selection under a limited budget. Specifically, we develop a variational Gaussian Process Item Response Theory (VGP-IRT) model, which leverages item-specific Gaussian process response functions to flexibly capture nonlinear prompt--model interactions beyond restrictive parametric response curves. Based on prompt features and predictive information derived from the VGP-IRT posterior, we further construct group-balanced candidate pools within local routed subspaces for adaptive selection. Experiments on four benchmarks demonstrate improved score estimation through our method, with the strongest gains in the low-to-moderate budget regime.

papers.title: AutoRepairBench: Benchmarking Long-Tailed, Safety-Critical Automotive Repair Reasoning
papers.abstract: Vehicle diagnosis begins with structured signals—an Electronic Control Unit (ECU) identifier, a Diagnostic Trouble Code (DTC), and trigger conditions—but technicians must translate them into an accurate fault description and appropriate repair measures. Automotive repair reasoning is both long-tailed and safety-critical: rare ECU/DTC combinations provide few training examples, while associating a fault with the wrong control unit or recommending unnecessary repairs can mislead maintenance decisions. Benchmarking this capability is challenging because diagnostic resources are fragmented, general-purpose large language models (LLMs) often fail to follow repair constraints, and exact-match metrics may reject valid answers expressed differently. We introduce AutoRepairBench , a BMW-centered benchmark and evaluation framework for long-tailed, safety-critical automotive repair reasoning. It supports single-turn diagnosis, multi-pair prompting, and frequency-aware analysis of common and rare cases. Its validated hierarchical evaluator accepts valid paraphrases while checking ECU/DTC associations, component relationships, repair severity, and unnecessary repair recommendations. We also develop RepairLLM-7B , a compact, retrieval-free model trained through two-stage distillation: the first stage reduces the dominance of frequent cases, while knowledge-graph-anchored online distillation emphasizes uncertain and rare cases. On a double-blind set of 585 cases labeled by three automotive experts, the evaluator achieved 94.19% accuracy and an F1 score of 94.67%. On the 500-instance main evaluation set, RepairLLM-7B achieved 95.0% single-turn joint accuracy (475/500) and 94.2% per-pair joint accuracy under multi-pair prompting (471/500); it also improved tail accuracy on the separate 100-instance generalization set and reduced safety-critical errors relative to supervised fine-tuning. These results demonstrate the importance of jointly benchmarking overall accuracy, rare-case performance, and repair safety in automotive repair reasoning.

papers.title: Internal Stability Signals for Selective Verification and Hallucination Mitigation in Vision-Language Models
affiliations: Shanghai University of International Business and Economics
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) are increasingly used for multimodal search, open-ended question answering, document understanding, and generated content analysis, yet they still produce claims that are fluent but unsupported by visual evidence. Existing hallucination mitigation methods often rely on external multimodal judges, language-model annotators, or human token labels to localize unsupported content, adding cost and introducing a mismatch with the target model's own failure modes. We propose HIS-Guard, a framework for trustworthy multimodal claim generation that diagnoses unsupported claims using the target LVLM's internal stability signals and routes those signals to selective verification or preference optimization. Its core diagnostic, Hallucination Instability Score (HIS), combines semantic convergence from cross-layer LogitLens entropy reduction with visual grounding coherence from cross-token attention-distribution consistency over image patches. By decomposing HIS into semantic and visual instability, HIS-Guard supports claim-level credibility analysis without external token-level hallucination localizers or auxiliary multimodal judges. We then instantiate a Diagnose-Treat-Prevent preference objective (DTP-DPO): semantic instability treats risky tokens by weighting DPO rewards, while visual and combined instability prevent visual neglect through gated auxiliary regularizers. Across Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B and InternVL2.5-2B, HIS-guided optimization provides downstream evidence that the diagnostic captures useful failure modes. On Qwen2.5-VL-3B, HIS-Guard reduces CHAIR_s by 32.2% and CHAIR_i by 45.6% over the baseline, improves over standard DPO trained on identical data, and largely preserves POPE accuracy. Scaling to Qwen2.5-VL-7B keeps HIS-Guard best on both CHAIR and POPE, while InternVL results suggest that the diagnostic signal is useful but the regularization strength is architecture-sensitive. Together, these results position internal stability as a practical signal for trustworthy multimodal information systems, selective verification, and hallucination-aware evaluation. The public implementation is available at https://github.com/20508Z/HIS-DTP-DPO.

papers.title: Emulating Expert Intuition: Retrieval-Augmented Cognitive Diagnosis for Student Cold-Start
papers.abstract: In intelligent education systems, cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) assess students' latent abilities through response records to enable personalized learning. However, existing CDMs struggle with inaccurate ability estimation under student cold-start conditions. Text-based CDMs, despite their strong generalization in data-rich scenarios, still suffer from ambiguous representations due to insufficient response records, which significantly hinders their practical deployment in real-world educational systems. Inspired by teachers' analogical reasoning when assessing new students, we propose Retrieval-Augmented Cognitive Diagnosis (RACD), a retrieval-augmented framework for CDMs. RACD fundamentally addresses student cold-start problems through a memory-retrieval-aggregation module that emulates teachers' analogical reasoning by retrieving and integrating similar student profiles from historical data. RACD is further enhanced by (1) Distinctiveness Regularization to align encoder outputs with distinctive representations and (2) Skill Shake that enforces contrastive learning for the retrieval module. Evaluations on three real-world datasets across four distinct cold-start configurations (different retention rates) show RACD outperforms both state-of-the-art CDMs and emerging LLM-based variants, with an average accuracy improvement of 1.2% and a peak gain of 2.1% over the best baseline in inductive scenarios, especially under student cold-start scenarios.

papers.title: PS²: Parameterized Control for Fine-Grained Student Proficiency Simulation
papers.abstract: Understanding how students with different proficiency levels respond to educational materials is a critical issue within the field of Education. However, acquiring sufficient real student response data for a robust evaluation is often hindered by cost, ethics, and security constraints. Consequently, LLM-based student proficiency simulation, especially prompt-based methods, has emerged as a practical alternative under data-scarce conditions. Despite their promise, current methods still exhibit limited controllability with coarse-grained proficiency representations, high sensitivity to prompt design, and the lack of calibration with academic performance. Therefore, we propose P arameterized S tudent P roficiency S imulation ( PS² ), an unsupervised and parameterized model-level framework that simulates students with different proficiencies by interpolating between a strong upper-bound LLM and a weaker, cognitive error-informed lower-bound student LLM via a hybrid ratio. Specifically, the lower-bound model is constructed by fine-tuning the weaker LM to exhibit cognitive errors when responding to educational materials. To ensure alignment with target proficiency levels, PS² further calibrates the interpolation ratio with academic performance. Experiments on two public datasets demonstrate that PS² achieves finer-grained and consistent proficiency simulation compared to existing baselines, leading to superior performance in student behavior similarity and item difficulty prediction.

papers.title: OPERA: Option-level Pedagogical Explanation via Reasoning for Augmented Knowledge Tracing
affiliations: Guangdong Institute of Smart Education, Jinan University
papers.abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) aims to predict learners' future performance by modeling their historical interaction data. In real-world educational scenarios, multiple-choice questions are deliberately designed so that each distractor exposes a specific misconception; however, existing KT models rely on randomly initialized ID embeddings and reduce each interaction to a binary correctness label, making it difficult to exploit such option-level diagnostic signals. To address these problems, we propose an option-level pedagogical explanation framework for augmented KT, i.e., OPERA, which combines LLM-based option-level explanation generation, multi-judge quality assurance, and offline semantic embedding injection into existing KT backbones, with all LLM computation confined to one-time offline preprocessing. Experiments on three multiple-choice datasets demonstrate our framework's superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy, consistently improving lightweight ID-based backbones to match or surpass much heavier process-aware models. To encourage reproducible research, we have made our code publicly available at https://pykt.org/.

papers.title: SKG-KT: Semantic Knowledge Graph Construction and Reasoning for Knowledge Tracing by Large Language Models
affiliations: Centre for Change and Complexity in Learning, Adelaide University
School of Artificial Intelligence, Shandong University
papers.abstract: Knowledge Tracing (KT), a core component of intelligent tutoring systems, aims to model the dynamic evolution of students' knowledge states based on their historical interaction data. However, mainstream methods rely heavily on large-scale students' response logs, hindering generalization to unseen students, and often overlook the semantic structure of knowledge points in knowledge graph construction. In this paper, we propose Semantic Knowledge Graph-Based Knowledge Tracing ( SKG-KT ), a novel KT framework that leverages the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs) to enhance the modelling of unseen students, without relying on numerous students with historical records. SKG-KT consists of two stages: ATC-ruled Semantic Graph Extraction and a Concept-aware Reasoning mechanism. In the first stage, we design a semantic student knowledge graph extraction method grounded in ATC rules, which captures the semantic structure across three hierarchical layers—domain, cluster, and standard—aligned with established educational theory. To extend beyond mathematics, we further introduce a multi-disciplinary semantic graph extraction method that induces an ATC-inspired hierarchical schema for other disciplines via LLM-based label induction. In the second stage, the Concept-aware Reasoning mechanism first applies knowledge concept reasoning to infer key knowledge concepts for unseen students with limited previous student data, and then fine-tunes an open-source LLM for correctness prediction based on the reasoned knowledge concepts, adapting the LLM to the KT task. Extensive experiments conducted on three publicly available educational benchmark datasets, namely Xes3g5m-small, Xes3g5m-large, and MOOCRadar, demonstrate that SKG-KT achieves state-of-the-art performance in knowledge tracing. Furthermore, SKG-KT has been validated to achieve robust predictive performance compared to others, while relying on a limited number of students with historical records. Our code and prompts are publicly available at the link (https://github.com/linqingliDestinyController/SKG_KT/tree/main).

papers.title: Incorporating Cognitive Load and Knowledge Transfer for Multi-Domain Knowledge Tracing
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China
State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence
papers.abstract: Knowledge Tracing (KT) aims to assess students' dynamic knowledge states from their learning histories. While most existing KT methods focus on single-domain learning with notable success, real-world learning scenarios often involve multiple domains simultaneously, introducing two critical factors: 1) Cognitive load, arising from managing learning across domains in both temporal and knowledge dimensions. 2) Knowledge transfer, where knowledge states in one domain influence related states both within and across domains. In this paper, we focus on exploring these factors to improve students’ knowledge state assessment in multi-domain learning scenarios and propose a novel method incorporating cognitive L oad and knowledge T ransfer for M ulti-domain K nowledge T racing ( LT-MKT ). Specifically, to bridge isolated domains, LT-MKT first integrates textual information from questions and their associated concepts to construct a Multi-domain Hierarchical Graph, leveraging the advanced representational capabilities of large language models (LLMs). Then, cross-domain features in both the temporal and knowledge dimensions are explicitly modeled to capture the effects of cognitive load. Additionally, a knowledge transfer module is designed to model the propagation of knowledge states within and across domains. By jointly modeling these factors, LT-MKT enables more accurate prediction of students’ future performance. Finally, extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance.

papers.title: Foundation-Assisted Cross-Domain Meta-Learning for Few-Shot Molecular Property Prediction
papers.abstract: Molecular property prediction is important for drug discovery, but labeled molecules are often limited for new prediction tasks. The difficulty is amplified in cross-domain few-shot settings, where target tasks differ from available source tasks and the model must adapt from sparse target-domain supervision. Existing few-shot and transferable few-shot methods mainly condition adaptation on the target support set, which can be unstable when the support molecules provide limited coverage of the target distribution. We propose Foundation-Assisted Cross-Domain Meta-Learning for Few-Shot Molecular Property Prediction (FACML), which augments cross-domain episodic learning with property-aware priors from a frozen Structure-Property Multi-Modal foundation model (SPMM). FACML represents each molecule using SPMM-derived SMILES features and graph features, and constructs support Property Vector (PV) prototypes and query PV representations from SPMM-predicted PVs based on molecular SMILES. A property-conditioned relation graph then integrates molecular nodes and PV-based prior nodes to refine episode representations for target-task adaptation. Across cross-dataset few-shot molecular property prediction benchmarks, FACML improves the average ROC-AUC over the strongest baseline by 6.36% and 8.12% under the 1-shot and 10-shot settings, respectively. An auxiliary zero-target-label analysis further examines the use of SPMM-generated molecules when labeled target support molecules are unavailable.

papers.title: IM 3 : Interaction Region-Augmented Multimodal Molecular Modeling for Precision Prescription
papers.abstract: Medication recommendation requires both therapeutic appropriateness and control of drug-drug interaction (DDI) risk. However, existing approaches face a semantic mismatch between the molecular mechanisms underlying DDIs and the clinical abstractions used for therapeutic assessment. This work addresses this limitation through a dual-level formulation that models interaction risk at the molecular level while incorporating therapeutic supervision and evaluation at the clinical class level. Building on this formulation, we propose IM 3 , an interaction region-augmented multimodal molecular modeling framework that integrates longitudinal electronic health records with quantum-informed drug representations. IM 3 employs the Interaction Region Indicator (IRI) to encode interaction-relevant electronic regions of drug compounds and combines global electronic characteristics with local chemical substructures. This representation incorporates molecular interaction information beyond static molecular topology and prescription co-occurrence. Experiments on two real-world intensive care unit datasets show that IM 3 substantially reduces DDI rates while maintaining competitive therapeutic performance relative to state-of-the-art baselines. These results indicate the complementary value of dual-level modeling and quantum-informed molecular representations for safer medication recommendation.

papers.title: HH-Track: Skeleton-Guided Visual Understanding with Prototype-Anchored RAG for Hand Hygiene Assessment
papers.abstract: Knowledge-grounded assessment of procedural compliance is a growing challenge in healthcare informatics. Such assessment benefits from explicit grounding in authoritative clinical references. Hand hygiene assessment offers a canonical instance, since hand hygiene is the single most critical defense against healthcare-associated infections (HAIs). Existing automated solutions often provide only coarse-grained compliance signals, while fine-grained technique analysis can incur substantial computational cost. Direct application of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) introduces additional challenges because processing long-form clinical videos is expensive and generic MLLMs lack grounded procedural references. We propose HH-Track, a knowledge-grounded retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework for fine-grained hand hygiene assessment. A skeleton-guided encoder first extracts structured clinical metrics and produces compact visual digests via boundary-progressive sampling. A prototype-anchored dual-stream RAG mechanism then retrieves step-aligned textual WHO guidelines and visual prototypes from curated reference resources. The MLLM uses these references for structured frame-level comparison during compliance assessment. To support this work, we construct Clinical-HHA, a hand hygiene dataset of 270 full-session recordings segmented into 1,408 step-level clips with template-guided expert compliance reports, paired with a curated visual prototype library. Release of both resources is subject to ongoing institutional review. Across five MLLM backbones, HH-Track improves compliance accuracy by an average of 36.1 percentage points over the Direct configurations, and the full dual-stream configuration further outperforms text-only grounding. Generated reports also show stronger agreement with expert-written references on average. These results support prototype-anchored multimodal retrieval for knowledge-grounded procedural assessment.

papers.title: DeDiff: Debiased Information Diffusion Prediction via Graph Disentanglement
affiliations: School of Computer Science and Technology, Tianjin University
School of Artificial Intelligence, Tianjin University
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a dominant paradigm for information diffusion prediction, yet their effectiveness can be undermined by biases inherent in observational diffusion data. In particular, skewed user activity and graph connectivity may encourage GNNs to exploit popularity-driven shortcuts rather than diffusion-relevant influence patterns. We attribute this limitation to the entanglement of predictive and bias-related signals in both graph structure and learned representations. To address this problem, we propose DeDiff, a disentangled graph debiasing framework that separates diffusion-relevant and bias-related signals at both the structural and representation levels. DeDiff first employs a low-rank adaptive edge mask to decompose the social and interaction graphs into complementary causal and bias views, preserving potentially informative diffusion pathways while isolating popularity-dominated shortcuts. It then introduces a dual-level representation disentanglement mechanism: causal–bias disagreement regularization discourages information leakage between the two branches, while inter-view contrastive learning preserves the distinct semantics of social and interaction relations and prevents excessive removal of useful structural information. Moreover, asymmetric branch supervision explicitly guides the bias branch to capture the empirical popularity distribution, reducing the incentive for the causal branch to encode the same shortcut and allowing it to focus on next-user prediction. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate that DeDiff achieves consistently strong ranking performance and remains substantially more robust than competitive baselines under amplified popularity bias.

papers.title: Learning Latent Process Knowledge via Variational Distillation for Low-Resource Social Experiment Prediction
affiliations: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become a promising tool for scaling social experiments with silicon samples. However, fine-tuning LLMs for real randomized controlled trials faces a dual low-resource challenge: structurally balanced experimental data are often small, and the process knowledge that explains how respondent profiles and treatments jointly shape outcomes is unobserved. Without reliable process-level supervision, existing fine-tuning methods may struggle to learn why a respondent gives a particular outcome, as the model prior often provides too few useful trajectories for such domain-specific prediction tasks. To address this challenge, we propose VPKD , a V ariationally motivated P rocess K nowledge D istillation framework. VPKD uses a teacher LLM to generate answer-conditioned posterior trajectories, filters them through masked reconstruction to retain student-useful process knowledge, and then distills the filtered trajectories into the student via SFT. By applying VPKD to a climate-policy attitude prediction task with only 500 data points and complex profile-treatment structure, we show that the learned process knowledge not only improves prediction accuracy, but also better recovers the causal effects of the original experiment.

papers.title: JECHO: Scalable Echo Chamber Detection via Jaccard-based Homophily and Seed Expansion
papers.abstract: Detecting echo chambers is critical for understanding and limiting negative social phenomena, such as online polarization, misinformation, and conspiracy theory diffusion. However, the echo chamber detection (ECD) problem yet lacks a rigorous algorithmic foundation. We address this gap by formalizing a unified definition of echo chambers based on three principles: internal opinion homogeneity, opinion extremism, and structural isolation. Under such a definition, we establish the theoretical hardness of the ECD problem, proving it is NP-hard via a reduction from the conductance minimization problem. To circumvent this computational barrier, we derive a theoretical lower bound on the Jaccard-based homophily (JHO) of nodes that reside within valid echo chambers. This guarantee motivates JECHO, a novel algorithm that detects echo chambers via local seed expansion rather than global enumeration. JECHO first identifies seeds that exceed the JHO threshold and then applies a score-based expansion to optimize structural isolation. Extensive experiments on real-world and synthetic networks demonstrate that our theory-guided approach detects more structurally isolated echo chambers than state-of-the-art methods while reducing runtime by orders of magnitude.

papers.title: Adversarial Creation and Detection of AI-Generated Social Bot Content
papers.abstract: The convergence of large language models and social bots allows malicious actors to manipulate the information ecosystem by generating human-like content at scale. Existing models for detecting AI-generated content often fail in the wild, primarily due to the lack of ground-truth data. We address this gap through an adversarial methodology that models the impersonation of real social media users by malicious actors. Using this methodology, we curate a multilingual, cross-platform dataset of paired human and AI-generated messages. Training on such adversarial data yields accurate detection of AI-generated text. Our approach significantly outperforms existing models for content-based bot detection in real-world, out-of-distribution data.

papers.title: CSC: Calibrated Simplicity for Conflict-Aware Social Bot Detection in the LLM Era
papers.abstract: Social bot detection is essential for protecting online platforms from misinformation amplification, coordinated manipulation, and distorted public discourse. However, large language models have made social bots much harder to detect from text alone because semantic camouflage is now cheap, fluent, and scalable. The resulting challenge is modality conflict: an account may look human-like in semantics while remaining suspicious in graph structure, profile attributes, or cross-modal consistency. Recent graph-based detectors tackle this limitation by adding graph-side complexity, such as sparse prototype selection, adaptive gating, or architecture-specific control logic, yet our experiments suggest that complexity alone is not the most reliable way to resolve such conflict. We therefore propose CSC, a calibrated-simplicity framework for conflict-aware LLM-era social bot detection. The framework combines three design choices: a simplified prototype-guided graph expert that retains useful structural biases while removing unstable graph-side heuristics, calibrated simplex-constrained fusion that aligns heterogeneous confidence spaces before late fusion, and a lightweight inconsistency expert that models cross-modal disagreement. Experiments on TwiBot-22, TwiBot-20, and MGStBot-large show that CSC improves calibrated operating-point decision quality while remaining competitive across external benchmarks. Further analyses show that calibration improves confidence reliability, the inconsistency expert mainly provides localized corrections in high-conflict or near-threshold regions, and simplified graph-side control yields a better stability-cost trade-off. A targeted semantic-camouflage stress test further shows that replacing selected bot text with matched human text sharply degrades the standalone text expert while leaving graph and fused evidence stable on a balanced challenge set. Overall, these results suggest that, when semantic evidence is easy to camouflage, robust bot detection benefits from preserving reliable structural signals and calibrating conflicting modalities before fusion, rather than continually increasing graph-side complexity.

papers.title: BotUmc: LLM-Enhanced Uncertainty-Aware Graph Learning for Bot Detection
affiliations: SKLCCSE, School of Computer Science and Engineering, Beihang University
papers.abstract: To detect social bots, many advanced methods have been proposed, especially graph-based approaches, their effectiveness is undermined by sophisticated bots that create spurious associations in network structures. As a result, current methods often struggle to provide high-confidence detection results. This motivates us to quantify the uncertainty of the output and reduce the interference of misinformation on detection, so as to determine the confidence of the results and output high-confidence results. Therefore, we propose an uncertainty-aware bot detection method to inform the confidence and use the uncertainty score to pick a high-confidence decision from multiple views of a social network under different environments. Specifically, our proposed BotUmc uses LLM to extract information from tweets. Then, we construct a graph based on the extracted information, the original user information, and the user relationship, and generate multiple views of the graph by intervention. Lastly, an uncertainty loss is used to force the model to quantify the uncertainty of results and select the result with low uncertainty in one view as the final decision. Extensive experiments show the superiority of our method.

papers.title: LABRA: A Label-free Graph Neural Framework for Illicit Account Detection in Large-scale Blockchain Transaction Networks
papers.abstract: Illicit account detection in blockchain-based cryptocurrencies seeks to pinpoint anomalies within large-scale, decentralized transaction networks, figuring prominently in financial risk control systems. Existing efforts typically formulate transaction networks as directed multigraphs and leverage graph neural networks (GNNs) to capture topological information under limited supervision. Despite their decent performance, supervised GNN models are capped by data scarcity and structural noise, with the former arising from the lack of annotated data and the latter stemming from malicious actors forging deceptive connections. In light of these, we in this paper propose LABRA, a novel label-free graph modeling for detecting illicit accounts in blockchain transaction networks. Operating in an unsupervised manner, LABRA (The source code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/bicheng1225/LABRA.) leverages a discrepancy-aware graph encoder to produce discriminative node representations, and subsequently employs an anchor-guided scoring mechanism to designate anchor nodes for anomaly detection. Furthermore, a tailor-made message-passing scheme is introduced to mitigate structural noise, which captures atypical financial flows within a transaction graph while attenuating the feature-smoothing effect caused by high-degree nodes. Extensive experiments on several cryptocurrency benchmark datasets demonstrate the feasibility and superiority of our method over several cutting-edge methods. To our knowledge, LABRA is among the first training-free frameworks for illicit account detection in cryptocurrencies, delivering robust performance without resorting to any learnable parameters or iterative model optimization.

papers.title: LENS: Reliability-Aware Stock Prediction via LLM-Extracted Priors and News-Driven Semantic Graphs
papers.abstract: Predicting stock returns requires modeling persistent company relations and time-varying market signals. Graph Neural Network (GNN) approaches combine static priors with dynamic relational graphs, but treat every extracted edge as a trustworthy binary fact, ignoring heterogeneous reliability across relational sources. We propose LENS ( L LM- E xtracted priors and N ews-driven S emantics), a static–dynamic graph framework for stock return prediction and ranking that models relational reliability as a first-class signal across the pipeline. On the static side, we extract a multi-relational company graph from a Large Language Model and aggregate it over multiple runs with confidence weighting to downweight low-consistency edges. On the dynamic side, we build a news-driven semantic graph with exponential-decay temporal aggregation to capture changing market context under uneven coverage. A context-dependent gated fusion module rebalances the two graphs at the per-stock, per-day level. On S&P 500, LENS improves AR@5 by 16.4% and SR@5 by 22.6% over the strongest baseline, and on NASDAQ 100 it achieves comparable improvements (15.5% and 20.9% respectively). Ablations isolate each component's contribution, and a human-validation study of sampled relations supports that the aggregation is grounded, providing evidence that reliability-aware LLM relations and news-based semantic graphs carry complementary information for graph-based financial prediction.

papers.title: FedMem: Memory-Aware Federated Continual Learning via Dual-Channel Memory Control
affiliations: Beijing Key Laboratory for Multimodal Collaboration and Advanced Application, Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.abstract: Federated continual learning (FCL) suffers from complex spatio-temporal catastrophic forgetting, driven by distribution drift along task streams and aggregation conflicts under non-IID client data. Existing studies often treat temporal and spatial forgetting as decoupled objectives, overlooking their interaction in the overall memory dynamics of the federation, where client-side acquisition and server-side consolidation jointly shape long-term performance. Motivated by the structural and functional correspondence between the dual-channel memory mechanism in collective cognition and FCL's client-server collaboration, we introduce Federated System Memory (FSM), a system memory metric that jointly models client-side short-term retention and server-side long-term consistency. Based on FSM, we further propose FedMem, a memory-aware FCL framework that utilizes dual-channel memory control to enable system-level closed-loop optimization. On the client side, FedMem constrains local learning with dual-channel decay indicators: short-term decay strengthens prototype-based retention, while long-term decay enhances memory-guided regularization for stable task-memory retrieval. On the server side, it regulates global updates through collective-consistency gated aggregation and adaptive update scaling based on long-term decay, while maintaining global prototypes and memory. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedMem consistently outperforms existing methods in both learning performance and system memory retention.

papers.title: ProRC: Prototype Personalization with Reliability Calibration in Heterogeneous Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Prototype-based federated learning (FL) provides a promising route for federated heterogeneity. By exchanging class prototypes rather than model parameters, it provides class-level semantic guidance under non-IID data and accommodates heterogeneous client backbones. Under severely skewed label distributions, however, two coupled limitations emerge. The broadcast global prototype is a cross-client average, and direct adoption can cause client semantic dilution. Meanwhile, local prototypes of rare classes are estimated from a few samples, leading to local margin erosion against well-supported neighbours. To address both, we propose ProRC, a prototype personalization framework grounded in shrinkage estimation. ProRC replaces naive alignment with a reliability-calibrated, margin-aware interpolation between global and local prototypes, and comprises two complementary client-side modules. The first module, Reliability-Calibrated Prototype Adaptation (RaPA), calibrates each global prototype by the reliability of its local counterpart, restoring client-specific semantics only to the extent the data warrant. The second module, Margin-Aware Prototype Refinement (MaPR), audits the candidate against the local true-class margin and attenuates margin-reducing steps. Together, the two modules are designed to mitigate client semantic dilution and local margin erosion, while preserving the prototype-exchange protocol and per-round payload of prior methods. Extensive experiments on label-skewed and real-world image benchmarks, together with ablation and reliability analyses, show that ProRC achieves the best overall average accuracy among the compared methods and improves the strongest prototype baseline in most heterogeneous settings.

papers.title: Progressive Collaboration Pruning for Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Collaboration-based personalized federated learning (Co-PFL) mitigates data heterogeneity by enabling clients to selectively exchange knowledge through a learned collaboration graph. Despite their success, existing Co-PFL methods often update collaboration weights mainly from pairwise similarity, which can produce graphs that are either overly sparse and hinder knowledge propagation or overly dense and weaken personalization, leaving graph connectivity largely uncontrolled. In this paper, we propose FedPGP, a Co-PFL framework that explicitly schedules collaboration from dense to sparse over training rounds, enabling clients to first exploit broadly shared knowledge and then refine specialized knowledge aligned with their local distributions. FedPGP builds on a connectivity-aware similarity regularization that jointly accounts for global graph connectivity and client-model similarity, together with an efficient greedy pruning rule that removes edges with the least contribution to the regularized objective. We further present FedPGP+, a module-specific extension that learns different collaboration graphs for different model modules, allowing collaboration intensity to vary along model depth. Extensive experiments across diverse non-IID settings show that FedPGP and FedPGP+ consistently outperform state-of-the-art Co-PFL baselines, achieving up to 5.52% absolute accuracy improvement, while producing interpretable dense-to-sparse collaboration schedules.

papers.title: FedCSOT: Model-Heterogeneous Personalized Federated Learning via Channel Semantic Optimal Transport
papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) provides a privacy-preserving paradigm for collaborative learning across distributed clients. In practical FL systems, clients often exhibit non-IID data distributions and deploy diverse model architectures under resource constraints. While model heterogeneity improves deployment flexibility under client resource constraints, it prevents direct parameter aggregation and makes cross-architecture knowledge transfer challenging. Existing methods mainly rely on shared structures, coarse-grained distillation, or projection-based feature alignment, which cannot explicitly capture channel-level semantic correspondences across heterogeneous architectures. This paper proposes FedCSOT, a model-heterogeneous personalized FL framework based on channel semantic optimal transport. FedCSOT induces sequence-driven channel semantics from channel responses over a shared unlabeled sequence, establishing a common semantic space for cross-architecture alignment. The framework models cross-architecture semantic alignment through entropy-regularized optimal transport to facilitate knowledge transfer. It further designs a divergence-aware personalized fusion strategy to adaptively balance consensus knowledge and local personalization under non-IID data distributions. Extensive experiments under diverse data and model heterogeneity settings demonstrate that FedCSOT consistently improves average test accuracy, convergence behavior, and robustness over representative baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/greenhead01/FedCSOT.

papers.title: DICE: Decentralized Incentive-driven Federated Learning for Efficient & Scalable Customization of Pretrained Models in Web3
affiliations: The State Key Laboratory of Blockchain and Data Security, Zhejiang University
papers.abstract: Customizing Pretrained Models (PMs) for downstream tasks demands task-specific data, which burgeoning Web3 applications provide abundantly. Blockchain-powered federated learning (BCFL) offers a secure and privacy-preserving paradigm to customize PMs among self-interested and untrusted Web3 participants. Yet, existing BCFL algorithms face severe efficiency and scalability challenges when applied to large PMs, due to their substantial computational and memory requirements and the hardware constraints of many participants. This paper introduces DICE, a novel BCFL algorithm that addresses the efficiency and scalability challenges of customizing large PMs in Web3 via two sets of synergistic techniques: (i) a dynamic progressive learning scheme and a model slice verification scheme to enable a wider range of honest participants, including those unable to deploy the full model, to engage in customizing PMs, while preserving model utility; (ii) a tree-structured committee consensus protocol and an efficiency-driven incentive scheme to address the dominant bottleneck that hinders existing BCFL algorithms from scaling to a larger number of data holders for customizing data-hungry large PMs, while maintaining security. Theoretical analysis and extensive experimental results on customizing vision and language PMs demonstrate DICE's efficiency, effectiveness, and security. A comprehensive technical report of DICE including its implementation details, extended analyses, discussions, and experiments is available at https://github.com/Hoho-Lin/DICE.

papers.title: Release the Potential of Relative Feature Consistency for Data Heterogeneous Federated Learning
affiliations: Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences
College of Intelligence and Computing, Tianjin University
papers.abstract: Federated Learning is a promising paradigm to achieve privacy-preserving collaborative training. However, its performance degrades severely under data heterogeneity. A main obstacle is the divergent local representations induced by data heterogeneity, which will degrade the quality of the aggregated global representations. In this paper, we discover that although local representation spaces contain client-specific biases, their internal inter-class structure remains consistent across clients, which we identify as relative consistency. Through theoretical and empirical analyses, we further show that a proxy dataset can serve as a common anchor to translate class prototypes into a relative space, where client-specific shifts are suppressed and cross-client class centers become better aligned. Based on these findings, we propose a novel framework named Federated learning with Relative Representation Alignment (FedReRA) with Relative Knowledge Extraction (RKE) and Relative Ensemble Inference (REI) to extract and leverage the relative consistency to address data heterogeneity. Specifically, RKE debiases the prototypes by translating absolute prototypes into the aligned relative space via a flexible proxy dataset, while REI conducts collaborative inference with bias-reduced prediction in the relative space. Extensive experiments validate FedReRA’s superiority over state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 3.83% average improvement under high heterogeneity and notably sustaining nearly 10% improvement on CIFAR-100 even when using random noise as the proxy data.

papers.title: FedEMoE: Towards Class-Aware Federated Learning via Evidential Mixture-of-Experts
papers.abstract: Federated learning under non-IID data suffers from client drift. Recent work introduces Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures to handle data heterogeneity by routing inputs to specialized experts, but two problems remain. Softmax routing produces overconfident expert assignments with no reliability measure. The parameter space carries no class-level information, forcing the server to aggregate all clients uniformly and destroying the expert specialization built during local training. We call this class-level specialization invisibility. To address these problems, we propose FedEMoE. On the client side, Evidential Mixture-of-Experts equips router and experts with evidential heads, dynamically adjusts the number of active experts based on routing uncertainty, and compresses accumulated evidence into a per-client signature. On the server side, Evidence-Guided Class-Aware Aggregation takes the signatures as input and adaptively performs class-aware parameter fusion and component recombination. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and FEMNIST show that FedEMoE consistently outperforms eight baseline methods across all settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/Stephen-Chow1/FedEMoE-CIKM.

papers.title: When Geometry Becomes Unreliable: Robust Federated Aggregation via Bounded Influence
papers.abstract: Robust aggregation in federated learning is often framed as down-weighting abnormal client updates.
