However, in realistic cross-device regimes, each round observes only a small number of high-dimensional updates, while benign updates can already be anisotropic, heavy-tailed, and strongly affected by non-IID data. In this setting, robustness depends not only on the final weighting rule, but also on whether the server-visible update geometry is estimable. We propose FedBIG ( Fed erated B ounded- I nfluence G eometry), a server-side aggregation framework that separates geometry construction from influence control. Instead of scoring raw updates directly, FedBIG builds a stabilized sketch-space geometry using robust centering, low-dimensional projection, calibrated scatter estimation, shrinkage, and whitening. It then maps stabilized deviations to bounded-influence weights and aggregates the original client updates. Experiments on heterogeneous federated learning benchmarks show that FedBIG improves the robustness–utility trade-off under statistical and triggered poisoning. Ablations, boundary stress tests, and runtime analysis further support the central claim: robust aggregation is effective when server-visible geometry is estimable, and weakens when this geometry collapses under extreme heterogeneity or sparse participation. Our code is available at https://github.com/ytma-phoenix/FedBIG.

papers.title: Operation-Guided Schema Evolution and Migration for Document Databases
affiliations: University of Science and Technology Beijing
papers.abstract: Document databases provide flexible data modeling, but long-running applications still rely on implicit schemas that evolve continuously. Legacy documents do not automatically follow schema changes, so a collection may contain documents conforming to different historical schema versions. This makes schema evolution an execution problem that spans change representation, operation reconstruction, and legacy-data migration. Existing studies typically address these tasks separately, leaving schema-level changes disconnected from the instance-level migration decisions. This paper proposes an operation-guided framework for executable schema evolution and migration in document databases. We first define a unified operation framework over field paths, types, and constraints, with explicit User-Defined Function (UDF) contracts for destructive changes. This framework specifies the valid operations from which schema evolution sequences are composed. We then reconstruct executable schema evolution sequences from schema snapshots through a two-stage method that combines multi-channel field-evolution association with instruction-tuned sequence generation. Finally, the generated sequences drive progressive migration: an instance-level Benefit–Cost Optimization (BCO) selector prioritizes affected documents, while a window-level allocator distributes migration budget under live workloads. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework directly expresses all 32 curated evolution cases, improves end-to-end sequence executability by 29.44%–31.51%, and reduces residual migration debt by 24.73% over the strongest adaptive migration baseline.

papers.title: Aligning Predicates with Database Content: A Type-Specific Query Reformulation Framework for Database Semantic Gaps
affiliations: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Inspur Cloud Information Technology Co., Ltd.
industryAffiliations: Inspur Cloud Information Technology Co., Ltd.
papers.abstract: Filtering textual columns based on user intent is a pervasive task in database applications, yet discrepancies between user predicates and concrete database values often cause keyword searches to fail. The Recall-Then-Verify (RTV) paradigm, which first retrieves a budget of candidate values and then verifies them using Large Language Models (LLMs), has emerged as a promising and widely adopted strategy; however, its overall efficacy remains inherently bounded by the recall of the initial retrieval stage. To improve this recall, we propose a type-specific query reformulation framework that adaptively aligns predicates with database content by addressing database semantic gaps. Specifically, the framework categorizes these semantic discrepancies into three distinct types—synonymy, conceptual hierarchies, and format inconsistencies—and executes a specialized, type-specific reformulation strategy tailored to each gap. The framework further grounds reformulation in the target database by reusing LLM-verified column values as feedback, enabling the system to capture database-local variants. Furthermore, to maintain low latency, it introduces an on-demand triggering mechanism that activates LLM reformulation only when a significant semantic gap is detected, supplemented by adaptive selection and early stopping strategies to prune redundant computation. Compared to existing RTV methods, experimental results demonstrate that the framework consistently enhances retrieval recall by up to 45.45% and improves end-to-end F1 score by up to 26.72%.

papers.title: The Backbone of Consistent Query Answering
papers.abstract: The existence of inconsistencies in databases has motivated the study of Consistent Query Answering (CQA) since the 1990s. Recent work proposed the use of Maximum Satisfiability (MaxSAT) for solving CQA for concrete types of inconsistencies. This paper shows that, for the types of inconsistencies solved with MaxSAT, it is the case that CQA corresponds to finding the backbone of a propositional formula. This observation not only yields a novel characterization in terms of the computational complexity of the problem, but it also enables significantly more efficient practical solutions. The experiments confirm that significant performance improvements can be obtained by computing the backbone instead of solving MaxSAT.

papers.title: Bounded-Memory Aggregate Query Processing on Streaming Temporal Graphs
papers.abstract: Time-window aggregate queries over temporal graph streams—COUNT, COUNT_DISTINCT, and label-filtered predicates—are central to agent memory, communication monitoring, and knowledge-base analytics, yet exact evaluation becomes increasingly costly as timestamped edges accumulate. Sketch-based approximate query processing (AQP) offers compact summaries, but the standard per-bucket design couples temporal resolution with cardinality state: placing a HyperLogLog (HLL) inside every Count-Min Sketch (CMS) bucket leaves only coarse time partitions under a fixed budget and still does not natively support all three query types. We present the Cardinality-Aware Multi-Resolution Sketch (CAMRS), a budget-decoupled multi-resolution sketch built on the observation that CMS and HLL have distinct budget elasticities. CAMRS separates fine-grained CMS buckets from coarse HLL segments, achieving a 9.6× temporal-resolution gain under the same 1 MB budget, and augments each bucket with Space-Saving label tracking to support predicate queries without global label thresholds. We further derive a closed-form COUNT error bound showing that temporal resolution, rather than CMS width, is the dominant accuracy lever; this bound drives a reliability-aware fallback mechanism that controls tail risk when predicted sketch error exceeds a user tolerance. Experiments on six real-world temporal graphs (60K–17.8M edges) show that CAMRS reduces COUNT error by up to 29.7× and predicate error by up to 7.9× over the coupled baseline while preserving native COUNT_DISTINCT support. The adaptive fallback policy further reduces worst-case tail error by up to 667×.

papers.title: Rewriting Ontology-Mediated Property Graph Queries into GQL
papers.abstract: Ontology-based data access is intended for graph data, but practical support remains limited to SQL-like languages lacking the navigational and path-matching features fundamental to graph querying. Theoretical algorithms for navigational queries have long been available. Still, they have never been implemented, largely because practical graph query languages fell short of their theoretical counterparts and lacked the expressive power needed to support rewriting common ontology languages. The recent standardisation efforts around GQL and SQL/PGQ finally allow us to overcome this barrier and present a practical query rewriting technique for ontology-mediated navigational graph queries. Ontologies are written in a DL-Lite variant tuned to property graphs, and the queries in a GQL fragment with nested two-way regular path queries and which can be evaluated in Cypher. Preliminary experiments with our proof-of-concept prototype suggest that querying graph data with ontological knowledge may finally be within reach.

papers.title: Path-Aware GQL Triggers for Property Graphs
papers.abstract: As property graphs become central to domains like network analysis, legislative and financial monitoring, there is an urgent need for reactive processing capabilities that can respond to complex structural changes. At the same time, the standardization of property graph processing has culminated in the ISO Graph Query Language (GQL) standard, which establishes a uniform and portable foundation for expressing triggers, ensuring portability across implementations. This paper introduces GQL-Triggers, the first trigger framework fully aligned with the ISO GQL standard that treats paths as first-class citizens. Unlike traditional approaches, GQL-Triggers allow developers to define declarative events, conditions, and actions over complex path patterns, incorporating GQL-specific features. We provide a formal semantic model for path-level event detection and transition sets computation. We present two alternative implementations of GQL-Triggers on top of Neo4j, respectively named Index-based and Query-based, and provide their experimental comparison in terms of time and memory efficiency.

papers.title: Cimos: Cost-Effective Multi-Query Oriented Continuous Subgraph Matching
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
papers.abstract: Continuous subgraph matching over dynamic graphs is a fundamental problem in graph databases, with broad applications in real-time pattern monitoring and risk control. In practice, applications often require monitoring multiple graph patterns simultaneously, making multi-query oriented continuous subgraph matching (MCSM) an increasingly important research topic. Although existing methods have achieved performance gains, their indexes offer limited filtering power and they lack high-quality query plans tailored to the multi-query setting. To address these limitations, we propose Cimos, a novel index-based framework for cost-effective MCSM. First, we design a data-centric index called DCL that serves multiple query graphs and prunes more non-candidate vertices by jointly considering the matching constraints of ancestor and descendant vertices in query DAGs. Second, we adopt a hybrid-order planning strategy that separates the query plan into static and dynamic ordering components. For the static component, we introduce a prefix order tree to extract isomorphic subgraphs shared across query graphs, and optimize vertex orderings using statistical upper-bound obtained via DCL-based subgraph sampling. For the dynamic component, we employ DCL-based cardinality estimation to adaptively determine vertex orderings during the matching process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Cimos achieves notable speedup of more than 4.2x against state-of-the-art CSM and MCSM methods.

papers.title: BLADE: A Bit-Level Learned Architecture for Dynamic Environments
papers.abstract: Learned indexes have significantly improved the query performance of in-memory databases by transforming traditional structural traversals into cumulative distribution function model predictions. However, existing dynamic learned indexes rely heavily on the core assumption of "local linear data distribution." Under highly skewed dynamic workloads in real-world scenarios, this linear assumption frequently fails, forcing the system to trigger extremely expensive model retraining and horizontal data shifting. This incurs severe cascading splits and leads to a sharp degradation in dynamic write throughput. To break this architectural bottleneck, this paper proposes BLADE, a bit-level learned index architecture designed for dynamic mixed workloads. BLADE abandons the strong reliance on complex mathematical models and achieves a structural decoupling of routing addressing and underlying data storage at the physical level. In the upper routing module, BLADE employs a pure integer bitwise partitioning mechanism for stateless memory addressing, eliminating the overhead of floating-point model computation. In the underlying leaf nodes, the system inherits the contiguous array layout with reserved gaps to absorb insertions efficiently. To address local congestion caused by data skew, BLADE introduces a vertical splitting strategy, which redistributes data by extending the routing level downwards, effectively avoiding large-scale physical data copying at the bottom layer. Comprehensive experimental evaluations demonstrate that under read-only and read-heavy workloads, BLADE achieves point lookup throughput of 8.2×, 4.1×, 3.2×, and 1.3× that of B+-trees, PGM-index, ART, and ALEX, respectively. Under high-frequency write dynamic mixed workloads, its throughput reaches up to 4.5×, 4.0×, 2.3×, and 1.2× that of PGM-index, B+ Tree, ART, and ALEX. Furthermore, by replacing learned internal-node models with deterministic bitwise routing, BLADE eliminates the iterative model fitting overhead, accelerating the index initialization and bulk-loading speed by 16× to 48.8× compared to the most advanced learned indexes. Under the tested skewed insertion patterns, BLADE's maximum observed RSS is only 1.17× that of its Uniform baseline. Parameter-sensitivity experiments further validate the default 30% target gap and 16 MiB maximum leaf capacity as a balanced configuration for insertion performance and space efficiency.

papers.title: Privacy-Aware Representation Decoupling in Federated Recommendation against Attribute Inference Attacks
papers.abstract: Federated recommender systems (FedRec) aim to preserve user privacy by keeping sensitive data on client devices and sharing only model parameters with a central server. However, FedRec is still vulnerable to attribute inference attacks (AIAs), where server-side adversaries exploit uploaded parameters to infer users’ private attributes. Existing FedRec approaches face a suboptimal privacy-performance trade-off. Privacy-focused methods mask attribute-related features in representations to protect sensitive information, but degrade recommendation accuracy. In contrast, performance-focused methods preserve accuracy by retaining these features but risk privacy leakage through uploaded representations. To balance privacy and performance, we propose PARD, a privacy-aware representation decoupling framework that explicitly decomposes representations into privacy-relevant and privacy-irrelevant components. Only the privacy-irrelevant part is uploaded to the server, and the privacy-relevant part is retained locally. We leverage Mutual Information (MI) objectives to facilitate this decoupling: (1) suppressing sensitive leakage by minimizing the MI between privacy-irrelevant representations and attributes, and (2) retaining attribute signals by maximizing the MI for privacy-relevant representations. Since exact MI computation is intractable, we derive variational bounds and estimate them using privacy estimators under adversarial and cooperative training paradigms. Experimental results demonstrate that PARD outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both recommendation accuracy and privacy preservation. The code is available at https://github.com/XuHao-bit/PARD.

papers.title: Dynamic Feature-Embedding Communication via Codebook Distillation for Federated Recommendation
papers.abstract: Federated recommendation systems commonly protect user privacy by keeping user parameters on local devices, while exchanging item parameters for collaborative model training. However, such item parameters usually model items independently and suffer from both efficiency and effectiveness challenges, making communication costs grow with the item space and limiting cross-item generalization and robustness to noisy feedback. To address these limitations, we propose to model items via shared latent feature embeddings for communication. Residual Quantization (RQ) provides a natural way to instantiate this communication by representing each item with a short sequence of discrete code IDs, i.e., Semantic IDs (SIDs). However, directly applying centralized and static RQ-based recommendation to federated learning is non-trivial due to 1) private and biased historical interactions and 2) evolving collaborative information. We propose RQFedRec, an RQ-based federated recommendation framework for dynamic feature-embedding communication. To construct globally aligned codebooks without accessing private interactions, RQFedRec introduces an information distillation module. Each client first learns item embeddings that encode local collaborative information from private interactions, and then distills such information into feature-indexed codebooks under globally shared SIDs, making sparse and biased local signals more compatible with server aggregation. To adapt to evolving collaborative information, RQFedRec introduces a self-refining SID update module that dynamically refines global SID assignments from aggregated codebooks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RQFedRec improves recommendation performance and reduces communication costs without relying on semantic information, while further benefiting from public semantics when available. Code is available at https://github.com/Mingzhe-Han/RQFedRec.

papers.title: MoSA: Multi-Modal Semantic-Anchored Feature Alignment for Federated Recommendation
affiliations: Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
papers.abstract: Federated recommendation (FedRec) suffers from sparse and highly heterogeneous interaction data, which can drive client-side item representations toward inconsistent semantic directions and cause feature conflict during aggregation. Addressing feature conflict in FedRec is non-trivial, as implicit feedback reflects user-specific preferences rather than stable item semantics, making it difficult to support prototype-based alignment as in standard FL. To address this issue, we propose MoSA, a FedRec-specific feature alignment framework that introduces multi-modal semantic anchors via item clustering. MoSA uses the resulting cluster assignments as globally consistent pseudo-labels and performs dual-level alignment: (i) a cluster-aware item representation alignment module to guide client-side item embedding matrix under partial item coverage, and (ii) a recommender modulation module to improve cross-client parameter compatibility while preserving personalization. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that MoSA consistently improves recommendation performance across representative federated recommendation backbones, and ablation studies validate the effectiveness of each component. The codes are available here. (https://github.com/SunJY1116/MoSA_Code.git)

papers.title: FedPerGen: A Personalized Generative Augmentation Framework for Federated Recommendation
affiliations: Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
papers.abstract: Federated recommendation is an emerging paradigm that enables collaborative model training while preserving user privacy by keeping raw interaction data on local devices. However, in this setting, each client performs local training solely on a single user's limited historical interactions, which further exacerbates the data sparsity issue that has long been a bottleneck limiting recommendation performance. In this paper, we delve into the data sparsity problem in federated recommendation and propose FedPerGen, a personalized generative augmentation framework for federated recommendation. Specifically, each client is required to upload a user preference proxy to the server. The server then feeds this proxy along with diversity-constrained random noise into a generative network to synthesize personalized pseudo-item embeddings for each client. To ensure the informativeness and diversity of the generated embeddings, we design three complementary optimization objectives: feature-contrastive loss, model-alignment loss, and embedding-diversity loss. Furthermore, a two-stage warm-up training strategy is proposed to guarantee reliable user preference proxies and high-quality pseudo embeddings. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that FedPerGen consistently improves various federated recommendation baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/xcheng202202/FedPerGen .

papers.title: FedHUR: Learning Hierarchical Utility-Guided Client Relations for Personalized Federated Recommendation
papers.abstract: Federated recommendation enables collaborative model training while keeping user interaction data on local clients. A central problem in federated recommendation is how to aggregate useful information across clients for personalized recommendation. Existing personalized aggregation methods usually construct client relations from predefined parameter-based assumptions, such as parameter similarity or complementarity, and use these relations to determine aggregation weights. However, such methods construct a single global relation, which is insufficient to capture the hierarchical and multi-granularity nature of user relations in recommendation. Moreover, these predefined relations cannot directly reflect whether the related clients can improve prediction performance after aggregation. To address these limitations, we propose FedHUR, a federated recommendation framework for learning hierarchical utility-guided client relations. FedHUR takes item-item filters as the object for relation construction and aggregation. Specifically, it first aggregates and clusters each client's local information to obtain global hierarchical information. Each client computes hierarchical utility signals based on its local information and the global hierarchical information, indicating which collaborative information is useful for improving its prediction. The server uses these utility signals to retrieve clients that are useful to that client for further personalized aggregation. Extensive experiments on five real-world datasets show that FedHUR consistently outperforms existing federated recommendation baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of hierarchical utility-guided client relation learning. Code is available at https://github.com/Mingzhe-Han/FedHUR.

papers.title: Transcending the Semantic Chasm: Knowledge-Graph Guided Aggregation for Cross-Silo Federated Session Recommendation
affiliations: Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications
papers.abstract: Session-based Recommendation (SBR) achieves high performance in traditional centralized settings by using global item transition graphs to capture user intent. However, Federated Learning (FL) mandates collaborative training on isolated data, which makes the construction of such global structures unattainable. We identify this critical dilemma as “Structure Collapse”, where the global graph remains fragmented despite model averaging. This collapse induces a “Semantic Chasm,” resulting in incompatible knowledge fusion and imprecise intent prediction. To break this impasse, we propose a novel Cross-Silo Federated Session-based Recommendation framework (CSFSR), which reconstructs global connectivity by harmonizing knowledge priors with local intents. Specifically, our Knowledge-Aware Initialization counteracts Structure Collapse by synthesizing shared attributes into a unified semantic space that anchors isolated clients. Further addressing the Semantic Chasm, the Graph-Guided Aggregation mechanism uses client signatures to direct personalized fusion, effectively filtering noise and ensuring robustness. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that CSFSR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art federated baselines and exhibits superior noise robustness. Our code is available at https://github.com/Is-Jiejie/CSFSR.

papers.title: FedCGR: Federated Cross-Domain Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Cross-domain recommendation (CDR) transfers preference knowledge across related domains, but federated deployment makes cross-domain alignment difficult because the behavioral anchors that align item spaces, such as overlapping users and shared interaction signals, are often sparse, unavailable, or privacy-sensitive across clients. To address this tension, we revisit federated CDR as generation over a stable semantic item language. By representing items as discrete semantic ID (SID) sequences derived from public item-side metadata, cross-domain item alignment is induced by a shared vocabulary rather than by exchanging private interactions or aligning domain-specific embeddings. Directly federating SID-based generators, however, introduces two design constraints: the SID tokenizer must remain fixed to preserve cross-client token consistency, which creates a semantic-only bottleneck because local collaborative filtering (CF) signals cannot be globally shared or aligned; meanwhile, standard federated averaging can cause negative transfer under domain heterogeneity. To overcome these constraints, we propose FedCGR, a federated generative CDR framework that keeps the item language stable and makes adaptation explicit. FedCGR injects local CF evidence through a reliability-aware semantic interface and trains a prototype-personalized generator that selectively aggregates shared parameters according to domain relatedness while keeping domain-specific quantities local. Experiments on six Amazon cross-domain scenarios show that FedCGR consistently outperforms federated generative baselines and achieves competitive performance against strong sequential and federated CDR methods under both full-ranking and sampled evaluation protocols. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ZhuodLiu/FedCGR.

papers.title: An Unseen Threat in Cross-Domain Recommendation: User Re-Identification Attacks and Practical Defenses
affiliations: Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
Nanjing University Of Aeronautics And Astronautics
papers.abstract: Cross-domain recommendation (CDR) boosts personalization by transferring knowledge across domains, but its privacy implications remain largely overlooked. In this paper, we uncover a critical threat in CDR: cross-domain user re-identification can be performed in realistic black-box settings using only the top-K recommended items returned by deployed systems. We propose a list-supervised shadow-model attack that treats the target model's top-K lists as implicit feedback and mimics its ranking behavior through a pairwise ranking objective. To amplify identity signals that persist across domains—even with disjoint item sets—the attacker learns disentangled user interests, separating domain-specific preferences from domain-invariant representations through contrastive constraints. The resulting representations support an effective classifier for determining whether two cross-domain accounts belong to the same individual. Extensive experiments across multiple CDR settings show that re-identification leakage is pervasive in modern models. Finally, we present practical defense mechanisms that mitigate linkability while preserving recommendation utility, highlighting the need for privacy-aware CDR design. The codes are available here. (https://github.com/SleepingZSJ/LiSA-Link.git)

papers.title: Sandwich Reasoning: An Answer-Reasoning-Answer Approach for Low-Latency Query Correction
papers.abstract: Query correction is a critical entry point in modern search pipelines, demanding high accuracy strictly within stringent latency constraints. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning improves accuracy but introduces excessive latency that limits real-time deployment. A natural alternative is to output an answer before reasoning to reduce latency; however, under autoregressive decoding, such an answer-first paradigm suffers from a decoupling problem : the early answer is generated independently of the subsequent reasoning, and therefore cannot benefit from it. To address this issue, we propose Sandwich Reasoning (SandwichR), a novel approach that explicitly aligns a fast initial answer with post-hoc reasoning, enabling low-latency query correction without sacrificing reasoning-aware accuracy. SandwichR follows an “Answer–Reasoning–Answer” paradigm, producing an initial correction, an explicit reasoning process, and a final refined correction. To align the initial answer with post-reasoning insights, we design a consistency-aware reinforcement learning (RL) strategy: a dedicated consistency reward enforces alignment between the initial and final corrections, while margin-based rejection sampling prioritizes borderline samples where reasoning drives the most impactful corrective gains. Additionally, unlike existing datasets that primarily focus on simple spelling errors, we construct a high-quality query correction dataset tailored to semantically sensitive errors. Experiments on three real-world domains show that SandwichR delivers the best accuracy-latency trade-off among evaluated methods at comparable model scale, achieving accuracy on par with standard CoT while reducing inference latency by 40–70%, and offering a promising solution for latency-sensitive applications.

papers.title: The ''Curse of Knowledge'' in LLM Query Simulation: Concept Provenance for Tracing Answer-Side Intrusion
papers.abstract: LLM-generated search queries are widely used to augment IR evaluation, yet they may contain concepts that presuppose answer-side document knowledge, violating the information-access boundary of pre-search users. Existing validation metrics—overlap, diversity, effectiveness—cannot distinguish rare human-tail variation from candidate answer-side intrusion. We introduce concept provenance , a framework that assigns query concepts to backstory-supported, human-central, human-tail, and candidate answer-side zones, operationalizing a boundary that retrieval metrics alone cannot detect. Applying concept provenance to 77,004 queries across 100 UQV100 topics, 8 LLMs, and 5 prompt conditions with two extraction pipelines (cross-pipeline token-HCIR Spearman ρ = 1.0 over five condition means), we find candidate answer-side concepts constitute 7.40% of non-generic concepts, appearing in 97 of 100 topics with topic explaining ≈67% of variance. Human validation yields 68.2% relaxed precision, revealing a dual mechanism: knowledge intrusion (45.5%) and deployment intrusion (45.0%). Diagnostic probes show these concepts carry disproportionate localized retrieval effects (deletion d = -0.47, exceeding random deletion d = -0.34) but explain less than 2% of aggregate evaluation variance, positioning concept provenance as a boundary-compliance diagnostic rather than an evaluation-shift predictor. Under the tested conditions, no prompt condition eliminates intrusion; post-generation concept-provenance selection achieves 99% elimination.

papers.title: LLMs Encode Relevance as a Layer-Wise Cross-Lingual Signal
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in information retrieval (IR) pipelines as relevance judges and re-rankers. Yet most analyses remain output-centric, evaluating generated labels or scores while offering limited insight into how relevance is represented inside the model. In this work, we study whether query-document (q-d) relevance is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations in instruction-tuned LLMs, how this internal signal compares with generated relevance judgments, and whether it transfers across languages. Using the TREC DL20 and MIRACL test collections, we guide medium-scale LLMs (4-9B parameters) with UMBRELA-style relevance judgment prompts, extract last-token activations from every transformer layer, and train linear probes to predict relevance labels. We compare probe predictions with generated judgments and use TREC DL20 to test whether probe-derived pseudo-labels preserve system rankings when compared with human judgments. Our results suggest that q-d relevance is encoded as a depth-dependent internal signal: probe performance is weak in early layers and strongest in middle-to-late layers, indicating that relevance becomes more linearly accessible after contextual integration. Most importantly, in several models, validation-selected probes match or outperform generated judgments and better preserve system rankings, revealing a separation between internal relevance representation and external expression. Multilingual experiments further suggest partial cross-language portability, although transfer remains weaker than within-language decoding. Overall, this work provides a representation-level perspective on LLM-based relevance assessment. Layer-wise probing can help diagnose where relevance emerges, when generated judgments fail to reflect internally available evidence, and how relevance representations vary across languages, datasets, and model families.

papers.title: Post-Calibration Reliability Reranking of Relevance Decisions via Label-wise Monotone Projection
papers.abstract: Web search, product search, and question-answering retrieval systems often assign a relevance label and confidence score to each query-candidate pair. The relevance label describes how well a page, product, or passage matches the query, while the confidence often guides downstream use or fallback decisions. Post-hoc calibration is therefore needed because misaligned confidence can make systems over-trust wrong predictions or unnecessarily defer correct ones. However, calibration mainly aligns confidence with average correctness, and does not remove predicted-label-dependent reliability differences that remain within the same calibrated confidence level. We address this gap with Label-wise Monotone Reliability Projection (MRP), which learns label-wise monotone functions that map calibrated confidence to correctness reliability while preserving the original predicted labels and class probabilities. The resulting reliability score reranks fixed predictions according to residual risk. Across six information access relevance datasets and multiple post-hoc calibrators, MRP improves reliability reranking and average fallback utility while preserving full-coverage accuracy and ECE. Structural ablations show that the main gains come from label-wise residual reliability rather than from global confidence remapping. We further analyze when MRP reliability scores can be embedded back into top-label probability geometry, showing that this projection is useful as a compatibility analysis but is distinct from the main reliability-reranking objective. The implementation is available at https://github.com/inu0104/MRP.

papers.title: Static Pruning Across Sparse Retrieval Regimes: What Transfers, What Breaks, and What Still Helps
papers.abstract: Static pruning is widely used to accelerate sparse neural retrieval, yet existing studies each validate their conclusions within a single custom pipeline, leaving it unclear which findings transfer to modern engines with different index organizations and dynamic pruning mechanisms. We present the first cross-engine pruning portability study, evaluating static pruning strategies across three engines—a controlled C++ pipeline (exhaustive inverted index), BMP (block-max pruning), and SEISMIC (clustered inverted indexes)—on two benchmarks (MS MARCO, Natural Questions) with two encoders spanning opposite query-density regimes (SPLADE: 44 avg. query terms; V3-GTE: 7 avg. query terms), totaling 1,140 experimental configurations, with an additional deep-judgment validation on TREC DL 2019/2020. We find that index-side pruning (document and posting-list) is portable: it consistently reduces latency (1.2–6.6×) and index size (18–82%) across all engines because sparse retrieval is memory-bound—a conclusion we support with cache-miss, TLB, and IPC profiling. In contrast, query pruning is already internalized by modern engines: it yields 4–11× speedup on the exhaustive pipeline but is subsumed by BMP's ? and SEISMIC's query_cut. Static pruning complements dynamic pruning: on BMP, combining document and query reduction yields 2.5× speedup with NDCG@10 within 0.003 of the exact baseline. Finally, NDCG@10 saturates while Recall@10 is still in the 85–95% range across all three engines, providing a portable stopping criterion: practitioners can push pruning to this knee without visible ranking degradation. Together, these findings answer what transfers (index-side pruning), what breaks (query pruning), and what still helps (static atop dynamic pruning). Code is available at https://github.com/zirui-song-18/cross_engine_static_pruning.

papers.title: Token-Level Credit Assignment Optimization for Generative Document Retrieval
papers.abstract: Generative retrieval models perform document retrieval by autoregressively generating document identifiers (DocIDs). This process naturally forms a sequential decision problem, i.e., the model makes a sequence of token-level decisions, selecting a DocID token at each decoding step, with the resulting complete sequence identifying the retrieved document. However, relevance feedback is available only after the complete DocID has been generated and mapped to a document, resulting in a granularity mismatch between token-level generation decisions and document-level retrieval supervision. Consequently, existing reinforcement learning methods for generative retrieval rely on sequence-level rewards, assigning the same document-level relevance signal to every decoding step. Such uniform credit assignment obscures the contribution of individual token decisions, making it difficult to identify which decisions contribute to retrieval success or failure. In this paper, we propose Token-Level Credit Assignment for Generative Retrieval (TCA), a fine-grained reinforcement learning framework that aligns the granularity of credit assignment with that of autoregressive DocID generation. Unlike assigning a single reward to an entire generated DocID, TCA derives fine-grained rewards by comparing the hidden-state trajectory of each generated DocID with the gold DocID trajectory obtained from a frozen reference model. These trajectory-based rewards provide differentiated feedback across decoding steps, allowing the policy to reinforce generation paths that remain aligned with the target DocID. Moreover, TCA decouples token-level credit assignment from policy optimization and can be instantiated with both GRPO and PPO. Experiments on MS MARCO and NQ benchmarks show that our method consistently outperforms baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of fine-grained supervision for aligning autoregressive DocID generation with retrieval objectives.

papers.title: Think-to-Personalize: Unifying Reasoning and Retrieval for User-Centric Personalized Dense Retrieval
affiliations: University of science and technology of China
University of Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: Dense retrieval has become a cornerstone of modern local-lifestyle e-commerce search by encoding queries and items into semantic embedding spaces. While recent advancements have transitioned from BERT-based embedding models to Large Language Models (LLMs), most approaches still treat LLMs as static text encoders, neglecting their inherent reasoning capabilities. Furthermore, standard dense retrieval models remain query-centric, which is insufficient in e-commerce scenarios where sparse and ambiguous queries create an intent gap that can only be bridged by the rich context of user history. Meanwhile, existing personalized retrieval methods typically rely on implicit embedding interactions, which lack the reasoning capability to effectively disambiguate user intent from noisy historical behaviors. To address these challenges, we propose Think-to-Personalize (TTP), a novel framework that unifies explicit user-centric intent reasoning with dense retrieval. By reasoning over the user's historical purchase sequence, TTP explicitly deduces latent personalized needs and generates an intent-enhanced query, which is then encoded into a unified dense embedding. Specifically, we design a two-stage training paradigm: (1) A Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) stage that establishes cold-start capabilities; (2) A Reinforcement Learning (RL) stage that aligns the reasoning process with retrieval utility using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Extensive experiments on both proprietary and public benchmarks demonstrate that TTP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, in online A/B tests, it achieved a +0.46% lift in order volume, validating its practical effectiveness and establishing a new paradigm for reasoning-driven personalized dense retrieval.

papers.title: Query-Aware Index Pruning for Retrieval Under Budget Constraints
papers.abstract: Production search indices operate under strict storage and latency budgets that prevent indexing the full corpus (e.g.: web documents). When only a fraction of documents can be retained, the system must decide which ones to keep. Existing pruning methods make this decision using query-agnostic signals, including lexical quality, embedding magnitude, and corpus centrality or single-feature query-aware heuristics (e.g., query similarity, nearest-neighbour coverage), without optimising which documents actually contribute to answering the queries the system will serve. We recast index pruning as query-aware subset selection: given a fixed budget and an expected query workload, the goal is to retain the document subset that maximises retrieval performance for the queries the system will serve. We introduce Query-aware Document Selection (QDS), a lightweight framework that scores documents using 13 retrieval-structural features derived from query–document interactions and index redundancy, capturing how many queries a document serves, whether viable alternatives exist, and how replaceable the document is within the retained set. A linear scorer trained with Evolution Strategies optimises nDCG@10 of the pruned index end-to-end, requiring no differentiable surrogate while remaining fully interpretable. % Across 10 IR benchmarks (1K–120M documents), four dense encoders plus BM25, and three modalities (text, image, audio), QDS consistently outperforms query-agnostic and single-feature query-aware baselines under aggressive pruning budgets. We show that coverage-oriented heuristics degrade at web scale by over-selecting high-frequency hard negatives, i.e., documents that are nearest neighbours to many queries but relevant to none. Given its simplicity, QDS can operate on existing indexes of 100M-1B documents in minutes with limited hardware.

papers.title: Two important things you must know! Revisiting Clickbait Detection from Perspectives of Humans' Cognition and Emotion
affiliations: Criminal Investigation Police University of China
papers.abstract: Clickbait headlines are purposefully designed to omit crucial news information, thus evoking strong curiosity and enticing readers to click. Naturally, such heightened curiosity is typically accompanied by more diverse imaginings of the news content and stronger emotional arousal among readers. Inspired by these cognitive and affective reactions, we develop a novel clickbait detection method, entitled C lickbait Detector with A ugmentation of C ognitive I magining and Emotion A rousal ( CACIA ). Specifically, a persona-induced multi-agent system (MAS), which simulates real-world news readers, is exploited to generate multiple content imaginings of a given headline. Meanwhile, we suggest a dimensional emotion recognition (DER) task within a multi-task learning framework to estimate the emotional arousal elicited by the headline. Accordingly, clickbait headlines tend to induce more diverse imaginings and stronger emotional arousal than non-clickbait ones. These relative differences are formulated as additional training objectives, thus enabling a more effective capturing of curiosity semantics in clickbait headlines. Finally, CACIA derives discriminative clickbait features augmented by human-like imaginings and emotion knowledge. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that CACIA consistently outperforms strong baseline methods.

papers.title: Emerging-Claim Stance Detection for Understanding Opinions in Voting Discourse
papers.abstract: Online platforms are increasingly shaping political communication, influencing how narratives emerge and gain traction. Unfortunately, this has led to an acceleration in the spread of false information. One way to analyze misinformation dynamics is to measure whether public discussions support or refute verified claims. However, most existing stance detection methods struggle to keep up with novel claims without retraining on new labeled data. In this paper, we extend claim-based stance detection research, explicitly focusing on generalization to unseen claim targets and model performance in-the-wild. We introduce a deep learning architecture designed to model the relational interactions between a claim and a post by combining a two-way cross-attention mechanism and supervised contrastive learning to learn stance features that transfer to unseen claims. Intuitively, this approach combines both instance-level reasoning associated with claim and post tokens and higher order reasoning associated with the stance detection task. Our experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate improved generalization performance across multiple domains when compared to state-of-the-art methods. Finally, we conduct a case study that uses our proposed model to measure the stance of voting claims on social media from the 2024 U.S. election, highlighting variations in misinformation across different voting-related themes and the benefit of our model for timely and scalable analysis of online discourse.

papers.title: Beyond Shortcuts: Semantic Decoupling and Dynamic Enhancement for LLM-Generated Fake News Detection
papers.abstract: As large language models advance, news increasingly contains both human-written and LLM-generated content. Existing models tend to exploit linguistic fingerprints in LLM-generated texts rather than deep semantics for veracity inference, leading to shortcut learning and detection bias when classifying both human-written and LLM-generated news. To address this issue, we propose a S emantic D ecoupling and D ynamic E nhancement ( SDDE ) plugin, which can be integrated into fake news detection models as a plug-and-play module to mitigate linguistic fingerprint interference and enhance transferable semantic information. Specifically, SDDE first obtains original text representations from the backbone model and denoises them to extract purified features. Subsequently, based on these features, adversarial training and auxiliary supervision are applied to reduce the influence of linguistic fingerprints while preserving deep semantics. Meanwhile, a cross-attention mechanism supplements semantic details of the purified features to obtain enhanced features. A token-level adaptive gating dynamically fuses enhanced features with the original text representations. Finally, the fused representations are reinjected into the backbone model for training. Experiments show that incorporating the SDDE plugin yields absolute accuracy improvements of 1.19%–6.29% across backbone models on two datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness and generalizability. The code is available at https://github.com/cgao-comp/SDDE.

papers.title: Adaptive Dual-Evidence Fusion via Policy-Driven Hybrid Gating for Multimodal Video Fake News Detection
papers.abstract: Effective multimodal fake news detection necessitates considering extracted cues not merely as features for passive aggregation but as distinct evidence for selective integration. Nevertheless, current methodologies primarily depend on static fusion architectures, lacking the ability to dynamically adjust to the particular evidence needed for each given sample. The constraint arises from their inability to effectively model the hybrid decision space: routing to specific evidence branches while regulating their respective contributions. To bridge this gap, we propose PAGE, a Policy-driven Adaptive Gating framework utilising Evidence fusion that explicitly decouples multimodal features into complementary content and editing evidence. To tackle the optimisation constraints of this hybrid action space, we formulate evidence fusion as a policy learning problem optimised via reinforcement learning. Specifically, an adaptive policy gate issues a hybrid action for each instance: it performs a discrete routing decision to establish the optimal fusion structure, while simultaneously predicting continuous gating values to calibrate branch interactions. Guided by task-level detection rewards, the framework jointly optimises these coupled decisions. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that PAGE achieves satisfactory performance, significantly improving detection accuracy over state-of-the-art baselines. The source code is available at https://github.com/cgao-comp/PAGE.

papers.title: GESR: Graph-Guided Evidence-State Repair for Citation-Grounded Multimodal Fact-Checking
affiliations: Chinese People's Armed Police Force Engineering University
papers.abstract: Multimodal fact-checking systems are increasingly expected to return not only a veracity label but also a citation-grounded re port. Yet a correct label may still be accompanied by query drift, hallucinated citations, unsupported evidence statements, or over strong conclusions. We argue that many such failures arise from evidence-state management errors in two local windows: retrieval plan formation before evidence retrieval and citation integration after evidence retrieval. We propose GESR, a training-free inference time framework that uses an executable claim-local evidence-state graph to constrain local repair actions under a fixed retrieval budget with one real retrieval call per example. Unlike graph-as-context prompting, GESR does not merely expose graph information to the generator. It uses graph checks to accept or reject typed actions, including entity, time, source, and modality edits before retrieval, and citation replacement, claim weakening, modality-support inser tion, and verdict downgrading after retrieval. To evaluate citation grounding, we build MR2-E, a controlled evaluation protocol on top of MR2 with a frozen retrieval index, opaque citation identifiers, top-5 citation resolution, and sentence-level support judgments. On MR2-E under the fixed single-retrieval-call setting, GESR shows statistically inconclusive label-level F1 differences but larger and more stable improvements in evidence consistency, citation accu racy, and human-judged citation grounding than verifier-repair and graph-exposure baselines.

papers.title: Evaluating and Improving Evidence-Grounded Fact-Checking in LLMs via Multi-Round Evidence Ablation
papers.abstract: Automatic fact-checking systems assess the veracity of claims given evidence from relevant documents. Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in fact-checking due to their general reasoning capabilities. However, it remains unclear whether they faithfully make use of the evidence provided to reach veracity judgments or rely on parametric knowledge. To investigate this, we introduce Fact-Ablated Evaluation (FAE), a new evaluation framework that iteratively ablates the cited evidence to assess whether LLMs revise their predictions accordingly. Our empirical results show that current off-the-shelf LLMs as fact-checking systems rely more on their parametric knowledge than on the evidence provided. To bridge this gap between prediction accuracy and evidence grounding, we propose REAL (Rigorous Evidence Ablation Learning), a training framework that promotes evidence-dependent verification through counterfactual evidence supervision for the LLM-as-verifier models. Experiments on four fact-checking datasets across different domains demonstrate that models trained with REAL obtain superior evidence-dependent capabilities compared to standard fine-tuned models. Our findings highlight that strong fact-checking performance can still coexist with weak evidence dependency, while REAL encourages veracity predictions to remain more closely tied to the availability of supporting evidence.

papers.title: Causal Modeling of Misinformation Diffusion via LLM-based Counterfactual Reasoning
papers.abstract: Misinformation diffusion at scale on social media poses serious societal risks, as it can distort collective decision-making, undermine public health interventions, bias political discourse, and trigger large-scale behavioral cascades during emergencies. Most existing approaches rely heavily on observable content signals or user-level features, primarily capturing surface-level correlations while overlooking the latent causal mechanisms governing diffusion dynamics. To bridge this gap, we formulate misinformation diffusion prediction from a causal perspective and propose MisTran, a mechanism-aware framework that models diffusion through causal mediation. Specifically, MisTran introduces a structured mediator to represent propagation mechanisms that connect persuasive content to cascade growth, enabling the model to move beyond correlation-based inference toward mechanism-oriented prediction. To further improve robustness, we incorporate LLM-based counterfactual reasoning to encourage causal consistency during training. By constructing hypothetical variations of posts, the model learns invariant propagation patterns that reflect stable causal structure rather than spurious correlations. Extensive experiments on a real-world misinformation diffusion benchmark demonstrate that MisTran consistently outperforms strong baselines. Ablation and interpretability analyses further validate the effectiveness of mechanism-constrained modeling and provide interpretable insights into the dynamics of misinformation diffusion.

papers.title: HybridDet: Redistribution-Robust Visual Content Provenance for Information Credibility
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: AI-generated images increasingly enter information-access systems where provenance signals inform search ranking, moderation, and news verification, often only after web and social-media redistribution. The practical task is therefore metadata-free visual content provenance rather than pristine-image classification: recompression, reposting, resizing, and re-digitization can alter the evidence available to a detector. Existing detectors typically rely on either low-level artifact cues or high-level representation cues, but these cues exhibit asymmetric reliability across the content life cycle. We present HybridDet, a representation-first dual-expert framework for redistribution-robust AI-generated image provenance. HybridDet combines Q-Table Transfer (QTT), which aligns real and synthetic samples through empirical JPEG quantization-table transfer during training, with Patch2DCT, which converts multi-scale DCT-band statistics into ViT-compatible patch tokens. Instead of dense fusion, HybridDet adopts a Confidence-Aware Router (CAR) that keeps QTT as the default path and invokes Patch2DCT only under validation-calibrated selective routing, yielding a validation-calibrated selective provenance signal. Experiments on ten clean-transfer and redistribution-oriented benchmarks show that HybridDet improves the robustness & generalization balance for binary AI-generated visual provenance, especially on real-world redistribution and recent text-to-image generators. Ablations, routed-subset analyses, calibration metrics, selective-decision analysis, and real-photo checks show that HybridDet selectively exploits complementary provenance evidence under distribution shift. Code is available at https://github.com/graydove/HybridDet.

papers.title: QA-Merging: Query-Adaptive Reasoning via Layer Selective Model Merging
papers.abstract: Recent large reasoning models (LRMs) have achieved strong performance on complex reasoning tasks by generating a long chain-of-thought (Long-CoT). However, such lengthy reasoning is often unnecessary for simple queries, leading to additional computation and latency. Existing approaches to adaptive reasoning typically rely on retraining the model or designing sophisticated prompting, which are either prohibitively expensive or highly sensitive to the prompt formulation. Model merging provides a more balanced alternative for adaptive reasoning by avoiding expensive training and integrating Long-CoT and Short-CoT behaviors. However, existing merging methods are often static and input-agnostic, or rely on costly all-layer calibration, which limits their effectiveness for query-adaptive reasoning. To tackle these challenges, we propose Query-adaptive Layer Selective Merging (QA-Merging), an activation-based merging framework that integrates a Long-CoT model and a Short-CoT model to obtain a query-adaptive reasoner without training from scratch or requiring large-scale additional data. QA-Merging first constructs a small pattern-labeled calibration set that assigns each query an appropriate reasoning pattern. Motivated by our empirical analysis that Long-CoT and Short-CoT behaviors diverge unevenly across transformer layers, QA-Merging identifies layers with high reasoning pattern divergence and calibrates only these layers through feature alignment and contrastive shaping, while applying closed-form hidden-state correction to the remaining layers. Experiments on seven widely used reasoning benchmarks across two model scales demonstrate that QA-Merging reduces inference cost and maintains strong performance. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/QA-Merging-q1a2.

papers.title: SemCoT: A Semantic Step-level Reasoning Optimization Approach for Collaborative Chain-of-Thought
affiliations: Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, with long or short variants, has become a central paradigm for enhancing the reasoning ability of large language models. Long CoT aims at achieving high accuracy in complex multi-step reasoning at the cost of high inference overhead, while short CoT focus on offering a more efficient but less capable alternative. To balance reasoning accuracy and reasoning efficiency, collaborative approaches combining long and short CoT have been widely explored. However, existing collaborative approaches either operate token-level pruning, risking disruption to reasoning coherence, or rely on instance-level routing, which over-look the excessive self-verification within long CoT reasoning. To address these limitations, a semantic step-level reasoning optimization approach for collaborative CoTs, named SemCoT, is investigated in this paper. Technically, verification redundancy and trigger mechanisms in long CoT reasoning are first analyzed. Specifically, a dynamic trigger leveraging lexical cues and logit uncertainty is designed to detect the onset of self-verification in long CoT reasoning. A finetuned short CoT model is subsequently employed to filter trivial verification, with redundant cases truncated through context steering. Confident phrases are finally embedded to ensure contextual coherence. Experimental results demonstrate that SemCoT reduces average reasoning length by 48% across several benchmarks while maintaining similar accuracy, highlighting its practical effectiveness.

papers.title: CriticRouter: Criticality-aware Step Router for Small-Large Collaborative Reasoning
affiliations: Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) achieve strong performance on complex reasoning tasks, but their long chain-of-thought trajectories incur substantial inference latency and computational cost. Small-large model collaborative reasoning mitigates this issue by offloading part of the reasoning steps to a small language model (SLM) while preserving large language model (LLM) computation for more demanding steps. Existing draft-and-verify methods use an external verifier to reject low-scoring SLM steps and regenerate them with the LLM, introducing per-step verification overhead. Moreover, we observe that many LLM rewrites remain semantically close to the rejected SLM drafts, causing unnecessary decoding cost. Further analysis shows that these redundant rewrites often occur on local derivation steps, whose content is largely constrained by recent context. Motivated by these observations, we propose CriticRouter , a verifier-free step-wise routing framework that reduces redundancy based on structural criticality as a routing signal. Specifically, structural criticality measures how sensitive the SLM's next-step generation is to perturbations in earlier reasoning history, and low-criticality steps are viewed as locally stable and delegated to the SLM, whereas high-criticality steps are treated as history-sensitive and routed to the LLM. To reduce probing overhead, CriticRouter further adopts short concurrent probes and progressive mask advancement for better cache reuse. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that CriticRouter achieves comparable accuracy to standard LLM reasoning while significantly reducing latency, demonstrating a better utility-efficiency trade-off.

papers.title: Semantic Caching: From Exact Hits to Close Enough
papers.abstract: The rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) has created demand for faster responses and lower costs. Semantic caching, reusing semantically similar requests via their embeddings, addresses this need but breaks classic cache assumptions and raises new challenges. In this paper, we explore offline policies for semantic caching, proving that implementing an optimal offline policy is NP-hard, and propose several polynomial-time heuristics. We also present online semantic aware cache policies that combine recency, frequency, and locality. Evaluations on diverse datasets show that while frequency based policies are strong baselines, our novel variant improves semantic accuracy. Our findings reveal effective strategies for current systems and highlight substantial headroom for future innovation. All of our code is open source.

papers.title: LSH-KV: Efficient KV Cache Retrieval for Long-Context LLM Inference via Locality-Sensitive Hashing
affiliations: Shanghai University of International Business and Economics
papers.abstract: As large language models increasingly support long-context inference, the computation and memory access overhead of attention and KV caches have become critical bottlenecks for inference latency and system scalability. Existing approaches mitigate these costs through KV cache dropping, approximate attention, or system-level optimizations, but often incur non-trivial trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, and implementation complexity. In this work, we propose LSH-KV, a coarse-to-fine KV retrieval framework for efficient long-context LLM inference. LSH-KV uses locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) as a lightweight, training-free coarse partitioning layer for similarity-preserving organization of global KV entries. Within each hash bucket, LSH-KV further uses product quantization with offline-precomputed codebooks for efficient approximate similarity estimation, followed by exact re-ranking to preserve attention accuracy. To further improve system efficiency, LSH-KV introduces a score-aware block-level cache management strategy that aligns KV movement between CPU and GPU with retrieval relevance. Experimental results on long-context benchmarks demonstrate that LSH-KV significantly reduces end-to-end inference latency while preserving generation quality, even when selective attention is performed using only a fraction of the input tokens. These results show that LSH-KV enables scalable, robust, and accurate inference under long-context settings. The code is available at https://github.com/HarryFunn/lsh-kv.

papers.title: Learning a Single Token to Replace Long System Prompts in LLMs
papers.abstract: Long system prompts are widely used to steer Large Language Models (LLMs), but repeatedly processing them at inference time is inefficient and consumes valuable context budget. This motivates a central question: can the behavioral effect of a long system prompt be retained using only a minimal learned representation? To enable this, we propose a lightweight training framework that learns a single Behavior-Equivalent Token ([BE]). The framework first trains [BE] to encode the semantic content of the original system prompt via reconstruction, and then distills the prompt's downstream behavior into this single token. Importantly, our method requires no update to the pretrained LLM weights, no auxiliary compression models, and no labeled responses. Empirical evaluations on three datasets show that replacing long prompts with a single [BE] token yields up to a 3000x prompt compression ratio, while retaining about 98% of the downstream performance of the original system prompts. This substantially reduces inference cost and frees nearly the entire context window for user inputs and model outputs. The implementation code is publicly available for reproduction.

papers.title: DATP: Training-Free Depth-Aware Token Pruning for Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: The massive redundancy of visual tokens in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) creates a critical computational bottleneck during large language model (LLM) prefill. Recent training-free pruning methods provide plug-and-play acceleration, yet their pruning decisions often rely on limited visual states or delayed in-LLM signals, which may underexploit both the layer-wise evolution of visual representations and the query-specific relevance of local regions. We propose DATP (Depth-Aware Token Pruning), a training-free early-pruning framework that selects compact visual tokens before they enter the LLM. DATP combines two complementary signals: Depth-aware Layer Aggregation (DALA), which aggregates multi-layer visual saliency trajectories to construct a high-recall structural prior, and Cross-modal Attention Gating (CMAG), which introduces a lightweight prompt-conditioned relevance signal to suppress visually salient but task-irrelevant tokens. Experiments on LLaVA-v1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, and Qwen2.5-VL show that DATP achieves a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off under aggressive token budgets. On LLaVA-v1.5, DATP preserves 95.7% of the full-token performance while retaining only 11% of the visual tokens. Across the reported multimodal reasoning and hallucination-sensitive benchmark settings, DATP generally outperforms the evaluated training-free pruning baselines.

papers.title: RI-Prune: Relation and Information Aware Visual Token Pruning for Multi-Image Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have recently been extended to handle multiple input images, but this extension dramatically increases the visual token budget, making visual-token pruning not merely an efficiency option but a practical necessity. Existing visual-token pruning methods, primarily designed for the single-image setting, rely on attention-derived saliency signals to estimate per-token importance. However, this attention-centric design transfers poorly to the multi-image regime: it causes substantial performance degradation on multi-image benchmarks, suffers from strong positional bias, and loses discriminative attention signals as the number of input images increases. To test whether attention-selected tokens are truly important for multi-image reasoning, we conduct two complementary causal probes—Leave-One-In and Leave-One-Deletion—which measure token importance by restoring individual tokens to a zeroed visual sequence or removing them from the full sequence. Attention-based pruners provide only marginal gains over random selection, showing that attention is a weak proxy for visual-token importance in multi-image reasoning. Motivated by this gap, we propose Relation and Information Aware Pruning (RI-Prune), a training-free, attention-free pre-decoder selector for multi-image visual token pruning. RI-Prune scores each visual token using a z-normalized combination of three signals computed from projector outputs: query relevance, cross-image correspondence with compact per-image prototypes, and intra-image representativeness. By integrating these signals, RI-Prune performs balanced per-image Top-K selection to preserve information across input images. Across multiple multi-image benchmarks and three LVLM backbones, RI-Prune achieves a stronger trade-off between token reduction and task performance than prior pruning methods, particularly under aggressive token budgets.

papers.title: MKG-CARE: Case-Aware Reasoning with Multimodal Knowledge Graphs for Explainable Medical Image Diagnosis
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: Medical image diagnosis has achieved significant progress with deep learning, yet existing methods often rely on isolated visual evidence and lack the ability to effectively leverage similar cases and external knowledge. In clinical practice, diagnosis is typically supported by similar historical cases and their associated symptoms. To explicitly model this evidence-based diagnostic process, we propose MKG-CARE, a framework that performs case-aware reasoning using multimodal knowledge graphs for explainable medical image diagnosis. Specifically, we construct a case-aware multimodal knowledge graph as a structured diagnostic memory, where diseases, images, and symptoms are hierarchically organized. Given an input image, MKG-CARE adaptively retrieves similar cases from this memory and extracts their corresponding case-centered subgraphs. We further introduce a knowledge propagation and injection mechanism, where an image-centric Graph Attention Network aggregates heterogeneous semantics within the retrieved case subgraphs, followed by bidirectional cross-modal attention to align and inject the aggregated case knowledge into visual representations. To mitigate retrieval noise, we design a confidence-calibrated decision refinement scheme that estimates each retrieved case’s reliability from prediction confidence and sample similarity, and reweights its contribution to the final prediction for interpretable case-level evidence attribution. Extensive experiments on multiple medical imaging datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines, while ablation and qualitative analyses validate the effectiveness and interpretability of our method. The code is available at https://github.com/lyxuan1022/MKG-CARE.

papers.title: DAMEC: Disease-Aware Multi-Expert Consensus Framework for Study-Level Radiology Report Generation
papers.abstract: Radiology report generation (RRG) translates medical images into clinical reports, yet existing systems diverge from real radiological practice in three respects. First, they are formulated at the image level, consuming a single image or a fixed pair of current/prior images, and discarding the variable visual evidence within a patient study. Second, report generation flows through a single end-to-end pipeline. Even when auxiliary classifiers or retrieved priors are incorporated, they remain auxiliary inputs rather than independent sources of clinical judgment. Third, both retrieval and validation operate without a finding-level clinical anchor: retrieval falls back on image-feature similarity, while validation relies on prompt-level heuristics, leaving generated reports weakly grounded. We propose DAMEC, a Disease-Aware Multi-Expert Consensus framework that recasts RRG as study-level, clinical-context generation. Four heterogeneous experts process a variable number of images from a patient study and emit per-expert clinical signals, which a trainable disease-aware consensus module aggregates into a unified consensus. The consensus, together with disease states, uncertainty, longitudinal changes, and attribute modifiers, is externalized into a structured Clinical Findings (CF) descriptor, serving as the finding-level anchor for both clinical-context retrieval and post-generation validation. On MIMIC-CXR, MIMIC-ABN, Two-view CXR, and CheXpert Plus, DAMEC consistently improves both natural language generation and clinical efficacy metrics over strong baselines. Code is available at: https://github.com/ku-milab/DAMEC.

papers.title: Discovering Hierarchy-Grounded Domains with Adaptive Granularity for Clinical Domain Generalization
papers.abstract: Domain generalization has become a critical challenge in predictive healthcare, where different patient groups exhibit shifting data distributions that degrade model performance. Still, regular domain generalization approaches often struggle in clinical settings due to (1) the absence of domain labels and (2) the lack of clinical insight integration. To address these challenges in healthcare, we aim to explore how medical ontologies can be used to discover dynamic yet hierarchy-grounded patient domains, a partitioning strategy that remains under-explored in prior work. Hence, we introduce UdonCare, a hierarchy-pruning method that iteratively divides patients into latent domains and retrieves domain-invariant (label) information from patient data. On public datasets (MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU), UdonCare shows superiority over eight generalization baselines across four representative clinical prediction tasks with substantial domain gaps, highlighting the potential of medical knowledge for enhancing model generalization.

papers.title: Weak Ordinal Supervision for Causal Structure Learning from Clinical Narratives
affiliations: Instituto Federal de Educação, Ciência e Tecnologia de Mato Grosso
papers.abstract: Causal structure learning in clinical domains faces a persistent challenge: tabular datasets are often limited, while valuable domain knowledge exists primarily in unstructured clinical narratives. Recent work has explored large language models (LLMs) as sources of knowledge to refine causal graph discovery or define causal relations. However, relying directly on LLM-generated causal judgments can be problematic, as such outputs may reflect spurious associations, domain bias, or statistical patterns learned from text rather than reliable causal mechanisms. In this work, we propose a different perspective: instead of treating LLM outputs as definitive causal judgments, we use them as weak ordinal supervision integrated into the Hill-Climbing score through a soft regularization mechanism that remains correctable by observational data. Our framework extracts candidate causal relations from clinical narratives and assigns them ordinal plausibility labels using a domain-specialized LLM. We evaluate this approach on three established Bayesian network benchmarks (Alarm, Child, and Hepar II) and a real-world clinical dataset from cBioPortal, comparing Hill Climbing with and without ordinal priors across varying sample sizes. The framework consistently improves structural recovery, with statistically significant gains persisting even in high-data regimes. Overall, the results suggest that ordinal LLM supervision provides a robust inductive bias that helps resolve statistical ambiguities and mitigate structural errors in clinical causal discovery.

papers.title: ClinSDT: LLM-Encoded Clinical Semantic Guidance for Sepsis Treatment via Decision Transformer
affiliations: East China University of Science and Technology
University of Science and Technology of China
University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: Offline sepsis treatment aims to learn treatment policies from retrospective ICU trajectories. Decision Transformer-based methods provide a natural sequence modeling framework for this task, but they mainly rely on raw physiological states and historical clinician actions. Such raw trajectory tokens may not explicitly capture clinical semantics that clinicians use in practice, such as patient severity, recent treatment response, and current risk priorities. To address this limitation, we propose ClinSDT , an LLM-assisted Decision Transformer framework for offline sepsis treatment. ClinSDT uses a frozen LLM as a semantic bridge rather than a treatment decision maker. It constructs three clinical semantic views from ICU trajectories, namely Profile, Context, and Advisory, and inserts their encoded representations as independent tokens into a Decision Transformer policy. To support policy refinement and rollout, ClinSDT further trains a Treatment-Response Forecaster to estimate the next physiological state, SAPS-II change, and predictive uncertainty from state–action inputs. In the second training stage, the forecaster screens local counterfactual treatment candidates, and only low-uncertainty candidates with lower predicted SAPS-II increase are distilled into the policy after semantic regeneration. During inference, ClinSDT performs closed-loop treatment rollout by refreshing semantic inputs from the currently available patient state. Experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV show that ClinSDT achieves consistent relative improvements over representative imitation learning, offline reinforcement learning, and Decision Transformer baselines under the same rollout protocol. Code and data are available at ClinSDT (https://github.com/KAG778/ClinSDT).

papers.title: Constructing Patient-Aligned References via Composition Modeling for Medication Recommendation
papers.abstract: Medication recommendation aims to generate effective drug combinations based on longitudinal clinical records of patients, where historical prescriptions and relevant candidate medications serve as important references to improve performance. However, existing methods treat these medications as individual entities and overlook structured interactions among clinically co-occurring drugs that jointly contribute to treatment effects. In addition, medications lack intrinsic principles to guide the modeling of semantic compositions describing such interactions, making it challenging to capture coherent clinical structures and resulting in a gap between structured patient representations and flat medication references. To address these challenges, we propose PACRM, a novel medication recommendation framework that captures semantic compositions to summarize collective drug effects through multi-level structures. Specifically, the model introduces a GAT-based voting strategy to organize drugs working as combinations jointly into structured compositions, and further performs temporally constrained and dynamically determined cross-combination voting over historical prescriptions and selected candidate medication to complete hierarchical effect propagation. This design summarizes individual drug effects into collective effects aligned with patient conditions, which are then integrated to generate effective prescriptions.
