Moreover, PACRM adopts a two-stage optimization to sequentially learn candidate relevance modeling and structured effect summarization. Experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV demonstrate that PACRM consistently outperforms competitive baselines, remains robust across varying sizes of medication sets, and is compatible with existing methods that leverage medication references.

papers.title: ECGTwin: Personalized ECG Generation Using Controllable Diffusion Model
papers.abstract: Personalized electrocardiogram (ECG) generation is to simulate a patient's ECG digital twins tailored to specific conditions. It has the potential to transform traditional healthcare into a more accurate individualized paradigm, while preserving the key benefits of conventional population-level ECG synthesis. However, this promising task presents two fundamental challenges: extracting individual features without ground truth and injecting various types of conditions without confusing generative model. In this paper, we present ECGTwin , a two-stage framework designed to address these challenges. In the first stage, an Individual Base Extractor trained via contrastive learning robustly captures personal features from a reference ECG. In the second stage, the extracted individual features, along with a target cardiac condition, are integrated into the diffusion-based generation process through our novel AdaX Condition Injector , which injects these signals via two dedicated and specialized pathways. Both qualitative and quantitative experiments have demonstrated that our model can not only generate ECG signals of high fidelity and diversity by offering a fine-grained generation controllability, but also preserving individual-specific features. Furthermore, ECGTwin shows the potential to enhance ECG auto-diagnosis in downstream application, confirming the possibility of precise personalized healthcare solutions. Our code is available at https://github.com/Raiiyf/ECGTwin.

papers.title: IC-DVLoRA: Input-Conditioned Dynamic Adaptation for Endoscopic Depth Foundation Models
affiliations: Beijing Information Science and Technology University
Southern University of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Transferring depth foundation models to endoscopic videos is promising for surgical geometric perception, but remains challenging under patient-level visual heterogeneity. Natural-scene depth models provide strong geometric priors, yet endoscopic imagery differs substantially in specular reflection, weak texture, tool occlusion, close-range anatomy, and acquisition conditions. Existing parameter-efficient adapters, including DV-LoRA-based methods, are typically static after training and apply the same adaptation to all frames, limiting their ability to handle input-dependent appearance shifts. We propose IC-DVLoRA, an input-conditioned dynamic adaptation framework for endoscopic depth foundation models. For each frame, a lightweight condition encoder extracts a compact token that captures appearance, texture, gradient, and structural cues. This token dynamically routes multiple DV-LoRA experts in a frozen transformer backbone and modulates a DPT-style decoder through feature-wise transformations, enabling sample-specific low-rank adaptation while preserving pretrained geometric knowledge. We train and validate IC-DVLoRA on SCARED and evaluate its zero-shot generalization on Hamlyn and C3VD without target-domain fine-tuning. Experiments show improved overall performance over static adaptation baselines and competitive results against recent endoscopic depth estimation methods. Further analyses of routing utilization, top-k selection, trainable parameters, and inference latency demonstrate that IC-DVLoRA provides an effective and efficient adaptation strategy for endoscopic depth foundation models.

papers.title: Bridge-Adaptive Continual Knowledge Graph Embedding with Topology-Aware Negative Sampling
affiliations: China University of Mining and Technology
papers.abstract: Real-world knowledge graphs evolve continuously, making retraining from scratch impractical. Continual knowledge graph embedding (KGE) updates representations with new triples while preserving historical knowledge. However, current methods face two challenges: (1) the stability-plasticity dilemma is pronounced for bridge entities connecting old and new subgraphs, where uniform updates may cause forgetting or rigidity; and (2) random negative sampling yields easy negatives and weak supervision near evolving graph boundaries. We propose KG-BRACE, a bridge-adaptive continual KGE framework combining topology-aware negative sampling with differentiated low-rank updates. KG-BRACE learns new entities via DoRA, updates bridge entities through a restricted Mini-DoRA branch, and freezes inactive historical entities. It also retrieves hard negative candidates from local neighborhoods. Experiments on six benchmarks show best or tied-best results on five datasets, consistent Hits@1 improvements, and competitive stronger freezing in extremely sparse graphs.

papers.title: FIETA: Few-Shot Inductive Knowledge Graph Completion via Task-Aware Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Few-shot knowledge graph completion aims to predict missing triplets involving few-shot relations, where each few-shot relation is associated with only a few examples of the relation, called support triplets. In few-shot knowledge graph completion, each few-shot task corresponds to predicting triplets for a few-shot relation. Most existing few-shot knowledge graph completion methods assume all entities and relations in knowledge graphs to be observed during training, making it challenging to deal with new entities and relations appearing at inference time. In this paper, we propose FIETA, a Few-shot InductivE knowledge graph completion method that introduces Task-Aware graph neural networks to handle few-shot tasks in knowledge graphs containing entities and relations unseen during training. Based on the local structures of support triplets, FIETA conducts task-centric modeling of relations to obtain relation representations reflecting relative positions to the few-shot relation, and performs task-guided message passing to compute entity representations optimized for each task by prioritizing triplets that are crucial in prediction. By learning to compute task-aware representations with structures, FIETA effectively handles few-shot relations on knowledge graphs with new entities and relations appearing at inference time. Experimental results show that FIETA outperforms 19 state-of-the-art baselines in various inductive scenarios.

papers.title: Structure-Conditioned Missing Modality Generation for Multi-modal Knowledge Graph Completion
papers.abstract: Multi-modal Knowledge Graph Completion (MMKGC) leverages entity-associated visual and textual information to infer missing facts in multi-modal knowledge graphs. However, real-world multi-modal knowledge graphs often suffer from modality missingness. Existing methods typically rely on deterministic reconstruction or modality alignment, which fail to model the uncertainty and diversity of missing modalities and overlook the impact of intra-modality noise and structural semantics, thereby limiting their reasoning capability. In this paper, we propose Structure-Conditioned Missing Modality Generation (ScMMG), a generative framework for MMKGC that recovers missing entity modalities under knowledge graph semantic guidance. ScMMG leverages diffusion-based modality generation to model the latent distribution of missing modalities and incorporates adversarial structural optimization to enforce relational consistency within a unified semantic space. As a result, the generated modality representations are encouraged to be both distributionally plausible and structurally coherent. To provide reliable semantic anchors, we introduce a Fragment-level Magnitude-aware Fusion (FlMaF) module that suppresses noise and captures intrinsic entity semantics at a fine-grained level. Furthermore, a Structure-Conditioned Driven Diffusion Generation (ScDDG) module with Adversarial Optimization Scoring (AOS) is designed to enforce structural consistency and improve training stability within a shared semantic space constructed by RotatE, a rotation-based knowledge graph embedding model. Experimental results on DB15K, MKG-Y, and MKG-W demonstrate that ScMMG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, while ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each proposed component.

papers.title: Structural Knowledge Induced Logical Learning for LLM Reasoning over Knowledge Graphs
affiliations: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) are fundamental for grounding Large Language Models (LLMs) in factually consistent reasoning across diverse data-mining tasks. However, when reasoning over complex graph topologies, LLMs can be brittle in maintaining structural consistency and may rely on spurious correlations. We propose SKILL (Structural Knowledge Induced Logical Learning), a novel paradigm that transforms relational rules from passive symbolic patterns into explicit, generation-time symbolic guidance for LLM-based reasoning. Unlike existing methods that isolate symbolic mining from neural inference, SKILL introduces a semantically aligned rule synthesis framework that filters spurious patterns and enables LLMs to leverage relational regularities during inference. By grounding generation in pruned, query-specific subgraph structures together with rule–path evidence, SKILL improves inductive generalization while preserving generative flexibility. Extensive experiments on three inductive benchmarks demonstrate that SKILL achieves state-of-the-art performance, with up to a 5% absolute improvement in Hits@1, highlighting a new and effective way to integrate symbolic structure into LLM reasoning over knowledge graphs. Source code is available at https://github.com/luilui97/SKILL.

papers.title: Existentially Consistent Skolemized Reasoning for Complex Query Answering on Knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract: Complex Query Answering (CQA) over incomplete Knowledge Graphs (KGs) formalizes compositional reasoning as Existential First-Order logic with one free variable (EFO 1 ), where existential variables link multiple atomic constraints within a query. Maintaining existential consistency helps prevent reasoning shortcuts that satisfy only part of these constraints. We identify a Grounding–Skolemization dichotomy in existing CQA approaches. Grounding-based methods preserve logical equivalence but incur combinatorial enumeration costs, whereas Skolemization-based methods enable efficient latent reasoning over KGs while risking reasoning shortcuts arising from existential inconsistency. To address this tradeoff, we propose existentially consistent Skolemized reasoning, instantiated by the Logic-constrained Vector Symbolic Architecture (LVSA). LVSA uses vector-symbolic operations to compose atomic constraints and differentiable Skolemization to construct and reuse a constraint-conditioned latent state for each existential variable. Logical negation is handled through a logic-regularized neural negator. Theoretically, LVSA is structurally expressive for EFO 1 queries with acyclic query graphs and offers favorable complexity. Experiments show that LVSA outperforms prior Skolemization-based methods in reasoning performance and empirical existential consistency, while incurring substantially lower inference costs than Grounding-based approaches.

papers.title: SEMAPHORE: Semantic Detour over Incomplete Knowledge Graphs for Multi-hop Numerical QA
papers.abstract: Numerical question answering (QA) over Knowledge Graphs (KGs) requires retrieving numerical values from structured sources. Knowledge Graph Question Answering (KGQA) and KG-augmented Large Language Model (LLM) methods exploit multi-hop connectivity for entity-centric questions but remain brittle for numerical queries, whose values typically appear as sparse attribute leaves. When required triples are missing, target values can become unreachable by explicit traversal; structural methods may retrieve values from the wrong numerical attribute, while numerical solvers assuming directly attached values cannot access non-local evidence. We propose SEMAPHORE , a neuro-symbolic framework that reformulates numerical QA over KGs as a semantic detour problem. SEMAPHORE combines symbolic path planning with embedding-based geometric navigation and decoupled scoring that separates relational navigation from numerical attribute grounding. This design identifies plausible detours while preserving the metric semantics required for accurate numerical answers. On numerical QA benchmarks derived from FB15K-237 and YAGO15K, SEMAPHORE outperforms strong LLM and KG-augmented baselines, demonstrating the value of semantic detours for robust numerical knowledge access over KGs. Sparsity and cross-dataset transfer experiments show that this advantage persists under severe graph incompleteness and when target-specific Knowledge Graph Embedding (KGE) training is replaced with transferred schema embeddings. Code is available at https://github.com/orcies8147/SEMAPHORE.

papers.title: Causality-Guided Spurious Evidence Pruning with GFlowNet for Faithful Graph Retrieval
papers.abstract: Knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) increasingly relies on graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG). However, graph retrievers are trained under path-level weak supervision, which treats every triple on an answer-reaching path as equally informative. Retrieved subgraphs thus contain spurious triples that reach the answer without causally supporting it, leaving noise filtering to the reasoner. We propose Causality-Guided Spurious Evidence Pruning with GFlowNet (CaseFlow), which internalizes spurious-evidence pruning into the retriever by reformulating retrieval as a flow-guided pruning process. Repurposed from a candidate generator into a pruner, the GFlowNet removes spurious evidence while retaining answer-supporting causal structure. To make this pruning causally informed and tractable, a relation-conditioned disentanglement encoder supplies a causal-relevance proxy for the chunk-level pruning prior, and adaptive relation-coherent chunks bound the action space. CaseFlow outperforms strong GraphRAG retrievers on the WebQSP, CWQ, and MetaQA-3hop benchmarks, with the largest gains in complex multi-hop reasoning. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChoiPi2/CaseFlow

papers.title: Role-Specific Agentic RAG: Asymmetric Hybrid-Path Reasoning over Semi-structured Knowledge Bases
papers.abstract: Hybrid Question Answering (HQA) over semi-structured knowledge bases (SKBs) is vital for high-stakes domains like clinical precision medicine. However, HQA over SKBs is challenging because evidence is split across documents and relations, while answers must satisfy both semantic and structural constraints. Standard RAG pipelines retrieve evidence from textual or relational sources separately, failing to jointly capture the semantic conditions and relational constraints required by HQA over SKBs. Meanwhile, advanced agentic RAG systems that rely on computationally intensive models incur prohibitive inference latency and cost. To address these limitations, we introduce RSA-RAG , a R ole- S pecific A gentic RAG method with an asymmetric hybrid-path reasoning framework. We propose Role-Specific Asymmetric Collaboration for Hybrid-Path Reasoning, which assigns high-level roadmap planning and final answer generation to the large model, while lightweight role-specific agents handle frequent retrieval-control operations. Additionally, we introduce Strategy-Guided Candidate Navigation for Semi-Structured Retrieval, where compact agents perform strategy routing, constraint extraction, and hybrid navigation over an initial candidate set to retrieve textual and relational evidence around candidate targets. Furthermore, we implement Candidate-Support Evidence Structuring for Grounded Generation, which uses evidence verification to organize supported textual-relational evidence into structured grounding contexts for final generation. Extensive experiments show that RSA-RAG achieves strong retrieval performance on STARK, with an average MRR of 54.6% and competitive top-ranked performance across the three subsets. It further improves CRAG accuracy by 11.1% relative to Agentic RAG and reduces token consumption by up to 56.9% compared with implemented LLM-intensive baselines.

papers.title: Compact Representations of Geometric Bipartite Graphs via Weighted Biclique Covers
papers.abstract: Bipartite graphs are a fundamental representation for relational data arising in recommendation systems, market-basket analysis, social networks, and communication graphs. A key challenge in these settings is to store and transmit large bipartite graphs compactly while preserving exact structural and path information. We study biclique-based representations of bipartite graphs G =( V , U , E ), where the edge set is encoded using a collection of complete bipartite subgraphs. We focus on the Weighted Biclique Covering problem, which minimizes the total number of vertices used across all bicliques, and introduce a generalized variant that additionally penalizes the number of bicliques, capturing practical overheads in storage, transmission, and model complexity. While the weighted biclique covering problem is known to be NP-Complete, we show that the generalized variant is also NP-Complete. Despite this hardness, many real-world bipartite graphs admit low-dimensional geometric embeddings or can be well approximated by them. Leveraging this observation, we develop the first approximation algorithms with provable guarantees for the (generalized) weighted biclique covering problem on geometric bipartite graphs. Specifically, for δ-disk bipartite graphs in low-dimensional ℓ ∞ d spaces, we design a polynomial-time algorithm that achieves an O(log | U | · log d | V |)-approximation, combining ideas from greedy set cover, geometric range searching, and densest subgraph optimization. We also show how our algorithms extend to ℓ α d metrics for any α≥ 1. Finally, we evaluate our algorithms on real-world bipartite datasets and show that they efficiently compute significantly smaller biclique-based representations than natural baselines, while scaling to large graphs.

papers.title: Authenticated K-core Community Search in Dynamic Graphs in Hybrid-Storage Blockchains
papers.abstract: Graphs model complex relationships in domains such as social networks, bioinformatics, and the Web, where structures evolve continuously. Many studies focus on k-core community search for applications like recommendation and advertising. Due to frequent graph updates and the large scale of real-world graphs, data owners often outsource graph maintenance and execution to third parties. This raises concerns that third parties may forge query results intentionally or due to external attacks, making it essential to ensure the integrity of query results. Blockchain offers transparency and reliability for secure data storage, and hybrid-storage blockchains use off-chain storage with smart contracts for scalability. However, current authenticated query methods in hybrid-storage blockchains primarily focus on key-value data or other types of graph queries, which cannot be applied to authenticated community searches. This is the first study on the authenticated k-core community search in dynamic graphs. We propose a baseline scheme enabling clients to verify query integrity via verification objects (VO) and design a precomputation-based authenticated data structure, the Merkle Core Tree (MCTree), to enhance efficiency and reduce communication costs. Considering that both of the above solutions are based on Merkle hash trees (MHT), MHT-based updates require modifying paths from leaf to root upon each change, limiting update efficiency. To address this issue, we introduce HCoreGen, an HMAC-based algorithm that updates only affected tuples without precomputation, significantly improving update efficiency. The effectiveness and efficiency of authentication solutions are verified by the extensive experiment results on real large dynamic graphs.

papers.title: Rethinking Community Consistency in Heterogeneous Networks
affiliations: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.abstract: Community discovery in heterogeneous networks commonly assumes that graph topology provides semantically useful neighborhoods. In human-centered systems, however, structural proximity may be weakly aligned with latent cognitive similarity, causing graph propagation to introduce psychologically inconsistent information. We revisit community discovery from this perspective and propose CogPHGNN, a cognition-aware graph learning framework that integrates multi-view psychological representations, semantic graph construction, and gated propagation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that graph learning becomes effective only when graph topology is sufficiently aligned with latent semantic and psychological similarity. The results show that graph construction quality and selective propagation critically affect cognition-aware community consistency, while mismatched neighborhoods or propagation mechanisms may degrade representation quality. Across graph constructions, propagation mechanisms, and psychological theories, the results consistently highlight structure-cognition alignment as a key factor governing cognition-aware community discovery.

papers.title: Representation-Aware Modularity with a Distance-Calibrated Null Model
affiliations: Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Modularity is a standard objective for community detection, comparing observed intra-community connectivity with its null-model expectation. Modern node embeddings capture structural and semantic proximity beyond raw topology, but replacing adjacency with representation-induced affinity while retaining the classical degree-based null model makes the observed term geometry-dependent and the expected term geometry-agnostic. This creates a null-model mismatch: the objective may reward affinity already expected from representation proximity. This paper introduces RAM, a representation-aware modularity objective with a distance-calibrated null model. RAM preserves the observed-minus-expected principle by calibrating expected affinity with both degree heterogeneity and representation distance. We analyse its relation to classical modularity and develop divisive and multi-level greedy optimisers. Experiments on seven real-world datasets and synthetic scalability tests show that RAM improves over topology-only, direct embedding-clustering, and deep learning-based baselines, remains competitive under classical modularity while improving community quality on large graphs, and scales efficiently. Ablations confirm that both degree correction and distance calibration are essential.

papers.title: Beyond Locality: Multi-scale Structural Tokenization for Unsupervised Community Search
papers.abstract: Community Search (CS) aims to retrieve query-dependent cohesive subgraphs from networks, playing a crucial role in modern applications such as computing power networks and biological systems. Given the high cost of labeling, unsupervised CS has emerged as a scalable paradigm. However, existing approaches often suffer from restricted structural receptive fields and the limitation of static node representations, which fail to perceive the evolving community boundaries during expansion.To address these, this paper explores the potential of unsupervised CS by proposing the ComPass framework. We first design an incremental graph augmentation strategy to generate views with enriched community information. These views are then processed via a multi-scale structural tokenization mechanism, which transforms the graph into hierarchical sequences that bridge fine-grained topological associations with coarse-grained community contexts. By feeding these sequences into a Transformer-based encoder, ComPass effectively captures discriminative community representations without supervision. During online search, an iterative score refinement mechanism enables the co-evolution of community structure and node scoring, mitigating semantic drift.Extensive experiments illustrate the promising performance of ComPass as an exploratory step. Notably, ComPass achieves a competitive advantage over the strongest baseline, TransZero, with an average F1-score improvement of 15.23%. This exploration suggests that integrating incremental augmentation, multi-scale tokenization, and adaptive search offers a potentially effective direction for advancing unsupervised community search.

papers.title: When Does Structural Entropy Track Labels? Margins, Diagnostics, and Failure Modes in Graph Clustering
papers.abstract: Structural entropy (H 2 ) is often reported beside normalized mutual information (NMI) and the adjusted Rand index (ARI), inviting the assumption that a lower structural objective implies better agreement with external labels. However, these metrics need not agree: H 2 measures random-walk compression, whereas NMI and ARI measure agreement with an external partition. For a fixed graph, we show that if every partition that differs substantially from a reference labeling has an H 2 value at least γ greater than that labeling's H 2 value, then any partition whose H 2 value is at most ε<γ above the reference labeling's H 2 value must also be close to the reference labeling. We measure this closeness using variation of information (VI), a standard distance between partitions, and derive a corresponding lower bound on NMI. These VI and NMI guarantees require a positive H 2 margin. Theoretically, we derive exact, checkable gap criteria for specified merge/split perturbations in balanced stochastic block models and for specified contact-domain boundary shifts. These criteria characterize when H 2 tracks external labels under the specified perturbations. Empirically, a sampled perturbation diagnostic assesses whether a graph–label pair exhibits a positive margin. Across 11 synthetic and eight real benchmarks, the pooled Spearman correlation between H 2 and NMI is -0.83 and -0.60, respectively. We identify four failure modes associated with departures from this trend: near-binary strong homophily, free-K over-segmentation, elongated-community fragmentation, and hub mis-assignment. A multistart local search makes the diagnostic practical. A Hi-C case study illustrates the method on two chromosome-19 contact maps. Code, experiment configurations, and saved result summaries are available at https://github.com/SuuTTT/se-when-tracks-labels.

papers.title: Inductive Correlation Clustering with Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Correlation Clustering (CC) is a natural formulation of clustering in combinatorial optimization, which uses a graph representation of the input and does not require a pre-specified number of clusters. Given n objects and a pairwise similarity function, the goal is to cluster the objects so that similar objects are put in the same cluster and dissimilar objects are put in different clusters. Despite its versatility, existing CC algorithms suffer from significant scalability issues and are inherently transductive: i.e., the algorithm must be executed from scratch for any new problem instance. In this work, we bridge this gap by leveraging Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to solve Inductive Correlation Clustering, a novel generalization of the CC problem designed to handle unseen graph instances. By learning to exploit common structural patterns and node features during training, our framework generalizes to new graphs drawn from the same distribution with minimal computational overhead with respect to standard algorithms. We demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of our approach through extensive experiments. Our framework not only excels in the inductive setting, e.g., lowering the inference time up to 5 order of magnitude, while maintaining an approximation ratio within 10% of the best baseline solution, but also achieves competitive results on standard (transductive) CC benchmarks. Finally, we showcase a practical application of our framework as a learnable pooling mechanism for graph classification. Our results indicate that our method serves as an efficient pooling layer, enhancing the ability of GNNs to capture hierarchical structural information in networks.

papers.title: ExplainCC: Explaining Correlated Clusters by Node Labels
papers.abstract: An increasingly important requirement for clustering algorithms is that decisions and outcomes need to be clearly understandable for human users. We address this requirement for the Correlation Clustering (CC) problem, in case the objects to be clustered are accompanied by labels. In CC one seeks to partition a set of objects into clusters based on pairwise similarity and dissimilarity information. Our proposed model only considers clusters that can be explained by a label tree, which is essentially a decision tree that partitions the objects according to labels. The goal is to find an explainable partition of the data that minimizes the CC objective function. We formalize this problem from a theoretical viewpoint, and prove several hardness of approximation results, also when constraining the size of the tree. Our proposed greedy method finds locally optimal splits, and works recursively in a top-down approach. To efficiently compute the best split, we carefully maintain certain counters. An experimental evaluation demonstrates its effectiveness. The proposed algorithm processes graphs with over million edges in a few minutes, can find the ground truth in synthetic data, and is able to produce interpretable clusters in real world networks.

papers.title: Towards Comprehensible Recommendation with Large Language Model Fine-tuning
papers.abstract: Recommender systems have become increasingly ubiquitous in daily life. While traditional recommendation approaches primarily rely on ID-based representations or item-side content features, they often fall short in capturing the underlying semantics aligned with user preferences (e.g., recommendation reasons for items), leading to a semantic-collaborative gap. Recently emerged LLM-based feature extraction approaches also face a key challenge: how to ensure that LLMs possess recommendation-aligned reasoning capabilities and can generate accurate, personalized reasons to mitigate the semantic-collaborative gap. To address these issues, we propose a novel Content Understanding from a Collaborative Perspective framework (CURec), which generates collaborative-aligned content features for more comprehensive recommendations. CURec first adapts the LLM with recommendation objectives through post-training, equipping it with instruction-following and chain-of-thought reasoning capabilities. Next, we use the LLM-generated features to train the recommender model. Then, we treat the user–item prediction scores produced by the trained recommender model as reward signals to guide RL-based refinement of the LLM, thereby improving the quality of generated reasons and pattern. The corrected reasons are directly integrated into the recommender model to enhance comprehensibility and recommendation performance. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of CURec over existing methods.

papers.title: SelfDR: Self-Distillation from Reasoning for LLM-Based Recommendation
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently emerged as powerful backbones for recommendation. To better elicit their capabilities, reasoning has been widely incorporated to help LLMs interpret rich textual signals and improve recommendation accuracy. However, explicitly generating intermediate reasoning traces often incurs substantial computational costs, which limits practical deployment in real-world recommender systems. To address this challenge, we propose SelfDR , a Self - D istillation from R easoning framework for LLM-based Recommendation. SelfDR distills an LLM's own reasoning-enhanced predictions to produce recommendations directly, improving recommendation effectiveness while maintaining inference efficiency. All components in the framework are built on the same base LLM, without relying on any external models. Specifically, the teacher recommender is constructed by training a reasoner with downstream performance as the reward, enabling it to generate targeted rationales that are later incorporated into the teacher’s input. A student recommender for direct recommendation, with the same underlying model, then learns from the teacher through self-distillation with a dynamic weighting strategy. Extensive experiments on three public datasets validate the effectiveness, rationality, and efficiency of SelfDR. Codes are available at https://github.com/JiangDeccc/SelfDistillation.

papers.title: SCoRD: Semantic-Assisted Continual Retriever-Reranker Distillation for LLM-Based Recommendation
papers.abstract: Recommendation systems increasingly adopt a two-stage pipeline, where an ID-based retriever retrieves candidates and an LLM-based reranker refines their rankings. To improve retrieval quality, reranker-to-retriever distillation is commonly used to transfer the reranker’s knowledge to the retriever. For practical deployment, however, this pipeline must continually adapt to evolving interests and incoming interactions. A naive solution is to repeatedly update the LLM reranker and distill its latest knowledge, but this incurs prohibitive costs. Updating the retriever alone is cheaper, but its limited capacity makes adaptation from sparse data difficult. We propose SCoRD, a continual knowledge distillation framework for LLM-based reranking pipelines under a non-stationary data stream. SCoRD introduces a semantic reasoning assistant that distills the LLM’s ability to infer underlying user intents into reusable intent-level guidance. It selectively distills reranker knowledge to the retriever on low-confidence sequences, guides retriever-only updates without repeated LLM inference, and feeds retriever-derived representations and intent-drift signals back to the reranker. Experiments on real-world datasets show that SCoRD enables effective and efficient retriever-reranker co-adaptation.

papers.title: SCAU-REC: Subspace-Constrained Adapter Updates for LLM-Based Recommendations
affiliations: The Education University of Hong Kong
papers.abstract: LLM-based recommender systems increasingly adapt frozen backbones with parameter-efficient adapters as user-item interactions arrive. However, continual updates can overfit transient feedback, amplify noise, and degrade long-term preferences. We therefore propose SCAU-Rec , a drift-conditioned adapter-control framework that uses an evolving reference coreset to detect preference shifts and trigger updates only when warranted. When triggered, SCAU-Rec modulates risk-aware alignment between consecutive model states and projects adapter gradients away from an online low-rank stability subspace, reducing interference with retained preferences. We provide theoretical analyses of interference control, bounded predictive shift, and robustness to approximate stability subspaces. Across multiple benchmarks, SCAU-Rec improves recommendation utility, retention, update efficiency, and robustness over representative continual adaptation and LLM-based recommendation baselines.

papers.title: TRACER: Balancing Stability-Plasticity-Cognitivity Trilemma for LLM Enhanced Continual Recommendation
affiliations: Pohang University of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Continual recommendation aims to capture evolving user interests from streaming data but struggles with sparsity. LLM enhancers mitigate this with semantic knowledge, but naive integration creates a new conflict. We identify this as the Stability-Plasticity-Cognitivity (SPC) Trilemma , where generalized LLM semantic priors (Cognitivity) conflict with retaining personalized historical preferences (Stability) and adapting to individual interest shifts (Plasticity). To address this, we propose T rilemma- R esponsive A daptive C ontinual E nhancement for R ecommendation ( TRACER ). TRACER synergistically combines three specialized modules, each targeting stability, plasticity, or cognitivity, while preventing any single lemma from dominating. This holistic design enables semantic knowledge to support history retention and adaptation to evolving interests without disrupting continual learning. Across five real-world datasets, TRACER effectively harmonizes the SPC trilemma and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by up to 14.38%. Our code is available at https://github.com/woo-joo/TRACER_CIKM26.

papers.title: PSCRec: Preference-Conditioned Semantic Calibration for LLM-Enhanced Graph Recommendation
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a dominant paradigm in recommender systems by modeling collaborative signals over user--item interaction graphs. Recent LLM-enhanced recommenders seek to complement such structural signals with semantic knowledge from Large Language Models (LLMs). However, most existing methods implicitly follow a direct semantic fusion paradigm, where LLM-derived representations are treated as reliable semantic features and directly fused with collaborative representations. We argue that this paradigm is incomplete: LLM semantics are informative, but not directly trustworthy for recommendation. Through controlled diagnostic analyses, we identify two failure modes of raw LLM semantics: Unreliable Semantic Signals, where representations are sensitive to task-irrelevant textual noise, and Semantic--Behavioral Misalignment, where semantic proximity does not necessarily imply behavioral relevance. To address these issues, we propose PSCRec, a model-agnostic framework for preference-conditioned semantic calibration in LLM-enhanced graph recommendation. PSCRec progressively transforms noisy LLM-derived priors into behavior-consistent semantic evidence by structuring semantic profiles, grounding them in dynamic user preferences, filtering unreliable semantic associations, purifying residual semantic redundancy, and aligning calibrated semantic representations with collaborative signals. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets show that PSCRec consistently improves multiple graph-based backbones and outperforms representative LLM-enhanced recommendation methods. Further ablation, robustness, semantic--behavioral calibration, and efficiency analyses demonstrate the effectiveness and practical feasibility of the proposed calibration framework.

papers.title: Scoring-to-Ranking: A Language Model-Guided Graph Framework for Multi-Criteria Preference Ranking
papers.abstract: Multi-criteria ratings provide user feedback on multiple aspects of an item, offering richer preference signals than a single overall rating. Early work mainly focused on predicting criterion or overall ratings, whereas practical scenarios require ranking items according to their overall utility inferred from sparse and heterogeneous criterion-level evidence, which constitutes the core problem of multi-criteria recommendation (MCR). This ranking-oriented formulation of MCR gives rise to two key challenges: learning reliable criterion dependencies under sparse interactions, and bridging the mismatch between semantic preference signals and collaboratively learned representations. To address these issues, we propose S2R-LMG, a scoring-to-ranking framework that jointly learns from semantic and collaborative views. Specifically, we construct a user–item–criterion tripartite graph to model criterion dependencies in the collaborative view, while using large language models (LLMs) to transform sparse multi-criteria feedback into criterion-aware contextual preference priors for users and items. These priors are then projected into the ranking space and coupled with collaborative representations via alignment and retrieval-based distillation, so that semantic guidance directly contributes to preference ranking. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets show that S2R-LMG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art models on top-N ranking, achieving an average improvement of 4.84% across all datasets and evaluation metrics over the strongest baseline. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/nunu1995/S2R-LMG.

papers.title: The Recall Ceiling of LLM Recommendation Reranking
affiliations: University of Southern California,Viterbi School of Engineering
papers.abstract: Some LLM-based recommendation rerankers are evaluated under an oracle protocol that guarantees the ground-truth item is present in the scored set, either by injecting it into the candidate list or by scoring it against sampled negatives. We show that this protocol overestimates realistic performance by 92-95% in NDCG@10 across three primary Amazon datasets, so oracle results do not transfer to deployment. The root cause is a recall ceiling: realistic retrieval covers only 2-19% of relevant items at K=100 across eight datasets in three domains (Amazon products, MovieLens movies, MIND news), placing a deterministic upper bound on any closed-candidate reranker's top-k NDCG (Theorem 1, E[NDCG@k] <= Recall@|W_pi| under LOO evaluation, where W_pi is the reranker's own candidate window). Under realistic retrieval, every optimisation strategy we tested fails to produce a statistically significant improvement over the CF baseline on our primary Amazon datasets: prompt engineering, model scaling across a 168x parameter range, sequential models, three supervised neural rerankers (LambdaMART, RankNet, MLP) under a disjoint train/eval user split, a LoRA-fine-tuned LLaMA-3.2-3B reranker, and a hybrid CF+BM25+Dense retrieval with reciprocal-rank fusion. Adding text-aware retrieval raises recall on Beauty but does not lift end-to-end NDCG. Giving the LLM the upstream CF ranks and scores directly--the fairest setting we can construct--narrows but does not close the gap to CF, and does so by making the LLM adhere more closely to the CF order rather than by adding information; an LLM+CF fusion tuned on the evaluation users themselves recovers CF's performance and no more. We propose the Recall-Aware Evaluation Protocol (RAEP) as a diagnostic: classify the regime by retrieval recall, then evaluate reranking only where the ceiling permits differentiation. In the retrieval regimes we can measure (Recall@100 of 2-19%), the path to effective LLM recommendation runs through retrieval improvement rather than reranker sophistication; we do not claim this ordering holds at the higher recall, richer feature sets, and online feedback available to production systems.

papers.title: Sliding-Window Reordering with Overlap Averaging: A Simple Time-Domain Augmentation for Multivariate Forecasting
papers.abstract: Augmentation has become a central technique for improving deep forecasting models, but classification-style transformations tend to break the coherence between the look-back window and its continuous future target. We describe a simple procedure that unfolds the joint input-target sequence into overlapping sliding windows, randomly reorders a controlled fraction of them-prioritized by a lightweight variance criterion-and reconstructs the sequence by averaging across the overlaps, producing synthetic samples with controlled variation while limiting temporal distortion. The procedure is model-agnostic, introduces only three interpretable hyperparameters, and achieves strong improvements over a comprehensive set of competing augmentations across nine long-term forecasting benchmarks with five backbone families (TSMixer, DLinear, PatchTST, TiDE, LightTS) and four short-term traffic benchmarks with PatchTST. Component-wise ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity studies, distributional-alignment diagnostics, probabilistic forecasting evaluation, and a transfer experiment to univariate and multivariate time series classification clarify the contribution of each design choice.

papers.title: SeleRT: Selective Retrieval of LLM Representations for Long-term Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Recent studies have explored the use of pretrained large language model (LLM) representations for long-term time series forecasting.While direct LLM-based forecasting methods adapt time series into LLM-compatible inputs, recent multimodal approaches further use LLM representations as auxiliary semantic representations and introduce interaction mechanisms between time series and language branches. However, existing methods mainly focus on aligning or combining these representations, leaving underexplored how LLM representations should be selectively utilized for different forecasting inputs. In particular, not all LLM layers are equally informative for time series forecasting, and different temporal regions may require different predictive cues from LLM representations. To address these challenges, we propose SeleRT (Selective Retrieval of LLM Representations for Long-term Time Series Forecasting), a multimodal forecasting framework designed to selectively utilize LLM representations for time series prediction. SeleRT consists of two key components: Statistics-Aware Dynamic Layer Fusion (SADLF), which dynamically generates layer weights from input time series statistics, and Patch-Wise Learnable Query Retrieval (PLQR), which enables patch-grounded queries to retrieve information from the fused LLM representation. We evaluate SeleRT on eight standard long-term forecasting benchmarks under full-shot and few-shot protocols. Experimental results show that SeleRT achieves state-of-the-art overall performance, with particularly strong gains in the few-shot setting. Ablation and visualization analyses further support the effectiveness of input-adaptive layer fusion and patch-wise selective retrieval.

papers.title: Recovering Lost Details: Multi-Scale Frequency Compensation for Long-Term Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Long-term time series forecasting has made significant progress by leveraging multi-scale information to capture hierarchical temporal patterns and model long-range dependencies. However, temporal downsampling in existing multi-scale methods inevitably smooths detailed temporal fluctuations, and this information loss is further aggravated by their emphasis on dominant trends across scales, resulting in insufficiently expressive representations. To address this, we propose a Multi-Scale Wavelet Mixing (MWMixer) model, which incorporates a Bidirectional Frequency-Bands Mixing strategy to recover lost temporal details across scales, enabling complementary cross-scale information interactions. Then, a Dynamic Scale-Adaptive Fusion module learns time-varying weights for each scale to fuse multi-scale forecasts into the final prediction, enhancing the flexibility of multi-scale aggregation. In addition, a cross-scale consistency loss aligns each coarse-scale prediction with the interval-averaged fine-scale outputs, while a multi-scale supervision loss enforces prediction accuracy at each scale, promoting consistent learning across scales. Extensive experiments on seven real-world datasets demonstrate that MWMixer achieves competitive performance in long-term forecasting.

papers.title: FAME: Frequency-Enhanced Pre-trained Model for Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: General time series forecasting models pre-trained on extensive datasets have recently gained significant attention for their strong domain generalization capabilities. Nevertheless, existing time series pre-trained models confront two critical challenges. First, previous approaches are insufficient in capturing the intricate relationships among variables from a global perspective. Second, the temporal relationships in time series are explored using a fixed patch size from a single frequency perspective that discards important information hidden in the data. To address these challenges, we propose a frequency-enhanced pre-trained model (FAME) for multivariate time series forecasting, which captures the temporal and variable relationships separately from a frequency perspective. In the temporal relation learning module, we design a multi-expert architecture that automatically determines the size of patches for time series and process them using the customized models based on the determined patch size. In the variable relation learning module, we model the variable dependencies from a global perspective in the frequency domain and propose to employ a frequency characteristic prompt which enhance the extraction of relationships between more correlated variables. Finally, the outputs of the two modules are aggregated to generate the final prediction. We pre-train FAME on the Time-300B datasets and extensive experiments on public real datasets demonstrate that our framework achieves superior performance. Our code is published for further research.

papers.title: Time Series Forecasting via Reasoning: A Slow-Thinking Approach with Reinforcement Fine-Tuned LLMs
affiliations: State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: To advance time series forecasting, a wide range of methods—from statistical techniques to deep learning architectures—have been proposed to improve prediction accuracy; however, most still follow a fast thinking paradigm that maps historical patterns to future values with limited explicit reasoning or interpretable intermediate steps, undermining adaptability to evolving temporal dynamics. Although slow-thinking LLMs exhibit strong multi-step reasoning, prompt-only solutions are constrained by cost, privacy, and insufficient domain alignment, motivating the training of LLMs to acquire slow thinking time-series reasoning skills. In this paper, we propose Time-R1, a reinforcement fine-tuning framework designed to enhance the multi-step reasoning ability of LLMs for time series forecasting. Training starts with supervised fine-tuning for warm-up adaptation, followed by reinforcement learning that improves the model’s generalization ability via reward-driven reasoning optimization. Specifically, we introduce a fine-grained multi-objective reward to provide training signals tailored to time series forecasting, and GRIP (group-based relative importance for policy optimization) to leverage non-uniform sampling for encouraging the exploration of effective reasoning paths. Experiments show that Time-R1 achieves competitive forecasting performance across diverse datasets (Code is at https://github.com/ustc-time-series/Time-R1).

papers.title: Beyond Noisy Temporal Contexts: Selective Event-Level Revision for Multimodal Time Series Forecasting
affiliations: Xinjiang Technical Institute of Physics & Chemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.abstract: Textual context can enhance time series forecasting when future dynamics are shaped by external events. In realistic forecasting pipelines, however, such context is typically retrieved rather than synchronously observed. Retrieved text is often sparse, temporally misaligned, and entangled with stale or non-predictive background information, making conventional multimodal fusion prone to negative transfer. We argue that the central challenge in multimodal forecasting is not to design increasingly sophisticated fusion mechanisms, but to determine when external textual context should revise a numerical forecast.To address this challenge, we propose Temporal Contextual Event Fusion (TCEF), an asymmetric selective revision framework that allows external textual context to influence numerical forecasts only when supported by relevant event evidence. TCEF first distills raw retrieved text into discrete timestamped events and estimates their horizon-specific relevance by jointly modeling event semantics, temporal recency, and the current state of the target series. Rather than treating text as an unconstrained forecasting signal, TCEF employs a prior-anchored revision branch to generate bounded residual corrections over a reliable numerical baseline. A reliability-guided trust gate then adaptively modulates textual influence across forecasting horizons, attenuating stale, weakly aligned, or uninformative signals while preserving the predictive structure of the temporal backbone.Experiments across nine Time-MMD domains and six temporal forecasting backbones show that TCEF consistently outperforms numeric-only forecasting and performs strongly against recent multimodal baselines. Further analysis shows that these gains are primarily driven by selective event-level revision rather than by simply incorporating more textual context.

papers.title: Koopman-Guided Diffusion for Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: While diffusion models have achieved impressive success in probabilistic time series forecasting, directly applying conventional noise injection may disrupt the continuity inherent in temporal data. Fundamentally, such additive Gaussian perturbations may sever the underlying dynamic continuity, generating intermediate states that are misaligned with the system's inherent evolution and making the recovery of valid sequential evolution exceptionally difficult. To resolve this misalignment, we introduce Koopman-Guided Diffusion (KoopDiff), a novel framework that restricts the generative process within an evolution-aligned subspace. Grounded in Koopman operator theory, our method lifts the diffusion dynamics into a coherent subspace where complex temporal dependencies are approximately linearized. Specifically, we establish this dynamically stable subspace by optimizing a Dynamical Subspace Alignment (DSA) objective, with analytical Koopman predictions serving as a Dynamical Prior to guide generative trajectories. Both theoretical analysis and a case study demonstrate that this formulation aligns the propagated noise with the dominant transition directions of the system, effectively maintaining dynamic continuity throughout the generative process. Extensive experiments on eight datasets show that KoopDiff achieves state-of-the-art forecasting performance while substantially enhancing inference efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/khwhk/KoopDiff.

papers.title: EvoGNN: Mutually Evolving Graph Neural Network for Time Series Forecasting with Variable Missing
papers.abstract: Time series forecasting with variable missing is a pervasive yet challenging real-world problem. Missing values from sensor malfunctions or communication disruptions severely degrade the performance of conventional models designed for complete data, limiting their practical utility. To tackle the dual challenge of simultaneous imputation and forecasting, we propose EvoGNN, a novel Mutually Evolving Graph Neural Network, centered on a Node-Edge Co-Evolution mechanism that moves beyond merely capturing time-varying dynamics. Its core innovation lies in establishing a closed-loop, iterative refinement process where adjacency relations (edge) and node representations dynamically and mutually enhance each other. This is realized through two synergistic modules: an Edge-Driven State Refinement (ESR) module, which fuses static prior knowledge with a dynamically learned graph to update node states, and a Node-Driven Adjacency Evolution (NAE) module, which evolves the graph adjacency by reasoning over refined node increments and global temporal contexts. A Recurrent Equilibrium Gate (REG) is further introduced to regulate the evolution dynamics, ensuring stable and convergent learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EvoGNN consistently outperforms SOTA baselines across various missing scenarios. We theoretically demonstrate the convergence, effectiveness and efficiency of the co-evolutionary process, providing analytical insight into reliability and scalability.

papers.title: BRAD: Enhancing Code summarization with Bytecode Retrieval-Augmented Deliberation model
papers.abstract: Comments and summaries play a critical role in program comprehension. However, high-quality summaries are often missing in large codebases. Existing code summarization methods improve linguistic fluency but still fall short in capturing program execution semantics. Furthermore, source-level retrieval methods struggle to identify code examples that are syntactically different but functionally relevant. To address these limitations, we propose BRAD (Bytecode Retrieval-Augmented Deliberation), a novel retrieval-augmented deliberation model for code summarization that integrates bytecode-level semantics with multi-pass deliberation. Specifically, BRAD (1) encodes bytecode control-flow graphs (CFG) with a Graph Attention Network (GAT) to preserve control flow semantics, and (2) retrieves exemplar drafts in the bytecode text space to capture execution-oriented functional cues. These are then fused with textual encodings in a deliberative refinement process to generate the final summary. We evaluate BRAD on a public Java dataset, and the results show that compared with the strong baselines, BRAD increases BLEU-1 by 18.7%, BLEU-2 by 16.2%, BLEU-3 by 8.5%, BLEU-4 by 2.8%, ROUGE-L by 13.4%, BERTScore-F1 by 6.3%, and CIDEr by 10.0%.

papers.title: CARE: When Not to Retrieve—Conflict-Aware Empathetic Dialogue via Intent-Gated Retrieval and Latent Critique
affiliations: Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region Information Center
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can undermine empathetic dialogue when retrieved content is tonally or emotionally misaligned with the user's expressed state: standard models forward the retrieved advice mechanically even when it is factually correct, eroding the supportive rapport the conversation calls for—a failure mode we term knowledge intrusion. We propose CARE (Conflict-Aware Reasoning for Empathy), which reframes retrieval-augmented generation as a decision to withhold: rather than treating retrieved documents as mandatory inputs to the generator, CARE introduces an explicit rejection action and learns when to take it. CARE cascades three mechanisms: Intent-Gated Retrieval, a probabilistic gate that suppresses retrieval when the user only needs emotional validation; Latent Critique, an explicit chain-of-thought step that decides whether to use or withhold the retrieved document on tonal and emotional grounds; and Conflict-Aware DPO, a preference objective trained on teacher-distilled robust/compliant response pairs to sharpen the rejection decision. At 50% injected noise, CARE improves Gating F1 over Standard RAG by up to 33.1 points, achieves a Context Rejection Score (CRS) above 70, and preserves generation quality. Our code is available at https://github.com/Zhizitan76/CARE-CIKM2026.

papers.title: GraFine: Retrieval-Time Refinement for Efficient Graph RAG over Corpus Graphs
papers.abstract: Graph RAG on corpus graphs enhances retrieval by leveraging intermediate node content as contextual clues to uncover unretrieved oracle nodes. However, existing methods suffer from two critical blind spots, namely semantically blind graph expansion and topology blind pruning, or else rely on prohibitively slow retrieval and generation interleaving. To address this, we formalize these limitations through an operational taxonomy and propose a retriever design that couples semantics- aware adding with graph- aware pruning under efficiency constraints. We instantiate this design as GraFine , which alternates between two refinement stages: Semantic Proximity eXpansion (SPX) for semantics-aware node addition, and a Graph Smoothing Reranker (GSR) for graph-aware pruning. Experiments on reference networks and text-rich knowledge graphs show that GraFine improves retrieval accuracy and generation quality while maintaining time-efficiency. Furthermore, we introduce Topological Recall (TR), a metric that quantifies the topological proximity between retrieved and oracle nodes. Our analysis using TR confirms that GraFine more effectively steers refinement toward undiscovered oracle nodes by leveraging intermediate contextual clues. Our code is available at this link: github.com/asmath472/GraFine (https://github.com/asmath472/GraFine).

papers.title: GraphLoom: Reliability-Calibrated Graph Evidence Routing for Multimodal KG-RAG
papers.abstract: Multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems often rely on long unstructured contexts or aggressively expanded evidence graphs, which can introduce noisy evidence, weaken multi-hop reasoning, and increase unsupported generation. We present GraphLoom , a reliability-calibrated multimodal knowledge-graph RAG framework for compact and faithful evidence routing. Given a question and its associated multimodal input, GraphLoom constructs an instance-level multimodal knowledge graph from grounded scene descriptions, extracted relational triples, and external commonsense knowledge. Instead of injecting all retrieved evidence into the generator, GraphLoom performs reliability-aware subgraph retrieval with bounded expansion and selectively routes high-utility evidence through hierarchical graph memory slots and joint graph–sequence attention in a frozen language model. To improve robustness in complex reasoning settings, GraphLoom further combines interleaved retrieval with budgeted corrective retrieval, enabling adaptive multi-hop evidence refinement under noisy retrieval conditions. We evaluate GraphLoom on ScienceQA , MultiModalQA , and OK-VQA , including large distractor evidence pools that approximate noisy external knowledge retrieval. Experimental results show consistent gains in answer quality and evidence faithfulness over strong multimodal RAG, graph-retrieval, and open-source vision–language baselines, with improved retrieval quality on MultiModalQA and stable performance under noisy evidence pools. Additional analyses using MiniCheck-based verification, human evaluation, and latency profiling show that reliability-calibrated graph evidence routing provides an effective alternative to long-context multimodal evidence injection.

papers.title: GeoRisk-RAG: A Hierarchy-Aware Risk Framework for Improving RAG Reliability through Selective Answering
papers.abstract: Current work on improving reliability in large language model (LLM)- generated answers has primarily leveraged Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), knowledge-graph augmentation, and reinforcement learning. While these methods are adept at enhancing and measuring reliability through semantic similarity and faithfulness, they often struggle to distinguish semantic similarity from geographic validity. This is especially critical in natural hazard management domains where geographic granularity (i.e., town vs. city vs. state) is significant for decision-making, as responses valid in one municipality may not transfer to another. In such domains, a confidently wrong answer carries greater risk than abstaining. We present GeoRisk-RAG, a novel hierarchy-aware framework that addresses this geographic-validity gap through selective answering. This framework explicitly estimates geographic applicability using a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)-based distance for context retrieval before response generation. Experiments on a novel held-out wildfire-related question-answering (QA) dataset show that GeoRisk-RAG significantly reduces false confidence rates for location-dependent questions, lowering the rate to 0.009 compared with 0.090 for standard semantic similarity and reranking baselines, while consistently achieving higher human preference alignment. This work provides a more comprehensive assessment of end-to-end RAG pipelines by integrating geographic validity and selective-answering behavior for safer decision-making in geospatial domains.

papers.title: Predicting the Benefit of Retrieval Augmentation in Open-Domain Question Answering
papers.abstract: While retrieval-augmented generation has become a common approach for enhancing question answering systems, retrieval is not universally advantageous. We study the problem of predicting whether incorporating external retrieved information is likely to improve response quality for a given question. To this end, we evaluate a range of prediction methods that are based on retrieval signals, answer characteristics, and semantic consistency between generated responses and retrieved passages. We further devise a predictor that probes the LLM's internal state. Its prediction performance significantly narrows the performance gap between post-generation methods which are computationally demanding and pre-generation (post-retrieval) methods. We use the prediction methods to devise a selective retrieval framework that dynamically chooses between retrieval and non-retrieval generation modes per question. Experimental results demonstrate that selectively applying retrieval augmentation yields answer quality that transcends that of using retrieval for all queries.

papers.title: LLM-Specific Utility for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
affiliations: State Key Laboratory of AI Safety
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is typically optimized for topical relevance, yet its success ultimately depends on whether retrieved passages are useful for a large language model (LLM) to generate correct and complete answers. We argue that such utility is often LLM-specific rather than universal, due to differences in models’ knowledge, reasoning, and ability to leverage evidence. We formalize LLM-specific utility as the performance improvement of a target LLM when a passage is provided, compared to answering without evidence. To systematically study LLM-specific utility, we construct a benchmark of LLM-specific gold utilitarian passages for four LLMs (Qwen3-8B/14B/32B and Llama 3.1-8B) on six QA datasets (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MS MARCO-FQA, HotpotQA, FEVER and 2WikiQA). Our analysis shows that utilitarian passages are model-dependent and non-transferable: each LLM performs best with its own utilitarian evidence, while evidence optimized for other LLMs is consistently suboptimal. Human-annotated evidence remains a strong general baseline but does not fully match individual LLM utility needs. We further introduce the LLM-specific utility judgment task and construct the corresponding benchmark, i.e., SpecUBench (LLM-Specific Utility Benchmark). Experiments show that existing utility-aware selection and scoring methods largely capture model-agnostic usefulness and struggle to reliably estimate LLM-specific utility. Overall, our findings highlight the limitations of current utility-aware retrieval and motivate generator-tailored evidence selection for improving RAG.

papers.title: State-Conditioned Evidence Coalition Selection for Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Question Answering
papers.abstract: Multi-hop retrieval-augmented question answering depends on compact evidence sets whose members complement one another rather than repeat already covered facts. In evidence selection over a candidate pool, prevailing relevance-based selectors score each candidate mainly as a standalone match to the question, which obscures its marginal role under the evidence already selected. A candidate that appears weak in isolation may complete missing support after another unit establishes a bridge, while a highly relevant candidate may become redundant once its fact has been covered. This paper introduces Marginal Evidence Coalition Selection (MECS), a state-conditioned evidence selector that treats the partially selected evidence set as a coalition and estimates the marginal value of adding each remaining candidate. MECS derives pairwise preferences from public supporting-fact annotations over partial evidence states, and its typed scoring channels align candidate value with support addability, bridge continuity, and coalition consistency. This formulation permits candidate value to vary across evidence states, promoting candidates that complete uncovered support while suppressing repeated or incompatible evidence. Evaluated as an evidence selector over shared candidate pools, MECS improves support recovery and downstream answer accuracy on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue with frozen readers. Mechanism and robustness diagnostics further support the role of state-conditioned marginal selection in recovering complementary evidence for multi-hop QA.

papers.title: End-to-End Delayed Matching Learning for Micro-View Order Dispatching in Ride-Hailing
papers.abstract: Micro-view order dispatching (MICOD) is a critical task in ride-hailing platforms, aiming to optimize driver--order matching within limited spatiotemporal contexts. Prior works predominantly employ Reinforcement Learning (RL) to learn delayed matching policies. However, RL-based approaches often suffer from sample inefficiency and instability due to the need for extensive trial-and-error exploration. Furthermore, the combinatorial nature of dispatching typically breaks differentiability, preventing end-to-end alignment between prediction models and optimization objectives. In this paper, we propose DML, an End-to-End Delayed Matching Learning framework. Unlike RL, DML formulates order dispatching as a learning-from-expert problem inspired by imitation learning. By leveraging the insight that a global offline optimal matching (OPT) can be computed from historical data, DML constructs an expert in hindsight and avoids the need for online exploration. To effectively clone this expert behavior while enabling end-to-end training, we address two key challenges: expert decomposition and combinatorial differentiability. First, we construct a Delay-Augmented Bipartite Graph (DABG) and theoretically prove that the global OPT can be equivalently decomposed into local sequential learning targets. Second, we incorporate a differentiable optimization layer based on the Sinkhorn--Knopp (SK) algorithm and introduce a Batch-SK (B-SK) implementation to efficiently handle variable-sized graphs in parallel. Experiments on a real-world dataset collected from Didi Chuxing demonstrate that DML significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both matching quality and training efficiency.

papers.title: Approximate Pareto Frontiers for Submodular Utility and Cost Tradeoffs
papers.abstract: In many data-mining applications, including recommender systems, influence maximization, and team formation, the goal is to pick a subset of elements (e.g., items, nodes in a network, experts to perform a task) to maximize a monotone submodular utility function while simultaneously minimizing a cost function. Classical formulations model this tradeoff via cardinality or knapsack constraints, or by combining utility and cost into a single weighted objective. However, such approaches require committing to a specific tradeoff in advance and return only a single solution, offering limited insight into the space of viable utility–cost tradeoffs. In this paper, we depart from the single-solution paradigm and examine the problem of computing representative sets of high-quality solutions that expose different tradeoffs between submodular utility and cost. For this, we introduce (α 1 ,α 2 )-approximate Pareto frontiers that provably approximate the achievable tradeoffs between submodular utility and cost. Specifically, we formalize the Pareto–⟨ f,c ⟩ problem and develop efficient algorithms for multiple instantiations arising from different combinations of submodular utility f and cost functions c. % Since the (α 1 ,α 2 )-approximate Pareto % frontier can often have a large number of solutions, We also provide an adaptive search algorithm that computes only a small subset of points that collectively summarize the entire Pareto frontier. Our results offer a principled and practical framework for understanding and exploiting utility–cost tradeoffs in submodular optimization. Experiments on datasets from diverse application domains demonstrate that our algorithms efficiently compute approximate Pareto frontiers in practice.

papers.title: BASAR: Bidirectional Sparse-Attentive Autoregressive Learning for Dynamic Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Task Assignment
papers.abstract: Dynamic heterogeneous task assignment is a fundamental problem in graph-based decision systems, where a scheduler must allocate continuously arriving tasks to multiple agents with diverse capabilities under coalition feasibility, deadlines, and resource constraints. Existing optimization-based methods often incur high replanning costs, while learning-based solvers usually struggle with weak task-agent coupling, sparse delayed rewards, and limited generalization under dynamic arrivals and coalition requirements. This paper presents BASAR, an end-to-end autoregressive framework for dynamic heterogeneous multi-agent task assignment on graphs. BASAR combines bidirectional task-agent cross-domain fusion, sparse-attentive state refinement, and feasible-action masked pointer decoding to generate online assignments over revealed task nodes and agent-specific fallback actions. To improve learning in collaborative scheduling, BASAR introduces an cooperative reward that evaluates the revealed task set and redistributes team utility through marginal service credits. Experiments on dynamic task assignment benchmarks show that BASAR achieves strong deadline-aware performance under fixed task workloads and high task throughput under fixed makespan execution, while reducing total planning time by up to 98.7% compared with the optimization-based baseline. Our code is available at https://github.com/wuwenjianw/BASAR.

papers.title: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach for Dynamic Route Optimization of Customized Shuttle Bus Services
papers.abstract: Real-time routing for customized shuttle buses presents a complex multi-agent control problem characterized by stochastic demands and strict topological constraints. However, efficient dispatching is frequently hindered by coarse-grained station representations, uncoordinated agent interactions, and the neglect of discrete operational constraints. To address these issues, HGA-PAC is presented as an event-driven framework where decisions are triggered upon vehicle arrival at stations. The framework operates through three synergistic components: a Heterogeneous Graph Attention encoder for fine-grained spatiotemporal dynamics, an attention-based communication module to mitigate resource competition, and a phaseaware decoder to ensure physical feasibility via dynamic masking. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly reduces operational costs and achieves a superior trade-off between service rate and travel efficiency compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

papers.title: Action-Aligned Frozen Credit: Storing Selected Feedback for Short-Session Contextual Bandits
papers.abstract: Short-session personalization and contextual recommendation often must improve later decisions from only a few selected-feedback observations. Standard online evaluation makes this improvement hard to interpret, because post-prefix reward may reflect both credit already stored from early actions and new reward information acquired while evaluation continues. We study this attribution problem through frozen-state credit storage, an adapt-then-freeze view in which rewards may update episode-local state during a short prefix, but later decisions can only read the state left at the freeze point. This boundary changes the design target: selected feedback is useful only if it is written before freezing into a state that remains readable afterward. Building on this insight, we introduce ReBEP, a bounded episodic-plasticity family organized around the action-local structure of selected feedback. ReBEP pairs a shared context scorer with resettable action-local memory, writes reward evidence only to the selected action slot, and reads the same slot after freezing. Its local-evidence update extends a scalar reward trace while preserving bounded action-local execution. Across latent-context tasks, supervised-to-bandit anchors, stress settings, and a short-session recommendation anchor, ReBEP stores prefix feedback more effectively as frozen decision credit than scalar traces, recurrent states, plasticity baselines, and frozen-prefix sequence summaries under the same write-read boundary. Memory interventions and component ablations show that the advantage depends on the frozen memory itself, action-slot assignment, bounded projection, and local-evidence writing rather than generic state capacity.

papers.title: Simple Actors and Deep Critics for Scalable Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Recent progress in offline reinforcement learning (RL) has been driven by expressive generative actors such as diffusion and flow-matching policies, which capture multimodal behavior in offline datasets. However, these actors require multiple denoising or integration steps per action and thus incur substantial overhead at every decision in deployment. In this work, we revisit where capacity should be invested in an offline actor--critic method. Since the critic is used only during training and is discarded at deployment while the actor runs at every decision step, allocating capacity to the critic rather than the actor is more favorable for inference-time efficiency. However, scaling MLP critics in offline RL is known to introduce several distinct instabilities that have, in practice, kept critics shallow. We identify three distinct failure modes that arise when critics are deepened in offline RL---optimization, bootstrap-noise amplification, and value-range drift---and address each with a corresponding ingredient: a residual MLP backbone, n-step bootstrap targets, and a categorical cross-entropy loss. Combining these ingredients with a lightweight deterministic actor, we propose LAC (Light Actor, deep Critic). On OGBench, LAC matches the strongest diffusion- and flow-matching baselines while achieving up to 4X lower inference latency, comparable to one-step distilled policies without distillation. Its critic recipe also transfers across actor parametrizations.

papers.title: On the Role of Language Representations in Auto-Bidding: Findings and Implications
affiliations: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.abstract: Auto-bidding is a crucial task in real-time advertising markets, where policies must optimize long-horizon value under delivery constraints (e.g., budget and CPA). Existing methods for auto-bidding rely on compact numerical state representations: while they can implicitly capture delivery dynamics, they offer limited support for explicitly representing and controlling high-level intent, evolving feedback, and operator-style strategic guidance in real campaigns. Meanwhile, Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a powerful method for encoding semantic information, it remains unclear when LLMs help and how to integrate them without sacrificing numerical precision.
