Building upon this, it embeds road network topology into its autoregressive modeling to capture physical movement constraints. During inference, rather than outputting an uninterpretable anomaly score, it dynamically constructs a physically coherent reference path to serve as a transparent baseline. Finally, by decoupling the detection into independent spatial and temporal dimensions, OSTAR explicitly pinpoints "spatial detours" and "temporal abnormal dwelling." This design effectively overcomes the opacity of traditional black-box scores. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate that OSTAR achieves excellent accuracy in fine-grained anomaly localization while maintaining competitive inference efficiency, meeting the real-time requirements of industrial deployment. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/lzxcompute/OSTAR.

papers.title: ELASTIC: Trajectory-Based Synchronization of Event and Tracking Data in Soccer
papers.abstract: Combining event and tracking data is fundamental to modern soccer analytics, yet the two sources are rarely well aligned: event timestamps recorded by human annotators often miss the true moment of the action, distorting the spatiotemporal context that downstream models rely on. Existing synchronization methods depend on noisy human-annotated event locations and fail to detect ball receptions, obscuring when each player gains ball possession. To address these limitations, we propose ELASTIC ( E vent- L ocation- A gno STIC synchronizer), a framework that infers the start and end timestamps of events solely from player and ball trajectories, without relying on annotated event locations. To recover ball receptions, ELASTIC enriches the event sequence by inserting virtual termination events between consecutive events, so that the end of each event is detected jointly with its start. It then extracts a sparse set of candidate frames where ball touches are physically plausible, and aligns the termination-inserted event sequence with the candidate-frame sequence using an extended Needleman-Wunsch algorithm. For reproducible evaluation, we construct a publicly available benchmark by annotating ground-truth timestamps on the Sportec Open DFL Dataset, on which ELASTIC substantially outperforms existing methods. Through downstream task evaluation, we further show that improved synchronization translates into measurable gains in soccer analytics. The source code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/hyunsungkim-ds/elastic.git.

papers.title: Node Importance Estimation in Multiplex Networks
affiliations: National Key Laboratory of Information Systems Engineering, National University of Defense Technology
School of Computer Science, University College Dublin
National Key Laboratory of Big Data and Decision, National University of Defense Technology
papers.abstract: Node importance estimation is an essential task in network science, with broad applications in recommendation systems and network dismantling. Existing GNN-based methods implicitly operate in a flattened relation space, where diverse interactions are either ignored or collapsed into a single propagation graph. However, real-world networks are far more complex. They comprise multiple types of nodes and edges, and are often multi-layered. As a result, single-layer methods fail to capture the intrinsic and extrinsic interactions among diverse relational categories. This study presents the first dedicated study on node importance estimation in multiplex networks, where a common set of nodes is connected through multiple relational layers. Our objective is to provide a comprehensive analysis by modeling distinct relationships as independent network layers while capturing both intra-layer connections and cross-layer dependencies. The proposed framework, namely HiGH, uses hypergraphs to learn intra-layer structures and capture higher-order interactions and grouping effects by modeling node influences. Specifically, an adaptive importance selector first identifies important nodes at each layer by integrating their local and global information. By constructing hyperedges from selected important nodes rather than from all nodes, the process becomes more targeted for importance-related tasks and reduces the complexity of hyperedge construction. Furthermore, a nested contrastive learning module with inter-layer bridge nodes facilitates cross-layer information transfer, allowing the model to discern node-level universality and specificity across layers. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets show that HiGH outperforms twelve competing baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness.

papers.title: HAWKEYE: Seeing One Layer Deeper --- A Cohesion-Aware Structural Channel for Temporal Link Prediction
papers.abstract: State-of-the-art temporal-link-prediction (TLP) models are, in essence, multi-channel information aggregators: they combine an interaction-history channel, a time-encoding channel, and a structure channel. The first two have been refined relentlessly; the structure channel remains a crude afterthought — DyGFormer encodes it as a 1–2-bit neighbour-cooccurrence count. We begin with a measurement: on sparse temporal graphs the classical 1-hop common-neighbour signal is near-random (discriminative AUC 0.50), because two nodes almost never share a direct neighbour; the genuinely discriminative signal lies one hop deeper — the 2-hop cohesive bridge, whose discAUC reaches 0.73–0.98, on both bipartite and non-bipartite graphs. Motivated by this, we propose HAWKEYE, a cohesion-aware structural channel that incrementally maintains the classical k-family of cohesiveness indicators (degree -> k-core -> k-truss) and forms 2-hop cohesive-bridge features. HAWKEYE is a drop-in replacement for a temporal-graph model's native structure channel, with no change to the backbone. Swapping HAWKEYE into DyGFormer improves test AP/MRR over the cooccurrence channel by +0.6 to +10.8 points across six multi-seed-validated datasets (uci, enron, USLegis, CanParl, reddit, mooc; wiki legacy single-seed). On the bipartite recommendation benchmark tgbl-subreddit, a 3-seed single-pass struct-only ablation shows HAWKEYE nearly doubling the baseline test MRR (0.103±0.003 -> 0.204±0.005, +10.1 points across all three seeds), demonstrating large-graph effectiveness; the streaming pipeline scales to the 67M-edge tgbl-flight in five minutes per pass. We further characterise when it helps: the gain tracks a graph's training-free 2-hop discAUC and vanishes on degenerate or saturated graphs — a predictable boundary. All code, data, drawio-editable figures, and figure-generation scripts are released.

papers.title: CCEC-TGN for Link Prediction in Large-Scale Continuous-Time Dynamic Graphs
papers.abstract: Temporal link prediction aims to forecast future connections from historical interactions. As a fundamental problem in temporal graph learning, existing methods exhibit three major limitations. (1) They usually focus on node-level interaction histories and information aggregated from temporal neighbors, while overlooking cohesive information from node-associated subgraphs. (2) They do not sufficiently integrate high-order topological information with temporal information. (3) They are susceptible to confounding factors, which may lead to spurious correlations. To address these limitations, we propose CCEC-TGN , a temporal graph neural network designed for continuous-time dynamic graphs (CTDGs). (1) We leverage continuous coreness to capture time-evolving cohesive information. (2) We use structural encoding, conditional structural interpolation, and gated residual fusion to integrate macro-level structural information with micro-level temporal information. (3) We apply counterfactual consistency regularization to mitigate confounding factors and improve robustness and generalization. Experiments on several real-world temporal graph datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of CCEC-TGN, especially in inductive prediction settings. The source code is available at https://github.com/BJHanjz/CCEC-TGN.

papers.title: Edge Sparsification via Temporal Forman-Ricci Curvature for Dynamic Graph Learning
papers.abstract: Temporal graph learning has become essential for analyzing real-world systems whose interactions continuously evolve over time, including financial transaction networks, communication systems, and online social platforms. However, learning from large-scale temporal graphs remains computationally challenging when networks are dense and rapidly changing. To address this limitation, we propose a network-curvature-inspired edge sparsification framework for dynamic graph learning. Our proposed method, TRicci, extends classical Forman-Ricci curvature to directed weighted temporal graphs by capturing structural support, temporal recency, and local interaction competition. Experiments on 9 transaction networks and 3 temporal graph benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework preserves predictive performance across multiple graph-level prediction tasks. The results show that TRicci sparsifies temporal graphs by approximately 80% while reducing end-to-end downstream training and inference time by an average of 55.94%, without substantial degradation in predictive performance. Our findings suggest that temporal curvature can serve as a principled basis for scalable temporal graph learning by preserving predictive temporal-structural information under substantial sparsification.

papers.title: Event-Aware Label Propagation Framework over Heterogeneous Graphs for Fake News Short-Video Detection
papers.abstract: Short video platforms have revolutionized information consumption but also accelerated the spread of fake news detection. Most existing detection methods use a single-sample paradigm, treating videos as independent instances and ignoring the macro-level event context. To address this issue, this paper proposes an E vent- A ware L abel P ropagation framework over H eterogeneous G raphs for fake news video detection( EALP-HG ). The framework constructs an event-centric heterogeneous graph that explicitly models hierarchical relationships among events, videos, and multimodal content, thereby enabling structured reasoning from event context to video evidence. A dual-level attention–based heterogeneous graph attention network is further employed to jointly aggregate node-and type-level information, enabling comprehensive representations for both event and videos. More importantly, EALP-HG introduces an explicit event-aware label propagation strategy, which uses predicted event labels as prior guidance to regularize video predictions. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance of EALP-HG. Under 5-fold cross-validation, it outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by 4.73% and 3.29% in accuracy, respectively. These results verify the effectiveness of incorporating event-aware supervision into fake news video detection. The code of our work is available at https://github.com/cgao-comp/EALP-HG.

papers.title: Effective Heterophilous Heterogeneous Graph Learning via Decoupled Spectral Filtering and Curriculum Learning
papers.abstract: Heterogeneous graphs (HGs) are widely used to model complex relational data in domains such as traffic networks, biology, and recommendation systems. While heterogeneous graph neural networks (HGNNs) demonstrate strong performance on homophilous benchmarks, they struggle to generalize to heterophilous HGs where connected nodes often hold different labels. Recent spectral HGNNs attempt to address this by modeling complex shift operations by positive non-commutative polynomials, but they suffer from severe over-parameterization and overfitting, especially when data are limited. Furthermore, existing methods often neglect the internal conflict between meta-path subgraphs with diverging homophily ratios. In this paper, we propose CLS-HGNN , a Curriculum Learning enhanced Spectral Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network. To mitigate over-parameterization, we replace dense learnable weight matrices with Jacobi polynomial bases, which decouple the spectral filtering process and significantly reduce complexity while preserving expressiveness. To reduce the impact of conflicts arising from inconsistent homophily, we introduce a curriculum learning strategy that quantifies node difficulty via training loss dynamics and embedding deviations across meta-paths. This allows the model to progressively learn from consistent (easy) patterns to conflicting (hard) ones. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CLS-HGNN achieves state-of-the-art performance on heterophilous HGs and significantly improves training efficiency compared to existing spectral methods.

papers.title: HERDGNN: Hybrid Error-Guided Regularization with Deviation for Highly Imbalanced Classification in Dynamic Graphs
papers.abstract: Risk monitoring tasks like financial fraud detection, money laundering detection, and cybersecurity often involve graph-native datasets that are characterized by extreme class imbalance and evolving structure, as well as deployment constraints that require incremental model updates under bounded temporal memory. Despite recent efforts in graph representation learning, the state-of-the-art Dynamic Graph Neural Networks (DGNNs) have several limitations: They are either designed for class-balanced settings and (some) offer a bounded temporal memory footprint, or are designed for class-imbalanced settings but do not offer a bounded temporal memory footprint. To bridge this gap, we propose HERDGNN: the first DGNN tailored for class-imbalanced settings while keeping a bounded temporal memory footprint. To address class imbalance, HERDGNN integrates deviation-aware regularization pushing abnormal entities away from the distribution of normal ones. To maintain bounded temporal memory, HERDGNN captures temporal information through a compact hierarchical memory whose size is fixed and independent of graph size, enabling live-update training without storing node-level temporal states. We evaluate the effectiveness of HERDGNN on 7 large-scale real and synthetic financial networks, under a live-update protocol, against 3 GNN baselines and 5 state-of-the-art DGNNs. The results show that HERDGNN achieves competitive or superior performance compared to the competing methods, and overall strikes the best balance between classification performance and memory consumption.

papers.title: From Auxiliary Views to Actions: Edge Augmentation for Strict Cold-Start Fraud Screening
papers.abstract: Fraudulent user detection in advance is crucial for risk control of real-world applications. One of the primary challenges lies in classifying new users as either benign or fraudulent when only limited user profile information is available. This scenario is often referred to as the Strict Cold Start (SCS) problem. Existing methods generally address this challenge by enhancing the topology or features of SCS nodes. However, these approaches can introduce task-irrelevant noise or require sharing raw cross-scenario features, which is operationally undesirable when scenarios are owned by different teams. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel graph learning framework called CoMGL. This framework employs a multi-view learning strategy to effectively tackle SCS tasks on graphs. Specifically, the CoMGL regards the interaction bipartite graphs from different scenarios as the multi-views for separately learning user representation, yielding more comprehensive representation for SCS users. Each view encoder consumes only its own scenario-local features, and only the resulting user embeddings are fused, which limits cross-scenario raw feature transfer. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework compared with the state-of-the-art approaches.

papers.title: RTDBStream: Efficient DBSCAN in Data Streams with Ray Tracing Cores
papers.abstract: Density-based clustering has been widely used in various applications such as hot spot detection, image segmentation, and geo-social network analysis. DBSCAN, as a representative density-based clustering approach, is known for expensive computation overhead, especially when the data volume is large. Specifically, performing DBSCAN on high-speed continuous incoming data with stringent realtime requirement poses challenges for modern applications, such as traffic monitoring and industry sensor monitoring. This paper proposes RTDBStream, a high-performance DBSCAN approach that utilizes ray tracing cores (RT cores) in modern GPUs for acceleration. RTDBStream transforms DBSCAN in data streams into an efficient ray tracing job in a three-dimensional space. To efficiently utilize the RT cores, two optimization techniques are designed in RTDBStream, namely Identifying Cores by Gridding and Clustering by Creating Mixed-radius Spheres, to significantly accelerate the clustering process. Experimental results show that RTDBStream outperforms existing implementations on both CPUs and GPU CUDA cores, and it achieves up to 16.4× over existing RT-based implementations.

papers.title: VoronoiSCAN: Enhancing DBSCAN with Voronoi Tessellation for Distributed Clustering
papers.abstract: DBSCAN, one of the most widely used density-based clustering algorithms in both research and industry, has proven to be a powerful tool for discovering complex patterns. Its robustness against noise and outliers has made it a cornerstone of density-based clustering. On large-scale datasets, DBSCAN is costly to compute and, hence, many distributed solutions have been proposed. However, many of them use naive partitioning strategies leading to suboptimal runtimes. To address this limitation, we propose VoronoiSCAN, a novel parallel and exact clustering algorithm that combines the DBSCAN algorithm with Voronoi tessellation for Euclidean distance and low dimensional datasets. By partitioning the input space into cells using Voronoi tessellations, we divide the problem into balanced, local clusterings. The subsequent necessary merging process relies on a novel density connectivity graph construction, which represents the neighborhood of the Voronoi cells. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm through comprehensive experiments on various datasets, showcasing its potential for large-scale clustering applications and its superior performance compared to other distributed DBSCAN algorithms.

papers.title: Manifold Diffusion Stability-Based Cross-view Graph Supplementation for Incomplete Multi-view Clustering
papers.abstract: Incomplete multi-view clustering aims to partition unlabeled samples when some views are missing. Recent graph-guided contrastive methods improve clustering by exploiting neighborhood structures from observed views. However, existing methods usually describe local structures with discrete pairwise affinities estimated from incomplete observations. Such affinities are sensitive to view-specific noise, sparse local density, and missing views, where accidental neighbor relations may be transferred across views and further affect contrastive supervision. To address these limitations, we propose Manifold Diffusion Stability-guided Cross-view Graph Supplementation (MDSCGS), a confidence-guided graph supplementation framework for incomplete multi-view clustering. Specifically, MDSCGS estimates manifold diffusion stability from observed view graphs to characterize stable local connectivity beyond direct pairwise proximity, and calibrates this stability through cross-view diffusion-neighbor consistency. Guided by the calibrated stability, high-confidence auxiliary structures are selected to supplement missing target-view relations, while unreliable cross-view relations are suppressed. The augmented view graphs are further integrated into graph-guided contrastive representation learning, enabling the model to exploit complementary cross-view information while preserving stable local manifold geometry. Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets under different missing rates demonstrate that MDSCGS consistently outperforms representative incomplete multi-view clustering methods.

papers.title: M2DNA: Multi-Modal Dual-Stream Representation Learning with Joint Relational Modeling for DNA Sequence Clustering
papers.abstract: Unsupervised DNA sequence clustering aims to group DNA sequences into biologically meaningful categories based on intrinsic similarities without relying on external annotations. While both global structural patterns and local sequential contextual information is essential for this task, existing methods predominantly rely on structural features, largely overlooking the rich biologically information embedded in the sequential context. To address this limitation, we propose M2DNA, a novel Asymmetric Dual-Stream framework designed for unsupervised clustering. Specifically, M2DNA converts DNA sequences into Frequency Chaos Game Representation (FCGR) images to extract structural priors via a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), while treating sequences as text to capture local biologically information using a genomic foundation model. These multi-modal features are aggregated via a fusion layer to drive clustering. To mitigate modality laziness in this architecture, we further introduce a Probabilistic Module Dropout (PMD) strategy that compels the learnable branch to extract discriminative semantic features. Extensive experiments on 11 benchmark datasets demonstrate that structural and sequential information are highly complementary, enabling M2DNA to significantly outperform state-of-the-art baselines. To foster reproducibility, our code is publicly released (https://github.com/Applied-Machine-Learning-Lab/CIKM2026_M2DNA).

papers.title: VISTA: Variable-length Interpretable Scalable Temporal Analysis for Industrial Time Series Event Clustering
papers.abstract: Clustering multivariate time series by operational conditions or fault types is important across industrial domains, but existing methods struggle with long, variable-length recordings, localized signatures, and interpretability. We present VISTA (Variable-length Interpretable Scalable Temporal Analysis), an unsupervised time series clustering model for industrial events that jointly captures local and global structure. First, a convolutional encoder embeds each sliding window. Then an eviction-attention mechanism, trained end-to-end via a straight-through estimator, maintains a bounded pool of the top-P most informative embeddings per series, and truncated SVD on this pool produces a fixed-dimensional representation that captures the principal directions of variation across the pooled embeddings of each time series, naturally accommodating variable length. Finally, K-means is applied to all the representations to assign a label to each event time series. Window- and series-level contrastive losses train the pipeline end-to-end. The bounded pool keeps memory usage constant per series and computation linear with sequence length. Intra-pool self-attention scores yield faithful temporal localization (“when”), and a per-cluster channel-attribution score identifies the sensors most relevant to each cluster (“what”). On five industrial datasets, VISTA outperforms all twelve baselines in time series event clustering. Faithfulness tests confirm that these interpretable scores identify windows and channels relevant to VISTA's clustering output and align with domain-expert physical interpretations.

papers.title: Causal Tracing and Algorithmic Recourse for Multivariate Time Series Anomalies
papers.abstract: Significant progress has been made in multivariate time series anomaly detection, enabling the effective identification of various anomalies. However, in time sensitive scenarios such as industrial control and microservice monitoring, a critical challenge remains: how to rapidly generate remediation measures that are both interpretable and incur low intervention cost after an anomaly is detected. To close this loop, a system must not only accurately identify anomalies but also trace their root causes. To this end, this paper focuses on algorithmic recourse in noisy multivariate time series and proposes a root cause localization mechanism that integrates causal inference, aiming to precisely identify the core variables that trigger anomalies. Based on the identified root cause variables, counterfactual windows are constructed, from which a downstream recourse generator produces repair suggestions that balance effectiveness with low intervention cost. We introduce a counterfactual based repair framework—CARE (Causal Algorithmic Recourse)—which not only reverses the anomalous time window but also provides causally interpretable remediation strategies. Experimental results on both synthetic and real world datasets demonstrate that CARE achieves precise root cause localization, maintains a high repair success rate, and significantly reduces the intervention cost. This work offers a feasible pathway toward shifting from passive anomaly monitoring to active, interpretable, and autonomous system repair.

papers.title: Frequency-Aware Anomaly Detection in Tabular Data
papers.abstract: The central challenge of one-class tabular anomaly detection lies not only in the absence of anomaly labels, but also in that abnormality can only be defined relative to normality. Such deviations do not have a fixed form in heterogeneous tabular spaces, and thus detection methods have to rely on implicit assumptions about anomaly patterns. For example, reconstruction-based paradigms expect anomalies hard to reconstruct through normal mappings, while distance-based paradigms expect anomalies to exhibit irregularity in local neighborhoods. However, real anomalies do not always follow these assumptions. They may be well reconstructed due to the generalization ability of deep models, or appear locally plausible. Therefore, this paper no longer seeks new reconstruction tricks or local constraints, but instead investigates whether discriminative cues can be discovered from the overall organization of normal patterns themselves. To this end, we analyze the inter-sample connection structure (T-Graph), and find that, under this data-dependent organization, anomalies induce stronger high-frequency responses. This suggests that spectral information captures structural changes induced by anomalous perturbations to normal connection patterns, thereby providing a new structural cue for distinguishing normal and anomalous data. Motivated by this, we propose FASEN ( F requency- A ware S pectral E ncoding N etwork). It first employs wavelet filters to decouple graph signals into multi-scale spectral representations. Subsequently, we design a Frequency Selection module to adaptively learn the frequency preference of normal data, thereby guiding the model to reconstruct utilizing the topological features dominated by normal patterns. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that FASEN outperforms SOTA methods. Further analysis indicates that this mechanism behaves as a physically interpretable matched filter. The complete code is available at https://github.com/criticcc/FASEN.

papers.title: Mitigating Convergence Collapse in Fixed-Target Anomaly Detectors via Kernel-Anchored Locality Regularization
affiliations: Université Paris-Saclay, CNRS, CentraleSupélec, LISN UMR 9015
Université Paris-Saclay, CNRS, CentraleSupélec, Laboratoire Interdisciplinaire des Sciences du Numérique
papers.abstract: A family of tabular anomaly detectors trains a neural map toward a fixed target under squared-error loss and scores anomalies by the test-time residual; contraction matching, one-step rectified flow, and reconstruction autoencoders all fit this template. We characterize a convergence collapse: better optimization makes the detector worse. At convergence, the learned map tracks the target even off-distribution, so the residual signal vanishes on anomalies as well as on normal data. These detectors therefore rely on implicit non-convergence (early stopping, capacity caps) to retain signal. We argue this is structural: effective anomaly detection requires a locality constraint that blocks unconstrained extrapolation. Classical detectors (kNN, KDE, isolation forests, LOF) enforce locality explicitly; fixed-target neural detectors do not. We formalize the connection by showing that the kernel-regression analog of a fixed-target detector is a finite-bandwidth Nadaraya–Watson smoother, which we call Kernel Contraction Matching (KCM). KCM is closed-form, training-free, and CPU-efficient, yet matches established neural baselines on ADBench. Building on this bridge, we introduce the Kernel-Anchored Regularizer (KAR), which penalizes deviation of the neural prediction from a kernel-weighted average of training targets. Across collapse-prone ADBench datasets and three backbones, KAR mitigates collapse and improves AUROC under prolonged training.

papers.title: Assessing Attack Surfaces in Generative Search Engines through Publisher Attributes: A Case Study in Political Domains
papers.abstract: We characterize the attack surface of generative search engines (GSEs) against poisoning attacks in the political domain, from the perspectives of citation selection and personalization. GSEs integrate web search and answer generation with user preferences and backgrounds using large language models (LLMs). They play a crucial role in how users access information on the web. Because anyone can publish content on the web, GSEs are vulnerable to poisoning attacks that manipulate citations to undermine reliable information delivery. Existing studies on citation evaluation focus on how faithfully answers reflect cited content. However, they leave unexamined the two critical aspects to capture the attack surface of GSEs against poisoning attacks: which publishers GSEs prefer to cite, and how personalization affects citation behavior. To fill this gap, we introduce an evaluation framework that characterizes the attack surface of GSEs against poisoning attacks. Our contributions are twofold: (1) we propose a novel metric, content-injection barrier , which quantifies the difficulty of injecting arbitrary content onto the web with a given level of publisher authority; and (2) we reveal how personalization affects citation behavior by embedding user profiles into GSEs. We conduct experiments on three major GSEs in the political domain of the United States and Japan. Our results show that (a) the attack surface differs across GSE models; (b) the web search functionality of GSEs shapes the attack surface; (c) ruling parties have a broader attack surface than opposition parties; and (d) user profiles have little influence on the attack surface.

papers.title: Retriever as an Attack Surface: Exploring Fairness Vulnerabilities in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
affiliations: State Key Laboratory of AI Safety
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems have recently been shown to be vulnerable to fairness and bias manipulation, with prior attacks predominantly targeting the data layer via corpus poisoning. In this work, we expose a fundamentally different and largely unexplored attack surface: the retriever itself. Motivated by the widespread deployment of off-the-shelf neural retrievers as plug-and-play components in modular RAG pipelines, we formalize the Adversarial Fairness Attack against RAG (AFA-RAG), where an adversary manipulates only retriever parameters, leaving both the corpus and generator untouched, to systematically skew evidence exposure toward a target demographic while preserving semantic relevance and stealth. To instantiate this threat, we propose AFA-RL, a reinforcement learning framework that treats the retriever as a strategic ranking agent interacting with a RAG environment. AFA-RL learns adversarial ranking policies that subtly reshape retrieved evidence to bias downstream response generation, guided by a fairness-aware reward with strict relevance and distributional constraints. Experiments across multiple datasets and large language model backbones show that AFA-RL can cause disproportionate fairness degradation with negligible impact on standard retrieval metrics. Our results uncover a previously overlooked supply-chain vulnerability in modular RAG systems and underscore the urgent need for robustness guarantees at the retriever level.

papers.title: Anchoring Bias: A Persistent Fairness Backdoor Attack against MLLMs under Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains where fairness is a critical safety requirement. In practice, these models are continually updated through continual learning (CL) to adapt to evolving tasks and data distributions. Prior work has shown that backdoor attacks can manipulate MLLM responses through hidden triggers, but naively implanted backdoors degrade as models undergo subsequent updates of CL. Although fairness has emerged as a central concern for MLLM deployment, whether backdoor-induced fairness violations can survive CL remains unexplored, leaving two critical questions unanswered: (1) whether a backdoor can reliably induce fairness violations in MLLMs, and (2) whether such fairness-targeted backdoors can persist through continual learning. We bridge this gap by proposing Persistent Fairness Backdoor Attack (PFBA) to inject persistent and group-specific discrimination into MLLMs. Specifically, PFBA achieves this through two novel mechanisms. The Latent Space Fairness Reinforcement reshapes the model's deep feature geometry by anchoring privileged-group representations to preserve utility while repelling and clustering targeted-group representations to sustain discrimination, and the Continual Learning Simulation iteratively optimizes the trigger against simulated parameter drift to ensure backdoor persistence across future updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PFBA induces severe fairness disparities that persist across continual learning rounds, evading standard backdoor defenses. The data and code are publicly available at https://github.com/lyygua/PFBA (https://github.com/lyygua/Persistent-Fairness-Backdoor-Attack-LVLM.git).

papers.title: MTBTime: Backdoor Attacks on Multi-objective Patterns under Multivariate Time Series Prediction
papers.abstract: Multivariate time series (MTS) prediction is widely used in safety-critical domains such as traffic management, energy systems, weather forecasting, and financial analysis. Recent studies have shown that MTS prediction models are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where poisoned training samples with hidden triggers can manipulate model predictions at run time. However, existing backdoor attacks on MTS prediction mainly focus on a single target pattern, forcing attacked variables to follow the same predefined trend. This setting overlooks a more realistic and challenging threat: in real-world multivariate systems, different variables are often causally correlated, sometimes positively and sometimes negatively, so an attacker may need to manipulate multiple target variables toward different target patterns simultaneously while keep the predictions normal for unpoisoned data. To address this gap, we propose MTBTime, a backdoor attack framework for multi-objective target patterns in MTS prediction. MTBTime first identifies vulnerable poisoning positions by combining Granger causality, neural causality scores, and prediction-error-based screening. It then constructs an adaptive causal graph convolutional trigger generator to learn inter-variable dependencies and optimize stealthy triggers that can jointly manipulate multiple target variables toward their respective target patterns. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets and mainstream MTS prediction models show that MTBTime achieves stronger attack effectiveness than existing methods in multi-target scenarios, while maintaining clean prediction performance and attack stealthiness. These results reveal a previously underexplored vulnerability of MTS prediction models under multi-objective backdoor attacks.

papers.title: Mind the Margins: Probing Link Prediction via Perturbations
affiliations: Data Science Group (DICE), Heinz Nixdorf Institute, Paderborn University, Germany
papers.abstract: Adversarial attacks pose a major threat to link prediction models. Carefully chosen triple-level perturbations can exploit weaknesses in the learned representations and change the model's ranking decisions. Despite their importance, adversarial attacks on knowledge graph embeddings (KGE) models remain less studied than their counterparts in areas such as image classification. One reason is that KGE inputs are discrete relational triples, not continuous pixel values. Moreover, KGE scores are computed within multi-relational prediction settings, where each relation can produce a different score distribution. As a result, score-based attack strategies cannot be directly transferred to KGE models. Studying training-data perturbations therefore both exposes vulnerabilities and identifies informative graph edits that can improve performance. In this work, we use adversarial triple modifications as controlled probes of KGE decision behavior. We introduce a decision-margin perspective that measures how clearly each training triple is ranked above its strongest negative alternatives. Our results reveal systematic vulnerability patterns, as well as improvement opportunities, that are shared across different KGE models. At the same time, these effects are not determined by the embedding model alone. The impact of training data perturbations also depends on the structure of the underlying knowledge graph. Overall, our study reframes adversarial probes as diagnostic instruments for KGE models.

papers.title: GrAP³: A Data-free Model Extraction Attack Framework under Graph Pre-training and Prompt Learning Paradigm
affiliations: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
The Chinese University of Hong Kong
papers.abstract: Graph pre-training and prompt learning paradigm have recently achieved remarkable success by improving the adaptability of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and alleviating the reliance on large task-specific datasets. However, we find that this paradigm inadvertently increases the vulnerability of GNNs to model extraction, a type of attack in which adversaries replicate a target model by observing its outputs. A particularly challenging and realistic scenario arises when attackers cannot access any target training data, known as the data-free setting. To address this, we propose GrAP 3 , a novel framework that enables the reconstruction of high-fidelity surrogate models under this resource-constrained condition. We first conduct a formal risk analysis to examine the impact of pre-training and prompt learning on model extractability. The analysis shows that these paradigms jointly tighten the theoretical upper bound of surrogate–target discrepancy. They are achieved by reducing representation, classification, and distribution gaps, which is the barrier to model extraction. Building on this insight, GrAP 3 generates structurally coherent and label-aware query graphs using a multi-class contextual stochastic block model. It further integrates a learnable prompt subgraph whose embeddings and structural connections are jointly optimized with a pre-trained surrogate through alternating optimization. Comprehensive experiments on six benchmark datasets demonstrate the superior model extraction performance of GrAP 3 without any access to the training data.

papers.title: Kernel-Complexity Edge Sanitization for Training-Free Defense against Structural Graph Attacks
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable success across diverse applications, yet they remain highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks that maliciously perturb graph structure. Existing defenses often lack rigorous theoretical grounding, rely on attack-specific heuristics, or require costly retraining procedures such as adversarial training. To address these limitations, we propose Kernel-Complexity Edge Sanitization (KCES), a training-free and model-agnostic framework for defending against structural attacks. KCES is built upon Graph Kernel Complexity (GKC), a principled metric derived from the graph Gram matrix that appears in a generalization upper bound on the GNN test error. From this bound, we define an edge-specific KC score that quantifies each edge’s structural influence via its induced change in GKC. KCES then identifies and prunes high-KC edges, which are empirically enriched with adversarial perturbations under structural attacks, to mitigate their harmful impact. Computationally efficient and scalable, KCES operates as a lightweight preprocessing step without retraining and can be seamlessly integrated with existing defenses. Extensive experiments demonstrate that KCES consistently outperforms representative robust baselines across diverse attack settings and scales effectively to large graphs. Supported by theoretical analysis and extensive empirical validation, KCES provides a principled and efficient framework for securing GNNs. Our code is available at https://github.com/karpning/KCScore.

papers.title: Towards Black‑Box Model Inversion Attacks via Lightweight Latent Diffusion Fine‑tuning
papers.abstract: Model inversion attacks (MIAs) aim to reconstruct high-quality copies of inaccessible private training data from deep neural networks, thereby posing a severe threat to data privacy. Training-based MIAs are only applicable to reconstructing low-resolution grayscale images. Optimization-based MIAs suffer from complex training of attack models, reconstruction quality degradation caused by iterative optimization, and high query and time overhead. Although diffusion-based MIAs achieve significant advantages in reconstruction quality and generation efficiency, this paradigm still faces two major limitations: 1) Unfiltered public datasets, which severely constrains reconstruction quality. 2) Low execution efficiency, particularly the substantial computational and time overhead incurred by training conditional diffusion models from scratch in the image space. Thus, we propose Lightweight Latent Diffusion Fine-tuning for Model Inversion Attack (LLDF-MI), a novel method that fine-tunes the pre-trained latent diffusion models (LDMs) via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to achieve efficient and high-quality black-box MIA. Specifically, we first constructs a Top-K positive face fine-tuning dataset via head pose detection and target model confidence filtering for precise visual-identity mappings. On this basis, we design a Multi-Identity LoRA module with a "partially identity-specific + partially shared" parameter allocation strategy, combined with conditional encoding and substitute-based identity loss, to precisely guide the generated images toward the target identity feature space. Experiments show that its attack performance significantly outperforms existing black-box and label-only MIAs, and is comparable to advanced white-box MIAs. Furthermore, it substantially reduces the training time overhead of the attack model and effectively improves the generation efficiency of attack images.

papers.title: Rich-Media Re-Ranker: A User Satisfaction-Driven LLM Re-ranking Framework for Rich-Media Search
papers.abstract: Re-ranking plays a crucial role in modern information search systems by refining the ranking of initial search results to better satisfy user information needs. However, existing methods show two notable limitations in improving user search satisfaction: inadequate modeling of multifaceted user intents and neglect of rich side information such as visual perception signals. To address these challenges, we propose the Rich-Media Re-Ranker framework, which aims to enhance user search satisfaction through multi-dimensional and fine-grained modeling. Our approach begins with a Query Planner that analyzes the sequence of query refinements within a session, decomposing the query into clear and complementary subqueries to enable broader coverage of users’ potential intents. Subsequently, moving beyond primary text content, we integrate richer side information of candidate results, including signals modeling visual content generated by the VLM-based evaluator. These comprehensive signals are then processed alongside carefully designed re-ranking principle that considers multiple facets, including content relevance and quality, information gain, information novelty, and the visual presentation of cover images. Then, the LLM-based re-ranker performs the holistic evaluation based on these principles and integrated signals. To enhance the scenario adaptability of the VLM-based evaluator and the LLM-based re-ranker, we further enhance their capabilities through multi-task reinforcement learning.

papers.title: Inference-Free Multimodal Learned Sparse Retrieval for Production-Scale Visual Document Search
papers.abstract: As large-scale visual-document corpora such as arXiv papers and enterprise PDFs continue to grow, visual-document retrieval has gained attention; yet it still lacks a deployable system that lexically indexes visual documents to serve queries without neural encoding at scale. Existing methods either achieve strong retrieval quality with VLM-based dense or multi-vector models but require neural query encoding at serving time, or avoid query encoding with OCR- or caption-based BM25 at the cost of time-consuming text extraction or generation. To fill this missing serving regime, we present V-SPLADE, an inference-free sparse retriever for visual-document retrieval. However, such inference-free multimodal learned sparse retrieval systems remain underexplored and have not yet shown dense-level effectiveness under high sparsity. We attribute this limitation to a lexical grounding problem: visual sparse representations often fail to capture the lexical content embedded in document images. To address this, we introduce caption-gated token supervision, a training-only signal that uses VLM-generated captions as lexical cues to activate retrieval-relevant vocabulary dimensions. With this supervision, V-SPLADE improves average NDCG@5 across six benchmarks by +13.7pp over the same-scale dense baseline and by up to +6.2pp over OCR- or caption-based BM25 baselines. On an 18.7M-document corpus, it doubles R@5 over the same-scale dense baseline and further improves competing retrievers through score fusion by up to +1.6pp R@5. Code and model weights are available at github.com/naver/v-splade and huggingface.co/naver/v-splade-quality, respectively.

papers.title: SAFE-G: Structure-Aware Faithful Evidence-guided Generation for Knowledge-Based Visual Question Answering
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: Knowledge-based Visual Question Answering (KB-VQA) aims to answer queries that necessitate reasoning over external knowledge sources beyond the visual content. Typically, current methods fuse multimodal features to retrieve external information, subsequently leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to derive answers from the retrieved evidence. However, these methods often struggle to capture structural associations within complex contexts to effectively filter noise. Furthermore, they frequently fail to ensure that the reasoning process remains strictly faithful to the retrieved evidence. To address these challenges, we propose SAFE-G, a Structure-Aware Faithful Evidence-guided Generation framework, which enables precise evidence localization and trustworthy reasoning. Specifically, we first employ a coarse-grained hybrid search fusing visual and textual modalities to recall candidate documents, and subsequently implement a structure-aware fine-grained graph retrieval that captures structural dependencies to filter noise and pinpoint precise evidence. Moreover, we introduce a reinforcement learning (RL) strategy with an evidence-grounded reward that assigns credit to correct answers only when the selected evidence is correct. This strict alignment constraint compels the model to anchor its response in the retrieved context, effectively enhancing its capability to locate evidence via multimodal features and perform faithful reasoning. Extensive experiments on the Encyclopedic-VQA and InfoSeek benchmarks demonstrate that SAFE-G outperforms prior methods by a margin of 8.9% and 3.5%, substantially enhancing the overall reasoning accuracy. Our source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/MINE-USTC/SAFE-G.

papers.title: Multi-View Hierarchical Graph Neural Network for Sketch-Based 3D Shape Retrieval
papers.abstract: Sketch-based 3D shape retrieval (SBSR) aims to retrieve 3D shapes that are consistent with the category of the input hand-drawn sketch. The core challenge of this task lies in two aspects: existing methods typically employ simplified aggregation strategies for independently encoded 3D multi-view features, which ignore the geometric relationships between views and multi-level details, resulting in weak 3D representation. Simultaneously, traditional SBSR methods are constrained by visible category limitations, leading to poor performance in zero-shot scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose Multi-View Hierarchical Graph Neural Network (MV-HGNN), a novel framework for SBSR. Specifically, we construct a view-level graph and capture adjacent geometric dependencies and cross-view message passing via local graph convolution and global attention. A view selector is further introduced to perform hierarchical graph coarsening, enabling a progressively larger receptive field for graph convolution and mitigating the interference of redundant views, which leads to more discriminative hierarchical 3D representation. To enable category-agnostic alignment and mitigate overfitting to seen classes, we leverage CLIP text embeddings as semantic prototypes and project both sketch and 3D features into a shared semantic space. We use a two-stage training strategy for category-level retrieval and a one-stage strategy for zero-shot retrieval under the same model architecture. Under both category-level and zero-shot settings, extensive experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that MV-HGNN outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: Prompt Contamination in Realistic Universal Cross-Domain Retrieval: Diagnosis and Text-Guided Rectification
papers.abstract: Universal Cross-Domain Retrieval (UCDR) requires models to generalize to unseen domains and unseen categories at inference time. Recent prompt-learning methods for vision–language models have achieved strong performance on object-centric benchmarks, yet their behavior under cluttered multi-object scenes remains under-explored. In such scenes, co-occurring objects can act as contextual distractors and induce prompt contamination : visually salient distractors may dominate the candidate tokens used for instance-adaptive prompt generation, causing retrieval representations to drift away from the designated primary target. To diagnose this gap, we construct DomainCOCO , a Realistic UCDR benchmark with 180,000 images across six domains, where each sample contains a designated primary category and contextual distractors. DomainCOCO is intended as a controlled diagnostic benchmark for studying target-aware retrieval under multi-object clutter and stylized domain shifts. We further provide Text-Guided Rectification Network (TGR-Net) , a practical rectification baseline that uses text embeddings as semantic guidance to re-weight patch-level visual evidence before prompt generation. Its Candidate Prompt Purification (CPP) module reduces distractor-dominated prompt synthesis, while a teacher–student strategy with a learnable null token enables label-free inference. Multi-scale feature fusion and gallery-side refinement are used as optional inference components for accuracy-oriented deployment. Experiments on DomainNet and DomainCOCO show that TGR-Net provides consistent gains over strong CLIP-based baselines, with larger gains in the more cluttered DomainCOCO setting. Code is available at https://github.com/YUEcjy13/TGR-Net.

papers.title: PRISM: Geometry-Aware Adaptation for Cross-Modal Retrieval under Distribution Shift
affiliations: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
Chengdu Jinfa Edge Intelligence Technology Co., Ltd.
industryAffiliations: Chengdu Jinfa Edge Intelligence Technology Co., Ltd.
papers.abstract: Cross-modal retrieval aims to identify semantically relevant instances from a gallery of another modality given queries of interest. Existing methods typically assume that online queries follow the same distribution as the source domain. However, due to the complexity and diversity of real-world queries, online query streams often substantially deviate from the source distribution; such deviations distort the geometry of the shared representation space and degrade retrieval performance. In this paper, we demonstrate that distribution shifts are inherently anisotropic within the representation space, where different geometric directions exhibit varying levels of semantic sensitivity and shift intensity. Leveraging this insight, we propose P rojected R epresentation via I nduced S pectral M etric ( PRISM ), which employs spectral decomposition to separate semantic-sensitive components from shift-intensive variations. During test-time adaptation, PRISM selectively confines adaptation updates to the subspace associated with high shift intensity but low semantic sensitivity, thereby suppressing distributional perturbations while preserving semantic consistency. We further show that PRISM achieves a tighter generalization bound under distribution shifts. Extensive experiments on six benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of PRISM across diverse distribution-shift scenarios. Code is available at: https://github.com/W2Wzj/PRISM.

papers.title: Residual Orthogonal Projection for Multi-Modal Molecular Retrieval
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to search biomedical knowledge bases. In this setting, queries describe the desired biomedical entity in natural language, and the system retrieves matching candidates. Existing methods typically represent candidate entities through text, leaving out available structural information such as molecular structure or protein sequence. Text descriptions can omit fine-grained structural information, making it difficult for text-only representations to distinguish candidates with similar descriptions but different structures. A natural idea is to introduce structural modalities. However, structural and textual representations of the same entity can encode partially overlapping information, creating cross-modal redundancy. Naive fusion can then reinforce shared information and reduce the contribution of additional structural signals. We present OrthoMol, a multi-modal framework for biomedical entity retrieval whose entity-side fusion explicitly accounts for this redundancy. Its core step, Residual Orthogonal Projection (ROP), decomposes the structural embedding into two parts: a text-aligned component and an orthogonal residual. ROP then removes the text-aligned component and uses the orthogonal residual to augment the text embedding as a complementary structural signal. We evaluate OrthoMol on STaRK-Prime and ProtDescribe, two biomedical retrieval benchmarks in which natural-language queries are matched against candidate entities described in text. On both benchmarks, OrthoMol outperforms foundation-model retrieval baselines and improves over the text-only version of the same backbone. Notably, on ProtDescribe, it reduces the mean rank of the target protein by 29% relative to the text-only backbone.

papers.title: S3-Prompt: Resolving Activity Cliffs via Structure-Disentangled Molecular Graph-Text Alignment
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented In-Context Learning (ICL) faces fundamental Information Retrieval (IR) bottlenecks when applied to continuous graph-structured data (e.g., molecules), as 1D textual representations (e.g., SMILES) fail to capture latent topological causalities. This representational bottleneck becomes catastrophic in Activity Cliff scenarios, where minor structural modifications trigger extreme target value divergences. In such environments, standard retrieval methods inject contradictory exemplars, causing LLMs to suffer from the Parroting effect—blindly mimicking the labels of retrieved neighbors rather than discerning true structural causality. Furthermore, existing retrieval strategies apply a uniform criterion regardless of the task nature, neglecting the distinction between local structural motifs and global physicochemical properties, thereby failing to provide optimal inference contexts. To address these challenges, we propose S 3 -Prompt , a novel framework integrating three key strategies: Structural Decomposition to preserve structural integrity via scaffold and side-chain soft embeddings; Structural Contrastive Learning to sharpen decision boundaries at inference time via an activity-aware contrastive loss; and Strategic Retrieval to employ task-adaptive retrieval modalities (topological vs. semantic) tailored to specific biochemical characteristics. To rigorously evaluate this, we introduce a Conflicting Context Subset to expose the vulnerabilities of the parroting effect. Experimental results demonstrate that S 3 -Prompt achieves state-of-the-art performance (e.g. up to 2.8% improvement in ROC-AUC) on MoleculeNet classification tasks while maintaining highly competitive results and consistent architectural synergies across regression tasks. Notably, it exhibits significant improvements in prediction robustness within challenging activity cliff regions.

papers.title: Embedding Surgery: Localized Updates for Adaptive Ranking Correction in Dense Retrieval
papers.abstract: Dense retrieval systems are core components of modern search engines, recommendation platforms, and retrieval-augmented generation pipelines. They encode documents and queries into dense embeddings, enabling efficient semantic search via vector similarity. However, because document embeddings are computed offline and stored in static indexes, these systems struggle to adapt to user feedback or evolving search intent. To address this limitation, we introduce embedding surgery , a lightweight approach for adaptive ranking correction in dense retrieval. The method applies localized, minimal updates to selected document embeddings at query time, guided by editorial feedback, user interactions, or pseudo-labels from large language models. We formulate embedding surgery as a convex optimization problem that enforces ranking constraints while minimizing modifications to the affected document representations. We integrate embedding surgery into standard dense retrieval pipelines and evaluate it on TREC Deep Learning, TREC Robust, TREC CAsT, and MS MARCO benchmarks. Results show consistent improvements (e.g., up to +60.64% relative improvement in nDCG@10 on DL-Hard under editorial feedback), even under noisy feedback, with low computational cost and without disrupting the global structure of the embedding space. Extensive experiments show that ranking corrections propagate to semantically related queries and that embedding updates can be applied safely and efficiently to scalable Approximate Nearest Neighbor indexes via simple in-place overwriting, without requiring costly index reconstruction. Finally, embedding surgery complements query adaptation methods such as CoRocchio, yielding additional gains while being more robust to noisy feedback.

papers.title: Building Better Encoder-only Cross-Encoders: A Controlled Study of Training Strategies for Neural Re-ranking
papers.abstract: Cross-encoders fine-tuned from Transformer backbones remain the standard for second-stage re-ranking, and recent knowledge-distillation strategies have closed much of the gap with LLM re-rankers. However, these strategies have not been compared under controlled conditions. In particular, it remains unclear how distillation from LLM rankers compares to distillation from strong cross-encoder teachers, or to purely supervised objectives. It is also unclear how much newer backbones (RoBERTa, ELECTRA, DeBERTaV3, ModernBERT) contribute compared to the original BERT. We run 162 controlled training runs (9 backbones × 6 objectives × 3 seeds), spanning pointwise, pairwise, and listwise losses with both human labels and two distillation signals, and evaluate on TREC-DL, MS MARCO dev, BEIR, LoTTE, and Robust04. We find that objectives emphasizing relative comparisons—pairwise MarginMSE and listwise InfoNCE—consistently outperform alternative objectives, including more complex listwise LLM distillation, across all backbones, and switching objective yields gains comparable to moving up one backbone size tier. A controlled disentanglement further shows that, once the negative-sampling pool is matched, even a simple pairwise Hinge loss with ColBERTv2 hard negatives matches—and on out of domain beats—listwise LLM distillation, indicating that the quality of the negatives is at least as important as the choice of loss. We release all 162 trained models on HuggingFace and a unified training codebase.

papers.title: Can LLM Annotations Replace User Clicks for Learning to Rank?
affiliations: State Key Laboratory of AI Safety
papers.abstract: Large-scale supervision is essential for training modern ranking models, yet obtaining high-quality human relevance annotations remains costly. Click data has long been used as a low-cost alternative, and recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have introduced LLM-based relevance annotation as another promising source of supervision. This paper investigates whether LLM annotations can replace click data for learning to rank (LTR) through a comprehensive comparison across multiple dimensions. Experiments on both a public dataset, TianGong-ST, and an industrial dataset, Baidu-Click, show that click-supervised models perform better on high-frequency queries, whereas LLM-annotation-supervised models are more effective on middle- and low-frequency queries. Further analysis suggests that click-supervised models better capture document-level signals, such as authority and quality, while LLM-annotation-supervised models are more effective at modeling semantic matching between queries and documents and distinguishing relevant from non-relevant documents. Motivated by these findings, we explore two training strategies, annotation-aware data scheduling and frequency-aware multi-objective learning, to integrate both supervision signals. Both strategies improve ranking performance across queries at all frequency levels, with frequency-aware multi-objective learning achieving stronger results. Our code is available at https://github.com/Trustworthy-Information-Access/LLMAnn_Click.

papers.title: PageLLM: A Multi-Grained Reward Framework for Whole-Page Optimization with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Whole-page optimization (WPO) decides how search and recommendation results are surfaced to users, and large language models (LLMs) open a new route to it by treating page generation as sequence generation. Adapting LLMs to web-scale WPO, however, remains bottlenecked by the need for costly human annotations and by the mismatched granularity between page-level coherence and item-level placement. In this work we show that these two challenges are coupled: implicit user feedback alone suffices for alignment, provided the reward signal is decoupled into two complementary granularities. We propose PageLLM, a reward-based fine-tuning framework that (i) turns implicit feedback into four contrastive preference-pair families covering relevance, ranking, diversity, and redundancy, (ii) learns a coarse page-level reward and a fine item-level reward that captures engagement-sensitive position swaps, and (iii) combines both rewards in PPO-based RLHF over a pre-trained LLM. Extensive experiments on seven Amazon categories against eleven baselines show that neither reward alone is sufficient—dropping the page-level or item-level signal reduces NDCG@100 by 17.8% and 15.2% respectively, whereas the joint reward improves NDCG@100 by up to 46.8%. Deployed in a 10M-user online A/B test, PageLLM raises GMV by 0.44% and click-through rate by 0.14%, confirming that multi-grained rewards from implicit feedback scale to production WPO.

papers.title: SGeture: Self-Guided Generative Reranking via Picturing the Permutation
papers.abstract: Reranking is instrumental in multi-stage recommender systems as it produces the target sequence of items exposed to users. Generative models have shown promise in this field recently, surpassing traditional discriminative paradigms. However, current methods generally follow an item-level generation manner. They either construct a sequence by irreversible autoregression, or iteratively refine a given sequence through item swapping and replacements. Such item-level decision horizons may cause the solution to be trapped in a local optimum, and also limit the ability to capture dependencies within the sequence, thus failing to pursue a global optimal objective. Furthermore, these methods mainly rely on historical contexts for modeling. We argue that in addition to such "past descriptors", the generation of a target sequence also requires directional guidance related to the future. In this paper, we propose SGeture ( S elf- G uided Ge nerative Reranking via Pic tur ing the P e rmutation), a sequence generation framework to address the above limitations. First, a self-guidance mechanism is designed to shape a future "guidance": (i) we enable the model to learn the correspondence between an exposed sequence and its own resulting future; (ii) at inference, the model is then equipped to self-control the future to be a desired one, therefore self-guiding the generation of a target sequence. Second, we present a holistic sequence generator for reranking. Specifically, a diffusion module is employed to progressively "picture" the permutation over candidate items in a sequence-level manner instructed by the above guidance, thereby avoiding local decision traps. Extensive offline experiments on public datasets and online A/B tests across different platforms of a real-world video application justify that our framework consistently outperforms existing generative approaches in reranking.

papers.title: GloRank: Generative Reranking for Deep Recommender Systems via Global Identifier Generation
papers.abstract: As a critical stage in the modern multi-stage recommendation pipeline, list-wise reranking determines the final exposed item sequence and directly shapes the user experience by modeling complex dependencies among candidate items within a list. Existing methods typically formulate this task as selecting indices from the local input list. However, this approach suffers from a semantically inconsistent action space: the same output neuron (logit) corresponds to different items across different samples, preventing the model from forming a stable, item-intrinsic representation. To address this, we propose GloRank (Global Action Space Ranker), a generative framework that shifts reranking from selecting local indices to generating global identifiers. Specifically, we represent items as sequences of discrete tokens and reformulate reranking as a token generation task. This design effectively decouples the scoring mechanism from the order of variable inputs, ensuring that items are evaluated against a consistent global standard. To further strengthen the framework, we adopt a two-stage optimization pipeline: supervised pre-training to initialize the model with high-quality behavioral demonstrations, followed by reinforcement learning-based post-training to directly maximize list-wise utility. Experiments on two public benchmarks and a large-scale industrial dataset, complemented by online A/B testing, demonstrate that GloRank consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and also achieves strong robustness in cold-start scenarios. GloRank has been deployed in production on our large-scale short-video recommendation platform, serving over a hundred million users daily.

papers.title: SWIM: Step-Wise Integrated Measure for Session-supervised List Evaluation in Generative Re-ranking
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: Modern industrial recommender systems have increasingly adopted the Generator-Evaluator (G-E) framework for the re-ranking stage. Within this paradigm, the generator produces candidate item lists from a pool filtered by upstream retrieval and ranking modules, while the evaluator scores these lists and selects the highest-scoring one for final exposure per request. However, on sequential platforms (e.g., short-video apps), users consume items continuously, ignoring artificial list boundaries. Conventional evaluators score lists by aggregating point-wise values, implicitly assuming exposure independence. This fails to capture critical session-level dynamics, such as contextual dependencies, user continuation, and diminishing marginal utility from repetitive content. To bridge this gap, we propose SWIM ( S tep- W ise I ntegrated M easure), a list-level evaluator that models user behaviors as a finite-horizon prefix session-level survival process. SWIM estimates the prefix-conditioned contribution of the current list to the session-level objective by factorizing it into a recursive survival distribution and reached-position conditional rewards. Leveraging a causally-masked Transformer, SWIM efficiently estimates continuation probabilities and utilities in parallel, satisfying strict industrial latency constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SWIM significantly outperforms baselines in listwise reranking tasks, yielding substantial improvements in overall recommendation engagement.

papers.title: Topology as a First-Class Object: Supervised Heterogeneous Attention for Robust Stock Ranking under Regime Shift
affiliations: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
papers.abstract: Stock ranking under non-stationary market conditions requires representations of inter-asset dependencies that adapt to changing market states. Prior work includes methods that learn dynamic stock--stock relations from price-based representations, as well as methods that incorporate market context into stock representations. We present HSCA (Heterogeneous Stock Conditioned Attention), which explicitly models the predictive affinity space. HSCA combines state-conditioned query modulation, State Anchors, and a supervised residual topology calibrator with Alpha-Guard stabilization. A State Gate conditions stock queries on the current market state, while State Anchors introduce global state references into the attention bank. During training, a Structural Hinge Loss supervises pre-softmax affinities using pairwise targets derived from cross-sectionally standardized forward returns. The loss penalizes violations of a margin that ranks directionally consistent peers above conflicting peers, whose directed stock pairs are identified as Toxic Edges. Experiments on CSI300 and CSI800 under a common evaluation protocol show consistent ranking and portfolio gains. Component and sensitivity analyses distinguish the roles of the proposed mechanisms. Regime-conditioned evaluation shows that residual topology calibration improves peer ordering and reduces conflicting exposure relative to the base peer topology in every decoded market state. The largest peer-margin and ordering gains and conflict reductions occur in bear regimes. At inference time, removing the learned residual topology correction or shuffling it within each source row produces lower mean IC and RankIC and higher mean Toxic Attention Mass than the learned correction in both universes.

papers.title: No Logs, Only Catalogs: Catalog-to-Supervision Training for Recommendation with LLM-Simulated Preferences
affiliations: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Most recommender systems remain fundamentally dependent on user–item interaction data for training. Recent studies suggest that LLMs can be used either as zero-shot recommenders or as user simulators, but whether LLM-generated signals can substitute for missing behavior data and train a recommender system remains an open question. We study Catalog-to-Supervision Training for recommendation: the model is trained using only the item catalog, with no user–item interaction logs or popularity statistics. At inference, the model receives the current user's observed short history as the query, exactly as in standard sequential recommendation. We propose CASTRec (CAtalog-to-Supervision Training for launch-time Recommendation), a catalog-to-supervision training framework that uses an offline LLM to generate supervised preference signals. Given only the catalog, CASTRec synthesizes catalog-grounded synthetic preference trajectories, grounds them in the actual catalog items, and trains a lightweight encoder for launch-time recommendation. Across benchmarks, CASTRec outperforms baselines, despite using zero interactions during training. It is especially effective in short-history and long-tail regimes, where interaction-trained models are most limited.

papers.title: Beyond Observed Auxiliary Relations: Environment-Conditioned Modeling for Multi-Behavior Recommendation
papers.abstract: Multi-behavior recommendation (MBR) leverages auxiliary behavioral signals, such as clicks and add-to-cart, to enhance target behavior prediction like purchases. While recent graph neural network–based approaches have achieved strong performance by systematically propagating auxiliary behavior signals, they still suffer from two fundamental challenges inherent to auxiliary behaviors: (1) missing auxiliary signals, which hinder generalization to items without auxiliary observations, and (2) unreliable auxiliary signals, which amplify noise misaligned with the target behavior. To address these challenges in a unified manner, we propose BOAR, an environment-conditioned MBR framework that addresses missing and unreliable auxiliary signals through two complementary modules conditioned on auxiliary observability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BOAR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving up to 7.82% gains in HR@10 overall and up to 44.2% gains for target items without auxiliary observations, highlighting its ability to capture hidden preferences beyond observed auxiliary relations. Our code is available at: https://github.com/LSH0411/BOAR.

papers.title: MoEFormer: A Unified Mixture-of-Experts and Transformer Architecture for Multi-Domain Recommendation
papers.abstract: Multi-Domain Recommendation (MDR) aims to model user behaviors across multiple domains with heterogeneous distributions while balancing knowledge sharing and domain-specific specialization. Mixture-of-Experts-style (MoE-style) architectures have become a dominant paradigm for MDR, but they often suffer from expert load collapse, where the routing network overuses a few experts and leaves others under-trained, thereby reducing effective model capacity and scalability. To address this issue, we introduce Dynamic Hyper-Routing (DHR), a hypernetwork-inspired routing mechanism that generates sample-conditioned routing parameters and alleviates expert load collapse without relying on sensitive load-balancing coefficients. More importantly, DHR reveals a mathematical isomorphism between MoE-style routing and Transformer self-attention when experts are viewed as tokens, providing a unified perspective for bridging expert modeling and Transformer-style scalable computation. Building on this insight, we propose MoEFormer, a unified architecture for MDR that reformulates expert-based domain specialization into a Transformer-style computation paradigm. Specifically, the MoEFormer consists of three key designs: (1) A Multi-Level Tokenization that converts heterogeneous multi-domain inputs into dimension-aligned tokens at the field, context, reasoning, and domain levels. (2) A Domain-Disentangled Mask that constrains token interactions to prevent negative transfer and enforce domain-aware information flow. (3) A Domain-Adaptive Transduction Unit that facilitates multi-level token interactions while balancing domain knowledge sharing and specialization. Extensive experiments on three large-scale offline datasets and one real-world online dataset demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of the MoEFormer. Moreover, the deployment of MoEFormer in a commercial online multi-domain advertising system achieves a maximum conversion rate improvement of 6.37%

papers.title: GPCDR: A General Graph Prompting Framework to Adapt Single-Domain Models for Cross-Domain Recommendation
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
papers.abstract: While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have established themselves as the state-of-the-art paradigm in recommender systems, their performance is often hampered by severe data sparsity. Cross-domain recommendation (CDR) offers a promising solution by leveraging multi-domain interactions. However, existing methods typically rely on specialized, end-to-end architectures. This isolation prevents the reuse of mature single-domain GNNs. Moreover, these methods typically employ static or uniform transfer mechanisms, failing to capture the interest heterogeneity across domains and the personalized nature of cross-domain correlations . To bridge this gap, we propose GPCDR , a general G raph P rompting framework for C ross- D omain R ecommendation. Designed as a plug-and-play solution, GPCDR transforms single-domain GNN-based recommenders into effective cross-domain recommenders via the graph prompting approach. Specifically, to handle interest heterogeneity across distinct graph structures, we introduce a multi-interest graph prompting module. It employs a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) mechanism to generate adaptive, user-specific graph prompts, enabling the backbone to capture diverse interest patterns. Furthermore, to address the rigidity of interest alignment, we design a personalized domain similarity module. Instead of enforcing uniform constraints, this module learns user-specific affinity scores to dynamically gate knowledge transfer, accommodating users with varying degrees of cross-domain consistency. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate that GPCDR not only significantly boosts the performance of various GNN backbones but also consistently outperforms state-of-the-art specialized CDR baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/liujinghong123/GPCDR.

papers.title: SGLP: Semantic-Guided Graph Structure Learning with LLM Structural Priors for Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation
papers.abstract: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation (CDSR) mitigates data sparsity and cold-start issues by transferring user preferences across domains.
