Although Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) effectively capture collaborative signals, they struggle with the inherent structural sparsity present in individual domains. Specifically, users or items with few interactions become "isolated nodes". Traditional cross-domain methods fail to rescue these nodes because they rely on explicit, overlapping interaction topologies that are often missing, severely hindering message passing. In contrast, Large Language Models (LLMs) encode rich semantic knowledge yet lack the inherent ability to interpret collaborative graph structures. To address this limitation, we propose SGLP (Semantic-Guided Graph Structure Learning with LLM Structural Priors), a framework that leverages LLM knowledge as a structural prior to reconstruct sparse interaction graphs. Specifically, SGLP employs LLMs to generate Item Semantic Embeddings and User Global Semantic Profiles, establishing a robust semantic foundation. Distinct from traditional Graph Structure Learning (GSL) methods that rely solely on intrinsic node features, SGLP introduces a Semantic-Guided Graph Modeling module. This module applies differentiable structure learning to dynamically construct a task-adaptive hybrid graph, transforming unstructured semantic similarities into structured collaborative connections. To resolve distribution discrepancies between the reconstructed structural and semantic views, we enforce a Semantic-Behavioral Alignment constraint via contrastive learning. Furthermore, a Bi-Level Sequence Prediction strategy is introduced to alleviate negative transfer arising from domain shifts. Extensive experiments on three real-world Amazon datasets demonstrate that SGLP outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, validating the efficacy of integrating semantic priors into graph structure learning for cross-domain recommendation.

papers.title: Bridging the Domain Gap: Domain-Aware Hierarchical Semantic Representation for Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation
papers.abstract: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation (CDSR) has emerged as a promising paradigm for alleviating data sparsity by transferring user preferences across domains. However, existing methods typically rely on sparse overlapping users or static LLM-derived embeddings, leading to two challenges: the Overlap Dilemma, where fragmented cross-domain connectivity impedes effective knowledge transfer, and the Semantic Gap, where identical items lack domain-specific contextual interpretations. To address these challenges, we propose D omain- A ware H ierarchical S emantic R epresentation ( DA-HSR ), a unified framework for learning transferable yet domain-sensitive representations. Specifically, we develop a Hierarchical Semantic Representation module that employs shared codebooks with domain-adaptive codeword refinements through Domain-adaptive Residual Quantization, thereby disentangling global static knowledge from layered dynamic semantics. We further design a Sequence-aware Routing Fusion module that treats the output of each codebook layer as an independent representation component and applies sequence-conditioned cross-attention to select the most relevant semantic granularity for each user context. To ensure robust cross-domain transfer, we introduce Cross-domain Sequence Encoding to retrieve informative global histories, together with Denoising Cross-domain Interest Transfer to suppress negative noise during preference alignment. Experiments demonstrate that DA-HSR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines while effectively bridging both the semantic and data gaps in CDSR. Code is available at https://github.com/zaixiaxiaowu/DA-HSR.

papers.title: Mitigating Negative Transfer in Search and Recommendation via Diffusion Denoising
affiliations: CCIIP Laboratory, Huazhong University of Science and Technology; Joint Laboratory of HUST and Pingan Property & Casualty Research (HPL)
Huazhong University of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Jointly modeling search and recommendation has emerged as a promising paradigm to capture diverse user preferences. However, the undifferentiated integration of cross-domain behaviors often induces negative transfer, driven by intrinsic intent ambiguity and extrinsic cross-domain semantic interference. To address this, we propose DiffuSAR, a diffusion-based framework designed to purify cross-domain behavioral sequences. First, we introduce a dual-branch intent disentanglement module to regularize domain-specific behaviors into discrete intent prototypes, which serve as explicit semantic anchors for the denoising process. Second, we devise a masked autoregressive denoising mechanism to efficiently suppress cross-domain semantic interference, leveraging preceding target-domain behaviors as guidance signals. Finally, we incorporate a trajectory loss to guide the reverse diffusion trajectory, progressively aligning cross-domain representations with target intents in a coarse-to-fine manner. Extensive experiments on two public datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on both recommendation and search tasks, validating the efficacy of generative denoising in mitigating negative transfer.

papers.title: Selection Meets Diffusion: Progressive Negative Sampling for Cross-Domain Recommendation
affiliations: Nanjing University Of Aeronautics And Astronautics
papers.abstract: Cross-Domain Recommendation (CDR) mitigates sparsity by transferring knowledge from source to target domains, yet its performance heavily depends on the quality of negative samples. Uniform random sampling is dominated by easy negatives that yield vanishing gradients, while hard negative sampling based on point-wise scores may suffer from false negatives and limited coverage of the global item structure. We propose SGNCDR, a progressive framework that unifies structure-aware negative selection and diffusion-based negative generation. SGNCDR selects diverse negatives from the observed item set by accounting for the global item-space structure, and constructs user-conditioned negative representations with a diffusion model using both domain-invariant and domain-specific user signals. With difficulty-controlled guidance, SGNCDR generates negatives at multiple hardness levels and integrates them into training via an easy-to-hard curriculum to refine preference modeling while maintaining stable optimization. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that SGNCDR consistently outperforms representative CDR baselines, and analyses confirm the effectiveness of each component. The codes are available here. (https://github.com/fanydan/SGNCDR)

papers.title: Latent Query Retrieval of Acoustic-Prosodic Evidence for Speech Toxicity Detection
papers.abstract: Speech toxicity detection is increasingly important in real-time voice-based interactions, where harmful speech can affect listeners before an utterance is fully observed. Existing approaches often treat speech as either transcribed text or a single audio embedding. However, toxic expressions can be lexically diverse, while vocal delivery may contain recurring acoustic-prosodic cues such as intensity, stress, rhythm, voice quality, or sarcastic tone. Motivated by this, we propose a latent query-guided acoustic-prosodic retrieval framework that learns class-specific latent queries to retrieve prediction-relevant local cues from speech tokens without relying on ASR transcripts or manually written prompts. Experiments on the combined English DeToxy+MuTox datasets show that our framework outperforms single-encoder, fusion, and retrieval baselines and improves early detection under prefix cropping. Analyses further show that the learned queries attend to temporally diverse regions and capture acoustic-prosodic differences associated with toxic and non-toxic speech. Latency measurements also indicate a lower-latency alternative to ASR-based text pipelines for real-time toxicity detection.

papers.title: Deconstructing Harmful Memes: Fine-Grained Analysis of Subtle Semantics
papers.abstract: Memes, widely shared on the internet as a form of cultural expression, present a challenge in identifying harmful content due to their compact format and subtle meanings. Current detection methods employ pre-trained models to extract image and text features from memes, subsequently combining these features through deep neural networks for classification. However, these approaches often overlook the underlying meanings embedded in memes, focusing solely on shallow semantics and surface-level harmful signals. This makes it difficult to capture the cultural connotations and subtle expressions inherent in memes. Moreover, they lack explanations for their judgments. To address these challenges, we propose a novel framework for explainable harmful meme detection. This framework combines the advantages of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and fine-grained heterogeneous semantic graphs. By leveraging multi-hop reasoning, we utilize MLLMs' extensive knowledge to provide comprehensive meme analyses, addressing meme literacy gaps. We extract key objects, relationships, and attributes from images to produce detailed scene graphs, which support a deeper understanding of the meme. The fine-grained heterogeneous semantic graphs filter and integrate multiple information sources to uncover hidden harmful elements. Additionally, through multi-hop reasoning and scene graphs, our approach generates reliable explanations via MLLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches on widely used datasets.

papers.title: Semantic-Guided Fine Alignment and Asymmetric Contrast for Multimodal Emotion Recognition in Conversation
papers.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition in Conversation (MERC) aims to identify the emotion of each speaker in every utterance by leveraging multimodal conversational signals. Existing methods typically employ graph structures to model contextual dialogue interactions; however, they often neglect fine-grained affective correspondences and implicitly assume equal reliability across modalities, making multimodal representations susceptible to modality-specific noise and semantic interference. To address these limitations, we propose SFAC, a semantic-guided fine alignment and asymmetric contrast framework with alignment-aware conversational graph modeling for MERC. Specifically, an optimal-transport-based fine-grained alignment objective captures flexible many-to-many correspondences among textual tokens, acoustic frames, and visual frames before conversational graph modeling. In addition, a semantic-guided asymmetric contrastive mechanism employs stop-gradient textual representations as semantic anchors to regularize acoustic and visual modalities after graph-based contextual reasoning, thereby preserving complementary multimodal information while mitigating interference from noisy auxiliary signals. Finally, the refined multimodal representations are fed into a decoder that formulates emotion recognition as an autoregressive text generation task. Extensive experiments on the IEMOCAP and MELD benchmarks demonstrate that SFAC consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the effectiveness of semantic-guided fine alignment and asymmetric contrastive learning. Our code is available at https://github.com/cgao-comp/SFAC.

papers.title: DGR-Net: Dynamic Gating and Retrieval-Enhanced Network for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
papers.abstract: Inferring human sentiment through the combined processing of language, audio, and vision signals is the core focus of multimodal sentiment analysis. Its effectiveness critically depends on high-quality multimodal representations that capture both modality-invariant and modality-specific features, while properly modeling the unequal contributions of different modalities. To address these challenges, we propose DGR-Net, a framework that jointly performs feature decomposition, hybrid dynamic gating, and complementary retrieval in a synergistic manner. Unlike prior purely work, our hybrid dynamic gating (HDG) module combines semantic attention with energy-based uncertainty for sample-level modality weighting, and our modality-specific retrieval (MSR) module is designed to selectively extract key cues from modality-specific features, thereby boosting the final prediction performance. Extensive experiments on MOSI and MOSEI demonstrate that DGR-Net achieves highly competitive performance and validate the contribution of each proposed module. Code is available at https://github.com/cgao-comp/DGR-Net.

papers.title: VGMR: Cross-Modal Value-Gated Modality Refiner for Robust Multimodal Learning
papers.abstract: Multimodal learning combines heterogeneous signals, such as text, audio, and vision, to improve prediction. However, adding modalities does not always help, because modalities may contain useful complementary cues together with noisy, redundant, or contextually unreliable components that interfere with full-modality learning. In this work, we propose Cross-Modal Value-Gated Modality Refiner (VGMR), a pre-fusion refinement module that estimates context-conditioned value evidence before modality features enter the backbone. VGMR models summary-level cross-modal agreement and discrepancy, estimates global-level and channel-level value signals, and uses them with raw and projected features to generate fine-grained gates over the original modality features. Different from conventional attention or generic gating, VGMR treats value as signed, context-conditioned impact evidence rather than a direct preservation probability, allowing the gate generator to learn whether each component should be enhanced, retained, or suppressed. We evaluate VGMR on MOSI and MOSEI with a Transformer backbone, and on MOSI, MOSEI, UCF101, AVE, and CREMA-D with a ResNet+Concat backbone. On MOSEI with the Transformer backbone, VGMR achieves 0.8446 Accuracy and 0.8029 Macro-F1, outperforming the strongest baselines by 1.09 and 0.89 percentage points, respectively. Ablation, controlled comparison, modality removal, noise robustness, optimization, and qualitative analyses suggest that VGMR can reduce unreliable modality responses before fusion and improve robustness under noisy multimodal inputs.

papers.title: Rebalancing Multimodal Learning via Adaptive Bidirectional Alignment
affiliations: Nanjing University of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Multimodal learning often suffers from modality imbalance, leading to an optimization dilemma. A key reason is that different modalities exhibit asynchronous learning dynamics during joint training. A representative line of existing methods seeks to rebalance multimodal learning through cross-modal alignment. However, such alignment is usually imposed in a static, symmetric, and fully coupled manner, making it prone to unreliable cross-modal interactions. To address this issue, we argue that cross-modal alignment under modality imbalance should be space-aware and status-aware, reducing feature-space discrepancy while selectively aligning transferable components according to modality learning status. Based on this principle, we propose an A daptive B idirectional A lignment (ABA) method. ABA first constructs class-conditional statistical projections to establish more robust semantic correspondences between heterogeneous modality spaces. It then employs feature-level partial optimal transport to selectively align reliable and transferable feature components. Furthermore, we introduce a dynamic bidirectional regulation mechanism to adaptively adjust the direction and strength of cross-modal knowledge transfer according to modality learning status, enabling more effective cross-modal collaboration. Empirical experiments on widely used datasets reveal the superiority of our method through comparison with various state-of-the-art (SOTA) multimodal learning baselines. The source code is available at our repository (https://github.com/yilnr/ABA)

papers.title: Accelerating Feature Aggregation for Imbalanced Multimodal Learning
affiliations: Nanjing University of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Imbalanced multimodal learning remains a critical challenge, as models often over-rely on dominant modality while under optimizing non-dominant one, ultimately limiting overall performance. Essentially, we observe that such over-reliance is closely associated with discrepancies in feature aggregation capability across modalities. More concretely, non-dominant modality lags in forming compact and stable representations, whereas dominant modality exhibits superior aggregation capability. To address this issue, we propose a simple yet effective approach called Dynamic Sample Retrieval for Efficient Feature Aggregation ( DSR-EFA ). Specifically, we first introduce a retrieval-driven near-neighbor sample augmentation strategy to build a candidate pool for each modality. Based on these pools, we propose a modality-aware dynamic ensemble scheme that allocates retrieval budget according to modality importance and constructs additional informative samples for classification. Consequently, DSR-EFA effectively reduces feature aggregation disparities and improves multimodal learning performance. Extensive experiments on widely used datasets verify the effectiveness of DSR-EFA.

papers.title: Multimodal Active Learning via Emotion-Aware Cross-Modal Contrastive Learning
papers.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) leverages diverse modalities such as text, vision, and audio to infer emotional states, yet suffers from prohibitively high annotation costs. As a promising solution, Active Learning (AL) strategically selects the most valuable data for annotation, enabling competitive model performance with substantially reduced labeling effort. To address this issue, this study proposes MALCC, a novel multimodal active learning framework that leverages emotion-aware cross-modal contrastive learning for emotion recognition. Specifically, to achieve task-specific alignment across modalities, we first design an emotion-aware cross-modal contrastive learning module, which embeds multiple modalities into a unified emotion-aligned representation space. Within this space, we propose a comprehensive reliability-aware query strategy that prioritizes cross-modal semantic consistency and modality contribution balance as two key reliability criteria, while incorporating informativeness and representativeness as complementary utility criteria to select more valuable instances for annotation. By leveraging this strategy, we then design a novel multimodal active learning algorithm tailored for emotion recognition. We further provide theoretical analysis to justify our design and conduct extensive experiments on three widely used MER datasets, demonstrating superior performance over state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods. Our code and supplementary materials are available at https://github.com/Atlantis-esh/malcc0425.

papers.title: TRACE: Tracing Temporal Constraints for Complex Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering
papers.abstract: Complex temporal knowledge graph question answering (TKGQA) requires composing multiple time-dependent facts under constraints such as validity intervals, temporal ordering, overlap, and set-style operations. Recent LLM-based approaches improve temporal reasoning through retrieval, decomposition, or planning, but the temporal constraints produced during intermediate reasoning are often left implicit: retrieved evidence may be temporally invalid, intermediate answers may be propagated without verification, and deterministic temporal operations may still be handled by free-form generation. We propose TRACE, a temporal-constraint-aware recursive framework that traces temporal constraints across retrieval, answer verification, constraint propagation, and execution. TRACE grounds temporal anchors and operators from sub-questions and intermediate answers, performs operator-aware temporal retrieval, verifies child-derived answers using grounding, bridge evidence, and operator consistency, and invokes symbolic temporal execution when root-level temporal operations are deterministically resolvable. Experiments on MultiTQ and TimelineKGQA show that TRACE improves multi-step and operator-sensitive temporal reasoning under the evaluated settings. Detailed analyses further show that verified answer propagation reduces error accumulation, while symbolic temporal execution is particularly effective for compositional temporal relations such as intersection and union. These results demonstrate that complex TKGQA benefits not only from retrieving or decomposing temporal questions, but also from explicitly tracing, verifying, and executing temporal constraints throughout the reasoning process.

papers.title: Time-Constrained Retrieval-Augmented Question Answering over Temporal Knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract: Temporal question answering over temporal knowledge graphs (TKGQA) requires retrieving evidence that is not only semantically relevant but also temporally valid. However, existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approaches primarily rely on semantic retrieval and often fail to enforce temporal constraints during retrieval, leading to temporally inconsistent evidence, especially for questions involving multiple events and implicit temporal dependencies. In this paper, we propose a time-constrained retrieval-augmented question answering framework for temporal knowledge graphs. Given a temporal question, our method decomposes it into an ordered sequence of structured event queries, each optionally associated with a temporal constraint and an event-time variable. Retrieval is conducted in a stepwise manner, where temporal constraints are enforced throughout the retrieval process via hard temporal filtering followed by semantic--temporal fusion re-ranking. Semantic relevance is modeled jointly from entity-, relation-, and sentence-level representations, while temporal relevance is incorporated as an additional ranking signal. We evaluate our approach on two temporal question answering benchmarks, MultiTQ and CronQuestions. CronQuestions involves year-level interval facts, whereas MultiTQ uses day-level time-stamped facts and includes questions with mixed temporal granularities and compositional temporal constraints. Experimental results show that our method achieves the best overall Hits@1 among the compared methods on both benchmarks. Ablation studies on MultiTQ further validate the effectiveness of structured temporal decomposition and time-constrained retrieval.

papers.title: SSR: Star-Shaped Rules for Link Prediction on Temporal Knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract: Link prediction on temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs), a.k.a. TKG link prediction, aims to predict missing facts from historical facts. Existing rule-based methods mainly rely on sequential temporal rules that propagate variables along chronological paths. However, such path-shaped rules cannot naturally capture a common prediction pattern in which a historical source-target interaction first identifies a candidate target, while subsequent source-side events provide contextual support before the query time. In this paper, we propose a new class of star-shaped temporal rules (SSRs) for TKG link prediction and a rule-based framework called PLSSR that discovers and applies SSR rules for link prediction. To discover SSRs, PLSSR employs a top-k pattern growth strategy over localized contextual relations. During inference, SSR rules are aggregated through Noisy-OR scoring, while sparse candidate sets are supplemented using subject-history and relation-level target priors. Experimental results demonstrate that PLSSR outperforms current embedding-based, rule-based, and LLM-assisted baselines with average relative MRR gains of 78.3%, 66.4%, and 57.9%, respectively, while preserving explicit, interpretable reasoning traces.

papers.title: HiTS-CL: A Continual Learning Framework for Long-Horizon Temporal Knowledge Graph Extrapolation
affiliations: Bejing University of Posts and Telecommunications
papers.abstract: Extrapolative temporal knowledge graph reasoning (TKGR) predicts future facts from historical snapshots. Most existing methods train once on an early prefix of the timeline and then use a frozen model for all future timestamps. We argue that this fixed-prefix protocol is misaligned with extrapolation. It learns from a static prefix, whereas the target stream is non-stationary: new entities and facts emerge, temporal dependencies shift across regimes, and recurring historical signals must be refreshed online. As a result, models trained only on early snapshots become outdated and degrade over long horizons. We address this mismatch by formulating extrapolative TKGR as continual learning over streaming snapshots. Under this view, effective extrapolation must jointly handle current dynamics , stable knowledge , and recurring historical evidence . Based on these requirements, we propose Hi story-enhanced T wo- S tep C ontinual L earning ( HiTS-CL ), a backbone-agnostic continual learning framework for extrapolative TKGR. HiTS-CL tracks current dynamics via continual fine-tuning, preserves stable knowledge via multi-teacher adaptive distillation, and retains recurring historical evidence via a selective memory of recent and frequent facts. We integrate HiTS-CL into five representative TKGR backbones and evaluate it on four benchmark datasets. HiTS-CL consistently improves extrapolation accuracy, reduces long-horizon degradation, and outperforms strong continual-learning baselines, including a recent method for temporal knowledge graphs. Source code and data are available at https://github.com/liuyansong98/HiTS-CL.

papers.title: HGNN-EAGE: Continual Event Knowledge Graph Evolution via Hypergraph Neural Evidence and Layered Alignment
papers.abstract: Event knowledge graphs (EKGs) must evolve continuously as new events emerge, while preserving temporal integrity and structural consistency. However, existing triple-completion and embedding approaches assume closed-world settings and lack mechanisms for open-world alignment and interpretable updates. Furthermore, real-world streaming data often suffers from out-of-order arrivals and information fragmentation, which exacerbates update conflicts and causal inversion in continuous evolution. We define the task of Continuous Event Knowledge Graph (C-EKG) Updating and introduce HGNN-EAGE , a unified framework that addresses these challenges through adaptive stream scheduling and hypergraph neural alignment. Specifically, we propose an adaptive dependency-aware sorting strategy that dynamically prioritizes information-rich and temporally antecedent events to initialize the topological basis. For event alignment, HGNN-EAGE models events as hyperedges and learns numerically stable embeddings via a degree-regularized hypergraph neural network. It decouples semantic, structural, temporal, spatial, type-level, salient-entity, and consistency cues into orthogonal evidence dimensions, driving a hierarchical decision process that maps interpretable alignment outcomes to atomic, version-controlled graph operations (insert, supplement, link-subevent). Extensive experiments on EventKG and DuEE-fin benchmarks demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms strong baselines in retrieval and classification accuracy. Moreover, the proposed streaming strategy substantially mitigates topological redundancy under high-load out-of-order data streams while maintaining near-linear scalability.

papers.title: Few-Shot Guided Knowledge Graph Population with Implicit Ontology Compliance from Partially Linked Tables
papers.abstract: Knowledge graphs (KGs) rely on structured representations of entities and relations to enable effective information access and integration. Building and populating KGs from semi-structured sources such as tables remains a challenging task, particularly due to the need to adhere to strict ontology constraints on valid entity types and relations. Large Language Models (LLMs) provide strong capabilities for understanding and generalising from text, but ensuring that their outputs conform to a target KG schema without explicitly providing the full ontology remains an open problem. In this paper, we propose WikiTabLLM, a few-shot, example-driven framework for ontology-compliant knowledge graph population. Instead of explicitly specifying ontology constraints, WikiTabLLM leverages partially linked Wikipedia tables to implicitly induce valid typing and relation patterns. Each table is partitioned into (i) rows containing entities already linked to the Wikidata knowledge graph, which serve as in-context supervision signals, and (ii) rows with unlinked entities, for which we aim to generate RDF triples for KG population. WikiTabLLM learns to infer valid properties and relations by conditioning on the structured patterns exhibited in existing triples, effectively enforcing ontology compliance through examples. We evaluate WikiTabLLM on a newly constructed dataset of Wikipedia tables and compare against Semantic Table Interpretation, relation extraction baselines, and zero-shot LLM prompting. Results show that our approach produces more accurate and schema-consistent triples (up to a 3x improvement in macro F1), demonstrating the effectiveness of leveraging in-context examples to guide ontology-constrained knowledge graph population.

papers.title: GrOIL: Graph-Grounded Domain Ontology Induction with Constrained LLM Mediation
papers.abstract: Constructing formal ontologies from domain documents requires simultaneously enforcing corpus grounding, vocabulary consistency, axiom-level expressivity, and end-to-end provenance, a combination no existing automatic system delivers. We present a seven-stage graph-grounded pipeline that converts domain documents into a complete, auditable Web Ontology Language (OWL) Terminological Box (TBox) without any unconstrained generation step. Documents are first encoded as Unified Discourse-Hypergraphs (UDH) capturing entity participation and discourse dependencies; subsequent stages transform this graph evidence into a class hierarchy, typed object and datatype properties, and restriction axioms, with Large Language Model (LLM) usage restricted to narrow, graph-grounded mediation tasks. A paired Assertional Box (ABox) population procedure grounds named individuals in the induced TBox, enabling SPARQL-based functional evaluation. Every emitted term carries a full decision chain from raw source passages through each pipeline stage, making the TBox directly auditable and suitable for targeted human refinement. Evaluated on the life insurance domain using two established benchmarks and a new 100-contract corpus spanning ten product types, our pipeline achieves strong results across all evaluation dimensions, outperforming direct and multi-agent LLM baselines on competency-question (CQ) coverage (0.85 vs. 0.63 and 0.62 on one term-life contract; 0.77 vs. 0.40 and 0.44 on another contract), while also attaining high keyphrase coverage comparable to a manually-constructed reference ontology and strong performance on structured gap-and-overlap reasoning, all without any manual TBox engineering. Ontology growth analysis provides evidence consistent with vocabulary saturation at scale, demonstrating that the pipeline produces stable, reusable domain representations from large document corpora.

papers.title: TaxoEvolve: Self-Evolving Taxonomy based LLM Memory Construction for Continually Growing Corpora
papers.abstract: Modern LLM-based applications increasingly rely on external memory for storing prior interactions, user-provided files, enterprise records, and domain-specific documents that can be reused in later interactions. However, as memory grows, current infrastructures provide limited support for understanding what the memory contains, how it is organized, and where retrieved evidence comes from. Vector indexes expose memory mainly through flat top-k similarity search, Knowledge graphs often require predefined schemas and fine-grained conversion of raw information into entities and relations which is difficult to navigate, meanwhile existing taxonomy construction methods are commonly static or one-shot. These limitations make current approaches difficult to maintain for continuously growing LLM memory. We present TaxoEvolve, an incremental framework that organizes memory items into a self-evolving taxonomy. It routes items to existing nodes, creates classes for emerging concepts, and refines overloaded nodes using a distribution-based split score that favors coherent groups with enough support. The taxonomy exposes an inspectable, editable memory structure, allowing humans or LLM-based agents to browse, search selected regions, and trace evidence through class paths and history tags. On TaxoBench, TaxoEvolve achieves stronger organization quality than clustering-based and LLM-based baselines, while some one-shot LLM baselines cannot process the full input due to context-window limits. Across scientific, medical, and financial retrieval tasks, taxonomy-guided search improves Recall@20, reaching 0.918 with hybrid retrieval and 0.923 with tag-aware retrieval.

papers.title: Adaptive-Path Wavelet Interpretation Maps for Auditing Neural Content Scorers
papers.abstract: Modern information and knowledge systems increasingly rely on frozen neural content scorers to rank, filter, recommend, moderate, and curate image, audio, and multimedia content. For trustworthy deployment, operators need attribution tools that explain not only salient input regions, but which structured signal components can locally restore or strengthen the scalar scores consumed by downstream ranking, filtering, and human-review workflows. We propose Adaptive-Path Wavelet Interpretation Maps (AP-WIM), a reference-input-free attribution method that computes nonnegative ascent-sensitivity maps in an invertible wavelet coefficient space. AP-WIM starts from the observed sample, advances along the local gradient field under an amplitude-proportional budget, and accumulates score-increasing sensitivity for input-aligned frequency-structured heatmaps. We characterize the origin-neighborhood risk of zero-baseline straight-line paths and, under local smoothness, derive a conditional score-improvement lower bound; the sign update is first-order optimal within its prescribed coordinate-wise budget box. On ESC-50 audio classifiers, paired-bootstrap tests show significant insertion gains under community-standard perturbation protocols, and a five-fold attribution stability check confirms that the insertion advantage is not unique to one audio fold. On a scorer-level Tiny-ImageNet query-gallery ranking audit, AP-WIM achieves the highest mean insertion AUC across target-score, Recall@1/5, MRR, and nDCG@10 endpoints, and significantly improves relevant-item score restoration over the strongest non-AP baseline. Together, the ranking audit, multimodal attribution benchmarks, runtime measurements, and robustness checks position AP-WIM as a resource-aware, frequency-structured explainability interface for frozen neural content-scoring pipelines. Code is available at: https://github.com/Davidjinzb/AP-WIM.

papers.title: Generating Intervention Hypotheses using Explainable Explanations on Graphs: G2I, a Two-Stage Greedy Framework
papers.abstract: Real-world decision-making in public health and social science can greatly benefit from predictive models, yet translating predictions into effective interventions requires explaining the model behavior. While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are well-suited for modeling relational data, existing explanation methods largely operate at the node level and fall short of supporting actionable, network-level intervention design. Existing counterfactual GNN explainers, such as CF-GNNExplainer and CF 2 , rely on continuous mask optimization over features and edges, which implicitly assume feasible edge manipulation, may allocate effort to immutable or non-actionable attributes, and incur substantial computational overhead. Further, the method of arriving at the explanation itself is difficult to explain to a domain specialist who is not an AI expert. Can simple methods generate good explanations? To explore this, we reframe counterfactual explanation as an intervention design problem. At the local level, we generate counterfactuals via a greedy search that directly identifies minimal, actionable changes to node features and neighbor-level conditions. We derive conditions under which the greedy search provides guarantees, and empirically show that these conditions are approximately met. These counterfactuals are converted into interpretable rules suitable for real-world intervention. At the network level, we formulate intervention selection as a Disjunctive Normal Form (DNF) coverage problem under a budget constraint, which is nondecreasing and approximately submodular, enabling a greedy algorithm with theoretical guarantees. Experiments on synthetic graphs and real-world suicide risk networks demonstrate that our approach produces scalable, cost-effective intervention strategies with significantly improved efficiency over mask-based counterfactual methods.

papers.title: AHFI: Adaptive Hierarchical Fairness Intervention for Fair Graph Neural Networks
affiliations: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are widely used for learning from relational data, but they can also propagate and amplify biases associated with sensitive attributes. Recent fair GNNs have moved from single-level debiasing toward multi-level intervention, but the strength of these interventions is still commonly governed by fixed coefficients, task-specific modules, or manually selected objectives. We propose Adaptive Hierarchical Fairness Intervention (AHFI), a fair GNN framework that performs adaptive constraint control at the input, representation, and output levels. AHFI monitors group disparity at each level with a geometric fairness proxy and assigns level-specific fairness pressure through learnable dual variables. To stabilize optimization, AHFI uses scale-invariant constraint violations, adaptive moving targets, and a finite-sample floor that prevents the controller from over-penalizing noise-level disparity. Experiments on six standard fair node classification benchmarks show that AHFI provides favorable fairness-utility trade-offs compared with representative fair GNN baselines across common message-passing backbones. Ablation studies show that the multi-stage design and the adaptive controller both affect the final fairness-utility trade-off. These results suggest that stage-wise adaptive control is an effective strategy for fairness-aware graph learning. Codes can be found at https://github.com/Dr-HZH/AHFI.

papers.title: Fair Graph Anomaly Detection via Multi-Disentangled Representation Processing
papers.abstract: Graph anomaly detection (GAD) identifies nodes deviating from normal graph patterns and is crucial in high-stakes applications such as fraud and social risk detection. However, existing GAD methods mainly prioritize accuracy while overlooking fairness. Sensitive information can be encoded in node attributes, homophilous links, and graph structures, and message passing may entangle these signals with anomaly evidence, causing group-imbalanced scores. Existing fair GAD methods are often detector-specific, limiting reuse and intensifying the fairness-utility trade-off. To address these issues, we propose Multi-Disentangled processing for Fair graph Anomaly Detection MDFairAD, built upon a Multi-Disentangled Fair Processor MDFP that serves as an upstream fair representation module jointly optimizable with off-the-shelf anomaly detectors. It performs multi-view disentanglement with causal- and representation-level debiasing to reduce attribute and structural leakage, and then nonlinearly fuses the disentangled branches to preserve cross-view anomaly evidence while suppressing sensitive information. The refined representations are further fine-tuned with anomaly detectors through a detection head. Experiments on real-world datasets show that MDFairAD achieves competitive detection performance while substantially improving fairness over existing baselines.

papers.title: Uncovering Locally-Persistent Bias with Formal Guarantees and Debiasing
papers.abstract: We propose the notion of Persistent-Bias-Aware (PBA) fairness and an approach to formally quantify locally-persistent bias. PBA fairness captures the bias in a model's predictions towards a certain outcome for a given input, compared to its counterfactual (where the sensitive attribute of the original input is flipped), in an entire region. As such, PBA fairness allows us to isolate the effect of the sensitive attribute, enabling formal identification of fairness disparities that are consistently present in the model behavior within a neighborhood. We evaluate our proposed approach under both fairness-agnostic and fairness-aware training methods and compare it to well-established fairness metrics on three benchmark datasets: Adult, COMPAS, and German Credit. The results demonstrate that our proposed approach identifies fairness disparities overlooked by other approaches and offers additional insights into model behavior. To address this challenge, we further propose a debiasing scheme by penalizing persistent bias. The results show that the models obtained under such debiasing scheme are consistently less prone to locally-persistent bias compared to the state of the art.

papers.title: FairRank: Fairness-Certified Premium Prioritization for Trustworthy Tiered Service Platforms
papers.abstract: Tiered service platforms in mobility, delivery, and cloud computing accelerate premium requests, and aggressive prioritization can silently degrade the experience of regular users. We study premium admission as an auditable admission-control problem over streaming telemetry: given per-region arrival rates, service-time moments, and a declared tolerance δ on the mean delay inflation of regular users, how many premium requests may be prioritized? Building on a two-class M/G/1 model with probabilistic gap insertion and head-of-line promotion, we derive a closed-form fairness certificate that maps three telemetry statistics and the platform's prioritization parameters to an admissible premium-to-regular ratio, prove its monotonicity, and show that it is a conservative surrogate of the exact nonpreemptive-priority formula whenever promoted requests wait at most one mean service time. The certificate composes across heterogeneous regions through a per-region cap layer and a shared-slack pooling rule with explicitly declared per-region budgets, and it acts as a state-dependent gate for online controllers. We evaluate FairRank on trace-driven replays of NYC TLC high-volume for-hire vehicle records from three weeks of 2024, comparing nine admission policies, including an established utilization-threshold admission-control baseline, across three premium-candidate definitions and sweeps over tolerance, calibration, scale, and time. Certificate-gated admission reduces mean regular-user delay inflation about five-fold relative to unconstrained prioritization at the evaluated operating points, and the telemetry-updated adaptive variant attains the lowest inflation of all tested policies. Because the certificate is model-conditional, we also isolate which assumptions matter: a synthetic study shows that heavy-tailed service times leave the certificate intact while bursty arrivals roughly double realized inflation, and a diagnostic on the real trace explains the remaining gap and gives operators a conservative parameterization that meets the nominal tolerance in every zone.

papers.title: FairStream: Adaptive Fairness Constraints for Streaming AutoML
papers.abstract: Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) systems are increasingly deployed in settings where data arrives continuously and evolves over time. In such streaming environments, fairness presents a distinct challenge: data distributions change, sensitive-group proportions fluctuate, models are updated incrementally, and fairness measurements become noisy and time-varying. Existing fairness-aware AutoML approaches are designed for static data and enforce fixed fairness thresholds, while streaming AutoML systems largely neglect fairness. To address this gap, we introduce FairStream, a fairness-aware AutoML framework for data streams that treats fairness as a dynamic control signal. FairStream introduces a streaming evaluation framework that jointly models predictive performance and group-based fairness through signals capturing temporal variation, estimation uncertainty, and both performance and fairness drift. These signals drive an adaptive fairness control mechanism that maintains a time-varying feasibility envelope and accumulated fairness debt to enforce consistent fairness over time. We formulate model selection as a sequence of online constrained optimization problems and solve it using constrained Bayesian optimization, enabling principled exploration under evolving fairness constraints. Experiments on diverse streaming benchmarks show that FairStream achieves strong predictive performance while substantially reducing fairness violations compared to fairness-agnostic and fixed-threshold fairness-aware baselines.

papers.title: CoShapley: Context-Structure Coupled Data Valuation for Data Markets
affiliations: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Data valuation is a fundamental problem in emerging data markets, where the value of data is inherently shaped by both the market context and the internal structure of the dataset. However, existing approaches typically capture only one side of this interplay. Classical Shapley-based methods treat data value as an intrinsic property of a fixed dataset, leading to inconsistent valuations across participants, while recent approaches that rely on global data distributions improve consistency at the cost of overlooking structural redundancy and incurring substantial computational overhead. In this work, we argue that data valuation should be understood as a context–structure coupling problem, where value arises from the interaction between global context and local data structure. Based on this perspective, we propose CoShapley ( Co ntextual-Structural Shapley ), a hierarchical valuation framework that explicitly models this coupling, producing valuations that are both stable across varying market contexts and sensitive to redundancy and correlation within the data. To make this formulation scalable, we introduce a signed decomposition that removes pairwise coupling in Shapley estimation, together with a hybrid two-stage sampling strategy that enables batch updates of all data points from a single model evaluation. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that CoShapley achieves superior valuation effectiveness and improves downstream task performance, while significantly reducing computational cost, achieving up to 14× fewer iterations to convergence and 4× speedup in end-to-end execution.

papers.title: OPERA: Automated Intra-Operator Parallel Pattern Generation for Distributed Transformer Training
papers.abstract: Designing intra-operator parallel patterns for large-scale Transformer training remains labor-intensive because it requires jointly coordinating tensor partitioning, local computation, and communication under hardware constraints. Existing automatic parallelization systems commonly select from predefined pattern libraries, limiting their ability to explore fine-grained execution alternatives. We present OPERA, a reinforcement learning framework for automatically generating executable intra-operator parallel patterns.OPERA formulates parallel pattern generation as a Markov Decision Process in which the environment tracks tensor placements, computation progress, and feasible computation and communication actions. A Transformer decoder encodes the history of layout and execution decisions, while its policy and value heads guide Monte Carlo Tree Search toward promising feasible trajectories. The resulting trajectories are reused to train the policy-value network, enabling the agent to progressively refine its decisions. A distributed program translator converts completed trajectories into executable programs and evaluates their numerical correctness, runtime, and resource consumption. Experiments on an eight-GPU NVIDIA A100 platform using BERT-Large and workloads derived from LLaMA and GPT configurations show that OPERA recovers 9 established intra-operator parallel patterns and generates additional feasible execution trajectories from primitive actions rather than selecting fixed templates.

papers.title: Gradient Interaction Graph Optimization
papers.abstract: Training large Transformer language models is dominated by the cost of synchronous parameter updates: every block of weights is moved at every step using a gradient computed before any block has moved. The resulting trajectory is wasteful, because per-block updates are evaluated on a frozen snapshot of the rest of the network that the next step will already invalidate. Second-order methods such as Shampoo and K-FAC address this spatially through preconditioning, and sharpness-aware methods such as SAM trade compute for sharper minima, but both leave the temporal coupling between blocks untouched. We introduce Gradient Interaction Graph Optimization (GIGO) , a meta-optimizer that estimates a sparse directed graph of cross-block gradient dependencies online, partitions each step into contiguous sequential stages along this graph, and refreshes downstream gradients using a stale-activation approximation. The framework wraps any base optimizer, adds one cached boundary activation per stage (∼32 MB at T seq =1024, scaling linearly with sequence length), and is compatible with mixed precision and data parallelism. On GPT-2 Small through XL (124M–1.5B), GIGO-Adam reaches the same OpenWebText/C4 perplexity in 32.0–34.0 % fewer optimizer steps than synchronous AdamW — a lead of 8–22 percentage points over the strongest 2024-vintage baselines (SOAP, Muon, Sophia, Lion, GaLore) on the Small comparison cohort — with a per-step overhead of 32–38 % and a net wall-clock benefit ranging from +5.2 % (Small) to +16.2 % (XL) across the four sizes tested. The benefit vanishes or reverses where the method's preconditions do not hold: a synthetic block-diagonal control (SRR = 0.0 %), the overhead-dominated Penn Treebank stress test (-18.5 % wall-clock), and a weak-coupling small-vision-Transformer diagnostic (-12.4 % wall-clock on CIFAR-100). Ablations decompose the mechanism: the partial-re-forward refresh primitive alone (random partition) accounts for 9.4 % SRR, the interaction-graph schedule contributes a further ∼22 pp, and the layer-contiguity constraint controls overhead. Our convergence theorem matches the standard Adam O(T -1/4 ) rate uniformly in graph-estimation quality, providing a safety guarantee; the empirical step-reduction is reported as an empirical regularity not formally predicted by the theory.

papers.title: Strong Lottery Ticket Hypothesis for Quantum Neural Networks
affiliations: Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) possess high expressivity via rich unitary transformations, offering abundant representational capacity while maintaining a parameter-effective architecture. In classical deep learning, the high expressivity of deep neural networks (DNNs) motivates the Strong Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (SLTH), which suggests that a randomly initialized DNN contains sparse subnetworks that achieve high performance immediately or serve as a warm start. On the quantum side, a key question is: Does a strong lottery ticket exist in QNNs? Our answer is, Quantum-Strong Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (Q-SLTH) , i.e., the first theoretical analysis for the existence of high-performing subnetworks in random scratch of QNNs. We validate our theory by proposing a quantum edge-popup algorithm to find strong subnetworks and empirically identifying winning tickets in randomly initialized QNNs on the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST benchmarks. For practice, Q-SLTH suggests a way to compress QNNs, allowing them to use fewer gates and thereby mitigating quantum-noise-induced degradation that is amplified across multiple layers of quantum gates.

papers.title: From Redundancy to Efficiency: A Similarity-based Filter Sharing for Deep Model Compression
papers.abstract: Deep CNNs have achieved significant performance across a variety of computer vision tasks. However, their effectiveness comes at a cost of overparameterization. This leads to extensive computation and memory requirements, thereby limiting practical deployment in resource-constrained environments. A growing body of evidence suggests that many of these parameters are redundant, motivating the need for compression strategies that go beyond parameter-level heuristics. To overcome these challenges, we propose a layerwise, similarity-based filter-sharing framework for optimizing parameters of deep models by identifying and exploiting redundancy among filters. By leveraging representational similarity of the filters measured via Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), our approach enables efficient filter-sharing over layers, significantly reducing the number of parameters, FLOPs and overall memory footprint. We form clusters of filters by measuring their feature-map similarity scores on the dataset, enabling compression decisions guided by representational behaviour rather than raw parameter values. We further use an entropy- and energy-based scaling mechanism that adaptively determines the number of shared filters per layer. Additionally, we extend the framework with a class-conditional formulation, enabling the construction of specialized compressed sub-models tailored to different subsets of tasks. This provides insight into how representational redundancy varies with task difficulty and allows the model to allocate capacity in a data-dependent manner. We conduct extensive experiments over VGG16, AlexNet, ResNet and MobileNetV2 models across standard benchmark datasets. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in achieving substantial parameter and FLOP reductions, while maintaining competitive accuracy. We compare our framework against several state-of-the-art compression methods from the literature. Our proposed framework offers a simple and effective approach to exploiting redundancy in deep networks, with practical implications for efficient deployment and adaptive model design.

papers.title: EPTQ: Fast and Accurate 2-bit Post-Training Quantization via Factored E8 Lattice
papers.abstract: Two-bit Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) offers an attractive path to deploying Large Language Models under strict memory budgets, yet scalar quantization suffers from catastrophic performance collapse at this extreme bit-width. While Vector Quantization (VQ) methods resolve the accuracy issue, existing approaches suffer from practical inefficiencies: complex optimization pipelines result in hours-long quantization, and some methods exhibit severely limited inference throughput. We propose EPTQ, a 2-bit PTQ framework available in two complementary variants (E8 and FE8), achieving high accuracy and practical efficiency through three contributions: (1) Factored E 8 (FE8) lattice quantization , which decomposes the E 8 codebook into a compact 4 KB structure that fits in the GPU L1 cache, enabling fast codebook lookup at inference time; (2) Lightweight scale normalization via row/column scaling vectors ( g , h ), which aligns weight distributions to maximize E 8 quantization efficiency, requiring only element-wise per-token scaling at inference; and (3) Adaptive critical weight preservation via knee-point threshold detection, which more accurately identifies Hessian-sensitive weights than approaches relying on fixed global criteria, consistently improving perplexity across models, with zero bit-overhead by encoding the preservation mask into the existing codebook index space. Evaluated across multiple LLMs including Llama-2 and Llama-3 families, EPTQ (E8) achieves accuracy competitive with or surpassing QTIP on Llama-2 models, while EPTQ (FE8) surpasses competing VQ methods in decode throughput on most models, achieving up to 38% faster inference than FP16, with both variants reducing quantization time by over 80% compared to competing approaches.

papers.title: Exploring Model Invariance with Discrete Search for Ultra-Low-Bit Quantization
affiliations: University of Alberta, Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute (Amii), Canada CIFAR AI Chair
papers.abstract: As language models continue to grow in size due to their success in a wide range of applications such as conversational agents and coding, there is a pressing need to make them more accessible. A popular technique is to reduce their memory footprint by post-training quantization, where we use fewer bits (e.g., 4--8 bits) to represent the model without retraining it. However, quantizing language models remains a challenging task, especially in the ultra-low-bit setup (e.g., 2 bits). In this paper, we propose InvarExplore, a unified framework that systematically explores different kinds of model invariance to maximize quantization performance. Importantly, InvarExplore features a discrete search algorithm that enables us to explore permutation invariance, which is under-studied as it cannot be optimized with gradient-based methods. Such exploration allows us to take advantage of the synergy between each type of invariance. Our results and in-depth analyses show that InvarExplore is compatible with existing state-of-the-art integer quantization methods, achieving an add-on performance improvement over strong competing methods.

papers.title: Pay Where It Matters: Accurate and Versatile Bit-Level Stream Analytics with Nino-Sketch
papers.abstract: Analyzing high-velocity data streams is critical for tasks like real-time monitoring, anomaly detection, and performance analysis, driving interest in sketches, probabilistic data structures that efficiently summarize fast streams. Traditional sketches often use large, fixed-size counters, leading to inefficient memory usage in skewed data distributions. Recent solutions, such as hierarchical structures and dynamic counters, attempt to improve memory efficiency but struggle to balance this with detection accuracy. In this work, we present Nino-Sketch, a memory-efficient and versatile sketch for data stream analysis. Nino-Sketch employs a flexible filter to exclude cold items (e.g., those with low frequency or persistence) while focusing on tracking hot items using variable-size counters. When a counter overflows, it reallocates memory by sacrificing the slot with the smallest counter value, enhancing the tracking of hot items. By using variable-length fingerprints (a short identifier derived from an item's key using hashing techniques) for different item types, Nino-Sketch further optimizes memory usage. Experimental results on various datasets show that Nino-Sketch surpasses existing methods, reducing relative error by up to 11.17× over prior baselines under tight memory conditions (e.g., 16KB) while retaining competitive update throughput. We further deploy Nino-Sketch as a synthesizable RTL design on a Xilinx Kintex-7 FPGA, confirming that the bit-level layout is implementable on reconfigurable hardware.

papers.title: AutoCSF: A Provably Safe Indexing Framework for Filter-Augmented Compressed Static Functions
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of building space-efficient indexes for static key-value datasets with highly skewed value distributions. A standard technique for this task is to augment a compressed static function (CSF) with an approximate set membership prefilter to handle a dominating value and break the one-bit-per-key barrier. However, we observe that prior approaches decide when to apply such a prefilter using idealized cost models or data-driven heuristics, and, as a result, can recommend using a prefilter in regimes where it actively increases space usage. We introduce AutoCSF, a principled algorithm for combining CSFs with prefiltering that comes with a provable safety guarantee: with high probability, it does not recommend a filter when doing so would harm space usage. Our key insight is that while modeling the absolute cost of each index appears intractable, the difference in cost between a CSF and a filter-augmented CSF admits clean analytical bounds via the optimality of Huffman codes. We derive a lower bound on this difference whose sign yields a provably safe decision criterion, along with a complementary upper bound on the maximum achievable savings from prefiltering. Because AutoCSF depends only on the dominant value fraction and a filter cost function, it applies to any approximate set membership structure with a known cost-versus-false-positive-rate tradeoff. We also validate our bounds empirically across three synthetic value distributions and four real-world genomics workloads, and show that the decision criterion never recommends a space-increasing filter while its parameter selection costs at most 0.02 bits per key more than an exhaustive search.

papers.title: Terminal-Optimal Graph Diffusion with Null-Model-Constrained and Structure-Preserving Noise
affiliations: Beijing Electronic Science and Technology Institute
papers.abstract: Graph diffusion models have emerged as a promising approach for generating complex networks, yet they typically face two major drawbacks. First, terminating the forward process in pure Gaussian noise eliminates the intrinsic structural signatures of the original network, which leads to suboptimal generation quality. Second, the absence of constraints along the diffusion trajectory causes progressive degradation of topological features, ultimately resulting in complete structural collapse. To overcome these challenges, we introduce Null-Model-Constrained Graph Diffusion (NMC-GD), a principled framework incorporating specialized designs for graph generation. Specifically, we substitute the conventional isotropic prior with a null-model distribution as the new forward diffusion endpoint, explicitly preserving critical statistical properties of the network. In addition, we develop a null-model-guided continuous-time stochastic differential equation (SDE) and design a directional noise term that enforces a global structural constraint on the diffusion trajectory, striking a balance between stochasticity and structural invariance. Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that NMC-GD achieves superior generation quality and computational efficiency.

papers.title: Equivariant Graph Neural ODEs for Modeling Physical Dynamics
affiliations: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
The City University of New York
papers.abstract: Modeling 3D dynamical systems is a fundamental challenge in the physical and engineering sciences, where Equivariant Graph Neural Networks (EGNNs) have emerged as a powerful paradigm by incorporating geometric symmetries. However, these models are fundamentally constrained by their discrete-time, Markovian framework, which neglects long-range temporal correlations and inevitably leads to error accumulation in long-horizon forecasting. To address this limitation, we introduce the Equivariant Graph Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (EG-NODE), a novel framework that directly learns the continuous-time evolution laws of physical systems. Instead of predicting discrete future states, EG-NODE leverages an equivariant GNN as its core to directly model the ordinary differential equation governing the system's instantaneous rate of change the physical laws of motion thereby natively preserving SE(3) symmetry within the learning process. This continuous-time paradigm enables high-precision predictions at arbitrary time points and allows for the use of adaptive step-size solvers to dynamically balance computational efficiency and accuracy. Extensive experiments on N-body, molecular, and fluid dynamics benchmarks demonstrate that EG-NODE significantly outperforms existing discrete models in long-horizon prediction accuracy and effectively suppresses error propagation. Our work establishes a more fundamental, first-principles-based paradigm for learning continuous physical laws from data. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/egno_egnn-436D/.

papers.title: Dynamic Fusion of Topology and History: The AdaGPS Architecture with GatEdgeformer
papers.abstract: Graph Transformers show immense potential in graph representation learning, yet adaptively capturing complex topological dependencies remains a critical challenge. This paper proposes AdaGPS, a novel adaptive architecture featuring three core improvements. First, the introduced GatEdgeformer module injects edge feature information through a dynamic gating mechanism, enhancing the global attention's perception of complex graph structures. Second, dynamically fusing local structure perception with global attention interaction effectively filters structural noise and accurately extracts long-range dependencies. Third, dynamically fusing historical representations from all previous layers enables the deep AdaGPS architecture to fully utilize rich positional and structural encodings preserved across preceding layers. Extensive experiments strongly demonstrate that the injection of edge features and historical information effectively improves model accuracy. Furthermore, the gated dynamic fusion of local and global features significantly enhances cross-domain generalization capability. Systematic ablations confirm robustness and stability, providing a highly expressive new paradigm for graph representation learning and potential computing power network applications.

papers.title: Advancing Edge Classification through High-Dimensional Causal Modeling of Node-Edge Interplay
papers.abstract: Edge classification, a crucial task for graph applications, remains relatively under-explored compared to link prediction. Current methods often overlook the potential causal influences of node features on edge features, leading to a loss of relevant prior information. In this work, we present an empirical exploration using the Causal Edge Classification Framework (CECF). Unlike conventional causal inference methods, CECF is the first framework to apply causal inference principles to the edge classification task and to explore modeling edge features as a high-dimensional treatment within a causal framework. Based on the node embedding of Graph Neural Network (GNN), CECF seeks to learn a balanced representation of high-dimensional edge features by mitigating the potential influence of node features. Then, a cross-attention network captures the complex dependencies between node and edge features for final edge classification. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CECF not only achieves superior performance but also serves as a flexible, plug-and-play enhancement for existing methods. We also provide empirical analyses, offering insights into when and how this high-dimensional causal modeling framework works for the edge classification.

papers.title: Seesaw Effect of Graph Neural Networks
affiliations: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable success in node classification tasks, but their performance often varies significantly across classes. Some classes benefit from highly accurate predictions, while others perform relatively poorly. Recent advances in imbalanced node classification have provided partial remedies, but often lead to a seesaw effect: improvements in the minority class come at the expense of the majority class. This phenomenon reflects a deeper problem of inter-class interference, where optimizing for some classes during training interferes with or inhibits learning in other classes. This imbalance is closely related to representation bias, where limited representational capacity is unevenly distributed across classes. To address this issue, we propose a graph balancing learning framework based on the structural rebalancing theory. Extensive node classification experiments demonstrate that our framework is applicable to various existing GNN models and effectively addresses the seesaw effect of GNNs. The code is available at https://github.com/linlin-oss/SSER-main.

papers.title: Quantifying and Optimizing Graph Neural Network Sparsification with An Approximation Framework
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown promising performance in learning from graph-structured data, but at the cost of prohibitive computational overhead due to a series of graph-scale operators. To reduce redundant graph operations, previous studies attempt to sparsify the graph by pruning or sampling graph edges, which enables popular GNN deployments in realistic tasks. However, these methods are mostly empirical, lacking a theoretical framework for bounding approximation precision and guiding sparsification policy. In this work, we present the first approximation theory for GNN sparsification that unifies both pruning and sampling paradigms, directly characterizing the representation error deviation in a layer-wise manner. Our theoretical bounds reveal that the pattern of error accumulation throughout iterative graph operators varies with key GNN model properties. Based on our framework, we further derive an optimal sparsification policy that minimizes the layer-wise approximation error under fixed computational constraints. Experimental evaluations confirm our theoretical findings on layer approximation bounds. Remarkably, our proposed optimal sparsification allocation reduces the representation error by up to 10× and retains better prediction accuracy compared to canonical sampling strategies. The code is available at https://github.com/Rechard16/QuOS/.

papers.title: BPB-GNN: Resource-Efficient Distributed GNN Training via Boundary-Aware Prefetching and Cost-Balanced Batch Construction
papers.abstract: Distributed graph neural network (GNN) training is essential for large-scale graph learning, but existing mini-batch frameworks still suffer from substantial inter-partition communication overhead and indirect, coarse-grained GPU memory control. In distributed mini-batch training, remote sampled neighbors cause frequent feature fetching, while fixed seed-node batch sizes cannot accurately reflect the computation graph expansion induced by multi-layer sampling. This paper presents BPB-GNN, a resource-efficient distributed GNN training system that jointly optimizes inter-partition feature access, hierarchical storage management, and mini-batch construction. First, BPB-GNN introduces a training-centric boundary-aware prefetching strategy to localize high-value remote neighbor features associated with boundary nodes in training-node receptive fields. Second, it uses a DRAM/NVMe SSD hierarchy with priority-aware placement and dynamic migration to manage prefetched features under limited DRAM capacity. Finally, it constructs seed-node batches according to estimated sampling-induced load costs rather than equal seed-node counts, thereby balancing batch-level workloads and reducing peak GPU memory usage and its inter-batch fluctuation. These resource-efficient mechanisms may also improve the efficiency of large-scale GNN computation in computing power networks and JointCloud environments. Experiments on real-world graph datasets show that BPB-GNN achieves up to 5× speedup over the baselines while reducing peak GPU memory usage by up to 36%.

papers.title: Q-Flow: Power-Balance-Aware Graph Learning for Power Flow Calculation with Partially Observed Reactive Power
papers.abstract: Classical AC power flow assumes that nodal active and reactive power injections are fully specified. In practice, however, reactive power at some PQ buses may be unavailable due to limited observability or implicit local control. In this paper, we study power flow calculation with partially observed reactive power, where network topology, bus types, active power, and only a subset of reactive-power injections are available as inputs. Specifically, we propose Q-Flow, a graph-based framework for predicting voltage states from such incomplete inputs. Q-Flow combines a Hierarchical Information Fusion (HI-Fuse) with a Multi-Order Gated Kolmogorov–Arnold Network (MoG-KAN), allowing the model to exploit local grid structure, bus-type information, and system-level context while modeling the nonlinear relationship between power injections and voltage states. AC power-flow equations are further incorporated as a physical consistency constraint during training. We evaluate Q-Flow on IEEE 39-, 118-, and 300-bus systems under fixed and sample-dependent reactive-power masks, as well as the complete-Q setting. Q-Flow consistently outperforms representative graph-learning baselines and maintains low voltage-state errors as reactive-power observability decreases.

papers.title: Outcome-aware Evaluation of Recommendation Rankings in Art Therapy Using Multimodal Physiological Utility
papers.abstract: Recommender systems are often evaluated using observable behavioral signals as surrogate relevance measures of user experience. However, in well-being and mental health support applications, user experience is inherently non-observable. To address this limitation, we introduce a multimodal physiology-driven framework for evaluating recommendation rankings in art therapy using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) and eye-gaze signals. We define a physiological utility scalar that captures item-level internal response by combining prefrontal hemodynamic responses with attention and engagement dynamics derived from gaze behavior, enabling direct comparison between system-generated rankings and rankings induced by internal user responses. We show that fNIRS-derived utility exhibits moderate alignment with system rankings (Spearman’s ρ ≈ 0.40, pairwise accuracy ≈ 0.69), with inter-hemispheric functional connectivity showing the strongest alignment among the evaluated neural descriptors. Gaze-derived utility yields stronger observed alignment (ρ ≈ 0.55, pairwise accuracy ≈ 0.75), particularly for attention continuity and engagement-related representations. Multimodal integration yielded the highest observed agreement between recommendation rankings and physiology-derived utility (ρ ≈ 0.61, pairwise accuracy ≈ 0.77). Our findings provide exploratory evidence that multimodal physiological signals may offer complementary information for evaluating recommendation rankings in outcome-sensitive art therapy.

papers.title: Beyond Static Profiles: Intent-Aware Behavioural Control for LLM-based Recommendation Simulation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in recommender systems for user modelling, ranking, and simulation. Among these applications, LLM-based user simulators provide a flexible way to evaluate recommender systems without relying on live user feedback. However, existing simulators typically reduce user behaviour to static preference matching based on fixed user profiles, overlooking the fact that real decisions may also reflect recent preference shifts and exploratory behaviour. To address this limitation, we propose IntRecSim ( Int ent-aware Rec ommendation Sim ulation), a plug-in behavioural control framework for LLM-based user simulation. IntRecSim introduces a lightweight intent mechanism that guides whether the simulated decision should follow long-term preferences, recent behavioural evidence, or exploratory behaviour. Since standard recommendation datasets lack explicit intent annotations, we construct pseudo-intent supervision from historical interactions using hybrid category and semantic preference signals. The inferred intent is injected into the LLM simulator as a dynamic control signal, making the framework compatible with different profile-generation backbones. Experiments on three benchmark datasets, covering discrimination and ranking tasks show that IntRecSim improves simulation performance in most evaluated settings. Further analysis highlights the importance of explicit behavioural control for modelling realistic user decisions in LLM-based recommender simulation.

papers.title: TMemAgent: Transferable Memory for Cross-Domain User Behaviour Simulation
papers.abstract: Reliable evaluation of recommender systems (RSs) often requires user studies or online interaction logs, both of which are costly to obtain for new or low-resource platforms. User behaviour simulation offers a scalable alternative, but existing simulators are typically trained and deployed within a single domain. Thus, they cannot easily reuse the same user agent across domains and often conflate stable user traits with domain-specific interaction evidence. In this paper, we study cross-domain user behaviour simulation: given a user agent learned from a source domain, simulate the same user's behaviour in a target domain. We propose TMemAgent, a transferable memory-based user simulator. The key idea is to treat memory as an actively managed behavioural representation rather than a passive store of past interactions. TMemAgent maintains two complementary memory banks: a transferable memory bank that captures stable user characteristics across domains, and a domain-specific memory bank that preserves local contextual evidence. A memory learning and management (MLM) policy, trained with an actor-critic objective, dynamically decides when to retrieve, add, reflect, update, or forget memory entries. Experiments on three Amazon domains show that TMemAgent improves user-agent prediction performance, yielding gains of around 12% in same-domain settings and around 14% in cross-domain settings compared with the strongest baseline. Moreover, the transferred agents preserve behavioural diversity close to the ground truth, demonstrating that explicit MLM supports scalable, transferable, and behaviourally realistic user simulation for RS evaluation.

papers.title: Beyond States: Investigating the Effects of Context on User Modeling with Feature-Conditioned Markov Models
affiliations: TH Köln - University of Applied Sciences
papers.abstract: User behavior simulation is widely used to evaluate interactive information retrieval systems, but classical state-based approaches (e.g., Markov models) have limited ability to incorporate contextual information relevant for decision-making. We address this limitation by introducing a feature-conditioned Markov-style user model, in which transition probabilities are modeled as functions of positional, content-based, and interaction-derived features, enabling context-aware decision making while preserving the structural simplicity and computational efficiency of state-based models. Applying a multi-level framework that assesses predictive fit and behavioral fidelity, we analyze how different sources of contextual information contribute to realistic user simulation across multiple datasets, search settings, and feature configurations.
