Our results show that incorporating contextual features improves the models' ability to reproduce key aspects of real user interactions, but that their effectiveness hinges on search scenario and modeling objective. Instead of a “one-size-fits-all” solution, effective simulation requires task- and setting-specific feature selection. Our framework provides a practical and interpretable basis for making these choices.

papers.title: Role of Personality in Conversational Information Seeking
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for information seeking, where users find, compare, and evaluate information through dialogue. In this role, the assistant does more than retrieve or generate content: it shapes how users articulate constraints, ask follow-up questions, verify claims, and decide when an answer is sufficient for action. Yet little is known about how user personality, assistant personality, and task context jointly influence these interactions. We examine personality as a controllable variable in conversational information seeking and study its effects on user behaviour and interaction quality. We conducted a controlled within-subject study in which assistant personality and task type were experimentally varied, while participant personality was measured using Big Five scores. Twenty-six participants each completed three information-seeking tasks under three assistant personality conditions: extraverted, conscientious, and neutral. Tasks covered exploratory travel planning, comparative smartphone shopping, and verification-sensitive health and diet information seeking. Data included conversation logs, behavioural traces, post-interaction questionnaires, an exit questionnaire, and Big Five measures. The assistant conditions were behaviourally distinct: the extraverted assistant produced longer turns, the conscientious assistant elicited higher user word share and more turns, and the neutral baseline fell between them. The strongest effect was a task-by-assistant interaction on trust and delegation, with preferred styles varying by task. No global winner emerged, but participants strongly preferred style choice or adaptation. These findings position assistant personality as a context-sensitive interactional design variable rather than a globally optimisable system property.

papers.title: How Cultural Background and Cognitive Style Shape Responses to Sustainability-Aware Explanations in Healthy Food Recommender Systems
affiliations: School of Hospitality and Tourism - Hue University
papers.abstract: Food recommender systems are increasingly expected to encourage healthier, more sustainable choices, often through sustainability-aware explanations that blend transparency with persuasive messaging. Yet little is known about how users' cultural backgrounds and cognitive styles shape their responses to these explanations. In this paper, we investigate the influence of cultural background and cognitive style on users' behavioral decisions and subjective evaluations of sustainability-aware explanations in food recommender systems. We conducted a user study using a web-based food recommendation prototype incorporating three Cialdini-inspired persuasive explanation strategies: Authority, Commitment, and Social Proof. The study compared Asian and European participants and further examined differences across cognitive-style groups. The results show that cultural background significantly influenced both recipe-selection behavior and users' perceptions of explanation quality, whereas cognitive style showed comparatively smaller effects that mainly affected subjective explanation evaluations. On the other hand, the persuasive explanation strategies themselves produced relatively stable behavioral effects across cultural and cognitive-style groups, with no significant interaction effects after multiple-comparison correction. These findings provide practical implications for designing food recommender systems that effectively balance persuasive support, transparency, and cultural adaptability to encourage healthier and more environmentally responsible consumption behaviors.

papers.title: On Mitigating Data Sparsity in Conversational Recommender Systems
papers.abstract: Conversational recommender systems (CRSs) infer user preferences from dialogue contexts, but they suffer from severe data sparsity in both dialogue and entity spaces. Dialogue data are linguistically diverse and open-ended, making it difficult to generalize across varied expressions. Meanwhile, existing CRS models often rely on large knowledge graphs, where only a small fraction of entities receive effective supervision during training, leaving the majority under-trained or entirely unseen at inference time. To address these challenges, we propose DACRS, a novel CRS framework consisting of three modules: Dialogue Augmentation, Knowledge-Guided Entity Modeling, and Dialogue–Entity Matching. The Dialogue Augmentation module adopts a two-stage augmentation pipeline to enrich dialogue contexts and improve robustness to linguistic variation. The Knowledge-Guided Entity Modeling module leverages knowledge graphs through entity substitution and an entity similarity constraint to enhance representation learning for sparsely supervised and unseen entities. Finally, the Dialogue–Entity Matching module integrates dialogue representations with mentioned entity embeddings via dialogue-guided attention aggregation, yielding user representations that capture both explicit and implicit preferences. Extensive experiments on two public benchmark datasets demonstrate that DACRS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art conversational recommender systems.

papers.title: POLAR: Policy Optimization through Larger Reasoners
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is a practical way to improve the reasoning and decision-making abilities of large language models, but its training signal is often sparse. When a policy faces prompts beyond its current ability, every sampled trajectory in a group may fail the verifier, resulting in an all-zero group. In this case, group-relative policy optimization gives little useful gradient even when the prompt contains valuable learning content. This capacity-difficulty mismatch is especially costly for smaller models used in knowledge-intensive and web-interaction tasks. We present POLAR, a difficulty-aware training framework that augments on-policy RL with conditional guidance from a larger reasoner. POLAR uses the standard GRPO branch when at least one sampled response succeeds, and switches to a supervised objective over verified teacher trajectories only when the whole student group receives zero reward. The method can turn otherwise wasted all-zero groups into targeted learning opportunities while keeping policy exploration on prompts the student can handle. We formalize the switching criterion, teacher selection objective, mixed RL/supervised loss, and compute overhead. We evaluate POLAR on WebShop, GAIA, and WebWalkerQA using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B policies. The results show consistent gains over matched GRPO baselines, with large improvements on hard web traversal questions for the two smaller policies. Ablations and diagnostics further show that the gains come from the proposed all-zero recovery mechanism.

papers.title: The Compaction Cliff in Long-Running AI Agent Memory
papers.abstract: A safety rule and an episodic log compete for the same tokens in an AI agent's context. When the budget overflows, both are summarized at the same rate; only the rule needs exact wording to remain enforceable. On 20 production agent configurations, Claude Code's /compact prompt on Sonnet 4.6 preserves 53% of safety rules after one compaction round and 10% after five. We name this the Compaction Cliff. We address it with Knowledge Triage, a framework that classifies each line of an agent's knowledge base by type and routes each type through its own retention policy. Three deterministic operators implement this triage across the three context-management operations: TypeCompact rewrites items in place under per-type fidelity, TypeDecompose partitions a topic too large to compact safely, replicating in-scope safety rules across partitions, and TypeRetrieve fetches items from external storage with in-scope rules pinned ahead of relevance. On five public corpora, TypeCompact preserves 2-4× more safety rules than the strongest single-shot LLM compactor at every ratio, with 96% recall over five rounds. TypeDecompose reaches 0% locality violations against 93% under uniform partitioning. TypeRetrieve reaches 100% recall@50 against 73% for the best single-shot LLM retriever. On three downstream behavioral benchmarks, we outperform the production Sonnet compactor on medical compliance (paired McNemar p < 10 -8 on preservation, N = 200), the full-policy and hierarchical baselines on retail task pass rate (p < 0.01, N = 115), and the hierarchical compaction on the airline domain (p = 0.024). We release AgentArtifactCorpus (396,934 agent configurations from 54,628 public GitHub repositories), the classifier, and the reference implementation.

papers.title: H-Mem: Hawkes-driven Adaptive Forgetting for Long-Horizon Agent Memory
papers.abstract: For long-horizon LLM agents, forgetting is not a housekeeping detail: it determines whether the agent preserves commitments, updates stale beliefs, and reasons coherently under finite memory. Yet existing policies mostly score each memory in isolation, so they cannot capture a central fact of agent interaction: a later event can revive or disambiguate an earlier memory. This mismatch makes budgeted forgetting a structural bottleneck for reliable agent memory. We propose H-Mem, a deceptively simple retention controller that turns forgetting into an event-coupled process. H-Mem first partitions memories into semantic clusters, allocates budget across clusters to avoid topic monopoly, and then runs cluster-local Hawkes excitation so that new related memories reinforce useful predecessors with diminishing returns. Bounded base intensity protects isolated but potentially important memories before relational evidence accumulates. This design confines propagation to semantically valid neighborhoods while keeping retention decisions auditable, causal, and budget-aware. We formalize an indistinguishability barrier for item-wise forgetting: when two memories share the same self history but differ in neighborhood evidence, any isolated scorer must make the same decision and can incur unavoidable regret. We also prove feasibility, bounded intensity, noise-stable influence, anti-monopoly quota behavior, optimal partition-matroid projection, monotone quota sensitivity, and end-to-end complexity. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S show that H-Mem consistently improves QA and evidence preservation; on LoCoMo at 25% memory, it raises Qwen QA from 42.6 to 47.4 and Evidence Survival@B from 41.3 to 61.1 over the strongest baseline under a matched memory pipeline.

papers.title: Predicting Partial Answer Quality and Utility in Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become a promising paradigm for multi-hop question answering, where a reasoning model iteratively issues queries to a retriever and incorporates newly retrieved context into subsequent reasoning steps. While this iterative process can improve final answer quality, current evaluations of agentic RAG largely focus on end-to-end outcomes and provide limited visibility into how a model's answer state changes during generation. In this work, we introduce an in-trajectory probing framework to study intermediate answer states in agentic RAG. Specifically, after each retrieval-reasoning iteration, we force an agentic model to stop reasoning and generate an intermediate answer based on its current state. This allows us to define two iteration-level measures: partial answer quality at each iteration, and partial utility as the change in partial answer quality across iterations. Our analysis across multi-hop QA benchmarks reveals that partial answer quality often plateaus before natural termination, with many later iterations contributing only small measurable improvements. Accordingly, we formulate two prediction tasks, partial answer quality prediction and partial utility prediction, and study trajectory-derived signals from intra-iteration, inter-iteration, and query-iteration perspectives. Experiments show that partial answer quality is more predictable than partial utility, with supervised models achieving Pearson's r above 0.43 for quality prediction. Finally, using predicted answer quality and utility for early stopping reduces average iteration count by about 11% while preserving about 98% of the final answer quality achieved by natural stopping.

papers.title: R2-Searcher: Calibrating Retrieval and Reasoning Boundaries for Agentic Search
papers.abstract: Recent search agents for multi-hop reasoning often fail by either retrieving incomplete evidence or reasoning over irrelevant portions of the retrieved content, leading to a retrieval-reasoning boundary shift. We propose R 2 -Searcher, a novel framework that explicitly explores and calibrates the retrieval and reasoning boundaries via fine-grained, query-token-guided evidence modeling and post-retrieval reflection. Specifically, R 2 -Searcher: (1) constructs fine-grained reasoning contexts by extracting precise facts from retrieved content based on query token semantics (e.g., subjects, actions, temporal markers, and degree modifiers), thereby guiding the attention of search agent; (2) introduces a retrieval reflection mechanism that evaluates and corrects boundary deviations after each retrieval step, guiding the generation of improved queries grounded in the extracted reasoning contexts; and (3) employs an end-to-end reasoning-reflection-guided reinforcement learning algorithm, R 2 PO, which jointly optimizes both boundaries through a tree-based exploration of reasoning regions and reflections. Our method significantly enhances the quality of both retrieval and reasoning, establishing an iterative loop where retrieval and reasoning mutually enhance each other. Extensive experiments on seven complex multi-hop QA benchmarks demonstrate that R 2 -Searcher significantly outperforms state-of-the-art agentic search methods in answer accuracy and retrieval-reasoning quality. Ablation studies further confirm the critical role of retrieval-reasoning boundary calibration. Implementation code is available for reproducibility: https://github.com/Applied-Machine-Learning-Lab/CIKM2026_R2-Searcher.

papers.title: Mind2Report: Expert-Level Commercial Report Synthesis via Cognitive Deep Research Agent
affiliations: State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China
State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, China
Artificial Intelligence Engineering Institute, iFLYTEK Co., Ltd
industryAffiliations: Artificial Intelligence Engineering Institute, iFLYTEK Co., Ltd
papers.abstract: Synthesizing informative commercial reports from massive and noisy web sources is critical for high-stakes business decisions. Although recent deep research agents (DRAs) achieve notable progress, their reports remain limited in quality, reliability, and coverage. These mainly stem from ambiguous intents that cause search drift, retrieved web content that rapidly saturates the context window, and single-pass synthesis that limits report comprehensiveness. In this work, we propose Mind2Report, a cognitive deep research agent that emulates commercial analysts to synthesize expert-level reports. Mind2Report first probes fine-grained commercial intent to establish a structured outline, then recursively explores web sources and distills validated evidence into research memory to preserve context efficiency. Meanwhile, the research memory and outline continuously co-evolve, refining the report structure to avoid rigid initial planning. Finally, Mind2Report iteratively synthesizes the report based on the evolving outline and accumulated evidence. Together, these designs enable reliable and context-efficient long-horizon commercial deep research. To rigorously evaluate commercial DRAs, we further construct QRC-Eval, comprising 200 real-world commercial tasks and a holistic evaluation framework covering report quality, reliability, and coverage. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Mind2Report consistently outperforms leading proprietary and open-source DRAs, while ablations verify the effectiveness of each module and further analyze the challenges they address. We expect this work to advance the development of commercial deep research agents. The implementation of Mind2Report and the QRC-Eval data are publicly available (https://github.com/ustc-ai4science/Mind2Report).

papers.title: HARE: History-aware Repository-Level Memory Retrieval for Conventional Commit Header Generation
papers.abstract: High-quality commit messages are crucial software knowledge that summarize the intent, scope, and rationale of code changes, which improves maintenance, code review, and repository traceability. As the Conventional Commits Specification (CCS) has been increasingly adopted in modern software development, commit header generation must produce not only fluent descriptions but also repository-appropriate structured header fields (type and scope). In this work, we study CCS-style commit header generation, focusing on the structural format [optional scope]: . We introduce CCHBench, a benchmark of 93,807 conventional commits from 119 repositories and nine programming languages, constructed with repository-level filtering, structural validation, and chronological splits. Our systematic evaluation shows that existing LLMs struggle in particular with repository-specific type and scope prediction, even when provided with generic in-context demonstrations. To address these limitations, we propose HARE, a novel H istory- A ware Re pository-level memory framework for generating conventional commit headers. Extensive experiments across multiple LLM backbones show that HARE substantially improves conventional commit header generation over zero-shot and ICL-based baselines. HARE improves the quality of natural language generation and the prediction of structured CCS fields, especially for repository-dependent type and scope fields. Ablation studies verify the contributions of episodic memory, evolutionary memory, and PMI-based reranking, while robustness analyses show that HARE remains effective across repositories with both sparse and extensive histories. Our framework implementation and dataset are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22006538.

papers.title: CURE: Circuit-Aware Unlearning for LLM-based Recommendation
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have opened new opportunities for recommender systems by enabling rich semantic understanding and reasoning about user interests and item attributes. However, as privacy regulations tighten, incorporating user data into LLM-based recommendation (LLMRec) introduces significant privacy risks, making unlearning algorithms increasingly crucial for practical deployment. Despite growing interest in LLMRec unlearning, most existing approaches formulate unlearning as a weighted combination of forgetting and retaining objectives while updating model parameters in a uniform manner. Such formulations inevitably induce gradient conflicts between the two objectives, leading to unstable optimization and resulting in either ineffective unlearning or severe degradation of model utility. Moreover, the unlearning procedure remains largely black-box, undermining its transparency and trustworthiness. To tackle these challenges, we propose CURE, a circuit-aware unlearning framework that disentangles model components into functionally distinct subsets and selectively updates them. Here, a circuit refers to a computational subgraph that is causally responsible for task-specific behaviors. Specifically, we extract the core circuits underlying item recommendation and analyze how individual modules within these circuits contribute to the forget and retain objectives. Based on this analysis, these modules are categorized into forget-specific, retain-specific, and task-shared groups, each subject to function-specific update rules to mitigate gradient conflicts during unlearning. Experiments on real-world datasets show that our approach achieves more effective unlearning than existing baselines.

papers.title: EchoTrace: Diagnosing Recursive Risks in LLM-Powered Recommender Systems
affiliations: Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST)
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into recommender systems as data augmenters, profile generators, and recommendation modules. While these roles can enhance semantic understanding and recommendation quality, they also introduce LLM-specific risks such as bias and hallucination. These risks become more critical in feedback-loop settings, where LLM-generated signals and recommendations recursively shape future training data and recommendation dynamics. In this paper, we propose a role-aware, phase-wise diagnostic framework for analyzing how LLM-induced risks emerge, propagate, and accumulate in LLM-powered recommender systems. Our framework combines controlled feedback-loop simulation with longitudinal phase-wise diagnosis across LLM-generated content, recommendation outputs, feedback-loop dynamics, and ecosystem-level effects. Experiments on widely used benchmarks show that LLM-based components can amplify popularity bias, introduce spurious signals through hallucination, and gradually produce polarized and self-reinforcing exposure patterns over time. The code for EchoTrace is available at https://github.com/DongUk-Park/EchoTrace.

papers.title: Diffusion-guided Disentanglement with Causal Debiasing for Cross-Domain Recommendation
affiliations: Nanjing University of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Cross-Domain Recommendation (CDR) effectively alleviates data sparsity by transferring knowledge from auxiliary domains. To achieve fine-grained transfer, disentangled learning is increasingly adopted to decouple user interaction motivations. However, existing paradigms predominantly rely on shallow linear assumptions that fail to decouple complex non-linear semantic noise and structural biases during knowledge transfer. Furthermore, their static training-stage debiasing exposes the inference phase to structural popularity bias and propagates confounding effects into final rankings. To address these challenges, we propose Diffusion-guided Disentanglement with Causal Debiasing for Cross-Domain Recommendation (DiDC-CDR). Specifically, DiDC-CDR extracts robust single-domain priors from global and niche subgraphs to explicitly capture long-tail interests. Conditioned on these priors, a diffusion module iteratively purifies cross-domain shared item attributes, which subsequently guide a geometric orthogonal constraint to rigorously isolate intrinsic interests from conformity. Finally, causal counterfactual intervention is executed to eliminate popularity-induced spurious correlations during inference. Extensive experiments across six diverse real-world dual-target CDR scenarios demonstrate that DiDC-CDR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Notably, in the Elec & Cloth task characterized by a substantial domain gap, our method achieves improvements of 14.32% and 16.33% in HR@10 and NDCG@10 for the target Cloth domain, respectively, thereby providing a novel generative and causal paradigm for robust knowledge transfer.

papers.title: POPCORN: Popularity-decoupled Interest Matching for Personalized News Recommendation
papers.abstract: To alleviate the information overload problem on online news platforms, personalized news recommendation aims to provide news articles aligned with users' interests. Most conventional methods suffer from popularity bias. To mitigate this, popularity-aware methods regard popularity-driven clicks as bias. Although these methods show higher accuracy, they still face three challenges: (C1) discriminating click types on popular news, (C2) topic-unaware popularity modeling, and (C3) dealing with interest signal attenuation. To jointly address these challenges, we propose POPCORN, a novel model-agnostic framework for POPularity-deCOupled inteRest matching in personalized News recommendation, with three key strategies: (1) Popularity-decoupled news modeling to discriminate interest-driven and popularity-driven clicks, (2) Candidate-guided user modeling to amplify a user's interest signal for a candidate news based on its topic, and (3) Popularity-penalized interest matching to suppress popular news not genuinely interesting to the user. Extensive experiments with three real-world datasets and eight state-of-the-art methods demonstrate that the methods augmented with POPCORN consistently outperform their original versions.

papers.title: Beyond Dense Propagation: A Remove-and-Reintegrate Framework for Debiased Short-Video Recommendation
papers.abstract: Graph neural network based recommender systems have achieved strong performance by propagating collaborative signals over user-item interaction graphs. However, in short-video recommendation platforms, the near-zero interaction cost produces substantially denser interaction graphs and amplifies popularity bias, where some high-degree nodes become connected to semantically heterogeneous neighborhoods and behave as incoherent hubs. These nodes propagate conflicting signals during message passing, degrading graph-based representation learning and recommendation performance. Existing methods reduce popularity bias by adjusting representations during or after graph propagation. However, in dense short-video graphs with high-degree nodes, conflicting signals can be repeatedly aggregated and amplified, making such adjustments less effective. Motivated by this observation, we propose a remove-and-reintegrate framework for short-video recommendation. To reduce popularity bias, we remove incoherent hubs and construct a purified interaction graph by analyzing the structure in an SVD-derived latent space. This is because SVD captures global interaction patterns and, thus, can identify such incoherent hubs. After that, we further design a lightweight reintegration module that aligns the removed nodes back into the recommendation space through ranking-aware optimization, allowing their representations to be preserved without reintroducing noisy propagation. Experiments on three public short-video recommendation datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently improves multiple graph-based recommendation backbones and achieves superior performance on both recommendation accuracy and popularity-aware evaluation metrics.

papers.title: GCL-Detox: Disentangling Uniformity for Robust and Effective Graph Contrastive Learning-Based Recommendation
papers.abstract: Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL) enhances recommendation via embedding uniformity, yet this very property introduces a critical vulnerability exploitable by poisoning attacks. Existing defenses overlook this geometric weakness. In this paper, we propose GCL-Detox , a defense framework that mitigates such attacks by systematically regulating embedding uniformity. Our key idea is a gradient-decoupled, tri-phase training strategy with progressive loss annealing, which enables a controlled transition from uniformity-driven representation learning to clustering-oriented recommendation optimization. We provide a rigorous theoretical analysis showing that the proposed training dynamics guarantee a monotonic increase in embedding non-uniformity, establish strict superiority over conventional joint training, and yield an explicit robustness bound against poisoning attacks. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets confirm that GCL-Detox significantly enhances robustness against state-of-the-art attacks while maintaining competitive accuracy, validating both our theoretical and empirical claims.

papers.title: From Interactions to Embeddings: A New Perspective for Poisoning Recommender Systems
affiliations: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.abstract: Recommender systems are essential tools for managing information overload. However, their vulnerability to data poisoning attacks presents substantial security concerns, where attackers can inject fake users to manipulate recommendations. Existing attacks, nevertheless, face two primary challenges, failing to fully reveal the vulnerabilities of recommender systems: First, representing fake users as a large constrained binary interaction matrix is hard to optimize, due to its high dimensionality and combinatorial nature. Second, modeling the poisoning effects of fake users across all training steps of the victim recommender is intractable. To address these two challenges, we propose FEO (Fake Embedding Optimization with Forward-looking), a novel poisoning attack with fake embedding optimization and single-step forward-looking . FEO encodes fake user behaviors through learnable embeddings, avoiding the complexity of optimizing the interaction matrix. Moreover, we focus on the critical training step when fake users form positive pairs with target items, to examine the poisoning effects of fake users in manipulating target item embeddings, instead of modeling the entire training process. Our framework enables fake user generation with both effectiveness and efficiency, revealing significant vulnerabilities of recommender systems. Extensive experiments across three real-world datasets, five victim models, and five scenarios demonstrate FEO's superior attack performance.

papers.title: EBD: Engagement-aware Bidirectional Debiasing with User Micro-Behaviors in E-commerce Recommendations
affiliations: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
State Key Laboratory of AI Safety, Institute of Computing Technology, CAS
papers.abstract: Click-through Rate (CTR) prediction and Conversion Rate (CVR) prediction, as core tasks in modern e-commerce recommender systems, are conventionally formulated as binary classification tasks using click/purchase labels. However, this approach suffers from Intention-Action Divergence (IAD) bias, where users' explicit actions (e.g., click/purchase) misalign with their implicit interest levels inferred from fine-grained interactions (e.g., dwell time, swipe velocity). In this paper, we focus on mitigating the IAD bias by leveraging users' implicit intentions. Specifically, we first mine more than one hundred kinds of user-device interactions in their decision-making process, termed Micro-Behaviors (MBs). Instead of constructing resource-consuming sequential features, we compress MBs into a lightweight sample-level engagement score that scalably quantifies users' intentions for billions of samples. Second, considering the inaccessibility of MBs in online serving, we propose a Pointwise-and-Pairwise Engagement Debiasing (P 2 ED) approach to mitigate the IAD bias in the CVR task, which utilizes the predefined engagement scores only in model training process. Finally, we extend the P 2 ED method to the CTR task with a novel Engagement-aware Bidirectional Debiasing (EBD) framework to address the limitation of missing engagement scores in non-click samples. Our method improves CVR and CTR performance, delivering +2.2‰/+1.4‰ AUC gains offline and driving 4.27% GMV growth and 1.38% IPV lift in online A/B tests. In addition, we also release a sampling version of our product dataset to enable future research, the first one containing abundant MB signals for the CTR task, which is available at https://taobao-ebd.github.io/.

papers.title: Graph Neural Delay Differential Equations for Continuous Epidemic Forecasting
affiliations: Southern University of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Reliable epidemic forecasting is essential for early warning and proactive public health decision-making. Existing spatio-temporal forecasting methods often model regional interactions on fixed discrete grids and rely on instantaneous or uniformly delayed transmission assumptions, limiting their ability to capture asynchronous epidemic spread and irregular surveillance records. To address these limitations, we propose EpiDDE, a continuous-time delay-aware framework based on graph neural delay differential equations for epidemic forecasting. EpiDDE first estimates latent epidemic delay priors from surveillance sequences, including both within-region temporal delays and cross-region propagation delays. It then constructs a Delay-Aware Transmission Graph (DATG) by combining sequence-derived delay priors with learnable regional representations, enabling data-driven modeling of directed and heterogeneous delayed dependencies. Conditioned on the learned DATG, EpiDDE evolves regional epidemic states through a graph-coupled neural DDE driven by delayed self-region and cross-region messages. Extensive experiments on four real-world epidemic datasets show that EpiDDE achieves competitive epidemic forecasting performance across multiple prediction horizons. Further analyses demonstrate the effectiveness of delay estimation, DATG learning, and DDE-based continuous evolution, particularly for long-horizon forecasting and irregular observations.

papers.title: ZoomLens Stock Forecasting: Adaptive Multi-Scale Modeling for Market-Aware Investment
affiliations: School of Computer Science and Engineering, Northeastern University
papers.abstract: Modern stock markets demand a sophisticated capability to simultaneously focus on fine-grained local volatility and perceive broader global trends. However, existing methods often remain limited by rigid temporal architectures and a neglect of dynamic cross-asset dependencies. To address these challenges, we propose an A daptive M ulti-scale signal S election and F usion M odel (AMSFM). Functioning as an intelligent ZoomLens , AMSFM incorporates an adaptive temporal scale selector that dynamically aligns modeling horizons with real-time market regimes, effectively capturing both microscopic fluctuations and macroscopic contexts. Furthermore, we propose an interpretable attribution and interaction mechanism to decompose forecasts into transparent feature contributions. To capture broader market influences, our model employs a market-aware forecasting strategy that integrates global context to perceive panoramic spillover effects without relying on rigid prior knowledge. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that AMSFM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks. The source code is available at: https://github.com/yizhibeijibei/AMSFM.

papers.title: Retrieve the Right Signal: Decomposition-Guided Retrieval-Augmented Forecasting for Financial Markets
papers.abstract: Financial time-series forecasting is important for portfolio construction, risk management, and investment strategy design, but financial markets are highly nonstationary and often lack stable periodicity. Retrieval-augmented forecasting is attractive in this setting because similar market conditions can lead to similar historical market responses. However, when retrieval is performed over the raw signal, similarity can be dominated by level or trend rather than by detrended temporal patterns that are more relevant to future market reactions. We propose a decomposition-guided retrieval framework for financial time-series forecasting. It decomposes each input into a trend component and a detrended component using a strictly causal moving average, and performs retrieval in the detrended space. The retrieved detrended futures are used both as a direct retrieval-based forecasting component and as Retrieval-as-Context (RAC) tokens that provide additional context to the forecasting backbone. This design separates trend modeling from retrieval over detrended temporal patterns, reducing misleading raw-signal matches while preserving historical market responses that are relevant to the current query. It also allows retrieved information to influence representation learning, rather than being used only through output-level fusion. Across eight real-world financial datasets and two TFB financial-market benchmarks, the framework outperforms retrieval-augmented, decomposition-based, attention-based, patch-based, clustering-based, and classical statistical baselines. On the eight real-world datasets, the framework ranks first in 23 out of 48 settings under both MSE and MAE; on the TFB benchmarks, it ranks first in 7 out of 8 MSE configurations.

papers.title: Anomaly-Regularized Foundation Models for Robust Electricity Market Forecasting
papers.abstract: In recent cases of multivariate time series forecasting, models are facing challenges that are due to complex interactions between multiple variables, rapid regime shifts and extreme events that cause problems, especially in the domain of electricity markets like the Australian National Electricity Market (NEM). In our research, we tried to improve the existing singular value decomposition autoencoder (SVD-AE) by introducing a spectral aspect to the anomaly scoring and coming up with a regularisation framework aimed at increasing the accuracy of the time series foundation model (TSFM). We used 5-minute resolution NEM data to evaluate our framework; specifically, the anomaly detection part was done on multiple variables influencing the Regional Reference Price (RRP), such as demand, generation, interconnector, temporal and weather, but the zero-shot forecasting and fine-tuning of the forecasting part were done solely on raw and regularised RRP against the same original ground truth. The forecasting outputs from our Hybrid-Scored SVD-AE (HS-SVD-AE) are then compared to the existing baseline SVD-AE. The experiments showed that in the fine-tuned scenario of TSFM, our proposed framework outperforms the existing SVD-AE regularisation by a good margin, but in the zero-shot scenario, SVD-AE performs better by a slight difference. Our findings in this research show that explicitly scored spectral information structure can complement multivariate anomaly detection, which produces more robust foundation model forecasting.

papers.title: A Deep Learning Framework for Quantile Demand Forecasting in E-commerce with Doubly Censored Data
papers.abstract: In recent years, a growing number of online retail companies have embraced deep learning models for demand forecasting, leveraging their scalability in processing large-scale datasets. Accurate demand forecasts enable improved planning and allow operational flexibility to adjust sales accordingly. Moreover, quantile estimation has gained widespread application as it offers valuable uncertainty quantification, thereby enhancing the robustness of decision-making processes. However, limited research has addressed the effective quantification of uncertainty when target labels are ambiguous. In retail, actual sales can be capped by stock and boosted by temporary promotions, whereas the target is underlying demand. Such scenarios are characterized by double censoring and no deep-learning pipeline yet exists for such data. In this paper, we introduce a straightforward framework for learning quantiles from doubly-censored observations and propose a tailored evaluation metric. Our approach is supported by theoretical guarantees, and we empirically demonstrate that our metric correlates well with the oracle calibration measure. Experimental results show that our estimator surpasses existing baselines. Finally, inventory simulations and real-world applications confirm the practical utility of our method in retail operations.

papers.title: EarthOracle: A Self-Correcting World Model with Observational Feedback for Long-Horizon Earth Forecasting
affiliations: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
The City University of New York
papers.abstract: While deep learning models have achieved unprecedented success in short-to-medium-range weather forecasting, they universally suffer from error accumulation, spectral decay, and climate drift during long-horizon autoregressive rollouts. We argue that this stems from a fundamental paradigm flaw: treating forecasting as an open-loop “one-shot extrapolation” rather than the closed-loop “predict-observe-assimilate” cycle inherent in operational numerical systems. To address this, we propose EarthOracle, a self-correcting Earth World Model that explicitly embeds sparse observations into its inference loop. At its core lies a Differentiable Data Assimilation (Diff-DA) module, which dynamically injects heterogeneous and sparse observations (e.g., satellite radiances, buoy data, radiosondes) directly into the latent state using learnable uncertainty weights. Coupled with a novel self-correction training objective based on perturbation consistency, EarthOracle actively digests new information to suppress error amplification over long trajectories. Furthermore, we introduce a Cross-Scale Memory mechanism that disentangles fast-evolving weather signals from slow-varying ocean-atmosphere coupled modes in the latent space, ensuring that observation feedbacks modulate the system at physically appropriate timescales. Extensive experiments on ERA5 (1979–2024) and multi-source sparse observations demonstrate that EarthOracle significantly outperforms pure autoregressive baselines in Subseasonal-to-Decadal (S2D) forecasting. It maintains stable energy spectra and climatology over long rollouts, and matches the predictive skill of dynamical S2D models on critical teleconnection indices (e.g., ENSO, MJO) at less than 0.1% of their inference cost. By redefining long-term Earth forecasting from open-loop extrapolation to closed-loop assimilation, EarthOracle provides a scalable and robust new paradigm for real-world AI climate prediction.

papers.title: MemPerceiver: Adaptive Multi-Scale Memory Reveals Biome-Specific Temporal Fingerprints in Carbon Flux Prediction
papers.abstract: Terrestrial carbon flux prediction is critical for quantifying ecosystem carbon sources and sinks. However, current deep learning models still struggle with cross-ecosystem generalisation across the heterogeneous biomes covered by global eddy-covariance networks. A fundamental reason is that different ecosystems are shaped by past climate over very different timescales: climate may continue to influence ecosystem processes for only weeks in tropical savannas but for months in temperate forests, while existing models apply a single uniform temporal context window to all ecosystems. To address this challenge, we propose MemPerceiver, a multimodal framework that augments the EcoPerceiver backbone with six ecologically motivated memory scales (-180 to -7 days) and a per-scale gating network, allowing the model to learn which of the predefined temporal horizons are most informative for each prediction, without requiring biome-specific lag labels. On the CarbonSense benchmark of 385 eddy-covariance sites across 15 IGBP classes, MemPerceiver achieves state-of-the-art performance on both Net Ecosystem Exchange (NEE) and Gross Primary Production (GPP), with particularly large gains in data-scarce settings: relative to EcoPerceiver, it reduces RMSE by 23.0% on the one-shot WAT class and improves NSE by 24.0% on the zero-shot SNO class. Averaging the learned gate activations within each biome yields an interpretable temporal fingerprint, and within-biome consistency analysis shows that these fingerprints provide a stable, model-derived view of biome-specific ecological memory. The code is available at https://github.com/gaoshan-bi/MemPerceiver.

papers.title: AquaNord-SE: A Large-Scale Longitudinal Multimodal Benchmark for Swedish Inland Water Quality
papers.abstract: Predicting inland water quality reliably requires integrating water quality observations, satellite remote sensing, meteorological reanalysis, and catchment descriptors, yet no benchmark provides these modalities jointly under reproducible evaluation protocols for optically complex, seasonally ice-affected inland waters. We introduce AquaNord-SE , a longitudinal multimodal benchmark of 883,325 samples from 18,743 Swedish lake and river monitoring stations over 2000-2025, integrating 38 water quality parameters from SLU Miljödata MVM with observations from five satellite sensor streams, ERA5-Land and MESAN meteorological reanalysis, 64 HydroATLAS catchment attributes, and 13 derived water quality indices. The dataset is structured as station-aligned multimodal feature sets and spatial-temporal archives, accompanied by a five-tier modality ablation design and three orthogonal generalization splits across spatial, temporal, and latitudinal axes. Benchmarking across tabular, spatial-temporal, and multimodal baselines under split conformal prediction and quantile regression reveals that static catchment attributes alone (R 2 =0.303 Chlorophyll- a , R 2 =0.642 Secchi) consistently outperform all non-tabular models, while total phosphorus proves intractable across all families (best R 2 =0.118). Conformal calibration error increases from 0.062 to 0.225 across the oligotrophic-hypereutrophic gradient, co-locating with the eutrophic regime where atmospheric correction (AC) failure exceeds 65% of optical retrievals. We additionally release a gridded water quality index (WQI) NetCDF at 5 km resolution over 2000-2025, supporting Water Framework Directive (WFD) compliance and long-term trend analysis. The dataset and evaluation protocols are publicly available to support reproducible research in environmental knowledge management and data-driven water quality assessment and monitoring.

papers.title: Multilayer Network Backboning
papers.abstract: Data collection comes with some amount of measurement error and network data is not exempt from this issue. Once a network is collected, it is necessary to test whether an edge exists with some degree of statistical certainty. This is a process called “network backboning.” There are a number of approaches to perform network backboning, but the approaches in the literature only work for directed, bipartite networks, and/or hypergraphs. To the best of our knowledge, there is no network backboning approach that takes into account the additional information that comes from multilayer networks. In this paper, we provide the first such approach, by extending the popular noise-corrected backboning approach using a similar Bayesian framework to consider potential layer-layer (anti)correlations. In synthetic experiments, we show that using the additional information that comes from the multiple layers is beneficial to find more accurate network backbones, at a minimal additional time complexity cost. We provide an extensive case study using a network from Wikipedia to show the real world usefulness of extracting multilayer backbones.

papers.title: Learning to Preserve Structural Backbones for Robust Graph Neural Networks
affiliations: Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are effective for modeling relational data, yet they remain vulnerable to adversarial structural perturbations. Existing defenses typically treat all edges equally, lacking targeted protection for the structural backbones, and struggle to balance robustness with clean accuracy. To address these issues, we propose PSB-GNN , a robust graph learning framework that learns to preserve structural backbones. Specifically, we leverage an explainer-derived prior to initialize a learnable defense policy, guiding a probabilistic structural denoising process that stochastically masks structural noise while preserving structural backbones. Additionally, we introduce a dual trust defense mechanism with a parallel feature-only pathway to enhance robustness without compromising clean accuracy, an asymmetric distillation framework to stabilize training, and a deterministic pruning strategy to filter adversarial edges during inference. Extensive experiments on three benchmarks show that PSB-GNN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art defenses, generalizes well across explainers, and maintains superior clean accuracy. The code is available at https://github.com/baxiansheng2/PSB-GNN .

papers.title: Gradual Adversarial Graph Transfer: Stabilizing Alignment with Dual Transitional Domains
papers.abstract: Graph domain adaptation under large source-target shifts is challenging because direct endpoint alignment often causes unstable adversarial optimization, while explicit intermediate-graph generation may introduce topology distortion and semantic artifacts. To address this problem, we propose Gradual Adversarial Graph Transfer (GAGT), which formulates cross-domain graph transfer as constructing a semantically feasible latent transition pathway. GAGT first learns domain-invariant and domain-specific representations through contrastive disentangled representation learning with tolerance-bounded reconstruction, where the reconstruction tolerance regularizes a semantically feasible region rather than forcing exact recovery. Based on this, GAGT synthesizes dual transitional domains as bidirectional bridge states and performs gradual adversarial alignment along the pathway. In this way, a large source-target discrepancy is decomposed into smaller and semantically constrained local discrepancies, yielding smoother adversarial signals and more stable transfer. Extensive experiments on diverse graph domain adaptation benchmarks demonstrate that GAGT outperforms nearly all state-of-the-art methods, especially under large structural and feature distribution shifts. Our code is available at https://github.com/GEEX-Weixing/GAGT-CIKM.

papers.title: SA-GSL: Simulated Annealing for Graph Structure Learning
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a cornerstone for applications involving graph data. However, the performance of GNNs is critically dependent on the underlying graph structure. This presents a fundamental challenge, as a predefined topology may not be optimal for the specific learning task, limiting the model's performance. This limitation is particularly pronounced in heterophilous settings, where the inherent homophily assumption of GNNs contradicts the actual graph structure, causing models that rely on raw topology to fail. Although Graph Structure Learning (GSL) aims to address this issue, most existing methods use continuous relaxations of the graph topology to enable gradient-based optimization. This approach can trap models in local optima and fail to capture the discrete nature of graph data. To address this issue, we introduce a novel GSL algorithm, S imulated A nnealing for G raph S tructure L earning (SA-GSL), that leverages Simulated Annealing (SA) to optimize the discrete graph structure, effectively adapting the topology to handle heterophily. The SA algorithm operates as a gradient-free refiner proposing new topologies, guided by a multi-objective energy function that uses a lightweight Label Propagation model as a proxy while simultaneously promoting sparsity. An ensemble of candidate structures is generated at each step and combined via majority voting. The final graph is weighted between the original topology and the SA refined ensemble structure. Our experiments reveal that SA-GSL is highly effective, achieving state-of-the-art results on several key node classification benchmarks (1.5% on Cora, 3% on Minesweeper). The code implementation is publicly available on our GitHub repository (https://github.com/ashba93/sa-gsl).

papers.title: Robust Node Classification via Noise-robust Views and Prototype Relabeling
papers.abstract: How do we classify nodes accurately on heterophilic graphs when training labels are infected by neighbors' majority classes? In many real-world applications, annotators lack sufficient evidence for each node in isolation and thus rely on its neighborhood context, causing labels to drift toward the neighborhood majority. We call this bias structural label infection, a graph-dependent corruption that makes supervision appear artificially homophilic even though the underlying graph remains heterophilic. This setting is particularly challenging because message passing quickly reinforces infected labels, making corrupted nodes look confident and rendering common loss- or agreement-based denoising methods unreliable. Structural label infection affects both hop selection and label correction. Because corrupted labels are aligned with neighborhood majorities, optimizing hop weights with these labels gives fake-homophilic neighborhoods an artificial advantage. This is especially harmful on heterophilic graphs, where useful propagation is not restricted to immediate neighbors. Moreover, predictions are produced by a model trained on infected labels, so directly copying them passes this infection to the next training round. We propose Recover (Robust nodE Classification under structural label nOise Via multi-score hop routing and prototypE Relabeling), a robust node classification framework that severs the feedback loop between infected supervision and structural propagation. Instead of allowing corrupted labels to dictate neighborhood aggregation, Recover secures robust representations by dynamically routing propagation through proxies based on static features and averaged task confidence. Subsequently, it directly rectifies the corrupted supervision by projecting these stabilized embeddings against reliable class prototypes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Recover achieves up to 29.41 percentage-point improvement in accuracy under infected-label settings.

papers.title: LLMTGL: Large Language Models for Robust Text-Attributed Graph Learning under Missing Text and Label Noise
affiliations: College of Computer Science, Inner Mongolia University
Department of Computer Science, Aalto University
School of Artificial Intelligence, Hebei University of Technology
papers.abstract: Text-attributed graphs have attracted considerable attention due to their extensive applications in domains such as social networks and citation networks. Existing methods typically rely on reliable text-attributed graphs. However, the frequent occurrence of missing text in real-world scenarios severely constrains model performance. Meanwhile, label noise is inevitably introduced during the data annotation process, leading to a degradation in the performance of graph learning. The large language model (LLM), with their text generation and semantic understanding, offers a unified solution to the challenges of missing text and label noise. To jointly address both challenges, we propose LLMTGL, a novel graph learning framework for text-attributed graph node classification. Specifically, we introduce graph topological properties to construct augmented prompts that guide the LLM in generating semantically coherent academic text descriptions for nodes with missing text. Subsequently, we design an LLM-driven pseudo-label expansion mechanism that selects high-confidence unlabeled nodes to the training set. This framework jointly optimizes for missing text and label noise by integrating graph topological structure with semantic information. Experimental results demonstrate that LLMTGL achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods on text-missing graphs with noisy labels. The source code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LLMTGL-EC24ssjs.

papers.title: Rethinking Graph-LLMs: Are Performance Gains Confounded by Data Leakage?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have advanced text-attributed graph (TAG) learning in recent years, leading to strong performance in Graph-LLM systems. However, these gains may partially arise from target-correlated parametric priors memorized during LLM pre-training rather than genuine graph reasoning. This issue is particularly critical in TAGs, where graph topology can propagate memory-triggered signals beyond individual nodes. Once encoded as node representations, memorized priors may spread through neighborhood aggregation, introducing topology-level bias amplification absent in conventional NLP tasks. Despite its importance, the interaction between LLM memorization and graph message passing remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we present a leakage analysis framework guided by Structural Causal Models (SCMs) for Graph-LLMs. Specifically, we investigate how prompt interventions influence downstream graph prediction and examine whether entity-level anonymization suppresses memory-triggering cues. We further construct globally consistent entity-anonymized graph benchmarks that preserve graph structure while masking identity-sensitive entities. Experiments on citation and person relational networks across multiple embedding models and graph backbones reveal three findings: (1) Target-related meta-information can act as shortcut signals when highly correlated with downstream labels; (2) Graph message passing may further propagate memory-induced bias across neighboring nodes; and (3) Graph-LLM performance drops notably after entity anonymization. These findings suggest that current Graph-LLM benchmarks may overestimate generalization ability when memorized priors are not properly controlled. The code and anonymized datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/mrjc12/GL-DataLeakage.

papers.title: GeoGNN: Quantifying and Mitigating Semantic Drift in Text-Attributed Graphs
papers.abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) on text-attributed graphs (TAGs) typically encode node texts with pretrained language models (PLMs) and propagate the resulting embeddings through linear neighborhood aggregation. Yet PLM representation spaces are geometrically structured, so linear aggregation can distort semantic geometry and cause semantic drift , where aggregated representations move away from the underlying manifold. We introduce a local PCA-based drift metric to quantify this effect across aggregation mechanisms, and propose Geodesic Aggregation , which aggregates neighbors along geodesics with log–exp mappings on the unit sphere, keeping representations on the spherical proxy while retaining unit-norm angular structure. GeoGNN instantiates this mechanism with spherical attention and manifold interpolation. Experiments on four benchmark datasets with multiple text encoders show that GeoGNN mitigates semantic drift and consistently outperforms strong baselines.

papers.title: COTA: Confidence-aware Opinion and Trust Assessment
affiliations: Luxembourg Institute of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Opinion consolidation is a common problem in crowdsourced knowledge collection and data integration, where multiple workers may provide conflicting opinions about the same statements. Accurately aggregating this knowledge is challenging, particularly when workers exhibit varying levels of reliability. Most existing approaches focus on binary or categorical inputs and ignore the confidence that workers assign to their own opinions, despite its potential to improve consolidation precision and robustness. In this paper, we introduce the Confidence-aware Opinion and Trust Assessment (COTA) algorithm, a confidence-aware opinion-consolidation method that aggregates numerical and binary opinions provided by multiple workers. COTA explicitly models the confidence that workers assign to each individual opinion and determines the uncertainty values that best reflect the collective trust of the worker population. Unlike many existing methods, COTA relies solely on workers' inputs and requires no additional data features. Experimental results show that incorporating workers' self-reported confidence significantly improves consolidation quality. In particular, COTA outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and remains effective even with inconsistent worker accuracy, provided that confidence correlates with opinion reliability. These results highlight the potential of confidence-aware opinion consolidation for aggregating uncertain knowledge in collaborative settings.

papers.title: Filter-then-match: Holistic Schema Matching via Small Language Model Filtering and Large Language Model Reasoning
papers.abstract: Schema matching (SM) is a critical step in data integration pipelines and serves as a foundation for tasks such as Table Search and Entity Matching. However, applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to SM is prohibitively expensive due to the task's inherent quadratic complexity, which hinders scalable and cost-efficient deployment. In this paper, we investigate two SM scenarios: the most common instance-based scenario where headers and their values are available, and the metadata-based scenario where only metadata is provided (e.g., due to privacy constraints). We propose Fermat, a unified framework designed to address both scenarios effectively. Fermat incorporates a Small Language Model (SLM)-based filtering strategy that significantly reduce the computational overhead of applying LLMs to SM. We also introduce a column synthesis workflow that enables a fully unsupervised solution, effectively mitigating the scarcity of ground-truth data. Additionally, we implement a specialized loss function with hard column mining to counteract the biases of the filter model on imbalanced data, ensuring improved recall of positive candidates. Finally, we conduct comprehensive reproduction and evaluation of recent schema matching methods on both metadata-based and instance-based datasets, providing insights into their generalizability across diverse scenarios.

papers.title: DataDescribe: Auto-Generated Source Descriptors for LLM-Agent Retrieval over Heterogeneous Data
papers.abstract: LLM agents over heterogeneous external data—databases, document collections, APIs—must decide which sources to load into a finite context before retrieval. Query-side embedding routing misses source-level properties (topic specialization, density, freshness); unifying all sources into one dense index dilutes retrieval and pays the per-engine retrieval cost across the entire federation. We introduce DataDescribe, a describe-then-decide method that auto-generates a compact six-facet descriptor per source (schema, size, variety, entropy, temporal density, freshness) once at ingestion and exposes it to plug-in source selectors composed with federated retrieval. The headline contribution is architectural: descriptor-driven two-stage retrieval (DD+RAG) matches or exceeds unified federated fusion while querying 5x fewer engines, under selectors as different as a zero-shot programmatic scorer and a supervised learned router. On FeB4RAG (790 queries, 16 heterogeneous BEIR collections), a zero-shot programmatic scorer (DD-Score) gives DD+RAG@M=3 0.500 nDCG@10 vs. unified Reciprocal Rank Fusion's 0.475 (p=0.0008); a supervised RAGRouter-style learned router trained on 395 labels amplifies the gap to 0.555 vs. 0.469 (+18% relative). Two supporting findings: (i) auto-generated descriptors beat expert hand-written ones (0.678 vs. 0.650, p=0.0001, surviving per-set weight retuning), so deployment does not require human curation; (ii) a per-facet ablation localizes the FeB4RAG signal to topic-variety (-32.5% when removed). Two controls bound the claim: on FeB4RAG's resource-selection labels a query-independent size prior matches DD-Score and a marginal-relevance prior beats it, yet neither transfers to the document level, where the two-stage gain requires a query-conditional selector. Where descriptors help: on homogeneous MuSiQue dense retrieval wins; on BRIGHT (12 reasoning-intensive corpora, independent of BEIR), the architectural and DD-Score patterns both replicate. DD-Score serves the cold-start regime—no labels, no query embedding, rotating federations—at zero per-query cost.

papers.title: AdaCAS: Balancing Efficiency and Effectiveness for Table Union Search via Adaptive Column Aspect Selection
affiliations: Key Laboratory of High Confidence Software Technologies, CS, Peking University
papers.abstract: In data integration, Table Union Search (TUS) retrieves tables suitable for union operations with a given query table. This task fundamentally relies on efficient and effective column similarity measurements. Recent studies model columns using fine-grained aspects such as number, pattern, and semantics to capture diverse information. However, as data volume expands, the growing heterogeneity and diversity of columns significantly raises the cost of encoding and searching all aspects during preprocessing and query stages. To address these challenges, we propose AdaCAS, a novel retrieval framework that balances efficiency and effectiveness for TUS via adaptive column aspect selection. First, we introduce a self-supervised aspect selection model that learns optimal aspect combinations from column statistics using an active-learning-based sampling strategy. Second, we design a cost-aware allocation mechanism to balance index expressiveness and preprocessing overhead. Third, we develop an early-stop query strategy that prioritizes indices with lower dimensionality and cardinality for fast ranking. Experimental results on real-world table collections show that our method achieves 4.3x speedup in preprocessing and 4.7x speedup in query execution over the state of the art, with peak acceleration exceeding 30x for certain queries. Notably, it consistently improves MAP@k by 1.5%, highlighting its ability to balance retrieval efficiency and effectiveness.

papers.title: Table-Guided Hyperspherical Diffusion for Preserving Semantic Dependencies in Column Type Annotation
papers.abstract: Column Type Annotation (CTA) is a fundamental task in Semantic Table Interpretation that assigns semantic types to table columns. In real-world tables, column meanings are often ambiguous because schemas are heterogeneous and metadata is limited. Therefore, the type of a column depends not only on its own cell values but also on its relationships with other columns. Recent Transformer-based CTA methods capture such contextual information during encoding. However, they rely on discriminative classification, where each column is independently assigned to a predefined type through a softmax classifier. As a result, semantic dependencies among column types are not explicitly preserved during inference. This limits accurate type prediction for context-dependent columns, such as ambiguous numerical columns and long-tail types. We propose SphereTab, a novel CTA framework that combines diffusion-based iterative denoising with hyperspherical representation learning to generate column type representations. SphereTab first learns table-guided signals from categorical and numerical columns to capture contextual relationships within a table. It then uses the signals to guide the iterative denoising process, allowing semantic dependencies to be progressively reflected in the generated representations. By modeling the representations in hyperspherical space, SphereTab preserves semantic dependencies through angular similarity rather than vector scale. Experiments on four benchmark datasets show that SphereTab outperforms state-of-the-art discriminative and LLM-based baselines.

papers.title: Structured Prediction for Scalable Spreadsheet Table Understanding: From Cell Types to Table Ranges
affiliations: DI ENS, ENS, CNRS, PSL, Inria
papers.abstract: Spreadsheets are a primary medium for publishing tabular data, yet automatically extracting structured content from them remains difficult due to heterogeneous layouts, diverse file formats, and inconsistent organizational conventions. We address two core tasks in spreadsheet understanding: Cell-Type Classification (CTC), which assigns roles to cells, and Table Detection (TD), which identifies table bounding boxes within sheets. We propose an efficient two-stage pipeline in which a learned CTC model feeds a deterministic TD algorithm. For CTC, we use a LightGBM classifier over 65 structured features together with a pairwise CRF enforcing spatial consistency across the cell grid. Our TD method extracts table ranges from predicted cell types by a deterministic five-stage procedure. For evaluation, we built and share StatSheets, a multilingual benchmark of 737 manually annotated sheets from 14 public data providers across multiple countries and file formats. Under 5-fold cross-validation, our CRF-LightGBM system achieves a Mean File-Macro F1 score of 0.937 on CTC, within 0.6 percentage points of the GPU-based TUTA Transformer, while requiring substantially fewer computational resources. For TD, our deterministic approach outperforms region-based baselines and remains competitive with recent LLM-based systems such as SpreadsheetLLM. These results demonstrate that combining non-linear structured prediction with deterministic range extraction provides a competitive, scalable, and computationally efficient approach to spreadsheet table understanding.

papers.title: Hierarchical and Permutation-Invariant Feature Transformation Learning via Policy-Guided Embedding Search
affiliations: Southwest University of Finance and Economics
papers.abstract: Feature transformation improves predictive performance on tabular data by constructing informative abstractions from raw features. Recent generative approaches encode transformation knowledge into continuous embedding spaces for efficient exploration of candidate strategies, but face three key limitations: 1) overlooking hierarchical relationships between low-level features, operations, and high-level abstractions; 2) enforcing order-sensitive embeddings on inherently permutation-invariant transformation sequences, introducing systematic bias; and 3) relying on gradient-based search ill-suited to non-convex transformation spaces. We propose a framework with two complementary components. First, a permutation-invariant hierarchical module captures interactions across features, operations, and abstraction levels, with a self-attention pooling mechanism that maps semantically equivalent structures to consistent embeddings aligned with downstream performance. Second, a policy-guided multi-objective reinforcement learning strategy initializes search from empirically strong seeds and jointly optimizes predictive accuracy and transformation efficiency. Extensive experiments on diverse tabular benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our framework against strong baselines. Our code and data are publicly available (https://github.com/RayLiu1103/PHER).

papers.title: Cavity-Calibrated Prediction Sets
papers.abstract: Conformal prediction equips black-box classifiers with finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees, but its standard application to structured outputs over probabilistic graphical models is hampered by two issues: per-node nonconformity scores derived from approximate beliefs are inflated by self-reinforcing local potentials, and a naive Bonferroni correction over N output variables produces prediction sets that grow with the size of the graph. We introduce Cavity-Calibrated Prediction Sets (CCPS), a framework that addresses both. From a single loopy belief-propagation pass we extract self-cavity beliefs b i cav ∝ b i / φ i that approximate exact leave-one-out scores at O(NL) amortized cost, recovering a Θ(N) speed-up over jackknife+. A two-level structured Bonferroni correction allocates significance across a proper graph colouring, recovering a factor-χ' tightening of the joint coverage bound. We prove distribution-free marginal and joint coverage guarantees and establish a correlation-decay condition under which cavity scores converge to true leave-one-out scores. Across seven primary benchmarks — CoNLL-2003 and OntoNotes 5.0 for NER, Pascal VOC, ADE20K and Cityscapes for segmentation, plus SensorNet and Ising synthetic graphs — evaluated over 20 calibration seeds at α=0.10, CCPS reduces mean prediction-set size by 34–58% relative to naive split-conformal and by 23–37% relative to RCPS while maintaining empirical joint coverage at or above the nominal level (all reductions p<0.001 under paired Wilcoxon with Holm–Bonferroni correction). On small Ising grids where exact leave-one-out is tractable, cavity scores rank-correlate with the exact LOO scores at Spearman ρ ≥ 0.985 in the sub-critical regime, and CCPS matches structured jackknife+ in tightness while running roughly 1,500× faster on a 32×32 grid.

papers.title: PACE: Prediction-Conditional Conformal Expert Aggregation for Known-Only Hyperspectral OOD Detection
affiliations: Nanjing University of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Closed-set hyperspectral image (HSI) classifiers are often deployed in scenes whose land-cover taxonomy is incomplete. In this setting, an unseen crop type, road material, or mixed surface may not look globally alien: it can lie near the known feature manifold and still be assigned to a known class with high confidence. We call this failure mode semantic absorption. It makes purely confidence-based, global feature-distance, and single logit-based scores unreliable, because the relevant question is whether the sample is plausible under the class into which the classifier absorbs it. We propose PACE, a known-only post-hoc framework for hyperspectral semantic OOD detection. PACE builds a prediction-conditional conformal anchor from class-geometry, global-support, and predicted-class-support evidence, converts heterogeneous OOD scores into conformal expert p-values, and combines compact expert sets by ACAT. A second conformal layer recalibrates the aggregate score into final p-values, which are used for OOD ranking and Benjamini--Hochberg (BH)-FDR-targeted unknown candidate mining. Across five HSI datasets under leave-one-class-out evaluation, PACE-Rank gives the best average AUROC and FPR95, while PACE-Discover gives the best AUPR-OOD and unknown recall at the BH target. All calibration and model selection use only known-center samples; no held-out-center samples, wild data, OOD labels, or target unknown labels are used.

papers.title: Information-Theoretic Neighbourhood Analysis for Detecting Confusion-Directed Label Noise
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks encode rich information about data samples through their training dynamics. The speed at which a sample is learned, the stability of its predictions across epochs, and the structure of its representation-space neighbourhood all carry signal about sample quality and label reliability. These dynamics can be exploited to detect mislabelled examples under confusion-directed noise, a regime where annotation errors are directed toward visually confusable classes, placing mislabelled samples in the confusion subspace where true and assigned classes have nearly identical logits. We prove that standard training diagnostics suffer a provable confusion-induced metric collapse in this regime. To escape it, we introduce the Neighbourhood Area Under the Margin (N-AUM), which replaces the logit margin with the collective vote margin of K representation-space neighbours. In order to make the proposed N-AUM more effective we propose the Layer Information Score (LIS), grounded in information bottleneck (IB) theory for neural networks, which weights each layer by its estimated class mutual information Î(Z ℓ ; Y) so that only class-discriminative representations contribute to the N-AUM score. Across four benchmark datasets, namely, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, and Tiny ImageNet, and across four diverse deep-neural network architectures, the IB-weighted N-AUM achieves the highest detection AUROC on every dataset while reducing collateral damage to clean-hard samples from 4.0% to 1.1% at a 2% detection budget (PR@1000 = 0.989 vs. 0.960 for AUM).

papers.title: PULSE: Support-Calibrated Class Prior-Free Positive-Unlabeled Learning with Hard-Negative Ranking and Lower-Tail Coverage
papers.abstract: Positive-unlabeled (PU) learning addresses weak-supervision settings where training data contain labeled positives and unlabeled samples, but no labeled negatives. In class prior-free PU learning, the hidden-positive proportion in the unlabeled pool is unknown and cannot be used for optimization. Existing prior-free methods, such as T-HOneCls [47], primarily control unlabeled data through aggregate objective corrections, reducing unlabeled-gradient domination by Taylorizing a variational PU loss. However, aggregate control does not explicitly distinguish the two critical tails of the unlabeled distribution: high-score negative-like samples that drive false positives and weak positive modes that drive false negatives. We propose PULSE, a class prior-free PU framework for calibrated support-region estimation. PULSE combines global unlabeled support control, teacher-weighted hard-negative ranking, lower-tail positive coverage, prior-free support calibration, teacher-student stabilization, and recall-guarded boundary regulation. Hard-negative ranking provides local precision control for negative-like unlabeled samples near the support boundary, while lower-tail coverage protects weak labeled positives whose scores approach the decision boundary. Support calibration uses positive anchors and low-score unlabeled lower-tail anchors to define calibrated threshold variants without labeled negatives or class-prior estimates. We evaluate PULSE on six benchmarks comprising 20 PU tasks, including five hyperspectral datasets and one RGB extension. The comparison covers label-noise representation learning objectives and class prior-based and prior-free PU methods, including the strongest baseline, T-HOneCls [47]. Across these benchmarks, PULSE improves precision-recall behavior on hyperspectral benchmarks and achieves higher overall accuracy on the RGB task, indicating that calibrated support-region estimation provides stronger boundary regulation than aggregate unlabeled-gradient control.

papers.title: Bias and Variance Inflation in Hierarchical Multi-Treatment DML: Diagnosis and Correction
papers.abstract: Many business and clinical decisions depend on the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) of each of several continuous treatments that move together: advertising spend and discount levels driven by the same campaign, or drug doses adjusted in a common protocol. Several estimator families produce CATE at every query point with a confidence interval, including meta-learners, doubly robust learners, Causal Forests and Double Machine Learning (DML); DML in particular gives both in closed form and is widely deployed. We show that, when treatments remain correlated after conditioning on covariates, the bias of the standard DML estimator is amplified along the directions in which two treatments are nearly indistinguishable. The plug-in confidence interval is asymptotically valid as long as the residual correlation does not reach one, but the convergence is so slow under strong correlation that coverage is far from nominal at practical sample sizes.
