We propose a hierarchy-aware bias correction that combines two CATE estimators of different complexity through a projector built from a user-supplied grouping of treatments by shared cause: the more flexible estimator on the directions where the data is informative and the less expressive estimator on the contrast directions among sibling treatments, where it has lower bias. Across four synthetic data-generating processes, the IHDP public benchmark and a treatment graph with two disjoint sibling triples, the correction lifts coverage on the correlated treatments from 30% for vanilla DML to 94%, reduces mean squared error by a factor of 51 and produces 30% narrower intervals. A second contribution adds a bias-augmented variance term that lifts coverage further to 99% at the cost of wider intervals, for use in extreme-correlation regimes where residual bias persists.

papers.title: Context-Aware Pruning for Ordering-Based Causal Discovery
papers.abstract: Ordering-based causal discovery decomposes DAG learning into topological order estimation and edge pruning. Existing work has focused on order estimation, while pruning often relies on component-wise additive tests that can miss parent effects expressed through co-parent context. We propose Context-Aware Pruning of Edges (CAPE), a plug-in pruning module that formulates post-ordering edge pruning as local model selection. For each candidate edge, CAPE computes the out-of-sample gain in conditional log-predictive density of the child when the candidate parent is included in the current parent context. It retains the edge only when this contextual gain exceeds an MDL-inspired adaptive structural penalty. This criterion evaluates conditional predictive evidence rather than isolated additive effects, enabling CAPE to retain interaction-driven dependencies while pruning weak finite-sample edges. Across six ordering backbones, CAPE improves SHD, SID, and F1 on synthetic nonlinear graphs and assumption-violation benchmarks, including simulated latent confounding, measurement error, post-nonlinear mechanisms, and non-i.i.d. sampling. On empirical benchmarks, CAPE lowers average SHD and SID under the same estimated orders. Its hierarchical group-pruning strategy reduces pruning time by up to 7.5 times on larger graphs. Source code is available at https://github.com/ku-milab/CAPE.

papers.title: FunnelCausalNet: Funnel-aware Joint Conversion-Revenue Uplift for Multi-tier Coupon Allocation
papers.abstract: Coupon campaigns aim to lift both conversion and revenue, but gross merchandise value (GMV) inherits a deterministic funnel structure from conversion and conditional order value and is typically zero-inflated and heavy-tailed. We propose FunnelCausalNet , an uplift estimator that couples a binary conversion head with a nonnegative conditional-value head under the funnel composition μ gmv =μ conv μ val . Under explicit RCT, support, rate-gap, and cross-head covariance-control assumptions, we derive an idealized leading-order MSE-ratio comparison that identifies a variance regime in which funnel composition can reduce pointwise estimation variance; it is a regime heuristic rather than a guarantee for the shared-representation neural implementation. The estimator is paired with marginal split-conformal summaries on each outcome's CATE (Bonferroni union for two-number joint coverage, treated as audit/monitoring bands) and a Lagrangian budgeted allocator that consumes RCT-anchored estimates for subsidy-aware ROI accounting. On semi-synthetic multi-tier Criteo-MT7 with oracle individualized treatment effects, FunnelCausalNet's mean AUUC_GMV is within one seed standard deviation of the leading recent feature-interaction baseline among eleven baselines, and a controlled funnel-coupling ablation reduces GMV effect error against direct GMV regression by 18–48% across the tested zero-inflation regimes. On de-identified industrial Hotel-Coupon RCT logs with ≈ 4.9 × 10 6 hold-out exposure records per seed, RCT-consistent expected-outcome (EOM) evaluation sweeps full LP frontiers, and FunnelCausalNet attains the best seed-averaged mean ΔROI at 7/7 correlated EOM anchors in 10%–60%; we treat this as descriptive frontier consistency rather than independent-anchor significance. On sparse binary-spend public benchmarks, revenue-focused rankers can dominate uplift-curve proxies; we foreground this regime boundary explicitly.

papers.title: Decision-Focused Learning for Budget-Constrained Coupon Allocation
papers.abstract: Coupon allocation optimization can be formulated as a multiple-choice knapsack problem (MCKP) that maximizes total reward subject to a limited budget, using the expected reward and cost when each coupon is assigned to each customer as coefficients. Since these coefficients are unobservable before assignment, the standard two-stage method (TSM) first estimates them with a prediction model and then solves the MCKP. However, because the prediction model is trained to minimize prediction error (e.g., MSE), improving prediction accuracy does not necessarily improve the quality of the MCKP solution. To bridge this gap, decision-focused learning (DFL) has attracted attention as a framework that trains the prediction model using a loss defined by the quality of the MCKP solution itself. Existing DFL methods for marketing design their losses based on the priority ordering of coupon assignments for each customer, but evaluate each customer's coupon assignment independently, failing to properly account for the shared budget constraint that couples all customers' assignments. In this paper, we propose LEOM-DFL (Lagrangian EOM-based Decision-Focused Learning), a method that directly optimizes the quality of the overall MCKP solution, including inter-customer dependencies arising from the budget constraint. Since rewards and costs of unassigned coupons are unobserved, LEOM-DFL employs an expected outcome metric (EOM) based on doubly robust (DR) estimators to estimate the total reward and total cost for any given assignment from logged data. Solving the Lagrangian relaxation of the MCKP with these estimates yields a budget-dependent trade-off weight, which is incorporated into the loss to capture inter-customer dependencies. Furthermore, the combination of entropy regularization and the implicit function theorem yields a closed-form gradient computation. Experiments on three datasets demonstrate that LEOM-DFL consistently outperforms existing DFL methods.

papers.title: Constrained Preference Dynamics: Energy-Based Minimization for Multi-Interest Recommendation
papers.abstract: In sequential recommendation, multi-interest models are widely deployed to capture diverse user preferences from behavioral histories. However, existing architectures typically extract multiple representation vectors and fuse them via conventional attention mechanisms. By computing a weighted sum, this paradigm implicitly assumes that distinct preferences are independent and can always be linearly combined. Consequently, when internal conflicts arise, such as budget constraints versus performance requirements, these feed-forward mechanisms compromise, yielding recommendations that combine incompatible signals. In this paper, we formulate conflicting preferences through explicit pairwise constraints. We propose Constrained Preference Dynamics (CPD), a framework that casts preference aggregation as a constrained dynamical system. CPD treats preference intensities as state variables evolving under learned pairwise constraints. By minimizing an energy function via unrolled gradient descent, the system moves preference states toward locally stable, low-energy configurations before scoring. On five real-world datasets, CPD improves overall accuracy while delivering larger gains under high-conflict scenarios. Specifically, on the Amazon Clothing conflict subset, CPD outperforms the strongest baseline MDGR by 19.8% in Recall@10 and 24.8% in NDCG@10. These results show that incorporating constrained dynamics improves recommendation performance under preference conflict.

papers.title: RouteRec: Behavior-Guided Sparse Routing for Sequential Recommendation
affiliations: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Sessionized interaction histories contain behavioral patterns that can improve sequential recommendation. However, existing models process all sessions through the same parameterized blocks, regardless of their behavioral differences. Mixture of Experts (MoE) enables conditional computation, but it leaves open what should guide expert allocation. We propose RouteRec, a sequential recommender that uses observed session behavior as the routing criterion. RouteRec summarizes four types of behavioral evidence from sessionized histories: interaction tempo, item-group focus, repetition and carryover, and popularity tendency. It uses these cues to route computation at macro, mid, and micro scopes. Cue-derived scores first select expert groups; within each selected group, the current backbone state then refines expert selection. Across six public datasets and 18 dataset–metric combinations, RouteRec ranks first in 12 and second in three, yielding the best overall average rank of 1.61 compared with 4.11 for the next-best baseline. Additional analyses suggest that the behavioral cues guide expert allocation beyond added capacity and produce routing patterns aligned with observed behavior. Our code is available at https://github.com/jy1559/RouteRec.

papers.title: SpikeRec: Accurate and Preference-Preserving Live-Streaming Recommendation under User-Sampled Signal Loss
papers.abstract: Given a user's past interactions and the set of channels that are currently live, how can a recommender choose the next channel when both channel availability and audience attention change within minutes? Live-streaming recommendation is difficult because the valid candidate set and each channel's audience state change continuously. In large-scale systems, an additional difficulty arises when training logs are subsampled at the user level for scalability: every interaction of the sampled users is kept and the rest are discarded. This user-level subsampling preserves each selected user's viewing history for learning personal preference, but removes many viewers from each channel's time series. As a result, standard sequential recommenders learn a user's revisit tendencies, but remain weak at detecting current channel-level signals such as sudden viewer-count surges. Simply boosting channels with global surges is also unsafe because many users return to channels they already know. In this paper, we propose SpikeRec (Spike-aware Recommender for live-streaming channels), an accurate recommender for live-streaming platforms. SpikeRec detects the spike of each live channel from the full streaming data, converting the viewer count into percentiles to make the spikes comparable across channels. It then enriches the representation of a user with the channels spiking around the recent interactions of the user, so that the spikes are reflected in the preference of the user. It finally adds a spike-scaled bonus to the channels that the user has watched before, so that the repeating tendency of the user is reflected as well. We also collect Chzzk, a new live-streaming dataset with de-identified chat and donation interactions together with the viewer counts of every channel. SpikeRec gives the best accuracy on every metric and every dataset, improving Hit@10 by up to 16.4% over the second-best method.

papers.title: Smart Predict then Optimize for Constrained Learning to Rank
papers.abstract: Ranking is a central problem in information retrieval. Traditional learning-to-rank methods aim to train a ranking model to predict the relevance of each item and then rank them according to the relevance scores. However, many real-world ranking systems must satisfy application-specific constraints to ensure the fairness, safety, or diversity of the ranking, so the ranking decision can no longer be obtained by decreasingly sorting the relevance scores. A straightforward solution is to utilize the predict-then-optimize paradigm: first training a ranking model to predict relevance scores and then feeding the predicted relevance into a downstream optimizer to generate a ranking list that satisfied the constraints. This paradigm can produce feasible rankings when the constrained problem is feasible, but its prediction training is separated from the optimization of the ranking objective, making it difficult to directly optimize the quality of the induced ranking. In this paper, we propose SPORank, a unified framework for constrained learning to rank. By adopting the SPO+ loss, SPORank jointly considers relevance prediction and constrained optimization during training, making it broadly applicable to constrained ranking problems. We instantiate SPORank on two concrete tasks. The experimental results demonstrate SPORank effectively improves ranking performance while satisfying the required constraints.

papers.title: Self-Evolving Memory for Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation has emerged as a promising end-to-end paradigm for personalized recommendation. In real-world recommendation scenarios, however, user preferences continuously evolve over time, making self-evolving an essential capability for generative recommender systems. Existing evolving strategies, such as continual retraining and distillation-based adaptation, directly update the shared model parameters using streaming interactions. Nevertheless, we find that directly applying such strategies to generative recommendation introduces a critical issue, termed evolution conflict. Specifically, heterogeneous preference shifts from different users are optimized within a fully shared autoregressive parameter space, causing dominant behavioral patterns to progressively dominate the model evolution process while underrepresented patterns become increasingly overlooked. To address this issue, we propose a self-evolving memory paradigm for generative recommendation, aiming to enable effective evolution across heterogeneous behavioral patterns. We further identify three key principles for effective self-evolving recommendation systems, including isolated memorization, reinforced evolution, and scalable application. Guided by these principles, we develop LION, a simple yet effective framework centered on a sparse Key-Value memory layer. Specifically, LION introduces sparse memory activation to isolate the evolution of different behavioral patterns, while a consolidation loss is designed to reinforce the learning of underrepresented preference dynamics during continual adaptation. Extensive experiments on diverse real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of LION under various continual evolution settings (e.g., per-period evaluation, user/item group evaluation, and evolution convergence analysis).

papers.title: Neither Black nor White: Balancing Semantic and Collaborative Signals with Graph-Informed Semantic IDs (GrIS)
papers.abstract: Existing work on Semantic IDs (SIDs) for generative recommendation treats SID construction as a representation learning problem: encode items into a quantised latent space and read off codes. We argue this view is incidental. SID construction is, at heart, a recursive clustering problem, and once stated this way the natural object to cluster is a graph whose nodes carry semantic content and whose edges carry collaborative signal; SID assignment becomes a hierarchical graph partition. This reframing yields a unified framework, Graph-Informed Semantic IDs (GrIS), that subsumes prior approaches rather than displacing them. RQ-VAE and RQ-KMeans are recovered as the special case where the graph is empty, exposing content-only quantisation as one corner of a larger design space along two so-far-collapsed axes: graph construction and recursive partition algorithm. We explore two contrasting instantiations: RecDMoN, which performs hierarchical assignment via differentiable graph pooling, and RQ-GAE, which extends RQ-VAE with graph-aware item representations and a graph reconstruction objective. On multiple real-world datasets, GrIS consistently improves over CF-aware SOTA, with gains of up to +52% Hit@10. Because graph construction and partition are explicit, separately configurable components, improvements on either axis can be combined and evaluated systematically.

papers.title: Profiling What Matters: Context-Aware Item Profiles from Large-Scale Metadata for LLM Recommenders
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly advanced reranking in recommendation, effectively leveraging item-side information remains challenging. Real-world items are described by vast, heterogeneous, and unstructured metadata, where decision-relevant signals are often implicit, noisy, or buried in long descriptions. Moreover, feature salience is highly context-dependent, varying not only across items but also across users. Existing methods often rely on item titles, fixed attributes, or static item summaries, which limit personalized and fine-grained item understanding. To bridge this gap, we propose CAIRO, a user context-aware item profiling framework for LLM-based reranking. CAIRO first structures raw metadata and reviews into objective features and subjective traits, and employs a lightweight profiler to select the most relevant information for each user–item pair with limited serving-time overhead. The resulting profiles are concise and context-specific, providing relevant item-side evidence for the LLM's ranking decision. Experiments show that CAIRO consistently improves LLM-based reranking, highlighting the importance of item profiling that effectively exploits vast item-side information.

papers.title: LiteUP4Rec: Efficient User Profiling from LLM-Derived Semantic Supervision
affiliations: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: LLM-derived user profiles improve recommendation quality but are costly to keep up to date: each new interaction requires regenerating the profile with another LLM call. We present LiteUP4Rec, a framework that amortizes LLM-based user profiling into a surrogate model, reconstructing the LLM-derived user representation from item embeddings and removing per-user LLM calls from the serving path while preserving the underlying preference signal. An LLM is used only during offline data preparation to produce user profiles and item descriptions; a lightweight transformer profiler is then trained under mean squared error against the encoded profile, and an alignment projection concatenates its output with collaborative features inside a two-tower retrieval formulation that inherits precomputable item indices and scalable nearest-neighbor lookup. Across benchmarks and baselines, LiteUP4Rec yields an average 40% (up to 74%) improvement. Latency and memory costs are significantly reduced, enabling LLM-derived user profiling under real-time latency budgets.

papers.title: SAERec: Constructing Fine-grained Interpretable Intents Priors via Sparse Autoencoders for Recommendation
affiliations: The Education University of Hong Kong
papers.abstract: Intent-based recommender systems have gained significant attention for enhancing accuracy and interpretability by modeling the underlying motivations behind user behaviors. Most existing models derive intents directly from user sequences via clustering or prototype learning. However, they are sensitive to the sequence quality, require presetting the number of intents and lack explicit semantic grounding. These issues lead to an incomplete and coarse intent set and limit the effectiveness of recommendation. In this paper, we propose the Sparse Autoencoder for intent-based recommendation (SAERec), a novel recommender that automatically constructs a fine-grained, interpretable intent space from a textual corpus to guide recommendation. Rather than treating texts as side signals, SAERec leverages them as high-information-density evidence for intent construction. Specifically, we first extract a comprehensive set of fine-grained interpretable intents from the latent space of Large Language Models (LLMs) by using a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) to disentangle and interpret text embeddings, which isolates intent-related semantics from substantial textual noise. Then, for each user, we retrieve relevant intents from the set as priors to guide recommendation. These priors include personal intents that match each user’s current interests and public intents that capture general item patterns shared across users (e.g., “quality” and “price”). Finally, to integrate retrieved intents into sequence modeling, we propose a multi-branch attention mechanism that captures temporal dependencies and injects both personal and public intent signals, followed by an adaptive fusion layer to construct the final user representation for recommendation. Extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate the superiority of SAERec, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art baselines while providing human-understandable explanations. Our code is available at https://github.com/jiangnanx129/SAERec.

papers.title: A Dual-Expert Strategy Integrating LLMs to Mitigate Negative Transfer in Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation
affiliations: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)
papers.abstract: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation (CDSR) predicts the next item a user will interact with based on their historical interaction sequences across multiple domains. Recent approaches leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) finetuned on textual representations of cross-domain user sequences to retrieve the recommended items, referred to as LLMRec. However, LLMRec primarily models the autoregressive patterns of token-level item texts, while overlooking item-level collaborative signals. This semantic misalignment often leads to distorted knowledge transfer across domains—termed negative transfer—degrading performance in the CDSR task. To address this issue, we propose a novel LLM-based CDSR model, DuELRec: Domain-Gated Dual Experts with LLMs for Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation. We propose a domain-gated dual-expert framework, equipped with an item-aware attention transformation module, which aggregates textual subtokens into item-level representations and enforces block-level attention masking. The single-domain expert restricts autoregressive attention to items within the same domain, while the cross-domain expert allows it across all domains. A gating mechanism adaptively fuses their outputs, using single-domain signals to reduce cross-domain noise that causes negative transfer. Second, we introduce a dual-sampling token-to-item contrastive learning objective that allows LLMs to capture the item-level collaborative signals from both single- and cross-domains. This is achieved by transforming token-level item texts into item-level representations and applying stochastic negative sampling from both single- and cross-domain item pools for contrastive learning. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets across ten domains show that our model outperforms 26 state-of-the-art methods in recommendation performance. Its deployment in our personal assistant app led to a 47.6% relative increase in click-through rate, demonstrating real-world impact. Our code and appendices are available at https://github.com/cpark88/DuELRec.

papers.title: RecSoup: Efficient Model Merging Approach for Controllable Multi-Objective Recommendation
papers.abstract: Recommender systems often need to balance multiple conflicting objectives. Controllable Multi-Objective Recommendation (CMOR) enables dynamic adjustment of objective trade-offs at inference time without retraining, adapting to shifting user or system requirements. Existing CMOR approaches typically rely on output-level reranking or parameter-generating modules, which either limit the scope of feasible trade-offs or incur substantial training and inference cost. Model merging provides a promising alternative by reusing multiple objective-specific models via parameter combination. However, its direct application to recommender systems is challenging due to the lack of a shared linear regime and cross-objective interference. To address these issues, we propose RecSoup, a lightweight two-stage approach for effective CMOR via specialized model merging. RecSoup first mitigates parameter interference across objectives through a pruning strategy that jointly considers objective-specific importance and cross-objective relevance. It then performs adaptive parameter merging via a learnable preference-to-coefficient mapping, allowing dynamic trade-off control at inference time without joint retraining or additional generative modules. Theoretically, we prove that RecSoup outperforms the parameter generation paradigm in effectiveness and efficiency, as it can fully navigate the Pareto front without smoothness constraints. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that RecSoup achieves improved Pareto front quality and effective controllability while delivers 165–228× faster inference-time latency than parameter generation approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/35798642/RECSOUP.git.

papers.title: A Transformer Architecture via Lightweight Sigmoid Attention for Graph Collaborative Filtering
papers.abstract: Transformer architectures have achieved strong performance in graph collaborative filtering by modeling complex user-item relationships. However, existing studies often rely on row-wise softmax attention, auxiliary modules, or constrained architectures, leading to three key challenges: relation modeling, architectural coherence, and computational efficiency. To address these challenges, we propose LiSA, a Transformer via lightweight sigmoid attention. LiSA replaces row-wise softmax attention with an element-wise sigmoid scoring formulation, enabling observed user-item relations to be modeled without normalization against other elements in the same row. It further incorporates a scaling parameter for attention sensitivity and score calibration, together with gated residual connections that preserve structural information across layers. Experiments on five real-world benchmarks show that LiSA consistently outperforms baselines while maintaining lightweight computation. Code is available at https://github.com/Burf/LiSA.

papers.title: The Edge Spectrum of Choice-Derived Item Graphs: Strong and Weak Edges Encode Different Relations in Collaborative Filtering
papers.abstract: Graph collaborative filtering relies on item–item graphs whose edges are used for positive smoothing, under the implicit assumption that stronger edges encode more of the same relation as weaker ones. We show that this assumption fails for a practically important class of graphs: those whose edge weights come from a choice model. On such graphs, strong and weak edges encode qualitatively different relations, which we call an edge spectrum . Specifically, strong edges concentrate on the in-slate competitors of clicked items, exactly the pairs that the within-slate ranking gradient pushes apart, while weak edges do not. We formalize this as a sign mismatch between the smoothing operator and the ranking gradient, and prove that co-click graphs cannot exhibit the same misalignment by construction. This diagnosis explains three empirical observations on MIND and EB-NeRD: (i) drop-in choice-derived operators do not beat co-click, despite indexing structurally distinct neighborhoods; (ii) uniform scalar fixes (sign flip, in-slate margin loss) fail predictably, because the misalignment lives in the graph, not in the loss; (iii) only edge-magnitude-aware operators, with the regime boundary located by the diagnosis rather than by tuning, recover the predicted ordering. The neighbor cutoff k is therefore a semantic switch , not a sparsification hyperparameter. Our claim concerns which interventions fail or succeed and why , not absolute headline gains, which the diagnosis itself predicts to be small under the attenuated propagation channel we observe. We turn the diagnosis into a reusable protocol practitioners can run before deploying any choice-derived item-side operator. Code: https://github.com/kyomusso/Edge-Spectrum-in-CF.

papers.title: Mixture-of-Experts Enhanced Parameter-free Hypergraph Contrastive Network for Next Point-of-Interest Recommendation
affiliations: Wuhan University of Science and Technology
Hubei University of Arts and Science
papers.abstract: Next Point-of-Interest (POI) recommendation aims to predict a user's next destination based on historical check-in sequences. Existing works have achieved notable progress by capturing human mobility patterns through spatio-temporal context modeling and by injecting global collaborative signals via graph neural networks and hypergraph neural networks to alleviate data sparsity. However, indiscriminate fusion may leave heterogeneous mobility signals, such as spatial constraints, temporal habits, and categorical preferences, insufficiently differentiated. Additionally, learnable transformations in parameterized hypergraph convolutions may perturb topology-driven collaborative signals during multi-layer propagation, particularly on sparse interaction data. Moreover, the user's static preference representation and the sequence-encoded dynamic intent representation originate from different embedding spaces, resulting in semantic misalignment. To address these challenges, this paper proposes the Mixture-of-Experts Contrastive Parameter-free Hypergraph Network (M-CPHNet). Specifically, a relative time-gap encoding preserves diurnal rhythms via modulo-24 operations for fine-grained temporal intent modeling. A user-conditioned intent excitation gate coupled with an adaptive soft-routing mixture-of-experts module adaptively weights multiple experts to model complementary spatial, temporal, and categorical mobility patterns, yielding sequence intent representations. These are then fused with relative time-gap embeddings and absolute position embeddings, encoded by a Transformer, and aggregated via an attention query into a short-term dynamic intent. A parameter-free hypergraph convolution (Pf-HGConv) layer introduces no learnable weights in its propagation operator and performs normalized aggregation solely on the user–POI and category–POI co-occurrence matrices to obtain topology-enhanced global POI representations, thereby reducing parameterization-induced distortion. Hypergraph-sequence contrastive learning aligns the user's static preference representation with the short-term dynamic intent representation, mitigating semantic misalignment. Experiments on three real-world datasets show that M-CPHNet achieves higher observed performance than the evaluated baselines, with an average improvement of 4.8% in Acc@5 across the three datasets; under the reported experimental settings, its per-epoch training time on Foursquare-NYC is substantially shorter than that of STHGCN.

papers.title: Learning Semantic Co-occurrence and Personalized Focused Representations for Multimodal Sequential Recommendation
papers.abstract: Multimodal sequential recommendation (MSR) leverages textual and visual content of items to capture the evolution of user interests over time. Prior efforts have largely concentrated on multimodal fusion strategies or downstream sequential modeling, while the question of how to obtain item representations genuinely aligned with the recommendation objective has received far less attention. Off-the-shelf encoders pretrained on generic corpora produce representations that emphasize broad semantic similarity rather than the specific cues that drive user choice in a recommendation scenario. In this work, we propose ScopeRec , a S emantic co -occurrence and pe rsonalized focus framework for multimodal sequential Rec ommendation, which reshapes multimodal representations from two complementary views. From the item view, items co-interacted within a behavior sequence carry rich sequence-level semantic associations, which we term semantic co-occurrence . ScopeRec mines such multi-level co-occurrence patterns directly from historical sequences and injects them back into the item representations, yielding embeddings that better reflect users' historical semantic preferences. From the user view, user attention typically concentrates on a few keywords in text or salient regions in images, which we term semantic focus . To exploit this property, ScopeRec employs a hierarchical mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture in which different experts independently capture fine-grained interest from distinct semantic perspectives. A specialized fusion module then adaptively combines representations across modalities and semantic levels in a personalized manner. Experiments on three public MSR benchmarks show that ScopeRec consistently surpasses state-of-the-art baselines, with relative gains of 13.8% to 28.7% on NDCG and Hit Ratio.

papers.title: FedTGC: Trajectory-Guided Graph Collaboration for Federated Recommendation
papers.abstract: Federated recommendation preserves user privacy by keeping interaction data on local clients, but this decentralization limits direct access to cross-user collaborative signals. Existing graph-based federated recommendation methods attempt to recover such signals by constructing client relation graphs. However, our empirical analysis shows that under a temporally faithful evaluation protocol, in which negative sampling and candidate construction are restricted to information available at the recommendation cutoff, client relations constructed by existing graph-based methods can become increasingly unreliable in practice. Consequently, clients may collaborate with mismatched neighbors, thereby introducing harmful collaborative signals and causing negative transfer. To address this problem, we propose FedTGC , a trajectory-guided graph collaboration framework for reliable federated recommendation. FedTGC represents each client by its local item embedding update trajectory, constructs a dynamic client relation graph from compact trajectory descriptors, and adaptively personalizes the calibration of collaboration strength across clients. This design enables effective knowledge sharing among similar clients. Extensive experiments on five real-world datasets show that FedTGC consistently outperforms representative federated recommendation baselines under the Honest Setting. Further analyses reveal that the commonly adopted Original Setting can substantially overestimate recommendation performance, highlighting the importance of temporally faithful evaluation and validating the effectiveness of trajectory-guided collaboration. The source code is available at https://github.com/Charleston77/FedTGC.

papers.title: When Can Social Network Recommendations Improve Precision and Mitigate Inequality?
papers.abstract: Link recommendation algorithms can reshape network topology and amplify structural inequalities through “rich-get-richer” dynamics: well-connected users may be disproportionately recommended, accumulating further connections at peripheral nodes' expense. Typical evaluations overlook how algorithmic choices interact with network topology behind this disparity. We introduce an auditing framework that isolates the effects of algorithmic design from those of network topology, on precision and structural equality. We define Equality Gain , a measure to quantify whether a recommender mitigates or amplifies structural disparities relative to a recommender-free baseline. To systematically vary topology, we introduce Counterfactual Graph Rewiring (CGR), which produces graphs with tunable clustering at a fixed degree sequence. We find that the precision–equality trade-off characterizing link-recommendation algorithms is contingent on network topology: sparse graphs exhibit a trade-off, whereas dense, highly clustered graphs admit a “win-win” regime in which models exploiting triadic closure around low-degree nodes attain both high precision and equality gains. These findings motivate a shift from model-centric optimization to network-aware link recommendation, aligning algorithmic mechanisms with network structure.

papers.title: Follow the COMPASS: Reasoning-Guided Advertiser Bid Modeling for Campaign Simulation under Auction Dynamics
affiliations: The Graduate University for Advanced Studies, SOKENDAI
papers.abstract: Advertisers launch ad campaigns to bid for potential customers and promote sales. In uncertain auction environments, accurate campaign performance forecasting (CPF) can help advertisers navigate toward efficient campaign configurations and successful marketing, much like a compass . However, existing CPF methods largely neglect auction dynamics, where competitors adjust their bids in response to evolving campaign states. Conventional log-driven models, which directly fit observable states to bid actions, overlook the deliberate reasoning process underlying advertiser behavior, leading to suboptimal forecasts. To fill the gap, we propose COMPASS , a reasoning-driven framework for modeling bid behavior during ad campaigns. COMPASS explicitly treats bid reasoning as a latent variable and progressively infers it under a Search-Optimization framework. Instead of a naive brute-force search, COMPASS adopts a hierarchical inference strategy: a high-capacity schema model searches over compact, high-level bid strategies, while a lightweight execution model expands them into concrete bid predictions and provides evaluation feedback. To simplify online deployment, we further propose an alignment-as-distillation mechanism with a self-evaluation trick. This avoids a separate knowledge distillation stage and produces a self-contained execution model that can be independently deployed without invoking the schema model at serving time. Extensive experiments on industrial and public datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of COMPASS. In large-scale online A/B tests, COMPASS achieves a 5.1% uplift in average revenue per user, validating its practical impact in real-world advertising systems.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Triggered Test-Time Selective Inference for Click-Through Rate Prediction
papers.abstract: Click-through rate (CTR) models estimate the probability of a user clicking on an item and exhibit varying prediction reliability across instances at inference time. Some feature combinations of model input are well-represented in training data and yield confident outputs, while others produce high uncertainty due to feature combination sparsity. Training-time approaches such as adaptive gating mechanisms learn a deterministic feature selection function, but this function is itself unreliable for under-observed combinations since it suffers from the same sparsity problem. More fundamentally, training and inference have asymmetric objectives: training benefits from diverse pattern exposure including sparse ones to learn generalizable representations, whereas inference should prioritize only combinations the model has already learned to evaluate reliably. This asymmetry motivates test-time optimization as a complementary paradigm. Rather than relying on a single learned function, test-time optimization explores multiple feature configurations per instance and aggregates predictions, deriving robustness from exploration diversity. By deferring computation decisions until the actual instance is observed, it further enables selective budget allocation that invests extra resources only in uncertain samples. However, CTR models with binary objectives lack built-in mechanisms for per-instance uncertainty assessment, and strict industrial latency constraints leave limited room for additional computation. Therefore, we propose a model-agnostic training-free Uncertainty-Triggered Test-Time Selective Inference framework (UTTSI) that operates directly on any already-trained CTR model without modifying its parameters. UTTSI estimates per-instance uncertainty via dual signals combining model logit confidence with a frequency-based prior, and selectively triggers feature path exploration only for uncertain samples, with the majority of confident instances served at zero additional cost. Finally, extensive experiments strongly validate the effectiveness of UTTSI.

papers.title: Generate to Accelerate: Improved Reranking via LLM-Generated Pivot Documents
affiliations: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
papers.abstract: Common approaches to reduce the computational overhead of reranking models include identifying a candidate set of documents for reranking or constructing comparison graphs to minimize redundant comparisons. For pointwise rankers, determining a candidate set typically involves estimating a query-dependent cutoff based on the scores of the top-ranked documents. In contrast, comparison graphs for listwise approaches are often derived using heuristics, such as propagating local comparisons within sliding windows in a bottom-up fashion or reducing comparisons via pivot-based strategies in a top-down manner. In this work, we argue that restricting these processes to existing documents in the collection is unnecessary. Instead, we propose leveraging the generative capabilities of large language models to synthesize a pseudo-relevant document for a given query. We then adapt existing reranking approaches and also propose a novel parallel reranking approach to leverage this LLM-generated document as a pivot. Our experiments demonstrate that using LLM-generated pivots for ranked list truncation reduces the number of pointwise ranker inferences by up to 66%. In both in-domain and out-of-domain settings, we observe speedups of up to 2.95× in listwise reranking, while maintaining comparable or improved retrieval effectiveness.

papers.title: When Do Anchor-Based Pointwise LLM Rerankers Help? Retriever Quality, Statistical Scope, and Anchor Design
affiliations: Missouri University of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Anchor-based pointwise LLM reranking scores each candidate against a shared reference passage to recover cross-document context at pointwise cost. We study when this actually helps, using GCCP/PAGC as a representative method. Our study is reproduction-first. We use reproduction as a starting point for a controlled component-level stress test of anchor-based pointwise reranking. Our initial reimplementation, based only on the paper text, achieves 0.24 nDCG@10 instead of the reported 0.66, revealing that several undocumented implementation details are necessary to reproduce the method. After identifying and recovering eight such details, we reproduce the reported results within 1.6% and use the validated implementation for controlled analysis. We find that the core contrastive scoring idea is robust under rigorous statistical correction. However, two design choices held fixed in the original paper are less reliable. First, we find that combining the contrastive score with the standard pointwise relevance score helps when the first-stage retriever is BM25, but gives little or no benefit when the first-stage retriever is a stronger dense model such as E5. Second, the paper's more complex method for constructing the anchor is unnecessary. A much simpler anchor, built by interleaving the top-ranked sentences, matches or outperforms it across datasets. These findings are consistent across different LLM backbones, including a 4-bit quantized 72B model. Overall, anchor-based pointwise reranking is effective, but its gains come mainly from contrastive scoring rather than from the more complex aggregation and anchor-construction choices, and they appear under narrower conditions than the original evaluation suggests.

papers.title: ASH: Asymmetric Scalar Hashing With Learned Dimensionality Reduction for High-Fidelity Vector Quantization
papers.abstract: For a long time, additive quantizers, such as product quantization, have been considered the gold standard in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Recently, scalar quantization has re-emerged from the depths of history with a new wave of data-agnostic techniques. Inscribed in this general framework, we turn our attention to data-driven methods, showing that new highs in recall and speed can be achieved by reducing the number of dimensions while increasing the bitrate per dimension. Critically, this dimensionality reduction needs to be learned from data to be successful. We present ASH (Asymmetric Scalar Hashing), a data-driven encoder-decoder framework that applies dimensionality reduction to database vectors via a learned orthonormal projection, followed by scalar quantization, while keeping queries in their original form. This asymmetric design enables higher accuracy than the best additive and scalar quantizers at iso-compression, while admitting highly efficient similarity computations via SIMD operations. ASH has short learning and encoding times, making it attractive for real-world deployment. Extensive experiments on a variety of datasets demonstrate that ASH achieves state-of-the-art ANN recall and speeds across all compression regimes.

papers.title: Transforming User Actions into Audit Signals: Participatory Auditing to Improve Search Results
papers.abstract: Regulatory frameworks, such as the European Union's Digital Services Act (DSA), have established new directives for the governance of online platforms, including Information Retrieval (IR) systems. In particular, the DSA mandates that IR systems should enable stakeholders, such as users, to independently audit the outputs of the system, for example, with respect to ranking quality or fairness. Moreover, users should be able to provide actionable feedback to the system's providers. In this work, we introduce a participatory audit strategy that transforms natural user interactions into actionable signals for identifying and correcting ranking errors, i.e., documents that have been systematically undervalued in the search results. We show that our strategy provides actionable feedback that can be used to improve the overall relevance of highly ranked documents. Our strategy uses a 3x3 grid presentation with 9x9 Latin-square counterbalancing as an unbiased audit interface, enabling auditors to identify ranking errors through their natural search behaviours. We evaluate our strategy with 108 participants across a Participatory Audit and separate Evaluation, complemented by an independent offline evaluation. Our findings show that our approach enables users to easily identify relevant documents that are ranked at lower positions by the system. We also show that these audit signals (the user's clicks and brief passage selections, collected while participants engage with the audit interface) can be used to rerank the results, and that the reranking elicits deeper user engagement. Our audit strategy produces measurable improvements in both online (user engagement) and offline (nDCG@10) evaluations. For example, participants preferred 6.7% of low-ranked documents identified by our strategy over every top-ranked document from the original ranking. We show that a reranking based on the obtained audit signals resulted in a statistically significant 6.81% relative gain in nDCG@10, according to a Bonferroni-corrected paired bootstrap test, with passage selection rates rising 6.1 percentage points in our online evaluation.

papers.title: Scalability Analysis of Cross-modal Text-to-Image Pipelines
papers.abstract: Cross-modal text-to-image retrieval systems are increasingly deployed over large-scale multimedia corpora, where retrieval effectiveness must be balanced against latency, energy consumption, storage, and candidate fidelity under approximate indexing. In this paper, we present a systems-level evaluation of text-to-image retrieval pipelines under realistic deployment constraints. We study representative single-index, retrieve-and-rerank, and ensemble pipelines on MS-COCO and Flickr30K, and evaluate their scalability on a 7M-image subset of LAION using Flat, HNSW, IVFPQ, and O-IVFPQ indexes. Our results show that strong rerankers can preserve retrieval quality provided the first-stage ANN index maintains sufficient candidate fidelity, but that low-fidelity indexes create unrecoverable candidate losses. At LAION scale, O-IVFPQ provides the strongest single-index operating point, maintaining high candidate fidelity while reducing latency, energy, and storage relative to HNSW. For retrieve-and-rerank pipelines, the reranker dominates end-to-end latency and energy, making index choice less important once sufficient candidate fidelity is preserved. Overall, our study shows that scalable cross-modal retrieval requires joint reasoning about pipeline architecture, candidate fidelity, and systems cost.

papers.title: Look Before You Leap: Teaching RAG Generators to TRACE Evidence Before Reasoning
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become a powerful paradigm for knowledge-intensive applications. To maintain high recall, retrievers often return extensive context, requiring generators to distinguish truly useful evidence. Previous approaches typically couple evidence identification and reasoning. This coupling, however, hinders the model's ability to explicitly decide which evidence to use before generating a response, limiting both verifiability and effective context utilization. In this work, we propose TRACE , a reinforcement learning framework that trains RAG generators to explicitly select evidence prior to grounded reasoning. TRACE trains models under a structured protocol that separates evidence selection from subsequent reasoning, and combines task-specific rewards for correctness, relevance, and structural validity with a high-weight holistic bonus that stabilizes the joint optimization of accuracy and attribution. To further mitigate policy-update instability under multiple reward signals, we employ a stabilized KL-divergence estimator. Experiments on three multi-hop QA datasets using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct show that TRACE improves answer accuracy by 10–30% while producing explicit, evidence-attributed reasoning traces. Its performance is competitive with advanced commercial LLMs. Further analyses demonstrate strong generalization across diverse QA datasets, retrieval settings, and an evidence-grounded summarization task. Our code is publicly available.

papers.title: S2R-Merge: Soft-Gated Routing with Structural Node Merge Optimization
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) have shown strong potential on complex reasoning tasks, but their scalability is limited by substantial communication overhead and token consumption. Recent methods reduce these costs by pruning redundant agents or edges, but such deletion-based optimization can discard role-specific information and often operates only after activating the full agent pool. To address these limitations, we propose S2R-Merge , a unified routing-and-merging framework that reframes MAS structural optimization from node deletion to information-preserving consolidation. S2R-Merge first uses an uncertainty-aware 2-Stage Soft-Gated Router to select a task-relevant agent subgraph, avoiding unnecessary full-pool activation. It then applies graph-based node merging to identify structurally inefficient agents from policy-gradient-learned communication pathways, absorbing them into strongly related partners while preserving their role-level information through Prompt-level Fusion. Experiments on six reasoning and code-generation benchmarks with Llama-3-8B-Instruct and GPT-4 show that S2R-Merge achieves the best average accuracy among all compared methods, reaching 77.22% and 92.37%, respectively. It also reduces average prompt token usage by up to 12.3× compared with full multi-agent collaboration and achieves the lowest token consumption among multi-agent graph-optimization baselines. These results demonstrate that S2R-Merge provides an effective cost-performance trade-off for scalable LLM-based MAS.

papers.title: MemDTG: Dynamic Temporal Memory Graphs for Evidence-Admissible Agent Memory
papers.abstract: Long-term agent memory is an online, non-monotonic retrieval problem. New interactions may reinforce, contradict, supersede, specialize, abstract, or expire earlier memories; the same fact can be a wrong current answer, a correct historical answer, or necessary transition evidence depending on query intent. Existing chunk, summary, and graph memories retrieve by semantic or graph relevance and treat time as post-hoc metadata, so they cannot determine whether a memory is observable, valid, lifecycle-admissible, and provenance-supported before it enters the candidate space. We propose MemDTG, a dynamic temporal memory graph that frames agent memory as temporal evidence admission. MemDTG separates immutable raw episodes from a mutable entity-state temporal graph and a memory-evolution graph over assertion versions. State slots localize mutable user and task states; an LLM-assisted slot-local resolver classifies semantic evolution only within bounded temporal histories; and deterministic commit rules update valid intervals, lifecycle states, and typed evolution edges. At read time, a query compiler instantiates observed-time, valid-time, version, edge-type, and role constraints before ranking, and QV-CTW retrieves evidence paths only inside the query-legal temporal subgraph. Evidence certificates record selected facts, sources, roles, and rejected stale or future alternatives, making retrieval auditable. On LongMemEval and LoCoMo, MemDTG achieves the best LLM-judge accuracy and Citation F1. Ablation and temporal error analyses confirm that provenance certificates and legal-subgraph pre-filtering are each essential for these gains, reducing stale-answer errors by 61.7% and future leaks by 80.1%.

papers.title: PrivMem: Privacy-Preserving Temporal Motif Mining over Cross-User Agent Memory Graphs
papers.abstract: Long-lived AI agents increasingly store private memory graphs of user goals, retrieved documents, tool calls, failures, and repairs. Mining these memories across users is crucial for discovering recurrent operational patterns, yet the problem remains unsolved: raw graphs cannot be centralized, and even aggregate motifs can reveal workflows supported by only one or two users. Existing local differential privacy (LDP) frequency-estimation and pattern-mining methods optimize top-K recovery, but they have no principled release-time defense against rare-workflow disclosure. We argue that the missing axis is not a stronger randomizer but a safer server-side release policy. We present PrivMem, which extracts retrieval-causal temporal motifs on device, perturbs them with per-coordinate randomized response, and releases them through a shrinkage ranker, a public-schema risk gate, and a Benjamini–Hochberg calibrated false-discovery filter. The analysis proves per-coordinate ε-LDP, derives concentration for the unbiased support estimator, establishes a support-gap condition for top-K recovery, and shows that the release stack preserves privacy by post-processing. On a 240-user planted benchmark, PrivMem reduces in-schema rare-workflow leakage by over 35× at matched utility; at ε=1,θ=8, it keeps top-20 F1 at 0.86 while cutting leakage from 0.27 to 0.007. It also drives out-of-schema leakage to zero and improves released-subspace clustering by over 10× ARI at ε=2. On a 1,757-user real-trace corpus across eight LLM-agent domains, PrivMem releases exactly zero rare motifs at every threshold, while LDP baselines leak 0.28–0.57.

papers.title: LuWu: Adaptive Layer-wise Heterogeneous KV Cache Quantization
papers.abstract: The KV cache is essential for efficient autoregressive inference in Large Language Models (LLMs), but its memory cost increases with context length, layer depth, and request concurrency, limiting long-context and high-throughput serving, particularly in Computing Power Network (CPN) environments. KV cache quantization reduces this cost by lowering the storage bit-width of keys and values. However, existing methods often rely on uniform precision or static mixed-precision policies, which cannot fully capture layer-wise differences in quantization sensitivity or decoding-time changes in precision requirements. This paper proposes LuWu, an adaptive layer-wise heterogeneous KV cache quantization method. LuWu first performs offline calibration to measure attention-output errors under different K/V precision pairs, clusters layers with similar error response patterns, prunes unsuitable candidate configurations, and searches an initial heterogeneous precision configuration under accuracy and bit-width objectives. During online inference, LuWu uses the Layer Activity Score (LAS) to adjust the precision of selected layers, while a hierarchical residual-code representation supports efficient promotion and demotion between precision levels. Experiments on representative reasoning, long-context, and language modeling tasks show that LuWu achieves a favorable accuracy–bitwidth trade-off. Compared with representative state-of-the-art K8V8 baselines, LuWu reduces the average equivalent bit-width by 29.5%–38.1% while maintaining competitive inference accuracy. These results highlight the effectiveness of adaptive layer-wise heterogeneous quantization for memory-efficient LLM inference.

papers.title: Double-down sandwiched learned Bloom filters for multiset membership query
papers.abstract: Multi-set membership query is a core operation in network and data systems, which requires simultaneous element existence verification and set category classification. Traditional multi-set Bloom Filters rely on fixed hash mechanisms and cannot adapt to data distribution characteristics, while existing Learned Bloom Filters (LBFs) are only designed for single-set scenarios and cannot support efficient multi-set parallel queries. To address these limitations, this paper proposes Double-Down Sandwiched Learned Bloom Filters (DDSLBF), a novel learning-enhanced architecture for multi-set membership queries. DDSLBF adopts a hierarchical sandwich structure composed of dual learned oracles and parallel Bloom Filter groups, realizing collaborative pre-filtering, verification and precise classification. We conduct comprehensive theoretical analysis on error rates, space efficiency, optimal space allocation and space-accuracy trade-off, and derive the theoretical performance bounds of the model. Extensive experimental results on three real-world network datasets show that DDSLBF achieves higher classification accuracy, eliminates classification failures completely, and reduces the false positive rate significantly compared with the baselines under the same memory constraints. This work extends the application scope of LBFs and provides a lightweight, high-precision solution for multi-set query tasks in network security and data systems.

papers.title: AdaptSteer: Workload-Adaptive Optimizer Steering via Execution-Derived Preference Supervision
papers.abstract: Database query optimizers often select suboptimal execution plans, and effective steering requires identifying configurations that improve query and workload performance without modifying DBMS internals. Existing external steering systems can reason over multiple optimizer configurations, but many rely on online feedback, exploration, or engine-specific steering mechanisms. More recent LLM-based SQL steering approaches avoid deeper optimizer integration, but often depend on narrow supervision and general-purpose embeddings that are costly, not explicitly aligned with execution behavior, and difficult to adapt under workload shifts. We present AdaptSteer, a novel workload-adaptive optimizer-steering framework that learns from execution-derived preference supervision. AdaptSteer converts latencies measured across diverse query–configuration pairs into preference-based contrastive training signals for a compact SQL encoder, without invasive DBMS modifications or external APIs. The resulting representation supports two lightweight decision heads: a calibrated classifier for safety-first binary steering and a pairwise Condorcet ranker that decomposes K-way configuration selection into binary execution-preference comparisons. We further apply Reptile-based meta-learning to the trained encoder, enabling few-shot adaptation to unseen workloads. Evaluations on the JOB and CEB benchmarks show that AdaptSteer reduces total workload latency by 70.1% relative to the PostgreSQL default and achieves 4.4% lower total workload latency than LLMSteer under the same binary protocol, without relying on external API calls. Beyond binary steering, AdaptSteer improves multi-action selection through pairwise preference ranking across the evaluated candidate sets and benefits from multi-configuration supervision across broader action spaces. Under CEB→JOB adaptation, AdaptSteer's meta-learned variant improves AUROC by 4.2 percentage points over the contrastive-only baseline with only 20 target-workload adaptation queries. Together, AdaptSteer unifies execution-derived preference supervision, binary and multi-action steering, and few-shot adaptation in a compact, deployable optimizer-steering framework.

papers.title: GAP: Privacy-Aware and Authenticated Knowledge Graph Queries in Hybrid-Storage Blockchains
papers.abstract: Hybrid-storage blockchain (HSB) has been a prevailing and efficient storage model in blockchain-based applications. It retains raw data off-chain and only stores metadata on-chain for integrity check to improve scalability. However, for widely provided query services, ensuring query integrity without compromising data privacy is an ongoing challenge in HSB since the off-chain storage provider may be malicious. Existing work has largely focused on authenticated keyword search or range queries over textual data, while several studies on authenticated queries on graph data either ignore user privacy or merely enable user-side verification, with limited support for various graph queries. This paper presents GAP, the first privacy-aware and publicly authenticated scheme for rich queries, including node keyword, edge type, connectivity, and subgraph matching queries, over knowledge graphs in HSB. The core of GAP lies in a novel authenticated data structure (ADS), which incorporates our modified hybrid index and an orthogonal list encrypted with inner product encryption (IPE). With such an ADS, we efficiently perform diverse graph queries with privacy protection, meanwhile generating verification objects (VOs) for public verifiability of the query integrity. Additionally, GAP supports dynamic node/edge updates with forward privacy and update integrity. Security analysis proves that GAP achieves L-adaptive security with desired privacy and integrity. Comparative experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets validate that GAP yields a 40%–50% reduction in trapdoor generation. It also outperforms others by over two orders of magnitude in search time, and its on-chain performance is around twice as efficient as the baselines.

papers.title: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly of Markov Boundary for Tabular Prediction
papers.abstract: Under standard graphical assumptions, the Markov boundary of a target variable is the smallest set of features that renders every other feature redundant. Once the boundary is observed, the target is conditionally independent of the rest of the table. This is a tempting object for tabular prediction, since it names exactly the columns a model should need. Yet modern regressors are still trained on the full feature set. We ask whether the Markov boundary is genuinely useful for prediction on SCMBench, a 3,450-task synthetic SCM benchmark with feature counts from 40 to 1000 and six SCM families, evaluated with six regressors. The answer is more nuanced than the theory suggests. Restricting a regressor to the oracle boundary often improves prediction substantially, and the improvement grows as the feature space becomes larger and sparser. But the natural pipeline of recovering the boundary with causal discovery and training on the recovered mask does not deliver. Existing estimators exhaust the compute budget before reaching the regime where the boundary helps most, and even where they run they rarely beat the full feature set. We trace this to three causes. Discovery optimizes structural recovery rather than prediction. False negatives and false positives carry sharply asymmetric predictive cost. The exact boundary is only one of many feature sets that beat all features. We then develop what these facts imply for prediction-aligned feature selection and for tabular models that learn to use causal structure.

papers.title: MCTS-KBQA: Monte Carlo Tree Search with Information Gain Rewards for Knowledge Base Question Answering
papers.abstract: This work investigates how to improve large language model (LLM)-based reasoning for knowledge base question answering (KBQA) via Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). Applying MCTS to LLM-based KBQA remains challenging because reward design is difficult and rollout-based search is computationally expensive. Existing MCTS-style methods either rely on direct LLM scoring or require substantial data to train separate reward models, and they often provide rewards only at terminal states. To address these limitations, we propose Fast MCTS, which replaces terminal rollouts with an information gain (IG) reward for intermediate states. The IG reward is implemented as a question-conditioned PPL-ratio proxy over sanitized interaction histories, computed by forward passes of an open-source instruction LLM without additional reward-model training. Experiments on four KBQA benchmarks show that Fast MCTS consistently outperforms linear baselines and generally improves the accuracy-cost trade-off relative to rollout-based Classic MCTS. (Code and data are available at https://github.com/JimXiongGM/MCTS-KBQA.)

papers.title: Continual Knowledge Graph Embedding via Community Hierarchies and Reconstruction Distillation
papers.abstract: Continual knowledge graph embedding (CKGE) aims to incrementally learn emerging knowledge in evolving knowledge graphs while preserving previously acquired knowledge. However, existing CKGE approaches suffer from two major limitations. First, they largely overlook the explicit graph structure that is crucial for robust representation learning. Second, newly arrived triples are often learned in a stochastic order, which disrupts topological coherence and fails to preserve the structural dependencies between historical and emerging knowledge, thereby leading to severe catastrophic forgetting. We propose CHR-KGE, a structure-first framework tailored for CKGE under evolving graph scenarios. Specifically, CHR-KGE organizes newly arrived triples into a structure-guided learning order through community partition and hierarchical prioritization, while preserving cross-snapshot structural continuity via structure-constrained reconstruction and aggregation module. Meanwhile, it selectively constrains representation drift in structurally important regions through learnable mask-guided distillation, enabling effective adaptation to new knowledge without sacrificing the stability of historical representations. Experiments on six datasets show that CHR-KGE consistently outperforms strong baselines in link prediction accuracy, knowledge transferability, and training efficiency. Compared with IncDE, CHR-KGE achieves average relative improvements of 3.39% in MRR, 5.36% in Hits@1, and 2.39% in Hits@10. Compared with re-train, CHR-KGE maintains highly competitive accuracy while reducing training time by 40%–60%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of CHR-KGE for continual knowledge graph embedding. The code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CHR-KGE/.

papers.title: SDiffusE: Structure-Aware Diffusion for Temporal Knowledge Graph Reasoning with Denoised Evolution
papers.abstract: Temporal Knowledge Graph (TKG) reasoning that aims to predict missing facts has been widely explored. Compared to static knowledge graphs, the introduction of temporal modalities makes reasoning about entities and relationships more challenging. Most existing methods assume that all the recorded TKG facts are credible, overlooking two critical challenges: TKGs are typically automatically constructed, thereby inevitably introducing noise; meanwhile, the temporal evolution itself inherently carries uncertainty. While recent works on KG error detection and uncertain KG have attempted to address KG errors and uncertainty, they heavily rely on hard-to-obtain labels and neglect temporal information in TKGs. In this paper, we propose SDiffusE , a novel framework that enhances TKG reasoning through S tructure-aware Diffus ion and denoised E volution, addressing the above issues. SDiffusE integrates three synergistic modules: The TKG diffusion module reconstructs authentic TKG structural interactions by denoising spurious edges; The recurrent relation-aware GCN module captures temporal dependencies for both original and denoised TKG snapshots; The dual-view contrastive learning module further leverages clean denoised signals to regularize learned representations. Experiments across four datasets show the superiority of SDiffusE over five categories of baselines.

papers.title: Disrupting Networks: Amplifying Social Dissensus via Large Language Models
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study how targeted content injection can strategically disrupt social networks. Specifically, we address a practical limitation of the basic variant of the Friedkin–Johnsen (FJ) model, which prevents increasing the polarization and disagreement of the network, making it unable to reproduce real-world scenarios. We overcome such limitation by using an enriched variant of the FJ model, further showing how altering a node inherent opinion to maximize disruption. Building on these preliminary considerations, we design a reinforcement learning framework to fine-tune a Large Language Model (LLM) for generating disruption-oriented text. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data confirm that tuned LLMs can approach theoretical disruption limits. Our findings raise important considerations for content moderation, adversarial information campaigns, and generative model regulation. Code is publicly available.

papers.title: Knowing When Evidence Is Insufficient: Supervising Claim-to-Evidence Reasoning for Multimodal Fact-Checking
papers.abstract: Not Enough Information (NEI) is the dominant failure mode in multimodal fact-checking, where current LVLMs routinely collapse NEI into Supported or Refuted. Our analysis on MOCHEG attributes this collapse to two challenges. The first challenge is a claim-driven shortcut, where supervised fine-tuning amplifies attention on claim tokens and lifts the claim-to-evidence attention ratio from 4.5 to 9.5. The second challenge is weak evidence-gap supervision, where training claims rarely expose where evidence is missing and models conflate linguistic ambiguity with genuine evidence insufficiency. To address these two challenges, we propose CEIR, a Claim-to-Evidence Insufficiency Reasoning supervision framework for multimodal fact-checking. CEIR aligns uncertainty with verified gaps between claims and evidence, helping LVLMs recognise insufficient evidence. CEIR anchors supervision by linking every atomic proposition of the claim to retrieved multimodal evidence via per-atom verification. It then rewrites only the verification-failing atoms with diverse uncertainty expressions while preserving anchor facts. Experiments on MOCHEG and Factify with advanced LVLMs show that CEIR improves NEI-F1/Macro-F1 over standard SFT by +27.5/+13.5 points on MOCHEG; on Factify, it improves merged-insufficient F1 and five-way Macro-F1 by +21.1 and +9.2 points.

papers.title: M-to-M: A Discipline-Mismatch Theory of Multimodal Fact-Checking
affiliations: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
papers.abstract: Multimodal fact-checking systems exhibit a persistent instability: an architecture that leads on one benchmark often loses ground on another, with no method best everywhere. We argue this reflects a structural property of the benchmarks themselves. Fact-checking benchmarks silently encode different verification disciplines —standards of evidential sufficiency that range from permissive, where broad multimodal consistency suffices, to strict, where each specific claim element must be independently grounded. We introduce M-to-M (Many-to-Many), a matrix-based framework that represents localized claim–evidence interactions before aggregation, and use it to instantiate two verification architectures—holistic and compositional—under identical retrieval and evidence conditions. Across three benchmarks ordered by discipline, the performance gap between the two architectures does not merely shrink but reverses sign: holistic verification wins under permissive labels, compositional verification under strict ones. We trace this reversal to a single verdict rule, show it persists when aggregation is learned rather than specified, and find that learned verdict heads fail to transfer across benchmarks. Our findings suggest that benchmark choice conditions which verification behaviors are rewarded, while M-to-M provides a methodological framework for isolating and studying these verification dynamics under controlled aggregation policies.

papers.title: Interpretation-Aware Image Manipulation Detection
papers.abstract: Image manipulation has been a common practice since the early days of photography, and has evolved into a sophisticated threat with the rise of powerful image editing tools and generative AI. It can be used to spread misinformation, manipulate public opinion, and cause harm to individuals and communities. In this article, we study the problem of determining whether an image is misleading, i.e. edited in a misleading way. We introduce a risk framework to assess the intrinsic interpretive shift (ITS) of an ordered image pair, which evaluates whether the final edited image changes the interpretation supported by a source reference image. We show our risk framework can be operationalized with the Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) provenance framework. We estimate ITS with a single-call vision-language implementation of our risk framework, which first checks for meaningful visual differences, then tests whether the differences induce interpretive shift, and finally determines whether the shift is fully explained by permissible transformations rather than content-level changes. The system outputs a binary label (potentially misleading or not) together with interpretive clues and a short justification. To test the approach and show that ITS is a measurable proxy for misleading edits, we built a benchmark of 418 ordered pairs, drawn from real-world fact-check cases and meaning-preserving transformations. The best-performing model configuration (gpt-5.4) achieves 88.2% precision, 94.2% recall, and 96.5% balanced accuracy. The code is available at https://github.com/liyu0x/ITS_detection/.

papers.title: SAVER: Selective and Adaptive Multi-View Routing for Visual Emotion Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Emotions elicited by visual content are formed through the interaction of multiple visual cues rather than a single visual element, and their importance varies depending on the context. This characteristic makes visual emotion analysis not merely a classification problem but a reasoning task that requires the selective integration of diverse visual cues. Existing approaches tend to represent images using a unified feature representation and fail to explicitly model the contributions of different visual cues. To capture the multifaceted nature of emotional cues, we propose SAVER, a framework for query-conditioned visual emotion reasoning. SAVER decomposes visual information into multiple view-specific representations corresponding to distinct aspects, such as facial expressions, scenes, objects, and colorfulness, enabling the explicit modeling of each cue. A semantic-aware routing mechanism dynamically selects and integrates the most relevant views by jointly considering the visual context and query semantics. This selective integration is combined with learnable soft prompts to enable structured emotion reasoning within a vision-language model. Extensive experiments on diverse emotion datasets demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms both vision-based and VLM-based approaches. Qualitative analysis provides interpretable insights into how different visual cues contribute to emotion prediction, highlighting the effectiveness of SAVER in improving both its performance and interpretability. The code is available at https://github.com/leeyubin10/SAVER.git.

papers.title: When Explanations Seem Helpful but Fail to Help: Evaluating XAI Interfaces for Model Diagnosis Across Modalities
papers.abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) methods, such as LIME and SHAP, are increasingly incorporated into AI-enabled information systems for model inspection, oversight, and diagnosis. However, it remains unclear whether these interfaces improve users' ability to diagnose model behavior, or whether such utility generalizes across data modalities. We report three controlled user studies comprising 108 modality-specific sessions in which participants with foundational AI knowledge diagnosed model errors across Tabular, Text, and Image settings using LIME, SHAP, or a No-Explanation baseline, jointly evaluating task-grounded behavioral outcomes and subjective perceptions. Explanation interfaces were consistently preferred and rated as more understandable and useful, and they increased completion time across modalities; however, their diagnostic utility varied by modality. Benefits were clearest in the Tabular setting, driven primarily by LIME. Explanations provided no reliable benefit in Text, and Image results reflected method-specific differences rather than a reliable advantage over the baseline. Qualitative findings suggest that explanations often strengthened users' sense of understanding but did not consistently help them detect model failures. We argue that the quality of explanations in multimodal information systems should be evaluated using task-grounded, modality-sensitive criteria rather than subjective perception alone.

papers.title: LG-PLO: Layout-Grounded Plackett–Luce Optimization for Instance-Aware Image Generation
papers.abstract: Layout-conditioned image generation aims to synthesize images that match specified object categories and bounding boxes. However, generated images often fail to follow the intended layout conditions, resulting in hallucinations such as missing or spurious objects and spatial misalignment. When such inconsistent image-layout pairs are used as augmented training data, they can degrade the performance of object detectors. To address this issue, we propose LG-PLO, a layout-grounded Plackett–Luce optimization framework for instance-aware image generation. LG-PLO jointly considers image- and layout-level preferences using three candidates: a preferred image with correct layout, a rejected image with correct layout, and a preferred image with incorrect layout.
