LG-PLO then optimizes a Plackett-Luce objective that ranks images satisfying both preferences higher than those satisfying only one. Experiments on the COCO benchmark show that LG-PLO achieves a better balance between visual fidelity and layout adherence compared to baselines, while also improving detector performance when generated images are used for data augmentation.

papers.title: Learning Video-Derived Behavioral and Physiological Representations for Automated Deception Detection
papers.abstract: Deception detection in video conferencing is increasingly important with the rise of remote interviews, online judicial hearings, and telemedicine consultations. Existing approaches either rely on observable behavioral cues (e.g., micro-expressions and head movements) or depend on specialized equipment for physiological sensing (e.g., thermal cameras or wearable devices). The former benefits from the ubiquity and non-intrusive nature of commodity RGB cameras but often suffers from limited accuracy, while the latter provides more reliable and discriminative signals at the cost of additional hardware, hindering scalability in real-world deployment. In this work, we bridge the gap between behavioral cue-based and physiological signal-based approaches and introduce DeceptSense, a video-derived multimodal framework for contactless deception detection using only RGB video. The key insight is that complementary signals, including motion dynamics, facial temperature variations, and cardiac activity, can be jointly recovered from RGB video. DeceptSense extracts these modalities using an iDT descriptor for motion dynamics, an RGB-to-thermal pipeline for temperature variation modeling, and an rPPG module for cardiac signal extraction. It then employs a cross-modal attention mechanism to align the three temporally asynchronous modalities. Extensive experiments show that DeceptSense achieves an AUC of 89.6% on the challenging Real-Life Trial dataset and AUCs of 64.5% and 65.1% on the BOL and MU3D datasets, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed video-derived multimodal framework for automated deception detection.

papers.title: TrojanShot: Reinforced Demonstrations Yield Sample-Efficient Jailbreaks and Guardrails for LLMs
papers.abstract: LLM-based applications increasingly rely on models served through third-party providers, where the model's own alignment is often the sole defense against misuse. In this regime, developers must implement both red-teaming and guardrails themselves, yet existing in-context methods address these objectives in isolation and do not refine demonstrations against the target LLM's responses. We propose TrojanShot , a unified framework that post-trains a demonstration generator via reinforcement learning to produce potent in-context examples for both attack ( Trojan shots ) and defense ( Guardian shots ), operating entirely at the prompt layer of the target LLM. On AdvBench, a single Trojan shot reaches 80.6% ASR on Mistral-7B, and averaged across four datasets TrojanShot exceeds 256-shot Many-Shot Jailbreaking by 14.6 p.p. while preserving human-readable prompts; ablations show RL post-training is the dominant factor in demonstration quality, with the untrained generator already surpassing 1-shot ICA. We demonstrate strong transferability, with a trojan-attacker trained on Mistral-7B reaching 81.2% ASR on Llama-3-70B, exceeding the 69.9% of an attacker trained on Llama-3-8B. Guardian shots reduce TrojanShot 's own ASR by 48.9 p.p. with helpfulness within 1.1 p.p. of the undefended model. Our results hold for models whose intrinsic alignment is the primary defense. Warning: this paper contains harmful model responses for academic reference.

papers.title: Evaluating Closed-Domain RAG Systems with Expert-Written MCQs
papers.abstract: Evaluating Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems in closed-domain settings --- where answers must be grounded in a fixed, domain-specific corpus --- remains an open problem. Existing approaches rely on synthetic question generation, manual annotation, or general-purpose benchmarks, each with structural limitations. We propose repurposing expert-written multiple-choice questions (MCQs) as a reusable evaluation signal for closed-domain RAG. MCQs are human-authored, curriculum-aligned assessment artifacts: they test concepts domain experts consider important, are written independently of the indexed corpus, and include expert-designed distractors that distinguish correct understanding from plausible misconceptions. Our methodology decomposes each correct answer into atomic factual claims, rewrites each option as a standalone declarative probe, and evaluates the RAG system through binary per-option judgments. We instantiate the methodology on a production university tutoring system and release a publicly reproducible benchmark. The per-option evaluation exposes differences in generation accuracy, abstention behavior, and distractor credulity that are not captured by retrieval-side evaluation alone. These results show that expert-written MCQs provide a practical and diagnostically rich evaluation resource for closed-domain RAG systems.

papers.title: Tasks over Application Manuals: Revealing Gaps in Long-Horizon Procedural Reasoning for Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance on a wide range of natural language tasks, and recent benchmarks suggest that they are increasingly adept at multi-hop reasoning. However, these benchmarks are typically short-horizon, requiring only a small number of retrieval or inference steps, and provide limited evidence of reliability on real-world tasks that involve following manuals spanning hundreds of pages with complex, interdependent guidelines. In this paper, we introduce Tasks over Application Manuals (TAM), a benchmark for evaluating long-horizon procedural reasoning. We construct TAM by curating real-world tasks from two domains—ICD-10-CM clinical coding (mapping medical conditions to diagnostic codes) and U.S. federal sentencing (computing crime sentencing guideline outcomes, specifically offense levels)—with human-validated labels. Each task requires following an authoritative manual with tens of thousands of rules and executing a sequence of interdependent steps across different sections to produce an exact answer. We evaluate general-purpose prompting approaches, including retrieval-augmented generation, ReAct-style prompting, and an agent-harness baseline on GPT-5, and find that the best exact-match performance remains extremely low: 1% on ICD-10-CM coding and 15.5% on sentencing tasks. These results show that current benchmarks may overestimate LLM reasoning ability and miss a key challenge: reliably following long, rule-based procedures.

papers.title: LogoGate: Object-Aware Logo-Exposure Backdoor Attack for Text-to-Image Models
affiliations: Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: As fine-tuning and customization of pre-trained T2I models have become prevalent, backdoor attacks that exploit this fine-tuning process to embed triggers have also emerged. In this context, an adversary can secretly embed a brand logo into the generation process to conduct covert advertising or brand sabotage through publicly released models. However, existing approaches do not constrain which objects carry the logo, allowing it to appear on semantically unrelated objects (e.g., a car-brand logo on a flower vase) and producing a conspicuous backdoor pattern that undermines the attack's stealthiness. To address this, we propose LogoGate, the first object-aware logo-exposure backdoor attack, which allows the adversary explicit object-level control over which objects the trigger activates on, while all other categories remain entirely inert. Specifically, LogoGate (i) identifies negative objects most strongly bound to the trigger via a memorization-based discrepancy between conditional and unconditional noise predictions, and (ii) trains the customized model with two complementary suppression objectives: one that suppresses the trigger's marginal contribution to noise prediction on negative objects, and another that aligns the trigger's classifier-free guidance direction with its trigger-free counterpart under inference-time amplification. Our experiments demonstrate that LogoGate achieves controllable logo exposure on target objects while preserving prompt fidelity and image quality. Human evaluations and qualitative results further validate the practical effectiveness of LogoGate in real-world logo-exposure backdoor attack scenarios.

papers.title: FedRGP: Robust Global-Consensus Prompting for Federated Vision-Language Adaptation with Noisy Labels
papers.abstract: Multimodal federated prompt learning provides a parameter-efficient pathway for adapting vision-language models in privacy-sensitive scenarios. However, most existing methods assume that client-side labels are reliable, making it difficult to suppress the propagation of noise-corrupted prompt updates during global aggregation and consequently impairing cross-modal semantic alignment and generalization performance. To address this issue, we propose FedRGP, a robust global-consensus prompting framework for federated vision-language adaptation with noisy labels. By taking the global-consensus prompt as a cross-modal semantic anchor, this framework establishes a noise-resistant prompt collaboration mechanism that integrates sample reliability estimation, dual-stream prompt decoupling, and purified aggregation of the clean prompt stream, thereby suppressing the contamination of shared prompts by label noise at both the local optimization and global aggregation levels. Furthermore, to mitigate the risk that the local clean prompt stream drifts toward the local noisy distribution, we further construct a global-consensus alignment constraint mechanism to enhance the consistency between local clean semantics and the globally shared view. In multi-random-seed experiments on seven datasets, FedRGP achieves an average improvement of 2.99 percentage points over the strongest baseline, and further enlarges the average advantage to 5.44 percentage points under the high-noise condition of 60%.The anonymized source code is available at: https://github.com/liaojiangmai/FedRGP.

papers.title: FedICL-KVc: Federated In-Context Learning via KV Cache
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly constrained by the scarcity of high-quality public data, making private data essential for further improvement. However, private data is typically distributed across resource-constrained devices and cannot be shared due to strict privacy requirements, rendering conventional federated fine-tuning of LLMs impractical under limited computation and communication budgets. To address these challenges, we propose Federated In-Context Learning via KV Cache (FedICL-KVc), a novel framework that enables effective utilization of private data without parameter updates. Instead of transmitting raw demonstrations, clients upload only the corresponding key--value (KV) caches generated during auto-regressive inference, which are compact, smaller than full-model parameter payloads, and subject to an empirical reconstruction-risk evaluation under a restricted attack model. To further enhance efficiency and effectiveness, we introduce a confidence-based demonstration selection strategy to identify informative client samples, and a server-side KV cache compression method guided by a proxy dataset to reduce inference cost and suppress irrelevant information. Experiments on multiple tasks demonstrate that FedICL-KVc achieves competitive performance without client-side parameter updates or full-model parameter transmission while avoiding direct raw-data transmission.

papers.title: FedHCA: Hierarchical Contribution-Aware Aggregation for Asynchronous Federated Class-Incremental Learning
affiliations: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.abstract: Federated class-incremental learning (FCIL) aims to learn emerging classes across decentralized clients while preserving previously acquired knowledge. Existing FCIL methods are often designed or evaluated under relatively synchronous new-class exposure settings, while in realistic federated systems, a new class may initially appear on only a few clients with limited samples. This creates a local-global propagation mismatch: scarce new-class samples make local updates unstable, whereas majority-dominated aggregation dilutes these updates and slows the global propagation of new-class knowledge. To address this problem, we propose Hierarchical Contribution-Aware Aggregation (FedHCA), a novel framework for FCIL under asynchronous new-class exposure. FedHCA stabilizes local new-class update formation via a prototype-guided local learning strategy, and further promotes global new-class propagation through coarse-to-fine hierarchical aggregation. Specifically, the server first distinguishes new-class-exposed clients from old-class-only clients, then groups exposed clients according to their semantic and update-direction consistency, and finally performs contribution-weighted group aggregation based on update magnitudes. This design amplifies informative new-class updates while maintaining old-class stability. Experiments on CIFAR-100, CIFAR-10, and SVHN show that FedHCA achieves the best overall accuracy and a better balance between old-class retention and new-class adaptation compared with representative baselines. Further analyses confirm its propagation efficiency, component effectiveness, and robustness under asynchronous exposure.

papers.title: HiMAC: Hierarchical Federated Learning with Mobility-Aware Collaboration
papers.abstract: Mobility-aware hierarchical federated learning (MobiHFL) is an emerging paradigm to support urban applications where clients continuously move across edge-server coverage areas. Existing methods mainly treat mobility as a scheduling challenge and often train a single global model across all edge-servers. This overlooks the spatial non-IID characteristics of urban environments, where regions exhibit distinct yet correlated data distributions. Region-wise personalization is a natural remedy, but mobility makes it difficult. Each edge model is trained on its current client population, while future arriving and departing clients may follow different distributions, causing cold-start degradation and feature-classifier mismatch after handover. We propose HiMAC, a personalized MobiHFL framework that turns predicted client movement into proactive inter-edge collaboration. HiMAC uses per-client LSTM trajectory predictors to estimate future client flows and builds a round-level transition matrix to guide collaboration. With a decoupled backbone-classifier architecture, HiMAC prepares each edge for expected incoming clients through incoming-aware classifier initialization and improves compatibility with likely destination edges through outgoing-regularized backbone training. Extensive experiments on image classification and object detection benchmarks show improvements of up to 12.18 percentage points in image-classification accuracy and 6.50 points in mAP@50 over state-of-the-art baselines across varying mobility intensities.

papers.title: Fair to Federate? Two-Sided Prediction of Performance and Fairness Outcomes in Healthcare Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for collaborative healthcare modeling under privacy constraints, yet institutions currently lack tools to anticipate how joining a federation will impact predictive performance and fairness. Existing work has primarily focused on post-hoc fairness mitigation, while overlooking the pre-collaboration decision itself. In this work, we introduce the Federation Assessment Problem, a two-sided prediction problem concerned with anticipating how federation would affect both a candidate institution seeking to join a federation and the institutions already participating in it, before collaboration occurs. To address this problem, we propose a two-stage meta-learning framework that predicts changes in performance and fairness metrics from institution-level metadata. We evaluate the framework on two healthcare imaging domains, across federations of varying sizes. Results show that federation-induced changes in both predictive performance and fairness can be estimated with high accuracy. The analysis further identifies label bias as one of the strongest predictors of fairness outcomes across both domains, often rivaling or exceeding demographic composition in importance. These findings demonstrate that informed federation assessment is possible without raw data sharing and highlight the need to explicitly measure multiple sources of bias when reasoning about fairness in healthcare FL.

papers.title: FairSEP: Harmonizing Multiple Fairness Metrics in Graph Neural Networks via Pareto Optimization
papers.abstract: Group fairness in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) aims to mitigate performance disparities across demographic groups. While existing methods primarily focus on Demographic Parity and Equal Opportunity, Predictive Equality (Δ FPR ) remains under-explored, potentially leading to disparate error risks. Furthermore, these methods often rely on a single surrogate loss of fairness, which is insufficient to achieve multiple fairness criteria simultaneously. Moreover, these methods often apply uniform debiasing across different label groups, making it difficult to separately address group disparities in the positive and negative classes. Consequently, achieving an optimal trade-off between utility and multiple fairness metrics remains challenging. To address these issues, we propose FairSEP, a unified Pareto-optimized framework. Specifically, we construct a sensitive subspace from per-class centroid differences between sensitive groups, debias embeddings by removing their subspace projections, and enforce prediction consistency between original and debiased representations. On this basis, we introduce a conditional Wasserstein loss that minimizes the Wasserstein distance between predictive distributions of sensitive groups conditioned on true labels, explicitly reducing disparate error rates across groups. Finally, we design a Pareto-based strategy that automatically adjusts the loss weights to resolve conflicts between different objectives. Experiments on five benchmark datasets demonstrate that FairSEP achieves a superior trade-off compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

papers.title: VFR-Audit: Verdict-Level Reliability for Fairness Audits in Hospital Length-of-Stay Prediction
papers.abstract: Fairness audits in clinical Artificial Intelligence convert continuous fairness metrics into binary pass-or-fail verdicts against operational thresholds, where hospital governance boards, payers, and regulators act on the resulting verdicts. Such audits are repeated over time and across hospital sites, thus the same verdict can flip between pass and fail across audits. Existing uncertainty methods such as Bayesian posteriors, bootstrap confidence intervals, and permutation tests address verdict instability only at the continuous-metric level. Converting metric-level uncertainty into a verdict-stability claim remains a manual step that scales poorly across the (model, metric, attribute) cells an audit covers. Existing uncertainty methods also leave open whether bias-mitigation steps, such as reweighing or per-group threshold shifts, yield a stable passing verdict at the cost of model discrimination measured as AUROC or AUPRC. To address this verdict-stability gap, we propose VFR-Audit, a framework built around the Verdict Flip Rate (VFR), a scalar bounded between 0 and 0.5 that measures the probability of verdict reversal under stratified bootstrap resampling. VFR-Audit reports VFR alongside three reliability axes, namely within-cohort resampling stability, audit-size sensitivity, and cross-hospital verdict agreement via Fleiss' kappa. The framework was evaluated on 925,128 administrative discharge records from 441 Texas hospitals, against an intersectional adaptation of Kamiran and Calders' reweighing. On the unintervened baseline, the audit detects verdict reversal in 43.5% of cells in the cross-model audit grid. After the canonical intervention, 11 of 28 cells continue to flip. Intersectional reweighing fails the four-fifths rule on this cohort regardless of regularisation strength, while per-cell threshold shifting is the main effective component of the canonical intervention. VFR translates continuous metric uncertainty into a probability of binary-verdict reversal, and a derived-baseline comparison attributes the verdict outcome to specific intervention components, so audit reliability and intervention effects can be reported together rather than as separate claims.

papers.title: Context-Aware Subgraph Explanations for Multi-Task GNNs
affiliations: Department of Statistics and Data Science, University of Seoul
School of Environmental Engineering, University of Seoul
Department of Statistics, University of Seoul
papers.abstract: Explanations for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) that perform graph-level prediction generally describe how substructures in an input graph contribute to a specific output. However, in multi-task settings, the input-output relationship and important substructures are heterogeneous across tasks, limiting the effectiveness of existing explanation methods. Existing approaches typically relied on task-specific independent explainers, underutilizing the shared representations across related tasks. As a result, it remains challenging to transfer explanatory patterns to data-scarce tasks. In this paper, we propose CAMIE, a Context-Aware Motif Importance Explainer designed for multi-task molecular classification. CAMIE leverages a Knowledge Distillation-inspired pseudo target to effectively distill assay-specific motif-removal responses, transferring explanatory patterns across tasks without requiring ground-truth labels. CAMIE utilizes assay context information as an input to the explainer, jointly capturing shared explanatory structures and task-dependent mechanisms. Our experiments on the ToxCast dataset show that our proposed method flexibly adapts explanations according to assay context and provides more faithful explanations across tasks, including tasks with limited data.

papers.title: To Rewire or Not to Rewire: Optimal Transport and the Limits of Graph Structure
affiliations: Télécom Paris, Institut Polytechnique de Paris
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) leverage message passing to learn on relational data, a mechanism that implicitly assumes homophily: connected nodes tend to share similar features. On heterophilic graphs, where this assumption breaks down, message passing can degrade node representations to the point where a simple Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) that ignores the graph entirely matches or outperforms spatial GNNs. While graph rewiring has emerged to address this topological misalignment, existing evaluations rarely tune rewiring hyperparameters jointly with the downstream model or include a competitive MLP baseline, which risks overestimating rewiring's benefits. We address this gap through a rigorous nested cross-validation protocol that jointly optimizes rewiring and classifier hyperparameters, guaranteeing that observed failures reflect intrinsic limitations rather than suboptimal configuration. As a practical instantiation of a rewiring approach based on joint feature-topology, we introduce OTR. It is a rewiring method based on the Multi-View Wasserstein distance that jointly models node feature similarity and graph topology via optimal transport plans, while maintaining the graph's structural density through a strict edge budget. Evaluating across the full heterophily-homophily spectrum on synthetic and real-world benchmarks, we characterize three operational regimes: rewiring is unnecessary under high homophily, beneficial in an ambiguous regime where it exposes latent homophilic structure, and insufficient under strong heterophily where a tuned MLP achieves better performance. We therefore advocate a Structure-First paradigm: establish the structure-agnostic performance ceiling before investing in topological preprocessing. Code and data are available at https://github.com/RichardSrn/GraphRewiring.

papers.title: Meta-ResGAD: Bi-Level Optimization for Topology-Adaptive Graph Anomaly Detection
affiliations: School of Computer Science and Engineering, Northeastern University
papers.abstract: Generative models have demonstrated significant potential in semi-supervised graph anomaly detection (GAD) by synthesizing pseudo-anomalies to mitigate extreme label scarcity. However, existing Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)-based frameworks face two key limitations: mode collapse during generation and poor topological adaptability. Specifically, traditional methods usually enforce rigid structural alignment, which wrongly treats normal heterophilic connections as anomalies, leading to performance degradation on heterophilic graphs. In this paper, we argue that these failures stem from indiscriminate learning, where models lack an adaptive mechanism to evaluate the quality and reliability of generated pseudo-anomalies and structural priors. To bridge this gap, we propose Meta-ResGAD, a novel bi-level optimization framework that introduces a "learning-to-reweight" paradigm into generative GAD. By reformulating GAD as a nested optimization problem, we divide the learning process into two levels: in the upper level, we utilize unrolled differentiation to optimize an upper-level Scorer using clean validation feedback; in the lower level, a structure-aware generation process explicitly decouples semantic and structural signals. Guided by meta-gradients, the Scorer acts as a dynamic sample filter that penalizes uninformative noise to prevent mode collapse, and adaptively down-weights unreliable structural priors to disentangle structural anomalies from normal heterophily. Extensive experiments on diverse real-world benchmarks demonstrate that Meta-ResGAD achieves state-of-the-art performance with robust topology-adaptive generalization, while maintaining the high inference efficiency and low memory consumption crucial for large-scale industrial deployment. Our code is now available at: https://github.com/TDSCX/AJAX.

papers.title: METrIC-G: Multigraph Enrichment and Time-Aware Message Passing for Imbalanced Classification in Transaction Graphs
papers.abstract: Modern digital ecosystems comprise entities connected through multiple directed interactions, forming complex transaction graphs. These graphs pose significant challenges for node and edge classification due to domain-specific interaction patterns spanning multiple hops and related transactions, multigraph structures with rich edge features, and often severe class imbalance. State-of-the-art graph neural networks often fail to fully exploit multigraph structures and effectively capture such structural-temporal patterns, resulting in suboptimal classification performance. To address these limitations, we introduce METrIC-G, a novel approach designed to capture multi-hop transaction patterns among connected entities occurring in close temporal proximity within a graph-neural-network-based architecture. METrIC-G builds expressive time-aware node- and edge-features from transaction sequences and time-based statistics. METrIC-G effectively identifies symbolic, class-discriminative patterns among transaction outliers to mitigate class imbalance. METrIC-G employs a time-aware message-passing mechanism that adaptively weights neighbor contributions based on a learnable temporal decay function. We experimentally demonstrate that METrIC-G outperforms all baselines by at least 5.15 percentage points (p.p.) in the minority class F1-score and at least 2.92 p.p. in macro F1-score across all datasets.

papers.title: PageRank Attributed Graph Subspace Clustering
papers.abstract: Attributed graph clustering aims to group nodes that are similar with respect to both graph structure and node attributes. However, effectively combining these two sources of information remains challenging, as structural proximity does not necessarily imply attribute similarity. The problem becomes even more difficult in high-dimensional settings, where clusters may depend on different subsets of features. To address these issues, we propose PRAGSC, a framework that integrates PageRank-based propagation with subspace clustering. Our propagation scheme incorporates a teleportation mechanism that mitigates over-smoothing by re-injecting the original node features at each iteration, while the subspace clustering component identifies cluster-specific attribute subsets. Experiments on six real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate that PRAGSC consistently outperforms recent state-of-the-art attributed graph clustering methods across different metrics, while enhancing interpretability through the identification of cluster-specific feature subspaces.

papers.title: Degree-Mass Message Passing for Betweenness Ranking in Directed and Undirected Networks
affiliations: National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology
Université Côte d'Azur, CNRS, Inria, I3S
papers.abstract: Computing the importance of nodes in networks is a long-standing fundamental problem that has driven extensive study of various centrality measures. A particularly well-known centrality measure is betweenness centrality, whose exact computation becomes prohibitive on large-scale networks. Graph Neural Network (GNN) models have thus been proposed to predict the ranking of nodes by betweenness centrality. However, existing GNN-based methods either have graph-size-dependent parameter counts or are limited to undirected graphs. We propose a lightweight GNN architecture that exploits the empirically observed relationship between betweenness centrality and multi-hop degree mass. This motivates the use of degree masses as size-invariant node features. To improve generalization, we train on synthetic graphs whose degree distributions more closely match those of real-world networks, including directed and undirected scale-free graphs and uniformly directed hyperbolic random graphs. We evaluate our model on 14 real-world networks spanning eight domains, including social, email, and citation networks, across both directed and undirected regimes. The experiments show that our model improves the Kendall τ b correlation by up to 24.6% on undirected and 10.9% on directed graphs, while using 56× fewer parameters than the lightest competing GNN baseline and achieving competitive inference time, with up to a 24.5× speedup on selected directed graphs.

papers.title: PAGT: Prototype-Guided Adaptive Graph Transformer for Mitigating Over-Globalizing
papers.abstract: For homogeneous data node classification tasks, Graph Transformers (GTs) have become highly promising frameworks, owing to their global attention mechanism that captures long-range correlations. However, existing models suffer from the over-globalizing problem in homogeneous graphs, where global similarity aggregation triggers multi-scale feature degradation and weak alignment of semantic and structural information, consequently allowing global noise to obscure local features and impede structural discovery. To solve this problem, we propose a Prototype-Guided Adaptive Graph Transformer for mitigating over-globalizing (PAGT). Firstly, a bi-branch local propagation module enhances multi-scale graph adaptive structural representation learning by decoupling and modeling residuals hierarchically, boosting training stability. Subsequently, a prototypically guided layered adaptive query mechanism mitigates feature degradation by generating global anchors from both microscopic and macroscopic levels, reducing noise and structure-irrelevant interactions. Finally, a teacher-guided semantic and structural alignment strategy enhances alignment between local and global representations via knowledge distillation and contrastive learning, guaranteeing alignment between local topological branches and global attention branches. Experimental results show that significant improvements with strong stability are achieved on all seven datasets, improving by 2.5% and 2.6% on the CiteSeer and Cora datasets, respectively. The code will be made publicly available upon publication.

papers.title: Dynamic Exploitation of Source Experts for Few-Shot Node Classification on Text-Attributed Graphs
papers.abstract: Cross-graph transfer on text-attributed graphs (TAGs) is challenging because different graph domains often encode different structure-semantic relationships. Existing unified-encoder methods jointly train a single encoder using multiple source graphs, but such a unified encoder yields only marginal improvements over the best single-source encoder due to knowledge conflict across domains. Recent multi-expert methods alleviate this issue by maintaining multiple experts, yet they also require joint training over all source graphs and do not adapt routing behavior to unseen target graphs. These limit scalability, flexibility, and applicability to unseen target TAGs under two realistic constraints of a source-free environment and few-shot node classification. To overcome these limitations, we propose DARGE (Dynamic Adaptive Routing of Graph Experts), a novel source-free few-shot cross-graph transfer method for TAGs. Instead of jointly training experts and a router, DARGE independently trains source-specific experts aligned via a shared universal LLM-derived codebook, allowing their outputs to remain directly comparable. Given an unseen target graph, DARGE dynamically combines experts using a two-level routing strategy: a label-free router first adapts to the unlabeled target graph structure through self-supervision, and an episode-level calibration further refines soft expert selection using lightweight few-shot class separation signals. Experiments on seven benchmark TAG datasets demonstrate that DARGE consistently outperforms both unified-encoder methods and multi-expert baselines. Further analysis shows that our routing strategy successfully recovers target-relevant expert preferences and scales well to large expert pools through signature-based pre-screening.

papers.title: Capture Invariants from Dynamics: Temporal Graph Learning by Decoupling Graph Context and Downstream Task
papers.abstract: Temporal graph learning aims to model the dependency between temporal graph (TG) data and downstream tasks. However, some temporal changes of nodes and edges contribute little to the essential task dependency, although they may show statistical correlations with task labels within certain time periods. Indiscriminately learning all dynamic patterns may therefore mislead the model to capture such period-specific correlations, leading to poor performance. To mask changes that could mislead model learning, we propose InvarTG, an invariance-based temporal graph learning method that decouples graph context modeling from downstream task prediction. Specifically, InvarTG first forecasts the evolving graph context by aggregating structural and temporal information through message passing and a temporal mixer, respectively. It then performs invariant task prediction by extracting invariant embeddings from multiple prediction-time graph contexts, thereby capturing invariant dependencies that consistently support downstream tasks. To preserve structural and temporal information while learning invariant dependencies, we further introduce a residual-guided joint optimization strategy to coordinate the forecasting and prediction processes. Experimental results on public datasets show that InvarTG outperforms state-of-the-art methods by at least 5.31% in F1 score.

papers.title: Heterogeneous Hypergraph Attention Network for Scholar Recommendation and Team Formation
affiliations: Missouri University of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Scholar recommendation and academic team formation are critical for collaborations fostering scientific breakthroughs. However, effective team formation presents challenges of balancing expertise from diverse scientific domains. Current recommendation approaches, although reasonably effective, fail to capture higher-order group semantics inherent in co-authorship of scientific manuscripts and funding communities, and also collapse entirely for scholars lacking sufficient interaction history. To address these challenges, we propose HyTeam , a hypergraph-based method for scholar recommendation and academic team formation comprising two tightly coupled components. First , a heterogeneous hypergraph attention network with TransE-based relational scoring that encodes multi-type scholarly relationships as hyperedges and ranks candidates via learned relational translation. Second , a query-decomposed diversity-aware team formation algorithm that jointly optimises team relevance, structural diversity, and skill coverage. HyTeam derives scholar embeddings from the hypergraph co-participation structure, naturally accommodating scholars with sparse or absent collaboration records. Our evaluations on a curated NSF award dataset and the public DBLP citation network demonstrate that HyTeam outperforms all baselines, achieving Recall@10 of 0.6005 and 0.4883 on the NSF and DBLP datasets, respectively. Our team formation evaluation further achieves consistently superior team configurations, attaining the best trade-off among all baselines with a team score of 0.6740.

papers.title: ResCrime: Residual Evolution Diffusion for Spatially Adaptive Multimodal Urban Crime Forecasting
papers.abstract: Urban crime forecasting aims to predict future spatial risk distributions from historical crime and urban context, supporting proactive public safety allocation. Existing methods have advanced this task with multimodal urban signals, but they often use historical crime risk maps only as conditioning inputs, without explicitly modeling their evolution into future risk maps. They also provide limited adaptation of point-of-interest (POI) semantics to local historical crime context, weakening their ability to capture spatially varying predictive relevance. To address these issues, we propose ResCrime, a history-anchored residual evolution diffusion framework for spatially adaptive multimodal crime forecasting. ResCrime initializes the reverse diffusion near the observed historical risk map and models future risk as a residual evolution of historical observations. A multimodal denoising backbone integrates crime, POI, satellite, and map features to support history-to-future risk estimation, while Crime History Spatial Adaptive Reweighting (CSAR) recalibrates POI semantic channels based on local historical intensity before multimodal fusion. Experiments on New York City and Los Angeles demonstrate that ResCrime outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, improving AP over DiffCrime by 6.68% and 5.21% and reducing RMSE by 10.71% and 6.52%, while maintaining efficient inference. Code is available at https://github.com/RooB1t/ResCrime.

papers.title: Retrieval-Corrected Conformal Prediction for Time Series
papers.abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) provides distribution-free prediction intervals for fixed forecasters, but its standard calibration procedure is often inefficient for time series data, where forecast errors are temporally dependent and change across time and operating conditions. Recent time series CP methods improve local calibration using recent, weighted, or localized residuals. Yet local calibration can remain indirect, since broad residual weighting or additional adaptation procedures may dilute the evidence most relevant to the current prediction. This motivates a simple retrieval and correction strategy that selects similar past residuals as local evidence and then corrects the coverage error left by retrieval. In this paper, we propose Retrieval-Corrected Conformal Prediction (RCCP), a retrieval-augmented calibration method for time series prediction intervals. RCCP builds an asymmetric interval from retrieved one-sided residuals and calibrates its normalized retrieval error with a scalar conformal correction. Thus, retrieval provides local residual evidence, while conformal correction determines the final scale needed for coverage. We provide a coverage-gap bound based on the stability of the normalized retrieval error distribution. Across standard benchmarks and backbone forecasters, RCCP attains the target coverage in every setting and achieves the lowest Winkler scores, with fewer severe misses. RCCP also achieves low calibration and inference overhead, showing that retrieval-corrected calibration is an effective and scalable approach to uncertainty quantification in time series forecasting. Code is available at https://github.com/jinsaaang/rccp.

papers.title: ReCast: Regime-aware Multi-scale Retrieval with Context--Evolution Coupling for Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Time series forecasting is essential in many real-world applications, but accurate prediction remains challenging when temporal dynamics are non-stationary and historical patterns recur at different temporal resolutions. Existing retrieval-augmented forecasting methods provide explicit historical evidence, yet they may retrieve dynamically mismatched samples and often integrate retrieved information only at the prediction stage. To address these limitations, we propose ReCast, a retrieval-augmented forecasting framework based on meta-guided multi-scale retrieval and context--evolution coupling. Specifically, we first construct lightweight statistical meta-features to characterize the global dynamics of each sample and organize historical data into latent regimes, so that retrieval is constrained to dynamically compatible candidates. We then perform retrieval across multiple temporal scales to capture recurring patterns at different resolutions. Beyond retrieved future representations, ReCast also introduces a retrieved historical context segment, termed Pre-key, which is aligned with the current input and concatenated as an informative historical prefix for encoder-side modeling. In parallel, the retrieved future representations from different scales are projected to the forecasting horizon and aggregated as a retrieval-based prediction branch. The final forecast is obtained by fusing the encoder-based parametric prediction and the retrieval-based non-parametric prediction. Experiments on both long- and short-horizon forecasting benchmarks show that ReCast consistently improves forecasting accuracy over competitive baselines, and the ablation results further demonstrate the contribution of regime-aware retrieval, multi-scale matching, and context--evolution coupling.

papers.title: Multi-Order Wavelet Derivative Transform for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
affiliations: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
papers.abstract: In deep time series forecasting, the Fourier Transform (FT) is extensively employed for frequency pattern modeling. However, it often struggles in capturing multi-scale, time-sensitive temporal patterns. Although the Wavelet Transform (WT) can capture these patterns through frequency decomposition, its coefficients are insensitive to abrupt changes in the time series, leading to suboptimal modeling. To mitigate these limitations, we introduce the multi-order Wavelet Derivative Transform (WDT) grounded in the WT, enabling the extraction of time-aware patterns spanning both the overall trend and subtle fluctuations. Compared with the standard FT and WT, which model the raw series, WDT operates on the derivative of the series, selectively magnifying rate-of-change cues and exposing abrupt regime shifts that are particularly informative for time series modeling. Practically, we embed the WDT into a multi-branch framework named WaveTS , which decomposes the input series into multi-scale time-frequency coefficients, refines them via linear layers, and reconstructs them into the time domain via the inverse WDT. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that WaveTS achieves state-of-the-art forecasting accuracy while retaining high computational efficiency. The code is available at https://github.com/zhouziyu02/WaveTS.

papers.title: GDformer: Going Beyond Subsequence Isolation for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
affiliations: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
China Mobile (Jiangxi) Virtual Reality Technology Co., Ltd.
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
industryAffiliations: China Mobile (Jiangxi) Virtual Reality Technology Co., Ltd.
papers.abstract: Multivariate Time Series (MTS) anomaly detection is crucial for maintaining the reliability of real-world systems, which can identify malfunctions from operational data and mitigate the potential financial losses. Given the scarcity of anomalies and difficulty in labeling MTS data, the MTS anomaly detection task is usually framed as an unsupervised learning problem to derive a compact and distinguished detection criterion without accessing the anomaly points. The existing deep learning methods are all confined to isolated subsequences with limited and subsequence-contained horizons, hardly deriving anomaly scores with series-level knowledge and promising the unified detection criterion. In this paper, we propose the G lobal D ictionary-enhanced Trans former (GDformer) with a renovated dictionary-based cross attention mechanism to cultivate the global representations shared by all normal points in the entire series. Accordingly, the cross-attention maps reflect the correlation weights between the point and global representations, which naturally leads to the representation-wise similarity -based detection criterion. To foster more compact detection boundary, prototypes are introduced to capture the distribution of normal point-global correlation weights. Extensive experimental results validate the effectiveness and efficiency of GDformer, compared with state-of-the-art unsupervised anomaly detection methods on six popular benchmark datasets. The source code is available at https://github.com/yuppielqx/GDformer.

papers.title: Imputation-Free Variable Subset Forecasting Based on Observed Subset Representation Enhancement
papers.abstract: Variable subset forecasting (VSF) addresses multivariate time series forecasting when an arbitrary subset of variables is absent at inference time. Most existing methods follow an impute-then-forecast pipeline in the original variable space, in which imputation errors can propagate into forecasting. Even methods that learn latent representations typically project them back to the original variable space before forecasting, which can discard information useful for prediction. These limitations raise the question of whether imputation is necessary at all. We observed that a forecasting backbone trained with sensor dropout alone, without any imputation, matched and in some cases exceeded state-of-the-art VSF performance. This led us to hypothesize that VSF benefits more from enhancing observed-variable representations in the embedding space than from imputing missing variables in the original variable space. To this end, we propose OSRE (Observed Subset Representation Enhancement), an imputation-free, backbone-agnostic framework for VSF that operates entirely in the embedding space via two complementary branches and is trained with sensor dropout. The Observed Variable Branch enriches observed-variable representations through unified attention, while the Missing Variable Branch marks missing positions with lightweight identification tokens. The combined embedding feeds into any standard forecasting backbone. Across four datasets and four forecasting backbones, OSRE outperformed prior state-of-the-art methods on METR-LA, Traffic, and Solar by an average of 12.7% in MAE and remained robust across varying missing rates. An Integrated Gradients analysis further suggests that observation-centric processing in the embedding space is a key contributor to these gains. The code is available at https://github.com/shykwon/CIKM26-OSRE.

papers.title: Quality Heterogeneity Matters: Adaptive Harmonization for Multi-Sensor Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Widely deployed multi-sensor networks are fundamental for the construction of digital twins. In the real-world, sensors often exhibit heterogeneous data quality due to differences in hardware designs and measurement principles. However, existing multi-sensor time series methods typically follow a quality-homogeneous modeling strategy, leading to representation aliasing and performance degradation. In this work, we propose QualityMoE , a plug-and-play quality-aware harmonization module to harmonize quality discrepancies across sensors. Specifically, we develop a quality-aware router to adaptively dispatch sensor data by integrating complementary static and dynamic quality characteristics. Furthermore, we employ a mixture of hybrid expert architecture where specialized experts distinguish heterogeneous qualities, while a shared expert fosters information interaction across sensors. We conduct white-box experiments to transparently validate the model's capability in perceiving quality-induced waveform heterogeneity within simulated circuits. Moreover, extensive experiments across 9 real-world datasets and 6 backbones demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of QualityMoE under multiple quality heterogeneity scenarios. QualityMoE further demonstrates its scalability on large-scale multi-sensor datasets and its broader applicability to another downstream task, i.e., multi-sensor time series classification.

papers.title: APILaNet: Adaptive Physics-Informed Latent Network for Single-Sensor Forecasting
papers.abstract: Forecasting river dynamics from sensor networks is often limited by sparse and noisy observations: in many catchments, operational monitoring provides only a single gauge and uncertain rainfall inputs. We propose an A daptive P hysics- I nformed La tent Network (APILaNet), a trustworthy physics-constrained forecasting model that learns a 1-D latent dynamical field while enforcing mass conservation through a weak-form residual weighted by a learned, normalized space–time measure. The normalization stabilizes training across discretizations and concentrates constraint enforcement on transient, event-driven regimes. To improve identifiability under single-gauge supervision, APILaNet uses a monotone Lipschitz measurement layer to map latent states to observed levels, and a bounded event-aware scheduler that increases conservation and smoothness regularization during high-impact periods while preserving optimization stability. Across synthetic 1-D conservation benchmarks and multi-catchment hydrological forecasting, APILaNet improves accuracy relative to strong sequence baselines and yields markedly lower error during extreme events, with consistent gains in Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency.

papers.title: A Hybrid Framework for Time Series Anomaly Detection with LLMs
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for time series anomaly detection (TSAD), yet their direct use often remains inferior to methods designed specifically for TSAD. In this work, we study whether this limitation arises primarily from weak forecasting or from insufficient exploitation of forecast residuals. Across LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, we find that parameter-efficient fine-tuning can improve forecasting accuracy, but does not consistently improve anomaly detection under fixed residual thresholding. The primary driver of detection performance is not forecasting quality, but how the resulting residuals are analyzed and refined in subsequent stages. Motivated by this finding, we propose a Forecaster–Detector–Imputer pipeline that restricts the LLM to forecasting normal temporal behavior, applies classical detectors to the resulting residuals using adaptive windowing and contamination-aware thresholding, and refines candidate detections through imputation via a time-series foundation model followed by a second detection pass. The proposed framework reaches F1 = 0.789 with LLaMA and F1 = 0.785 with Mistral, roughly doubling the zero-shot baselines, with results confirmed on an independent NAB benchmark. These results suggest that LLMs are most effective for TSAD when used as forecasting components within a hybrid residual-analysis pipeline, and that the primary bottleneck lies in post-hoc residual exploitation rather than forecasting quality alone.

papers.title: Bridging Local Geometries via Adaptive Convex Multi-graph Fusion for Unsupervised Manifold Representation
papers.abstract: The quality of unsupervised manifold learning relies fundamentally on the underlying neighborhood graph. Standard linear methods utilizing a single affinity matrix often fail to capture the multiscale complexity of high-dimensional data. While multi-view algorithms integrate complementary information, additional views may be unavailable or costly to acquire in some practical scenarios. Consequently, effectively exploiting the multi-scale structural information within a single reliable view remains an important research problem. To this end, we propose Multi-Affinity Matrix Fusion-based Locality Preserving Projections (MAMF-LPP). This framework bridges fragmented local geometries through a unified joint optimization paradigm, dynamically coupling adaptive convex multi-graph fusion with manifold projection. To optimize the resulting non-convex objective, we develop an efficient Block Coordinate Descent (BCD) algorithm featuring exact row-wise probabilistic simplex projections, thereby eliminating standard heuristic approximation errors. Theoretical and empirical analysis establishes the monotonic descent of the objective, while empirical results demonstrate rapid convergence. Across multiple benchmark datasets, MAMF-LPP achieves competitive performance against representative single-graph, nonlinear, and joint-learning baselines. A case study further shows that exploiting multi-scale intra-view geometries can yield performance competitive with selected multi-view configurations under the evaluated protocol.

papers.title: Diagnosing and Correcting Geometric Bias in Diversity-Driven Code Instruction Data Selection
papers.abstract: Diversity-driven data selection offers a scalable way to reduce code instruction-tuning costs, yet it relies on a fragile assumption: geometric spread in representation space should correspond to training-useful semantic coverage. In code data selection, our diagnosis reveals a geometric bias behind this assumption: dense embedding geometry can be strongly influenced by rare surface forms, verbose constraints, and implementation artifacts, causing diversity objectives to over-explore locally sparse or globally peripheral samples whose training utility is not guaranteed. To correct this bias, we propose Semantically Anchored Geometric Coverage (SAGC), a framework for reshaping representation geometry using LLM-generated macro-intent labels as semantic anchors for dense micro-context representations. Rather than replacing standard diversity objectives, SAGC reshapes the geometry exposed to them, using macro-intent anchors to constrain dense-space exploration toward high-level algorithmic structure without requiring downstream validation signals, gradient feedback, or evaluation results. Using only 20k samples selected from a 446k pool, SAGC reaches 0.4006 on LiveCodeBench, approaching full-data training at 0.4027. Further diagnostics and out-of-benchmark evaluations show that semantic anchoring provides a structured correction to this geometric bias.

papers.title: EndoBudget: Capacity-Controlled Learning for Stable Information Systems under Endogenous Feedback
papers.abstract: Modern information systems increasingly operate in closed feedback loops: recommenders shape exposure, retrieval and generation pipelines influence future content, agentic systems change the environments they query, and human-AI interfaces alter the logs used for subsequent training. In these settings, data are not merely sampled from an external distribution. They are endogenously produced by prior model decisions, creating deployment drift that can accumulate over time and change finite-run reliability estimates. This paper develops EndoBudget, a learning-theoretic framework for analyzing deployment discrepancy in information systems trained on feedback-generated data and for auditing explicit update budgets. We formalize closed-loop learning as a sequential process in which each deployed model induces the next data distribution. Our main generalization result bounds the long-horizon absolute deployment gap by a classical capacity-dependent estimation term plus an accumulated endogenous drift term. We further state a sufficient stability condition for temporal capacity budgeting: under an explicit update-stability condition, a summable budget yields finite feedback path length and convergence of the induced data distributions in complete metric spaces. An auxiliary continuous-time limit provides a formal view of the discrete retraining process as dynamics over probability measures. Controlled diagnostics and a semi-synthetic closed-loop recommendation study report finite-run measurements of cumulative exposure drift, absolute deployment-gap variability, exposure dispersion, and ranking utility for the compared update rules within the studied protocol. The framework provides a finite-run audit for stating, measuring, and evaluating explicit capacity and update constraints in adaptive information systems that retrain under long-term feedback, subject to the regularity assumptions made explicit below.

papers.title: Support-Adaptive Complexity Control for Longitudinal Counterfactual Prediction
papers.abstract: Longitudinal counterfactual prediction aims to forecast future outcomes under candidate treatment sequences from observational trajectories. Existing methods mainly address time-varying confounding and temporal representation learning. We identify a complementary finite-sample challenge: counterfactual queries often lie in history-action regions with highly heterogeneous logged support. This leads to the support-complexity mismatch for the fixed-capacity prediction heads used by existing methods. Motivated by finite-sample learning theory, where reliable generalization depends on function-class complexity relative to the number of relevant samples, we propose Support-Adaptive Complexity Control (SACC) to address this issue, a backbone-agnostic method that replaces the fixed action-conditioned prediction head with a support-adaptive one. SACC estimates rollout-conditioned local support for each query and uses it to progressively activate residual prediction blocks. It shrinks toward a stable low-complexity base predictor in weakly supported regions while enabling richer corrections when support is strong. We provide theoretical analysis and experiments showing that SACC improves the finite-sample reliability of longitudinal counterfactual outcome estimation, especially for weakly supported treatment plans.

papers.title: Asymmetry-Aware Local Structure Alignment for Conditional Average Treatment Effect Estimation
papers.abstract: Estimating conditional average treatment effect (CATE) is crucial for characterizing treatment effect heterogeneity at the individual or subgroup level. Existing methods mitigate confounding bias by capturing local structures within treatment and control groups to enhance representation balancing. However, they still overlook cross-group local structure asymmetry, including capacity asymmetry from imbalanced sample sizes and semantic asymmetry from unreliable cross-group correspondences, which may induce spurious matching and ultimately compromise CATE estimation. To address these issues, we propose an A symmetry-Aware L ocal S tructure A lignment (ALSA) method for CATE estimation. ALSA enables reliable cross-group local alignment by modeling subgroup capacity imbalance and constructing soft barycentric correspondences. Specifically, to handle capacity asymmetry, samples within each group are clustered into prototypes, and non-uniform capacity priors are constructed based on the number of samples covered by each prototype. This enables optimal transport (OT) to explicitly account for subgroup-level capacity imbalance. Moreover, we design a prototype-guided contrastive learning strategy to encourage intra-subgroup consistency and inter-subgroup separability. To tackle semantic asymmetry, ALSA employs an OT-based bidirectional barycentric alignment mechanism, which softly aligns samples lacking reliable correspondences to the weighted barycenters of multiple relevant prototypes, thereby reducing spurious matching. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ALSA outperforms existing methods and significantly reduces CATE estimation error.

papers.title: Discovering and Preserving Category Correlation Knowledge via Adaptive Reciprocal Knowledge Distillation
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation aims to improve the performance of lightweight student models by transferring knowledge from larger and more powerful teacher models. However, a substantial size gap between teacher and student models often impedes effective knowledge transfer. Most existing approaches adopt a static, one-way teacher-to-student distillation paradigm, which overlooks the dynamic nature of student learning and fails to provide targeted guidance on hard samples. In this paper, we propose adaptive reciprocal knowledge distillation (AR-KD), a novel method that improves knowledge transfer by simplifying the teacher’s output distribution. Specifically, AR-KD performs reciprocal adaptation on the teacher by matching its class correlation matrix to the student’s relational representation, which reshapes the teacher’s prediction structure to better suit the student’s capacity. This relational alignment mitigates the collapse of inter-class dark knowledge caused by overconfident teachers, enabling the student to learn from richer and more compatible supervisory signals. We evaluate AR-KD on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1k classification datasets, where it outperforms state-of-the-art knowledge distillation baselines. Specifically, AR-KD improves student performance across homogeneous and heterogeneous setups: up to 7.13% accuracy gain for students, 1.42%–4.15% higher than vanilla KD on average, and further improvements when integrated with other advanced methods. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ARKD/.

papers.title: FinMamba: Market-Aware Graph Enhanced Multi-Level Mamba for Stock Movement Prediction
papers.abstract: Recently, combining stock features with inter-stock correlations has become a common and effective approach for stock movement prediction. However, financial data presents significant challenges due to its low signal-to-noise ratio and the dynamic complexity of the market, which give rise to two key limitations in existing methods. First, the relationships between stocks are highly influenced by multifaceted factors including macroeconomic market dynamics, and current models fail to adaptively capture these evolving interactions under specific market conditions. Second, for the accuracy and timeliness required by real-world trading, existing financial data mining methods struggle to extract beneficial pattern-oriented dependencies from long historical data while maintaining high efficiency and low memory consumption. To address the limitations, we propose FinMamba, a Mamba-GNN-based framework for market-aware and multi-level hybrid stock movement prediction. Specifically, we devise a dynamic graph to learn the changing representations of inter-stock relationships by integrating a pruning module that adapts to market trends. Afterward, with a selective mechanism, the multi-level Mamba discards irrelevant information and resets states to skillfully recall historical patterns across multiple time scales with linear time costs, which are then jointly optimized for reliable prediction. Extensive experiments on U.S. and Chinese stock markets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed FinMamba, achieving state-of-the-art prediction accuracy and trading profitability, while maintaining low computational complexity. The code is available at https://github.com/TROUBADOUR000/FinMamba.

papers.title: SenseFlow: A Physics-Informed and Self-Ensembling Iterative Framework for Power Flow Estimation
papers.abstract: Power flow estimation plays a vital role in ensuring the stability and reliability of electrical power systems, particularly in the context of growing network complexities and renewable energy integration. However, existing studies often fail to adequately address the unique characteristics of power systems, such as the sparsity of network connections and the critical importance of the unique Slack node, which poses significant challenges in achieving high-accuracy estimations. In this paper, we present SenseFlow, a novel physics-informed and self-ensembling iterative framework that integrates two main designs, the Physics-informed Power Flow Network (PPFNet) and Self-ensembling Iterative Estimation (SeIter), to carefully address the unique properties of the power system and thereby enhance the power flow estimation. In specific, SenseFlow enforces the PPFNet to gradually predict high-precision voltage magnitudes and phase angles through the iterative SeIter process. On the one hand, PPFNet employs the Virtual Node Attention and Slack-Gated Feed-Forward modules to facilitate efficient global-local communication in the face of network sparsity and amplify the influence of the Slack node on angle predictions, respectively. On the other hand, SeIter maintains an exponential moving average of PPFNet's parameters to create an ensemble model that refines power state predictions throughout the iterative fitting process. Experimental results demonstrate that SenseFlow outperforms existing methods, providing a promising solution for high-accuracy power flow estimation across diverse grid configurations. The code is available at https://github.com/ZhenZHAO/SenseFlow.

papers.title: CFDA: A Plug-and-Play LLM-Driven Code Functional Diagnosis Framework for Programming Knowledge Tracing
papers.abstract: Knowledge Tracing (KT) models the evolution of students' knowledge states from historical learning interactions. However, most KT models are designed for traditional subject domains and exhibit limited generalization ability in programming knowledge tracing (PKT). Programming submissions are open-ended and repeatedly revised, and the same code change may indicate an effective repair, an ineffective attempt, or a functional regression. Moreover, programming progress is functional in nature: the educational meaning of a submission depends on whether it satisfies problem requirements rather than on code structures alone. To address these issues, we propose CFDA, a plug-and-play LLM-driven Code Functional Diagnosis and calibration framework for general KT and PKT models. CFDA analyzes problem requirements and student submissions, assigning fine-grained diagnostic signals including functional completion, semantic error, skill-level application, and transition cues. These signals are then injected into existing KT backbones through a lightweight calibrator that corrects hidden knowledge states while preserving the original tracing architecture. Experiments on two public programming datasets show consistent AUC and probability-error improvements across multiple backbone models and competitive performance against 14 representative KT and PKT baselines.

papers.title: Psy-GRAG: Evidence-Based Subgraph-Augmented LLM Reasoning for Mental Health Attribution
papers.abstract: Mental health disorders have emerged as a critical global public health challenge, with automated classification of social media text offering significant value for early risk detection. Fine-tuned pre-trained language models (PLMs) achieve reasonable in-domain performance but generalize poorly across tasks. Large language models (LLMs) with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) offer improved flexibility, yet both approaches lack the structured domain knowledge required for fine-grained psychiatric reasoning. To address these gaps, we propose Psy-GRAG, an evidence-based subgraph-augmented LLM reasoning framework. First, we construct a three-layer heterogeneous knowledge graph comprising a linguistic feature layer, an intermediate semantic layer, and a task label layer, modeling the cognitive reasoning path from surface expressions to mental health classifications. Second, a multi-round graph optimization strategy iteratively refines edge confidence weights and prunes noisy connections via supervised learning. Third, a psychology-informed retrieval strategy extracts disorder-relevant reasoning paths to guide pre-trained LLMs with fixed parameters for training-free inference without further parameter updates. Extensive experiments on CAMS, SWMH, and MultiWD demonstrate that Psy-GRAG generally outperforms traditional ML models, fine-tuned PLMs, and existing graph-augmented RAG methods across Accuracy, Macro-F1, and cross-run stability.

papers.title: HyBrain: Spatiotemporal Hyperedges for EEG Seizure Detection and Prediction
affiliations: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Seizure detection and prediction from EEG are clinically important but challenging because seizures are rare, temporally localized, and propagate as coordinated events across multiple channels. Recent dynamic graph neural networks model this by running a temporal model over a sequence of per-time-step pairwise channel edges. However, this pairwise construction misses the spatiotemporal coupling that constitutes a seizure, at substantial training cost. We propose HyBrain, which summarizes spatiotemporal EEG evidence through a small set of soft hyperedges rather than pairwise edges. A per-channel Mamba backbone produces one token per (channel, second), and a spatiotemporal hyperedge block pools these tokens into E h shared group embeddings through soft memberships and broadcasts them back. The same encoder serves three downstream tasks: window-based detection, one-second point-wise detection, and preictal seizure prediction. On TUSZ and CHB-MIT, HyBrain achieves the best AUROC on every reported setting against ten baselines, with the largest gap on long-clip preictal prediction. It also matches the most efficient baselines in training time and peak GPU memory. A qualitative analysis shows that even a single learned hyperedge cleanly captures the preictal → ictal → postictal trajectory on a real seizure clip.

papers.title: In-Context Learning as Approximate Belief Propagation
papers.abstract: Few-shot in-context learning (ICL) cannot revise its belief about an early demonstration once a later, contradicting one arrives, so a single misleading example can derail the prediction. Existing remedies are split: retrieval methods choose which examples to include but weight them uniformly; calibration methods adjust the output without identifying which demonstration to distrust; mechanistic interpretability reveals the latent inter-example structure but offers no way to act on it. We introduce ICL-BP, an inference-time augmentation that addresses all three. ICL-BP constructs a sparse pairwise factor graph from the model's own late-layer attention maps, runs a small fixed number of loopy belief propagation iterations to obtain per-example relevance beliefs, and uses those beliefs to additively edit the residual-stream context at the query token before decoding. Conditional on a linear-representation hypothesis, an attention–similarity alignment proxy, and a belief-collapse condition that we verify empirically rather than rate-prove, the bias of the implicit concept estimator falls quadratically in the fraction of misleading demonstrations; when no demonstration is misleading, ICL-BP reduces exactly to Standard ICL under uniform beliefs, with at most a 1/N 2 noise inflation in the empirically-observed near-uniform case. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with 16 demonstrations, ICL-BP improves over Standard ICL by a median +7.4 pp across eight benchmarks (+5.2 to +12.0) and over the strongest reweighting baseline BatchICL by +1.8 pp median (+1.2 to +2.4). Composed with SC-CoT on Llama-3.1-70B, it reaches 90.4% exact match on GSM8K and 80.5% on MMLU at under 10% wall-clock overhead.

papers.title: Curvature Graph Mergeability: Predicting Model Compatibility from Per-Layer Hessian Geometry
papers.abstract: Merging independently trained neural networks — via weight averaging, model soups, or task-vector arithmetic — is increasingly central to large-scale model reuse, yet the success of any merge hinges on whether two parameter vectors occupy the same loss basin, a property currently certified only by expensive multi-point interpolation barriers. We introduce Curvature Graph Mergeability (CGM) , a scoring framework that predicts the interpolation barrier from only cheap, per-layer Hessian curvature features at each endpoint. CGM extracts two scalar curvature statistics per layer using Hutchinson's trace estimator and the power method, organizes them into a chain-structured factor graph whose latent compatibility states encode qualitative regimes of layer alignment, and computes a mergeability score from the negative variational free energy of the chain. For deep linear networks under balanced factorization, we prove that the interpolation barrier is upper-bounded by a multilinear function of per-layer curvature mismatch, and we identify a diagonal-dominance condition under which the score is monotone in mismatch; the bound is stated as an implicit joint bound on the per-layer mismatch vector, with the regime of validity made explicit. Across four meta-training architectures and four held-out OOD architectures (ResNet-110, ViT-B/ImageNet, WRN-28-10, 3-layer LSTM), CGM attains Spearman ρ=0.86 on leave-models-out splits and ρ=0.81 pooled OOD, outperforming zero-order distance, CKA, Fisher overlap, REPAIR, midpoint-barrier, and architecture-agnostic curvature-MLP baselines at Holm–Bonferroni-corrected p<0.01. It is approached only by Git Re-Basin + barrier (ρ=0.90), which costs ∼14,500× more per pair; CGM closes the gap to permutation-based merging at 35× amortized speedup over direct 11-point barrier when screening 50 candidates, with negligible memory overhead. Per-layer posterior marginals additionally pinpoint specific layers that act as merge bottlenecks.

papers.title: Retrieve-then-Adapt: Test-Time Retrieval-Augmentation for Sequential Recommendation
papers.abstract: The sequential recommendation (SR) task aims to predict the next item based on users' historical interaction sequences. Typically trained on historical data, SR models are frozen after deployment, limiting their ability to handle test-time patterns that are rare during training. Existing approaches to address this limitation include test-time training, test-time augmentation, and retrieval-augmented fine-tuning. However, these methods either introduce significant computational overhead, rely on random augmentation strategies, or require a carefully designed two-stage training paradigm. In this paper, we argue that the key to effective test-time augmentation lies in achieving both effective retrieval and efficient fusion. To this end, we propose Retrieve-then-Adapt ( ReAd ), a novel framework that augments a deployed SR model through retrieved user preference signals. Specifically, given a trained SR model, ReAd first retrieves collaboratively similar items for a test user from a constructed collaborative memory. A lightweight retrieval learning module then integrates these items into an informative augmentation embedding that captures both collaborative signals and prediction-refinement cues. Finally, the initial SR prediction is refined via a fusion mechanism that incorporates this embedding. Extensive experiments across five benchmark datasets demonstrate that ReAd consistently outperforms existing SR methods. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/xingt-tang/ReAd.

papers.title: SEDRec: Semantic Entanglement for Generative Diffusion-based Sequential Recommendation
papers.abstract: Sequential recommendation (SR) predicts a user’s next action by modeling their historical interaction sequence, and it underpins many real-world platforms where accuracy directly impacts engagement and conversion. Recently, diffusion-based SR has gained traction by iteratively denoising corrupted representations, improving robustness and handling uncertainty when user intent is ambiguous. However, most diffusion-based SR methods still rely mainly on item IDs and learned latent embeddings, complemented by conditioning or regularization techniques. This ID-centric design limits semantic expressiveness: semantically similar items can remain distant under sparse feedback, while unrelated items may be confounded by co-occurrence and popularity biases. Prior work has attempted to inject semantics through contrastive learning or auxiliary objectives, but semantic signals are often incorporated indirectly and can weaken along the denoising trajectory, especially at inference when generation starts from noise. To address this limitation, we make semantics an explicit denoising target by introducing a semantic token whose target is the next-item semantic embedding in the same latent space as item embeddings, and we jointly denoise the item sequence and the semantic token. Building on this idea, we propose SEDRec ( S emantic E ntanglement generative D iffusion for sequential Rec ommendation), which entangles semantic and ID-based signals through history semantic conditioning, synchronized noise levels, semantic-to-target mixing, and intermediate alignment to a fixed semantic anchor. Across multiple benchmarks and evaluation metrics, extensive experiments demonstrate that SEDRec consistently outperforms strong baselines, and ablation studies confirm the contribution of each semantic entanglement component.

papers.title: Faithful Evaluation of Semantic-ID Tokenizers for Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation based on Semantic IDs (SIDs) represents each item as a discrete sequence of SIDs and is conventionally evaluated by matching the generated SID sequence against the target item's SID sequence. This evaluation is faithful only when each SID sequence uniquely identifies one item. In practice, SID collisions violate this condition: across the evaluated SID tokenizers and datasets, collision rates reach 30.52%, and SID-level Hit@10 is inflated by up to 103.36% relative to item-level Hit@10.
