To address this evaluation gap, we introduce Collision-Corrected Evaluation (CCE), which defines collision-aware item-level metrics (ItemHit@K, ItemNDCG@K) computed from generated SID sequences, and Zero-Collision Reassignment (ZCR), which constructs zero-collision SID assignments for existing tokenizers via minimum-cost reassignment. Applying these methods to four datasets and five representative SID tokenizers, we find that metric inflation scales with collision rate and is large enough to flip pairwise tokenizer comparisons under item-level re-evaluation. This finding calls into question the reliability of SID-level rankings reported in prior work and indicates that faithful tokenizer evaluation requires item-level correction or zero-collision SID assignments.

papers.title: Accumulative Modality Tokenization for Multimodal Generative Recommendation
affiliations: DCST, Tsinghua University; Quan Cheng Laboratory
Quan Cheng Laboratory; DCST, Tsinghua University
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation has attracted widespread attention as a new paradigm in recommender systems. Its core idea is to discretize item semantic representations into semantic IDs and leverage the generative model's sequence modeling capability to predict the next item the user may prefer. Early approaches mainly focused on textual semantics, and recent multimodal generative recommendation methods incorporate additional modalities to provide richer semantics. However, existing methods typically handle modalities independently during both tokenization and generation, leading to insufficient modality fusion in semantic ID construction and inadequate cross-modal integration during recommendation. Moreover, the modality tokenizers are optimized with representation-level reconstruction or alignment objectives and lack recommendation-aware supervision, resulting in sub-optimal performance. To address these issues, we propose A ccumulative M odality T okenization for Multimodal G enerative R ecommendation, namely AMTGR . Specifically, we harness the Multimodal Large Language Model as the unified tokenizer to progressively accumulate and tokenize multimodal information, and design a collaborative-aware reconstruction task as the tokenizer's optimization objective to achieve recommendation-oriented multimodal semantic IDs, which will be jointly fed into the generative model to achieve effective cross-modal integration during recommendation. Experiments on public datasets demonstrate that AMTGR significantly outperforms baselines, and further analyses verify the effectiveness of high-quality multimodal semantic IDs and the unified modality integration.

papers.title: Personalized Context-Conditioned Tokenization for Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) represents user actions as sequences of discrete tokens (often referred to as semantic IDs) and predict future interactions through autoregressive generation. This paradigm offers advantages such as compact representations, scalability, and the potential to unify retrieval and ranking. However, existing tokenization schemes are typically static and agnostic to user-specific context. In most cases, semantic IDs are derived solely from item attributes, implicitly assuming a shared notion of item similarity across all users. Under autoregressive decoding, tokens with identical prefixes tend to receive similar probabilities, meaning that a fixed tokenization enforces a universal similarity structure that may not reflect individual user perspectives. In reality, users may interpret the same item in fundamentally different ways depending on their preferences and intents. To better capture such diversity, we introduce a context-conditioned tokenizer that integrates a user’s historical interactions into the tokenization process. This approach allows a single item to be mapped to multiple semantic ID sequences under different user contexts, enabling the model to represent heterogeneous interpretations and produce more personalized recommendations. Empirical results on three public benchmarks show that our method achieves up to 11.44% improvement in NDCG@10 compared with non-personalized tokenization approaches. The implementation is available at https://github.com/YoungZ365/Pctx.

papers.title: Learning from Unreachable Rewards: Hint-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning for Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Semantic-ID generative recommenders represent each item as a short sequence of discrete semantic tokens and predict the next item by autoregressively generating this token sequence. This paradigm enables a unified generation interface for item IDs, histories, and item text, but it also creates a structured optimization bottleneck during reward-based post-training: when an early semantic token enters the wrong branch of the item-token space, finite rollout groups rarely reach the ground-truth item, so group-relative optimization receives identical zero rewards and produces no useful advantage. We propose Hint-Conditioned Generative Recommendation (HCGRec), a semantic-ID generative recommendation framework that recovers learning signal for such hard training instances. HCGRec diagnoses each instance with checkpoint rollouts and supplies a minimal target-prefix hint only when the current generator cannot reach the correct item. The model then generates the unhinted suffix under the hinted semantic branch, turning zero-reward groups into informative comparisons over item-token completions. Hinting also changes token identity: hinted prefix tokens are oracle-provided item context, while unhinted suffix tokens are sampled generation actions. We therefore introduce hint-aware credit decomposition , using supervised learning to preserve item-semantic and prefix-structure alignment for hinted tokens and GRPO to optimize the sampled suffix. Experiments on sequential recommendation benchmarks show that HCGRec substantially improves over supervised fine-tuning and vanilla reward-based post-training, while reducing zero-advantage training samples from over 70% to below 20%. The code is accessible at https://github.com/WncFht/GRec.

papers.title: Towards Efficient Federated Time Series Forecasting under Structural Data Heterogeneity across Nodes
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: Time series data is highly valuable yet sharing-sensitive across nodes, making federated learning a promising paradigm to leverage distributed temporal data. However, varying sampling standards lead to heterogeneous data structures across nodes, with diverse time granularities and inconsistent variable sets being particularly prominent, posing significant challenges for conventional federated learning frameworks. In this paper, we propose PiXTime, a novel Transformer-based time series forecasting model designed to tolerate and exploit such structurally heterogeneous distributed data. Specifically, we redesign the internal modules and adopt the parameter-decoupling philosophy by carefully designating each module as either local or shared to handle the unique challenges of the federated scenario. To address granularity misalignments, PiXTime retains a personalized set of local modules for each node, acting as a crucial bridge between the node-specific raw temporal granularities and the unified feature dimension of the federated network. To tackle variable inconsistencies, we design a shared VE Table that explicitly injects globally unified variable categorical identities into specific auxiliary tokens, enhancing PiXTime's capability to collaboratively train under highly diverse auxiliary variable distributions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PiXTime not only establishes state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in handling structurally heterogeneous distributed data but also achieves superiority in conventional benchmarks. We open-source our code at https://github.com/WearTheClo/PiXTime.

papers.title: Scaling Up Unified CTR Prediction via Dynamic Sequence-to-Feature Interaction
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: Industrial CTR prediction requires unified modeling of long user behavior histories and heterogeneous non-sequential features. Existing methods usually follow two paradigms: encode-then-concatenate methods independently encode behavior sequences and then coarsely concatenate them with non-sequential features, while token-level joint modeling methods flatten sequential and non-sequential signals into a shared interaction space. The former may ignore the heterogeneity between sequential and non-sequential representations, limiting fine-grained cross-feature interaction; the latter may suffer from capacity dilution, since behavior tokens often far outnumber high-value user, item, and contextual fields. To address these challenges, we propose Dy namic S equence-to- F eature I nteraction (DySFI), a unified sequence-conditioned dynamic feature interaction framework for CTR prediction. DySFI separately models sequential and non-sequential features with a temporal-aware sequence encoder and a DLRM backbone. The candidate-specific sequential representation generates dynamic parameters to transform the DLRM representation, enabling behavior histories to explicitly guide non-sequential feature interaction. We further introduce candidate-aware residual-update aggregation and stabilization designs to improve efficiency and training stability. Experiments on two industrial CTR scenarios show that DySFI consistently outperforms competitive baselines. Online A/B tests on Huawei AppGallery further demonstrate a 1.57% eCPM improvement over the production model, leading to full deployment.

papers.title: AlphaCast: A Human Wisdom-LLM Intelligence Co-Reasoning Framework for Time Series Forecasting
affiliations: State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: Time series forecasting is typically treated as a single-pass numerical prediction task based on historical observations. However, real-world forecasting often requires expert-like reasoning, where temporal patterns, contextual cues, case-based references, and domain knowledge are jointly considered and iteratively revised. Existing statistical, deep learning, foundation, and LLM-based forecasting models mainly rely on pattern fitting, direct prompting, or static context augmentation, leaving interactive and reflective forecasting insufficiently explored. In this work, we propose AlphaCast, a human wisdom–LLM intelligence co-reasoning framework for interactive time series forecasting. AlphaCast does not require real-time human intervention; instead, it operationalizes human wisdom as structured forecasting support, including time-series features, contextual cues, case-based references, and domain knowledge. Built upon an expert-like think–forecast–reflect workflow, AlphaCast comprises three agents: an Investigator that constructs forecasting context from available evidence, a Generator that produces context-grounded forecasts, and a Reflector that evaluates plausibility and provides feedback for refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AlphaCast improves forecasting accuracy and produces interpretable forecast explanations, offering a promising step toward interactive and context-aware time series forecasting (https://github.com/ustc-time-series/AlphaCast).

papers.title: Latent Residual Reasoning for Ranking in Generative Recommendation
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) models for ranking typically adopt a fast-thinking direct prediction paradigm with strong practical efficiency. However, ranking requires fine-grained scoring across multiple candidate items, while existing GR models still mainly rely on one-shot prediction. This raises the question whether additional inference-time computation can further improve ranking quality. Recently, inspired by Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in large language models (LLMs), some work has begun to introduce reasoning into recommendation systems. Some of these methods rely on LLM reasoning frameworks to perform explicit reasoning in textual space, but such designs are not suitable for more widely deployed non-textual recommendation models. A more relevant direction is to introduce latent reasoning into ID-based recommendation models. Although recent work has extended latent reasoning to industrial ranking, how successive reasoning steps should improve fine-grained candidate scores remains less explored. To address this problem, we propose Refiner , a latent residual reasoning framework with parameter-efficient fine-tuning for generative ranking. Our approach introduces three key components: (1) a residual reasoning mechanism that progressively refines ranking scores through cumulative additive corrections, (2) history queries that provide condensed user behavior representations to enhance candidate-specific reasoning, and (3) a parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategy that leverages LoRA modules to adapt pre-trained models for latent reasoning. Extensive experiments on two public benchmarks, an offline industrial dataset, and an online A/B test demonstrate that Refiner consistently improves over direct prediction, validating its effectiveness and practical utility.

papers.title: TAG-Rec: Grounding LLM-based Recommendation via Trigger-Anchored GRPO
affiliations: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated significant potential in recommendation systems; however, employing Reinforcement Learning (RL) to align them with ranking metrics in the query-generation formulation of large-scale recommendation remains a critical challenge. Current RL-based approaches often suffer from reward sparsity and generating too general queries. In this paper, we propose TAG-Rec, a framework that grounds generative recommendation via Trigger-Anchored Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Built upon a verifiable-anchor training principle, TAG-Rec enforces a “Trigger-First” generation strategy in which the model explicitly identifies a salient historical item as a verifiable anchor before generating a search query, structurally transforming open-ended generation into grounded reasoning. TAG-Rec combines three components: (i) Trigger-Grounded Data Curation via reachability verification, which concentrates training supervision on samples that admit a verifiable historical anchor; (ii) the Trigger-First generation strategy that anchors generation in a salient prior interaction; and (iii) a Trigger-aware Reward that supplies dense intermediate feedback to mitigate reward sparsity. On real-world sequential recommendation benchmarks, TAG-Rec achieves up to 23.6% and 13.8% average improvement over strong SFT and RL baselines, with notable gains on long-tail and novelty metrics.

papers.title: Auditing Multimodal Claims: A Controlled Reproducibility Study of Graph-based Conversational Recommendation
papers.abstract: Multimodal conversational recommender systems (CRS) integrate dialogue, knowledge graphs, and visual signals. Recent work reports substantial gains over the knowledge-graph baseline KGSF on the INSPIRED dataset (R@10: 0.132→0.257). However, this pipeline couples ViT-based image embeddings with zero-fill handling for 23.7% of items missing poster data and augments training with LLM-generated synthetic dialogues, failing to isolate the visual modality. We present a controlled reproducibility study, maintaining the MSCRS backbone and training fixed while intervening on data and image-embedding inputs. To isolate item-specific visual correspondence from representation-level artifacts, we replace ViT embeddings with three distractor conditions: random Gaussian vectors, zero vectors, and shuffled real ViT embeddings. We also apply an artificial 23.7% missingness mask to ReDial and probe synthetic-dialogue training using a valid-best checkpoint protocol. Across INSPIRED and ReDial, the distractor conditions do not consistently separate from the original ViT condition; the multi-seed mean R@10 spread is only 0.007. Conversely, synthetic dialogue shows a directional paired difference (Δ R@10 = +0.031 ± 0.020, Cohen's d z =1.59). Furthermore, selection bias introduces a max-test versus valid-best gap of up to +0.035 R@10. These results do not imply that images are unhelpful, but rather that modality-specific visual effects are currently confounded by missing-node graph effects and augmentation artifacts. We propose a reproducibility-oriented audit procedure for multimodal CRS evaluation, covering distractor controls, missingness validation, and strict checkpoint selection.

papers.title: Less is More: Concise Retrieval and Critic-based Re-ranking for Composed Image Retrieval
papers.abstract: Zero-shot composed image retrieval (ZS-CIR) aims to retrieve a target image based on a reference image and modification text. Recent approaches commonly rely on large vision-language models to generate target image captions for retrieval. However, these captions may include redundant semantic details, introducing noise when retrieving the target image and leading to suboptimal retrieval results. To address this issue, we propose Less-is-More CIR, a two-stage training-free framework that combines Concise Retrieval and Critic Re-ranking. In the first stage, concise target-oriented captions are generated that preserve only the most discriminative modification semantics, thereby reducing semantic noise in the retrieval. In the second stage, a critic re-rank module further evaluates the retrieved candidates from the perspectives of modification consistency and reference preservation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed framework for the ZS-CIR. Our code is available at: https://github.com/dxlabskku/LM-CIR.

papers.title: Large Language Model-Guided Adaptive Source-Domain Weighting for Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation
papers.abstract: Sequential Recommendation Systems (SRS) aim to predict the next item based on their historical interaction sequence. To address the data sparsity issue that commonly existed in SRS, Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation (CDSR) has emerged, which aims to improve recommendation performance in a sparse domain (usually called target domain) by transferring knowledge from an information-rich domain (usually called source domain). However, existing CDSR methods mainly rely on ID-based representations and provide limited semantics across domains. With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), recent studies have begun to incorporate LLM-generated item or user embeddings with rich semantic information into CDSR models, substantially enriching the representation space and improving modeling expressiveness. However, these LLM-enhanced methods typically treat all source domains equally and overlook the varying semantic relevance of different domains, which will lead to low-relevance domains introducing noise and consequently degrade recommendation performance. To tackle these issues, we propose LLMAW4CDSR, a Large Language Model-guided Adaptive source-domain Weighting framework. The core idea is to first leverage the semantic reasoning abilities of LLMs to produce semantically enriched user and item representations, and then use them as semantic guidance for more effective cross-domain knowledge transfer. Building on this guidance, we design an source-domain weighting mechanism that estimates the contribution of each source domain to the target domain. By integrating LLM-driven semantic alignment with adaptive domain weighting, LLMAW4CDSR highlights relevant domains while suppressing noisy ones, enabling fine-grained cross-domain knowledge transfer. Comprehensive experiments on four cross-domain datasets demonstrate that LLMAW4CDSR consistently outperforms both state-of-the-art CDSR methods and LLM-based baselines.

papers.title: DREAM-CF: Diffusion-deficiency Repair via Adaptive Multi-view Semantic Bridging for Collaborative Filtering
papers.abstract: Long-tail items are ubiquitous in collaborative filtering recommendations, and due to sparse interactions, it is difficult to extract sufficient collaborative propagation signals from the original user–item graph, leading to inadequate representation learning and a bias toward popular items. Existing Graph ODE-based collaborative filtering methods enhance propagation flexibility by continuously modeling the evolution of user and item representations. However, they typically assume that the input graph already possesses reliable information diffusion paths, thereby overlooking the issue of insufficient diffusion for long-tail items within the original interaction structure. To address this, we propose DREAM-CF, which stands for Diffusion-deficiency Repair via Adaptive Multi-view Semantic Bridging for Collaborative Filtering. DREAM-CF first integrates item text semantic representations with user historical behavior to construct a time-aware semantic initial state, thereby reducing the reliance of continuous diffusion on random ID embeddings. Subsequently, we design an ODE-aware Diffusion-deficiency Diagnosis mechanism to identify items with genuine information reception deficiencies on the original user–item graph, rather than simply classifying long-tail targets based on interaction frequency. Furthermore, DREAM-CF constructs high-confidence item-item bridge edges from three perspectives—textual semantics, co-occurrence, and metadata relationships—transforming external semantic information and behavioral priors into structured signals that can participate in graph propagation. Experimental results demonstrate that DREAM-CF effectively improves recommendation performance in long-tail and sparse interaction scenarios.Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/XiQier/Dream-CF.git.

papers.title: MUSER: Memory-Augmented Multimodal Sequential Recommendation
affiliations: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
Institute of Artificial Intelligence (TeleAI), China Telecom
papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models offer unprecedented capabilities for sequential recommendation, yet their deployment is fundamentally bottlenecked by the conflict between finite context windows and unbounded interaction histories. Existing methods typically compress multimodal behaviors into textual summaries, inevitably precipitating semantic degradation and interest homogenization. To resolve this, we propose MUSER , a M emory-augmented framework for m U ltimodal SE quential R ecommendation, built upon a collaborative dual-agent architecture. Specifically, a User Agent maintains a parametric memory via structured input, forget, and rerank operations, guided by a dynamic personality parameter and an Isomorphic Consistency Planning mechanism to ensure long-term preference stability. Concurrently, a Recommendation Agent leverages this stateful memory under a decision-reason bi-objective scheme to jointly optimize recommendation accuracy and high-fidelity textual explanations. Extensive experiments on three real-world benchmarks demonstrate that MUSER significantly outperforms state-of-the-art (SoTA) baselines.

papers.title: Neutralizing Popularity Bias in LLM-based Recommendation via Counterfactual Reasoning Guidelines
papers.abstract: In the era of generative AI, recommender systems are moving from precise prediction to trustworthy generation. Large language models (LLMs) support this shift by inferring user interests and producing natural-language explanations. However, LLM-based recommendation suffers from a fundamental obstacle: popularity bias. Pre-training on massive corpora, LLMs tend to rely on global statistics and trend signals, yielding recommendations that follow popularity rather than genuine preference. As this bias is entangled in model parameters and is hard to remove directly, we propose Neutralizing Popularity Bias in LLM-based Recommendation via Counterfactual Reasoning Guidelines (NPRec), a model-agnostic framework that mitigates popularity bias through external semantic intervention. NPRec performs counterfactual refinement to causally separate intrinsic user interests from popularity-driven conformity, producing debiased textual guidelines that reflect actual user preferences. These guidelines are injected at inference time to shift the LLM from unconstrained generation to guided reasoning, without any parameter updates. Serving as explicit premises, they both ground faithful explanations and improve recommendation quality. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that NPRec achieves promising performance in recommendation accuracy, explanation quality and debiasing capability.

papers.title: Mitigating Popularity Bias in Sequential Recommendations with Sparse Prior-Regularized Objective
papers.abstract: Popularity bias is a well-known challenge in recommender systems, often leading to the over-exposure of popular items and reduced catalog coverage. In this work, we propose PR-entmax, a sparse prior-regularized objective that makes popularity correction context-dependent. We derive our method from a generalized variational principle in which an item popularity prior is incorporated directly into a sparse probability mapping, yielding a popularity-aware active support: the set of items receiving non-zero probabilities and hence non-zero gradients is determined jointly by contextual relevance and item popularity. As a result, the prior affects not only item probabilities, but also which items participate in gradient updates during training. The method requires no architectural changes and can be integrated into existing training pipelines by modifying only the loss function. At inference time, the prior term is removed, and items are ranked by the learned contextual relevance alone. Experiments across multiple benchmark datasets and sequential recommendation architectures show that PR-entmax consistently reduces popularity bias while preserving or improving recommendation relevance, advancing the relevance-debiasing trade-off.

papers.title: Near In-Distribution Watermarking for Recommender Systems
papers.abstract: Recommender systems constitute valuable intellectual property for modern platforms, driving the need for reliable ownership protection. Existing out-of-distribution (OOD) memorization-based watermarking methods for sequential recommendation preserve recommendation utility by constructing watermark sequences outside natural interaction patterns. However, this separation can introduce detectable behavioral deviations that expose new vulnerabilities under black-box deployment. We identify two such inconsistencies– distributional and trajectory inconsistency–and propose a unified inference-time attack framework that exploits them via lightweight output suppression, requiring neither retraining nor parameter modification. To mitigate these vulnerabilities while preserving watermark verifiability, we propose Near In-Distribution Watermarking (NIDW), which shifts watermark construction from extreme OOD patterns toward a controlled near-ID region. NIDW comprises three components: (1) seed prefix initialization from real user sequences, (2) near-ID sampling guided by a popularity prior and semantic smoothing, and (3) progressive multi-stage training with a lightweight OOD-retention constraint. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed attacks substantially degrade existing OOD watermarks, while NIDW maintains competitive recommendation utility and achieves improved robustness against inference-time attacks, distillation, and fine-tuning. Our code is available at https://github.com/powell4322/NIDW.

papers.title: The Role of User-Item Connectivity in CTR Prediction
papers.abstract: Click-through rate (CTR) prediction is a central problem in recommendation systems. Modern CTR models are largely feature-centric. They encode users, items, and contextual variables as independent feature fields, even though the same training data also define a user-item interaction graph. Graph-based methods can exploit this structure, but less is known about the role of connectivity itself. These efforts do not ask why connectivity helps, when it produces reliable gains, and which user groups receive them. This paper studies user-item connectivity as the object of analysis rather than as another architectural component. We use a deliberately minimal message-passing (MP) operator as a controlled intervention that enriches user and item representations with graph-based information while leaving the CTR architecture unchanged. We first show that MP smooths learned representations over the interaction graph and reduces sensitivity to small input perturbations, with stronger effects for nodes with more observed interactions. Experiments across datasets with different interaction densities show that connectivity is not uniformly beneficial. Denser graphs produce more consistent gains, while sparse graphs benefit less consistently. We further find that connectivity-aware embeddings can be efficiently integrated by fine-tuning existing CTR models. Finally, we introduce the Marginal Cost of Improvement (MCI), which measures the effective effort associated with improving each user group. Across our experiments, MP shifts more predictive improvement toward under-served user groups, leading to a more balanced distribution of predictive performance.

papers.title: H2CE: Modeling Geo-Semantic Interactions for POI Reranking with Heterogeneous Two-Stage Cross-Encoders
papers.abstract: Point-of-Interest (POI) reranking in local search must model query-conditioned tradeoffs among lexical semantics, geospatial proximity, and numerical quality signals such as rating and review count, while remaining practical under real-time serving constraints. A close POI may only partially satisfy the query intent, while a farther one may offer stronger semantic and quality evidence. We present H2CE, a Heterogeneous Two-stage Cross-Encoder for latency-bounded POI reranking. H2CE represents numerical attributes in two complementary ways: bucketized natural-language descriptors are inserted into the cross-encoder input to support semantic–numeric attention, while exact scalar values are processed by dedicated MLPs to preserve magnitude information. The resulting semantic and numerical embeddings are fused through latent-space aggregation, enabling nonlinear interactions beyond scalar weighted sums. H2CE then applies a two-stage architecture: Stage 1 scores all candidates pointwise for scalable filtering, and Stage 2 performs head-to-head pairwise comparison among the top-K candidates with Copeland aggregation, making fine-grained relative tradeoffs explicit while reducing pairwise cost from O(N 2 ) to O(N+K(K-1)). On a 5,743-query local search test set, H2CE achieves 67.48% NDCG@5, improving over XGBoost LTR by +22.82% absolute and over a zero-shot LLM reranker by +35.89%. The pairwise stage adds +1.98% NDCG@5 over the pointwise model alone. Ablations confirm the value of numerical features, latent aggregation, top-K pairwise reranking, and aligned training.

papers.title: Beyond Exposure: Dynamic Income-Fair Ranking under Time-Varying Provider Value
papers.abstract: Ranking systems in web search and recommendation must balance relevance-based effectiveness with fairness for item providers. Exposure Fairness seeks to allocate position-induced attention according to item merit, but exposure is only an intermediate signal whose conversion into provider utility varies with context. We therefore define income as the context-dependent provider utility induced by exposure. We formalize Income Fairness , which requires cumulative provider income to be proportional to relevance, and develop a corresponding metric based on a context-dependent unit-income function. We propose DIDRF ( D ynamic- I ncome- D erivative-aware R anking F airness), which exploits the quadratic structure of income-fairness violations to derive a prefix-aware, state-calibrated scoring rule that balances effectiveness and income fairness. Experiments on standard learning-to-rank datasets in semi-synthetic income environments calibrated from real advertising and e-commerce logs show that DIDRF achieves lower income unfairness than representative fair-ranking baselines while maintaining competitive effectiveness.

papers.title: One Metric Does Not Fit All: How Platform Type Shapes the Validity of Online Evaluation Metrics in Conversational Search
papers.abstract: The shift from traditional web search to conversational search has introduced new challenges for online evaluation. While prior work has begun to rethink evaluation for conversational search systems, the role of platform type remains underexplored. This study investigates how metric-satisfaction relationships differ between a generation-centric platform (ChatGPT) and a retrieval-centric platform (Perplexity) in conversational search. We categorize online evaluation metrics for conversational search into two categories: traditional metrics adapted to conversational contexts, and novel metrics designed specifically for conversational interactions. Through a controlled user study with 72 valid participants, we collect fine-grained interaction logs and post-task satisfaction ratings. Our results show that user behavior and the predictive power of online metrics for satisfaction differ significantly across the two platforms. Notably, novel conversational metrics exhibit stronger predictive power on generation-centric platforms, while adapted traditional metrics remain effective on retrieval-centric ones. Qualitative interviews further reveal underlying mechanisms: divergent cognitive load, verification strategies, and perceived efficiency are reflected in these cross-platform differences. Our findings highlight the necessity of context-aware evaluation frameworks tailored to platform characteristics, although the findings are based on two specific platforms and should be generalised with caution.

papers.title: CoVer-CIR: Constraint-Aware Retrieval Calibration and Self-Verification for Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: Zero-shot composed image retrieval aims to retrieve a target image given a reference image and a modification instruction, without task-specific annotated triplets. Existing methods typically conflate the multimodal query into a single textual query, leveraging VLMs such as CLIP to rank candidates by overall similarity. However, this conflated representation is insufficient for CIR, where the instruction specifies multiple edit constraints relative to the reference image, such as preserving certain visual content while adding, removing, or replacing others. This makes it difficult to distinguish hard negatives that are globally plausible but violate a decisive edit constraint, especially when the violation is local and subtle. To address this limitation, we propose CoVer-CIR, a training-free framework that progressively turns edit constraints into ranking evidence. It first makes the edit constraints explicit by deriving a positive target, negative constraints, and contrastive pairs from the query. During retrieval, CoVer-CIR calibrates retrieval scores with adaptive negative penalties estimated from images favored by the positive target, producing a cleaner Top-\(K\) candidate set. For re-ranking, instead of using an expensive candidate-level verifier, CoVer-CIR performs lightweight pairwise verification with the contrastive pairs. Each pair compares a required local condition with a confusing alternative, and the resulting relative margin provides local evidence for the edit constraints. Experiments on CIRCO, CIRR, and FashionIQ show strong performance across CLIP backbones, especially in top-ranked retrieval results.

papers.title: Process In-Context Learning: Confusion-Aware Demonstration Retrieval and Dynamic Insertion for Mathematical Reasoning
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) has achieved strong results across a wide range of large language model (LLM) tasks. However, its effectiveness for problems that require step-by-step deduction, such as mathematical reasoning, is still not well understood. One major limitation of existing ICL methods is that demonstrations are chosen before inference and remain unchanged throughout reasoning. As a result, they cannot respond to confusion points that emerge during multi-step problem solving, such as uncertain calculations or missing logical transitions. When these confusion points are not resolved, they may propagate and ultimately degrade answer accuracy. To address this limitation, we propose Process In-Context Learning (PICL), a dynamic demonstration insertion framework for mathematical reasoning. PICL consists of two stages: 1) it identifies potential confusion points by analyzing semantics and entropy in the reasoning process and summarizes their core characteristics; 2) upon encountering these points, it retrieves relevant demonstrations from the demonstration pool that match the confusion context and inserts them directly into the ongoing reasoning process to guide subsequent steps. Experimental results show that PICL outperforms representative baselines by alleviating mid-process confusion, demonstrating the effectiveness of adaptive demonstration insertion for complex mathematical reasoning.

papers.title: CDAR-RAG: Cross-Distributional Alignment-Based Retriever for Online Community Jargon Understanding
papers.abstract: Online communities often use jargon, which is a set of specialized terms that can only be understood implicitly and in context by a specific group of users. Although large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable achievements in various tasks, understanding community jargon is challenging, as it introduces more complex, high-context comprehension. In-context learning (ICL) can help LLMs achieve better jargon understanding by providing demonstrations of jargon usage-definition pairs, yet using appropriate demonstrations is critical. However, which jargon terms are appropriate demonstrations for the given target jargon term is unclear; no true relationship between jargon terms is known. This makes typical retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) struggle to obtain appropriate demonstrations, as labeled query-document relations are often required for task-specialized RAG. For this problem, we propose CDAR (Cross-Distributional Alignment-based Retriever), a retriever training method that requires no explicit query-document relevance labels, by aligning the distribution of cosine similarities between pairs of jargon usage examples to that between their corresponding definitions. Our results show that CDAR effectively increases jargon understanding across five LLM generators of varying scales, consistently outperforming zero-shot, random, vanilla RAG, and triplet-loss baselines, and that a retriever trained on one jargon domain transfers effectively to unseen jargon domains. Notably, Qwen3 8B + CDAR significantly surpasses GPT-OSS 120B performance, showing that CDAR serves as an efficient framework, especially with smaller LLMs.

papers.title: A Contrastive Framework for Enhanced Automatic Attribution Evaluation Through Error Generation
papers.abstract: Attributed Large Language Models learn to cite supporting documents in their generated text, thus improving factuality and traceability. Research on the automatic evaluation of this capability either focuses on proposing new specialized metric-models or on defining attribution evaluation frameworks that rely on base models at a granular level, such as Natural Language Inference (NLI) models, for their implementation. While the latter have become the standard for attribution evaluation, their reliance on repurposing base models of different tasks hinders their full potential. In this work, we propose a comprehensive study that examines existing attribution evaluation solutions for a fine-grained understanding of model errors and current limitations. To achieve this, we survey existing works on attribution evaluation and construct a comprehensive taxonomy of persistent error types. We leverage this analysis to design synthetic examples that mimic error types to quantify the ability of existing models to overcome them. We additionally follow a contrastive framework and propose a new model better aligned for the attribution evaluation task that can be seamlessly integrated into existing evaluation schemes. We use two standard attribution and faithfulness evaluation benchmarks, the AttributionBench and the TRUE Benchmark, covering 18 datasets, and show that our proposed model allows for better generalization and robustness to a wide range of errors while maintaining baseline performance.

papers.title: Risk-Aware Reranking for Agentic Tool Retrieval
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China
University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: Tool retrieval determines which external tools are exposed to an LLM agent for a user query or task, making retrieval a critical pre-execution safety boundary. Unlike document retrieval, tool retrieval exposes executable actions: a tool that is useful for one task may be unnecessary or risky for another. However, existing tool-retrieval methods primarily optimize semantic relevance, and safety evaluations often focus on failures after tool execution rather than risks introduced during retrieval. We study risk-aware tool retrieval, where the goal is to retrieve useful tools while reducing exposure to higher-risk tools. We propose a lightweight reranking framework on top of a frozen first-stage retriever. The framework models query-conditioned relevance and tool-level exposure risk separately, combines them through an explicit parameter controlling the tradeoff between safety and utility, smooths scores over a ToolGraph, and optionally applies rule-based safety constraints. To support retrieval-time safety evaluation, we annotate 6,108 tools across UltraTool and Seal-Tools with five ordinal risk levels and define metrics that measure risky-tool exposure in the top-k results. Experiments on UltraTool and Seal-Tools show that our approach improves the relevance–safety tradeoff over relevance-only retrievers and reranking baselines, with the rule-filtered variant providing a conservative operating point for safety-critical deployments. These findings indicate that retrieval-stage filtering can reduce the candidate action space exposed to agents before execution, complementing downstream tool-use safeguards. The code and supplementary materials are available at: https://github.com/qli447/risk-aware-tool-retrieval-release https://github.com/qli447/risk-aware-tool-retrieval-release.

papers.title: S-VEAM: A Shared Spectral Memory for Cross-Session Retrieval in Long-Horizon LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents in multi-session deployments must answer through a bounded prompt window while their histories grow without bound. Surfacing the right history within that budget is a retrieval and ranking problem over a state that never stops growing. We present S-VEAM, a shared spectral memory controller for long-session agents in which construction and retrieval are two phases of one persistent spectral state (P, V, ?) that unifies writing new sessions into the state and reading evidence back out. Both phases use non-generative spectral operations: the controller issues no generative-LLM call at memory-management time, and the spectral indexing rank — distinct from the retained verbatim pool — remains fixed as trajectories grow. In the tested long-session settings this yields a low-latency retrieval profile while preserving verbatim evidence for the downstream model. We evaluate S-VEAM under the Cross-Session Stress Test Protocol (CSSTP), a source-faithful evaluation over existing benchmarks with controlled long-session stress conditions. LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S provide the main long-session evidence: S-VEAM is top-ranked on both answer containment and evidence-backed answer containment on every LoCoMo cell and on LongMemEval-S native, with non-generative fixed-rank maintenance and low-latency retrieval. MuSiQue Tier 3 enters as an auxiliary multi-hop evidence-split diagnostic where S-VEAM achieves the highest evidence-backed answer containment. Stateful memory peers enter as cost-matched counterparts under the same budget and reset policy. S-VEAM thus marks a fixed-rank, non-generative indexing operating point for long-session memory under tight retrieval budgets.

papers.title: Bethe Consensus Decoding: Joint Inference on Empirical Pairwise Factor Graphs for Structured LLM Outputs
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly serve as zero-shot extractors for structured outputs whose fields are mutually dependent: a salary range is correlated with experience level; a destination is correlated with the airline. The dominant unsupervised aggregator, independent majority voting (IMV), decodes each field marginally and therefore commits combinatorially inconsistent outputs whenever the per-field modes do not co-occur. We introduce Bethe Consensus Decoding (BCD), a training-free post-hoc aggregator that reconciles K samples drawn from a frozen LLM by minimising a Bethe free energy on a sparse pairwise factor graph. The graph is constructed from empirical mutual information using a cardinality-aware χ 2 threshold, sum-product loopy belief propagation with damping yields pseudo-marginal beliefs, and a sequential greedy clamping procedure with a pairwise-belief ratio correction extracts a globally coherent output. We show that on tree-structured factor graphs in the population limit, BCD strictly dominates IMV in the induced tree distribution. On five real datasets ranging from slot filling to 15-field resume parsing, BCD with Llama-3-70B-Instruct improves average exact-match accuracy by 4.6 points over IMV and by 2.2 points over the strongest unsupervised structured baseline. We additionally evaluate BCD on Llama-3-8B, GPT-4o-mini, and Gemini-1.5-Flash and observe strong absolute performance on each (up to 44.96 EM on GPT-4o-mini), though backbone-matched IMV baselines are out of scope for this study. BCD is competitive with a supervised pairwise CRF that uses the same graph topology: the margin is small (≤ 1.3 pp) on the three data-rich benchmarks (D1, D2, D4) and substantially larger (3.7–4.7 pp, statistically significant under Holm–Bonferroni correction) on the two data-scarce benchmarks (D3, D5). Aggregation runs in milliseconds on CPU and reduces to IMV exactly when the empirical edge set is empty.

papers.title: AegisKV: Runtime Headroom Control for Online LLM Serving via Adaptive Attention Offloading
papers.abstract: This paper presents AegisKV, a runtime-adaptive attention offloading system for heterogeneous GPU environments. AegisKV dynamically offloads decode attention and KV cache at the request level based on runtime KV pressure and auxiliary GPU capability. AegisKV treats attention offloading not simply as KV-capacity expansion, but as a runtime KV headroom control mechanism for continuous batching in online LLM serving. To realize this design, AegisKV integrates (i) a pressure-aware request offloading scheduler, (ii) heterogeneous KV-cache management across serving and auxiliary GPUs, and (iii) a cross-device execution pipeline that overlaps KV transfer and decode execution. By selectively offloading only necessary requests, AegisKV mitigates preemption and recomputation while avoiding unnecessary auxiliary-path overhead. We implement AegisKV on top of vLLM and evaluate it using realistic online serving workloads on heterogeneous GPU configurations. On Llama-2-13B, AegisKV achieves up to 1.23× lower normalized token latency than baseline vLLM and 1.80× lower than static full offloading. Furthermore, on Qwen2.5-72B with MPS-based optimization, AegisKV achieves 15.07× lower TTFT and delays the onset of latency saturation by up to 1.43×.

papers.title: Accelerating Scientific Data Analytics Using Reconstruction-Free Error Control
papers.abstract: Error-bounded lossy compression is widely used to reduce scientific data volume and alleviate storage and I/O bottlenecks. However, downstream analyses often require different accuracy levels, forcing users to rerun compression with multiple settings or store multiple compressed files. In addition, many applications focus on derived quantities of interest (QoIs), making it difficult to determine how much information should be retrieved to satisfy a prescribed QoI error bound without repeated reconstructions. In this work, we focus on QoI-aware progressive retrieval and develop reconstruction-free QoI error-control methods for both univariate and multivariate QoIs. Our approach uses basic statistics from the original data to construct conservative upper bounds, which determine a sufficient retrieval amount before reconstruction. This avoids trial-and-error reconstruction while supporting different QoI accuracy requirements from a single progressive representation. We compare our method with two categories of QoI-aware baselines: methods requiring separate compression runs for different QoI accuracy levels, and reconstruction-based progressive search methods requiring repeated reconstructions to identify a sufficient retrieval amount. The results show that our method satisfies prescribed QoI error bounds while reducing reconstruction overhead, with up to an 80.37% reduction in reconstruction time compared with the reconstruction-based search method.

papers.title: CubeFlow: Accelerating Multidimensional Query Chains for Interactive Data Analytics
affiliations: Nanjing University of Finance and Economics
papers.abstract: Interactive data analytics tools enable users to explore data incrementally, often generating a sequence of dependent SQL queries, called a SQL chain. Even for moderately sized datasets, executing such chains on traditional database systems incurs significant overhead due to multiple rounds of intermediate aggregations, joins, and other compute-intensive operations. This paper focuses on multidimensional query chains and presents CubeFlow, an acceleration layer that sits between the analytics platform and the underlying database. By decoupling dimension columns from measure values, CubeFlow represents intermediate results as cube structures and models execution as a sequence of cube transformations along the chain. We introduce shadow dimensions to preserve regular cube structures across transformations in the chain, and propose coordinate-based aggregation and join algorithms that reuse dimension mappings and hash integer coordinates rather than raw attribute values. We implement a single-threaded prototype of CubeFlow and evaluate it on six multidimensional query chains over TPC-H, Online Retail, and Stocks. Despite the overhead of data conversion and coordination, our approach achieves average speedups of 5.4× over DuckDB and 7.6× over ClickHouse under single-threaded settings.

papers.title: SCoP: Structured Constraint Parsing for Evidence-Space Control in Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering
affiliations: Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.abstract: Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering (TKGQA) requires answer inference from evidence that is both structurally valid and temporally admissible. Existing methods often leave anchor-event binding, temporal admissibility, and ordinal selection implicit in model reasoning, task-specific training, or similarity-driven retrieval, allowing locally relevant but invalid facts to enter the answer context. We formulate complex TKGQA as evidence-space control and propose SCoP (Structured Constraint Parsing), a constraint-centric framework that externalizes temporal decisions before answer inference. Instead of treating retrieved facts as admissible evidence by default, SCoP separates answer-seeking event patterns from temporal anchor events, conservatively grounds them to canonical TKG entities and relations, and translates temporal intent into executable constraints with optional ranking requirements. These constraints operate over normalized point and interval ranges, enabling deterministic filtering of structurally compatible candidates and producing a compact evidence space for generation. Experiments on MultiTQ and TimelineCronQ-R assess SCoP across timestamped point-fact and interval-oriented settings with richer temporal relations and ordering dependencies. Without task-specific parameter updates, SCoP achieves 0.825 Hits@1 on MultiTQ and 0.761 Hits@1 on TimelineCronQ-R, with gains on constraint-intensive question types. These results support explicit evidence-space control over unconstrained retrieval or implicit temporal reasoning.

papers.title: Intent2Chain: Multi-Task Knowledge Graph Reasoning for Network Intent Completion
affiliations: College of Computer Science, Inner Mongolia University
papers.abstract: Intent-Driven Networking (IDN) is important for autonomous network management. It aims to translate high-level user goals into structured network configurations. However, user intents in real-world scenarios are often incomplete. They may lack specific service functions (SFs), proper function sequences, and necessary attributes. This makes it difficult to obtain a complete Service Function Chain (SFC) representation. In this paper, we propose a multi-task knowledge graph reasoning method, named Intent2Chain, for network intent completion. We construct an Intent-Network Knowledge Graph (INKG) to unify business intents and network service knowledge in a shared semantic space. To bridge the gap between abstract intents and structured SFC representations, we decompose the completion process into three related subtasks: SF set prediction, SFC link prediction, and SF attribute completion. Specifically, we combine global attention with local graph learning to capture structural dependencies among SFs. We further introduce SFC order prior constraints and weighted topological sorting to ensure structural validity and avoid loops. Experimental results on real-world operational logs show that Intent2Chain can effectively recover missing SFs, order relations, and attributes for incomplete network intents.

papers.title: From Ontology Alignments to Executable Code: Automating Data Integration with Fact Generating Functions
papers.abstract: Data integration remains labor-intensive, making projects lengthy, costly, and difficult to automate end to end. Although substantial progress has been made on core subtasks such as schema matching, ontology alignment, and entity matching, these subtasks often stop short of producing executable transformations. In ontology-based data integration, mappings can identify corresponding classes and properties, but value normalization, literal conversion, and multi-fact generation are still commonly implemented through bespoke scripts. We introduce Fact Generating Functions (FGFs), executable triple-conversion functions that transform RDF triples expressed under source semantics into semantically corresponding triples under target semantics. FGFs bridge the gap between ontology alignment and RDF materialization by making transformation logic explicit, inspectable, and executable. We present an automated pipeline that instantiates the approach by converting relational data into RDF, identifying source-to-target correspondences, generating intermediate logical rules, and materializing target triples through executable FGFs. We evaluate the method on benchmark scenarios for relational data-to-ontology integration and show competitive results across diverse mapping settings. The results demonstrate the feasibility of using FGFs as a practical abstraction to automate semantic data mapping and reduce the need for manually engineered transformation scripts.

papers.title: Who Do We Trust? Investigating the Human-AI Trust Gap in Scientific Social Media Discourse
affiliations: GESIS - Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences
papers.abstract: As social media continues to be one of the primary communication channels, it has become a critical hub for the dissemination of scientific information. The nature of these platforms allows for the quick sharing of scientific claims, even without a reference. Users often rely on contextual cues such as comments accompanying posts for validation, while some platforms are increasingly integrate LLM-based systems that participant in online discourse by generating comments, explanations, and fact-checks. In this paper, we investigate how comment attribution (Human vs. AI) affects perceived trustworthiness of comments and posts and how it changes with the presence of a reference to a scientific publication and the comment's stance. We conducted a preregistered within-subjects user study (N=152) using a web-based platform that simulates a social media timeline containing posts and comments. We compared eight conditions: two types of comment attribution (Human vs. AI), two types of comment stance (Endorsing vs. Refuting), and two types of reference existence (Reference vs. No Reference). While we did not find evidence for a difference in overall trustworthiness between Human- and AI- attributed comments, we found that comments without a reference that were attributed to an AI were perceived as more trustworthy than those attributed to a human, highlighting the risk of over-reliance on AI. Exploratory analysis further indicate differences in comment and post trustworthiness between Human- and AI-attributed comments, depending on whether posts' claims aligned with scientific consensus. These observed differences suggest a potential interplay of trust and confirmation bias in the context of AI-attributed comments, which warrants further investigation by future research.

papers.title: PACIFIER: Pacing Opinion Depolarization via a Unified Graph Learning Framework
papers.abstract: Online social networks often form opposing echo chambers that reinforce opinion polarization. Under the Friedkin--Johnsen (FJ) model, ModerateInternal (MI) and ModerateExpressed (ME) reduce polarization by neutralizing selected users' internal or expressed opinions, but existing solutions are largely model-specific and learning-based depolarization remains underexplored. We study FJ-based moderation as feedback-free autoregressive sequential planning and propose PACIFIER, a unified graph-learning framework that constructs ordered intervention sequences from the initial graph--opinion instance without using recomputed post-intervention expressed opinions as intermediate feedback. PACIFIER combines history-aware node representations with Greedy and RL variants for immediate and long-horizon action scoring, and supports MI, ME, continuous opinions, cost-aware moderation, and node removal. We evaluate intervention trajectories by Accumulated Normalized Polarization (ANP). Trained only on synthetic graphs with fewer than 50 nodes, PACIFIER transfers to 15 real-world Twitter networks with up to 155,599 nodes. It improves over the strongest non-PACIFIER baseline by up to 35.3%, while PACIFIER-RL improves over PACIFIER-Greedy by up to 37.69%. Compared with oracle-style Greedy, PACIFIER retains 98.94% and 97.39% near-oracle quality on MI and ME, respectively, and is about 600× faster at the 450-node range. The source code is available at https://github.com/RickyYY-SZU/PACIFIER.

papers.title: Multi-stage Interpretable Temporal Mixture of Experts for Information Diffusion Prediction
affiliations: Henan University of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Information diffusion prediction, which aims to identify potentially infected users for a given message, is essential in domains such as public opinion analysis, fake news detection, and social recommendation. However, existing methods still suffer from several limitations: (1) They usually divide the historical cascades using a fixed time interval, ignoring the heterogeneity of multi-stage information diffusion dynamics. (2) Present methods primarily focus on sequential dependencies among users, while overlooking explicit temporal information and the interpretability of the prediction results. To address the aforementioned issues, we propose a Multi-stage Interpretable Temporal Mixture of Experts model (MITMoE). Specifically, we first introduce an adaptive temporal-scale segmentation method, which can dynamically adjust the temporal granularity according to diffusion dynamics at different stages, preserving temporal consistency while accounting for variations in diffusion density. We then present an Interpretable Temporal Mixture of Experts (ITMoE) interaction mechanism for explicit temporal information fusion, providing interpretable temporal interaction patterns at both local and global levels. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets show that MITMoE outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, with each core component contributing effectively.

papers.title: Predicting Narrative Virality on Social Media Streams for Pre-Peak Misinformation Triage
affiliations: INESC-ID / Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa
papers.abstract: Misinformation narratives that reach virality on social media typically do so within a median of 1.5 days, while professional fact-checkers require a median of 4.5 days to publish corrections. When a false claim circulates unaddressed, polarization sets in around it, eroding the corrective impact of fact-checks that arrive after peak spread. Existing virality prediction operates either on individual posts (will this tweet trend?) or on coarse events (will this topic dominate?), missing the narrative, a cluster of semantically equivalent claims, as the natural unit of analysis for fact-checking workflows. We introduce narrative-level streaming virality prediction as a new task formulation, supported by an end-to-end pipeline with four components: streaming clustering of semantically equivalent posts into evolving narratives, online kernel-density anomaly detection over cluster activity, LLM-based claim normalization, and cluster-level spread prediction via a novel Post-Detection Spread Ratio (PSR) metric that quantifies the remaining intervention window at detection time. The pipeline surfaces actionable triage decisions before peak virality. Our downstream components also advance the state of the art on two established Automatic Claim Detection (ACD) tasks. On the N=300 CT2025 English claim-normalization test subset, a contrastive few-shot approach with Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 exceeds the strongest published baseline by 10.0 METEOR points despite using a smaller model than the published baselines. On CheckThat! 2024 check-worthiness, our 4-Parallel-Heads DeBERTa-v3-large achieves F1=0.833 with dimension-wise confidence decomposition, generalizing zero-shot to ClaimBuster (F1=0.973) and CheckThat! 2023 (F1=0.933). We release the first dataset and baselines for narrative-level streaming virality prediction, with virality labels, check-worthiness annotations, and intermediate features over 535 narratives derived from 1.52M tweets of a US political-event Twitter stream.

papers.title: ContextClaim: A Context-Driven Paradigm for Verifiable Claim Detection
papers.abstract: Automated fact-checking pipelines typically begin with a filtering stage that decides which claims are worth verifying, given that the later evidence retrieval and verification components are expensive to apply at scale. A central task in this stage is verifiable claim detection, which asks whether a statement is in principle checkable against external evidence. Prior work on this task, as well as on the closely related notion of check-worthiness, conditions its decisions only on the claim sentence itself. We argue that this is restrictive, because deciding whether a statement is checkable often depends on identifying the entities and events it mentions, and on whether external information about them is actually available in the first place. Motivated by how downstream verification systems rely on retrieved evidence, we move retrieval upstream into the detection stage and introduce ContextClaim. Given an input claim, the approach identifies entity mentions, queries Wikipedia as a structured background source, and uses large language models to compress the retrieved material into short contextual summaries that are then passed to a classifier. Experiments are conducted on two domains and genres, namely the CheckThat! 2022 Twitter collection and the PoliClaim corpus of political debates, and cover both encoder and decoder only models under fine-tuning, zero-shot, and few-shot settings. The added context yields gains on verifiable claim detection in several configurations, although the size of the improvement varies with the dataset, the backbone model, and the training setup. We further find that the same retrieved summaries are useful beyond detection. Feeding them into a downstream verification model on FEVER improves verification F1. Component level analyses, human annotation, and error inspection further clarify the conditions under which retrieved context helps, and where it does not.

papers.title: HARA: A Hierarchical Artifact-Aware Residual Adapter Framework for AI-Generated Image Detection
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: With the rapid advancement of generative models, AI-generated image (AIGI) detection has become crucial. However, current pretrained encoder-based methods still face two key limitations: (i) late feature fusion , where local artifact cues are progressively suppressed by stacked ViT encoder layers before being exploited; and (ii) source-domain overfitting , which limits robustness to unseen generative models and domains. To address these challenges, we propose HARA , a H ierarchical A rtifact-aware R esidual A dapter framework for AIGI detection. HARA introduces a dual-branch adapter architecture that jointly models semantic representations and generation-induced artifact cues through lightweight low-rank adaptation and local convolutional feature extraction. Instead of restricting feature interaction to the final stage, HARA progressively injects adapter-enhanced features into selected shallow, intermediate, and deep ViT layers, enabling hierarchical refinement of artifact-aware representations while preserving the pretrained representation space. This progressive fusion strategy effectively preserves and exploits fine-grained artifact traces that are often diluted in deeper semantic representations. Furthermore, to improve out-of-distribution generalization, we introduce two feature-space regularization strategies: structured noise perturbation and stochastic adapter scaling. These mechanisms act as implicit feature-space augmentation, encouraging the model to learn more invariant and transferable representations under distribution shifts introduced by different generative pipelines. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that HARA consistently outperforms existing methods, particularly in challenging cross-generator and cross-domain evaluation settings.

papers.title: Prototype-Rectified Iterative Self-supervised Manifold Denoising under Severe Acoustic Shift
affiliations: Indian Institute of Science Education and Research Bhopal
papers.abstract: Audio-Text Foundation Models (ATMs) fail catastrophically under severe acoustic noise, yet existing adaptation strategies either rely on gradient-based Test-Time Adaptation (TTA), which reinforces noise rather than signal, or on prompt tuning that requires privileged noise annotations unavailable at inference. We address these failures with PRISM (Prototype-Rectified Iterative Self-supervised Manifold Denoising), a training-free, source-free TTA framework grounded in the Affine Noise Hypothesis: severe acoustic noise induces a low-rank affine shift in the multimodal latent space, with more than 90% of distortion energy confined to the leading 60 principal components. PRISM estimates and reverses this distortion from an unlabeled target batch using frozen text prototypes as geometric anchors via three closed-form geometric corrections compiled into a single static projection matrix by Affine Bias Regression. In inference, adaptation reduces to one matrix-vector multiplication in 9 × 10⁻⁴ ms, making it substantially faster than gradient-based TTA while requiring no additional training. On UrbanSound8K, PRISM improves over the zero-shot baseline by +12.94 pp and surpasses an oracle-assisted TTA baseline by +9.41 pp, which requires privileged augmented noise prompts PRISM never sees. We further identify the Polyphonic Trap, a principled failure mode of subspace deflation for broadband classes, and resolve it via Confidence-Aware Regression (CAR), recovering up to 8.16 pp for the worst-affected class. The code is available at https://github.com/Ashish-1108/PRISM.

papers.title: SAND-CBM: Image-Side Basis Reconstruction for Concept Bottleneck Models
papers.abstract: Concept bottleneck models are only as useful as the concept space they expose. Existing concept-annotation-free CBMs often treat this space as text-pool retrieval: an image is explained by whichever prompt words score highly, so visual evidence that is fine-grained, compositional, or hard to name can be missed. We introduce SAND-CBM, which shifts the bottleneck from prompt retrieval to image-side basis reconstruction in a frozen vision–language space. Text-similarity channels are retained as named anchors, but they are complemented by learned visual-factor channels that can surface candidate evidence beyond the vocabulary. The core design is a signed–nonnegative–calibrated–shared (SNCS) representation contract: signed dictionary rows preserve CLIP-space directions, nonnegative activations give additive channel strengths, training-set calibration makes channels rankable, and a class-conditional selector reuses one shared dictionary across classes. SAND-CBM is concept-annotation-free rather than label-free: it uses no concept names, concept annotations, or concept-level targets for the learned image-side basis, while task labels train the final readout and an explicit low-bandwidth class gate. This design provides a more diagnostic interface: important channels should be removable, low-contribution or random removals should have weaker effects, discovered activations should align above null controls, and class gates should reuse rather than duplicate evidence. Across four visual benchmarks, SAND-CBM remains competitive in accuracy while showing a more concentrated and intervention-consistent concept-candidate interface than matched controls. Core code is available at https://github.com/LMBTough/SAND.

papers.title: Robust Chart Information Extraction via an LVLM Ensemble and Pairwise Reasoning
affiliations: TIB - Leibniz Information Centre for Science and Technology
Marburg University and Hessian Center for Artificial Intelligence (hessian.AI)
papers.abstract: Data visualizations are essential for communicating findings in scientific literature since they convey significant insights such as experimental results, trends, and distributions. However, due to the diverse nature of charts in real-world settings, automatic chart information extraction (CIE) remains challenging. Current state-of-the-art models demonstrate limited generalization across a variety of charts and benchmarks, performing adequately on basic chart types but failing to recognize complex visualizations, particularly when the characteristics (e.g., resolution, axis, complexity) differ from the datasets used to train them. To address these challenges, we make several contributions. (1) We propose an ensemble-based approach that aims to leverage the synergies of models trained for CIE and general-purpose large vision-language models (LVLMs). (2) We propose several inference strategies for our ensemble approach, including a multiple choice and two binary choice approaches based on league- and tournament-style inference to prevent excessive context length and positional bias of generative AI models. (3) For a fair comparison, we suggest a novel evaluation metric that resolves fundamental problems of existing metrics used for CIE task. (4) Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed ensemble approach can efficiently leverage synergies across various models achieving superior results and generalization across four benchmarks in comparison to the state of the art.

papers.title: R 2 -Net: Efficient Low-Light Image Enhancement via Dynamic Routing and High-Frequency Refinement
papers.abstract: Low-light image enhancement aims to recover images with clear details and natural colors from low-light observations. However, existing enhancement algorithms often struggle to simultaneously ensure global illumination consistency, preserve local high-frequency textures, and effectively increase brightness, which is prone to noise residue or detail loss. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel low-light image enhancement network named R 2 -Net. First, to overcome the limitations of traditional Transformers, such as their high computational complexity and difficulty in adaptively capturing long-range dependencies under low-SNR conditions—we introduce the Dynamic Routing Global Block (DRGB), which adopts a content-aware dynamic routing mechanism to perform sparse global contextual modeling. Second, to alleviate the local texture blurring problem commonly observed in deep enhancement networks, we design a High-Frequency Detail Residual Refinement (HDRR) module that accurately recovers edge and texture details by selectively enhancing high-frequency responses. Extensive experiments on several real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art algorithms in both objective metrics and subjective visual quality, exhibiting superior enhancement performance and generalization ability. With a moderate size of only 7.37M parameters, our model achieves a superior trade-off between restoration quality and model capacity. R 2 -Net also serves as a robust front-end enhancement module that restores semantically meaningful visual features, improving the resilience of multimedia retrieval systems under challenging illumination conditions. Code is available at https://github.com/jiaQi224/R2-Net.

papers.title: FortMem: Secure Stateful Data Management for Long-Term LLM Agent Memory
papers.abstract: Long-term LLM agent memory has become a critical state layer where records are written once and reused across sessions, turning prompt poisoning from a one-shot hazard into persistent database corruption. Traditional stateless RAG defenses reset per query and fail to evaluate the trustworthiness of persistent records over time. To address this, we present FortMem, a structurally robust memory layer, and PASTP (Provenance-Anchored Signed Trust Propagation), a zero-trainable-parameter trust score that formulates provenance as the teleport vector over a signed ANN–NLI corroboration graph. Theoretically, our Closed-Coalition and Open-Boundary Trust Caps prove that adversarial coalitions can inflate trust solely via their boundary fraction, a runtime-measurable structural channel. To counter advanced provenance spoofing, an enhanced variant (PASTP + ) automatically audits and demotes the priors of spoofed records contradicted by trusted neighbors. Extensive evaluations across three real-passage memory stores demonstrate that PASTP maintains resilient retrieval correctness under persistent poisoning, whereas vanilla dense retrieval degrades catastrophically. Furthermore, our boundary diagnostic accurately detects 96.3% of poisoned snapshots with zero false alarms, and downstream evaluations confirm that FortMem severely limits poisoned-answer adoption without compromising standard generative capabilities.

papers.title: SpecGuard: Source-Aware Heterogeneous Agent Placement for Defending LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems against Adversarial Communication
papers.abstract: Large Language Model based Multi-Agent Systems (LLM-MAS) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for solving complex tasks through collaboration among multiple agents. Nevertheless, this graph-structured communication inherently introduces a vulnerable attack surface, allowing adversarial instructions to propagate from compromised nodes across the entire system. Existing defenses often rely on runtime intervention or topology modification, which are often inapplicable to practical LLM-MAS deployments constrained by fixed communication structures, predefined roles, and execution protocols. A practical alternative is to selectively upgrade some agents to stronger model backbones before deployment. However, upgrading all agents to strong-tier models is costly, and the placement decision should be source-aware because adversarial content enters from specific attacker agents. To address this problem, we propose SpecGuard, a heterogeneous agent placement framework for fixed-topology LLM-MAS. SpecGuard upgrades a small set of weak agents before execution while preserving the original graph, agent set, and runtime protocol. Within SpecGuard, we design H-NetShield, a source-aware algorithm that estimates the exposure risk considering attacker locations, graph structure, deliberation horizon, and calibrated model susceptibility. It also incorporates a structural score to reduce redundant placements caused by overlapping protection. Empirical evaluations on CommonsenseQA across representative topologies demonstrate that upgrading just a single selected agent recovers 54.8%-90.3% of the defense benefit of an all-strong deployment. Moreover, H-NetShield further outperforms common graph-based baselines, and its exposure risk aligns well with empirical attack success rates.

papers.title: Revealing Hidden Vulnerabilities in Autoencoders via Gradient Signal Restoration
papers.abstract: Adversarial robustness of deep autoencoders (AEs) has received less attention than that of discriminative models, although their compressed latent representations induce ill-conditioned mappings that can amplify small input perturbations and destabilize reconstructions. Existing white-box attacks for AEs, which optimize norm-bounded adversarial perturbations to maximize reconstruction damage, often converge to suboptimal perturbations, thereby potentially overstating AE robustness. We show that this limitation is linked to vanishing adversarial loss gradients during backpropagation through ill-conditioned layers, associated with near-zero singular values in their intermediate weight matrices. To address this, we propose GRILL (Gradient Signal Restoration in Ill-Conditioned Layers), a framework designed to mitigate gradient degradation and improve the reliability of adversarial robustness evaluation in encoder--decoder architectures. GRILL is designed to mitigate adversarial gradient degradation during optimization, enabling attacks to better approximate high-distortion perturbations under fixed norm constraints.
