Through extensive experiments across multiple AE architectures, under both sample-specific and universal attacks, as well as standard and adaptive attack settings, we show that GRILL significantly increases attack effectiveness, thereby exposing vulnerabilities hidden by existing attack limitations. Beyond AEs, we provide preliminary evidence that modern multimodal encoder–decoder architectures exhibit similar vulnerabilities.

papers.title: SURF: Subtractive Updates for Recommender Forgetting
papers.abstract: The increasing demand for user privacy and compliance with regulations such as GDPR has made machine unlearning a fundamental requirement for modern recommender systems. However, Sequential Recommender Systems (SRS) pose unique challenges for unlearning due to their reliance on temporal interaction patterns. Existing approaches either require computationally prohibitive full retraining or fail to account for the sequential nature of user behavior. We propose SURF (Subtractive Updates for Recommender Forgetting), a lightweight framework for approximate machine unlearning in SRS. SURF operates in three stages: (i) identifying the neighborhood of the entity to forget via K-nearest neighbors in the embedding space, (ii) training an auxiliary model on this compact local subset, and (iii) subtracting the auxiliary model's scores from the original model at inference time. Experiments against five baselines on 7 datasets show that SURF achieves unlearning effectiveness comparable to full retraining while substantially reducing computational cost, yielding up to a 32% improvement in NDCG and requiring as little as 0.02x of the retraining time. We share our code at https://github.com/FilippoBetello/SURF .

papers.title: QD-RDFL: Resources-decoupled Collaborative Computation for Data Assetization
papers.abstract: Computation is increasingly collaborative: data, models, and computing resources are indispensable yet rarely co-located. As their demands grow, especially the computational requirements of modern large language models, it is increasingly impractical for any participant to simultaneously possess high-quality data, advanced models, and sufficient computing resources. In settings such as federated learning (FL), participants typically control only one component; for example, a hospital may own patient data but lack powerful models or large-scale computing resources. We refer to this emerging paradigm as resource-decoupled collaborative computation. A key challenge to its sustainability is fair reward attribution, as data, ubiquitous yet critical to model quality, becomes a valuable digital asset. We propose a Resource-Decoupled FL framework (RDFL) that enables data owners, model owners, and computing centers to jointly train high-quality global models while maximizing data assetization value. We introduce a Tripartite Stackelberg Model for global utility optimization under strategic interaction and develop QD-RDFL, a Quality-aware Dynamic Resource-Decoupled FL algorithm that quantifies data-quality contributions and allocates rewards accordingly. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our approach.

papers.title: FedCSN: Mitigating Skewed Feature via Class-wise Selective Normalization in Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables multiple distributed clients to collaboratively train a shared model without directly exchanging raw data. However, heterogeneous feature distributions across clients often lead to inconsistent local optimization and degraded model performance. Existing normalization-based augmentation methods attempt to alleviate this issue through cross-client statistic sharing. Nevertheless, most existing methods do not explicitly consider class consistency during normalization perturbation, where statistics from different classes may be indiscriminately applied to local samples. Through our investigation, we observe that class-consistent statistic sharing can improve model performance, while cross-class statistic perturbation may introduce noisy augmentation under heterogeneous edge environments. Motivated by these observations, we propose FedCSN, a lightweight normalization-based augmentation framework based on class-wise selective normalization for FL under feature distribution skew. Specifically, FedCSN constructs class-wise normalization statistics from local datasets and adopts an adaptive dominant-class statistic selection strategy to improve the reliability of uploaded class-wise statistics. During local training, each sample is augmented using normalization statistics associated with its class label, thereby reducing cross-class statistic mismatch. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedCSN achieves the highest dataset-level average accuracy among the evaluated methods across all three datasets using both AlexNet and ResNet18 under severe Non-IID settings. In particular, using AlexNet, FedCSN improves the average accuracy on Office-Caltech-10 by 6.12 percentage points compared with the state-of-the-art normalization-based augmentation method. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/MereIN0211/FedCSN.

papers.title: FedMCS: Federated Multi-Granularity Chemical-Semantic Distillation for Molecular Graph Learning
affiliations: School of Computer and Software Engineering, Southwest Petroleum University
National Key Laboratory of Oil and Gas Reservoir Geology and Exploitation, Southwest Petroleum University
papers.abstract: Federated molecular learning enables collaborative molecular property prediction across distributed institutions while keeping raw molecular graphs decentralized. However, most existing federated molecular methods transfer knowledge through shared parameters, whole-molecule representations, or label-dependent prototypes. This makes collaboration vulnerable to scaffold, domain, endpoint, and label-space heterogeneity. These coarse or task-bound signals struggle to capture chemical patterns that can be reused across clients while remaining consistent with each client's local prediction objective. To address these issues, we propose Federated Multi-granularity Chemical-Semantic Distillation (FedMCS), which builds a reusable substructure-level channel regularized by a fixed fingerprint prior. FedMCS summarizes client-side substructure embeddings as compact Gaussian prototypes, allowing recurring chemical motifs to serve as transferable carriers while raw molecular graphs and task heads remain local. A gate conditioned on a client-local task embedding selectively reuses refined global mean prototypes when the same fragment has different relevance across endpoints. On the server, Soft Chemical Distillation regularizes prototype relations with fingerprint-derived similarity, encouraging the shared prototype space to preserve a fingerprint-induced neighborhood structure. Experiments on eight MoleculeNet benchmarks show that FedMCS consistently outperforms federated baselines in intra-dataset scaffold non-IID settings and obtains the best weighted average among collaborative methods in the cross-dataset setting. These results support substructure prototypes as an effective transfer granularity for federated molecular learning.

papers.title: Attribution as Click: Understanding and Modeling Attribution Bias in RAG
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds LLM outputs in retrieved documents to address hallucination, but its retrieval-and-generation pipeline could still introduce various biases. Prior work studies biases such as social bias only in generated content while overlooking the bias present in the cited references, referred to as attribution bias. In this paper, we study gender-related attribution bias in RAG, addressing three questions: (i) with the ranking fixed, how do document position and gender shape citation decisions; (ii) in a realistic ranking setup with various irrelevant documents in the ranking, how does the gender composition of irrelevant documents influence attribution; and (iii) how are relevance, position, and gender associated with attribution after conditioning on the other measured factors? Across open-ended RAG experiments with four LLMs, document position strongly affects attribution, neutral documents partially absorb gendered citation preferences, and model-specific gender preferences persist after controlling for position and relevance. Attribution bias is therefore jointly shaped by retrieval and generator behavior. Our framework positions whom a RAG system cites as an axis of fairness alongside what it says.

papers.title: Adversarial Edge Generation: A Generator-Discriminator Game for Sparse Graph Learning
papers.abstract: Most existing graph learning methods are limited by the sparsity of the initial graph, which leads to biased node classification on the refined graph structure. Although adversarial training has shown strong performance in computer vision tasks, there is still no study that uses adversarial training to generate edges that approximate the true data distribution on a graph. In this work, we propose AEG (Adversarial Edge Generation), a generator-discriminator game framework for sparse graph learning. By incorporating high-confidence edges and hard negative edges into adversarial training, we perform edge adversarial generation on the sparse graph. This allows us to obtain a reliable refined graph that approximates the true data distribution, and then supports the following node classification. Moreover, to address the imbalance and sparsity issues in the refined graph, we introduce a new pseudo-label evaluation strategy in which edges between unlabeled nodes and labeled nodes are added to improve connectivity on the graph, based on their prediction confidence, neighborhood information and structural centrality. Experimental results show that AEG can effectively perform both edge generation and node classification, even on extremely sparse graphs.

papers.title: RAD: Rule-Augmented Relational Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Anomaly detection is often applied to relational databases, yet most existing methods require flattening multiple tables into a single feature matrix. This can obscure entity identity, schema structure, and multi-hop dependencies, limiting detection of anomalies that depend on relational context rather than isolated feature values. Relational anomaly detection also raises the challenge of incorporating symbolic behavioral evidence into learned relational representations. We propose RAD, a rule-augmented relational anomaly detector that combines heterogeneous graph representation learning with refined symbolic rule signals. RAD derives candidate rules from random-forest paths over flattened entity or event summaries, refines them into compact predicates, injects the resulting rule features into the graph model, and learns anomaly scores using reconstruction and pairwise-ranking supervision. We introduce a relational anomaly detection benchmark spanning three settings: LANL cybersecurity event detection and two unexpected user-churn tasks derived from Amazon and H&M relational databases. RAD improves anomaly ranking over flattened tabular detectors and relational baselines under natural class imbalance, achieving the best average rank on AUROC and AUPRC across the benchmark. Ablations show that direct rule injection and ranking-based supervision are key contributors to performance, while edge reconstruction is not uniformly beneficial. Code and data are available at https://github.com/noahd15/RAD_RelationalAnomalyDetection.

papers.title: Capturing Collaborative Structure in Graph Anomaly Detection by MoE-Gated Neural Common Neighbor
papers.abstract: In real-world graphs, anomalies usually exhibit collaborative structure, manifested as densely connected sub-graphs. Capturing multi-hop relationships is essential to identify and characterize the connections among these anomalous nodes. Existing graph anomaly detection (GAD) methods fail to capture such structures due to two core challenges: 1) standard recursive neighbor aggregation paradigm causes over-squashing of high-order neighbor information, which is vital for detecting collaborative suspicious behaviors; 2) different collaboration patterns depend on specific hop counts, with irrelevant hops introducing substantial noise. In this paper, we propose MoE-Gated Common Neighbor Attention (MCNA), an auxiliary parallel branch of the Graph Neural Network based (GNN-based) GAD backbones that can effectively distinguish collaborative structure to enhance the backbone's performance. MCNA explicitly encodes neural common neighbor information to capture the arbitrary k-hop collaborative structure among anomalies. To balance the information and noise from multi-hop neighbors, an MoE mechanism is employed to choose the valuable hops in terms of structural information. The structural collaborative patterns captured by MCNA and the attribute-based patterns captured by backbones are finally fused with a gating mechanism. Extensive experiments on 10 real-world datasets and 8 different backbones demonstrate that MCNA achieves average improvements of 5.36% on AUROC and 7.76% on AUPRC, showcasing the comprehensive universality of our proposed method.

papers.title: Sipu: Accurate Graph-based Positive-Unlabeled Learning under Heterophily
papers.abstract: How can we accurately train a binary node classifier on heterophilic graphs when only positive and unlabeled nodes are available? This setting commonly arises in real-world applications such as fraud detection, where only detected fraudsters are labeled as positive, while the remaining users are unlabeled and may include both normal users and undetected fraudsters. The key challenge is that heterophilic edges connect nodes from different classes, causing conventional graph-based PU methods to propagate label-inconsistent information. At the same time, simply suppressing such edges discards useful higher-order homophilic information connected through heterophilic paths. This creates a trade-off between reducing negative transfer and preserving structural information, which is further complicated by the absence of negative labels. We propose Sipu, an accurate graph-based PU learning method for heterophilic graphs. Sipu models the given unsigned graph as a latent signed graph, where positive and negative signs correspond to homophilic and heterophilic relations, respectively. Through sign-aware propagation, Sipu mitigates negative transfer from heterophilic neighbors while preserving higher-order homophilic information through positive paths. To accurately estimate unobserved edge signs, Sipu iteratively refines the classifier and the edge-sign estimates using node-label and edge-homophily marginals computed via graphical inference as soft targets. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that Sipu gives state-of-the-art performance, consistently outperforming existing graph-based PU learning methods.

papers.title: FEIM: Fair Event-Aware Influence Maximization Over Microblogs
affiliations: Shenzhen Institute for Advanced Study, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: Microblogs have become an important source for disaster resilience (DR). A typical problem for DR is to maximize the influence of event messages to effectively engage the maximal number of social users in disaster activities. Traditional Influence Maximization (IM) approaches focus on spreading a single message to activate as many users as possible, overlooking that users vary in event sensitivity and propagation capability. As a result, existing methods may overload highly influential users with irrelevant messages while failing to activate poorly connected ones. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes the Fair Event-aware IM (FEIM) problem and a new framework that coordinates message propagation in an event-sensitive and fair manner. We propose an event-aware social graph that captures each user’s activation probability across different events, and develop a Fair Ensemble Activation (FEA) model with seed selection and diffusion optimization algorithms to ensure equitable propagation. To further improve efficiency, we design a Dijkstra-like Fast Reachability Calculation (DFRC). Extensive tests prove the superiority of FEIM.

papers.title: LEAP: Learning Evolutionary Advantage Policies for Fixation Maximization via Deep Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Diffusion processes on networks are central to social network analysis and data mining, where influence maximization provides a canonical framework for identifying influential nodes. However, many real-world diffusion processes are competitive and reversible, making classical irreversible influence maximization models inadequate. The positional Moran process captures such dynamics by modeling stochastic competition with position-dependent fitness and motivates the fixation maximization problem: selecting an initial active set that maximizes the probability of eventual population-wide dominance. Existing methods rely on static structural heuristics or simulation-intensive greedy search. These approaches either ignore long-horizon evolutionary effects or scale poorly because they require repeated stochastic simulations. This limitation raises a fundamental question: Can we learn scalable active node selection policies that capture the evolutionary dynamics governing fixation? We answer this question with LEAP, a deep reinforcement learning framework for amortized fixation maximization under the positional Moran process. LEAP formulates active node selection as a Markov decision problem and learns fixation-aware representations that combine graph structure with mutant invasion and stability signals. Its fixation-modulated message passing mechanism models selection pressure through learned fitness contrasts, while fixation-weighted pooling constructs a global evolutionary representation. Experiments on real-world networks show that LEAP matches the solution quality of simulation-based greedy methods with approximately five orders of magnitude faster inference and outperforms all baselines in at least two-thirds of experimental settings. These results show that deep reinforcement learning can optimize long-horizon competitive diffusion when equipped with fixation-aware mechanisms that capture evolutionary dynamics.

papers.title: Aligning the Spectrum: Hybrid Graph Pre-training and Prompt Tuning across Homophily and Heterophily
affiliations: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.abstract: Graph “pre-training and prompt-tuning” aligns downstream tasks with pre-trained objectives to enable efficient knowledge transfer under limited supervision. However, current methods typically rely on single-filter backbones (e.g., low-pass), whereas real-world graphs exhibit inherent spectral diversity. Our theoretical Spectral Specificity principle reveals that effective knowledge transfer requires alignment between pre-trained spectral filters and the intrinsic spectrum of downstream graphs. This identifies two fundamental limitations: (1) Knowledge Bottleneck: single-filter models suffer from irreversible information loss by suppressing signals from other frequency bands (e.g., high-frequency); (2) Utilization Bottleneck: spectral mismatches between pre-trained filters and downstream spectra lead to significant underutilization of pre-trained knowledge. To bridge this gap, we propose HS-GPPT. We utilize a hybrid spectral backbone to construct an abundant knowledge basis. Crucially, we introduce Spectral-Aligned Prompt Tuning, which learns filter-specific prompt graphs to improve spectral alignment between downstream graphs and frozen pre-trained graph filters, facilitating knowledge transfer across both homophily and heterophily. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness under both transductive and inductive learning settings. Our code is in https://github.com/luohaitong/HS-GPPT.

papers.title: Molecular Knowledge Guided Prompt Adaptation for Pre-trained 2D Graph Encoders
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
University of Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: Pre-trained 2D graph encoders have achieved strong performance in molecular representation learning by capturing transferable topological patterns from large-scale unlabeled molecular graphs. However, downstream molecular applications often involve rich chemical and geometric information associated with atoms and bonds, which is not explicitly modeled by conventional 2D graph pre-training approaches. Existing molecular pre-training methods typically incorporate such knowledge during large-scale pre-training, requiring specialized architectures and substantial computational cost. In this paper, we investigate how to enhance pre-trained 2D graph encoders through lightweight downstream prompt adaptation with molecular knowledge. We propose a molecular prompting framework that integrates heterogeneous molecular information into downstream graph learning without modifying the pre-trained encoder parameters. Specifically, molecular knowledge is first projected into the latent space of pre-trained topological representations to reduce the discrepancy between topology and molecular semantics. Based on the aligned representations, we further employ knowledge-conditioned prompt generators to produce adaptive prompts for different molecular components, enabling fine-grained and instance-aware downstream adaptation. The proposed framework can be flexibly incorporated into existing 2D graph pre-training methods while maintaining strong parameter efficiency. Extensive experiments on molecular classification and molecular property prediction benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over representative graph pre-training and molecular representation learning baselines, particularly under low-resource settings.

papers.title: CausalExplainer: Causal Explanations for Temporal Graph Neural Networks
affiliations: RIADI Laboratory, National School of Computer Sciences, University of Manouba
SAMOVAR, Telecom SudParis, Institut Polytechnique de Paris
papers.abstract: Temporal Graph Neural Networks (TGNNs) have demonstrated remarkable performance in modeling complex dynamic interactions over evolving graphs. However, explaining their predictions remains highly challenging because asynchronous temporal dependencies often entangle causal signals with spurious patterns. We introduce CausalExplainer, a causally informed explanation framework that learns intervention-stable latent factors underlying TGNN predictions. Unlike methods that directly explain observed interactions, our approach trains a generative model to disentangle intervention-stable temporal representations from spurious variations. A multi-objective causal formulation promotes compact and faithful explanations by jointly enforcing predictive sufficiency, counterfactual necessity, and disentanglement. To further address biases arising from dynamic graph evolution, we model the confounding effects of temporal node attributes and interaction histories within a disentangled spurious latent space. We then introduce counterfactual perturbations in the learned latent causal space to encourage the identification of intervention-necessary explanatory factors and improve explanation robustness. CausalExplainer is model-agnostic, operates post-hoc on latent representations extracted from diverse TGNN architectures, and does not rely on input feature independence assumptions. Experiments conducted on real-world continuous-time dynamic graph benchmarks using TGN and TGAT demonstrate that CausalExplainer produces explanations that are more faithful and structurally cleaner than those produced by state-of-the-art baselines.

papers.title: CHARM-Mamba: Calibrated Hierarchical Adaptive Routing Multi-Source Mamba for Cross-City Traffic Prediction
papers.abstract: Cross-city transfer learning is pivotal for traffic prediction in data-scarce regions, yet impeded by structural limitations in existing frameworks. Conventional decoupled spatio-temporal modeling often struggles to fully capture the entangled, topology-dependent nature of congestion propagation. Moreover, indiscriminately aggregating heterogeneous source domains without granular pattern-specific filtering frequently induces negative transfer on incompatible data. Compounding these issues, full-parameter adaptation incurs prohibitive computational costs, severely hindering scalable few-shot deployment in dynamic real-world settings. To address these challenges, this paper proposes CHARM-Mamba, a Calibrated Hierarchical Adaptive Routing Multi-source transfer framework. First, the architecture integrates a Deep-Coupled Mamba backbone where State Space Models and dynamic spatial graphs mutually modulate to learn joint representations. Second, to mitigate negative transfer and support reliable knowledge reuse across heterogeneous sources, a routing mechanism on normalized feature spaces is introduced. By selectively retrieving compatible source prototypes via uncertainty-based calibration, it prioritizes transferable knowledge while discarding irrelevant noise. Third, to ensure parameter efficiency, a lightweight hypernetwork dynamically generates target-specific adapter parameters driven by routed patterns, facilitating pattern-aware adaptation with the backbone frozen. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CHARM-Mamba significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in few-shot generalization. Notably, it achieves up to a 5.7% reduction in Mean Absolute Error (MAE) while utilizing fewer than 5% of the trainable parameters, highlighting its potential for scalable, trustworthy knowledge modeling in dynamic urban environments. The code and datasets used in this paper are available at: https://github.com/JOJOJISHENGWU/CHARM-Mamba.

papers.title: CivicPulse: Efficient Hotspot Mining and Parsing in Municipal Hotline Data
papers.abstract: Municipal hotlines accumulate massive complaint narratives, yet effective governance requires more than closing individual tickets---it demands hierarchical event understanding: first surfacing recurring hotspots from complaint streams, then parsing each hotspot into actionable sub-events with distinct causes, scenarios, and citizen requests. Two challenges make this difficult. At the hotspot level, expression diversity and administrative ambiguity fragment evidence for the same civic issue, leaving conventional clustering with unstable boundaries. Within each hotspot, shared topical background overwhelms the representation space, masking the fine-grained distinctions needed for targeted intervention. We present CivicPulse, a two-stage framework that addresses both challenges. For hotspot mining, CivicPulse aggregates complementary semantic and administrative evidence to consolidate fragmented complaints into governance-aligned hotspots. For sub-event parsing, it suppresses hotspot-shared background and clusters the residual representations to expose cause- and intent-specific sub-events. On a real-world municipal hotline corpus, CivicPulse achieves a human-judged pairwise hotspot agreement of 0.7137, substantially outperforming density-based, graph-based, and taxonomy-matching baselines. Scenario-based evaluation with municipal hotline staff further confirms that its outputs are more interpretable and better support downstream dispatching and cross-department coordination.

papers.title: Quantifying Event Impacts on Time Series via Multiscale Contrastive Learning
papers.abstract: Shocks that spread through the web, such as cybersecurity breach disclosures, can abruptly disrupt financial time series and cause substantial abnormal losses. While these events are disclosed as discrete records through news reports, regulatory filings, or public databases, their consequences unfold through continuous market dynamics. This creates an event-conditioned impact prediction problem: given pre-event market history and limited event metadata, the goal is to estimate short-term post-disclosure abnormal loss rather than reconstruct the full post-event trajectory. However, most time-series forecasting models focus on endogenous regularities such as trend, seasonality, and autocorrelation, and thus struggle with rare and heterogeneous external events. The challenge is further amplified by sparse high-impact events and background market noise. We introduce EventTime, a multi-resolution framework that combines long-horizon market context, short-horizon pre-event dynamics, and event metadata. It incorporates an event fusion module that couples temporal representations with event attributes to identify relevant recent market patterns. To mitigate sparse supervision, EventTime further introduces a dynamic contrastive objective that constructs event- and time-series-aware positive and negative pairs during training. We also construct SECURE, a real-world dataset aligning cybersecurity incidents with stock-market time series and structured and LLM-derived semantic features. Experiments show that EventTime consistently outperforms state-of-the-art time-series and event-aware baselines in estimating post-event financial losses. Further analyses demonstrate more event-sensitive representations, greater robustness to incomplete metadata, and more interpretable estimates of short-term market impact following cybersecurity disclosures.

papers.title: Forecasting Functions, Not Points: Time Series Forecasting via Polynomial-Fourier Coefficient Prediction
papers.abstract: Environmental sensor signals, including meteorological, air-quality, and eco-hydrological measurements, are highly characterized by a slowly varying trend and a small number of low-frequency periodic components. In long-term forecasting benchmarks for these signals, the models that explicitly capture trend and seasonality have consistently achieved strong performance. However, in practical deployments, the dominant periods of environmental signals vary between regimes, which heavily forces a deployed forecaster to operate over a wide range of varying prediction horizons H. Standard point forecasting models, such as DLinear, PatchTST, and TimeMixer, tie the output projection weights directly to H. Consequently, any change in the horizon severely increases the decoder parameter count and requires complete, expensive retraining. To the best of our knowledge, no prior studies have proposed a flexible forecasting framework that eliminates this horizon-dependent structural rigidity. Therefore, we propose a novel functional forecasting framework called the Coefficient-prediction Network , which approaches long-term time-series forecasting by predicting the coefficients of a continuous function f(t) composed of polynomial and Fourier terms. The decomposition into trend and seasonality is explicitly encoded in the structure of f(t) itself, allowing the same trained coefficients to be evaluated on any arbitrary target grid without additional parameters or retraining. Since a pure polynomial-Fourier basis captures global trend and periodicity but may not capture the detailed local variations of signals, we further propose a per-sub-window low-rank modulation scheme. This adaptable scheme captures localized fluctuations by perturbing the shared coefficients at a minimal 4% parameter overhead. As a result, the Coefficient-prediction Network successfully achieves the coarse-to-fine prediction property without requiring post-hoc interpolation. Extensive experimental results on four datasets of real-world environmental sensors demonstrate that the proposed approach is robust against varying horizons, attaining state-of-the-art performance in 13 of 16 settings against nine baselines for standard point forecasting.

papers.title: PaDi: Patch-wise Decomposition and Latent Interaction for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Multivariate long-term time series forecasting aims to predict the future trajectories of multiple variables. However, many existing methods oversimplify temporal patches and channel interactions: they encode each raw patch as a single token and model channel relations directly in the original variable space. Such simplification leads to two limitations. At the patch level, raw-patch similarity can diverge from predictive-pattern similarity, since local state shifts may dominate the observed values, even when fluctuation patterns are similar. At the channel level, useful shared dynamics are often concentrated in compact latent structures rather than being uniformly distributed over all pairwise channel interactions. These two limitations reveal patch-level temporal heterogeneity and channel-level structural heterogeneity, suggesting that forecasting models should preserve such structures rather than force them into undifferentiated patch and channel tokens. To address these issues, we propose PaDi, a patch-based forecasting framework that captures such heterogeneity through patch-wise decomposition and latent interaction. Specifically, PaDi disentangles each input patch into base and deviation components and injects a compact base summary into future patch queries as temporal anchors, enabling stable coarse-grained cues to guide the reuse of deviation patterns. It further introduces Latent Channel Attention to exchange cross-variable information through learnable latent channel bases, thereby avoiding redundant dense channel mixing in the original variable space. Extensive experiments on seven public benchmarks under four prediction horizons demonstrate that PaDi achieves superior performance compared with several state-of-the-art baselines, highlighting its effectiveness and stability across diverse forecasting scenarios. The implementation of our model is available at: https://github.com/HYYAlex/PaDi.

papers.title: Dynamic Spectral Decoupling for Time-Series Forecasting
affiliations: Pohang University of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: While frequency-domain approaches have advanced time-series forecasting, many existing methods process spectral components through a unified pathway, despite substantial energy disparities across frequencies. High-energy components can dominate the learning process, making it difficult to capture weaker residual dynamics that may contain both predictable structure and stochastic fluctuations. To address this issue, we propose Dynamic Spectral Decoupling (DSD), a model-agnostic module that separates frequency components based on instance-wise energy concentration. DSD uses a Lorenz-curve-based adaptive mechanism to determine instance-wise separation boundaries, separates dominant components from the residual spectrum, and assigns the resulting components to separate prediction pathways. This design reduces interference between energy scales without assuming that all low-energy components are equally useful. Extensive experiments on five real-world datasets show that DSD improves the average performance of diverse forecasting backbones and outperforms existing model-agnostic methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/anthi7-google/DSD.

papers.title: Technology Forecasting through Data-Driven Analysis of Patents
papers.abstract: Forecasting technology lifecycle phases is a key enabler of data-driven innovation scouting, helping coaches and decision makers anticipate future technological developments and plan accordingly. Patent data offers structured, time-stamped records of innovation activity, making it a valuable basis for modeling and forecasting technology lifecycle trajectories. In this paper, we propose a systematic, domain-agnostic framework for technology forecasting using patent count time series from the European Patent Office (EPO). After identifying trends that are likely to capture a complete technology lifecycle, we derive a universal eight-phase lifecycle pattern within the retained EPO series. Based on this pattern, we annotate the trends and evaluate a two-stage pipeline combining neural time series forecasting with lifecycle phase classification. The evaluation yields three key results: (1) a Transformer-seq2seq classifier achieves F1-macro 0.785 on the eight-phase labeling task using only raw patent counts; (2) the top neural forecasters converge to within MAE 7.85 patents (57% below Prophet), relative to the median per-series peak; and (3) the best combined pipeline configuration (Transformer-Direct paired with LSTM-seq2seq) predicts lifecycle phase transitions with a mean year-delta of 1.8 years and a median of 0.650 years, without relying on any domain-specific features or patent text content.

papers.title: RNEC: Reference-Guided Neighborhood Evidence Calibration for Multivariate Time-Series Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Multivariate time-series anomaly detection commonly relies on reconstruction errors produced by autoencoders as anomaly scores. However, in real-world industrial systems, normal states are often heterogeneous: normal windows that are difficult to model may yield large reconstruction errors, whereas some anomalous windows can still be well reconstructed. As a result, raw reconstruction errors are not always directly comparable across different test windows. To address this issue, we propose RNEC, a post-training reference-guided neighborhood evidence calibration framework. Without modifying the parameters of a trained autoencoder, RNEC constructs a latent representation–reconstruction error reference field from training windows. During inference, it combines the relative reconstruction difficulty measured against latent neighbors with the degree to which a test window is covered by the training reference distribution, thereby producing calibrated anomaly evidence. Experiments on five public multivariate time-series anomaly detection benchmarks show that RNEC achieves the best macro-average F1, AUROC, and AUPR, with the best performance in 11 out of 15 dataset–metric combinations, while remaining lightweight and plug-and-play. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/RNEC-code/rnec.

papers.title: GT-PSSM: Unified Probabilistic Framework for Stochastic Dynamics Modeling and Dependency Learning in Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Multivariate time series anomaly detection (MTAD) is crucial for ensuring the safe and reliable operation of complex systems. Many existing methods learn normal patterns by training reconstruction or forecasting models on predominantly normal data. However, a large portion of these approaches rely on deterministic models and their associated point-wise output errors for anomaly scoring. Since real-world multivariate time series are inherently stochastic due to measurement noise and intrinsic system randomness, purely error-based scores can be unreliable, as large errors may arise from benign fluctuations rather than true anomalies. Probabilistic approaches address this limitation by quantifying uncertainty in model outputs. In particular, probabilistic state-space models (PSSMs) provide a principled framework by modeling stochastic system dynamics through latent state transitions and measurement noise via emission models. Despite this advantage, existing PSSM-based MTAD methods often struggle to capture long-range temporal dependencies and inter-variable dependencies, as they typically rely on noise-sensitive recurrent architectures and lack explicit cross-variable structure modeling. To address these limitations, we propose Graph-Transformer-Enhanced Probabilistic State-Space Model (GT-PSSM), a novel PSSM-based MTAD method that tightly integrates PSSM-based probabilistic modeling of stochastic dynamics with Graph Transformer-based learning of temporal and inter-variable dependencies. Specifically, GT-PSSM leverages temporal multi-head self-attention to capture long-range temporal dependencies and graph convolution over a learnable graph to explicitly model inter-variable dependencies, while retaining principled stochastic modeling of system dynamics and measurement noise. By jointly modeling stochasticity, long-range temporal dependence, and variable interactions within a unified probabilistic framework, GT-PSSM enables more robust anomaly detection. Extensive experiments on real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate that GT-PSSM achieves state-of-the-art performance.

papers.title: S2CSR: Self-Supervised Contrastive Learning for State Recognition in Multivariate Time Series
papers.abstract: The recent proliferation of sensors has enabled the collection of extensive time series data from cyber-physical systems. These time series can typically be segmented into distinct states, each carrying rich semantic information. For example, time series recorded during patient rehabilitation may represent sequences of activities such as standing, walking, and sitting. However, annotating these states remains both labor-intensive and costly. Although recent state-of-the-art recognition approaches utilize self-supervised learning to identify such states, many of them overlook informative frequency-domain characteristics, which are often crucial for distinguishing different states. As a result, these methods may fail to accurately identify state boundaries, particularly during periodic state transitions. In addition, existing methods often struggle to effectively capture inter-channel correlations and intra-channel temporal dependencies within multivariate time series. Furthermore, they are susceptible to false negative samples during contrastive learning, which can degrade the quality of learned representations. To address these limitations, we propose S2CSR, a cross-domain contrastive learning framework for multivariate time series state recognition. Specifically, S2CSR jointly performs representation learning and state discovery by introducing contrastive objectives at both the instance and temporal levels. Moreover, the framework encodes time series data in both the temporal and frequency domains, enabling the model to learn more robust and discriminative representations through cross-domain contrastive learning. To further improve representation quality, we design a false negative elimination mechanism to alleviate the adverse impact of incorrect negative samples during contrastive learning. Finally, a nonparametric clustering algorithm is employed to automatically discover latent states. Extensive experiments conducted on six benchmark datasets demonstrate that S2CSR consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both effectiveness and robustness.

papers.title: Streaming Semi-Supervised Adaptive Isolation Forest
papers.abstract: Anomaly detection in data streams is vital in areas such as network security, finance, and IoT, but it is hindered by the scarcity and cost of labels. We propose the Streaming Semi-Supervised Adaptive Isolation Forest (S 3 AIF), which extends the Adaptive Isolation Forest to partially labelled data, evolving streams by using discrimination power as a unifying principle to: (i) weight isolation trees when scoring; (ii) replace the least discriminative tree at each window; and (iii) select query instances for active learning by path-length disagreement. Across 22 benchmark datasets with a labelling budget below 1%, S 3 AIF outperforms HiLAD in both ROC-AUC and PR-AUC while running more than three times faster and ranks first against 10 unsupervised baselines in ROC-AUC. An ablation confirms that discrimination-power-based tree replacement is the main driver of S 3 AIF's performance.

papers.title: Resilient Deep Multi-View Clustering via Dual-Time-Scale Kernel Attention
affiliations: Xi'an University of Posts and Telecommunications
papers.abstract: Multi-view clustering aims to cluster data into different groups by leveraging both the consistency and complementarity across multiple views. Nevertheless, existing methods commonly face two primary limitations. First, cross-view information fusion often lacks fine-grained sample-level modeling, leading to semantic drift during feature alignment. Second, the dynamic optimization process suffers from inherent inertia, failing to correct accumulated errors stemming from infrequent pseudo-label updating during training. To address these problems, this paper proposes a novel framework named Resilient Deep Multi-View Clustering via Dual-Time-Scale Kernel Attention (DKAMVC). Specifically, we first adopt an autoencoder coupled with a capacity-adaptive MLP to extract latent representations. Then, the unified features obtained by connecting the latent representations are fed into a dual-time-scale model which integrates slow anchor updating with fast weight learning for resilient noise suppression. Next, these reinforced features are directed into a decoupled dual-pathway architecture, which utilizes a Local Kernel Attention (LKA) module to accurately quantify localized confidence. This design completely separates distribution modeling and weighting functions to establish fine-grained sample-to-target matching in the Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS). Finally, the multiply-augmented global features are clustered to yield the ultimate results. Experiments conducted on eight multi-view data sets demonstrate that the clustering performance of DKAMVC outperforms state-of-the-art comparison methods.

papers.title: Beyond Local Centers toward Prototypes: Joint Learning of Self-Representation and Adaptive Clustering
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose a prototype-learning framework that addresses a common limitation of proximity-based methods: the need to specify proximity weights in advance. Rather than relying on a fixed proximity matrix computed from raw observations, the proposed method jointly learns the prototype representation and the proximity structure. We implement this idea by extending the convex-clustering framework, replacing the pre-specified proximity input with a self-representation matrix learned from the prototype-level representation. The resulting adaptive proximity matrix captures intrinsic relationships among prototypes, yielding prototypes that better reflect the underlying data geometry rather than merely serving as cluster centers. We solve the resulting nonconvex optimization problem using an optimization algorithm based on multiaffine ADMM. Experiments on synthetic non-Euclidean datasets and real benchmark datasets show that the proposed method learns prototypes that better cover the underlying data geometry than standard convex clustering, while removing the need to manually specify proximity weights.

papers.title: GeoHIL: Geometry-Supervised Hierarchical Invariant Learning for Molecular OOD Generalization
affiliations: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
papers.abstract: Reliable molecular property prediction is fundamental to accelerating scientific discovery, yet Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) often fail to generalize when exploring new chemical spaces—a classic out-of-distribution (OOD) challenge. A popular line of research is graph invariant learning, which aims to extract environment-invariant rationales that remain stable across distribution shifts. However, existing graph invariant learning methods often rely on coarse environment partitions, which are insufficient to reflect continuous real-world shifts. Moreover, molecules are inherently 3D, and purely 2D graph-based invariant learning can extract formally invariant yet physically invalid rationales. To address these issues, inspired by 3D-enhanced graph pretraining, we propose GeoHIL, a geometric hierarchical invariant learning framework for molecular OOD generalization. GeoHIL introduces a hierarchical environment characterization, with global environments capturing dataset-level shifts and local environments capturing intra-molecular conformational variations. At the global level, GeoHIL adopts a stochastic-attention rationale learner to extract environment-robust 2D subgraphs. At the local level, we encode each conformer with a 3D encoder and aggregate the resulting representations. Then we propose geometry-supervised local invariance that uses the aggregated 3D representation as a training-time supervision signal to regularize 2D rationales to be conformation-consistent. This local invariance is instantiated with two variants: MC uses a Mahalanobis-distance consistency objective to match the conformation distribution, while vMF-C uses a von Mises--Fisher objective to enforce hyperspherical consistency. Additionally, we provide theoretical insights by interpreting the proposed local objectives as likelihood-based regularizers and providing quantitative stability insights for local invariance. Experiments on DrugOOD and GOOD-HIV show strong OOD performance, with particularly large gains in low-data settings over invariant-learning and 3D-enhanced baselines.

papers.title: Online Meta-Expert Learning
affiliations: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics
papers.abstract: Online meta-learning combines the strengths of online learning and meta-learning to handle continuously evolving task streams. It updates the model sequentially as new data arrive, while also learning transferable knowledge that enables rapid adaptation to newly emerging tasks. However, most online meta-learning methods require explicit task boundaries, which are often unavailable in real-world scenarios such as evolving illicit transaction detection or user preference prediction. Experiments show that when tasks are blurred by injecting 20% samples from adjacent tasks into each task, the test error of online meta-learning increases by about 25.3%. Existing approaches typically either use task boundary detection to guide updates or apply threshold-based parameter adaptation, but both are highly sensitive and not robust in non-stationary environments. We address this challenge by proposing an Online Meta-Expert Learning (OMEL) framework. OMEL dynamically maintains multi-timescale experts based on geometric covering (GC) intervals and adaptively updates their weights to reduce sensitivity to task variations, guiding a meta-learner toward robust online adaptation. Because explicit parameter-space aggregation is computationally expensive, OMEL uses prediction-space distillation to efficiently transfer knowledge from the expert ensemble to the meta-learner. OMEL attains sublinear strongly adaptive regret of Õ(√τ), where τ is the interval length. Experiments on image classification and transaction anomaly detection show state-of-the-art performance.

papers.title: Incorporating Rank Distributions into Uplift Modeling
papers.abstract: Uplift modeling estimates the individual treatment effect (ITE) by predicting the difference in outcomes between treated and control groups, enabling optimal targeting strategies in applications such as precision marketing and personalized medicine. Existing methods mainly focus on minimizing pointwise uplift errors yet fail to exploit the ranking information among samples fully. Studies in other areas have shown that ranking loss is helpful to learn more generalizable feature representations and mitigate overfitting on sparse data. Moreover, in many applications, the relative ranking often matters more than the absolute values. Thus, we propose RUM, a rank distribution-enhanced uplift modeling framework that jointly optimizes uplift estimation and ranking objectives. In the framework, we develop a full-ranking evaluation module with a SoftRank loss to enable end-to-end optimization of population-level ranking performance, which can be integrated with existing uplift models. We theoretically prove that minimizing the SoftRank loss provides a robust upper bound on ranking risk. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets show that models built upon our proposed framework consistently achieve superior performance over all benchmark models.

papers.title: A Game-Theoretic Spatio-Temporal Reinforcement Learning Framework for Collaborative Public Resource Allocation
affiliations: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
papers.abstract: Public resource allocation involves distributing resources, including urban infrastructure, energy, and transportation, which are typically limited in capacity, to meet social demands. In real-world scenarios, resources are typically limited in capacity, which makes coordination among multiple resources essential. However, existing methods often optimize resource movements in an isolated manner and do not explicitly account for capacity-aware collaboration under spatio-temporal dynamics. To address this limitation, we introduce the Collaborative Public Resource Allocation (CPRA) problem, and propose a Game-Theoretic Spatio- Temporal Reinforcement Learning (GSTRL) framework to solve it. Our contributions are twofold: 1) We formulate CPRA as a potential game and construct the potential function based on the objective function of CPRA, laying a theoretical foundation for approximating the Nash equilibrium of this NP-hard problem; and 2) Our GSTRL framework effectively captures the spatio-temporal dynamics of the overall system. We evaluate GSTRL on two real-world datasets, where experiments show its superior performance. Our source codes are available at https://github.com/thunderlrr/GSTRL.

papers.title: Special Orthogonal Hyper-Connections for Geometry-Preserving Deep Routing
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks increasingly suffer from progressive information geometry degeneration as network depth scales, manifested as gradient attenuation, representation collapse, and feature homogenization across layers. Existing connection mechanisms, including residual routing and manifold-constrained hyper-connections, primarily focus on numerical stabilization but fail to preserve the intrinsic geometric structure of feature propagation. To address this issue, we propose SOHC ( S pecial O rthogonal H yper- C onnections), a geometry-preserving routing framework that formulates inter-layer information propagation as exact manifold transformation on the special orthogonal group. Specifically, SOHC parameterizes routing matrices through the Cayley transform, ensuring analytically exact isometric propagation along the geometry-preserving routing stream throughout network depth. This exact orthogonal residual path preserves signal energy and spectral geometry along the isometric stream, providing a stable backbone for deep information propagation. Moreover, we design a gated dual-stream architecture that combines globally stable isometric propagation with locally adaptive semantic refinement, balancing structural stability and representation expressiveness. Extensive experiments on deep language modeling and sequential recommendation benchmarks demonstrate that SOHC consistently improves optimization stability, representation diversity, and downstream performance over existing hyper-connection methods. Further analyses show that SOHC effectively mitigates representation rank degeneration and preserves stable feature geometry throughout deep signal propagation, validating the importance of geometry-preserving routing for deep neural architectures.

papers.title: PERO: Efficient Robust Post-Training Foundation Models for Encrypted Traffic Classification
papers.abstract: Encrypted traffic classification is vital for network security, yet real-world deployments are inherently sensitive to rare but high-loss errors such as misclassification of malicious traffic. The encrypted traffic foundation model, as a promising general-purpose technique, can achieve impressive overall performance. However, employing standard objectives such as empirical risk minimization often overlooks high-risk tail events, and commonly used performance metrics hardly reflect robustness limitations in risk-sensitive scenarios. Directly applying robust optimization objectives, such as conditional value-at-risk, to post-training is computationally prohibitive for large models, as identifying high-loss samples exhausts substantial computation. To this end, we propose P re- E valuation R obust O ptimization ( PERO ), an efficient robust post-training framework for encrypted traffic foundation models. PERO employs a lightweight proxy to estimate sample-wise risk and selects a subset of high-risk samples to update the foundation model, decoupling risk estimation from expensive large-model optimization. Extensive experiments on typical encrypted traffic datasets show that PERO achieves competitive or superior robustness and average performance compared to outstanding robust post-training methods, while significantly reducing computational and memory costs.

papers.title: Multi-View Molecular Representation Learning with Hierarchical Graphs and Contextualized Fingerprints
papers.abstract: Molecular property prediction requires representations that generalize from limited labeled data to structurally novel compounds. Existing molecular pretraining methods often rely on a single view: graph-based approaches model atom-bond topology but provide limited fragment-level supervision, whereas fingerprint descriptors encode chemical patterns but are typically used as fixed auxiliary features. We propose HiFi-Mol , a multi-view framework that separately pretrains a hi erarchical graph encoder and a contextualized fi ngerprint encoder before downstream integration. The graph branch uses fragment-aware masking with multi-resolution supervision to capture substructure-aware representations, while the fingerprint branch tokenizes active entries from seven fingerprint families and applies masked language modeling to learn contextualized embeddings. During fine-tuning, HiFi-Mol combines projected multi-resolution graph features with fingerprint embeddings for downstream prediction. Evaluated on MoleculeNet benchmarks under the scaffold split, HiFi-Mol achieves a 2.77% improvement in average ROC-AUC over the best baseline across eight classification tasks while maintaining competitive performance on three regression tasks. Further analyses reveal that fragment-aware masking improves graph representation quality, and classification results demonstrate dataset-dependent strengths of the individual graph and fingerprint variants, confirming that the two views provide complementary predictive signals.

papers.title: Language Model-based Knowledge Tracing: A Comprehensive Study on Architectures, Domain Adaptation, and Cold Start Problem
papers.abstract: Knowledge Tracing (KT) models student learning from interaction histories. Recent work has begun applying large language models (LLMs) to KT through prompting, option weighting, and test-time reasoning, but the resulting AUC remains substantially below ID-based KT. We propose Language Model-based Knowledge Tracing (LKT), a PLM-agnostic supervised KT framework that reformulates each interaction as a natural-language sequence of concept text, question text, and a response token, allowing any encoder-based pre-trained language model (PLM), or any decoder LLM after LLM2Vec adaptation, to be fine-tuned end-to-end under a unified protocol. Across three datasets, LKT achieves the highest supervised AUC among Language Model-based KT methods on every dataset, outperforming LOKT and Thinking-KT (best 0.7105 and 0.7185 on DBE-KT22) and frontier LLM prompting baselines (AUC near 0.5 to 0.6). Among the LKT backbones, ModernBERT provides the most cross-dataset stable performance and is our recommended deployment default. Beyond benchmark performance, we analyze LKT's behavior with performance comparisons and explainable AI (XAI) techniques, including attention maps, LIME, and t-SNE visualization of the [MASK]-position embeddings, to characterize which textual cues drive predictions and how the learned representation encodes correctness. Our work contributes a PLM-agnostic and interpretable KT framework that future PLM advances can directly plug into.

papers.title: SynEHR: Joint Modeling Inter-visit Temporal Evolution and Intra-visit Clinical Structure for Longitudinal EHR Synthesis
papers.abstract: Longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) document patients' sequences of clinical visits over time, preserving the temporal evolution of disease progression and care delivery. However, real longitudinal EHRs are difficult to access because they contain large amounts of fine-grained, patient-specific information. Synthetic EHR generation therefore provides a valuable approach for preserving the statistical patterns and clinical structure of patient visit trajectories, enabling broader modeling and analysis when real records are limited. Although recent generative models have made progress in producing future visit sequences, they remain limited in explicitly integrating inter-visit irregular temporal evolution and intra-visit clinical event structures in EHRs, leading to clinically inconsistent and temporally unrealistic visit sequences. In this work, we propose SynEHR, a lightweight adaptive LLM-based framework for longitudinal EHR synthesis. There are two novel designs in SynEHR, i.e., a Temporal State Conditioning Module captures irregular temporal states across visits and a Temporal-Relational Adaptation Module combines these states with patient history to dynamically construct patient-specific relational representations. SynEHR then builds on a parameter-efficient LoRA-adapted language-model generator with next-visit generation capability to train the two modules for temporally and clinically informed generation. Extensive experiments on real-world EHR datasets across fidelity, privacy, and downstream utility evaluations demonstrate that SynEHR outperforms state-of-the-art models by generating more clinically coherent and temporally faithful longitudinal EHR data.

papers.title: Performance-Adaptive Instruction-Template Assignment for Clinical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Instruction-tuning corpora are commonly constructed by pairing fixed input–output examples with static or randomly sampled instruction templates. However, for clinical reasoning, different candidate instruction templates may emphasize different learning signals, including diagnostic conclusion, evidence synthesis, and explanation structure. This paper studies instruction-template assignment as a training-time corpus-construction problem: given fixed clinical input–output examples and a pool of candidate templates, can performance feedback guide template assignment during fine-tuning? This paper presents Performance-Adaptive Instruction-Template Assignment (PAITA), a framework that uses validation feedback to assign instruction templates to fixed clinical input–output examples during fine-tuning. Unlike static assignment, which repeatedly applies one template, or random assignment, which samples templates without regard to observed performance, PAITA balances exploration of alternative templates with exploitation of templates associated with stronger validation feedback. We evaluate PAITA primarily using LLaMA-3-8B and further examine instruction-template assignment across additional model settings using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and BioMedLM-2.7B on the Clinical Reasoning task; Clinical Diagnosis and Medical QA serve as auxiliary evaluations. PAITA improves clinical reasoning conclusion accuracy over static assignment (0.397 vs. 0.372; +2.5 percentage points, p=0.001) and random template assignment (0.397 vs. 0.383; +1.4 percentage points, p=0.044), with additional gains in several reasoning-quality metrics. Auxiliary results and template-assignment analyses further suggest that performance-adaptive assignment can provide benefits beyond instruction diversity alone. These findings support instruction-template assignment as an important design variable in supervised instruction tuning of clinical LLMs.

papers.title: PHASE: A Modular LLM Pipeline for On-Premise Phenotype Profile Extraction from Clinical Referral Reports
papers.abstract: The automated extraction of structured phenotypic profiles from clinical narratives is a critical step in genetic diagnosis, but it is hindered by the unstructured nature of medical reports, the contextual complexity of clinical language, and strict privacy requirements that forbid sending clinical data to external services. We present PHASE, a modular pipeline for the extraction of phenotypic profiles from clinical referral reports, designed to work under on-premise deployment constraints. Instead of using a single Large Language Model (LLM) monolithically, PHASE decomposes the task across specialized modules that interleave generative reasoning with explicit ontological alignment: a high-recall semantic extractor, a hybrid ontological aligner against the Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO), a generative concept normalizer, and an ontology-grounded validator. The resulting phenotypic profile consists of records that link each phenotype to its HPO concept, identify its subject (proband or family member) and assertion status (confirmed, negated, or suspected), and provide a natural-language rationale supporting the prediction. We further propose an ontology-aware evaluation metric that complements strict identifier matching with bounded partial credit based on HPO topology. We evaluate PHASE on a public dataset of clinical case reports, against five state-of-the-art systems, and show consistent improvements in precision, recall, and F1 score under both exact-match and ontology-aware metrics, while operating exclusively on quantized LLMs deployable on a single workstation GPU. An ablation study quantifies the antagonistic and complementary contributions of generative normalization (recall amplifier) and ontology-grounded validation (precision filter), with consistent qualitative behavior across two open-weight LLMs.

papers.title: Data-Driven Near-Optimal Regional Epidemic Surveillance
papers.abstract: In the early stages of an epidemic outbreak, when the incidence data is limited, policy makers actively try to establish the scale and scope of the outbreak. Two of the most pertinent questions they seek to answer are i) has the outbreak started in a particular region (e.g. a country) and ii) how many sub-regions (e.g. a state or a county) have been affected thus far? We study these problems as a data-driven knowledge extraction task, i.e., given mobility and epidemiological data, we aim to extract actionable knowledge about which regions should receive additional surveillance resources so that an outbreak is detected early and its spatial footprint is accurately characterized. To this end, we formulate two discrete-lattice optimization objectives for epidemic surveillance, 1) maximizing the probability of detecting at least one infected sub-region and 2) maximizing the expected number of infected sub-regions detected. Both objectives turn out to be NP-hard. However, we prove that they are both submodular, which paves the way for efficient epidemic surveillance from limited data. We use this structure to derive curvature bounds for the objective. We also relate the bound with the parameters of the metapopulation disease dynamics. We propose a scalable algorithm, Lattice-Adapted Modified Greedy (LAMGreedy), that uses the curvature, and marginal-gain machinery to establish constant factor approximation guarantee. Extensive experiments on real-world mobility networks for COVID-19 and Influenza across three U.S. states show that LAMGreedy consistently outperforms natural and the state-of-the-art baselines under multiple cost models. The empirical results validate the prevalence and curvature estimates, and demonstrate that the proposed tools extract high-quality surveillance knowledge from mobility and epidemic data under realistic budget constraints.

papers.title: STMoE: Multi-Scale Mixture-of-Experts for Single-Cell Gene Expression Prediction from Histology
papers.abstract: Predicting single-cell molecular state from routine histology could make spatial profiling more scalable, but existing histology-to- expression methods are mostly limited to spot-level targets, re- stricted gene panels, or organ-specific settings. This leaves three gaps for practical single-cell deployment: a lack of large aligned- cell resources, limited support for direct multi-organ prediction, and incomplete full-gene expression recovery from whole-slide images. We address these gaps by curating CellST-24M, a 23.94M- cell histology–transcriptomics resource spanning 66 studies, 25 organ categories, Visium HD, and Xenium, and by introducing STMoE, a WSI-only organ-routed prediction framework for full- gene single-cell expression inference. STMoE detects cells from H&E slides, encodes cell-centered and tissue-context crops with a frozen UNI2-h pathology foundation model, aligns image and expression embeddings with soft contrastive learning, and predicts full-gene profiles through organ-routed retrieval from training-only reference banks. On matched human lung benchmarks, STMoE achieves state-of-the-art cell-level performance, outperforming cell- adapted BLEEP, sCellST and GHIST under both in-domain and cross-patient settings. Across 22 organs, STMoE supports direct multi-organ prediction and achieves gene-wise Pearson up to 0.6451 and cell-wise Pearson up to 0.8379, while retaining approximately 60% predictive capability under cross-patient transfer. In down- stream marker-derived analysis, predicted profiles recover coarse cell-state structure with 0.5935 accuracy and 0.5922 balanced accu- racy. Together, CellST-24M and STMoE establish a benchmark and modeling framework for WSI-only, multi-organ, full-gene single- cell histology-to-expression prediction.

papers.title: Recommender System as Slow and Fast Thinkers
affiliations: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
University of Science and Technology of China
GAIR-Lab - School of Computing Science, University of Glasgow
papers.abstract: Sequential recommendation models are foundational to modern personalized services, yet their effectiveness varies substantially across heterogeneous user environments. In particular, static one-pass recommenders often perform well on common behavior patterns but degrade on operationally challenging user groups, such as users with longer histories or less mainstream item profiles. To address this limitation, we propose DS-Frame, an adaptive fast–slow inference framework for sequential recommendation. DS-Frame combines a Fast System for efficient routine prediction, a Slow System for iterative latent refinement, and a learned selector that routes each sample under a controllable computation budget. Experiments on five real-world datasets show that DS-Frame consistently improves representative sequential recommendation backbones, with larger gains on challenging groups and effective accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. This highlights the potential of adaptive inference for more efficient and robust recommendation. Code is available at https://github.com/ZichenYuan233/Recommender-System-as-Slow-and-Fast-Thinkers

papers.title: From Overlooked to Explored: Recovering Item Relations via Mixture of Perspectives for Sequential Recommendation
affiliations: Pohang University of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Capturing user preference from a user's interaction sequence is the central challenge of Sequential Recommendation (SR). This preference intuitively emerges from inter-item relations: each item transition reflects a preference embedded in the relations between items, making the faithful capture of these relations essential for accurate recommendation. For this reason, self-attention is dominant in sequential recommendation for its ability to compute pairwise item interactions, yet our empirical analysis reveals that it consistently suffers from similarity bias across various types of transformer-based SR models: dot-product attention scores disproportionately favor similar items, systematically overlooking heterogeneous relations with meaningful preference signals and directly limiting recommendation performance. To address this, we propose PRISM ( P erspective-based R elational I nsight S ynthesis M odule), a module that re-examines item relations from multiple perspectives. PRISM employs K Perspective Lenses to calibrate attention from distinct viewpoints, combining an Affinity View that refines homogeneous relations and a Contrast View that exposes heterogeneous ones suppressed by similarity bias, enabling the model to capture the full spectrum of user preferences. Extensive experiments on seven real-world benchmarks demonstrate that PRISM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/327aem/PRISM/.

papers.title: PRISM: Pruning-Enhanced Intent Sampling for Recommendation Multi-List Generation
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation has emerged as a prominent paradigm, unifying retrieval and ranking through large-scale sequence transducers. However, existing generative recommenders are basically pointwise: they optimize for next-item prediction, leaving the construction of the final exposure list—a slate—to heuristic post-processing. This creates a structural gap between pointwise candidate generation and industrial listwise delivery, which demands holistic reasoning over contextual opportunity, position bias, and intent uncertainty. To bridge this gap, we introduce List Composer , a decoupled module that transforms pointwise candidate pools into deliverable exposure lists within generative recommender systems. We instantiate this concept through PRISM , an autoregressive listwise generation model featuring two core mechanisms. First, a CVAE-based IntentSampler module models user interests as a latent distribution, sampling distinct intent facets as initial states averts the Deterministic Collapse phenomenon, wherein standard autoregressive generators converge onto nearly identical sequences despite repeated decoding. Second, a Listwise Pruning strategy dynamically culls low-utility beam paths using position-discounted pointwise scores, concentrating computational resources on promising trajectories. Extensive offline experiments and real-world online A/B tests validate the effectiveness of PRISM, which achieves consistent improvements in recommendation quality and serving efficiency, including a 0.288% gain in video views on a major short-video platform.

papers.title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
affiliations: Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Cross-domain sequential recommendation aims to improve next-item prediction in a target domain by leveraging user behavior from auxiliary source domains. However, real-world deployment faces two critical challenges: business constraints that isolate interaction data across domains, and user heterogeneity, where many users lack cross-domain activity. This makes existing cross-domain methods difficult to apply. In this paper, we propose a simple and practical framework for cross-domain sequential recommendations that transfers information exclusively through learned user representations, without sharing raw interaction data or item embeddings across domains. We introduce a lightweight adapter that projects the source-domain user representation into the target-domain embedding space and integrates it with the target interaction sequence. Importantly, when source data is unavailable (i.e., the user observed only in the target domain), the model seamlessly defaults to a robust target-only sequential recommender, retaining benefits from joint training across all users. Extensive experiments were conducted under two setups; one targets benchmarking against previous baselines, while the other focuses on realistic and scalable conditions. Both sets of experiments demonstrate consistent performance gains for shared and unshared users.

papers.title: ClusterRec: Cluster-Aware Recommendation with Large Language Models for Efficient and Scalable Inference
affiliations: School of Big Data and Software Engineering, Chongqing University
Department of Electronic Engineering, Tsinghua University
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have significantly improved recommender systems by enabling richer semantic modeling of user preferences. However, existing LLM-based recommenders typically require expensive per-user inference over long interaction sequences, causing computational costs to scale rapidly with both model size and the number of users. To address this challenge, we propose ClusterRec, a framework that decouples LLM-based recommendation into two stages: (1) group-level preference modeling and (2) user-level personalization. Specifically, users are first clustered based on behavioral representations, and LLMs are employed to construct a group-level semantic representation for each cluster. Individual user representations are then constructed by integrating shared group representations with personalized collaborative filtering embeddings. This design amortizes LLM inference at the group level, substantially reducing computational overhead while preserving personalization. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate that ClusterRec achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods, including conventional CF-SRec (e.g., SASRec) and recent LLM-based recommenders, while significantly reducing LLM inference cost. These results highlight that group-level semantic modeling provides an effective and scalable paradigm for integrating LLMs into practical recommender systems. The code is available at https://github.com/tsinghua-fib-lab/ClusterRec.

papers.title: Semantic-Structural Cross-Calibration for Multi-Behavior Recommendation
papers.abstract: Multi-behavior recommendation (MBR) alleviates target behavior sparsity by leveraging abundant auxiliary behaviors. However, most MBR methods are trapped in a dilemma. Separately aggregating multiple behaviors struggles to fully exploit cross-behavior interaction information, while collectively aggregating different behaviors into a unified graph may cause the target behavior to be submerged among massive auxiliary behaviors. To this end, we propose the Semantic-struCtural crOss-calibRation modEl (SCORE), a structure-conditioned calibration framework for MBR. SCORE adopts a decouple–enhance–calibrate strategy to fully exploit cross-behavior interactions while robustly reconstructing target-related user representations. Specifically, SCORE first decouples target semantics from unified representations through a shared modulation space under joint multi-behavior supervision. It then enhances unified representations through structural refinement on the target-behavior graph, reconstructing target-consistent structural context. Finally, SCORE reconciles semantic and structural references through structure-conditioned gating to obtain calibrated representations. Extensive experiments on three real-world benchmarks demonstrate that SCORE greatly improves over thirteen competitive baselines by up to 61.73% on HR@10 and 46.04% on NDCG@10.

papers.title: BUGLE: Balanced Fusion with Graph Modality Experts for Multimodal Recommendation
papers.abstract: Multimodal recommendation effectively alleviates the data sparsity by integrating historical interaction behaviors with multimedia content (e.g., image, text).
