However, fusing these heterogeneous modalities faces two critical balance dilemmas: (1) Modality Knowledge Balance: Overemphasizing modality shared knowledge leads to homogeneous modality representations, while overemphasizing modality unique knowledge creates semantic gaps between modalities and deviates from the recommendation objective. (2) Modality Allocation Balance: Dominant modalities are often overestimated, resulting in modality bias; conversely, suppressing them may overlook their contributions to user preferences, causing excessive balance. To address these issues, we propose a novel B alanced f U sion with G raph moda L ity E xperts for multimodal recommendation ( BUGLE ). Firstly, inspired by the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) mechanism, we design independent graph expert subnetworks for each modality to perform disentangled modeling over a shared interaction graph structure. We further introduce preference-disentangled contrastive learning to align modality representations and interaction supervision signals in the semantic spaces of each modality to enhance modality discriminability, thereby achieving a balanced utilization of both shared and unique modality knowledge. Additionally, we propose a dual-task routing balanced mechanism that combines expert routing entropy loss with result-guided loss. This mechanism ensures equitable modality allocation during fusion while highlighting the dominant contributing modalities. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that BUGLE significantly outperforms various state-of-the-art methods. Our code is available at: https://github.com/GarethJellingham/BUGLE.

papers.title: Generative Multimodal Intent Modeling with Adaptive Integration for Recommendation
papers.abstract: Multimodal recommender systems have attracted increasing attention for their potential to enhance recommendation performance by leveraging textual and visual item information. However, existing approaches often treat multimodal signals as auxiliary features for item-level discrimination, overlooking two intrinsic characteristics of real-world multimodal data: 1) noise and uneven informativeness across modalities and items, and 2) fine-grained intent-related semantics embedded in multimodal representations. In this paper, we propose GEMIA, a Generative Multimodal Intent modeling framework with Adaptive integration for recommendation, which infers target-side multimodal semantic representations related to user preferences which explicitly models intent-related multimodal semantics while adaptively integrating heterogeneous modality signals. GEMIA consists of two key components: a Multimodal Semantic Inference (MSI) module that adopts a generative representation-inference approach to generate the next item’s text and image representations in a continuous multimodal semantic space, enabling the model to capture fine-grained intent-related information; and an Adaptive Multimodal Fusion (AMF) module that integrates multimodal representations via item-specific gating, accounting for item-dependent modality noise and uneven informativeness. Furthermore, GEMIA aggregates item-, text-, and image-based scores using item-wise weighting to flexibly adjust reliance on multimodal and item-level information. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate that GEMIA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, with more pronounced improvements in long-tail scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/kCMI113/GEMIA.

papers.title: Beyond Spatio-Temporal: Frequency-Gated Hypergraphs for Next-POI Recommendation
papers.abstract: Next Point-of-Interest (POI) recommendation aims to predict a user's subsequent location from historical trajectories. The task is challenging because user mobility is shaped by short-term intentions, long-term preferences, calendar effects, and structured spatial relations. Existing methods have improved sequential modeling and representation robustness, but they often treat temporal, spatial, and semantic contexts as loosely coupled signals and provide limited control over frequency-domain mobility patterns. To address these limitations, we propose ST-HFCR (Spatio-Temporal Hypergraph-enhanced Frequency-domain Contrastive Recommendation). ST-HFCR first constructs a multi-type hypergraph with time-slot, spatial-proximity, calendar-aware, and user-personalized hyperedges to model both macro-level contexts and individual preferences. It then introduces a gated frequency fusion module, GatedKAN, which learns separate gates for real and imaginary spectral components to balance amplitude- and phase-related information. Finally, ST-HFCR uses multi-level contrastive learning to align node- and graph-level representations under semantic-aware perturbations. Experiments on three real-world datasets show that ST-HFCR achieves consistent gains over competitive baselines in both HR and NDCG, suggesting that structured spatio-temporal hypergraphs and frequency-aware gated fusion provide complementary signals for next-POI recommendation. The code is available at https://github.com/MyCode12-maker/STHGCN/.

papers.title: Popularity-Aware Complementary Preference Distillation for Diffusion Recommendation
affiliations: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: Diffusion recommender models have shown promising results by reconstructing user preference signals through denoising. Since user-item interactions typically follow a long-tailed distribution, the denoising process tends to favor signals from popular items with high-frequency interactions. This makes recommendation results overly concentrated on popular items and limits the exposure of long-tail items. Directly suppressing popular items may increase tail exposure, but it can weaken useful collaborative signals and degrade overall accuracy. To address this limitation, we propose P opularity-Aware C omplementary P reference D istillation ( PCPD ), a diffusion-based recommendation method that mitigates popularity bias in the denoising process. Instead of simply suppressing popular items, PCPD incorporates mainstream collaborative signals and sparse long-tail preference signals as complementary supervision. Specifically, PCPD preserves mainstream collaborative preferences, calibrates the recovery of tail-item preferences, and distills the resulting complementary supervision into a unified diffusion recommender. At inference time, PCPD relies only on the distilled student model, without requiring auxiliary branches or online score fusion. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets show that PCPD consistently improves long-tail recommendation performance and alleviates item-side exposure imbalance while maintaining competitive overall recommendation accuracy.

papers.title: One Size, Many Fits: Aligning Diverse Group-Wise Click Preferences in Large-Scale Advertising Image Generation
papers.abstract: Advertising image generation has increasingly focused on online metrics like Click-Through Rate (CTR), yet existing approaches adopt a “one-size-fits-all” strategy that optimizes for overall CTR while neglecting preference diversity among user groups. This leads to suboptimal performance for specific groups, failing to satisfy group-wise visual preferences. To bridge this gap, we present One Size, Many Fits (OSMF), a unified framework that aligns diverse group-wise click preferences in large-scale advertising image generation. OSMF begins with product-aware adaptive grouping, which dynamically organizes users based on their attributes and product characteristics, representing each group with rich collective preference features. Building on these groups, preference-conditioned image generation employs a Group-aware Multimodal Large Language Model (G-MLLM) to generate tailored images for each group. The G-MLLM is pre-trained to simultaneously comprehend group features and generate advertising images. Subsequently, we fine-tune the G-MLLM using our proposed Group-DPO for group-wise preference alignment, which effectively enhances each group's CTR on the generated images. To further advance this field, we introduce the Grouped Advertising Image Preference Dataset (GAIP), the first large-scale public dataset of group-wise image preferences, including around 600K groups built from 40M users. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework achieves the state-of-the-art performance in both offline and online settings. Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/JD-GenX/OSMF.

papers.title: An Automated Multi-Agent Search-then-Evolution Framework for Lifetime Value Prediction
papers.abstract: Lifetime value (LTV) prediction is a key component of decision-making in online advertising, e-commerce, and recommender systems. In practice, however, LTV modeling is scenario-dependent because data distributions differ across applications. Practitioners often rely on scenario-specific pipelines with repeated feature engineering, objective adjustment, and tuning. These workflows require manual effort and are hard to transfer. We propose AgentLTV, an automated multi-agent search-then-evolution framework for lifetime value prediction. AgentLTV treats each candidate solution as an executable pipeline program. LLM-driven agents generate code, run and repair pipelines, and analyze execution feedback. Two decision agents coordinate a two-stage search. The Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) stage explores a broad space of modeling choices under a fixed budget, guided by the Polynomial Upper Confidence bounds for Trees criterion and a Pareto-aware multi-metric value function. The Evolutionary Algorithm (EA) stage refines the best MCTS program via island-based evolution with crossover, mutation, and migration. Experiments on a large-scale proprietary dataset and a public benchmark show that AgentLTV consistently discovers strong models across ranking and error metrics. Online bucket-level analysis further indicates improved ranking consistency and value calibration, especially for high-value and negative-LTV segments. We summarize practitioner-oriented takeaways: use MCTS for rapid adaptation to new data patterns, use EA for stable refinement, and validate deployment readiness with bucket-level ranking and calibration diagnostics. The proposed AgentLTV has been successfully deployed online. Details of our optimal model and prompts are available at https://github.com/wuchaowei123/AgentLTV.

papers.title: Cold-Start Constrained Autobidding via Implied-Dual Calibration
papers.abstract: When a new ad enters an existing auction market, an autobidding system must choose its first constrained bid before observing feedback from that ad. We study this cold-start decision under budget and CPC-style constraints. The standard warm start is to reuse a historical constrained policy, which is strong under stationarity although sensitive to shifted prices or response curves. Instead of replaying the full historical optimum, we propose implied-dual variable calibration (IDVC), which learns an admissible, low-dimensional implied-dual surface from historical contexts. For CPC constraints, the reusable margin is m=s(z)v+α(z)Cμ, where s(z)>0, α(z)∈[0,1], v=CTR·CVR, and μ=CTR. SPA/VCG auctions can bid this margin directly, and first-price/hybrid auctions require a supported map from margin to bid. We prove that calibration and bid-map error control first-period bid, reward, and constraint error under local support. On the public BAT dataset, we report benchmark-target calibration; in BAT-shaped semi-synthetic known-transform studies with validated bid maps, guarded IDVC improves early constrained bidding relative to historical reuse.

papers.title: CASTLE: Contrastive and Seed-Guided Training for Cold-Start Natural Language Search
papers.abstract: Deploying natural language search systems presents a critical cold-start challenge: no real user queries to learn linguistic patterns, and no relevance labels to train ranking models. We present CASTLE (Contrastive And Seed-guided Training for natural Language sEarch), an LLM-based framework for generating synthetic queries and relevance labels from structured catalog data, powering Airbnb's natural language search across its full lifecycle. CASTLE makes three contributions. First, we generate realistic queries by combining structure-guided prompting with seed queries from user research, using template, few-shot, and attribute-grounded prompt variants together with explicit variety mechanisms to prevent query collapse. Second, we produce relevance labels by construction via contrastive listing pairs derived from booking sessions---achieving near-zero false positives without LLM judgment. Third, CASTLE's structured input design is flexible: incorporating richer signals---such as guest reviews and photo captions---alongside listing attributes enables generation of niche, long-tail queries that reflect subjective user preferences (e.g. "cozy cabin with fireplace") beyond what catalog attributes alone can express. Compared against InPars-style, Promptagator, and contrastive-only baselines, CASTLE achieves KL 1.01 vs. real users---a 9.2× improvement over the best baseline (9.33)---and the lowest attribute-type KL divergence (0.08), outperforming even survey seed queries (0.09). A human evaluation on 200 sampled triplets confirms label quality: annotators agree with CASTLE labels at 91--93%. We deploy production pipelines generating synthetic examples daily for embedding-based retrieval and ranking evaluation. Synthetic data remains valuable beyond cold-start: it targets tail queries underrepresented in organic traffic and extends naturally to multi-turn conversational search.

papers.title: Effective Re-Ranking with DIMEs using Few Noisy LLM-Generated Relevance Judgments
papers.abstract: State-of-the-art Information Retrieval (IR) pipelines often rely on dense neural models to index and retrieve large document collections. After an initial retrieval stage, precision-oriented re-ranking approaches can further refine the ranked list. However, re-ranking quality strongly depends on the availability of reliable relevance signals. Recent work has explored the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) to automatically generate relevance judgments that can serve as such signals. However, achieving strong alignment with human gold labels generally requires either very large and complex LLMs or extensive human supervision. In this work, we investigate whether relatively small LLMs, despite producing limited and often noisy relevance assessments, can still be leveraged to improve the ranking of documents retrieved by dense bi-encoder models. Specifically, we introduce new approaches based on the recently proposed Dimension IMportance Estimators (DIMEs), incorporating LLM-generated relevance judgments into the re-ranking process. Our study assumes a practical setting: we consider access only to relatively small LLMs and to very small sets of relevance judgments generated for the top-retrieved documents of each query by dense retrieval models, and we investigate how to leverage these sparse, often noisy signals to refine the ranking of the entire retrieved set. Our method leads to substantial improvements in document ranking, boosting nDCG@10 and AP by up to 9% and 15%, respectively, across different datasets, LLMs, and bi-encoder backbone retrieval models. These results show that even a few noisy relevance judgments from small LLMs can provide a powerful signal to improve the effectiveness of IR systems.

papers.title: Tree-Compatible Personalized Ranking via Linear Latent-Trait Decomposition
papers.abstract: Learning-to-rank systems often use a global scorer despite systematic variation in user preferences. We propose a model-agnostic latent-trait framework for probabilistic ranking objectives. A low-dimensional profile activates shared ranking directions linearly, enabling tractable profile inference with nonlinear document-feature effects. Our iterative route encodes all traits as G profile features in one ranker rather than learning or serving G factor models. Ranker fitting reuses an unmodified standard LTR package, and serving uses one model. An offline module probes the ranker to construct an additive surrogate for profile updates across neural and tree rankers. To our knowledge, this is the first continuous user-specific latent personalization under a ranking loss for standard LambdaMART without architecture changes. In simulation, the method outperforms non-personalized and history-encoder baselines, incurs a modest penalty when G is overestimated, and yields probe-surrogate updates that transfer to the trained ranker. In a retrospective offline Message Search evaluation, personalized LambdaMART outperforms its non-personalized baseline. TreeSHAP provides model-relative trait interpretations.

papers.title: Efficient Offline Learning of Ranking Policies via Top-k Policy Decomposition
papers.abstract: Many recommender systems such as for e-commerce and news platforms aim to provide users with rankings they are likely to interact with. Off-Policy Learning (OPL) of ranking policies enables us to learn new ranking policies using only historical logged data. However, ranking settings make OPL remarkably challenging because their action spaces consist of permutations of unique items, being extremely large. Existing methods primarily use either policy- or regression-based approaches. The policy-based approach, which typically uses importance-weighted policy gradients, can suffer from high variance due to large action spaces. The regression-based approach, on the other hand, estimates the expected reward using conventional machine learning methods, avoiding variance issues but potentially suffering from severe bias. To circumvent these issues of existing methods, we propose a new OPL method for ranking, named Ranking Policy Optimization via Top-k Policy Decomposition (R-POD) , which combines the policy- and regression-based approaches in an effective fashion. Specifically, R-POD decomposes a ranking policy into a first-stage policy for selecting top-k actions and a second-stage policy for choosing the bottom actions given the top-k actions. It learns the first-stage policy using a new policy gradient estimator and the second-stage policy via the regression-based approach. This method can substantially reduce variance, since it applies importance weighting only to the top-k actions. We also demonstrate that our policy-gradient estimator for the first-stage policy is unbiased under a conditional pairwise correctness condition, which only requires that the expected reward differences of pairs of rankings sharing the same top-k actions can be estimated correctly. Comprehensive experiments illustrate that R-POD provides substantial improvements in OPL for ranking.

papers.title: Personalized kNN Query Execution in Vector Databases
papers.abstract: Modern vector databases enable search over high-dimensional embeddings, but query execution engines rely on a specific similarity metric that cannot reflect how individual users perceive similarity. We advocate a metric-level perspective on personalization, keeping the shared embedding space and the underlying index unchanged, and representing each user's specific search needs by a small matrix for Mahalanobis distance learned using relevance feedback and metric learning. Using a lower bounding relationship between Mahalanobis and Euclidean distances, we propose a query execution strategy for personalized k-nearest neighbour search that retrieves an enlarged candidate set using a standard Euclidean (or inner product) index and refines it under the user’s subjective metric. Experiments on CLIP embeddings from Profiset and LAION-2B-en datasets using FAISS-based indices show that this approach can be layered on top of existing vector databases with predictable behaviour, high overlap with precise Mahalanobis kNN search results, and only a small overhead over standard Euclidean search. When the Euclidean–Mahalanobis discrepancy becomes too large for efficient refinement, we propose approximation techniques and show that a Cholesky-based whitening transformation can reorganize embeddings so that personalized search reduces to Euclidean indexing again.

papers.title: Persona Conditioning as an Assessor-Sensitivity Probe for LLM-Based IR Evaluation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as relevance assessors in information retrieval (IR) evaluation, raising questions about how assessor framing affects judgment reliability and downstream system comparison. We study persona conditioning as a diagnostic mechanism for exposing LLM assessor sensitivity. Using task-oriented personas drawn from two complementary sources (PersonaHub and NVIDIA Nemotron-Personas-USA), we instantiate five assessor roles emphasizing intent interpretation, domain expertise, contrastive judgment, evidence verification, and global search-quality assessment, compared with a standard UMBRELA baseline. Across six LLM backbones on TREC DL20 and RAG24, our analyses reveal structured rather than uniform assessor sensitivity. Judgments usually remain close to the baseline while shifting assessment strictness, evidential threshold, or interpretation emphasis rather than producing widespread relevance reversals. At the system level, high-capacity models preserve system-ranking agreement, while smaller models amplify persona-induced instability. Local rank-displacement analysis shows sensitivity concentrates on particular retrieval systems and system types, especially neural ranking/reranking systems on DL20 and RAG-oriented pipelines on RAG24. Persona source matters less than assessor role and model capacity. These findings position persona-conditioned judging as a controlled sensitivity probe for stress-testing LLM-based IR evaluation pipelines and identifying systems whose evaluation outcomes are sensitive to assessor framing.

papers.title: On Multiple Comparison Procedures Involving Multiple Measures and Collections
papers.abstract: When a researcher has m (>2) IR systems to compare and is interested in the difference in mean (say) nDCG for each of the m(m-1)/2 system pairs, a multiple comparison procedure (MCP) should be performed in order to avoid inflating the familywise error rate (FWER). However, we go beyond this rather limited view of multiple comparisons, as IR researchers often employ multiple evaluation measures and multiple test collections, and tend to make a research claim based on whatever statistically significant results found in any part of the experiment. More specifically, we consider MCPs by treating null hypotheses over multiple measures and over multiple collections as a family, using FWER-based MCPs (Holm adjustment, Tukey HSD test with Bonferroni adjustment) as well as a more recent approach of setting the desired False Discovery Rate instead of the FWER. Using real data from NTCIR and TREC with ten evaluation measures, we demonstrate the impact of introducing these more holistic MCP approaches, and provide practical recommendations for IR experimenters.

papers.title: BiFocus: Evidence-Grounded Patch and Query-Token Calibration for Visual Document Retrieval
papers.abstract: Visual document retrieval has recently shifted from OCR-heavy document parsing pipelines toward screenshot-based late-interaction retrievers such as ColPali. These models preserve fine-grained token–patch matching, but their supervision remains misaligned with their scoring mechanism: relevance is accumulated over query-token MaxSim scores, while training signals are typically page-level and, at best, patch-side. We argue that this creates a supervision asymmetry: existing methods can teach visual retrievers where to look on the page, but provide limited explicit supervision for which query tokens should drive the match. We propose BiFocus, an evidence-grounded late-interaction framework that repurposes explicit evidence boxes from BBox-DocVQA to calibrate both page-side patch grounding and query-side token contribution. The framework first converts bounding-box evidence into soft patch-level targets, then induces token-level evidence credits from token–patch alignment and uses them to train a lightweight query-token scorer. At inference time, no evidence boxes or teacher models are required; the model computes a calibrated weighted late-interaction score that emphasizes query tokens supported by document evidence while preserving the original page-level retrieval interface. On ViDoRe V2, BiFocus improves ColPali-v1.3 by +6.15 nDCG@1 and +3.80 nDCG@5, and improves ColQwen2.5-v0.2 by +7.12 nDCG@1 and +4.72 nDCG@5 under the same-backbone setting. On the more extractive and saturated ViDoRe V1 benchmark, BiFocus preserves the strong baseline performance. Code is available at https://github.com/YUEcjy13/BiFocus.

papers.title: Do RAG Systems Cite Themselves? Measuring and Preventing Source Displacement in Self-Updating Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: Self-updating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems store generated answers, summaries, or evidence cards for later retrieval. We show that this reuse creates a provenance risk: generated memories can displace primary sources and later be cited without recoverable root evidence. We call these failures source displacement and citation-lineage collapse. Controlled 100-round streams on HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA show that unrestricted memory reuse places unverified generated memories in 27.6–28.4% of late-stage top-5 retrieval slots and produces citation-lineage collapse in 10.7–11.7% of answers. We then introduce LineageGuard, a lightweight provenance contract that attaches root-source metadata, admits only verified extractive memory cards, caps generated-memory exposure, and expands generated citations to primary sources. Under correct verifier and lineage metadata, LineageGuard enforces zero unverified exposure and zero collapse; these are policy guarantees rather than learned outcomes. Empirically, it improves primary-source recall by 5.0 points on HotpotQA, while lowering answer F1 on 2WikiMultiHopQA, exposing a safety–utility trade-off. An audit of 150 admitted memories finds 91.3% joint support-lineage precision. These results position LineageGuard as a practical control layer, not an accuracy-improving retrieval method, and show why self-updating RAG should treat generated memories as derived evidence rather than ordinary documents.

papers.title: Routing by Contract: Evidence-Gated Skill Selection for Language Agents
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics
papers.abstract: Agentic language systems increasingly rely on reusable skill libraries, but skills with similar surface descriptions often differ in their operational contracts---source of truth, recipient scope, evidence policy, and output format. We study this operational-contract under-specification problem and demonstrate its practical consequences: end-to-end agent experiments on WildClawBench, an independently published benchmark, show that incorrect skill selection causes task-completion penalties of up to 0.514 on a 0--1 verifier scale---far exceeding the offline ranking gap. To address this, we propose query-conditioned operational schema induction with evidence-gated correction. A schema induction module produces a declarative QueryRuleSpec from the query alone (without inspecting candidate skills), deterministic extraction applies the same schema to query and all candidates, and an evidence gate accepts correction only when grounded operational-contract fields are present. The correction layer works on top of any base ranker. On ContractBench, spanning 10 skill families and 6 orthogonal contract policies, schema induction reaches 0.7833 Top-1 versus 0.6917 for path-graph and 0.7167 for semantic text. Evidence-gated correction recovers 6 additional correct selections on each base ranker, empirically never reducing accuracy below the base ranker. The method is regime-aware: it preserves the strong path-graph baseline outside the contract regime and provides auditable, evidence-bearing routing decisions deployable on any base ranker.

papers.title: Bringing Agentic Search to Earth Observation Data Discovery
papers.abstract: NASA and its data centers hold thousands of geoscience datasets and tools like Worldview, Giovanni, the Science Discovery Engine, and Harmony. Finding the right one is hard even for domain experts. We present an agentic search framework for geoscience data discovery that takes a natural-language research query and returns matching datasets and tools. We demonstrate that, in the era of large language models, the latent value of knowledge graphs (KGs) can be substantially amplified through agentic search. From the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph (NASA EO-KG) we derive NASA-EO-Bench, an open benchmark of 47k query–dataset pairs (21k task-based queries). A neural scorer fine-tuned on NASA-EO-Bench beats cosine and BM25 baselines. Further combining it with BM25 via score fusion raises both Recall@10 (R@10) and MRR to over 5× the unadapted cosine baseline. On top of this supervised pipeline, a zero-shot reranking stage lifts MRR by 16%, significant under a paired bootstrap, with no additional training, and autonomous web and arXiv tool use adds a further gain, showing that LLM reasoning is complementary to supervised retrieval.

papers.title: Do Large Language Models have Lateral Thinking in Puzzle-Solving Games?
affiliations: School of Information, Renmin University of China, School of Smart Governance, Renmin University of China
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show exceptional skills in a wide range of tasks, with their ability in lateral thinking standing out as a particularly intriguing area. Lateral thinking in LLMs allows them to understand deeper or suggested meanings from the context, which is essential for making sense of complex scenarios, especially in puzzle-solving games. To delve deeper into and improve the lateral thinking capabilities of LLMs in the realm of puzzle-solving, we introduce the “Lateral Thinking Puzzles” and construct the accompanying dataset. Our novel PuzzleVerse framework aims to enhance LLMs' lateral thinking in puzzle-solving games. Complementing this, we propose a creativity metric to ensure comprehensive evaluations. Experiments show that the selected LLMs, after being trained with PuzzleVerse, have an average improvement of 93.1% compared to their performance before PuzzleVerse training among all metrics. We also validate the robustness of PuzzleVerse that trained LLMs perform better in other reasoning tasks.

papers.title: GPU-Accelerated Parquet Compaction and Index Construction for High-Cardinality Time-Series Databases
papers.abstract: Time-series databases commonly employ LSM-Tree with Parquet columnar storage, where compaction and index construction act as major performance bottlenecks in high-cardinality IoT and cloud monitoring scenarios. Traditional CPU-only compaction suffers from low parallelism and high computation overhead, while mainstream GPU solutions such as cuDF fail to adapt to time-series features. They load complete Parquet files without optimization for string primary keys and lack an end-to-end accelerated index building workflow. This work presents a CPU-GPU collaborative framework for Parquet compaction and index construction. It partitions Parquet row groups into overlapping and non-overlapping segments by primary key ranges to avoid unnecessary global sorting. A global dictionary alignment scheme transforms variable-length string keys into integers to eliminate GPU warp divergence and enable efficient radix sort. Combined with lazy materialization, the framework only processes sorting keys and delays metric field parsing, significantly reducing GPU memory consumption and data transfer cost. A two-phase adaptive cost model enables effective heterogeneous task scheduling. Additionally, a parallel GPU pipeline accelerates tag inverted index construction, leaving only FST and bitmap generation to the CPU. Evaluated on the TSBS benchmark, our framework outperforms CPU baselines and cuDF substantially. It cuts compaction time by nearly an order of magnitude, speeds up index construction by 3.8×–5.2×, and boosts end-to-end throughput by 7.0%–16.0% with stable query latency.

papers.title: GSPARC: A Mode-Aware GPU-Based Method for Large-Scale Sparse Tensor Contraction
papers.abstract: Sparse tensor contraction (SpTC) is a core operation for high-order sparse data analytics in recommendation, knowledge graph analytics, large-scale tensor mining, and scientific computing. Existing methods are limited by SpTC-misaligned representations, overlapping outputs across partitions, and memory-inefficient accumulation over large output spaces. We propose GSPARC, a GPU-based SpTC method that combines a new mode-aware bit-wise representation with mode-decoupled output partitioning and memory-efficient accumulation. These techniques improve index matching, eliminate inter-partition merging, and avoid full output-space allocation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GSPARC outperforms state-of-the-art SpTC methods in contraction speed and scalability. Our code is available at this link: https://github.com/seohyeon0322/GSPARC.

papers.title: Hide-And-Seek-Pair: Efficient Two-Stage Privacy-Preserving Deep Entity Resolution
papers.abstract: Entity resolution solutions based on deep learning have been gaining more attention due to their improved performance in linking records of the same entity. However, due to the complexity of models (especially state-of-art language models) used for entity resolution, it is challenging to provide privacy-preserving variants of deep entity resolution models to comply with data privacy constraints in applications like medical data analysis. In this paper, we propose Hide-And-Seek-Pair (HASP), an efficient privacy-preserving deep entity resolution protocol that utilizes and optimizes homomorphic encryption with deep models in a two-stage computation fashion that provides a practical balance between robust privacy guarantees and computational efficiency. Additionally, by employing Synthetic Ranging, Polynomial Degree Optimization and Differential Loss Term, HASP ensures accurate non-linear function approximation in encrypted neural networks. Overall, the framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in various benchmarks while offering a secure and efficient method for privacy-preserving entity resolution.

papers.title: Seq2Synth: Benchmarking Temporal Fidelity in Synthetic Sequential Tabular Data
papers.abstract: Synthetic sequential tabular data are increasingly used for privacy-preserving data sharing and research, yet conventional tabular metrics often overlook temporal structure. Existing single-table and relational evaluation protocols largely collapse records into static distributions, leaving key temporal properties insufficiently evaluated. We introduce Seq2Synth, a unified benchmark for assessing these properties. Its taxonomy characterizes temporal and schema properties to determine applicable evaluations, covering timestamp, cross-sectional, longitudinal, and structural fidelity, alongside trajectory-aware utility and privacy. Across seven core datasets from a 13-dataset benchmark and eight generators, models with near-perfect static fidelity still violate basic temporal constraints, producing duplicate timestamps, irregular intervals, and incomplete observation grids. Moreover, static and temporal-aware rankings diverge substantially, showing that temporal fidelity must be evaluated directly rather than inferred from static or relational scores. Project page and online appendices are available at: https://seq2synth.github.io/.

papers.title: SERA: Evaluating LLM-based SEmantic RAnking over Structured Tables
papers.abstract: LLM-based data systems are moving beyond text-to-SQL toward semantic query processing, where natural language requests are executed through operators that combine relational processing with LLM-driven inference. A central operator in this setting is SemanticRank, or semantic top-k: given a user intent and a set of relational records, the system orders rows according to a user-defined criterion. Current systems implement this operator as a single black-box LLM prompt. This abstraction hides a key execution problem: the reliability and cost of semantic ranking depend on the criterion being evaluated, the evidence available in the table, and the physical strategy used to compare candidate records. We study semantic ranking as a logical database operator and introduce a multi-domain benchmark for identifying the factors that govern reliable execution over tabular data. Our framework evaluates five dimensions: criterion complexity and specification, computable versus semantic execution, evidence availability, and ranking strategy. We compare proprietary, open-source, and reasoning-oriented LLMs across datasets, specification regimes, evidence conditions, and execution strategies using rank-aware metrics. Our analysis shows that SemanticRank cannot be implemented reliably as a single prompting primitive. Ranking quality is shaped by criterion structure, and formula-based specifications help reasoning-oriented execution. Real-world names can introduce prior-knowledge bias that anonymisation reduces. Full execution is competitive on small candidate sets, while partitioning changes the cost-quality trade-off without consistently improving accuracy. These findings identify key factors for reliable SemanticRank execution.

papers.title: Query-Graph Compatibility: A Formal Pre-Condition for Faithful Knowledge-Grounded Language Model Generation
affiliations: Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic University
papers.abstract: Knowledge-graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (KG-RAG) grounds large language model (LLM) outputs in structured facts by retrieving a query-relevant subgraph before generation. However, existing KG-RAG systems often assume that the retrieved graph contains sufficient evidence to answer the query. When this assumption fails, the LLM may produce an answer that is factually plausible but not faithfully grounded in the KG. To address this problem, we introduce Query-Graph Compatibility (QGC), a formal, model-independent pre-condition for faithful KG-grounded generation. Given a natural-language query parsed into a typed conjunctive query and a KG with schema, QGC checks whether the query has a valid typed match in the graph, formalized as a typed homomorphism. If QGC=0, the KG lacks the structural evidence required by the query, so no generation model, regardless of architecture or scale, can produce a faithful answer from the KG alone-a consequence that follows directly from our definitions but yields a checkable pre-generation condition. QGC inherits the classical complexity of conjunctive-query evaluation: NP-complete in general, yet tractable for the bounded-width query structures that cover all KGQA queries in our evaluation. We validate QGC across six datasets and four domains. Under controlled edge deletion on MetaQA, QGC predicts LLM failure with AUC 0.78-0.93 for 1-2 hop queries across five LLMs, with accuracy gaps of +55 to +86 percentage points. Under natural incompleteness in clinical KGs (MIMIC-III, CORAL), all five evaluated models show positive QGC accuracy gaps (+5 to +31 percentage points), while PrimeKGQA exposes a boundary condition: structurally simpler QGC=0 contexts can yield higher correctness despite lacking faithful grounding. QGC checking runs in under 0.1 ms per query, making it practical as a real-time pre-filter or retrieval stopping criterion.

papers.title: Multi-dimensional Evolution Model with Attribute and Structure Interactions for Entity Alignment
papers.abstract: Entity alignment aims to identify equivalent entities across different Knowledge Graphs (KGs), serving as a fundamental task for knowledge graph integration. It is inherently a multi-dimensional problem, where graph topology, entity attributes, and alignment evidence should mutually reinforce one another. However, most existing methods fail to establish such a loop. They typically expand or refine alignment supervision alone, while keeping the underlying graph structure and attribute importance static. Moreover, they lack a global view of which attributes are discriminative across the alignment set. As a result, structural sparsity persists, noisy attributes cannot be suppressed, and alignment supervision remains scarce. To solve these problems, we propose MEASI, a Multi-dimensional Evolution model with Attribute and Structure Interactions for entity alignment. MEASI comprises three evolutionary modules that establish a self-reinforcing loop. First, a Graph Structure Evolution (GSE) module progressively enhances graph topology by leveraging newly discovered alignments. Second, a Global Attribute Weight Evolution (GAWE) module iteratively updates global attribute weights via alignment feedback, emphasizing discriminative attributes and reducing the influence of attribute noise. Finally, an Alignment Signal Evolution (ASE) module continuously discovers new aligned entities from both structural and attribute views to fuel the next iteration of GSE and GAWE, compensating for limited pre-aligned entities. Extensive experiments show that MEASI outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: CodeGraph: Open-Taxonomy Knowledge Graph for Source Code with Wikidata Grounding
affiliations: LTCI, Télécom Paris, Institut Polytechnique de Paris
papers.abstract: Public software repositories, like GitHub and Software Heritage Archive, store billions of files, yet extracting their implicit engineering knowledge ---i.e., the algorithms they implement, the paradigms they follow, the patterns they instantiate, and the application domains they serve--- remains challenging, as current tools are constrained to syntactic and token-level analysis. We present a pipeline for building an open-taxonomy semantic annotation of source code using a code-specialised Large Language Model. The extracted entities are grounded in Wikidata through a three-stage linking procedure: a deterministic SPARQL stage handles unambiguous entities, a Deep Research Agent resolves the residual long tail, and a hierarchy-rollup stage imports the parent-of closure of each resolved Wikidata identifier. The resulting annotations are materialised as a source-code-specific open-taxonomy knowledge graph. We further introduce a calibrated quality-assurance protocol that quantifies annotation precision by combining a small human gold set with an LLM-as-a-judge filter. We applied our pipeline to the 167 million files of the Stack-Edu corpus, creating the first known large-scale open-taxonomy knowledge graph for source code. Our graph, named CodeGraph, contains approximately 158 million nodes, which include around 145 million files, about 63,000 extracted concept entities (such as algorithms, paradigms, design patterns, and application domains), and roughly 19,800 grounded Wikidata entities. Furthermore, CodeGraph features approximately 1 billion typed edges that connect files to their respective concepts, link these concepts to their grounded Wikidata identifiers, and relate them to their parent categories, covering 14 programming languages.

papers.title: LSRTopic: Contextual Sparse Topic Modeling via Corpus-Vocabulary Alignment
affiliations: Federal University of São João del-Rei
papers.abstract: Topic modeling still struggles to combine contextual expressiveness with lexical interpretability. Sparse models are transparent but semantically limited, whereas dense contextual models capture meaning at the cost of direct interpretability. We argue that Learned Sparse Representations (LSR) offer a promising alternative but remain underused in topic modeling due to a vocabulary misalignment problem: their activations are over subword vocabularies, whereas topic models require stable corpus-level terms. We introduce LSRTopic, a framework that maps and aggregates contextual sparse activations into the target corpus vocabulary, producing semantically enriched and lexically interpretable document--term matrices for factorization methods such as NMF. Experiments on six benchmark datasets against 10 baselines show that LSRTopic achieves the strongest overall performance across coherence, embedding-based proximity, topic uniqueness, and document-representation separability. Additional LLM-as-judge word-intrusion evaluation with human validation, ablations, and efficiency analysis confirms that resolving vocabulary misalignment enables topic models that jointly support contextual semantics, interpretability, and practical efficiency.

papers.title: Anytime-Valid Multi-Objective Online Experimentation with Contrast Certificates
affiliations: Southern University of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Large-scale search and recommendation systems routinely run online experiments for ranking models, feed policies, user-interface treatments, and ad/recommendation blending strategies. These launches are rarely single-metric decisions: teams often need to improve click-through rate, conversion, dwell time, retention, or revenue while controlling negative feedback and latency. We propose AV-MO-SOPTIMA++, an anytime-valid framework for multi-objective online experimentation under adaptive traffic allocation and optional stopping. Instead of relying only on marginal arm-objective confidence sequences, AV-MO-SOPTIMA++ uses prospective two-sample contrast confidence sequences for decision-relevant arm pairs; these contrasts may be pre-activated for a fixed decision mode or activated online when new bottleneck constraints appear. The method derives Pareto and guardrail certificates from these contrasts and propagates certified dominance through a dominance graph. The framework further uses decision-specific stopping rules for full Pareto, relaxed Pareto, and guardrail launch decisions, together with a bottleneck-aware allocation policy that prioritizes comparisons currently blocking a valid decision. Experiments show that the anytime-valid controller maintains calibration under optional stopping, exposes false certificates from nominal multi-objective peeking, and supports safe guardrail launch decisions with fewer samples than fixed-horizon A/B or full-Pareto PSI in a launch benchmark. Component ablations show that contrast certificates reduce guardrail stopping time and bottleneck allocation sharply reduces bad-arm exposure. In full Pareto identification, contrast variants reduce samples on separated instances, while near-boundary instances remain challenging for all validity-first methods.

papers.title: RoE-FND: Synergizing LLMs with Experiential Learning for Effective and Generalizable Evidence-Based Fake News Detection
papers.abstract: The proliferation of deceptive content in social networks necessitates robust Fake News Detection (FND) systems. Existing pipelines either train detectors on labeled data or leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) for their reasoning ability. However, current approaches remain either limited in generalizability or prone to over-commitment to persuasive yet flawed rationales, lacking systematic experience and mechanisms to expose subtle reasoning errors. We propose RoE-FND ( R eason o n E xperiences FND), an LLM-based framework that combines self-reflective experience building with deliberation through retrieved experiences for FND. RoE-FND builds an experience bank via reflective learning that compares an unconstrained analysis with a label-conditioned analysis using the ground-truth label as posterior supervision, then summarizes their critical divergence into reusable reasoning guidelines. During inference, RoE-FND generates two opposing deductions via a flipped pseudo-label provided as posterior, retrieves the most relevant experiences for resolving their key disagreement, and adjudicates the better-supported rationale as the final prediction. Experiments across five popular benchmarks, including text-only datasets, i.e., CHEF, Snopes, PolitiFact, and multimedia datasets, i.e., FakeTT, FakeSV, demonstrate that RoE-FND outperforms strong baselines without optimizing LLM parameters on dataset distributions, while exhibiting strong cross-dataset generalization.

papers.title: SADI: Spatial-Aware Dynamic Intervention for Mitigating Hallucinations in LVLMs
affiliations: Qilu University of Technology (Shandong Academy of Sciences)
China Telecom Digital Intelligence Technology Co, Ltd
industryAffiliations: China Telecom Digital Intelligence Technology Co, Ltd
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) persistently suffer from object hallucinations, generating plausible yet factually incorrect outputs that fabricate objects non-existent in the visual input. Existing mitigation methods typically fall into three paradigms: fine-tuning with targeted data, which incurs prohibitive computational costs; applying contrastive decoding, which introduces high inference latency and may penalize beneficial language priors; or intervening in attention weights via heuristic hard-truncation or head-homogeneous shifts, operations that may discard information from selected attention paths. Building upon the third paradigm, we present Spatial-Aware Dynamic Intervention (SADI). SADI discards conventional rigid truncations in favor of a spatial-aware soft mask to adaptively correct visual-semantic misalignments. Specifically, it establishes a robust median consensus among multiple attention heads to anchor reliable visual representations. Guided by the spatial variance across these heads, SADI dynamically allocates intervention weights and employs a soft mask to gently suppress anomalous attention distributions. As a lightweight, training-free inference solution, our method reframes attention modulation as a smooth, continuous recalibration process. Ultimately, SADI effectively rectifies semantic drift while maintaining comparable generation fluency and description richness in our evaluations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SADI significantly reduces both sentence- and instance-level hallucinations while maintaining description richness. Across the evaluated CHAIR, POPE, and MME benchmarks, SADI shows consistent gains in the tested settings. Code is released at https://github.com/yz-8/SADI.

papers.title: OmniHandwritingOCR: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Evaluating Multimodal LLMs in Handwritten OCR Scenarios
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used for OCR in document and knowledge-processing pipelines, yet their ability to faithfully read real handwriting remains underexplored. Existing benchmarks emphasize printed text or clean single-line inputs and provide limited coverage of multilingual handwriting, writer errors, and structurally complex mathematical expressions. We introduce OmniHandwritingOCR, a diagnostic benchmark for evaluating MLLM/OCR systems on handwritten OCR. It covers handwritten text recognition and handwritten mathematical expression recognition across six subtasks and twelve subsets, totaling 77.57K labeled images from public datasets and newly collected student writings. A difficulty-stratified multi-line formula corpus tests robustness as structural complexity increases. We evaluate thirteen open- and closed-source systems with five complementary metrics under a unified protocol. Results show that current systems remain far from faithful transcription: performance drops sharply on complex multi-line formulas, model rankings vary across language and formula settings, and several generative models hallucinate plausible but visually unsupported corrections. OmniHandwritingOCR provides a challenging testbed for diagnosing language, content, structural, and visual-grounding failures in handwritten OCR.

papers.title: Anchoring Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge Systems: Prior Scores Compromise Evaluation Independence
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly assess generated content, giving rise to the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm. These systems now score outputs, filter content, and gate iterative refinement in production pipelines, where each judgment is often assumed to be independent of earlier evaluations. We test this assumption using three prompt conditions: no metadata, revision framing, and anchored metadata containing revision, attempt, and prior-score fields. We show that prior scores, even when included only as context metadata, anchor judgments and systematically shift ratings toward their values. Across 192,000 attempted evaluations (185,271 successful) seven out of the eight evaluated models have 95% task-stratified bootstrap intervals below zero for the total anchored-metadata effect on 20 fixed texts. Cohen's d, a standardized measure of the difference between score distributions, reaches an absolute value of 0.71. Token-level analysis of selected model-task probes suggests a threshold-like response pattern: introducing anchored metadata produces a marked redistribution of output-score probabilities, while changing the anchor value within the tested below-threshold range produces comparatively little additional variation. On categorical industry data with human-labeled ground truth, anchored metadata blocks 48% of error corrections and flips 10.18% of correct judgments toward assigned wrong label, demonstrating the bias extends beyond numerical scoring to categorical decisions. Neither Chain-of-Thought nor a metadata-disregard warning reduces the total effect, although warning improves the paired accuracy effect relative to baseline in the industry experiment. Reliable LLM evaluation demands careful context engineering rather than passive assumption of impartiality, where effective mitigation must be validated for intended model, and specific task or domain.

papers.title: RoSafetyBench: A Culturally-Native Safety Benchmark for Romanian Language Models
papers.abstract: Romanian, like most non-English languages, has no dedicated safety benchmark for large language models—existing multilingual efforts (XSafety, M-ALERT) cover 10 and 5 languages respectively, none of them Romanian, and derive their non-English prompts by translating a source set written for other languages, which leaves culturally-specific risks like anti-Roma discrimination and Romanian profanity patterns with no source to translate from. We introduce RoSafetyBench, a Romanian-first benchmark of nearly a thousand prompts across six dimensions (toxicity, bias, hallucination, jailbreak, over-refusal, cross-lingual transfer), and evaluate 17 open-weight models (0.5B–27B) plus three frontier APIs (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro). Methodologically we contribute a dual-judge refusal-scoring protocol pairing a primary LLM judge with a second-rater from a different vendor (? = 0.79 over 1663 responses), with bootstrap intervals on every agreement statistic. Two findings follow that the keyword protocols of prior multilingual benchmarks could not have produced: over-refusal of benign Romanian prompts spanning 0–53% and largely missed by keyword detection (? = 0.11 over all 2000 judgments); and a positive size–safety association within Gemma 3, Qwen 3, and Qwen 2.5 (with a small 14B dip), reversing an apparent inverse-scaling artefact. Independently of the scoring protocol, Romanian factual accuracy stays below 32% across the entire open-weight range. Comparing English and Romanian within prompt pairs rather than between marginal rates, the transfer gap reverses sign by category—English refuses more on harmful intent, Romanian more on bias probes—so the near-zero aggregate reported by unpaired analyses averages two opposite panel-level differences away. A scoped comparison with a 40-prompt machine-translated HarmBench control finds none of our prespecified Romanian-specific risk markers and much higher refusal than on the separate native-toxicity set; because the sets are not content-matched, this is descriptive rather than a causal translation effect. We release the benchmark, harness, all model responses, and the complete categorical judge-label table on Zenodo and Hugging Face (Section 9).

papers.title: BenchGuard: A Calibrated, Adversary-Aware Triage Layer for Reward-Hacking Agentic Trajectories
papers.abstract: Agentic AI systems are increasingly evaluated on executable benchmarks, and a now well-documented failure mode is reward hacking: agents inspect graders, spoof expected outputs, hijack binaries, or extract hidden test inputs. The dominant operational response is to monitor every trajectory with a strong LLM judge, but at $0.4–$3.8 per 100 trajectories and several minutes of latency, judge-everywhere is impractical for the millions of runs produced by continuous benchmark development. We present BenchGuard, a strict command-only forensic triage layer: TF-IDF word n-grams over agent shell commands feed a class-balanced LinearSVC that is recalibrated with Platt scaling and reports prevalence-aware operating points. On Terminal Wrench's 5,984 paired trajectories, BenchGuard reaches ROC-AUC 0.928 [task-grouped bootstrap 95% CI 0.918, 0.939] at 50% prefix and TPR 0.70 at 5% FPR. We then run a head-to-head LLM judge experiment on the same balanced 100-trajectory sample under three configurations: command-only (judge AUC 0.806), full-context with a generic prompt (0.727, DeLong p=0.012 vs. BenchGuard), and full-context with a rubric-tuned prompt (0.837, p=0.237). BenchGuard is point-estimate-best across all three at $0 vs. $0.77–$1.50 per 100 trajectories. Two cheap baselines (BM25 max-similarity AUC 0.451, a distilled hashed-n-gram MLP AUC 0.931) bracket the result: pure lexical similarity is insufficient, but capacity at this scale is also not the bottleneck. Three static lexicon-evasion attacks plus an LLM-paraphrase adversary that drops token-Jaccard to 0.42 cost only 0.013–0.030 AUC (-9 pp at TPR@5%FPR for the paraphrase); adversary-aware retraining recovers the static gap. Platt-recalibrated flag rates on a 34,029-trajectory external corpus drop from 13.3% (raw) to 0.4% (Platt p >= 0.99), demonstrating calibration transfer. We document a sharp construct-validity boundary: against the realistic union-negative class (legitimate solves + no-reward attacks), AUC drops to 0.700 and operating-point precision collapses — and we translate this into a three-step deployment recommendation. All code, data extracts, judge response logs (scores and verdicts), the LLM paraphrase outputs, and calibration models are released as a reproducible artifact.

papers.title: TRACE: Graph-Aware Anomaly Detection for Trust Routing in Adversarial Decentralized Marketplaces
affiliations: Akhilesh Das Gupta Institute of Professional Studies
papers.abstract: Decentralized agent marketplaces route paid work to pseudonymous providers, and any trust mechanism for doing so has to balance three pressures: bound fraud exposure, stay open to newcomers, and survive coordinated graph manipulation. We introduce TRACE (Trust Routing with Adversarial Coordination Evidence), a routing policy that scores providers using uncertainty-aware evidence weighting and structural coordination detection rather than propagating trust through the graph. We compare TRACE against three baselines, reputation-only, price-only, and EigenTrust, across four attack regimes at N=1,000 agents with 30% adversaries and ten seeds per cell. Two results drive our findings. Trust propagation amplifies coordinated attacks: EigenTrust routes 81.7% of jobs to malicious agents under Sybil attack, while reputation-only contains the same attack to 29.0%. Exploration is also costly under score-based adversaries: disabling Thompson sampling in TRACE lowers mean fraud from 10.7, 46.5, 19.0, and 83.7 sats to 4.7, 6.4, 7.1, and 31.7 sats on strategic-default, collusion-ring, sybil-cluster, and game-theoretic-adversary, respectively. This greedy variant has the lowest fraud on the first three attacks; EigenTrust attains lower game-theoretic fraud (4.4 sats) but only by routing 41.2% of jobs to malicious agents. A scale run at N=5,000 (five seeds per baseline policy, ten for TRACE-no-bandit) confirms EigenTrust's pathology persists, and the same propagating-versus-non-propagating ordering replicates on two real-world signed-trust graphs (Bitcoin Over-The-Counter, Bitcoin Alpha). Together, these findings caution against trust propagation in adversarial settings and motivate risk-conditioned exploration as a principled extension.

papers.title: Backdoor Poisoning Mitigation for Federated LoRA via Structural Adaptive Control
papers.abstract: Large pre-trained models are increasingly adapted on user devices, but direct fine-tuning in federated settings is constrained by computation, memory, and communication limits. These constraints have motivated the use of parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, among which LoRA is widely adopted by concentrating adaptation in low-rank parameters. While this design improves efficiency, it also changes the security setting. In federated LoRA, backdoor behavior can exploit the low-rank adaptation structure and persist across communication rounds, making defenses designed for full-model updates less reliable. To address this gap, we propose StrAP, a server-side defense tailored to federated LoRA fine-tuning. StrAP combines reliability control before aggregation with structure-aware regulation after aggregation. Before aggregation, client updates are softly weighted based on their alignment with a clean validation gradient and tracked across rounds using a stateful trust mechanism, which suppresses persistent anomalies while allowing benign recovery. After aggregation, StrAP analyzes the LoRA parameter structure to identify suspicious rank channels using robust cross-client statistics and applies utility-calibrated structural actions guided by clean validation loss. Extensive experiments show that StrAP consistently reduces backdoor attack success rates with minimal impact on clean accuracy. Our code is available at https://github.com/HwhCN-ui/StrAP.

papers.title: Cross-Architecture Semantic Backdoor Attack in Data-Driven Federated Learning
affiliations: Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications
papers.abstract: Traditional Federated Learning (FL) relies on iterative parameter exchange, which limits architectural flexibility and introduces high communication overhead for large foundation models. To address these issues, Data-Driven Federated Learning (DD-FL) has recently emerged as a scalable alternative. Instead of exchanging model parameters, DD-FL adopts a one-shot data-centric pipeline, where heterogeneous clients collaboratively annotate a shared unlabeled public dataset and the server performs knowledge distillation through soft-label aggregation. While DD-FL improves scalability and supports heterogeneous architectures, it also introduces a new attack surface on the shared public dataset. These public datasets are often collected from web crawlers or collaborative platforms with limited integrity validation, making data poisoning feasible. Moreover, since DD-FL removes parameter-level interactions and relies on soft-label aggregation across heterogeneous models, traditional FL backdoor attacks designed for individual models are easily diluted and exhibit poor cross-architecture transferability. In this paper, we propose a semantic backdoor attack for DD-FL. Our method generates poisoned samples by aligning image perturbations with target semantic directions in a shared vision-language space. This enables poisoned samples to induce semantically aligned target predictions across heterogeneous client models, making the backdoor more transferable during soft-label aggregation. We also study how biased aggregation weights further strengthen the attack effect. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet show that our method achieves higher attack success rates and robustness than existing baselines, while maintaining high clean accuracy and strong visual stealthiness.

papers.title: DuetDP-DD: Size-Adaptive Differentially Private Dataset Distillation for Heterogeneous Users
affiliations: Centre for Frontier AI Research (CFAR), Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR)
papers.abstract: Differentially private dataset distillation (DP-DD) enables privacy-preserving data sharing by releasing compact synthetic datasets with formal privacy guarantees. However, existing DP-DD methods typically optimize for a fixed images-per-class (IPC) setting, making them ill-suited to heterogeneous users who require distilled datasets with different IPC sizes. Straightforward extensions to support multiple IPC requirements either incur cumulative privacy costs across separate DP-DD runs or sacrifice adaptability by relying on a predefined maximum IPC size. To address this issue, we introduce Size-Adaptive DP-DD , a strategy that decouples private data access from the construction of IPC-specific distilled datasets under a single privacy budget. Building on this strategy, we propose DuetDP-DD , which constructs a reusable DP-synthetic candidate space and derives IPC-specific distilled datasets through tailored post-processing. DuetDP-DD employs a dual-classifier guidance scheme: the Semantic-Anchor Classifier identifies semantically central candidates within each class, while the DP-Classifier provides discriminative guidance, with its feature space supporting diversity-aware selection, thereby preserving class representativeness, inter-class discriminability, and intra-class coverage of distilled datasets across IPC settings. This design allows DuetDP-DD to serve emerging IPC requests with utility-preserving distilled datasets without additional private optimization. Extensive comparative experiments demonstrate that DuetDP-DD achieves competitive utility across IPC settings without incurring the repeated privacy cost of separate fixed-size DP-DD runs. Additional analyses confirm the effectiveness, flexibility, and cross-architecture generalization of DuetDP-DD, underscoring its applicability to privacy-preserving distilled dataset sharing for heterogeneous users.

papers.title: GraphMemShield: Auditing Cross-Session Leakage in Graph Memories
affiliations: Ho Chi Minh City University of Technology (HCMUT), Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City
papers.abstract: Graph-backed assistants increasingly write user utterances into a provenance-tagged knowledge-graph memory and later retrieve k-hop neighborhoods to ground responses. Because the retrieval surface is multi-user and append-only, an edge written by one session can enter the context of another. This boundary is neither model memorization nor document-RAG leakage; it is a retrieval-control problem that existing benchmarks do not isolate. We introduce GraphMemShield , a benchmark and audit suite for cross-session leakage in dynamic KG memories, packaging a JSONL trace schema, gray- and black-box leakage probes, a response-leakage scorer, and four policy baselines: global retrieval, owner-only isolation, label filtering, and bounded provenance-aware sharing. Two structural results frame the suite. First, we prove that any policy with cross-session QA accuracy a must expose at least ⌈ a N cs /ρ⌉ victim-owned determining edges; a retrieval-time budget guard attains this bound to within 1.06× on a structured workload (the enterprise bank). Second, we apply the standard private-selection lower bound to show that post-retrieval answer-level ε-DP cannot match the deterministic guard's utility in the small-margin regime our graph-memory workloads exhibit empirically: our DP-GraphQA mechanism lands at 0.15–0.18 accuracy at usable ε on these workloads because measured margins are only 0.54–1.24. The operational rule is therefore to bound exposure before unsafe cross-session edges enter the context, and add post-retrieval DP only when the application can pay the margin cost.

papers.title: GhostEdges: Measuring Neighborhood Leakage After Deletion in Retrained GNNs
papers.abstract: The machine unlearning literature treats retraining a GNN from scratch as the gold standard for deletion privacy, yet this assumption has never been empirically tested. If even full retraining fails to prevent attackers from recovering deleted neighborhood information, then the entire framework of approximate unlearning methods built on this premise would be undermined. We formalize this question as Model-level Deleted Neighborhood Inference (M-DNI) and conduct the first systematic measurement across five attack strategies, six GNN architectures, and two signed trust networks. A key methodological challenge is that heavy-tailed degree distributions dominate the signal: simply guessing that a deleted user was connected to high-degree nodes achieves AUC 0.83, making raw attack accuracy meaningless. We therefore introduce degree-calibrated ΔAUC, defined as attack AUC minus the degree-prior baseline, as the primary metric. The strongest attack achieves raw AUC 0.761 but ΔAUC = -0.070 (p<0.0001), performing worse than naive degree guessing. Every attack and architecture yields ΔAUC ≤ 0, and after accounting for degree, the residual deletion-specific signal collapses to AUC 0.44, indistinguishable from random. Even an MLP with no access to graph structure matches the degree prior, confirming that the observable signal originates from degree features in the input, not from the GNN having memorized neighborhood structure. On the networks tested, these findings support the retraining assumption and suggest that efficient approximate unlearning methods may be sufficient for deletion privacy in GNN-based trust systems, since even the gold standard does not create exploitable neighborhood leakage.

papers.title: FUCH: Non-IID Federated Unlearning via Classification-layer Hybrid-order Constraints
affiliations: School of Information Science and Technology, Yunnan Normal University
School of Software Engineering, Chengdu University of Information Technology
papers.abstract: Federated unlearning (FU) aims to support the “right to be forgotten” by reducing the influence of target samples without full retraining. However, when applied to deep neural networks (DNNs) in practical non-IID scenarios, existing FU methods suffer from low unlearning efficiency and deviate from the retraining reference's predictive behavior. Specifically, they require costly full-model updates or multi-round communication, failing to disentangle the complex coupling of target-sample influence and retained knowledge. In this work, we revisit the necessity of full-model updates for sample-level FU and investigate the formation of this complex coupling. We reveal key empirical insights: (1) updating solely the final classification layer can effectively approximate the predictive behavior of full retraining; and (2) disentangling target-sample influence under non-IID settings requires separately resolving distinct intra-client and cross-client knowledge couplings. Based on these insights, we propose FUCH, a classification-layer-based hybrid-order-constrained FU framework. To improve unlearning efficiency, FUCH freezes the feature extractor and performs a single-round update on the final classification layer. Furthermore, to disentangle the complex knowledge coupling, FUCH employs a coupling-aware hybrid-order mechanism combining local second-order and global first-order information to constrain the unlearning updates. Extensive experiments across diverse non-IID benchmarks validate our empirical insights and demonstrate that FUCH achieves efficient unlearning while significantly outperforming SOTA baselines in closely approximating the retraining reference's predictive behavior.

papers.title: FDA-Opt: Federated Fine-Tuning via Dynamic Update Schedules
papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables the utilization of vast, previously inaccessible data sources. At the same time, pre-trained Language Models (LMs) have taken the world by storm and for good reason. They exhibit remarkable emergent abilities and are readily adapted to downstream tasks. This opens one of the most exciting frontiers in FL: fine-tuning LMs. Yet, a persistent challenge in FL is the frequent, rigid communication of parameters—a problem magnified by the sheer size of these contemporary models. The FedOpt family of algorithms has become the go-to approach for FL, relying on fixed but arbitrary intervals for model exchanges. Recently, the FDA algorithm prescribed a dynamic approach by monitoring the training progress. However, it introduced a hard-to-calibrate parameter and imposed a rigid synchronization scheme. In this work, we address these limitations by proposing the FDA-Opt family of algorithms—a unified generalization of both FDA and FedOpt. Our experimental evaluation focuses on fine-tuning LMs on downstream NLP tasks and demonstrates that FDA-Opt outperforms FedOpt even when it is configured with hyper-parameters specifically optimized for the latter. In other words, we show that FDA-Opt is a practical, drop-in replacement for FedOpt in modern FL libraries and systems: it requires no additional configuration and delivers superior performance out of the box.

papers.title: When Is Shallow Enough? Adaptive Split Federated Learning with Client-Specific Sufficiency Estimation
papers.abstract: Split Federated Learning (SFL) enables distributed model training by splitting networks between the server and clients. However, under client heterogeneity, the conventional static split strategy may be suboptimal because clients can differ in data distributions, adaptation dynamics, and representation learning progress, making a single split point insufficient to accommodate client-specific training states. In this paper, we propose FedSGA, a S ufficiency- G uided A daptive split Fed erated learning framework that addresses this question through client-specific shallow sufficiency estimation. First, we introduce a client-specific adaptation channel based on private prompt tokens, which tracks local adaptation dynamics separately from the shared backbone and provides a lightweight signal for detecting whether client adaptation remains active. To further avoid repeated online probing over multiple candidate depths, we design a shallow sufficiency estimator that combines cross-client semantic alignment, temporal interface stability, and prompt-state variation to estimate whether the shallowest split is already sufficient. Finally, we introduce a split-compatible interface harmonization module that projects activations from different split depths into a shared semantic space, improving the comparability of heterogeneous client interfaces before server-side prediction. Extensive experiments on multiple heterogeneous benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of FedSGA in improving model performance compared with state-of-the-art methods while reducing unnecessary client-side computation.

papers.title: Federated Personalization of Early-Exit Networks
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong Shenzhen Research Institute
papers.abstract: Personalized Federated Learning (PFL) excels at tailoring clientspecific models, which is particularly critical for decentralized and heterogeneous data environments, yet existing methods produce static models with a fixed tradeoff between accuracy and efficiency. This inherent static nature limits their ability to adapt to inference demands that vary with context and resource availability, posing a challenge for real-world deployment. Early-exit networks (EENs), which enable adaptive inference via intermediate classifiers, offer a promising solution. However, integrating EENs into PFL introduces two intertwined conflicts: client-wise heterogeneity across clients and depth-wise interference arising from conflicting exit objectives. Prior studies fail to resolve both conflicts simultaneously, leading to suboptimal performance. In this paper, we propose X-FED, a novel Conflict-Aware Cross-Client Federated Exit Distillation framework that jointly addresses both client- and depth-wise conflicts while extending PFL to early-exit networks. At its core, X-FED employs a progressive, depth-prioritized student coordination mechanism that mitigates interference among shallow and deep exits while enabling effective personalized knowledge transfer across clients. Furthermore, we introduce a client-decoupled formulation that reduces communication overhead with theoretical soundness. Extensive evaluations on various datasets show that compared to state-of-the-art PFL and PFL-EE methods, X-FED achieves higher accuracy while reducing inference costs by 30.79%–46.86%.

papers.title: DualFed-RCGC: Dual-Track Personalized Federated Learning via Covariance-Transferred Rare-Class Geometric Completion
papers.abstract: Personalized federated learning under extreme data heterogeneity suffers from two coupled structural issues: local majority-class gradients contaminate the globally shared representation, while rare classes lack sufficient local support, making reliable local discrimination difficult. To address these issues, we propose DualFed-RCGC, a dual-track personalized federated learning framework. First, it employs a Y-shaped architecture with explicit gradient-path isolation, decoupling global representation learning from local adaptation to mitigate majority-dominated gradients from biasing the shared backbone. Second, to improve discrimination for underrepresented classes, we introduce a Covariance-Transferred Rare-Class Geometric Completion (RCGC) module. It calibrates local decision boundaries by synthesizing geometry-aware virtual features using fixed Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) anchors and covariance structures transferred from local majority classes. Finally, a class-aware masked distillation strategy selectively injects global knowledge to further improve rare-class discrimination. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet demonstrate that DualFed-RCGC consistently improves personalized local accuracy while retaining a usable shared branch for federated aggregation.

papers.title: Feature Evolution and Migration during Vision Transformer Training
papers.abstract: We present a novel view on feature evolution in Vision Transformers (ViTs) by visualizing the training process over two dimensions – network depth (layer) and training time (epochs). We employ Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to extract candidate sparse features from CLS-token representations and compare their activation profiles across epoch–layer pairs. This allows us to study feature-level dynamics that are not directly visible from representation-level similarity measures. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this framework of feature evolution allows us to describe feature migration , the change in the layer where a feature is most detectable during training. Our experiments show that migration is concentrated early in training, occurs more often toward earlier layers than toward deeper layers, and declines as feature organization stabilizes. We further find that deeper layers stabilize earlier and more strongly than shallow layers. The results show that our approach can be employed as a tool for understanding how ViTs learn and evolve.

papers.title: GroupSegment-SHAP: Shapley Value Explanations with Group-Segment Players for Multivariate Time Series
