Existing methods with static trigger representations cannot adequately capture real-time intent drift or disentangle fine-grained preferences such as brand versus category. We propose C ontext- A ware User I ntent M odeling (CAIM) to address these limitations. CAIM incorporates an Intention Enhancement Module (IEM) that integrates real-time context to dynamically reconstruct the trigger representation, serving as an adaptive anchor. An Intention Retrieval Module (IRM) retrieves relevant long-term user behaviors, while a Sub-intention Extraction Module (SIEM) decomposes the overall intent into attribute-level sub-intentions. Experiments on industrial datasets show that CAIM outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Deployed in a large-scale e-commerce platform under strict latency constraints, CAIM yields a 6.9% increase in orders and a 7.7% increase in Gross Merchandise Value (GMV), validating its effectiveness and practical applicability.

papers.title: Learning from What You Retrieve: Online RL Fine-Tuning for Semantic Retrieval
papers.abstract: In large-scale e-commerce retrieval, dual-encoder retrievers are optimized for contrastive similarity, whereas downstream rerankers capture finer-grained relevance preferences; this objective mismatch limits end-to-end retrieval quality. Reinforcement Learning offers a way to use reward-model feedback for retriever adaptation, but we observe that standard policy-gradient updates can degrade embedding geometry, especially when the document index must remain frozen due to industrial constraints. To address this, we propose PAO (Positive-Advantage-Only) , a selective RL optimization method. Our analysis reveals that indiscriminate penalization of negative samples (pushing away) in a frozen high-dimensional space disrupts pre-trained semantic manifolds. PAO selectively applies gradient updates only to retrieved items with positive advantages, effectively pulling query embeddings toward high-reward regions while preserving global topological stability. Experiments on both a massive industrial dataset and public benchmarks demonstrate that PAO significantly outperforms standard RL and distillation baselines.

papers.title: Unleashing the Power of LLMs in Dense Retrieval with Query Likelihood Modeling
affiliations: State Key Laboratory of AI Safety
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.abstract: Dense retrieval is a fundamental task in Information Retrieval (IR), forming the foundation for downstream applications such as re-ranking and augmenting generation. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have exhibited remarkable semantic understanding capabilities, drawing significant interest from researchers in dense retrieval. While LLMs, as decoder-style generative models, excel in language generation, they often struggle to capture global information due to their lack of attention to subsequent tokens. Motivated by the classical word-based language modeling approach in IR, particularly the query likelihood (QL) model, we seek to exploit the generative advantages of LLMs through QL maximization. Instead of using QL estimation directly for document ranking, we introduce QL maximization as an auxiliary task to strengthen the backbone, thereby facilitating the subsequent contrastive learning of the retriever. We introduce our model, LLM-QL, which incorporates two key components: Attention Block (AB) and Document Corruption (DC). AB blocks the attention of predictive tokens to the document tokens before the document's ending token, while DC corrupts a document by masking a portion of its tokens during prediction. Evaluations on the in-domain (MS MARCO) and out-of-domain dataset (BEIR) indicate LLM-QL's superiority over other LLM-based retrievers. Furthermore, comprehensive analyses also validate the efficacy of LLM-QL and its components.

papers.title: On Non-Relevance Signals in Pointwise LLM-based Reranking
papers.abstract: Pointwise reranking with large language models (LLMs) evaluates query-document pairs independently and allows parallel processing, but it often struggles with absolute relevance estimation. In this work, we investigate whether non-relevance prompting provides a signal that differs from ordinary relevance prompting in LLM-based pointwise reranking. Specifically, we compute both relevance and non-relevance scores for each query-passage pair and examine two simple ways to combine them: (1) a simple product and (2) a probability-weighted RMSE to the ideal label targets. We evaluate these scores on 10 datasets from TREC and BEIR using nDCG@10 with GPT-4o-mini and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. With GPT-4o-mini, bidirectional scoring significantly improves over relevance-only scoring and achieves performance comparable to RankGPT, although gains over a two-prompt relevance-only control are not statistically significant. Further analysis on highly relevant DL19 pairs shows that flipped non-relevance scores often raise the scores of documents underestimated by the relevance prompt. In contrast, the effectiveness of using non-relevance scores for Llama varies across datasets, suggesting that the utility of non-relevance prompting is model-dependent.

papers.title: Difficulty-Gated Fusion of Reasoning Views for Temporal Retrieval
papers.abstract: Reasoning-intensive temporal retrieval requires matching a query to documents whose relevance depends on shared temporal reasoning rather than lexical overlap. Expanding a query into several reformulations that make its temporal intent explicit, and retrieving with each, supplies this reasoning, but fusing the resulting rankings with equal weights wastes accuracy: for any single query, only some reformulations are reliable. We propose query-difficulty-gated fusion of reasoning views. From each view we read an eight-dimensional signature of its score distribution, built from query-performance-prediction quantities such as softmax entropy, score gaps, and dispersion, and a gate of roughly one thousand parameters maps these signatures to per-query view weights. The fused ranking uses no relevance labels at inference, no re-ranking, and no fine-tuning of the retriever; the gate is trained leave-one-task-out. On the Tempo benchmark, the method improves all six retrievers we evaluate, from BERT encoders to 7B decoder retrievers, with the largest gains on the weaker backbones. The strongest retrievers reach 0.297 and 0.303 nDCG@10, and the per-query gain over the original query is significant under a paired bootstrap (p<0.001). A per-query oracle reaches 0.364 against our realized 0.297, exposing headroom that identifies per-query view selection as a concrete next step (https://github.com/DataScienceUIBK/difficulty-gated-reasoning-view-fusion).

papers.title: Learning to Act, Failing to Retrieve: Diagnosing Reward-Effectiveness Mismatch in Proactive Conversational Information Retrieval
papers.abstract: Proactive conversational information retrieval (CIR) requires an agent to decide not only what to retrieve, but how to act: when to ask the user for clarification, when to issue a new retrieval, and when to reuse evidence it has already gathered. We study this as a sequential dialogue-management problem over Ask, Push, and Reuse. We train the interaction policy with reinforcement learning in an LLM-driven environment providing user simulation, query reformulation, and a relevance judge that scores the training reward; evaluation instead uses held-out human relevance judgements (qrels). The resulting agent learns coherent, state-dependent behaviour and accumulates high shaped reward, yet its qrel-based retrieval effectiveness (nDCG, MAP) falls at or below simple non-learned baselines on iKAT. We argue that this reflects a reward–effectiveness mismatch: the shaped reward, scored by an LLM judge and crediting cheap reuse of buffered evidence, is only loosely coupled to held-out qrel effectiveness. We localize this mismatch to reward design and show that replacing the dialogue-shaped signal with a retrieval-gain-aligned reward recovers much of the gap to the strongest non-learned baseline—roughly doubling nDCG@10 and MAP, with the residual gap traced to clarification quality—suggesting that reward formulation is a key lever for aligning proactive dialogue behaviour with retrieval quality.

papers.title: Distributional Approximate Nearest Neighbour Search for Uncertainty-Aware Retrieval
papers.abstract: Approximate Nearest Neighbour search indices form the backbone of real-world recommender systems, enabling real-time candidate retrieval over million-item catalogues. Typically, a single point estimate embedding is learnt for every user and every item. At serving time, the user embedding queries the index for relevant items. Since these representations are learnt from sparse interaction data, they are noisy and might fail to capture all the nuances that contribute to “ relevance ”—ignoring the fundamental uncertainty that is inherent to them. The result is a retrieval pipeline that is systematically biased toward the small minority of popular head items with well-estimated embeddings, at the expense of the long-tail majority of niche, diverse, and serendipitous content. We propose dinosaur ( Di stributional Approximate Nearest N eighb o ur S e a rch for U ncertainty-Aware R etrieval): a simple and infrastructure-compatible framework to incorporate embedding uncertainty into candidate generation. Rather than indexing point estimates, dinosaur samples S i embeddings per item and constructs an index on this augmented set. Analogously, at query time, a user embedding is sampled. This two-sided stochastic retrieval process implicitly marginalises over embedding uncertainty, without requiring changes to model architecture or ANN index infrastructure. On the analytical side, we show that dinosaur recovers standard point-estimate retrieval as uncertainty vanishes, and we characterise how increased embedding variance expands the regions of latent space in which uncertain items are retrievable. Reproducible empirical observations align with these expectations, showing large coverage gains with small losses in offline recall.

papers.title: AdaMerge: Tuning-Free Patch Compression for Multi-Vector Visual Document Retrieval
papers.abstract: Multi-vector visual document retrieval (VDR) models such as ColPali and ColNomic achieve strong accuracy by representing each document with hundreds to thousands of patch-level embeddings, at substantial storage and latency cost. Existing compression methods either prune unimportant patches or merge similar ones into clusters; the recent state-of-the-art merging method Prune-then-Merge (PtM) consistently outperforms pruning-only baselines at high compression, but requires a per-dataset cluster budget m to be tuned by grid search. We observe that the merge-cosine sequence produced by hierarchical clustering exhibits a sharp cliff separating mergeable redundancy from salient signal, and that the location of this cliff is concentrated in a narrow band across more than 11,000 documents from 14 datasets. This suggests the merge boundary can be detected per document rather than tuned per dataset. Building on this observation, we propose AdaMerge, a plug-and-play compression method that (i) detects each document's own cliff via gap analysis on the merge-cosine trajectory, and (ii) builds attention-weighted cluster centroids to preserve salient signal. On the long-document benchmark ViDoRe-V2 (4 datasets, two backbones), AdaMerge significantly outperforms tuned PtM across the operating range (p < 10^-4); on the short-document benchmark ViDoRe-V1 (10 datasets, two backbones), where all merging methods are already near-lossless, AdaMerge matches tuned PtM without any per-dataset tuning. AdaMerge adds only about 10 ms per document and exposes a single global hyperparameter shared across all datasets and backbones.

papers.title: No Target-Language LLM? Simple English-Side Augmentations for Cross-Lingual Cross-Modal Retrieval
papers.abstract: Cross-lingual cross-modal retrieval (CCR) for low-resource languages typically relies on machine-translated (MT) captions that lack diversity and carry language-specific flaws. Recent work addresses this by enriching queries with more detailed visual descriptions via multimodal LLMs and complex alignment. We instead take a data-centric view: rather than adding richer semantics, making existing supervision more challenging and diverse better strengthens the target-language encoder, without requiring any target-language LLM. Specifically, we design two lightweight English-side augmentation strategies: semantic perturbation to construct hard negatives, and semantic-preserving rewriting to foster expression robustness. Generated once in English and shared across target languages via MT, our approach is both broadly applicable and cost-efficient. An adaptive selection mechanism chooses the most suitable perturbation per sample, while a visual-guided weighting down-weights noisy rewrites. Experiments on standard CCR benchmarks show consistent improvements across target languages, confirming that simple English-side augmentations effectively boost CCR.

papers.title: Query-Adaptive Statutory Evidence Construction for Statutory Question Answering
papers.abstract: In statutory question answering, a provision similar to the question may define an exclusion by citing other provisions elsewhere in the statute. Correct answers may therefore require scope context around the retrieved provision, other provisions listed alongside it, or provisions cited by number elsewhere in the statute. Most retrieval-augmented generation approaches either enlarge the retrieved chunk or apply a fixed neighborhood expansion. These strategies can miss provisions cited by number or include unrelated intervening text in the answer model's context. We exploit chapter, section, and article hierarchy plus parsed citation links to construct compact statutory evidence. From a single retrieved provision, the method follows only the relations the question needs: scope context, remaining items of an enumerated list, or specific cited provisions. We build a bilingual Japanese and English QA dataset covering these evidence types. On this QA dataset, the method gives the highest overall necessary-evidence coverage and final answer score among the tested baselines, with the clearest gains on citation-target questions. It also uses about half the broad-expansion context.

papers.title: SCAR: Semantic Continuity-Aware Retrieval for Efficient Context Expansion in RAG
papers.abstract: Fixed-length chunking in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) often leads to boundary fragmentation, where critical evidence is split across segments, degrading retrieval recall. While static windowing and parent retrieval improve recall, they introduce significant token overhead. We propose SCAR (Semantic Continuity-Aware Retrieval), an adaptive retrieval policy that selectively expands neighboring chunks by weighing query-neighbor relevance against a structural continuity penalty. SCAR uses a relative expansion threshold tied to each retrieved chunk's own query-relevance, yielding an approximately scale-invariant decision rule that transfers across embedding models without recalibration. Across four diverse corpora (RFC, GDPR, a 10-K report, and a Merger agreement; N=320 queries; 160 boundary-fragmented), SCAR achieves 92.8% recall on boundary-fragmented queries with only 7.84 chunks, a 22.9% reduction compared to static windowing (10.16 chunks). Paired bootstrap tests (B=10,000) confirm the chunk reduction is highly significant (p<0.0001, Cohen's d=-1.49, large effect), with a small recall difference (Cohen's d=-0.33). The policy transfers across three embedding models (text-embedding-3-large, BGE-large-en-v1.5, zembed-1) using the same single hyperparameter setting, and downstream RAGAS evaluation on the 10-K corpus confirms SCAR preserves generation faithfulness while reducing context tokens by 27.1%.

papers.title: FailSafe-RAG: Evidence-State-Aware Generation under Retrieval Failures
affiliations: Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves factual grounding by conditioning language models on retrieved evidence, but its reliability depends on whether the retrieved list is relevant, consistent, and semantically grounded. When retrieval fails under coverage gaps, conflicting passages, or lexical matching traps, generators may still produce definitive but unsupported answers. We propose FailSafe-RAG, a lightweight and training-free framework that treats retrieval failure as an explicit post-retrieval evidence state. Inspired by Query Performance Prediction (QPP) and retrieval-list coherence analysis, FailSafe-RAG estimates three evidence-risk indicators: coverage insufficiency, conflict risk, and evidence noise. A risk-prioritized policy maps the resulting risk state to behavior-conditioned generation, enabling clarification, abstention, cautious answering, or direct assertion without model fine-tuning or architectural changes. Experiments on failure-oriented splits derived from NQ, HotpotQA, and conflict-annotated QA instances show that FailSafe-RAG reduces overconfident failures while preserving competitive answer accuracy. The results highlight IR-based evidence assessment as a practical guardrail for reliable RAG.

papers.title: The Small-Model Graph-RAG Gap Is a Faithfulness Gap
papers.abstract: On multi-hop benchmarks, modern Graph-RAG retrieves the gold answer for 77-90% of questions, yet a budget open-weight 8B model answers only 31-77% correctly. We show that faithfulness (reading the retrieved evidence rather than guessing) and calibration (abstaining when it is insufficient) account for a large, recoverable part of this gap. A leak-controlled decomposition finds that on the hardest, least-contaminated benchmark (MuSiQue), 43% of questions have their supporting facts in the retrieved context yet are answered wrong, and on these the model gives a confident answer 82% of the time rather than abstaining. A grounding-and-calibration prompt makes the model answer from the retrieved context or abstain when it cannot, a more trustworthy operating point at no accuracy cost. A re-ask step then spends some of that calibration for coverage, turning abstentions into correct answers for a gain of +9 pp on KET-RAG and +13 pp on LightRAG (MuSiQue, answer-present slice) that closes about half the gap to a 70B model on KET-RAG and most of it on LightRAG. Few-shot example source moves the model along the same faithfulness-accuracy frontier, better for calibration than accuracy. Unlike structure-exploiting augmentations that degrade on uniform-relevance retrieval, grounding helps most there. For small-model Graph-RAG the target is faithful, calibrated use of retrieved evidence. Code is available at https://github.com/thomouvic/graphrag-faithfulness.

papers.title: Forward-Looking Guidance for Iterative RAG in Multi-Hop Question Answering
affiliations: Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Multi-hop question answering aims to answer complex queries by identifying and integrating evidence distributed across multiple documents. Existing iterative RAG approaches address this task by decomposing complex questions into plans or sub-questions, followed by repeated retrieval, evidence extraction, and reasoning to accumulate the information needed for the final answer. Nevertheless, intermediate outputs produced during this iterative process are often optimized locally rather than guided by future reasoning needs, making them useful for the current iteration but suboptimal for the overall multi-hop reasoning process. We empirically investigate the potential of forward-looking guidance in iterative RAG, where the remaining planned reasoning trajectory is incorporated into each iteration. We analyze its effect across retrieval, evidence extraction, and reasoning, and find that such guidance is especially beneficial for evidence extraction and reasoning, leading to more effective intermediate outputs and consistent improvements over iterative RAG baselines.

papers.title: HyperMind: Claim Resolution and Reputation Tracking for Trustworthy Multi-Agent LLM Aggregation
papers.abstract: The quality of knowledge produced by multi-agent generative AI systems depends not on the capability of individual agents but on the reliability of the communication layer between them. When agents disagree, that reliability is entirely invisible: no outcome is recorded, no agent is accountable, and the system learns nothing. This paper presents HyperMind , a protocol that makes disagreements productive by treating each resolved dispute as a verifiable calibration event, through three co-designed components: a seven-state Claim Resolution Finite State Machine (FSM) issuing signed provenance receipts; a Beta reputation system updated exclusively from FSM-verified outcomes; and DiversityGuard, which detects and interrupts premature consensus. On a 100-question enterprise benchmark spanning five domains, HyperMind achieves the lowest Brier score on all four tested LLMs; paired-difference 95% BCa confidence intervals exclude zero on two models (Gemma-4-26B [+0.0321,+0.0913], Wilcoxon p=0.0005, surviving Bonferroni correction across four models; Qwen-3.6-35B [+0.0021,+0.0737], p=0.037, not correction-surviving), though the n=100 evaluation is underpowered for the remaining two models (5–6% power). The full run costs $0.005 per 100 questions, and every resolved claim produces an auditable chain of custody over agent reliability.

papers.title: AdaCon: Learning Adaptive Trust Regions for Consistent LLM Agent Reasoning
affiliations: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly operate over long horizons, yet they drift, contradict themselves, and abandon working strategies as interaction lengthens. At each step, an agent may produce exploratory and conservative candidates, but their disagreement alone does not reveal which one should be executed. We formulate this choice as context-conditioned online prediction using environmental feedback from executed exploratory proposals. We therefore propose Adaptive Consistency (AdaCon), which uses similarity only to identify divergent proposals and applies a critic that learns from context whether to execute them, trained online from the environment's own reward without human labels. We establish a squared-error lower bound for similarity-only rules and a no-regret guarantee for a convex linear-critic special case. On ScienceWorld, AdaCon achieves higher reported mean scores than strong reinforcement-learning, reasoning, and consistency-supervised baselines across all task horizons, with the largest gains on long-horizon tasks.

papers.title: Redundancy-Aware Self-Consistency for Efficient LLM Reasoning
affiliations: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly solve multi-step reasoning tasks, where a single sampled chain of reasoning is frequently unreliable. Reaching a correct answer therefore requires aggregating many sampled reasoning paths into one trustworthy decision. The dominant family, self-consistency and its sampling-and-voting variants, suits such reasoning tasks, but its raw-count vote treats sampled paths as separate units of evidence, even when their reasoning is highly redundant. Within this regime, adaptive-budget methods curb the cost by deciding when to stop, yet their stopping signals are commonly based on the same redundancy-blind counts. We therefore propose Redundancy-Aware Consistency (RAC), which strengthens self-consistency by aggregating reasoning paths according to their effective support rather than their raw count. We establish the boundedness of this effective support and show that RAC recovers self-consistency when within-answer paths are mutually dissimilar. Experiments on four benchmarks with the primary backbone and a three-benchmark subset with a second backbone show that RAC achieves higher observed accuracy than the evaluated self-consistency and adaptive-budget baselines. On the primary backbone, it also uses substantially fewer samples.

papers.title: RATED: Reliability-Aware AI Agent Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics
papers.abstract: As AI agents increasingly rely on external tools, accurate retrieval is essential for reliable behavior. Existing methods optimize semantic relevance but largely ignore tool availability during execution. To address this gap, we propose RATED ( R eliability- A ware T ool retrieval via E xecution D ynamics), a retrieval framework that combines robust semantic matching with dynamic reliability adaptation. RATED employs a frozen dual-encoder with contrastive fine-tuning for semantic matching, and a lightweight contextual bandit module that re-ranks candidates based on real-time execution feedback. This design enables rapid adaptation to runtime tool failures without expensive model retraining. We introduce EcoAgent , a benchmark of 5,172 real-world tools and over 210,000 query–tool pairs for offline retrieval and dynamic reliability evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that RATED achieves a 52.2% relative MRR improvement over the ToolLLM API retriever on real-world queries, and reduces fault selection rate from 86.2% to 2.9% under severe API outage scenarios with a 30% failure rate, while incurring negligible latency overhead of less than 1 ms over encode-only inference. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Elliotes/EcoAgent.

papers.title: Entropy Interventions Do Not Transfer: Why RLVR Entropy Control Misfires in On-Policy Distillation
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) controls policy entropy by reweighting tokens against an external scalar advantage. On-policy distillation (OPD) faces the same surface problem, a student that can sharpen too fast, but it replaces that advantage with a per-token teacher target. That shared symptom makes an RLVR entropy fix look reusable. We show the reuse fails for a simple reason. Re-deriving the token-level entropy change of the OPD objective shows its governing factor is the covariance between the teacher-student probability gap and the log policy, not an advantage. The two decompositions disagree on which tokens drive entropy, so transplanting an RLVR entropy reweighting such as STEER into OPD damps exactly the teacher-corrective tokens the student must learn. A preliminary API analysis makes this failure mode visible before training, with corrective tokens over-represented in the high-entropy tail a STEER-style reweight suppresses. A controlled four-seed distillation run then confirms the prediction. Transplanting STEER collapses GSM8K accuracy from 38% to 7%, with corrective-token retention falling in step, while the MATH-500 effect stays within seed noise. We propose a corrected reweighting that reads the teacher-student sign before damping. It restores corrective-token retention and returns to the vanilla OPD band on GSM8K within seed noise.

papers.title: SymGRPO: Preventing Mode Collapse in Group Relative Policy Optimization via Symmetric Anti-Reinforcement
papers.abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has become the dominant critic-free method for reinforcement learning from human feedback in large language models, with growing adoption for fine-tuning LLM-based retrievers, query reformulators, rerankers, and agentic search systems. We identify a fundamental failure mode of GRPO in multi-prompt training: prompt-blind mode collapse, where the policy converges to a single output regardless of input prompt—a critical concern for information retrieval applications where prompt-conditioned behavior is essential. We prove this arises from a quadratic gradient vanishing at the collapsed state: GRPO's entropy restoration rate is ?(?²|log ?|) where ? = 1 ? ?_max. We propose SymGRPO, which augments GRPO with an anti-reinforcement log-barrier on unchosen tokens, raising the restoration rate to ?(?|log ?|)—a diverging ratio of ?(V?1)/?. Critically, this benefit appears only when the batch advantage sum S ? 0, which holds under EMA baselines but is forced to zero by standard mean-zero normalization. Across four small-scale reasoning tasks, GRPO mode-collapses to 19–50% accuracy while SymGRPO reaches 100% on multi-solution tasks. The modification is three lines of code.

papers.title: TriAgent: Granularity-Stratified Multi-Agent Routing with a Multilingual Semantic Cache and a Free Trust Signal for LLM Inference Pipelines
papers.abstract: LLM-based information pipelines—retrieval, classification, entity linking, intent inference—share a structural cost problem: the reasoner LLM dominates the per-query bill, yet a large fraction of queries are trivially handled by far cheaper specialists. We present TriAgent, a generic multi-agent inference router that stratifies agents by contextual granularity (word / sentence / cross-sentence) and gates routing with a three-way Semantic Divergence Index (SDI). On two financial testbeds we report four findings. (i) The critic plateau is calibration-conditional: on FPB (where FinBERT is well calibrated, ECE=0.016) critic protocols collapse 1.5B-7B Qwen to a single F1≈0.87 (bootstrap CIs overlap), while a same-size 3-persona vote drops to 0.66; on TFNS (where the specialist collapses to F1=0.66) the critic plateau fails, falling below the LLM-alone baseline. (ii) A Shared Consensus Dictionary on multilingual sentence-BERT answers 95% of Chinese queries from an English cache at F1=0.99 — a cross-lingual canonicaliser at zero marginal cost. (iii) The same SDI doubles as a post-hoc LLM-hallucination detector at AUC=0.90. (iv) At a 10M-user scale the architecture saves $363M/year against a GPT-4 baseline. The router, cache, and trust signal are domain-agnostic and apply directly to LLM-based IR pipelines.

papers.title: LEAD-Route: An Adaptive Language-Calibrated and Entropy-Aware LLM Selection for Homologous Model Routing
papers.abstract: With the increasing language diversity on the web, the demand for multilingual Question-Answering (QA) has grown significantly. To maximize QA performance, a common way is to equip multilingual large language models (MLLMs) with more parameters, which also incurs significant costs. To improve efficiency without losing performance, we propose a novel task, Homologous Model Routing (HMR) . Given a set of homologous MLLMs of varying parameter counts (such as Qwen2.5 1.5B, 3B...), HMR tries to select the minimum model that can just correctly answer the current question. Then, we propose a Language-Calibrated Entropy-Aware Dynamic Routing (LEAD-Router) that performs homologous model routing by estimating question difficulty based on response entropy and language-aware calibration. Experiments on the two datasets show that LEAD-Router achieves consistently better routing accuracy and QA performance than baselines.

papers.title: Weight-Adjusting Binary Transformation: A Dynamic Label Ranking Model for Multi-Label Data Stream Classification
papers.abstract: Multi-label data stream classification has unique challenges compared to typical classification tasks. The models do not have access to the entire data as classification is done instance by instance and the multi-label association makes predictions significantly more complex. Many of the existing solutions in this area do not scale well in terms of time efficiency and predictive accuracy when the number of labels grows. We propose Weight-Adjusting Binary Transformation (WABT), a lightweight problem transformation model which dynamically ranks labels with each arriving instance and applies binary transformation. WABT handles the problem of information loss typical in binary transformation models without increasing computational complexity. We evaluate WABT on 10 datasets, most with large numbers of labels, and compare it against four state-of-the-art problem transformation models. Overall, we demonstrate that WABT delivers the strongest average ranking across three effectiveness measures, achieves second-best performance on Hamming Score, while ranking highest in terms of time efficiency.

papers.title: Coordination-Free Schema Evolution for Replicated Property Graphs
affiliations: ENSIIE, Inria Paris, IRIF, SAMOVAR (Télécom SudParis)
papers.abstract: Collaborative applications increasingly manage interconnected data as property graphs whose data and schema both evolve at runtime. Under concurrent updates, schema migration either incurs high latency or risks data divergence, and concurrent schema changes must be merged correctly and reflected onto the data. We present Refract, a coordination-free middleware built on conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs). It combines a graph schema CRDT that deterministically merges concurrent Schema Modification Operators (SMOs), such as renames, property and label changes, and type splits and joins, into a single schema; a property-graph lens engine that lazily translates raw data into the current schema at query time, and a graph data CRDT that stores and merges schemaless data. To the best of our knowledge, Refract is the first system to treat property graph schema evolution itself as a replicated convergent object . Preliminary experiments on the LDBC Social Network Benchmark show that Refract matches the overhead of Cambria, the state-of-the-art document-level baseline, while adding graph-native schema merging, and cuts schema-change downtime by over two orders of magnitude compared to eager migration.

papers.title: Relational-View Ensemble Learning for Tabular Prediction
papers.abstract: Tabular prediction can benefit from relational information at multiple levels, including global feature relations, feature interactions within each sample, and relations among similar samples. Existing deep tabular methods exploit such information through attention-based, graph-based, and retrieval-based modeling. However, they often focus on only part of the relational structure or merge relational information into a shared representation, making it difficult to distinguish the predictive role of each relation type. We propose a relational-view ensemble framework for tabular prediction. Instead of simply integrating multiple relations into a single representation, the proposed model decomposes them into three distinct predictive views: global feature relations, intra-sample feature interactions, and inter-sample relations. Each view produces an independently supervised prediction logit, and the final prediction is obtained through learnable logit-level fusion. This design treats different relational axes as explicit predictive sources within a single architecture without training multiple model instances. Experiments on eight public tabular datasets show that the proposed framework achieves competitive performance against strong baselines, including gradient-boosted decision trees and recent deep tabular models, while achieving the best average rank across the evaluated methods. Ablation studies further show that the full three-view model achieves the best or tied-best performance on five of the six evaluated datasets, supporting the benefit of jointly modeling multiple relational views.

papers.title: Benchmarking Agentic Text-to-SPARQL for Multi-Hop Scholarly Knowledge Graph Exploration
papers.abstract: Conversational access to scholarly knowledge graphs promises more intuitive ways of exploring research fields, but current approaches remain limited by two major barriers: the lack of realistic multi-hop benchmarks and the brittleness of Text-to-SPARQL methods over real-world schemas. We address these gaps by introducing a benchmark of challenging, researcher-authored questions grounded in a domain-specific subset of DBLP. The benchmark targets realistic multi-hop scholarly information needs rather than synthetic or template-based queries. We evaluate five large language model-based SPARQL generation pipelines with increasing levels of schema grounding, decomposition, rule guidance, and endpoint feedback. Our results show that baseline and sequential approaches remain brittle, while a rule-augmented pipeline substantially improves execution accuracy and semantic alignment with the intended information need. The study contributes both a new testbed for evaluating conversational access to scholarly knowledge graphs and practical design insights for building more reliable, schema-aware Text-to-SPARQL agents.

papers.title: OntoForge: Continual Ontology and Knowledge Graph Construction via Multi-Agent Consensus and Self-Refining Procedures
affiliations: Shanghai Key Laboratory of Data Science, College of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence, Fudan University
JR Talent Technology Limited Company, Advantage AI Agent Lab
papers.abstract: Constructing domain ontologies and knowledge graphs (KGs) remains challenging when extraction procedures must operate across heterogeneous schemas and reuse feedback over time. Fixed prompts often miss valid triples, mis-handle canonicalization, and cannot adapt to recurring errors. We propose OntoForge, a multi-agent framework for continual ontology and KG construction. OntoForge generates recall-oriented and ontology-conformant candidates, verifies them through evidence- and schema-aware consensus, and maintains a self-refining Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) memory that converts recurrent conflicts into reusable procedural rules. On Text2KGBench across four Wikidata-TEKGEN domains, OntoForge improves triple-level F1 over direct prompting and static-SOP baselines across several LLM backbones, mainly through higher recall. Ablations show that gains are not explained by extra LLM calls alone, and sequential diagnostics show that persistent SOP adaptation benefits later construction windows after cold start.

papers.title: Automated Construction of FAIR Digital Object Knowledge Graphs from Flat Cultural Heritage Records
affiliations: Fraunhofer Institute for Applied Information Technology
Fraunhofer Institute for Applied Information Technology FIT
papers.abstract: The FAIR Digital Object (FDO) framework mandates that metadata attribute values be expressed as persistent identifiers (PIDs) wherever possible, producing a fully machine-actionable graph in which every reference is resolvable. The Europeana Data Model was designed long before the FDO specification and stores most metadata values as plain text. This supports human browsing, but gives an automated agent little to follow across records or collections. We present a pipeline that transforms flat Europeana records into an FDO-compliant knowledge graph structured with CIDOC-CRM. Following the FDO specification, we model every heritage entity as a discrete FDO with its own PID, type, profile, and metadata layer. The core technical challenge is automating the FDO-prescribed distinction between values that must become PID references (resolvable entities) and those that may remain literals (terminal leaves such as notes, measurements, and dates). We address this challenge using a large language model that classifies each metadata value, routes it to a controlled vocabulary (Getty AAT, Wikidata, VIAF, or PeriodO), and links it to a shared entity FDO. We evaluate the approach on 637 archaeological records from five Europeana providers. The pipeline links 86% of metadata slots and resolves 58.5% of values that Europeana had not already enriched. It also merges cross-lingual surface forms that byte-identical matching keeps separate; 17 of 33 such merges were correct on manual review. Graph connectivity alone does not distinguish this approach from string matching; what distinguishes the FDO graph is that every node is typed and resolvable.

papers.title: Formal-Informal Mathematical Alignment through and beyond Human Annotations
papers.abstract: Formalized mathematics libraries such as Lean's mathlib provide machine-verifiable representations of mathematical knowledge, including definitions, theorems, and their relationships. If effectively connected to informal mathematical resources, formal mathematics could help uncover previously implicit links between mathematical concepts and improve access to existing formalizations. However, connections between informal and formal mathematics libraries are currently sparse and unsystematic. In this paper, we make first strides towards better formal integration. We construct a dataset linking informal statements from the Stacks Project to their formalizations in mathlib by exploiting expert annotations. We evaluate retrieval, LLM-based reranking, and LLM-assisted verification to discover new unannotated informal-to-formal links. To facilitate exploration and reuse of formalized knowledge, we integrated the newly discovered alignments into the MaRDI knowledge graph, enabling mathematicians to find formal counterparts to informal mathematical content. We discuss the difficulties and challenges in using LLMs for linking formal and informal mathematical content. All code and data necessary for reproducing this paper can be found at: https://github.com/AnkitSatpute/Formal-Informal-Mathematical-Alignment

papers.title: When One Gold Entity Is Not Enough: Label Weakening for Robust Candidate Generation
papers.abstract: Entity linking and entity-centric question answering systems rely on candidate generation to retrieve a small set of plausible entities for a mention or question. This stage is commonly trained with hard labels, although entity annotations are often sparse, ambiguous, or noisy: semantically similar entities may be confused, plausible alternatives may be unannotated, and corrupted positives may be memorized during contrastive training. To mitigate this, in this short paper, we propose label weakening , a simple ambiguity-aware training strategy for robust entity candidate generation under noisy supervision. Instead of assuming a single reliable gold entity for each input, label weakening constructs a small set of plausible entity candidates from the observed annotation and model confidence, and optimizes a superset-ranking objective over this set. This weakens uncertain supervision without explicitly correcting labels or estimating a noise transition model. We evaluate label weakening on mention-to-entity and question-to-entity retrieval tasks. Results show that label weakening is particularly effective for preserving gold-entity Recall@10 in the candidate generation stage under high noise.

papers.title: Scaling Creative Writing Beyond Story-Centric Data with Attribute-Guided Genre Expansion
papers.abstract: High-quality creative writing data for language models remains dominated by story-centric data, limiting models' ability to follow the structural and functional conventions of diverse creative formats. We propose an attribute-guided genre expansion framework for scaling creative writing data beyond story generation. By separating thematic breadth from genre-form control, our framework leverages human-authored story prompts as diverse creative seeds, while utilizing manually curated genre attributes to enforce distinct structural, stylistic, and formatting conventions. We combine these to prompt strong models for genre-faithful query–response pairs, which are then quality-filtered. Applying this framework, we construct the Multi-Genre Collection , a 50K-example corpus spanning 13 creative genres, including story, lyrics, game design, and other creative formats. Experiments demonstrate that models fine-tuned on our data consistently surpass not only base models and writing-specialized baselines, but also models trained on existing writing corpora. Genre-count ablations further indicate that genre expansion is a key driver of robust creative writing capability.

papers.title: Simplify, Then Retrieve: Evaluating Meaning Preservation through Search Behavior
papers.abstract: Text simplification eases document understanding while preserving meaning, but this balance remains difficult to evaluate without reference simplifications. We propose a retrieval-based perspective: if a simplified document preserves the information content of its source, it should remain retrievable for the same queries. We test this idea on BEIR collections from biomedical, news, and Wikipedia domains, comparing original and simplified documents under BM25 and dense retrieval. We analyze both retrieval effectiveness and ranking stability and relate them to a diverse set of indicators that capture different aspects of faithfulness and simplification quality. Experimental results demonstrate that simplification can substantially affect retrieval behavior, especially when models aggressively compress or delete content. Conversely, conservative simplifiers tend to better preserve search effectiveness. These findings suggest that search behavior provides a practical and complementary reference-free signal for evaluating meaning preservation in text simplification.

papers.title: From Preferences to Values: Evaluating Latent User Understanding and Transfer in LLMs
papers.abstract: Personalized LLM agents should adapt to users who often reveal preferences through behavioral cues rather than explicit statements. Because existing benchmarks mainly evaluate surface-level profile matching, we propose PALETTE, a theory-driven benchmark designed to evaluate value-based user understanding in LLMs. Grounded in Schwartz's ten basic values, PALETTE contains 25,200 dialogues across 400 personas, pairing a historical dialogue that reveals a situational preference with a new context request that necessitates the same underlying value. We evaluate models on Dialogue-Based Understanding and New-Context Application to examine whether they can infer latent values from behavioral signals and generalize them across contexts. Our experiments with seven LLMs demonstrate that while models generate contextually appropriate dialog responses, they struggle to project an understanding of hidden values onto new contexts. PALETTE thus provides a diagnostic framework for verifying whether personalized agents can move beyond mere preference matching toward genuine, value-based user understanding. We make PALETTE publicly available at https://taehyungnoh.com/cikm26-palette/.

papers.title: The Wisdom of the Right Crowd: Platform Governance via Local Vote Authority Ranking
papers.abstract: Online communities require governance to function, yet enforcement has not kept pace with the scale of participation. Automated classifiers struggle with community-specific nuance, while crowdsourced approaches are reactive and slow. We ask whether communities themselves hold latent moderation expertise expressed through organic voting behavior, and introduce Vote Authority Ranking (VAR), a closed-form estimator computed per community that scores users from their voting history by weighting correct votes on minority classes, applying temporal decay toward recent activity, and regularizing against sparse evidence. We evaluate our approach on 83K moderation logs and voting actions across 11 Reddit communities over three years, against nine baselines. Our findings show that community votes carry a reliable signal about moderator decisions, and that VAR identifies high-authority users more reliably than every baseline. This authority does not transfer across communities, and integrating the votes of VAR-identified users into automated classifiers improves their performance. This study offers a practical and effective path for platform governance that is based on the voting activity communities already produce.

papers.title: TextZGCA: Text-Guided Zero-Gated Cross-Attention for 3D Human Motion Prediction
affiliations: Institute of Automation Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.abstract: 3D human motion prediction (HMP) forecasts future joint trajectories from a short observed pose sequence, but pose alone is often a narrow description of human behavior. A person who is turning, sitting down, or preparing to reach can have similar short-term pose dynamics while implying different futures. Modern vision-language models can turn simple stick-figure renders into natural-language descriptions, making semantic context available without changing the motion input itself. The challenge is to use this context without overwhelming a strong pose-only predictor with heavy language-conditioning machinery. We propose TextZGCA, a text-guided zero-gated cross-attention recipe for 3D HMP. Starting from a DCT-based spatial-temporal Transformer backbone, we encode each VLM-generated caption with a frozen plain CLIP-L text tower, project it into a small set of conditioning tokens, and insert a zero-gated cross-attention adapter after every motion encoder block. Because each adapter gate is initialized to zero, the model is initially identical to the no-text baseline and can learn to use text only where it improves prediction. On Human3.6M, TextZGCA achieves the best short-horizon and overall MPJPE among representative state-of-the-art methods in our comparison, while avoiding FiLM branches, auxiliary heads, and retrieval banks. The same recipe also achieves competitive results on CMU-Mocap, supporting a simple view of language in HMP: captions are useful as a semantic prior attached to a strong motion model.

papers.title: Beyond Answer Accuracy: Diagnosing Perception Failures in Multimodal Mathematical Reasoning
papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown strong performance on mathematical reasoning tasks that combine textual and visual information. However, final-answer accuracy offers limited insight into whether errors arise from incorrect perception, modality-dependent information extraction, or downstream reasoning. We introduce a perception-aware diagnostic framework for bimodal mathematical reasoning that represents a model's perceived problem understanding as knowledge graph triples and evaluates them using an Auxiliary Perception Set (APS), a human-verified collection of perception-oriented questions grounded in directly observable input information. We apply the framework to Plane Geometry problems from MathVerse, evaluating three MLLMs across two input representations: text and diagram embedded in a single image, and text and diagram provided separately. We also test controlled textual and visual perturbations to examine robustness under modality-specific noise. Results show that perception accuracy and final-answer accuracy often diverge: models that generate more accurate perception triples do not necessarily achieve higher final-answer accuracy, and the same problem content can produce different behavior depending on input representation. Cross-model triple transfer further shows that downstream performance depends on both the quality of extracted perceptual structure and the model's ability to reason over it. These findings suggest that perception-aware evaluation exposes failure modes hidden by answer-only evaluation and provides a finer-grained diagnostic view of bimodal mathematical reasoning. (Detailed implementation code, prompts, our multimodal noise-variant dataset, and results are available on GitHub: https://github.com/Anshu-Mehta/CIKM-2026. An interactive project website is available at https://perception-in-mllms.netlify.app/.)

papers.title: Direct Answers, Hidden Criteria: Empirical Trade-offs in LLM Responses to Underdetermined Prompts
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in question answering, recommendation, and conversational decision support. In many such settings, the user asks for a single answer even though the prompt does not specify the criterion needed to justify a unique choice. We study this setting as semantic underdetermination: multiple answers remain compatible with the prompt unless an additional ranking criterion is supplied. Rather than claiming a formal impossibility result, we study an empirical tension among three properties: premise-entailment correctness, criterion neutrality, and single-turn decisiveness. We evaluate 140 manually curated underdetermined prompts across seven categories on six LLMs, from 4B to frontier scale, under four response policies that handle under-specification differently. Forcing a direct answer makes models far more decisive (decisive rate 32%→93%) but lowers judged utility (4.06→3.53 out of 5, a large effect), because a confident answer must commit to a criterion the user never gave. Asking for the missing criterion instead gives the highest judged utility (4.53/5) and LLM-predicted satisfaction (4.48/5) but is rarely decisive in one turn (5.4%). A criterion-sensitivity score supports the mechanism: differences are small in size, but every one of the six models is most criterion-sensitive when forced to answer and least when it asks for the criterion. These findings suggest that asking for the missing criterion is a practical and transparent strategy for LLM systems facing under-specified user requests.

papers.title: Beyond Benchmark Scores: How Synthetic and Authentic Query Distributions Diverge in RAG Evaluation
papers.abstract: RAG systems are routinely evaluated using synthetic question sets generated from the target document corpus. While this practice provides a useful check on overall retrieval capability, relying exclusively on synthetic benchmarks can mislead under distribution shift and overstate deployment readiness. Synthetic generation spreads questions evenly across the corpus, formulating long, detailed queries; real users put most of their traffic on a few administrative and procedural topics in short queries, while also asking about matters the generator never covers at all. We demonstrate this gap on a university faculty information system, comparing 1,851 synthetic questions generated via Gemini Notebook against 322 authentic queries collected via a student survey. The synthetic and authentic query sets differ significantly: authentic queries average 6.8 words versus 15.7 for the synthetic ones, and draw from only 53 unique sources compared to 165. Consequently, configurations that appear highly effective on synthetic benchmarks experience a substantial performance drop on authentic queries. Importantly, optimizing on synthetic queries selected a higher-latency hybrid retriever. In our setting the sparse retrieval component benefited long synthetic questions but not short authentic ones, costing up to 8× the latency of the fastest configuration we tested. We propose treating synthetic and authentic query sets as complementary extremes of the query-quality spectrum: synthetic data verifies maximum retrieval capacity under idealized conditions, while authentic queries test system robustness to the imprecise, underspecified inputs of real users.

papers.title: Cite Unseen: Measuring Citation-Channel Vulnerabilities in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: Citation-grounded retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems expose source URLs alongside answers, extending user trust to cited links. Prior corpus-poisoning research primarily targets answer corruption, overlooking cases where answers remain largely unchanged while citations route users to unsafe destinations. We identify this citation-channel vulnerability and introduce Citation-stage Attack Success Rate (C-ASR) to separate citation manipulation from answer degradation. Across four BEIR corpora, three retrievers, and four generators, changing only the source URL of a single injected document reaches 71% C-ASR on the most vulnerable generator at well under 1% corpus pollution. The attack persists with paraphrased or answer-derived content, while citation behavior differs sharply across generators under our fixed pipeline. These results expose a model-dependent safety surface missed by answer-centric RAG evaluation.

papers.title: Embedding-Space Attacks on Pathology Foundation Models for Histopathology Retrieval
papers.abstract: Pathology Foundation Models (PFMs) are increasingly being used as frozen encoders for content-based retrieval in histopathology archives. In this context, a malicious actor does not need to alter a class label; a slight modification to the query image can shift its embedding and change the retrieved neighbors. We examine this vulnerability within an input-only white-box threat model, wherein the adversary has access to encoder gradients, but not to labels, classifier heads, retrieval pairs or the protected gallery. We instantiate PGD attacks with embedding-space objectives, comparing them with a random-noise baseline and evaluating training-free input transformations defenses under retrieval protocols that measure both embedding stability and ranking quality. Results across recent pathology encoders and benchmark datasets show that rankings can be severely degraded without gallery access, while simple symmetric preprocessing can partially restore retrieval performance.

papers.title: Trigger-Invariant Contrastive Unlearning for Backdoor Removal
papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks embed hidden triggers that cause malicious model behavior at inference time. Gradient-ascent-based unlearning methods attempt to remove such behavior by maximizing loss on poisoned samples, but they may redirect the trigger’s effect to other classes rather than eliminate it. We propose Trigger-Invariant Contrastive Unlearning (TICU), an invariance-based framework that constructs clean and trigger-inserted counterfactual pairs and aligns both output distributions and hidden representations. Across multiple datasets, model architectures, and attack settings, TICU reduces triggered-accuracy drift compared with strong unlearning baselines, suggesting improved mitigation of trigger shifting. However, TICU exhibits a trade-off: it often better preserves triggered-task behavior while leaving higher residual label-flip rates than some baselines. These findings highlight both the promise and limitations of invariance-based backdoor unlearning.

papers.title: BIRDNet: Mining and Encoding Boolean Implication Knowledge Graphs as Interpretable Deep Neural Networks
affiliations: BITS Pilani, K K Birla Goa Campus
papers.abstract: Tabular data in knowledge-rich domains often carries a latent prior in the form of Boolean implication relationships (BIRs) between pairs of features. We mine such relationships with a sparse-exception binomial test. We encode the resulting typed graph as the connectivity of a layered neural network, called BIRDNet, in which each hidden unit corresponds to one mined rule and binds only to its two features. We show two consequences of this design: First, the architecture is sparse: at most 2/d of the weights in each BIR layer are active, where d is the input dimension. Second, the model is intrinsically interpretable: every trained unit keeps a stable symbolic identity, so rules can be read off the network without surrogate models. Unlike most neurosymbolic models, BIRDNet does not consume an external rule base; its structural prior is mined from the data. We evaluate BIRDNet on six transcriptomic and proteomic benchmarks. Our results show that BIRDNet stays within 0.02 AUROC of the strongest dense baseline, while using up to 95× fewer active parameters than an architecture-matched dense MLP. First-layer rules align with known biological signatures across multiple cancer subtypes and tissue types. Matched-topology controls show that the mined graph contributes symbolic meaning rather than predictive advantage: shuffled or random pairings match or improve AUROC but no longer correspond to mined implications. Data and code are available at: https://github.com/MAHI-Group/BIRDNet.

papers.title: Adversarial Deception-based Detection of Anomalous Network Communities
papers.abstract: Detecting anomalous communities in complex networks is a fundamental task in network science, cybersecurity, and social network analysis. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework for anomalous community detection that accounts for the intentional manipulation of community structures through adversarial deception strategies. Intuitively, our notion of anomalous community captures communities whose structure can be deliberately perturbed to evade community detection algorithms while preserving their internal cohesion. The rationale underlying this novel notion is that well-formed communities are more difficult to hide within the overall network structure and are inherently difficult to conceal, whereas anomalous ones are particularly vulnerable to deception. We formalize the notion of deception anomaly by combining community deception metrics with statistical unexpectedness measures derived from the distribution of deception scores across candidate communities. Building on these definitions, we propose DACAD (Deception-based Adversarial Community Anomaly Detection). We perform a preliminary evaluation of the proposed approach on synthetic benchmark networks, analyzing the effectiveness of the proposed approach for different network topologies and deception budgets and comparing our method with related competing approaches.

papers.title: MASK: Minority-aware Semantic Alignment via Knowledge Enhancement for Long-tailed Graph Clustering
papers.abstract: Text-attributed graph (TAG) clustering seeks to identify node groups by jointly exploiting the semantic information encoded in textual attributes and the structural information captured by graph connectivity. Despite significant progress, their performance often becomes less satisfactory under long-tailed distributions. To address this challenge, we introduce Minority-Aware Semantic Alignment via Knowledge Enhancement (MASK), an unsupervised framework designed for long-tailed TAG clustering. The core idea of MASK is to integrate the textual understanding capability of large language models (LLMs) with canonical correlation maximization to construct minority-aware semantic groups. More specifically, MASK first leverages LLMs to augment textual attributes and generate multiple textual views, which are then aligned via canonical correlation. Subsequently, we randomly assign samples into balanced groups with mixed semantics for consistency learning and then emphasize those with higher semantic discrepancy as minority candidates. To enhance clustering with external knowledge, we leverage LLMs to fine-tune the model with ranking guidance, which is then formulated as a regularization term. Extensive experiments on four datasets under two varying imbalance ratios demonstrate the effectiveness of MASK. The implementation of MASK is publicly available at https://github.com/fuyw-aisw/MASK.

papers.title: SparkAlign: A Star-Hopping Heuristic for Efficient Unsupervised Plain Graph Alignment
papers.abstract: Unsupervised plain graph alignment (UPGA) seeks corresponding nodes between two graphs from topology alone, without attributes or seed anchors. The dominant embed-then-match paradigm is expensive on both fronts: it repeatedly retrains node embeddings and then solves a costly global assignment, so it scales poorly to large graphs. We present SparkAlign, a training-free heuristic that, inspired by star-hopping in celestial navigation, locates a node's counterpart by measuring its heat-diffusion proximity to a shared set of high-confidence landmark matches. Although heuristic in spirit, the descriptor is principled: diffusion makes structurally equivalent nodes comparable across graphs, and a short stability analysis justifies a finite diffusion depth. Matching then uses two sparse, highly parallel strategies that avoid dense global assignment, one favoring speed and one preserving one-to-one consistency on a restricted candidate set. On three benchmarks SparkAlign attains accuracy approaching a structural identifiability reference while running up to two orders of magnitude faster than the strongest baseline and seeding markedly more accurate pseudo-anchors. Our code is available at https://github.com/MaxQ545/SparkAlign.

papers.title: PRISM: Reliable LLM Knowledge Distillation from Graph-Context Perspectives for Text-Attributed Graph Learning
papers.abstract: Text-attributed graph (TAG) learning aims to leverage both textual attributes and graph structures for node classification. Recent studies have utilized Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate pseudo-labels and rationales for few-label TAG learning. However, existing approaches typically rely solely on the textual attribute of target nodes, making the generated knowledge susceptible to noise and unreliability. To address this limitation, we propose PRISM (Perspective-based Reliable Imitation with Semantic Multiplicity), a reliability-aware knowledge distillation framework for few-label TAG learning. PRISM constructs multiple structural-context perspectives for each target node and estimates the reliability of LLM-generated knowledge based on cross-perspective consistency. The resulting reliability weights are then incorporated into the distillation process, enabling GNNs to place greater emphasis on more reliable supervision signals. Extensive experiments on five TAG benchmark datasets demonstrate that PRISM consistently outperforms existing methods in few-label node classification.

papers.title: Hyperlink Prediction on Hypergraphs of Text
papers.abstract: Hypergraphs are powerful tools for modeling high-order relationships in complex real-world data, and hyperlink prediction has emerged from the need to infer relationships that are missing or have not yet formed. Existing hyperlink prediction methods primarily emphasize the structural connectivity encoded in the network, overlooking the rich semantic information associated with nodes and hyperedges that can be expressed in text. In this work, we propose a novel framework for hyperlink prediction on Hypergraphs of Text (HoTs), where both nodes and hyperedges are enriched with textual attributes. Our model jointly leverages these semantic and structural signals by combining hypergraph convolutional operators with cross-attention mechanisms that iteratively refine node and hyperedge representations. Experimental results demonstrate that integrating semantic information from nodes and hyperedges with structural features consistently improves performance over baselines that rely solely on topology, thereby highlighting the effectiveness of contextual representations for hyperlink prediction and opening new directions for semantic-aware hypergraph learning.

papers.title: Classification-Aware Graph Construction and Learning for Time Series Classification
papers.abstract: Recent GNN-based time series methods often fail to align graph and mini-batch construction with the classification objective, weakening target-neighbor interactions essential for accurate classification. In particular, time series similarity-based graphs may induce structural distortions by over-connecting different classes or under-connecting the same class, and random mini-batches may exclude the important neighbors of a target from the same batch. To address this, we define the Class-Discriminative Neighborhood ( CDN ), a graph neighborhood structure beneficial for classification, and analyze it from two perspectives: quality and connectivity . Quality refers to how strongly a target is connected to same-class neighbors and weakly to different-class ones, while connectivity refers to how sufficiently these neighbors are utilized in GNN message passing. To enhance both aspects, we propose the Classification-aware Graph Construction and Learning ( CGCL ) framework with two key modules. First, Embedding-Aware Graph Learning improves CDN quality by first learning embeddings from a time series graph and then further reconstructing it from more discriminative embeddings. Second, Target-Aware Mini-Batch strengthens CDN connectivity by including a target and its neighbors in the same batch. Experimental results on the UCR datasets show that CGCL improves classification accuracy by 10.7%p on average over SOTA classification models.

papers.title: SemSTG: Semantic State Transition Graphs for Time Series Event Forecasting
papers.abstract: Accurate time-series event prediction is critical in many real-world domains, such as web traffic monitoring and industrial system management. It relies on identifying distinct underlying states or representative patterns from observed data. However, existing studies mainly focus on state detection and pattern extraction, yet the evolutionary correlations and transition dynamics between states have largely been overlooked. In this paper, we propose a data-driven framework, called the semantic state transition graph network (SemSTGN). Specifically, SemSTGN constructs a semantic state transition graph (SemSTG) from time series with a self-supervised state recognition approach. Furthermore, we introduce a novel graph neural network to learn robust representations of the semantic state transition graph. SemSTGN can capture node-level and graph-level features in the SemSTG, then fuse such characteristics to predict future events in an end-to-end manner. Experimental results on four real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach consistently outperforms 16 baseline methods.

papers.title: ICLFS:Inverted Contrastive Learning For Unsupervised Feature Selection
papers.abstract: Unsupervised feature selection is important for high-dimensional data analysis, yet many existing methods rely on graph construction, spectral objectives, or reconstruction-based criteria that may be difficult to adapt across domains. We propose Inverted Contrastive Learning for Feature Selection (ICLFS), a contrastive unsupervised feature selection method that treats each feature as a training instance and learns feature representations from multiple perturbed views of its sample-profile vector. Experiments on benchmark datasets from multiple domains show that the proposed method outperforms strong classical and neural baselines on the selected evaluation suite, suggesting that feature-wise contrastive learning is a promising direction for unsupervised feature selection and other feature-related tasks.

papers.title: Evaluating Interestingness Functions for Automated Exploratory Clustering: A Scenario-Based Benchmark
papers.abstract: Automated Exploratory Clustering returns a set of diverse, high-quality clusterings rather than a single solution, supporting practitioners in discovering multiple valid knowledge structures within a dataset. A key open question is how to quantify the interestingness of such a clustering set, i.e., its likelihood of providing actionable insight to a user, so that it can serve as an optimization objective in an automated system. We formalize four practical usage scenarios with distinct requirements (e.g., prioritizing the best clustering vs. minimizing evaluation effort), propose four novel interestingness functions, and benchmark all six functions (including two from prior work) across 136 datasets using seven scenario-aligned evaluation measures. Our results show that the choice of interestingness function substantially impacts set composition and utility: MMR-based interestingness yields the highest-quality individual clusterings but produces unnecessarily large sets, whereas our proposed functions generate compact sets better suited to cost-sensitive or exploration-focused scenarios. We provide actionable recommendations for matching interestingness functions to usage scenarios in automated knowledge discovery systems.

papers.title: Attribution-Aware Active Learning for Pairwise Constrained Clustering
affiliations: IRIT, UMR 5505 CNRS, Université de Toulouse, UT2J
IRIT, UMR 5505 CNRS, Université Toulouse Capitole
Université de Toulouse, CNRS UMR 5070, INSERM U1301, EFS, ENVT, Institut RESTORE
papers.abstract: Active constraint-based clustering iteratively incorporates user knowledge through pairwise constraints to improve clustering quality while minimizing annotation effort. Existing approaches rely on two main heuristics: representativeness and uncertainty. Although effective, these strategies may select constraints that do not accurately capture the underlying data structure. In this paper, we introduce a novel active constraint-based clustering approach that formulates constraint selection as a hybrid learning task. Our method first identifies a small set of representative samples to build a supervised model. We then exploit feature attribution scores derived from this model, using SHAP values to build an attribution-based representation space that captures the contribution of each feature. This space enables the identification of highly uncertain regions of the data. By jointly leveraging representativeness, uncertainty, and attributions, our approach selects pairwise constraints from the most informative regions of the data space, leading to more effective clustering guidance and improved query efficiency.

papers.title: Label-Free Pairwise Embedding Comparison via Local Map Spectra
papers.abstract: We study label-free pairwise comparison of embedding spaces for model selection. Existing unsupervised quality metrics usually assign one scalar score to each embedding matrix and rank candidate models by these scores. This ignores the object-level correspondence available when two embedding spaces are computed on the same unlabeled objects. Using this correspondence, we compare embedding spaces through local maps between their point clouds. Spectral summaries of these maps produce pairwise scores that are evaluated against downstream classifier accuracy differences. Across the reported matched comparisons---four spectral summaries on four datasets, plus effective-rank results on two additional datasets---the map-based score improves the matched global metric in 16/18 comparisons by correct ranking ratio. Mean signed Spearman correlation increases from 0.199 for the matched global metrics to 0.591 for the corresponding local-map scores. Ablations show the role of neighborhood scale, comparison with one-directional maps, adaptive neighborhood selection, and full-spectrum map summaries.

papers.title: Transferability of Knowledge-Distilled Lottery Tickets Across Object Classification Tasks in Images
papers.abstract: The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) states that large neural networks contain sparse subnetworks, referred to as "winning tickets", that can match the performance of the original dense model when trained in isolation. Recent work has shown that knowledge distillation improves training stability and produces sparser subnetworks that retain the performance of the original ticket, leading to the Knowledge-Distilled Lottery Ticket (KDLT) framework. In this work, we investigate whether sparse subnetworks discovered using KDLT can be used effectively for downstream tasks. We evaluate the performance of these subnetworks across several vision datasets with varying levels of task similarity. Experiments are conducted on three settings: CIFAR-100 to CIFAR-10, Tiny-ImageNet to CIFAR-10, and Tiny-ImageNet to CIFAR-100. Our results show that KDLT-discovered subnetworks can be trained effectively across related vision tasks, particularly at low to medium sparsity levels. Even at high sparsities, the subnetworks retain strong performance, although, as is expected, a modest drop relative to the directly trained target-dataset tickets is observed. Furthermore, KDLT matches or modestly exceeds standard LTH in most settings.

papers.title: Judging a Review by its Cover: A Reliability Analysis of LLM-based Peer Review Evaluation Metrics
papers.abstract: Peer-review evaluation is increasingly being automated with LLM-as-a-judge metrics, but this creates a measurement risk. A review may receive a high score because it is fluent, organized, and polished, rather than because it provides a strong evaluation of the paper. This risk is especially important in AI-assisted reviewing, where reviewers may use LLMs to improve clarity or presentation while preserving the underlying judgments. We propose a statistical framework for testing whether peer-review evaluation metrics capture substantive review quality beyond surface-level linguistic form. The framework compares original human reviews with faithful LLM rewrites that preserve the same evaluative content while changing wording and presentation. Using a dataset comprising 4,044 meaning-preserving rewrites derived from 674 human reviews from ICLR and NeurIPS, we evaluate 29 content-oriented peer-review evaluation metrics drawn from four prior works through complementary tests of surface sensitivity and robustness . Although these metrics are intended to capture review properties beyond surface-level, writing-dependent characteristics, we find that sensitivity to rewriting is widespread. Under our primary analysis, 23 metrics assign significantly different scores to reviews whose evaluative content is preserved, while only six satisfy our robustness criterion. The patterns are largely consistent across two LLM judge models, suggesting that the issue is not specific to a single judge. These findings show that many peer-review evaluation metrics partially conflate review quality with linguistic presentation, and indicate that robustness to meaning-preserving rewriting should be validated before such metrics are used to compare human-written, AI-assisted, and AI-generated reviews. All evaluation results, prompts, and implementation code are publicly available in our GitHub repository: https://github.com/Reviewerly-Inc/llm_judge_reliability_analysis.

papers.title: Verification-Guided Specification Synthesis with Large Language Models for Intrusion Detection Rules
papers.abstract: Attacks against Internet-connected IoT devices continue to increase; however, transforming observed attack traffic into deployable intrusion detection system (IDS) rules remains largely a manual process. Recent studies have explored using large language models (LLMs) to generate IDS rules; nonetheless, existing approaches often require auxiliary information beyond observed traffic or generate rules without validating their detection logic against benign traffic. This study presents a verification-guided specification synthesis framework for generating Suricata rules directly from HTTP request traces. Instead of having an LLM generate IDS rules in a single step, an LLM first identifies a vulnerable parameter and synthesizes a semantic detection specification. These specifications are iteratively refined through counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS), in which benign traffic samples serve as counterexamples during synthesis and verification. Verified specifications are then deterministically compiled into Suricata rules. Experiments on 281 real-world CVEs and benign traffic collected from real IoT devices show that the proposed method achieves a detection rate of 81.5% while maintaining a false positive rate of 0.0%. An ablation study also demonstrates that CEGIS-based verification improves detection performance while maintaining a low false positive rate.

papers.title: Can Frontier LLMs Capture $40 Billion in Supply Chain Value?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform well on many NLP tasks, but their ability to reason about complex supply chain relationships remains unclear.
