We introduce the Supply Chain Intuition Exam (SCIE), a benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can identify and infer direct and indirect supplier relationships. We compare standard LLMs, models with grounding-based retrieval, and deep research (DR) systems. Despite access to public financial reports and real-world data, recall remains low: standard and grounded models achieve approximately 3--16%, while the best DR systems reach only 22%. These results suggest that retrieval alone is insufficient for professional-grade supply chain reasoning. SCIE highlights the need for methods that better integrate domain knowledge, retrieval, and multi-step reasoning in business and finance applications.

papers.title: Beyond Event Prediction: A Loss Function for Operational Ordinal Wildfire Risk
affiliations: Université Marie et Louis Pasteur, CNRS, institut FEMTO-ST (UMR 6174)
papers.abstract: Wildfire prediction is often framed as classification or regression, yet operational management relies on coherent ordinal risk levels. We propose the Cluster-Centered Latent Transition Loss (CCLLT), a novel ordinal objective designed for operational wildfire risk. Rather than predicting event occurrence directly, the proposed framework learns ordinal operational risk systems whose levels correspond to increasing real-world operational consequences. CCLLT combines latent ordinal centers, hierarchical EMA priors, monotonic ranking constraints, coverage regularization, and adaptive threshold calibration to directly optimize the ordinal consistency of risk signals. Unlike standard classification, it enforces monotonic operational transitions while preventing collapse toward dominant low-risk classes. Evaluated via a monotonic explainability framework, our approach successfully moves prediction beyond event-centered metrics to produce stable, interpretable, and operationally meaningful risk signals.

papers.title: SemIKT: Semantic-driven Inductive Knowledge Tracing
affiliations: The University of New South Wales
papers.abstract: Knowledge Tracing (KT) is a core component of Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS), enabling adaptive learning by modelling a student's evolving knowledge state to predict future performance. Most KT methods rely on question identifiers, limiting generalisability to newly introduced questions without retraining, a significant constraint for real world deployment. We present SemIKT , a semantic-driven inductive KT framework that replaces question identifiers with generalisable pretrained language-model embeddings, augmented with expert-annotated difficulty labels and contrastive auxiliary objectives. We evaluate against 16 baselines on XES3G5M, a benchmark dataset, and SFSD, a private, de-identified education dataset. SemIKT outperformed all baselines on SFSD, achieving a 1.3% AUC improvement over the strongest baseline. Under a strict unseen-question setting where 25% of questions were held out from all stages of training, SemIKT achieved an AUC of 76.10%, demonstrating viable zero-shot prediction for unseen questions.

papers.title: Agentic Reasoning Is Not Always Better: Evidence from Clinical Time-Series Explanation
papers.abstract: Continuous physiological monitoring is central to emergency care, yet building trustworthy, clinically usable AI remains challenging. While LLMs translate complex physiological signals into natural-language clinical narratives, it remains unclear whether agentic reasoning frameworks improve the quality of explanations over zero-shot inference. We present Vivaldi, a role-structured multi-agent system for explaining multivariate physiological time series in emergency department settings. We evaluate through a controlled clinical pilot involving a small cohort of emergency medicine experts. Their assessments challenge the assumption that increasingly complex agentic reasoning uniformly improves performance. Our experiments show agentic pipelines substantially benefit non-reasoning and medically fine-tuned models, improving expert-rated explanation justification and relevance by +6.9 and +9.7 points, respectively. Contrarily, for reasoning models, agentic orchestration often degrades explanation quality, including a 14-point drop in relevance, while improving diagnostic precision (ESI F1 +3.6). We also find explicit tool-based computation is decisive for codifiable clinical metrics, whereas subjective targets, such as pain scores and length of stay, show limited or inconsistent changes. Expert evaluation indicates gains in clinical utility depend on visualization conventions, with medically specialized models achieving favorable trade-offs between utility and clarity. Together, these findings show that the value of agentic AI lies in the selective externalization of computation and structure rather than in maximal reasoning complexity, highlighting concrete design trade-offs that are broadly applicable to explainable AI in safety-critical healthcare settings.

papers.title: Contrastive Captioning for Clinical Time-Series: Learning Joint ECG–Text Representations through Retrieval and Generation
papers.abstract: Recent approaches to clinical time-series report generation increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) and retrieval-augmented pipelines, achieving strong performance at the cost of substantial computational complexity. Consequently, the fundamental factors that govern effective multimodal representation learning for physiological signals remain poorly understood. We present a systematic study of contrastive captioning for electrocardiogram (ECG) report generation using a lightweight adaptation of the Contrastive Captioners (CoCa) framework. Across both the curated PTB-XL dataset and the large-scale MIMIC-IV-ECG corpus, we investigate the effects of decoder architectures, diagnostic representation quality, semantic supervision, and uncertainty-aware latent regularization on joint ECG--text representation learning. Our experiments reveal four key findings: (i) Encoder--decoder models substantially outperform decoder-only architectures for conditioning text generation on continuous physiological representations. (ii) Replacing clinical reports with demographic pseudo-text induces severe degradation in cross-modal retrieval performance, suggesting that demographic-only text is insufficient for robust ECG--text alignment at scale. (iii) Frozen contrastive ECG–text embeddings encode clinically meaningful diagnostic structure, as shown by strong linear-probe performance on PTB-XL diagnostic superclasses. (iv) While conventional latent regularization strategies improve performance in data-scarce settings, they do not transfer effectively to larger-scale datasets. We show that multimodal uncertainty conditioning alleviates this limitation and yields improved report generation performance at scale. Together, these findings establish practical design principles for scalable multimodal learning from clinical time series

papers.title: BERT4DTI : BERT-based Model for Predicting Drug-Protein Interactions
affiliations: Imaging and Orthopaedics Research Laboratory, CHUM Research Center
papers.abstract: Understanding how drugs interact with protein targets is fundamental to drug discovery, drug repurposing and the early identification of promising therapeutic candidates before costly experimental testing. Sequence-based DTI models face three practical limitations: labelled interactions are scarce and unevenly distributed, large pretrained chemical and protein encoders are expensive to fine-tune end-to-end, and independently encoded sequences do not capture pair-specific dependencies. We present BERT4DTI, which encodes SMILES strings with ChemBERTa and amino-acid sequences with ProtBERT, applies bidirectional mutual attention between token-level representations, and classifies the resulting interaction features using convolutional layers and a multilayer perceptron. To reduce trainable size, ProtBERT is truncated to 18 retained layers and only the last two layers of each encoder are fine-tuned. On BIOSNAP, DAVIS and BindingDB, BERT4DTI is competitive, achieving the best ROC-AUC and PR-AUC on BIOSNAP and the highest sensitivity on all three benchmarks. An ablation on DAVIS shows that mutual attention improves PR-AUC and specificity. With 125M trainable parameters compared with 353M for full BERT fine-tuning, BERT4DTI provides a favourable performance--parameter trade-off for sequence-based DTI screening, while leaving runtime profiling, calibration and leakage-audited validation for future work.

papers.title: TG-SEG: Text-Guided and Presence-Aware Temporal Propagation for Medical Image Segmentation
papers.abstract: Segmenting anatomical structures or lesions in medical image sequences using natural language descriptions is challenging due to subtle visual cues, ambiguous boundaries, and temporal appearance variations across frames or slices. Existing text-guided segmentation methods typically operate on individual images and lack explicit temporal modeling. This results in unstable predictions when the target is temporarily absent. In this work, we propose TG-SEG, a text-guided segmentation framework that integrates vision-language alignment with propagation-based temporal tracking and a novel presence-aware gating mechanism to ensure consistent sequence-level predictions. We evaluate our method on four medical imaging datasets with sequence characteristics, including ACDC, MSD Spleen, Prostate, and CVC-ClinicDB. Compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, TG-SEG achieves consistent improvements across all evaluated datasets, with Dice gains of upto 3.13% and IoU gains of upto 4.41%. Ablation studies show that TG-SEG reduces false negative rates by 21.8-47.5% across datasets. Furthermore, stronger visual backbones such as SwinV2 provide additional gains of up to 9.26% Dice and 13.67% IoU, demonstrating the backbone-agnostic nature of the proposed framework. These results highlight the effectiveness of presence-aware gating for accurate and reliable medical image sequence segmentation. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/cse-iitbhu/TG-SEG.

papers.title: Group-Relative RL Post-Training for Sequential Recommendation
papers.abstract: Sequential recommender systems are typically trained with next-item cross-entropy (CE), yet evaluated by top-N ranking metrics that reward relative item ordering in the recommendation slate. This mismatch remains unaddressed for strong collaborative sequential models. Recent group-relative reinforcement learning has shown promise for LLM alignment and LLM-based recommenders, but whether a critic-free post-training paradigm can reliably improve standard collaborative sequential recommenders remains unclear. We introduce GRFT (Group-Relative Fine-Tuning), a GRPO-style post-training framework that aligns a pretrained sequential recommender directly to slate-level ranking rewards. GRFT samples multiple top-K slates per user context via Plackett-Luce sampling without replacement, scores them with ranking rewards, and updates the model with a PPO-clipped group-relative objective anchored to the frozen supervised reference. We instantiate rankwise and listwise variants to support position-level and whole-slate credit assignment. Under leakage-resistant global temporal splits on four datasets, GRFT consistently improves a strong sequential backbone, achieving gains of up to 25.3% NDCG@20 and 19.5% Recall@20. The improvements remain complementary to stronger supervised initialization, showing that reward-aligned post-training adds value beyond better supervised training alone. GRFT thus establishes that GRPO-style, critic-free post-training can improve strong collaborative sequential recommenders.

papers.title: Generative Chain of Behavior for User Trajectory Prediction
papers.abstract: Modeling long-term user behavior trajectories is essential for understanding evolving preferences and enabling proactive recommendations. However, most sequential recommenders focus on next-item prediction, overlooking dependencies across multiple future actions. We propose Generative Chain of Behavior (GCB), a generative framework that models user interactions as an autoregressive chain of semantic behaviors over multiple future steps. GCB first encodes items into semantic IDs via RQ-VAE with k-means refinement, forming a discrete latent space that preserves semantic proximity. On top of this space, a transformer-based autoregressive generator predicts multi-step future behaviors conditioned on user history, capturing long-horizon intent transitions and generating coherent trajectories. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that GCB achieves strong multi-step prediction performance while generating coherent long-horizon behavior trajectories. Beyond these results, GCB provides a unified generative formulation for modeling user preference evolution.

papers.title: Leveraging Language Models for Music Recommendation with Bayesian Residual Quantization
papers.abstract: Generative recommendations (GRs) reframe recommendation as autoregressive generation over Semantic IDs (SIDs), enabling Large Language Models (LLMs) to model user intent and sequential preference patterns in a unified manner. Most existing systems discretize continuous item representations into SIDs via codebook-based residual quantization, and then generate subsequent SID tokens through next-token prediction. However, conventional residual quantization relies on deterministic, hard nearest-neighbor assignments. This rigid mapping fails to account for semantic ambiguity, suffering from error propagation across quantization levels and often leading to under-utilized codebooks. To address these limitations, we propose the Bayesian Residual Quantized Variational Autoencoder (BRQ-VAE), a probabilistic reformulation of residual quantization that introduces stochastic quantization and stochastic dequantization under an ELBO-driven objective. We further develop alignment strategies to integrate language semantics and collaborative signals for end-to-end LLM-based recommendation. Experiments on public benchmarks, large-scale industrial datasets, and online A/B tests on a commercial music platform show that BRQ-VAE consistently improves codebook quality, downstream recommendation performance, and key engagement metrics over strong baselines.

papers.title: SRCRec: Staged Reverse Curriculum Learning for Conversion-Oriented Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Conversion-oriented generative recommendation (GR) is challenged by sparse conversion supervision, where the decoder must learn conversion targets from long interaction histories with limited positive signals. Existing multi-behavior GR methods enhance behavior-aware representation learning, but still optimize the original full-history prediction task directly, leaving the difficulty of sparse conversion modeling insufficiently addressed. Recent reverse-curriculum-inspired methods further show that conversion-related intermediate behaviors are useful, yet they mainly instantiate the curriculum as one-shot decoder-prefix conditioning, which does not provide a staged reverse curriculum process and will increase online serving latency. To address these limitations, we propose SRCRec , a staged reverse curriculum learning framework for conversion-oriented GR. SRCRec constructs difficulty-aware curriculum contexts over the historical sequence, trains the model from target-near easy contexts to harder historical contexts, and finally recovers the original no-prefix conversion objective. This staged optimization enables the model to progressively learn from curricula with increasing difficulty while keeping inference identical to standard GR. Experiments on public and industrial datasets show that SRCRec achieves superior offline performance, and online A/B tests further improve orders by 3.52% and Gross Merchandise Volume by 2.98%.

papers.title: CDNet: Efficient Sequential-Contextual Feature Interaction via Core-Behavior Selection and Interest-Distribution Compensation
papers.abstract: Effective click-through rate (CTR) prediction hinges on capturing the interactions between user behavior sequences and non-sequential contextual features. Existing approaches face a fundamental dilemma in this interaction: aggregation-based methods compress the sequence into fixed-length vectors before interacting with contextual features, sacrificing the fine-grained behavioral details critical for capturing how specific past behaviors relate to the current candidate; full sequence unrolling enables direct interaction between every behavior and every contextual feature, but incurs quadratic computational cost and allows noise from irrelevant behaviors to overwhelm the signals from the truly relevant ones. To resolve this dilemma, we propose CDNet , a C ore-Behaviors and D istributional-Compensation Dual-View Interaction Net work that models sequential-contextual feature interaction from two strictly complementary and mutually indispensable angles. The Fine-grained Core-Behaviors Module selects the most relevant behaviors for explicit fine-grained interaction with contextual features, providing local behavioral semantics at low computational cost. The Global Interest-Distribution Module addresses an orthogonal question that core behaviors structurally cannot answer: how broadly does the user's full history align with the candidate? This global interest-intensity signal, encoded as a compact relevance distribution over the entire sequence, enables contextual features to calibrate their interaction with the precise behavioral signals, a capacity entirely absent when only core behaviors are considered. Extensive experiments on public and industrial datasets demonstrate that both modules are necessary and their combination achieves superior accuracy and efficiency over state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: Learning Collaborative and Discriminative Embeddings with LLMs for Sequential Recommendation
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise as embedding generators for sequential recommendation. Effective adaptation typically involves two stages: collaborative signal injection and discriminative representation learning. However, optimization objective and item semantic misalignments arise between these two stages, resulting in catastrophic forgetting of collaborative relationships learned in the first stage. To address these issues, we propose a novel LLM-based embedding method called GCTP, which obtains both collaborative and discriminative embeddings. Specifically, we maintain a generative training objective throughout the training process, thereby alleviating potential optimization conflicts. Moreover, we preserve local semantics to ensure semantic consistency during training, and capture global semantics with minimal modifications when extracting item embeddings. Experiments on real-world datasets show that GCTP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art LLM-based embedding methods.

papers.title: E²L³AE: End‑to‑End Text Encoder Tuning for LLM‑Enhanced Linear Autoencoders
affiliations: Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology
papers.abstract: Enriching sparse user–item interactions with semantic item knowledge is essential for robust recommendation, particularly for long-tail items where collaborative signals are weak or unreliable. L³AE integrates frozen LLM embeddings into linear autoencoders, but fixed text representations can be suboptimal for recommendation because consumption-relevant item characteristics often deviate from general textual semantics. We propose an end-to-end extension that fine-tunes the text encoder within the same linear autoencoder framework, encouraging its embeddings to reflect item relatedness derived from user–item interactions, thereby adapting pretrained textual knowledge to recommendation objectives while remaining grounded in pretrained semantic knowledge. Experiments on public datasets show that our end-to-end trained hybrid model improves upon the original L³AE and other baselines. Moreover, the fine-tuned encoder alone serves as a competitive semantic-based recommender.

papers.title: Ask to Be Sure: Informative Interactions for Confident Multi-Turn LLM Recommendation
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled their use as conversational recommender systems (CRS), demonstrating strong recommendation accuracy and natural dialogue. However, guiding multi-turn interactions to elicit user preferences effectively remains challenging. Existing approaches either use separate reinforcement learning agents with templated interactions or optimize for interactivity judged by another LLM, without measuring how much useful information is actually gained. We propose a new approach that quantifies the effectiveness of each interaction by the reduction in the assistant’s uncertainty, measured via entropy over recommendations. We apply this entropy reduction as a reward—without relying on ground-truth recommendations, which are often unavailable in real-world scenarios—to fine-tune the LLM, enabling strategic interaction generation. Empirical results with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and direct preference optimization (DPO) on the INSPIRED and ReDial datasets show that our method improves both recommendation quality and conversational efficiency.

papers.title: Retrieval, Scoring, and Decoding Shape Performance and Stability in LLM-based Conversational Recommendation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as rerankers in conversational recommender systems, yet measured gains depend strongly on the retrieval and inference protocol. On the ReDial conversational movie recommendation benchmark, we compare proprietary, open-weight, and fine-tuned LLM rerankers with collaborative-filtering and sequential baselines in a shared retrieve-then-rerank pipeline. We vary candidate-pool size, first-stage retriever, and decoding temperature. With a shared semantic top-250 candidate pool and strict candidate-aware scoring, the best proprietary reranker reaches NDCG@10 of 0.1497, compared with 0.0939 for the strongest non-LLM baseline. The same reranker reaches 0.2925 in zero-shot generation, showing that unconstrained scoring can yield a much larger apparent advantage than matched-pool evaluation. No evaluated open-weight LLM outperforms the tuned shallow autoencoder baseline under this protocol. For the strongest proprietary and open-weight rerankers, switching from semantic to collaborative-filtering candidates raises NDCG@10 by more than 50%, showing that measured reranker performance is highly sensitive to candidate generation. For the best proprietary reranker, raising temperature from 0 to 1.0 increases top-10 Jaccard distance from 0.0900 to 0.1240 while mean NDCG@10 changes negligibly, whereas weaker LLMs show larger degradation. These ReDial results support treating candidate generation, candidate-pool size, scoring policy, and decoding configuration as required reporting fields rather than implementation details.

papers.title: Conformal Prediction for Statistically Reliable LLM-as-a-Judge in Recommender Systems
papers.abstract: LLM-as-a-judge has emerged as a promising strategy for evaluating recommender systems. Yet, treating simulated ratings as real feedback can make unreliable evaluation appear reliable. This risk is especially consequential in sensitive domains such as nutrition and health. In this paper, we treat the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm as a calibrated relevance simulation problem: an LLM-based simulator predicts human preferences from user and item representations, and conformal prediction converts them into uncertainty intervals. To account for the nature of recommendation, we introduce stratified conformal calibration by user rating variance. Experiments under three LLMs and seven conformal prediction methods show that point estimates of preferences hide failures on low-rating items, while conformal interval width is driven by user-level heterogeneity. Source code and data : https://github.com/maddalena-amendola/conformal_prediction_recsys.

papers.title: A Behavioral Trait Leaks into Preferences: Diagnosing Trait Interference in LLM User Simulators
papers.abstract: LLM-based user simulators aim to bridge the offline–online gap in recommender evaluation by emulating users through injected traits, where preference attributes determine what a user engages with and a behavioral activity trait governs how long they browse. However, we show this intended trait independence collapses during simulation, causing two failures: (i) Trait Interference, where amplified activity distorts preference boundaries and forces interactions with mismatched items to sustain browsing, and (ii) Evaluation Invalidity, where satisfaction scores inflate with activity-driven page counts despite taste mismatches, biasing evaluation toward trait distributions rather than recommender performance. To resolve this, we propose PQA, a page-level quality anchoring method that guides simulators using a personalized anchor reflecting each user's intrinsic preference standard. By assessing whether a page meets this standard before further browsing, PQA enables proactive exits from low-quality pages, letting the activity trait retain its intended role of modulating browsing depth within preference-conforming pages. Experiments show PQA mitigates trait interference and improves the reliability of LLM-based simulator evaluation under activity shifts. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaehyun1/PQA.

papers.title: Personalized Task Dependency Graphs for Mitigating Signal Erosion in Multi-Task Recommendation
papers.abstract: Optimizing multiple conversion objectives is a core challenge in industrial recommendation, often limited by signal erosion in rigid architectures. Existing Multi-Task Learning (MTL) methods typically enforce uniform dependency strengths across a static conversion funnel, overlooking how task correlations naturally vary based on item characteristics. Hierarchical message passing along these fixed chains leads to cumulative signal attenuation, which degrades performance on sparse, deep-funnel objectives. To address this, we propose the Personalized Task Dependency Graphs ( PTDG ). While respecting necessary physical causal constraints (e.g., Click → Pay ), PTDG dynamically “rewires” the intensity of dependency pathways for each item via low-rank approximation to ensure structural robustness. We implement a GCN-based propagation with hard causal masking to establish adaptive information shortcuts. Additionally, we introduce an Adaptive Progressive Masking (APM) strategy that decouples shared parameters according to task sparsity, helping to stabilize optimization. Experiments on KuaiRand1K and an industrial dataset show that PTDG significantly improves AUC on sparse conversion tasks by up to 1.45%, while maintaining comparable performance on dense objectives. Online A/B testing shows PTDG improves Conversion Rate (CVR) by 1.2% and effective Cost Per Mille (eCPM) by 1.9% relative to the baseline.

papers.title: Revisiting LLM-Enhanced Collaborative Filtering: A Text-Free Alternative with Heterogeneous Interaction Signals
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently improved collaborative filtering (CF) by adding text-derived signals, but often require rich textual data and costly inference. In this work, we revisit RLMRec [11], a representative LLM-enhanced CF framework, and examine whether its gains come from LLM-specific knowledge or from complementary representations. Our analysis suggests that a substantial part of the improvement can be attributed to auxiliary heterogeneous signals, rather than solely to intrinsic LLM knowledge. Motivated by this, we propose HetRec (Heterogeneity-aware Recommender), a text-free, model-agnostic CF framework that replaces LLM-derived textual embeddings with interaction-derived heterogeneous signals. HetRec constructs auxiliary embeddings from heterogeneous-view CF models and enriches them via similarity-aware k-nearest neighbor aggregation, capturing neighborhood-level collaborative patterns. Under the same RLMRec-style alignment framework, HetRec improves over RLMRec variants on the Amazon-book, Yelp, and Steam datasets without textual inputs or LLM inference. Our code is available at https://github.com/Jaeeun-Lim02/HetRec.

papers.title: TEDI: Target-Review-based Knowledge Distillation for Effective Recommendation
papers.abstract: Review-based recommendation systems (RBRS) leverage textual reviews to capture rich information about user preferences. A target review , which is directly associated with the target rating, contains highly relevant information for rating prediction but is unavailable during inference. Existing RBRS approaches try to reproduce the target review's semantic embedding by leveraging historical reviews. However, this semantic embedding often includes rating-irrelevant information, limiting its effectiveness in rating prediction. To address this issue, we propose TEDI, a novel RBRS based on privileged feature distillation (PFD). TEDI consists of a teacher module that distills rating-relevant knowledge from both target and historical reviews, and a student module that reproduces this knowledge by leveraging historical reviews during inference. Experiments on six datasets demonstrate that TEDI outperforms nine state-of-the-art RBRS methods, validating the effectiveness of utilizing knowledge from target reviews. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/Bigdasgit/TEDI.

papers.title: Neural Tree Collaborative Filtering: Rethinking Graph Collaborative Filtering as Tree Collaborative Filtering with Curvature-Aware Propagation Depth
affiliations: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Graph Collaborative Filtering (GCF) has become the dominant paradigm in modern recommender systems by modeling user--item interactions as a bipartite graph and propagating embeddings through a fixed number of message-passing layers. However, applying a uniform propagation depth to every node ignores a fundamental property of real interaction graphs: nodes differ substantially in their local connectivity, so peripheral nodes quickly suffer from over-smoothing while hub-like nodes remain under-explored beyond their immediate neighborhood. In this paper, we revisit GCF from a tree-structured perspective and propose Neural Tree Collaborative Filtering (NTCF), a framework that re-interprets each node's local neighborhood as a rooted tree and assigns a node-specific propagation depth based on a closed-form local-degree-imbalance score that serves as a discrete Ricci-curvature proxy. We provide a theoretical analysis showing that (i) NTCF strictly generalizes NGCF, degenerating to NGCF when all curvature-induced depth adjustments vanish (a lower bound on its representation power), and (ii) the curvature-aware schedule retains strictly more discriminative information at deep layers on positively-curved (peripheral) nodes than uniform-depth propagation. NTCF can achieve higher performance than most widely used GCF backbone models and can be integrated into existing advanced self-supervised models as a backbone, replacing their original backbone to achieve enhanced performance. Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate the superiority of NTCF.

papers.title: Sequential Modality Dropout for Robust Multi-Modal Sequential Recommendation
papers.abstract: Multi-modal sequential recommenders assume every item carries every modality, but real product catalogs often miss images or text, and a model trained on complete data loses much of its recommendation accuracy when a modality is unavailable at serving time. We propose Sequential Modality Dropout (SMD): during training, each modality stream (image and text) is independently erased with probability p for an entire user interaction history, so the model learns to predict the next item without relying on any single modality. We measure robustness by retention, the fraction of a model's full-modality accuracy (HR@10) that survives when a modality is removed at test time. Across four backbones (MM-SASRec, IISAN, MISSRec, and fMRLRec) on four Amazon domains, SMD raises text retention by 1.0 to 3.2× at essentially no cost to full-modality accuracy; under an extreme 95% per-item missing rate, it retains 61% of HR@10 versus 22% without (a 2.8× improvement). An optional cross-modal reconstruction loss further lifts retention from 90% to 98% on a simple additive backbone under severe text missingness. SMD is a four-line, architecture-agnostic change that makes multi-modal sequential recommenders robust to the missing modalities they actually encounter in deployment. Code: https://github.com/guanqun-yang/SMD

papers.title: Adaptive Preference Allocation and Semantic Hard-Negative Supervision for Multimodal Recommendation
affiliations: Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
papers.abstract: Multimodal recommendation enhances user preference modeling by leveraging visual and textual content. However, existing methods generally adopt a unified modality fusion strategy, making it difficult to capture users’ diverse reliance on visual and textual signals. Meanwhile, random negative sampling provides limited ranking supervision and is insufficient for modeling fine-grained preference boundaries. To address these issues, we propose an Adaptive Preference allocation and Semantic Negative supervision framework called APSN, which explicitly models personalized preferences through user-level modality contribution allocation, thereby learning more fine-grained multimodal user representations. To enhance ranking supervision, APSN samples informative semantic negatives from dynamically constructed user communities, guiding the model to better capture users’ preference boundaries. In addition, APSN improves feature robustness via masked semantic consistency and complements local structural information through a sparse collaborative view. Experimental results on multiple public datasets demonstrate that APSN can achieve consistent and effective improvements in recommendation performance. Code is available at https://github.com/jcs12123/APSN.

papers.title: Seeing Double? Multimodal Duplicate Detection for Recommendation Lists in Fashion E-Commerce
papers.abstract: Duplicate products frequently appear in fashion e-commerce recommendation lists because the same item may be offered by multiple vendors with inconsistent product information. This paper introduces recommendation-list validation as a multimodal duplicate-detection task and presents a scalable and interpretable framework that combines visual, textual, and metadata signals through attention-based representation learning and pairwise classification. We also release the first large-scale public benchmark for list-level fashion product deduplication, comprising more than 1 million products and 800,000 validation instances. The experimental results demonstrate substantial improvements over existing baselines.

papers.title: PGBid: Platform-Wide Generative Auto-Bidding via Macro-Micro Decoupling
papers.abstract: Automated bidding in Demand-Side Platforms (DSPs) aims to maximize overall value while satisfying diverse advertiser constraints. However, scaling to practical deployments reveals two structural challenges: cross-granularity constraint conflicts between advertiser-level decisions and business-line KPIs, and bid homogenization under first-price auctions that erodes platform surplus. Existing single-advertiser AI Generative Bidding (AIGB) methods fundamentally fail to address these platform-wide issues. We propose PGBid (Platform-Wide Generative Auto-Bidding), a macro-micro decoupled framework. At the macro level, a Strategist uses convex optimization to decompose global constraints into per-advertiser targets. At the micro level, a Tactician combines a conditional diffusion model with a distribution-aware inverse dynamics model to translate these targets into bidding distributions for fine-grained bid shading. Extensive offline experiments and large-scale online A/B testing demonstrate that PGBid significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Moreover, PGBid has been fully deployed on our DSP platform, reliably processing billions of bid requests daily.

papers.title: When Is Complex Chunking Worth It? A Multi-Objective Evaluation of Chunking Methods at Scale
papers.abstract: Dense retrieval is commonly evaluated on benchmarks that represent each document with a single embedding, even though real-world retrieval systems often index long documents that require chunking. In these settings, the chosen chunking method not only affects retrieval quality, but also indexing throughput, query latency, and memory usage. Prior comparisons of chunking strategies have mainly focused on retrieval performance, leaving operational trade-offs underexplored. To address these issues, we evaluate eight representative chunking strategies across two scalable corpora, three embedding models, and multiple corpus sizes, measuring both retrieval effectiveness and system-level costs. Our results show that computationally expensive methods rarely provide consistent gains over simpler chunking. Instead, the best performing strategy depends on the embedding model, dataset, corpus size, and target retrieval metric. Methods with similar performance can also differ substantially in operational cost, showing that chunking should be seen as a multi-objective design decision. Our code and datasets are available on GitHub (https://github.com/casparil/chunking-eval) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/PaDaS-Lab/kilt-nq) (https://huggingface.co/datasets/PaDaS-Lab/CoRE).

papers.title: Sentence Operators: Second-Order Representations for Retrieval
papers.abstract: Sentence embedding models typically compress contextual token states into a single vector and compare texts with cosine similarity. We study a second-order alternative that represents each sentence as a trace-normalized positive semidefinite (PSD) operator over normalized token directions, preserving geometry discarded by pooling. We compare mean-pooled cosine with full-operator similarities and two low-rank eigenspace scores, computed through token Gram matrices without forming dense d × d operators. We also fine-tune encoders on MS MARCO using contrastive objectives defined by these similarities. Across multiple encoder families and MTEB retrieval tasks, normalized and low-rank scores expose retrieval-relevant structure beyond pooled cosine. Unnormalized Hilbert–Schmidt overlap is generally weaker, while low-rank subspace comparison produces the strongest gains for BERT-based encoders. On frozen bert-base-cased, which lacks sentence-level training, the best projection score more than doubles average retrieval quality. The gains shrink or disappear for backbones already optimized for retrieval, indicating that the value of sentence operators is backbone-dependent. Overall, sentence operators provide a scoring and diagnostic framework for identifying when retrieval benefits from multi-directional token-state structure.

papers.title: Seek: Self-Evaluative Exploration for Knowledge Retrieval
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based retrievers and rerankers have advanced passage ranking, yet both paradigms interact with the corpus in a single pass and commit to the resulting candidate set, leaving relevant documents permanently unrecoverable once missed. We introduce Seek, S elf- E valuative E xploration for K nowledge Retrieval), a training-free framework that addresses this limitation through iterative corpus interaction at test time. At each round, an LLM generates pseudo-passages conditioned on accumulated relevance feedback, a retriever surfaces fresh candidates, and a dedicated assessor assigns graded relevance judgments that guide subsequent rounds. On TREC Deep Learning, Seek matches trained rerankers in ranking quality while consistently improving Recall@100 over single-pass BM25. On the reasoning-intensive BRIGHT benchmark, Seek with Qwen2.5-7B achieves an 82% relative gain over BM25, surpassing all trained baselines, and Seek with GPT-4.1 reaches 37.4 average nDCG@10, exceeding the strongest baseline by 37%. We make our code, prompts, and data publicly available at https://github.com/aminbigdeli/SEEK.

papers.title: Reasoning About Query Difficulty to Predict Retrieval Effectiveness
papers.abstract: Pre-retrieval query performance prediction methods estimate the effectiveness of a query prior to retrieval and enable control of the search pipeline through tasks such as query routing, selective expansion, and retriever selection. However, because they operate solely on query features without access to retrieved documents, pre-retrieval predictors often struggle to provide accurate predictions. They typically treat query difficulty as a latent statistical property rather than one that can be reasoned about. We propose a new pre-retrieval framework that leverages the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to uncover and encode interpretable reasons of query difficulty. By integrating these reasons with transformer-based neural regressors, our approach allows the predictor to be both aware of and conditioned on reasons that make a query challenging. Our experiments on MS MARCO Dev, TREC DL 2019, TREC DL 2020, and DL-Hard demonstrate that our method consistently achieves reliable and stable correlations across various TREC DL datasets. Our code, models, and difficulty reason annotations are made publicly available at https://github.com/ls3-lab/draq.

papers.title: The Plug-and-Play Illusion: Cross-Encoder Brittleness to Retrieval Noise under Fixed Recall
papers.abstract: Cross-encoder rerankers are often treated as safe, drop-in quality boosts once a first-stage retriever has recalled a candidate pool. The hidden assumption is simple: if the gold document is present, the reranker should still pick it out from whatever negatives the retriever supplies. We test that assumption with a recall-controlled stress test that keeps recall at 100% and varies only the distractor distribution. Under this protocol, a small cross-encoder's NDCG@10 falls by up to 50% when negatives shift from random documents to retriever-mined hard negatives. The collapse repeats across four rerankers spanning 4M-278M parameters and two training families, so it is not one weak model. We then ask whether zero-shot LLM rerankers fail in the same way. A listwise language-model reranker, with gpt-4o-mini as the strongest case, is less sensitive to BM25 hard negatives across three BEIR corpora, but the controls complicate the story. On nfcorpus, the advantage relies on the BM25-seeded listwise order. On fiqa and scifact, it survives pointwise scoring and shuffled-order controls, indicating intrinsic model robustness. Dense hard negatives still hurt all rerankers. The conclusion is therefore not that "LLMs are robust," but that negative distributions are part of the retriever-reranker interface and should be checked before deployment. We end with a no-new-label diagnostic.

papers.title: Cost-Sensitive Listwise Optimisation for Sensitivity-Aware Search
papers.abstract: In typical search tasks, the goal is to return a list of k documents that are ordered by their relevance to a user-issued query. However, not all information that is contained in a collection should be made available to users, i.e., sensitive information should not be revealed. Sensitivity-Aware Search (SAS) is a bi-objective retrieval task that aims to make collections that potentially contain sensitive information safely searchable by producing a ranked list of documents that are (1) relevant to the query and (2) non-sensitive. Previous work on SAS leveraged pointwise relevance-only loss functions in combination with SAS-specific negative sampling techniques. We argue that modelling SAS in a pointwise manner at training time limits how effectively the task can be expressed to the model. Hence, we investigate listwise loss functions for SAS. Further, we propose a sensitivity-aware listwise distillation loss function that penalises the model for highly ranking sensitive documents during training. We perform experiments on two test collections labelled for relevance and different types of sensitivity, and observe that listwise loss functions outperform pointwise and pairwise losses, retrieving up to 58% fewer sensitive documents. Our proposed sensitivity-aware listwise distillation loss function outperforms a relevance-only listwise loss function by 12% and a pointwise loss function leveraging SAS training data by 15% in relevance-sensitivity tradeoff metrics. We release model checkpoints with PyTerrier integrations on HuggingFace.

papers.title: PMC: Build-Time Per-Modality Centroid Correction for Cross-Modal Binary-Quantized Retrieval
papers.abstract: Approximate nearest neighbor search is a core operator in large-scale retrieval, where vector quantization is widely used to reduce memory cost. Binary quantization methods encode each dimension as a single bit, but they assume queries and database vectors share a common centroid. This assumption fails in cross-modal retrieval, where each modality clusters around a different centroid, producing a modality gap that corrupts the centroid's dual role as inverted-file routing pivot and sign-bit decision boundary. We propose Per-Modality Centroid Correction (PMC), which shifts database vectors toward the query centroid at build time, rewriting routing and code boundaries at the source rather than merely adjusting queries at serving time. A selective variant confirms that concentrated gap energy in a few dimensions drives most recall loss. PMC adds no index memory or serving overhead; at ?=1, the correction is fully absorbed into the index with zero query-time cost. Experiments on five cross-modal benchmarks, three encoders, and four binary-quantized index types show gains over uncorrected and query-shifted baselines that scale with modality-gap magnitude, up to a 400M-vector deployment. Code: https://github.com/sehoon787/PMC.

papers.title: Recovering Graph ANN Search on Attention-Derived Workloads via a Query-Agnostic Spherical Transformation
papers.abstract: Graph-based indexes such as HNSW are widely used for approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search due to their strong empirical performance. Prior work (Morozov and Babenko, NeurIPS 2018) suggests that these methods remain effective even for non-metric maximum inner product search (MIPS). We show that this assumption fails for the attention-derived embeddings from modern large language models available in the recent VIBE benchmark. We trace the failure to HNSW's neighbor-selection heuristic, which prunes almost every candidate at build time and yields graphs too sparse to effectively support greedy descent. As a remedy we revisit an index-agnostic transformation that maps the database onto the unit hypersphere while preserving the inner-product ranking, without any knowledge of the query distribution. The transformation restores the assumed geometry of the datasets and raises HNSW recall above 95%. Moreover, a query-agnostic adaption of the query-aware index RoarGraph (Chen et al., VLDB 2024) stays below 40% recall. This means that RoarGraph's strong performance needs access to the query sample rather than purely relying on its bipartite graph construction.

papers.title: CoALANN: Cross-Query Node-Fetch Coalescing for Batched Full-Precision Disk ANN Search
papers.abstract: Concurrent approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) queries over full-precision, disk-resident indexes often traverse overlapping graph regions, yet batched runtime paths can issue duplicate logical node-fetch requests independently. We study this redundancy in Vamana-style search and propose CoALANN, a traversal-round coalescer that synchronizes a batch of beam searches at bounded traversal rounds, deduplicates pending requests for the same node record, issues one deduplicated batched request set through io_uring (the Linux asynchronous I/O interface), and shares completed reads with all requesting queries. In the n = 20 headline paired runs at B = 64 across four ANN datasets (SIFT1M, DEEP1M, DEEP10M, and LastFM64) under an NVMe OS page-cache-cold stress protocol, duplicate logical node-fetch submissions account for 40.4–55.2% of requests. Relative to the same round-synchronized, batched io_uring harness with only cross-query deduplication disabled, CoALANN improves QPS by 1.09–1.35×, with identical Recall@10 in the paired runs. CoALANN leaves the index unchanged and reads full float32 vectors.

papers.title: Surrogate Inverse-Variance Weighting for Intervention Harvesting on Heavy-Tailed Click Logs
papers.abstract: Under the Position-Based Model (PBM), the probability that a user clicks a document d shown for query q at position k factorises as p_k * r q,d , where p_k is the position examination probability and r q,d is the query–document relevance. Intervention harvesting estimates the ratio p_k/p k' from naturally occurring ranking variation by aggregating per-cell click-rate ratios over (q,d) cells. On real logs, cell impression counts are extremely heavy-tailed: on the full KDD Cup 2012 Track 2 log, 60% of interventional pairs have at most five impressions while 0.1% of pairs account for 42% of all impressions. The weighting of cells is therefore central to finite-sample efficiency. We study count-only weighting schemes for intervention harvesting. Beyond the uniform weighting of Agarwal et al., we propose two new count-only weights: the min-count weight omega_i = min(N_k^i, N k' ^i) and the harmonic weight omega_i = N_k^i N k' ^i / (N_k^i + N k' ^i), where N_k^i is the number of impressions of cell i at position k. The harmonic weight arises from an inverse-variance approximation to per-cell click-rate differences under PBM: after replacing the relevance-dependent variance terms with a common factor, the resulting count-only surrogate variance is minimised by harmonic weighting. A Cauchy–Schwarz argument shows that harmonic improves this surrogate variance over uniform aggregation for any impression counts. We evaluate finite-sample efficiency via the closed-form delta-method asymptotic variance of the weighted ratio estimator. On the full KDD log, harmonic weighting achieves a 4.5x asymptotic relative efficiency improvement over uniform and remains robust under weight capping. Synthetic and Yahoo-LTR semi-synthetic experiments with ground truth corroborate the prediction, with up to 54% variance reduction under high imbalance. We also make explicit an estimand caveat: under PBM mis-specification, different weights target different weighted averages of cell-specific ratios. Overall, harmonic weighting offers a simple count-only replacement for uniform intervention harvesting with a count-only surrogate-variance guarantee and consistent empirical gains; min and harmonic perform comparably, with harmonic preferred for its theoretical justification.

papers.title: Better Together: Human-LLM Pairs for Reliable System Rankings
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of assigning two bronze (i.e. "non-topic-creator") assessors per topic for constructing an IR test collection, where the quality of human assessors is unknown. Given the advent of LLM-as-a-judge strategies in IR evaluation, replacing one or both of the human assessors with an LLM certainly seems appealing. But which is the best assessor pairing strategy for the purpose of obtaining an effective system ranking that represents a collective view of human assessors? To address this question, we leverage a unique existing web search test collection whose relevance assessments were contributed by a total of 24 assessors. The collection consists of non-overlapping subcollections, each with over 50 topics. For each subcollection, our target system ranking reflects the collective view of eight assessors. We then form all possible pairs from a pool of 12—comprising the original eight assessors plus four LLMs—and evaluate how well each pair's generated ranking approximates the target ranking with only two assessors. Across the three subcollections, the best performing pair type is Human-Human (H-H), but the Human-LLM (H-LLM) pair is only 0.009 Kendall's (τ) behind on average. Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) further show that H-LLM pairs are practically equivalent to H-H pairs under a pre-defined margin. Furthermore, H-H pairs are not uniformly strong, as human assessors have larger performance variance and can occasionally underperform H-LLM pairs when a reliable LLM is used. When Llama 4—which produced output format errors during label generation—is excluded, H-LLM pairs surpass H-H on average. Our results suggest that pairing one human with a reliable LLM can closely approximate the collective view of the eight assessors for ranking systems.

papers.title: Modeling Uncertainty in LLM-Based Information Retrieval Evaluation via Hierarchical Bayesian Models
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in Information Retrieval (IR) evaluation to annotate query-document pairs for relevance, enabling significant cost reductions compared to the traditional human-only assessment process. However, LLM-generated human judgements are not error-free and, compared to humans, are more prone to introducing systematic latent biases and producing spurious results. Therefore, since the evaluation target remains the human, it is necessary to understand how to align observations derived from LLM-generated annotations with those that would have been made using human relevance judgments. This work introduces a novel framework for estimating the performance we would observe if relevance judgements were human-made, using a large amount of LLM-generated judgments with a limited pool of human-annotated queries. The proposed approach exploits hierarchical Bayesian modeling and calibration to build Credible Intervals (CrIs) providing statistical guarantees on the estimated performance. The obtained results show how the computed CrIs allow (a) over 95% coverage while exploiting a limited number of human annotations and (b) to jointly take into account the LLM error and the variance due to topics, enabling future use of the computed CrIs for statistical hypothesis testing.

papers.title: Remote Sensing Image-Text Retrieval via Hierarchical and Targeting Semantic Alignment
papers.abstract: Remote sensing image-text retrieval (RSITR) can facilitate visual language mining in spatial scenarios, which holds significant importance for aviation and aerospace applications. Existing RSITR methods often lack joint coarse-grained and fine-grained alignment, or their unified learning strategies are inefficient. Additionally, there is no analysis of remote sensing characteristics in these fine-grained feature learning. To address these issues, this paper proposes Hierarchical and Targeting Semantic Alignment (HTSA) for remote sensing image-text retrieval, which simultaneously considers the construction of global and local features. In coarse-grained semantic alignment, cross-modal classification learning and inter-modal matching learning are combined. For fine-grained semantic learning, targeted semantic alignment is introduced to highlight essential objects, which are overlooked by current RSITR methods, but crucial for remote sensing scenarios. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of the proposed framework, while different ablation studies discuss the functions of specific components.

papers.title: RankGap-RAG: Rank-Discrepancy Contrastive Feedback for Multi-Paraphrase Retrieval
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is sensitive to the wording of the original query, and iterative query refinement can further amplify early retrieval errors when misleading passages are reused as feedback. We propose RankGap-RAG, a training-free query refinement framework that uses bi-encoder/cross-encoder rank discrepancy to select inference-time hard-negative feedback. Rather than treating retrieved passages as uniformly useful feedback, RankGap-RAG pairs cross-encoder-selected positive evidence with rank-gap negatives to guide the LLM toward relevant evidence while discouraging misleading semantic directions. We further introduce a Diverse Multi-Chain extension that combines contrastive feedback with multiple refinement trajectories. Experiments on SQuAD 2.0, Natural Questions, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue show consistent gains over original-query retrieval, while component ablations on SQuAD 2.0 and Natural Questions show improvements over positive-only feedback.

papers.title: From Oracle Gains to Repair Priorities: Conservative Split-Conditioned Diagnosis for Modular RAG
papers.abstract: Gold-evidence interventions are widely used to evaluate retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, but they are often reduced to one average oracle gain. This aggregation mixes evidence access, context ordering, and answer-extraction failures, which can turn local evidence effects into an overinterpreted repair claim. We propose Conservative Split-Conditioned Oracle Diagnosis (CS-RAG), a compact diagnostic method that converts paired oracle traces into guarded subset-level repair priorities. CS-RAG treats each example as a bounded vector of gains from three evidence-control actions. Our method aggregates these vectors within registered splits, maps action gains to repair-label scores via a split-valid incidence map, and outputs a priority only when the support, gain, and label-margin guards all hold. On 1,500-example Natural Questions and TriviaQA diagnostic subsets, aggregate oracle probes reveal substantial headroom across stages. Preliminary repair experiments further show that retrieval repair improves both datasets, whereas conservative generation repair does not yield consistent gains. Our code is available at https://github.com/sungchaewon/rag-diagnostics.

papers.title: RAG-X: Systematic Diagnosis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medical Question Answering
papers.abstract: Automated question-answering (QA) systems increasingly rely on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to ground large language models (LLMs) in authoritative medical knowledge, ensuring clinical accuracy and patient safety in AI applications for healthcare. Despite progress in RAG evaluation, current benchmarks focus only on simple multiple-choice QA tasks and employ metrics that poorly capture the semantic precision required for complex QA tasks. These approaches fail to diagnose whether an error stems from faulty retrieval or flawed generation, limiting developers from performing targeted improvement. To address this gap, we propose RAG-X, a diagnostic framework that evaluates the retriever and generator independently across a triad of QA tasks: information extraction, short-answer generation, and multiple-choice question answering. RAG-X introduces Context Utilization Efficiency (CUE) metrics to disaggregate system success into interpretable quadrants, isolating verified grounding from deceptive accuracy. Our experiments reveal an “Accuracy Fallacy”, where a 14% gap separates perceived system success from evidence-based grounding. By surfacing hidden failure modes, RAG-X offers the diagnostic transparency needed for safe and verifiable clinical RAG systems. Our code is available at https://github.com/AswiniS94/RAG-X_Evaluation.

papers.title: Training Uncertainty-Aware Adaptive Reasoning Budgets with Policy Entropy
affiliations: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: Generative question answering and knowledge access systems increasingly use reasoning language models to synthesize retrieved or domain-specific information, but verbose rationales can raise latency and serving cost. We study whether policy entropy can serve as a training-time signal for uncertainty-aware compute allocation in such information access settings, rather than only as an online stopping heuristic. Our method estimates token-level entropy from repeated samples, assigns each question to a reasoning-budget tier, compresses traces for lower-uncertainty cases, and trains compact student models with mixed-granularity supervision and optional reinforcement learning. On five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two knowledge-intensive QA settings in healthcare and finance, the method reduces reasoning length while preserving or improving accuracy. These results suggest that uncertainty estimates can shape supervision for resource-efficient generative AI and help models learn adaptive reasoning behavior without adding an inference-time controller.

papers.title: LACE: Unsupervised Concept Drift Detection in Multi-Label Data Streams Through Label Cluster Evolution
papers.abstract: Concept drift detection in multi-label data streams is challenging when true label vectors are delayed or unavailable. Most existing drift detectors monitor prediction errors, and therefore assume immediate access to ground-truth labels. This assumption is often unrealistic in stream settings, where reliable feedback may not be available at detection time. We propose LACE (Label Cluster Evolution), an unsupervised drift detector that uses changes in predicted label-dependency structure as evidence. It maintains a sliding window of recent predictions to compare label-cluster structures across consecutive subwindows. These clusters summarize evolving co-occurrence patterns among predicted labels, and changes in their structure are treated as evidence of drift in label dependencies. Cluster evolution is quantified using the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI), while Normalized Variation of Information handles degenerate cases and a Monte Carlo permutation procedure resolves ambiguous comparisons. We provide a comprehensive evaluation of LACE against several supervised error-based drift detectors and LD3, the only prior unsupervised drift detector for multi-label data streams to our knowledge. On real datasets, LACE achieves the best cumulative rank across predictive metrics despite requiring no immediate ground-truth labels. On synthetic datasets with known drift points, LACE reduces Delay For Detection by 63.51% on average relative to LD3, the next-best method, while achieving a 0% Missed Detection Rate. All code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/mehmetkadri/LACE.

papers.title: SchemaLens: Explainable Design-Space Reduction for Workload-Aware Document Schema Selection
papers.abstract: Document-schema design is a workload-dependent trade-off: embedding, referencing, and duplication affect latency, document growth, update cost, and the performance of other workload queries. Exhaustively benchmarking plausible MongoDB schemas is impractical, and selecting a schema too early can obscure relevant trade-offs. We present SchemaLens, an EER-guided framework for explainable design-space reduction. Rather than recommending a single schema, it extracts conceptual and workload signals and uses them to activate a compact family of MongoDB configurations for empirical benchmarking. Across representative workloads, SchemaLens reduces the benchmarked configuration space while preserving empirically competitive alternatives. The main benefit is an auditable reduction step that focuses benchmarking on semantically justified normalised, denormalised, bridge-based, and hybrid alternatives, while final schema selection remains empirical.

papers.title: Cross-Modal Attribute Consistency Verification for E-Commerce Products via Relational Graph Embedding
papers.abstract: Product attributes on e-commerce pages are often distributed across two modalities, textual content and embedded images. Such cross-modal presentation can introduce inconsistencies in wording, units, values, and attribute presence. Existing approaches match representations across modalities, but such alignment only indicates correspondence and cannot determine the relation type between paired attributes, such as equivalence and value conflict. We propose a framework that verifies attribute consistency at the attribute-pair level. First, it aligns cross-modal attributes by combining representation normalization with semantic embedding matching. Second, it classifies each aligned pair into four relation types. Third, it represents the inferred relations as typed triples in a relational graph for relational embedding learning. Finally, we evaluate the proposed framework on a real-world dataset in terms of relation classification, link prediction, and structural triple injection.

papers.title: RecipeNet: A Hierarchical Transformer for Recipe Data
papers.abstract: Recipe data arises in domains such as materials synthesis, pharmaceutical formulation, and industrial manufacturing, where procedures are represented as ordered sequences of steps containing heterogeneous structured fields. Existing tabular learning methods typically flatten this structure into fixed-schema representations, limiting their ability to capture hierarchical field interactions and procedural dependencies. We propose RecipeNet, a hierarchical Transformer architecture that encodes field-level interactions within each step and sequential dependencies across steps through stacked Transformer encoders. Experiments on multiple recipe datasets and tasks demonstrate that RecipeNet consistently outperforms existing tabular models, highlighting the value of hierarchical and sequential modeling for recipe representation learning.

papers.title: Less Is More: Knowledge Graph Construction and Schema-Guided Canonicalization with LLMs
papers.abstract: Knowledge graphs (KGs) are widely used in domains such as healthcare and finance, but existing LLM-based construction methods often produce redundant triples and semantically inconsistent representations. We propose a unified framework combining LLM-based triple extraction with schema-guided canonicalization. Our approach extracts triples and induces a schema to constrain canonicalization candidates, enabling consistent entity and relation merging. Experiments on five benchmark datasets show that our method produces more compact KGs with higher F1 scores than existing approaches. Ablation studies show that schema-guided canonicalization reduces redundancy with minimal loss of semantic fidelity. Our canonicalized KGs also improve retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) question-answering performance. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HwangSeonPark/less-is-more-kg

papers.title: Beyond Keywords: Training-Free Entity Linking for Multilingual Research Metadata
papers.abstract: Research collections in the humanities and social sciences describe overlapping subjects under divergent cataloguing practices, so records that belong together stay unconnected across databases. Stable identifiers would make the overlap machine-readable, but assigning them means disambiguating keywords that are short, multilingual, and largely without context. We present Context-Aware Routing for Entity Linking (CAREL), a training-free pipeline that links research metadata keywords to Wikidata QIDs through a four-layer cascade. Its core is Cross-lingual Retrieval Consensus (CRC), a novel signal that turns the agreement of retrieval ranks across language-specific queries into a measure of linking confidence without requiring annotated data. Rule-based layers resolve the clear cases, and only genuinely ambiguous keywords reach a locally deployed open-source large language model (LLM), which bounds inference cost and avoids sending research metadata to external services. On two manually verified benchmarks from multilingual African studies metadata, subject headings anchored in the Library of Congress Subject Headings (LCSH) and researcher-supplied tags, CAREL reaches 89.8% and 90.9% accuracy on the headings with Gemma4-31B-it and Qwen3.5-27B, and holds 88.8% and 89.5% on the anchor-free tags. It also detects the keywords for which no Wikidata entity exists, at an F1 of 88 on the tags.

papers.title: Pair-Level Essay-Scale Republication and Reuse from Fragmented Historical Text Reuse: A Workflow Study on Eighteenth-Century Books and Newspapers
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the recovery of essay-scale republication and reuse from fragmented text-reuse evidence, a setting whose central challenge is pair-level evidence consolidation and not fragment retrieval alone. The study focuses on a candidate set centered on essays by eighteenth-century Scottish philosopher David Hume, spanning books from ECCO (Eighteenth Century Collections Online) and historical newspapers. Because the input consists of fragmented reuse hits instead of clean document pairs, and positive coverage is inherently incomplete, we formulate the task as pair-level evidence consolidation into plausible transmission relations and compare three methodological families: a staged rule-based workflow, baselines (a decision tree and two direct LLM settings), and automated rule adaptation. On labeled ECCO--ECCO slices, pair-level feature aggregation alone already reaches 0.948 F1 on the main labeled slice, while the final workflow gives the strongest overall precision-recall trade-off among the tested rule stages. On the full ECCO--ECCO candidate universe, direct LLM baselines flag up to 14,886 pairs as reprints compared to 771 for the final workflow, behaving in this direct-prompt setup as high-recall candidate expanders rather than precision-controlled deployment classifiers. On ECCO--Newspaper, manual audit confirms all 176 predicted positives as genuine cases of republication or reuse, while issue duplication and source-side multiplicity reveal additional provenance structure. Under incomplete ground truth, auditable pair-level evidence consolidation provides a practical way to produce compact candidate spaces for historical inspection.

papers.title: Lost in Extraction: RE-ErrorTax, A Fine-Grained Taxonomy of LLM Errors in Relation Extraction Across Multiple Benchmarks
papers.abstract: Relation Extraction (RE) is a fundamental information extraction task that identifies semantic relationships between entities in text. Recent Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled zero-shot RE, reducing the need for task-specific training data. However, existing evaluations rely primarily on aggregate metrics such as F1 score, which provide limited insight into the underlying causes of model failures. To address this limitation, we introduce RE-ErrorTax, a fine-grained error taxonomy for analyzing LLM-generated relation triples. We evaluate 13 open-source and proprietary LLMs on five widely used RE benchmarks and categorize their errors using the proposed taxonomy. Furthermore, we investigate the feasibility of using LLMs as automated error evaluators and compare their judgments against human annotations on a manually annotated subset. Our analysis reveals that relation-level errors are substantially more common than entity-level failures and that LLM judges achieve moderate agreement with a human annotator. The results demonstrate the value of taxonomy-driven evaluation for understanding LLM behavior and highlight the potential of LLM-based judges for scalable RE error analysis.

papers.title: When Persona Simulations Are Informative: Graph-Structured Signals for Pluralistic Opinion Sensing
affiliations: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Persona-conditioned large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate survey responses across diverse domains. However, apparent response variation can reflect unconditioned model priors or token sampling noise rather than systematic persona conditioning. We argue that persona-conditioned variation is informative when semantically similar personas exhibit concordant response shifts. To operationalize this principle, we introduce Persona-Conditioned Informativeness (PCI), an unsupervised diagnostic metric that measures whether semantically similar personas deviate in concordant directions relative to item-level sample baselines. By modeling personas as a similarity graph, PCI uses Local Moran's I to quantify local spatial coherence and extract compact persona subsets without using construct labels. To evaluate PCI without external human benchmarks, we test its ability to recover established latent value structure using the 57-item Portrait Values Questionnaire-Revised (PVQ-RR). Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) shows that a PCI-selected 10% subset substantially improves overall construct recovery relative to response-stability and random selection. These findings support PCI as a principled internal diagnostic for screening synthetic respondents in survey pipelines.

papers.title: GRAIN: Detecting AI-Generated News via Article-Level Structure
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate news articles that closely resemble human-written journalism, raising concerns about misinformation and the reliability of online information. Existing AI-generated text detectors primarily rely on lexical, stylistic, or contextual representations, which often struggle to generalize to unseen generators and do not explicitly model article-level structure in news. We propose GRAIN, a framework for AI-generated news detection that jointly models semantic representations and article-level structural patterns. Through empirical analysis, we identify recurring article-level structural patterns in AI-generated news that remain consistent across multiple LLM families and a real-world AI-generated news dataset. Experiments on RAID, DetectRL, an in-house dataset comprising 157K AI-generated news articles from 11 LLMs, and the real-world NewsGPT dataset show that GRAIN improves ROC-AUC over the strongest baseline by 7.9 percentage points on average across evaluation settings. These results suggest that article-level structural patterns provide effective complementary signals for improving the robustness and generalization of AI-generated news detection. The code is available at: https://github.com/DSAIL-SKKU/GRAIN-CIKM-2026.

papers.title: Grounded Distractor Probing: A Diagnostic Protocol for Hard-Distractor Sensitivity in VLM Multiple-Choice Evaluation
papers.abstract: Multiple-choice evaluation for vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly relies on stronger distractors, but recent work has mostly emphasized distractor construction or generic option bias. We introduce Grounded Distractor Probing (GDP), a matched original/permutation/hard diagnostic protocol that probes how models respond to same-type, visually plausible near-miss distractors under a controlled intervention. GDP is instantiated on GDP-Slice, a manually curated 98-item diagnostic slice, and additionally characterized on an overlap-inclusive 198-item GDP-v2-lite silver set. Across four VLMs, we find that evidence-first prompting is not a universal improvement: under the same hard-distractor probe, some models improve hard-condition accuracy or reduce distractor selection, while others show lower hard-condition accuracy or increased distractor selection. We therefore argue that MCQ-based VLM evaluation should report distractor sensitivity together with model-dependent intervention response, rather than aggregate accuracy alone.

papers.title: Auditing Ethical Value Misalignment in LLM-Based Human Simulation: A Dual-Metric Cross-National Study with Persona Injection
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose MIRAGE ( Mi salignment and R epresentation A udit for G lobal E thical Simulation), a cross-national, multi-LLM framework that empirically audits how faithfully persona-injected LLMs represent human ethical values along two axes: directional bias —a systematic skew of LLM responses toward a particular ethical direction—and distributional diversity —how well LLM responses preserve the spread of human responses. Our method (1) constructs a seven-category taxonomy from the 23 items in the World Values Survey (WVS) Wave 7 Ethical Values and Norms section, (2) generates 10,000 stratified personas per country across eight countries from WVS demographic distributions and injects them into LLMs, and (3) measures ethical value misalignment between LLM and human responses. Category-level paired tests (7 categories × 3 LLMs = 21 comparisons) reveal significant human–LLM differences in 18 of 21 for distributional diversity and 12 of 21 for directional bias, with the item-level tests (23 items × 3 LLMs = 69 comparisons) confirming that this misalignment is pervasive (44/69). LLMs show lower distributional diversity than humans across nearly all categories, indicating that they fail to represent response diversity, and LLMs show lower permissiveness in Dishonesty & Corruption, while directional bias in Political Violence varies by model. These findings demonstrate that researchers should jointly audit LLM-based personas for directional bias and distributional diversity before using them as proxies for human populations.

papers.title: When Cheap Answers Are Not Delivered Answers: Contract-Aware Costing and Repair for Multilingual LLM Systems
papers.abstract: Multilingual LLM systems are often paid to deliver objects, not merely facts: localized final answers, parseable sections, visible traces, or JSON fields consumed by downstream tools. Standard cost per correct answer (CPC) prices factual correctness but can ignore whether the requested object was delivered. We operationalize Contract-Aware Delivered-Answer Evaluation: specify a visible language/format contract, label reliable delivery as correctness plus non-truncation plus contract compliance, replay deployable verifier-triggered repairs, and compare system variants by cost per reliable-correct delivered answer (CPRC). In a 5,040-output human-reviewed MGSM audit over six models, seven languages, and four requested language-path contracts, the English-trace/target-answer condition preserves 89.7% answer accuracy but falls to 53.7% visible reliable-correct delivery. Under target-final-only scoring, where the trace is ignored, delivery remains 62.0%, so the mismatch persists even without scoring the trace. Under the fixed English-trace/target deliverable, CPC and CPRC select different lowest-cost deployable prompt or visible-verifier repair variants in 19/35 complete model-language cells (problem-level bootstrap 95% interval: 16–22). DeepSeek/GPT account for 12 disagreements and the largest finite penalties, with median CPRC penalties of 3.07× and 2.77×; in 8 cells, the CPC-selected variant delivers zero reliable-correct outputs. A 500-output triple-labeled reliability check yields Fleiss' ?=0.911 for visible-contract compliance and ?=0.961 for reliable delivery. We release the ContractCostBench protocol and code, including contract specifications, prompt templates, visible-verifier logic, and rerun scripts. Belebele final-text and search-style JSON views show how the same contract-cost ledger extends to non-MGSM contracts. For the audited systems, visible compliance is not only an instruction-following label; it is a costed deployment variable.

papers.title: When Is Debateability a Model Property? Cross-Interlocutor Validation in Multi-Agent Debate
papers.abstract: Multi-agent debate (MAD) evaluations often treat resistance to false persuasion and receptiveness to truthful correction as model-level capabilities.
