We test whether such persuasion-derived scores support stable target-model inference in a controlled one-turn target–interlocutor persuasion setting. Across multiple models, interlocutors, and reasoning benchmarks, single-context scores fail to identify reliable target rankings and are strongly conditioned on the interlocutor. Leave-one-interlocutor-out evaluation shows that aggregating multiple interlocutors partially recovers a transferable combined signal, but the component behaviors generalize differently, with false-attack resistance remaining weakly transferable. Independently sampled response instability predicts acceptance of both false attacks and truthful corrections, indicating that answer revision is not inherently evidence of successful deliberation. In our downstream pruning setting, fixed-interlocutor rankings do not provide consistent cross-task evidence of agent contribution. These findings establish that interlocutor sampling is part of the measurement design and that single-interlocutor persuasion scores should not be interpreted as stable target-only properties of persuasion behavior without cross-interlocutor validation.

papers.title: Human Indirect Prompting Vulnerabilities and Intention-Aware Conversational Defenses for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can explain sensitive topics across domains, but harmful goals may be concealed behind educational, fictional, historical, or research-oriented framing. We study Human Indirect Prompting (HIP), a conversation-level behavior in which a user steers an LLM toward restricted information without explicitly stating the unsafe objective. We construct a controlled, redacted dataset of 25 HIP prompts spanning five risk domains and ten prompting strategies, and evaluate five LLM families. Across 123 valid responses, indirect prompting achieves an overall attack success rate of 53.66% with substantial cross-model and cross-strategy variation. We then introduce Controller-Guided Intention-Aware Conversational Defense (IACD), a wrapper that uses structured experiment context and conversation-level control before the target model completes a request. In an ablation study using the most and least vulnerable target models from the five-model evaluation, direct harmful leakage is 88% and 20%, respectively, and falls to 0% under controller-guided conditions. Exact paired tests confirm significant reductions relative to direct prompting. These results characterize HIP and provide initial evidence for dialogue-level safety control, while the controlled use of benchmark intent metadata limits claims about autonomous intent inference.

papers.title: Semantic Boundary: A Framework and Benchmark for Policy-Constrained Semantic Disclosure
papers.abstract: Privacy-preserving AI systems must determine what information crosses from trusted collection contexts into downstream analytics, observability, evaluation, and agentic workflows. Existing approaches such as redaction, tokenization, and sanitized rewriting primarily limit disclosure by transforming surface representations. However, modern AI systems depend on feedback loops over operational traces (e.g., conversations, tool use, logs, and reports), and aggressive suppression can remove the semantic information they need for debugging, monitoring, evaluation, and learning. This challenge is particularly acute for longitudinal behavioural traces: interaction routines and inferred intent can function as identifying signatures even after explicit identifiers have been removed. Privacy and utility are therefore coupled through the semantic information that remains available after privacy-preserving transformations have been applied. We introduce Semantic Boundary, a framework for reasoning about what meaning may cross system boundaries under explicit disclosure policies and downstream purposes. Under this framework, sensitive inputs are transformed into policy-governed exports with transformation provenance before release to a downstream consumer. To evaluate alternative disclosure strategies, we construct the Semantic Boundary Benchmark (SBB), a counterfactual export-lattice benchmark over synthetic behavioural traces with injected sensitive attributes, quasi-identifiers, latent behavioural patterns, analytical tasks, and provenance targets. We find that risk-constrained selection on this lattice varies by registered purpose and linkage tolerance: surface-token suppression can coexist with persona re-linking; different tasks favour different lattice conditions; and forcing one condition across consumers incurs measurable utility regret. SBB makes these purpose-conditioned comparisons measurable and reproducible.

papers.title: Adaptive Authorization Execution for Authorized Retrieval via TFHE-Aware Predicate Compilation
papers.abstract: Modern retrieval and RAG systems commonly fill a candidate set before enforcing access, allowing unauthorized documents to consume candidate slots and displace authorized evidence. We present an authorization-aware routing operator under bitwise TFHE. Its attribute-family TFHE compiler (AFTC) reuses public predicate instances across policy templates, while repeated policy nodes can execute through a shared DAG. We evaluate two real-TFHE paths separately: a Base-ADAPT execution path that selects between per-template and shared-DAG execution, and a fixed-PT AFTC compiler ablation. We do not report an end-to-end AFTC-adaptive runtime. At the largest tested setting, Base-ADAPT achieves a 7.39±0.14× speedup over Naive-DOC, whereas AFTC-PT achieves a 1.918±0.012× speedup over Base-PT. A five-seed MS MARCO replay using the ABAC Lab E-Document workload for the view action raises Recall@10 from 0.382 to 0.513 among answerable query–user pairs (10.8% mean coverage), with a conditional mean routed-corpus fraction of 39.5% over that subset. A trusted policy enforcement point (PEP) materializes routes and performs exact final enforcement. The large-corpus experiment replays a common BM25 run with a plaintext authorization oracle; it does not measure full-corpus TFHE retrieval or physical-index latency.

papers.title: Toward TabUL Rasa in Tabular Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Generative models are increasingly adopted as they become more capable of synthesizing realistic data. Across various domains, this has urged improved control of the data that influence their behavior. Central herein is the ability to remove or alter data used during training post-hoc. While unlearning methods show promise for visual and language generators, they remain understudied in the tabular context. Both generally and specifically in attribute-level (column) data removal. In this work, we aim to empirically characterize the latter vertical unlearning using our proposed framework to quantify the ability of post-training methods to remove features (columns). Our evaluation of existing unlearners and a new variant, Vertical Negative Preference Optimization, provides insights into the dynamics of feature removal. Therewith uncovering a consistent limitation: categorical features pose an additional challenge. Our code is available online: https://gitlab.ewi.tudelft.nl/dmls/publications/tabul-rasa.

papers.title: Correlation-Guided Latent Sharing for Non-IID Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed clients without centralizing raw data, but its performance often degrades under non-independent and non-identically distributed (non-IID) data. This degradation is especially severe when clients observe only a limited subset of the global label space, causing biased local updates and client drift. Standard aggregation methods such as FedAvg and FedProx mainly address this problem at the optimization level, but they do not directly enrich the incomplete local data distributions that cause heterogeneity. This paper proposes Correlation-Guided Latent Sharing (CGLS), a federated learning framework that selectively augments client training using latent information received from statistically aligned peers. CGLS identifies compatible clients through gradient-direction correlation and mixes local training data with synthetic latent information from correlated neighbors. We formulate this process as a mixed-distribution federated objective and explain how targeted mixing can reduce gradient dispersion under severe label skew. Experiments on MNIST, FashionMNIST and CIFAR-10 under Dirichlet and balanced one-class non-IID partitions show that CGLS improves accuracy and macro-F1 over FedAvg and FedProx, with the largest gains appearing in the strongest heterogeneity settings.

papers.title: Many Cultures, One Label: Investigating Cultural Alignment in Harmful Meme Detection
papers.abstract: Harmful meme detection has become an important multimodal classification task. However, existing approaches are trained and evaluated against a single ground-truth binary label (harmful/not harmful), implicitly assuming a universal notion of harmfulness despite evidence that perceptions of harmful content are shaped by cultural and social context. In this paper, we investigate whether culture-aligned Large Language Model (LLM) agents can surface cross-cultural variation in harmful meme perception and reveal potential biases in benchmark annotations. To this end, we instantiate six culture-aligned LLM agents. Given a meme, each agent independently evaluates its harmfulness and provides a culturally grounded rationale. These assessments are integrated with OCR text and image captions into a concept graph representation of the meme, and combined with complementary vision language features to train a downstream classifier. Experiments on the Facebook Hateful Memes (FHM) benchmark show that the resulting model achieves competitive performance (AUC = 0.804), outperforming several baselines. More importantly, our analysis reveals substantial cross-cultural variation: the six agents disagree on 34.9% of 10,000 evaluated memes, while maintaining an overall agreement level (k = 0.690) remarkably close to that reported for human annotators (k = 0.684). We further find significant differences in alignment with the ground-truth labels, with agents representing Brazil, South Africa, and the United States exhibiting consistently higher agreement than agents representing India, Japan, and Saudi Arabia. These findings suggest that harmfulness benchmarks may implicitly privilege particular cultural interpretations of harmful content.

papers.title: Explaining Neural Combinatorial-Optimisation Policies: LP-Weighted Attribution, CSP-Certified Counterfactuals, and Bonferroni-PAC Sufficient Subsets
papers.abstract: Most neural policies for combinatorial optimisation (CO) rely on opaque autoregressive decoders. Operators therefore cannot tell whether a routing or scheduling choice is driven by a near-binding capacity, a tight time window, a budget envelope, or a geometric shortcut. We introduce CAX, a post-hoc explainer built around three primitives from the constraint-programming relaxation already supplied by the problem. The Λ primitive is a Lagrangian-weighted gradient × feature decomposition that scales each family's attribution by its LP shadow price. The ζ primitive is a sample-and-verify counterfactual whose accepted perturbations carry a CSP feasibility certificate. The S primitive is a Bonferroni-corrected Hoeffding sufficient-subset test. Along the greedy attribution ordering, this test bounds the smallest subset of nodes that preserves the policy's argmax, with family-wise probability 1-δ. We compare three multiplier backends using the counterfactual-derived signal on CVRPTW, OP, and FJSP, which have contrasting rank profiles. In the rank-mismatch regime, the LP-anchored backend improves over the proxy gradient by +21.5 and +42.0 percentage points on CVRPTW and OP, respectively (McNemar p ≤ 10 -14 on ≥ 281 certified flips). In the rank-aligned FJSP regime, it matches the proxy, with both backends reaching 100% on the 59 certified flips. This pattern supports CAX's account of when LP duals add information and when they do not. Across a 54-configuration robustness sweep, the CF-derived top family remains unchanged on all three problems.

papers.title: When Representation Drift Does Not Reflect Functional Contribution: A Regime Analysis of Prompt Tuning
papers.abstract: Representation similarity metrics are commonly used to validate parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods that adapt large pre-trained language models by updating only a small subset of parameters under the implicit assumption that a large drift implies meaningful adaptation. In the encoder-based classification settings of this study, we demonstrate that this assumption is regime-dependent rather than universal. In Regime A (frozen encoder, trainable classifier), learned soft prompts exhibit drift comparable to Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) yet are entirely dispensable: removing, scaling, or randomizing them changes fewer than 0.3% of predictions (well within the variance of a random seed). A geometric decomposition explains this: 98% of prompt drift lies in the null space of the multi-class classifier weight matrix, computed across all heads and five seeds. In Regime B (frozen encoder, frozen task-fitted head, trainable prompts), we run two controlled variants: (B1) head taken from a converged Regime A model and (B2) head re-initialised from a different random seed. We find consistent, statistically significant gains in both, ruling out re-alignment artifacts. In Regime C, C(LoRA) and C(BitFit) produce representational drift of comparable Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) magnitude that aligns closely with the decision boundary (orthogonal fraction 0.52–0.55), yielding large performance gains. Three similarity metrics, namely CKA, Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA), and Projection-Weighted Canonical Correlation Analysis (PWCCA), agree on drift magnitude across every regime yet cannot distinguish functional from non-functional adaptation. We do not claim these metrics are generally invalid; rather, we characterise the specific architectural condition under which they become uninformative, that is, the presence of a free trainable component downstream of the drift source.

papers.title: Attention to those tokens! Ensemble Clustering can explain Attention-based Text Classifiers
papers.abstract: Recent research has questioned the reliability of attention weights as faithful explanations for Transformer-based text classifiers, showing that highly attended tokens are not necessarily responsible for model predictions and that attention distributions can be manipulated without affecting outputs. In this work, we argue that, although attention scores alone are not suitable feature-importance measures, attention patterns still encode meaningful semantic relationships among tokens that can be exploited for explainability purposes. We propose ECAM (Ensemble Clustering from Attention Maps), a novel framework for attention-based text classifiers. ECAM leverages attention maps extracted from Transformer layers to build token similarity structures and identify semantically coherent token clusters through an ensemble clustering strategy. We demonstrate that clusters produced by ECAM can be used to produce faithful explanations while requiring substantially fewer black-box evaluations than perturbation-based approaches such as LIME. Importantly, since ECAM is agnostic to the explanation task, in that it relies on semantically-driven token aggregations induced by attention patterns, our findings also provide broader evidence about the intrinsic relational properties encoded by Transformer attention mechanisms. This suggests that attention maps capture stable explainability-oriented relational structures beyond their direct use as token-importance indicators.

papers.title: When Do Gradient-Based Explanations Identify Important Video Frames? A Global-Local Evaluation of Time-Series Explanations
papers.abstract: Gradient-based methods are widely used to explain deep video models, yet their ability to identify temporally important evidence remains insufficiently understood. We study gradient-based video explanation as frame-level temporal evidence detection. Using a global-local spatiotemporal attention network trained with weak video-level labels, we convert VanillaGrad, SmoothGrad, and Grad-CAM outputs into frame-level importance scores and evaluate them against annotated activity frames across four medically relevant video classification tasks. The results show that combining full-frame global views with local region-of-interest views improves both video classification and important-frame detection. The global-local model achieves 96.49 F1 for classification, and its SmoothGrad explanations achieve 86.68 F1 for important-frame detection. At the same time, the evaluation reveals failure modes: Grad-CAM is less effective for the transformer-based model, and CNN-based gradients are more reliable for long videos. These findings suggest that video explanations should be evaluated by their ability to identify relevant frames, not only by visual inspection of saliency heatmaps.

papers.title: MINT: Mitigating Structural Inconsistency via Attentive Message Passing for Financial Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Illicit account detection is a critical task for financial risk control systems, aiming to pinpoint malicious actors within transaction networks. Existing efforts typically recast transaction networks into directed multigraphs and leverage graph neural networks (GNNs) to detect anomalies via topological structures under the homophily assumption. However, directly grafting GNNs onto transaction graphs is faced with at least two pivotal challenges, i.e., structural inconsistency and label scarcity. The former arises from deceptive connections forged by malicious actors, while the latter stems from the lack of annotated data. In light of these, we introduce MINT, a novel graph neural framework that mitigates structural inconsistency via an attentive message-passing scheme on transaction graphs. Specifically, MINT introduces a discrepancy-aware feature propagation, which tracks malicious actors by quantifying deviations between nodes across bi-directional transaction flows. A transaction salience module is proposed to mitigate structural inconsistency by adaptively regularizing the interaction strength between nodes. Furthermore, to alleviate label scarcity, MINT is optimized via Positive-Unlabeled (PU) learning, which exploits only a minority of illicit nodes coupled with a majority of unlabeled ones. Extensive experiments conducted on three financial transaction benchmarks, including two large-scale public and one in-house real-world datasets, validate the superior effectiveness of MINT over several cutting-edge baselines.

papers.title: CARE: Calibrated Attribute Imputation with Deviation Refinement for Attribute-Missing Graph Clustering
papers.abstract: This paper studies the problem of attribute-missing graph clustering, which involves a subset of nodes with missing attributes. Existing approaches typically integrate neighborhood-aware imputation with graph autoencoders for self-supervised graph learning, resulting in suboptimal performance due to potential imputation biases and representation collapse. To address these issues, we propose Calibrated Attribute Imputation with Deviation Refinement (CARE) for attribute-missing graph clustering. The core of CARE is a self-iterative optimization scheme that jointly improves attribute imputation and graph clustering within a teacher-student framework. Specifically, our CARE introduces two complementary masking strategies, including a fixed permanent masking set and a dynamic temporal masking set, to provide reliable reconstruction supervision. The student network is optimized through attribute reconstruction over all originally observed nodes from corrupted inputs, and the teacher network is optimized using the exponential moving average of the parameters in the student network to provide stable predictions for consistency regularization. In addition, we introduce a deviation refinement strategy to iteratively update cluster prototypes and stabilize representation learning. Experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of CARE against seven competing baselines.

papers.title: Improved Streaming Algorithm for Balanced Hypergraph Partitioning
papers.abstract: Balanced hypergraph partitioning is an essential task for massive hypergraph analysis in distributed computing. Existing methods usually use the entire hypergraph to obtain structural information before the assignment process. However, many applications require online partitioning, motivating the development of streaming algorithms. In the streaming order, vertices are assigned in real time and their ownership does not change. Therefore, partitioning the streamed vertices under the balance constraint is challenging. In this paper, we propose a method for balanced hypergraph partitioning in the streaming mode. By defining a modularity function under the Erdos-Renyi random hypergraph model, we build the Erdos-Renyi Hypergraph Modularity Greedy. We approximate the hypergraph as a uniform hypergraph and optimize the modularity function with lower computational complexity. Compared with other modularity functions, our modularity function is more suitable for streaming algorithms. Finally, we design a data structure to reduce the execution time for finding the block with minimum capacity. Overall, our method achieves the state-of-the-art performance when evaluated with the cut-net metric.

papers.title: SBAND: Spectral Band-wise Score Debiasing for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
affiliations: Seoul National University of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Reconstruction-based multivariate time-series anomaly detection (MTSAD) typically assigns anomaly scores using the mean squared reconstruction error (MSE). We show that this score has a spectral blind spot : because MSE responds strongly to large errors, anomaly signals in low-energy bands of the training spectrum are ignored by the score. The per-dataset oracle headroom, measured on 9 of 12 well-known benchmark datasets, objectively confirms this diagnosis. From this, we propose SBAND (Spectral Band-wise Score Debiasing for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection), a post-hoc correction determined in closed form from the spectrum statistics of the training input alone, without labels, validation, or separate tuning. SBAND is attached only at the scoring stage without retraining: an activation gate automatically disables the correction on diffuse datasets, and a closed-form gain determines the correction strength from the training spectrum negentropy. On the 12 benchmark datasets, SBAND, with an average AUROC of 0.802 (only 0.007 below the per-dataset oracle of 0.809), outperforms the state-of-the-art model CATCH (0.759) by +0.043 as well as all 13 external baselines. SBAND is backbone-agnostic. We apply it on CATCH, replacing the FFT with a real-valued FFT (rFFT) for efficiency, yielding a 2.6× training speedup over CATCH (6.48h vs 16.97h) and improving both accuracy and efficiency over the state of the art. The code is available at https://github.com/bigbases/SBAND.

papers.title: Redundancy-Aware Sensor Array Optimization for Electronic Nose Classification
papers.abstract: Electronic nose (E-nose) systems rely on multi-sensor arrays to classify gases or volatile compounds, but dense sensor arrays increase hardware cost, power consumption, and deployment complexity. This work studies compact E-nose sensor array optimization while preserving classification performance. We propose MOMENT-R3S, a redundancy-aware optimization framework based on pre-trained time-series foundation model representations. MOMENT-R3S ranks sensors by jointly considering task relevance, class separability, single-sensor utility, and inter-sensor redundancy, and determines a compact deployment budget through a performance retention constraint. Experiments on five E-nose datasets show that MOMENT-R3S reduces 40.0%–54.0% of sensors while preserving 95.61%–99.29% of full-sensor Macro-F1 performance. Under the same fixed sensor budgets, MOMENT-R3S consistently outperforms prototype-distance methods, TSelect, mutual information, and mRMR. These results show that time-series foundation model representations and redundancy-aware ranking provide an effective solution for low-cost and compact E-nose sensor array design.

papers.title: XGIF: An Explanation-Guided Anomaly Detection Extention of Isolation Forest
affiliations: IRIT, UMR 5505 CNRS, Université Toulouse Capitole
papers.abstract: Isolation Forest ranks among the most widely used unsupervised anomaly detection algorithms due to its simplicity, scalability, and computational efficiency. However, its tree construction process relies exclusively on randomly selected splitting features and split values, ignoring informative signals about how anomalies are characterized in the feature space. In this paper, we propose XGIF, an explanation-guided extension of Isolation Forest that exploits feature attribution signals to drive the isolation process. Our core insight is that anomalous instances tend to exhibit unstable attribution patterns across the tree ensemble, while normal instances are characterized by more consistent attributions. XGIF introduces attribution stability as a novel criterion for evaluating leaf purity and adaptively extends tree growth when unstable explanatory patterns are detected. Furthermore, the growth process is guided toward features that contribute most to anomaly characterization, enabling more effective isolation of outlying instances. By integrating explainability directly into the learning mechanism, rather than confining it to post-hoc interpretation, XGIF leverages attribution signals as an active driver of anomaly detection performance. Experiments on 20 benchmark datasets from ADBench demonstrate that XGIF significantly improves detection performance, outperforming Isolation Forest on 17 of 20 datasets.

papers.title: Calibration before Recognition: Sensor-Level Domain Generalization for Cross-Session HD-sEMG Gesture Recognition
papers.abstract: Cross-session HD-sEMG gesture recognition is a zero-shot domain generalization problem central to deployable myoelectric interfaces. Existing approaches typically treat the session gap as a generic distribution mismatch and address it through larger models, uniform normalization, or latent feature alignment. We argue that, in HD-sEMG, part of this gap arises before representation learning: electrode reattachment perturbs the sensing interface, producing structured drift that is frequency-selective in amplitude and non-uniform across electrodes. Motivated by this observation, we propose a calibration-before-recognition paradigm for cross-session HD-sEMG generalization and instantiate it as Frequency–Electrode Calibration (FEC), a lightweight plug-in framework that recalibrates band-wise spectral magnitudes and down-weights unreliable electrodes before backbone feature extraction, without target-session labels or model updates. On the Hyser cross-session benchmark (20 subjects, 2 recording days separated by 3-25 days), FEC with a MobileNet3D-SE backbone achieves 70.96% zero-shot accuracy using only 99.2K parameters, improving the naive backbone by 9.33% and the strongest normalization-style calibration baseline by 4.99%. These results suggest that explicitly modeling sensor-level drift can shift cross-session generalization from purely model-centric compensation toward pre-recognition calibration, offering an interpretable view of cross-session HD-sEMG degradation and enabling a parameter-efficient framework for resource-constrained edge deployment in real-world wearable myoelectric systems.

papers.title: Not All Segmentation Is Equal: How Quality Filters Evaluate Structure
papers.abstract: Classifier-based quality filtering (CQF) increasingly determines which web documents compose language-model pretraining corpora, yet its structural preferences remain poorly understood. Prior work shows that broad presentation changes can shift CQF scores, but it remains unclear how specific forms of document organization affect this judgment. This paper studies heading- and list-based organization, a common surface structure in web text, through a fact-mediated structural probe. For each source document, the probe extracts factual propositions and generates three variants from the same fact list: prose-like continuity, balanced heading/list organization, and over-segmented structure. Across examples generated from 9,973 seeds and ten public CQF and data-quality scores, CQF preferences vary sharply by objective. QuRater and several FineWeb-style educational filters favor balanced structure over Prose, while NVIDIA Quality DeBERTa and CLIMB-based scores favor Prose. Over-segmented presentation is broadly penalized relative to balanced structure, and threshold-level analyses show that structural presentation can change which documents would pass FineWeb-style educational filters. These results show that CQF models encode model-specific preferences over document organization, suggesting that data-quality filters should be evaluated not only by which documents they select, but also by which structural presentations they systematically reward. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/k391160334/cqf-structure-preference.

papers.title: Dual-Level Consensus Alignment for Multi-Agent Cooperation
affiliations: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.abstract: Centralized training exposes cooperative agents to information that is unavailable during decentralized execution, creating a problem of representation recovery: task-relevant cooperative information must remain independently inferable from each agent's local information. Existing latent-consensus approaches commonly impose a single uniform sharing scope, although team-wide consistency and interaction-local compatibility place different requirements on a cooperative representation. We characterize this limitation as consensus-scope mismatch and introduce multi-scale cooperative sufficiency, which requires the representation at each cooperation scope to preserve task-relevant information while remaining locally recoverable. Based on this principle, we propose Dual-Level Consensus Alignment (DLCA). DLCA combines a team-level posterior aligned with a privileged global anchor and a neighborhood-level posterior aligned only across interaction-defined neighbors. Scale-specific reconstruction discourages uninformative agreement, while both posteriors are inferred locally during execution. Experiments on the discrete SMAC and SMAC-HARD benchmarks and on the continuous MAPDN benchmark show that DLCA consistently outperforms strong actor-critic and value-based baselines.

papers.title: Prototype-Driven Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Active Voltage Control via Contrastive Latent Conditioning
affiliations: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.abstract: Active voltage control (AVC) in low-voltage distribution networks requires cooperative multi-agent policies that adapt to highly non-stationary operating conditions driven by photovoltaic generation, load fluctuation, and topology reconfiguration. Existing centralized-training-decentralized-execution multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) methods rely on entangled recurrent hidden states that lack explicit semantic abstraction, while prototype-aware variants depend on manually defined discrete prototype sets that limit adaptability across diverse operating regimes. We therefore propose Prototype-Driven Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (PD-MARL), which equips each cooperative agent with a continuous latent task prototype that summarizes its recent operating context and conditions its policy accordingly, and we ground the design in a unified mutual-information framework that justifies the joint training objective. On the MAPDN active voltage control benchmark across 33-, 141-, and 322-bus networks, PD-MARL achieves the best overall performance among all evaluated methods.

papers.title: Analyzing Stream Collapse in Hyper-Connections: From Diagnosis to Mitigation
papers.abstract: Multi-stream architectures augment standard Transformer residual pathways with several interacting streams. Focusing on Hyper-Connections (HC), we study whether residual information is distributed across streams or concentrated in a small subset. We use fine-grained diagnostics that expose both inter-stream routing and representation structure. We find that stream usage often becomes strongly imbalanced. After an early seeding stage, residual mixing tends to preserve same-stream flow, limiting exchange between streams. At the same time, representation magnitude and interpretable sparse features concentrate in a dominant stream. This indicates that the added residual pathways are used non-uniformly. Finally, symmetry-breaking stream initialization reduces dominant-stream behavior and improves validation performance across mHC variants.

papers.title: Automated Software Ticket Generation Using Large Language Models and Code Graphs
papers.abstract: High-quality tickets are essential for software development, serving as a means of knowledge transfer between product owners and developers. Poorly written tickets create additional work and increase development costs. Creating tickets is time-consuming, and product owners often lack insight into the codebase, resulting in descriptions that may not reflect existing implementations. Large language models (LLMs) excel at processing natural language and possess strong programming knowledge, making them promising tools for automating ticket generation. However, research on LLM-based ticket generation remains limited. Recent work has shown that combining LLMs with code graphs improves querying of large codebases, which may benefit ticket generation. We propose TicketAgent, a repository-aware workflow for automated software ticket generation that combines LLM-based ticket writing with code-graph-based code localization and project-specific domain knowledge. We evaluate TicketAgent alongside two baselines: an LLM-only workflow and a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) workflow. Across automated and human evaluations, providing LLMs with additional information sources consistently improves ticket quality. In particular, structured access to the source code via code-based querying yields the largest improvements, outperforming both the LLM-only and RAG baselines.

papers.title: Feature or Penalty? A Placement Diagnostic for Graph-Risk Signals in Learned Portfolio Decisions
papers.abstract: Graph-derived domain signals create a placement problem in learned decision systems: they may inform the predictor, or they may enter the downstream decision layer directly. We study this question in learned portfolio contracts, where a graph-risk score can be supplied as a neural feature (Feature-only contract) or additionally priced as an explicit penalty on risky exposure (Graph-penalty contract). To separate placement from asset-specific graph-score ordering, we introduce a within-state permutation diagnostic. The control permutes the graph-risk scores across assets within each decision state, preserving the state-level marginal distribution and the explicit penalty placement while breaking the asset-specific graph-risk assignment. On Fama-French industry portfolios and an external universe of exchange-traded funds (ETFs), explicit penalty placement reduces conditional value-at-risk at the 95% level (CVaR95), crowding, and co-crash risk relative to feature-only placement over ten seeds, with essentially matched effort. All variants use matched architecture, decision rule, benchmark, and feasibility constraints. The diagnostic separates two channels: explicit penalty placement, not graph ordering, accounts for the aggregate CVaR reduction; the permutation control attains lower CVaR than the true ordering in both universes, while the true ordering helps most clearly for industry crowding. We therefore identify explicit decision-layer placement as the more reliable source of risk control in this setting.

papers.title: Beyond Rote Memorization: A Cognitive Framework for Tracing Knowledge in Open-World Scenarios
papers.abstract: Knowledge Tracing (KT) models commonly represent exercises with learned problem identifiers, which limits their ability to handle new problems whose IDs have not accumulated sufficient interactions. We propose MKT-LLM, a content-aware framework for new-problem KT that combines problem-content representations with learner interaction history in an LLM-compatible latent space. The framework contains three components: (1) Perceptual Harmonization, which fuses learned problem embeddings with semantic content embeddings; (2) Adaptive Generalization, which synthesizes an ID-like representation for an unseen problem from semantically similar seen problems; and (3) Cognitive Synthesis, which models the learner's evolving knowledge state from the resulting interaction sequence. MKT-LLM uses content similarity to place new problems in the same latent space as observed problems and performs prediction from latent states rather than relying on token-level answer generation. Experiments on NIPS2020 and Junyi show consistent improvements over representative KT and cold-start baselines, and the model degrades more gracefully as the proportion of new problems increases.

papers.title: LCSR-LLM: Longitudinal Cognitive State Reasoning for LLM-based Knowledge Tracing
papers.abstract: Knowledge tracing aims to infer a student's evolving mastery from historical learning interactions. Recent large language model (LLM) approaches offer a natural way to encode textualized learning histories, but they are often evaluated primarily as next-step predictors. This leaves open whether the model forms a stable and diagnostically meaningful latent trajectory of student state, or merely exploits shallow statistics such as recent correctness rates. We introduce LCSR-LLM, a longitudinal cognitive state reasoning framework that uses marker-aligned LLM hidden states to estimate a soft latent cognitive-state trajectory at each prediction step. The framework combines state-conditioned prediction with trajectory-level regularization, especially dynamic consistency and entropy control, to encourage smoother and non-collapsed state posteriors. We further propose Longitudinal Aggregation Drift (LAD), a diagnostic protocol that measures sequence-level prediction drift, posterior uncertainty, and trajectory volatility. On ASSIST2012, LCSR-LLM with Qwen2.5-7B reaches 0.7684 AUC, 0.7705 ACC, and 0.8610 F1, achieving the best AUC among our controlled runs and the best F1 among the listed results, while remaining competitive in ACC. Paired trajectory diagnostics show that dynamic consistency and entropy control improve internal trajectory behavior beyond final predictive accuracy.

papers.title: Temporal-Aware Graph Attention for Sequential Knowledge Tracing
papers.abstract: Knowledge tracing aims to model student learning trajectories and predict future performance from historical question–response interactions. Many recent works approach knowledge tracing with graph-based modeling, where concept dependencies (question-concept relations) are represented as graphs and learning is driven by message passing or attention over these structures. Existing graph-based KT methods often rely on predefined or weakly learned graphs and lack a principled mechanism to jointly account for temporal distance and contextual relevance when aggregating past interactions. As a result, they may overemphasize non-informative signals while under-utilizing informative recent context. In this work, we introduce a graph attention-based knowledge tracing model, TAGAKT, and reframe the problem as implicit graph learning over a causal directed acyclic graph. Our proposed graph attention model incorporates context-aware, learnable temporal bias that adjusts the importance of historical interactions based on their distance to the current prediction point. In addition, we integrate an efficient channel recalibration module that performs lightweight cross-channel reweighting to suppress noisy feature dimensions arising from interaction aggregation, improving prediction robustness. Extensive experiments on six datasets show that TAGAKT outperforms baselines on most datasets and achieves the best overall rank.

papers.title: Robust Survival Analysis via Fuzzy Interval Learning
papers.abstract: Survival analysis plays an important role in healthcare applications, yet learning reliable time-to-event predictions remains challenging under censoring, limited data, outliers, and distributional shift. Existing uncertainty-aware approaches typically rely on Bayesian inference, ensemble methods, or higher-order probabilistic models, which often require multiple stochastic forward passes or introduce additional modeling complexity. To bridge the gap, we propose Fuzzy-AFT, a single-pass uncertainty-aware survival model that represents predictive uncertainty as output-space imprecision through fuzzy interval-valued predictions on the log-time scale. Our model is embedded within an accelerated failure time (AFT) framework and trained using a hybrid objective that combines censored likelihood estimation with interval-score-based regularization. This formulation enables direct optimization of interval-valued predictions without Bayesian sampling or second-order distributions. Experiments on two survival datasets demonstrate that Fuzzy-AFT maintains competitive predictive performance while improving robustness under covariate shift, outlier corruption, and data scarcity. Furthermore, the learned imprecision provides informative uncertainty signals for out-of-distribution detection. These results suggest that output-space imprecision offers a simple and effective alternative for robust uncertainty-aware survival analysis.

papers.title: Feasible by Construction: Preference-Guided Itinerary Optimization with Cross-Entropy Search
papers.abstract: Trip itinerary planning requires optimizing user preferences while satisfying hard constraints: opening hours, travel times, visit durations, daily schedule, and budget tier. We present Iterative Itinerary Optimizer, a feasibility-first framework that builds plans through projected insertions, where each proposed POI visit is retimed and kept only if the schedule stays feasible. A learned reward model trained from pairwise itinerary comparisons scores completed plans, and a cross-entropy-style update adapts the construction scorer toward high-reward candidates. Our main goal is to identify where itinerary quality actually comes from. On 891 controlled scenarios, the adaptive optimizer raises mean learned reward from 7.460 to 8.008 over the initial construction baseline. A separate equal-budget comparison attributes the improvement: most of it comes from evaluating several feasible candidates and keeping the best, while the adaptive update adds a smaller but reliable improvement over random sampling (+0.041). Because every edit is checked before it enters the plan, all variants are feasible by construction. The study positions feasible construction as a strong baseline and quantifies what an adaptive preference loop adds on top.

papers.title: Higher Capacity Transfer into JPQ Item Codes for Scalable Sequential Recommendation
papers.abstract: Although transformer models have improved the effectiveness of sequential recommendation, their computational and memory costs make it challenging to scale to item catalogues containing millions of items. To address this limitation, RecJPQ, a recommendation method based on joint product quantisation, represents each item using compact discrete codes rather than large embedding tables, substantially reducing training memory requirements. These codes are typically initialised from a memory-efficient bootstrap representation, such as truncated SVD, before being quantised. However, this process introduces an information bottleneck: because quantisation is inherently lossy, information may be lost when the bootstrap representation is mapped to the fixed-budget discrete item-code space, resulting in suboptimal code assignments. To address this capacity transfer problem, we initialise JPQ item codes using a higher-dimensional bootstrap representation and adopt product quantisation (PQ) to compress this representation into the fixed-budget discrete item-code space prior to training; we refer to this method as RecJPQ-HC (Higher Capacity). Experimental results show that RecJPQ-HC consistently improves downstream recommendation performance over the original RecJPQ code assignment strategy. Across multiple datasets and sequential recommendation models, it achieves statistically significant average relative improvements of approximately 30% in NDCG@10 while preserving memory efficiency.

papers.title: Latent Intent Anchoring for Robust Sequential Recommendation
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
papers.abstract: User behavior sequences are often driven by stable, high-level intents. Existing intent-aware sequential recommendation methods typically extract intents from derived sequence representations to serve as post-hoc supervisory signals. Although effective, this post-hoc paradigm prevents intents from explicitly participating in the semantic shaping of sequential representations. Without a structural high-level semantic anchor, the sequence representations become vulnerable to local item transitions and user behavioral noise. To overcome this challenge, we propose IASRec , an I ntent- A nchored S equential Rec ommendation framework that shifts user intents from post-hoc supervisors to architectural anchors. IASRec consists of three synergistic modules: (1) a Latent Intent Distiller (LID) to extract multi-faceted latent intents from interaction sequences; (2) an Intent-Anchoring Encoder (IAE) that infuses intent semantics into item representations to guide temporal dependency modeling; and (3) an Intent Consistency Regularizer (ICR) that ensures robustness across different intent views. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that IASRec achieves an average 7.7% improvement over state-of-the-art baselines and exhibits superior robustness, with markedly better resilience to 20% behavioral noise compared to competing methods. The source code is available at https://github.com/x-labs-xyz/iasrec.

papers.title: CoRe-Rec: Budgeted Consistency Policy Re-Rolling for Sequential Recommendation
affiliations: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
papers.abstract: Real-time sequential recommendation requires policies that are both expressive and efficient. Diffusion policies can model diverse user preferences, but their iterative denoising process introduces high serving latency. Standard reinforcement learning (RL) actors usually execute a single sampled action without checking whether the action is likely to trigger a positive user response before exposure. We propose CoRe-Rec , a budgeted consistency-policy re-rolling framework for RL-based slate recommendation. CoRe-Rec uses a shared consistency actor to generate continuous hyper-actions in one or few denoising steps. Each hyper-action induces a provisional slate through top-K item scoring. Before execution, a frozen user response model (URM) evaluates multiple low-cost candidates generated with different sampler configurations and noise seeds, and an early-stopping rule selects the best slate under an inference budget. The re-rolling step is a detached test-time search procedure: gradients are not propagated through the discrete sampler selection or the top-K slate construction; instead, the selected branch is recomputed for actor-critic learning. Experiments in simulated environments built from RL4RS, BookCrossing, and MovieLens 1M show that CoRe-Rec improves cumulative reward and episode depth while providing a favorable reward–latency trade-off.

papers.title: From Head to Tail: Asymmetric Knowledge Transfer in Long-tail Recommendation with Generative Semantic IDs
papers.abstract: Long-tail recommendation in real-world e-commerce platforms remains challenging due to severe data imbalance. Existing methods often struggle to combine content-based multimodal features with collaborative signals. Many of these methods also ignore an important asymmetry in knowledge transfer between head and tail IDs: noisy signals from tail IDs can hurt representation learning for head IDs. This paper presents AKT-Rec, a framework for Asymmetric Knowledge Transfer in long-tail Recommendation that uses LLM-generated semantic IDs. AKT-Rec uses Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) with supervised fine-tuning to align content representations with collaborative information for both items and users, producing semantic representations. It then discretizes these representations into semantic IDs with a Residual-Quantized VAE (RQ-VAE), which yields semantic clusters of similar entities. AKT-Rec has two main components: (1) Cluster-Guided Adaptive Embedding, which decomposes each ID representation into a cluster-level embedding that captures shared semantics and an individual embedding. Through an asymmetric contrastive objective and an activity-aware gating mechanism, this module directs knowledge transfer from head to tail IDs. (2) Hierarchical Feature Aggregation, which builds parallel feature views and adaptively fuses them to optimize predictions for samples with varying activity levels. Extensive experiments on both a public benchmark and a large-scale industrial dataset, together with online A/B testing on a major e-commerce platform, demonstrate the effectiveness of AKT-Rec. AKT-Rec improves offline performance by 0.35% in AUC and 1.53% in GAUC, outperforming several competitive baselines. In online A/B testing, AKT-Rec achieves a 2.76% increase in CTR and a 3.47% increase in GMV, validating its utility in real-world production environments.

papers.title: Preference-Aligned Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Semantic IDs (SIDs) are becoming a practical interface for generative recommendation. Existing pipelines usually build them by quantizing frozen content embeddings, implicitly assuming that content similarity is the right geometry for recommendation. This assumption is often too strong: items that look similar in content space may play different roles in user behavior, while behaviorally related items may be far apart in text embedding space. We propose a simple pre-quantization alignment step for SID construction. Starting from frozen content embeddings, we train a lightweight content-to-item adapter inside a sequential next-item prediction model. The adapted vectors replace the standard item embedding table and are optimized with the recommender’s cross-entropy objective. After training, the sequential model is discarded, and the adapted item vectors are quantized using a standard SID tokenizer such as RQ-KMeans. The resulting codes preserve the content-based SID interface while aligning the underlying continuous space with user behavior. This design separates two roles that are usually coupled: learning a recommendation-useful item geometry and assigning discrete codes. It is easy to add to existing SID pipelines and requires no changes to the tokenizer or the downstream generative recommender. Experiments show that aligning embeddings before quantization improves ranking quality over content-only SIDs, collaborative-only SIDs, and compression baseline.

papers.title: Do Recommenders Need to Think in Words? Latent Reasoning for Efficient LLM-Based Recommendation
papers.abstract: LLM-based recommender systems increasingly generate chain-of-thought (CoT) text before each item prediction to activate the LLM's reasoning capacity, costing tens to hundreds of extra tokens per recommendation at inference. We ask whether inference-time reasoning artifacts (textual or latent) can be replaced by training-time supervision alone, without loss of accuracy. We propose LatentRec, a framework for LLM-based generative recommendation that replaces inference-time reasoning artifacts with training-time per-step head supervision. LatentRec has three components. A 2.5M-parameter Continuous Thought Module iterates K latent reasoning steps over the LLM's hidden state during training. Soft Token Selection bridges the approximately 14x norm gap between hidden states and input embeddings. A Per-step Reasoning Loss (PRL) supervises every intermediate state through the LLM's prediction head against the first token of the target Semantic ID. The trained LLM retains this accuracy without the module at inference, so the module can be discarded at deployment. On three Amazon benchmarks, LatentRec improves HR@10 by 4.0–5.0% (relative) over a CoT-distilled baseline at 18.3x lower latency (batch=1). Per-step training supervision consistently improves accuracy across three datasets, paid once at training rather than at every recommendation.

papers.title: Training-Free LLM-Based Recommendation with Post-LLM Item Refinement Using Collaborative Signals
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise for training-free recommendation, but LLM-generated user interests are often too broad for fine-grained item retrieval. Existing methods incorporate collaborative filtering (CF) signals in a pre-LLM manner through candidate reranking or prompt augmentation, yielding limited gains. We propose CoRRe, a training-free recommendation framework with a post-LLM paradigm that injects CF signals into LLM-generated item representations, which are later matched with LLM-generated user interests for ranking. Specifically, CoRRe refines the directions of item embeddings using an item-item co-purchase graph and their magnitudes using item popularity. Experiments on real-world datasets show that CoRRe consistently outperforms existing training-free methods and achieves competitive or superior performance compared with training-based methods, without requiring any model training or task-specific fine-tuning.

papers.title: Typed Counterfactual Preference Optimization for Multi-Turn Conversational Recommendation Agents
papers.abstract: Large language models have enabled conversational recommendation agents (CRAs) that interact with users through preference clarification, tool-based retrieval, and natural-language recommendation. Existing prompt-based and preference-optimization methods can improve the interaction capabilities of CRAs, but they provide limited direct guidance for a critical multi-turn decision: when should the agent ask for more preferences, invoke the retriever, or present recommendations? To address this issue, we propose PAPO, a progress-anchored typed counterfactual preference optimization framework for multi-turn CRAs. PAPO identifies critical dialogue states where the current policy is likely to make strategically suboptimal action choices. For each critical state, PAPO constructs typed counterfactual candidates across Ask, Search, and Respond, and verifies them with action-type-specific criteria: information gain for clarification, item reachability progress for retrieval, and recommendation readiness and response grounding. The verified counterfactual actions are used to build preference pairs for direct preference optimization. Experiments in three AILO-Agent-based interactive recommendation environments show that PAPO improves recommendation-oriented performance over strong prompt-based and training-based baselines while maintaining competitive simulator-assessed satisfaction. Ablation and action timing analyses further confirm the effectiveness of typed counterfactual construction, type-specific verification, and readiness-aware recommendation.

papers.title: From Counterfactual Edits to Human Narratives: LLM-Driven Interpretations for Recommender System Explanations
affiliations: Faculty of Information Technology, Czech Technical University in Prague
Department of Computer Science, University of Innsbruck
papers.abstract: Recommender systems increasingly influence what users discover and consume online, yet the decision logic behind their outputs often remains opaque. Counterfactual explanation (CFX) methods provide an effective way to show which changes to a user's interaction history would alter a recommendation. In recommendation settings, however, CFXs often require many edits, producing long, low-level lists that are hard for users to interpret. Moreover, most evaluations emphasize edit counts while largely overlooking whether the resulting CFXs are coherent and actionable for users. We argue that this gap between generating valid CFXs and communicating model behavior stems from the lack of user-centered abstraction and limited qualitative evaluation. To bridge this gap, we investigate large language models as mediators that summarize raw CFX interaction edit lists into concise natural language explanations describing higher-level preference patterns. We optimize these mediators for correctness, informativeness, and linguistic quality through preference optimization, and evaluate the resulting explanations with human-calibrated metrics derived from separate human-labeled datasets. On the MovieLens-1M dataset, across multiple counterfactual generators and language models, the resulting summaries achieve high overall linguistic quality, while the strongest semantic results are obtained with high-success CFX methods such as ACCENT and SPINRec. Direct Preference Optimization improves the semantic metrics in almost all evaluated settings.

papers.title: Revisiting N2DCG: An Empirically Grounded Reformulation of Carousel Recommendation Evaluation
papers.abstract: Carousel interfaces have been widely used in video and music streaming services, yet it remains unclear how to properly evaluate recommender systems in these two-dimensional layouts. N2DCG has been proposed to address this gap by adapting NDCG to carousel-based recommendation, but it relies on unverified assumptions borrowed from the single-list web-search setting that do not transfer well to two-dimensional carousel layouts. We identify two substantial limitations of N2DCG: its ideal ranking, used for normalization, violates carousel constraints, and its discount function does not reflect user browsing behavior observed in empirical data. To address both limitations, we propose a reformulation of N2DCG that normalizes appropriately by respecting constraints and uses an empirically grounded discount function. We validate the proposed metric, showing that it better reflects users' empirical behavior on real-world eye-tracking data and better predicts the comparison results of carousel layouts simulated based on empirical examination patterns.

papers.title: Diagnosing Lexical Text-Anchor Retrievability in Sequential Recommendation Benchmarks
papers.abstract: Aggregate accuracy on text-rich sequential recommendation benchmarks can obscure whether gains reflect broader sequential preference modeling or local item-text matching. We operationalize lexical text-anchor retrievability with a BM25-over-title diagnostic for identifying next-item cases recoverable from recent history items. On Amazon Beauty, Sports, and Toys, last-title BM25@10 retrieves the target for 6.6%, 3.6%, and 8.8% of test cases, while a recent-5 anchor-union diagnostic retrieves the target for 12.8%, 7.8%, and 14.4%; the same diagnostic is much weaker on ML-1M and Steam. As an aggregate-sensitivity test, we inject normalized recent-title evidence into ID-based sequential models without additional model training. On Amazon datasets, this bounded, validation-tuned perturbation shifts Recall@10 by an amount comparable to differences among recent learned retrieval-oriented references under our evaluation setting. These results indicate that the Amazon product benchmarks considered here contain a recency-concentrated text-anchor-retrievable regime that can disproportionately influence aggregate evaluation. We therefore recommend reporting performance separately on text-anchor-retrievable and non-retrievable cases alongside aggregate Recall/NDCG. The code is available at: https://github.com/keito0329/Retrievability.

papers.title: Cross-Country Code-Mixing for Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Cross-country recommendation on modern e-commerce platforms is typically deployed with disjoint user and item ID spaces across markets, removing the shared anchors that conventional cross-domain methods rely on. Generative recommendation (GR) mitigates this by mapping items into a shared token space and training a unified model, but existing approaches keep behavior sequences strictly country-specific, so knowledge transfer occurs only at the parameter level and remains absent at the data level. Inspired by code-switching corpora in multilingual natural language processing, we propose CMRec, a cross-country GR framework that injects cross-country supervision at the data level via dual-constrained, context-aware code-mixing. CMRec first learns a shared semantic codebook from multi-modal content and behavioral co-occurrence across countries. It then uses this codebook to synthesize mixed-country sequences via token-level substitutions that satisfy both static (content) and dynamic (e.g., price, audience, popularity) constraints. Finally, it introduces a context-aware loss that reweights mixed samples according to their plausibility in the current sequence. Experiments on two real-world multi-country datasets and an online A/B test show that CMRec substantially improves recommendation quality in data-sparse countries while preserving performance in data-rich countries, achieving +1.77% advertising revenue and +2.64% orders on a large-scale e-commerce platform.

papers.title: Taxonomy-Guided Contrastive Learning with Competency-Calibrated Graphs for Job Recommendation
papers.abstract: The goal of job-skill matching is to predict appropriate job opportunities for job seekers based on their skill-sets. Prior studies encode unstructured skill data into latent representations using simple mappings within job classification systems. However, such approaches often fall short in capturing the multi-level and asymmetric associations between jobs and job-relevant competencies. To address these limitations, we propose TaxoCal, a Taxonomy-guided contrastive learning framework with competency-Calibrated graph propagation for skill-based job recommendation. TaxoCal combines skill-taxonomy augmentation with degree-normalized bipartite graph propagation to mitigate generic skill bias and preserve job-specific competency signals. The model learns both skill and job representations using path/depth cues from the taxonomy and competency-aware interaction patterns in the job-skill graph. Experimental results on real-world datasets show that our method improves accuracy by +13.6%, NDCG@3 by +10.6%, and MRR@3 by +11.7%, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines.

papers.title: DualSpectralCF: Training-Free Sign-Aware Spectral Collaborative Filtering
papers.abstract: Real-world recommendation platforms routinely collect explicit negative feedback such as 1-star reviews, hate-button clicks, distrust between users, and very-low watch-ratio videos. Learned sign-aware recommenders exploit this signal for clear accuracy gains, but only at the cost of gradient-based training. In parallel, a line of training-free spectral collaborative filtering methods matches or beats learned graph recommenders at a fraction of the cost, yet operates on positive interactions alone. We bridge these two lines with DualSpectralCF, a training-free framework of two components that attach to any spectral backbone of the form r̂ u = F( M ) r u : a signed input signal r u ± that encodes the user's explicit dislikes, and a signed item-item operator M ± that blends like-together and dislike-together similarity. The framework is backbone-agnostic and adds just two scalar hyperparameters. We instantiate DualSpectralCF on ChebyCF, GF-CF, and Turbo-CF, and evaluate on five sign-aware benchmarks: every instance matches or beats its unsigned backbone on all 5 datasets at Recall@20 and in 14 of 15 cases at NDCG@20, with Recall@20 lifts up to +32.6% with backbone-specific (γ, κ) tuning and +1.9% to +16.0% for DualSpectralCF on ChebyCF at the fixed default (γ=-0.5, κ=0.1), and the family runs 7.7 to 155.3× faster than SIGformer while reaching 70.7% to 90.7% of its accuracy. Sign-awareness helps most for cold-start users, with up to +29.2% Recall@20 on Epinions users with 1 to 5 training items. Code: https://github.com/guanqun-yang/DualSpectralCF

papers.title: Norm Removed, Bias Remains: Gradient-Decoupled Sampled Softmax for Collaborative Filtering
papers.abstract: Popularity bias in collaborative filtering is known to manifest in embedding norms, which grow with interaction frequency. Sampled softmax (SSM) paired with cosine scoring addresses this by normalizing norms out of the score, and has become the dominant training objective. However, our gradient-level analysis reveals that two further mechanisms reintroduce degree bias during training. First, per-update norm drift under plain SGD recreates degree-dependent gradient magnitudes. Second, per-epoch gradient accumulation scales linearly with the interaction count, conflating genuine preference with exposure opportunity. To address these problems, we propose Gradient-Decoupled Sampled Softmax (GD-SSM). Our method combines L 2 projection to stabilize per-update gradients with a closed-form degree prior that rebalances per-epoch contributions. Across three benchmarks with MF and LightGCN backbones, GD-SSM achieves the best performance in all configurations, improving over the strongest baseline by up to +33.3% and lifting the lowest-degree group by up to +114% over SSM. We further validate GD-SSM on production data from a real streaming service. Our code is available at https://github.com/yunwooseong/GD-SSM.

papers.title: FairMB: A Multi-behavior Group Fairness Model for Recommendation with Representation Augmentation
affiliations: Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications
Nanjing University, State Key Laboratory of Novel Software Technology
papers.abstract: Ensuring fairness in modern recommender systems is an ongoing imperative, yet current methodologies fail to effectively capture the complex interplay between long-tail distributions and biases. Specifically, sparse interactions cause tail user nodes to undergo semantic homogenization, progressively entangling their preferences with sensitive attributes. Consequently, such entanglement severely degrades recommendation utility and fairness for tail users. In this paper, we propose FairMB, a multi-behavior fairness paradigm designed to mitigate the tail-node degradation by leveraging rich collaborative signals from auxiliary behaviors. Specifically, a tail-aware aggregation mechanism exploits additional auxiliary signals to provide tail-node compensation. Furthermore, to prevent additional biases from auxiliary behaviors, a dual-guided debiasing augmentation network is employed. Driven by downstream tasks and projection-based purified residual embeddings, it constructs fair augmented targets for contrastive alignment, guiding the original representations to disentangle biases from preferences and ultimately achieving an optimal utility-fairness trade-off. Comprehensive evaluations across diverse recommendation benchmarks confirm that FairMB effectively achieves accuracy-fairness trade-off, establishing state-of-the-art standards for fair representation learning in multi-behavior environments.

papers.title: Multi-Attribute and Intersectional Exposure Fairness in Recommender Systems
affiliations: University of Applied Sciences St. Pölten
papers.abstract: Ensuring fair exposure across demographic groups of content creators in recommender systems is crucial, as it affects the real-world visibility of minorities and underrepresented groups. Existing work on provider-side exposure fairness has primarily considered single demographic attributes, leaving multi-attribute and intersectional exposure fairness largely unexplored. Yet in real-world platforms, fairness concerns may arise simultaneously across multiple intersecting provider attributes. We introduce multi-attribute and intersectional perspectives on exposure fairness in recommender systems, propose an evaluation framework taking both perspectives into account, and present a post-processing approach for multi-attribute exposure fairness informed by online settings in social choice theory. Our experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets show a clear distinction between the two perspectives, as baseline approaches demonstrate a tendency to trade attribute-level fairness for improvements on the intersectional level. Our proposed method achieves a more favorable fairness-utility trade-off across attribute-wise exposure objectives and robust improvement of both exposure fairness aspects on the real world data. On synthetic data no method shows consistent improvement of both attribute-level and intersectional exposure fairness across all backbone models, highlighting the challenging nature of the task and the need to evaluate multi-attribute exposure fairness from both perspectives. With this work we aim to kick off the research on provider exposure fairness in recommender systems at a more granular level.

papers.title: Bandit-Quota: Latency-Budgeted Multi-Retriever Selection via Contextual Thompson Sampling
affiliations: Birla Institute of Technology and Science, Pilani
papers.abstract: Dense-retriever ensembles improve ranking quality but invoke every expert per query, routinely violating production latency SLAs. We present Bandit-Quota, a training-free, per-query selector that picks a budgeted subset of dense retrievers under a strict wall-clock cap. We cast multi-retriever selection as a Knapsack-constrained contextual bandit: a 16-dimensional neural–linear query sketch (PCA-projected bert-tiny [CLS], ?3 ms on CPU) feeds Linear Thompson Sampling (LinTS) posteriors, and a Lagrangian utility trades expected post-reranking quality against estimated per-arm latency, with a Jaccard coverage bonus that suppresses redundant experts. A budget-feasible greedy constructor resolves the per-query knapsack online, and a cached Reciprocal-Rank-Fusion fallback protects tail latency. Across seven BEIR collections spanning biomedical, finance, scientific and argumentative domains, Bandit-Quota reduces end-to-end latency by 2.4× to 9.3× over a 10-arm full ensemble, matches or improves nDCG@10 and MRR@10 on six of seven datasets, and outperforms a matched-capacity supervised router on all seven by adapting online to test-time query-distribution shifts. The policy exposes explicit operator knobs (B, M, ?) for the quality–latency trade-off with no retraining.

papers.title: Exploring the Capabilities and Limits of Late Interaction
papers.abstract: Late interaction with MaxSim scoring is the ranking mechanism of the very effective multi-vector bi-encoder retrieval model ColBERT. In this paper, we investigate how important the representational capacity and ColBERT's lexically-bound token embeddings are for late interaction. Our experiments on TREC Deep Learning and on BEIR data indicate that late interaction is only more effective than a single-vector bi-encoder's dot product scoring when late interaction can use a higher representational capacity or when the embeddings are bound to lexical tokens.

papers.title: Reducing Representational Interference in Retrieval Embeddings with Trainable Prefix Tokens
papers.abstract: Embedding models compress variable-length text into fixed-size vector representations, but this compression can entangle semantic content with residual token-level information, such as artifacts arising from attention sink behavior. We propose a simple method that prepends trainable [DUMP] tokens to the input during embedding model training. The method keeps the model architecture, pooling strategy, and training loss unchanged, while optimizing the added tokens through the standard contrastive retrieval objective. By introducing trainable prefix positions that interact with regular tokens during encoding, [DUMP] tokens help reduce the influence of residual or uninformative token-level signals on the final retrieval representation. Experiments on standard retrieval and long-context benchmarks show that our method consistently improves over finetuned baselines across encoder and decoder embedding models. Further analysis shows that [DUMP] tokens alter token-level activation and attention patterns associated with low-information tokens. These results suggest that trainable prefix tokens provide a lightweight way to improve retrieval representations.

papers.title: LLMs Propose, Verifiers Decide: Selective Intent Classification for Short Web Queries
papers.abstract: Short web queries are difficult to classify: they contain few lexical cues, and query logs are dominated by informational intents. Recent work shows that LLMs improve recall on this task, but direct top-1 LLM prediction does not consistently meet the requirements of precision-sensitive annotation. We find that, in this setting, LLMs are better suited as candidate proposers than as final classifiers: their top-2 intent candidates often contain the gold label even when top-1 predictions are skewed. We introduce CAVE-NV, a selective candidate-verification framework that asks an LLM for a small candidate set, scores each candidate with a label-conditioned MiniLM verifier, and uses a split-calibrated acceptor to output a label or reject the example. On ORCAS-I-gold, GPT-4o and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct reach top-2 candidate recall of 0.976 and 0.974. In the query-only setting, CAVE-NV accepts 54.8% and 45.4% of examples with 0.985 and 0.984 micro accepted precision. With clicked-URL evidence and the ranking verifier for offline query-log annotation, prediction coverage reaches 63.5% and 59.5% with 0.988 and 0.987 precision. Selective verification can therefore label a high-precision subset of query-log examples without forcing a prediction for every query.

papers.title: EviQE: Evidence Selection for LLM-Based Query Expansion
papers.abstract: LLM-based query expansion increasingly conditions reformulation on documents retrieved from the target corpus, yet most work focuses on how to generate expansions rather than which documents the model should read. We propose EviQE, which aggregates documents retrieved by multiple reformulators, selects a compact evidence set, and uses it for one grounded expansion step. This separates evidence selection from generation and treats reformulators as complementary retrieval perspectives. Across three TREC DL and five BEIR benchmarks, reformulators frequently retrieve distinct relevant documents, so pooled candidates provide higher relevant-document coverage than any individual source. The strongest gains come from relevance-based evidence selection: LLM-Score consistently outperforms direct reformulation, cold-start expansion, and single-source seeded expansion. Additional retrieval-generation rounds provide little benefit once strong conditioning evidence has been selected and can reduce effectiveness.

papers.title: Reasoning-Aware Utility Estimation for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems increasingly rely on retrieved documents to ground large language model outputs, yet evaluating whether those documents are truly useful for generation remains an open challenge. Recent work has shown that retrieval quality measured by conventional relevance-based metrics does not necessarily align with end-to-end RAG performance: a document judged relevant to a query may not help the model answer correctly, while an irrelevant document may actively distract generation. Existing utility-aware evaluation methods address this limitation by estimating the utility of retrieved documents through isolated document-level probes. However, these approaches estimate document utility independently of the reasoning process. We argue that a document is useful not because it can answer a question in isolation, but because it contributes to the reasoning process that produces the final answer. To capture this behavior, we introduce Trace Utility Gain (TUG) , a family of retrieval evaluation metrics that estimate document utility directly from chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning traces generated over the full retrieval context. Specifically, TUG measures utility through three complementary signals: citation behavior, semantic alignment between retrieved documents and reasoning traces, and model self-assessment of document reliance. By estimating utility from the model's observed reasoning process, TUG captures how retrieved evidence contributes to answer generation rather than how useful it appears in isolation. We evaluate TUG on five question-answering benchmarks using three instruction-tuned large language models. Results show that TUG consistently achieves stronger correlation with end-to-end answer correctness than both traditional retrieval metrics and prior utility-aware approaches.

papers.title: What Limits Does Quantization Place on Dense Top- k Retrieval? A Theoretical Study
papers.abstract: We establish conditions for embedding a corpus of N documents as d-dimensional vectors such that every k-subset S ⊆ [N] is realizable as a top-k retrieval by some query vector. Recent work shows that d = O(k) suffices for such embeddings to exist in R d , independently of N. We show that this corpus-independent bound is specific to infinite precision. With B bits per coordinate, perfect top-k retrieval requires Bd = Ω(k ln N), so at any fixed precision the dimension must grow at least logarithmically with N. Specializing to an ℓ 2 -normalized B-bit uniform scalar quantization model, we also identify a sharp critical precision B * = O(ln ln N) below which no dimension suffices, together with two further regimes that bound the feasible (B, d) pairs. Our result implies that in practical vector databases and dense retrieval systems where quantization is standard, the embedding dimension cannot be chosen without reference to corpus size.

papers.title: Multi-Aspect Joint Retrieval for E-Commerce: Bridging Product Catalogs and Customer Reviews
papers.abstract: E-commerce platforms support diverse retrieval needs, from finding relevant products to identifying useful information in customer reviews. In these settings, relevance depends not only on textual content, but also on structured aspects such as brand, category, price, rating, and popularity. Recent multi-aspect dense retrievers show that these signals improve product search, but they are typically designed for a single task over a single corpus, leaving open whether aspect-aware representations can be shared across related e-commerce retrieval tasks. In this paper, we study joint multi-aspect dense retrieval for e-commerce, where a single model supports retrieval over both product catalogs and customer reviews.
