We propose J-MADRAL, a joint dense retrieval model that learns shared aspect-aware representations from textual content and structured metadata across product and review search. To evaluate this setting, we construct Search ESCI, a novel synthetic review-search benchmark derived from Amazon Reviews 2023 and ESCI-related product resources, and evaluate on Amazon ESCI, TREC Product Search 2023, and Search ESCI. Experiments against sparse, dense, and multi-aspect retrieval baselines show that joint training substantially improves review search while maintaining competitive product search effectiveness. These results demonstrate the value of shared aspect-aware representations for integrated e-commerce search. To support reproducibility, we release the source code, data, and model weights at https://github.com/alemarco96/J-MADRAL.

papers.title: Robustness of IR Models to Collection Growth
papers.abstract: Information Retrieval (IR) systems seek to identify relevant documents within a collection. In practical applications, collections are dynamic, with documents frequently added. We argue that ideally, a retriever's effectiveness should not decrease when non-relevant documents are added to a collection. This study formalises this concept and empirically evaluates it by merging two collections with negligible topic overlap. We hypothesise that the way an IR model conditions its ranking on other documents in a collection (e.g., the IDF component in BM25 or contextual documents in listwise rerankers) plays an important role in its robustness to the addition of non-relevant documents. We broadly classify models as those that do not depend on other documents (Multi-Document-Agnostic, MDA) and those that do (Multi-Document-Dependent, MDD). Our results show that neither MDD nor MDA models are fully robust to the addition of non-relevant documents, as all models exhibit some performance degradation. Interestingly, among the models we test, MDA is more effective than MDD for retrieval, whereas MDD and MDA rerankers are equally effective.

papers.title: Retrieval-Stage Interactions in Cross-Modal Text-to-Image Retrieval Pipelines
papers.abstract: Cross-modal retrieval systems enable searching content in one modality using queries from another. Recently, retrieving images using natural language queries – text-to-image retrieval – has received a lot of attention due to advances in deep learning vision models and interest in multi-modal processing in general. While several modeling approaches exist, ranging from simple keyword matching to joint embedding models and neural rerankers, there is limited understanding of how candidate generation, reranking, and fusion interact across retrieval pipelines. In this paper, we present an analysis of retrieval-stage interactions in text-to-image retrieval pipelines, spanning a comprehensive set of categories drawn from recent advances in information retrieval: single index pipelines, multi-stage retrieve and rerank pipelines, and ensemble pipelines. We compare the effectiveness of these pipelines on the MS-COCO and Flickr30K benchmarks revealing several retrieval-stage phenomena governing reranking effectiveness, candidate-set expansion, and ensemble behavior.

papers.title: First News Report Retrieval for Short-Form Videos
affiliations: Department of Applied Artificial Intelligence, Sungkyunkwan University
Department of Computer Education, Sungkyunkwan University
Department of Immersive Media Engineering, Sungkyunkwan University
papers.abstract: Short-form videos are increasingly used to consume and share news, but they often omit explicit links to the underlying articles. Tracing the first news report from these videos is challenging because the same event is often reported repeatedly across multiple news outlets and platforms, while short-form videos may summarize the event using different expressions. In this paper, we formulate First News Report Retrieval for Short-Form Videos, a task that aims to identify the first news report of the event described in a short-form video. We construct a manually verified benchmark consisting of 99 news topics and 865 Korean Shorts videos. We also introduce a stepwise retrieval-and-verification framework designed to improve first news report tracing from short-form videos. Experiments with strong frontier LLMs show that retrieving the first news report remains challenging: general tool-augmented search often returns follow-up reports or articles about related but different events. Our framework provides an initial approach for systematically investigating this task by combining structured query generation, candidate retrieval, and article-level verification.

papers.title: PT2PR: A Benchmark for Multimodal Patent-to-Product Retrieval
papers.abstract: Detecting patent infringement requires identifying products whose design or functionality falls within the scope of a patent's claims—a task that demands sophisticated legal reasoning and is difficult not only for experts but also for LLMs. A crucial first step is to identify candidate products that are potentially related to a given patent, allowing a detailed legal analysis to focus on a small set of cases. However, patent documents and product descriptions differ substantially in language, structure, and level of abstraction, making the retrieval a challenging cross-domain problem. Yet no datasets and methods exist for this task. As a first step, this paper introduces Patent2Product (PT2PR), a benchmark for multimodal patent-to-product retrieval consisting of datasets, metrics, and baselines. Our pipeline mines patent-product pairs from patent references in product texts using high-recall rules, followed by high-precision manual validation; it can be applied to any catalog with patent references in product text. Applied to the datasets Amazon Reviews 2023 and ESCI, the pipeline yields 11,303 and 1,351 patent-product pairs, respectively. The PT2PR-Amazon dataset not only contains text, but also patent drawings and product images, enabling multimodal retrieval experiments. As baselines, we evaluate state-of-the-art LLMs, VLMs, and lexical retrieval. Our experiments show that (1) dense retrieval outperforms lexical retrieval, (2) incorporating visual information can improve retrieval, although the gains are model-dependent, and (3) the effect of using longer context windows for patent documents is also model-dependent.

papers.title: Beyond One-Shot Expansion: Contrastive Evidence Exploration for Multi-Hop Retrieval
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) critically depends on retrieving the evidence necessary for effective reasoning. However, this remains particularly challenging in multi-hop question answering (QA), where supporting passages are often linked through intermediate entities and relations that must be progressively uncovered. Existing retrieval approaches typically rely on a single retrieval intent or one-shot query expansion, limiting their ability to adapt to newly retrieved evidence and potentially introducing noisy or redundant retrieval signals. To address these limitations, we propose a training-free multi-hop retrieval framework that integrates evidence-conditioned exploration, passage-specific contrastive refinement, and coverage-aware final ranking. During offline indexing, the framework constructs passage-specific contrastive facets that characterize each passage relative to its semantically similar neighbors, providing fine-grained signals to distinguish closely related candidates. At inference time, the framework iteratively retrieves evidence, generates probes targeting unresolved information needs, refines candidate relevance using the contrastive facets, and selects a complementary set of passages that collectively cover diverse evidence-seeking intents. Experiments on MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and 2WikiMultihopQA demonstrate consistent improvements in retrieval quality and downstream QA performance over baselines.

papers.title: Support Selection Survives under Official-Context RAG: A Same-Backbone Boundary Study
affiliations: Technology and Engineering Center for Space Utilization, Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.abstract: We study bounded Agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for knowledge-intensive question answering. The task is to answer multi-hop or domain questions from auditable external evidence under a fixed inference budget. Existing Agentic RAG evaluations often vary the model, retriever, corpus interface, controller, training signal, and search budget together. As a result, observed gains do not show whether planning, repair, active retrieval, or support selection is the useful mechanism. We conduct a same-backbone boundary study with fixed Qwen-based retrieval, generation, evaluation, and call budgets. We decompose bounded agentic control into same-stack mechanism controls and seven ablations. The evaluation uses official-context HotpotQA, 2Wiki, and MuSiQue. It also includes a secondary native-retrieval Chinese aerospace QA stress test. Across three seeds, the full Agentic workflow is not the best answer-F1 design. Corrective achieves the highest F1 on the public benchmarks, and Active retrieval achieves the highest F1 on the domain set. In this access regime, Agentic mainly adds lexical grounding and trace structure at higher latency. The most consistent positive component is sentence-level support selection. Removing it reduces F1 on every dataset. Bootstrap CIs support this drop on HotpotQA, MuSiQue, and the domain stress test, but not on 2Wiki.

papers.title: PCD-RAG: A Diagnostic Framework for Auditing Parametric Contamination in RAG Distillation
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) distillation offers an efficient paradigm for deploying compact language models, yet it raises a critical safety concern: Does evidence-conditioned supervision inadvertently encode transient retrieved facts into the student model's parametric memory? If transient retrieved facts pollute model parameters, the core premise of externalizing knowledge in RAG is compromised. To audit this risk, we introduce PCD-RAG, a negative-control diagnostic benchmark and metric suite. By utilizing 5,000 synthetic facts with 0% pre-training exposure baseline, this atomic-level probe cleanly disentangles closed-book memorization from context-conditioned reading. Under these strictly controlled zero-exposure settings, our comprehensive evaluation across Qwen2.5 students reveals a counterintuitive finding: RAG distillation does not induce surface-level exact-match retention. Answer-only distillation leaves retrieval-free answer recovery near zero (<= 0.8%). Furthermore, extending our probe to realistic noisy multi-document distillation reveals a stark contrast in training stability: while traditional supervised fine-tuning (SFT) triggers catastrophic optimization collapse when architectural constraints are relaxed (e.g., LoRA R=16), distillation targets (Hard KD) act as an implicit regularizer that successfully stabilizes the model. By bounding parametric contamination and identifying complementary architectural safeguards, our framework lays the empirical groundwork for future community exploration of complex multi-hop reasoning, safeguarding the deployment of reliable RAG pipelines.

papers.title: Caching Hyperedges: KV-Cache Reuse for Hypergraph RAG
papers.abstract: Hypergraph-based retrieval captures the n-ary relational facts that binary-graph methods fragment, but answering a query is slow: the model must read the text of many retrieved units before it can answer. We present Cachy, which removes this reading cost by precomputing a key-value (KV) cache for each retrieval unit and reusing it whenever a query retrieves that unit. Because retrieval is hyperedge-grounded, each cached unit is a short, self-contained passage, so caches fuse at query time without fine-tuning and with no detectable loss in generation quality. To keep storage tractable, Cachy caches only the units that queries actually reach (demand caching) and compresses each cache by up to 8× with INT8/INT4 quantization and 50% K-norm token pruning. Together these cut storage from 1.9 TB to 109 GB on our workload. On UltraDomain across five domains, Cachy matches the uncached hypergraph pipeline on generation quality while cutting mean query time from 21.61 s to 8.52 s, matching the latency of lightweight RAG. Code and resources are publicly available (https://github.com/PRAISELab-PicusLab/Cachy-Hypergraphrag).

papers.title: CiteAlign-Table: Verifying Citation Faithfulness when LLMs Attribute to Structured Data
papers.abstract: Attributed Question Answering systems increasingly ground answers in tabular structured corpora—Wikipedia infoboxes and relational tables, the dominant structured evidence in open-domain RAG—yet citation faithfulness methods remain designed for text passages. This mismatch allows LLMs to cite the correct table but the wrong row, silently aggregate values without justification, or attribute claims to schema fields that do not semantically entail them. We formalize multiple structural hallucination modes specific to structured-data attribution and introduce CiteAlign-Table, a hybrid neuro-symbolic verifier that checks schema-path validity, cell-level semantic alignment, and arithmetic consistency between claims and their cited records. A schema-aware entailment module detects entity and content misalignments, while a lightweight program synthesizer verifies numerical aggregation, temporal consistency, and unit correctness. Experiments on a hybrid benchmark of Wikipedia infoboxes and WikiTables show that CiteAlign-Table achieves 0.84 F1 in detecting unfaithful structured citations, while text-only baselines degrade to 0.61 F1. By extending citation faithfulness from passages to structured records, our work makes attributed QA trustworthy over the heterogeneous data that production RAG systems actually retrieve.

papers.title: The Fellowship of the Query: Learning Retrieval Actions
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented question answering requires control decisions about when to decompose a question, search, reformulate, extract evidence, synthesize facts, verify progress, and stop. We study whether trajectory fine-tuning can improve small language models (SLMs) as next-action controllers. We additionally evaluate a low-resource setting in which a single SLM serves as both the controller and the final-answer generator. From accepted teacher search traces, we build a seven-way action-prediction task, where the model predicts the next structured teacher action from the current trajectory state, and evaluate LoRA-supervised fine-tuning across SLMs and xSLMs as controllers. On 1,646 held-out action examples, Granite 4.1 3B trained on 13,194 actions reaches macro-F1 0.6536, compared with 0.1736 for zero-shot prompting of the same model and 0.5399 for a TF-IDF logistic-regression baseline. In an end-to-end controller/generator swap evaluation over 149 held-out trajectories, using the fine-tuned model for both roles improves Exact Match from 0.7530 to 0.7946 and token F1 from 0.7783 to 0.8295 compared with using the base model as both controller and generator. The cross-role conditions show that the fine-tuned controller increases evidence-fact recording when the generator is fixed, while controller-only final-answer gains are not statistically clear. Overall, trajectory supervision improves action prediction and evidence-recording behaviour in this evaluated pipeline. The code used in this paper is publicly available.

papers.title: RAH: Recursive Agent Harnesses for Long-Context Reasoning through Delegation-as-Code
affiliations: Commercial Technology Innovation Office, PricewaterhouseCoopers, U.S.
papers.abstract: When an agent recurses over a long-context task, should the recursive unit be a bare model call or a full harness with filesystem tools, code execution, and planning? We study this question on long-context aggregation, tasks where a single instance may contain thousands of key–value pairs each requiring individual model reasoning. Coding agents reduce per-entry reasoning to regex heuristics. Recursive language models (RLMs) invoke LLMs recursively but lack tool access. We introduce the Recursive Agent Harness (RAH) , in which a parent agent generates and runs an executable script that programmatically spawns full subagent harnesses in parallel for fine-grained workloads and uses structured function calls for subtasks of 1–5 entries. We call this harness recursion and study it against model recursion , recursion over bare model calls as in RLMs, on long-context aggregation. With the backbone held fixed at GPT-5 to match the published Codex and RLM baselines, RAH improves the Codex coding-agent baseline from 71.75% to 81.36% on Oolong-Synthetic (199 samples, 13 context-length buckets up to 4M tokens), a gain attributable to the harness rather than the model. With a stronger backbone, Claude Sonnet 4.5, the same design reaches 89.77%.

papers.title: PyRAMIND: Auditable Deterministic Pyramid Memory for Long-Running LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Long-running LLM agents are increasingly considered for regulated, high-consequence domains such as finance, compliance, and audit, where memory must be accurate, traceable, replayable, and inspectable after a decision. Existing agent-memory systems often invoke an LLM during maintenance operations such as fact extraction, consolidation, updating, summarization, and forgetting. Although effective, this design makes it harder to reconstruct why a memory existed, changed, or was removed at a particular point in time. We present PyRAMIND (Pyramidal Retention with Arithmetic Memory for Inference-time Determinism), an auditable memory architecture in which write consolidation, reinforcement, forgetting, tier promotion, and retrieval scoring are closed-form arithmetic over cached embeddings. Only optional entity tagging at ingest and answer generation at query time call an external LLM. Given fixed embeddings, cached boundary-model outputs, parameters, and software, each maintenance transition is replayable from ordered inputs. PyRAMIND stores memories in a four-tier Pyramid (raw→facts→themes→worldview) and ranks them with a max-ensemble retention score modulated by local semantic density. Under a matched harness, PyRAMIND achieves competitive accuracy on long-horizon memory tasks ( 0.93 on LongMemEval-S) despite eliminating LLM calls from the memory-maintenance path, while reducing memory-lifecycle token expenditure to 1.4k LLM tokens per turn versus 3.1k for reproduced Mem0 OSS and 4.2k for Zep v3. Performance is weaker on temporal and multi-hop reasoning tasks ( 0.62 on LoCoMo), highlighting the continued value of richer relational memory structures for compositional reasoning. These results suggest that strong long-term memory performance is possible without LLM-mediated maintenance, and motivate future replayable memory systems that add temporal and relational structure while preserving auditable deterministic maintenance.

papers.title: Beyond Uncertainty: Multi-Solver Disagreement Rewards for Self-Evolving Reasoning Curricula
papers.abstract: Self-evolving reasoning frameworks train a Challenger to generate questions exposing a Solver's weaknesses, creating adaptive curricula without human data. However, existing approaches use a single solver's sampling uncertainty as the Challenger's reward. This creates a fundamental bottleneck: as the solver grows confident on the Challenger's question distribution, all sampled answers converge identically, collapsing the reward to zero and starving the Challenger of learning signal. Critically, this single-model reward cannot distinguish genuinely easy questions from those that merely align with one solver's learned biases. We propose a multi-solver disagreement reward using a heterogeneous ensemble varying in model capacity and sampling temperature. A normalized Shannon entropy over the ensemble's per-question plurality answers explicitly rewards questions where solvers produce conflicting solutions—capturing difficulty as inter-model divergence rather than intra-model sampling variance. This richer gradient enables the Challenger to discover questions targeting true capability boundaries, producing a curriculum that forces downstream Solvers to develop robust reasoning strategies generalizing across problem types. Our approach is a drop-in reward function replacement requiring no framework modifications or additional data. Experiments with Qwen3-4B show that Solvers trained on disagreement-Challenger questions achieve +1.34 points average improvement on competition-math benchmarks (MATH-500, AMC, Olympiad), suggesting that multi-solver disagreement provides a complementary and scalable signal for curriculum generation in self-play reasoning systems.

papers.title: Detecting Routing Collapse Early and Label-Free in LLM Cascades
papers.abstract: LLM cascades save cost only when easy queries stay on the cheap model, yet learned routers often collapse and send nearly all traffic to the expensive tier. Prior work links this failure to an objective-decision mismatch; we ask why that mismatch is systematically one-sided. Under a weak per-query signal, collapse follows from regression to the mean. Even a correctly specified regression router estimates the conditional mean gain, discarding unpredictable noise and pulling predictions toward the global mean. If that mean exceeds the cost threshold, thresholding the contracted scores routes too much traffic upward. The same view predicts two counterintuitive scaling effects: collapse strengthens as the signal weakens, and more same-kind data can deepen it by removing estimation noise around an already-contracted target. It also gives a no-new-label diagnostic: compare the expensive-tier route fraction to the strong-win base rate already present in training labels. Across all 45 viable RouterBench cascades, regression over-routes by 7 to 49 points, with every bootstrap interval above zero. In 1068 real routers, 240 of 534 regression routers collapse, versus 0 of 534 decision routers. The diagnostic reaches AUROC 0.999 at convergence and 0.92 after one quarter of training. Since the failure is a rank-preserving level shift, base-rate recalibration removes it.

papers.title: Knowing When to Correct: Cost-Aware LLM Routing for OCR Post-Correction in Historical Documents
papers.abstract: Historical digital archives present new challenges for retrieval systems because of OCR errors introduced by degraded page quality, old typefaces, and complex page layouts. Large language models (LLMs) offer an effective means of correcting transcription errors. However, applying LLM-based correction at scale can become prohibitively expensive. We investigate a selective, cost-aware strategy for LLM-assisted OCR post-correction, using a regression-guided router to predict when LLM correction is likely to improve transcription quality, thereby reducing unnecessary LLM processing and associated costs while preserving historically valid text. We evaluate this strategy on a dataset comprising historical Swiss newspapers published between 1733 and 1945. Our results show that selective correction can retain most of the quality gains of full correction while substantially reducing the LLM token cost. Using Tesseract OCR, sending all text segments for LLM correction improves CER from 6.3% to 2.9% (best approach). In contrast, our regression-guided router achieves CER of 3.1% (0.2% worse) while avoiding routing 40% of segments for LLM correction. Finally, we show that our regression-guided LLM router closely trails the decisions of an oracle that knows in advance which segments benefit from correction.

papers.title: Conservative Hybrid SQL Rewriting with Rules, Retrieval, and LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: SQL query rewriting improves database performance by transforming queries into semantically equivalent but more efficient forms. Rule-based rewriting is reliable for standard cases, but often misses boundary scenarios involving NULL semantics, outer joins, nested queries, or workload-specific constraints. Large language models (LLMs) can reason over such cases, but direct application risks hallucinations and semantic errors. We propose Conservative Hybrid SQL Rewriting, a rule-anchored framework that combines deterministic rules, retrieval-guided LLM refinement, and verification-gated fallback. The LLM refines a rule-generated candidate, and is accepted only if validation passes; otherwise, the deterministic candidate is returned. Experiments on PostgreSQL workloads show that rules dominate standard scenarios, while constrained LLM reasoning improves boundary-case coverage. Our results suggest LLMs are most effective as conservative coverage extenders, complementing rather than replacing deterministic rules.

papers.title: KITDG: Knowledge-Infused Tabular Data Generation
papers.abstract: Tabular data generation has advanced in distributional fidelity, yet no framework systematically enforces domain-level associative structure during synthesis. We introduce KITDG (Knowledge-Infused Tabular Data Generation) – which infuses Apriori-mined association rules into a generative backbone through a differentiable Logic Tensor Network (LTN) knowledge base with gradient-isolated three-stage training, and ARFD (Association Rule Fidelity Distance) – a novel metric decomposing associative fidelity into rule preservation (P 1 ) and rule strength (P 2 ), applicable to any tabular generator as a drop-in evaluation complement to distributional metrics. Across 13 benchmark datasets under TSTR, KITDG matches or outperforms its backbone in 48 of 52 (dataset, classifier) pairs. We further report the top-k phenomenon , to our knowledge the first characterization of a quality-over-quantity regime in rule-infused tabular generation, supporting association rule infusion as a general, transferable principle for tabular synthesis.

papers.title: PROCS: Uncertainty-Aware Knowledge Graph Embeddings via Conceptual Spaces
affiliations: Mohamed Bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI)
papers.abstract: While deep reasoning models (e.g., NBFNet, ULTRA) have advanced knowledge graph completion, they often sacrifice the efficiency and interpretability of geometric embeddings for increased expressivity. We present PROCS, a framework that combines the best of both worlds through region-based representations inspired by Gärdenfors' Conceptual Spaces, realised as a scalable probabilistic embedding layer. Unlike deterministic point embeddings, PROCS models entities as Gaussian distributions where variance explicitly encodes vagueness and conflict. By introducing a scalable geometric inference mechanism that avoids intractable sampling, PROCS achieves 0.417 MRR on FB15k-237, matching the performance of heavy reasoning models while retaining the O(1) inference of embedding methods. Its uncertainty estimates enable risk-aware retrieval, validated by a Defence-domain case study. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/ubaidazam/PROCS.

papers.title: Leave-One-Signature-Out: Auditing Recurrence in Episode-Structured Temporal Benchmarks
papers.abstract: Held-out train/test evaluation remains necessary, but episode-structured temporal benchmarks can preserve recurring signatures across random/time splits, so scores may partly reflect recurrence rather than broader out-of-signature generalization. We propose leave-one-signature-out evaluation (LOSO), which holds out all instances sharing a target-free structural signature. LOSO removes the audited recurrence channel by construction and enables an oracle-collapse diagnostic: the standard-to-LOSO gap indicates how strongly a score depends on the audited recurrence channel. In TKGs, repeated test triples account for 44–84% of cases against train+validation history, while LOSO audits target-free signatures such as (s,r). On UCI Diabetes EHR, LOSO exposes rank instability: temporal kNN significantly outperforms the majority baseline and logistic regression on hard folds (p = 0.004), while static kNN drops from second to last. A six-crop agricultural benchmark adds a directional case: the top random-split method drops by 0.468 macro-F1 under LOSO. We add a non-degenerate ICEWS14s (s,r)-LOSO audit to test recurrence without unseen-relation degeneracy.

papers.title: Do General NLP Embeddings Capture Ontological Reasoning?
affiliations: TIB Leibniz Information Centre for Science and Technology
papers.abstract: General-purpose NLP embedding models perform well on linguistic tasks, but their ability to capture symbolic ontological structure remains unclear. We introduce AVA, a systematic framework for evaluating whether embeddings distinguish logic-sensitive relational semantics in ontologies and knowledge graphs. AVA comprises 171,007 contrastive triplets derived from 163 heterogeneous ontologies using hierarchy inversion, relation substitution, and disjointness injection. Each triplet contains an ontology statement, a semantically equivalent paraphrase, and a logic-sensitive hard negative with contradictory relational meaning. We evaluate more than 25 state-of-the-art embedding models and find substantial limitations: the best model achieves only 0.739 triplet accuracy, while hard negative accuracy falls to 0.135. Fine-tuning improves discrimination by a large margin but transfers poorly to downstream Semantic Web tasks, including taxonomy discovery and ontology alignment. Further analysis suggests that improvements stem partly from perturbation-specific pattern recognition rather than robust ontological understanding. These findings reveal a persistent gap between linguistic representation learning and ontology-level discrimination, challenging the assumption that strong NLP benchmark performance translates to Semantic Web competence.

papers.title: Improving Precision in Cluster-Level Pricing Experiments with Temporal Switchbacks
papers.abstract: Online pricing systems often cannot randomize treatments at the user level because prices are deployed over operational units such as routes, regions, or markets. This creates low-powered A/B tests due to persistent cluster heterogeneity, seasonality, and autocorrelated demand. We study temporal switchback designs for cluster-level pricing experiments, where each cluster alternates between treatment and control over time. Using LATAM Airlines ancillary-pricing data and calibrated simulations, we show that switchbacks can substantially reduce standard errors relative to parallel cluster designs. We further characterize how switching cadence interacts with temporal dependence, highlighting when daily or weekly switchbacks are preferable. The results provide practical guidance for experimentation in pricing and transportation platforms where fine-grained randomization is infeasible.

papers.title: TMRP-Net:Temporal-Aware Multimodal Retrieval for Social Media Popularity Prediction
affiliations: National Key Laboratory of Big Data and Decision
papers.abstract: Predicting the popularity of user-generated content (UGC) is challenging because content diffusion depends not only on the post itself but also on its publication time and the historical performance of similar content. Retrieval provides a natural way to incorporate historical evidence, but semantic similarity alone is an insufficient proxy for retrieval utility. A retrieved post may appear relevant in content while being temporally mismatched, unavailable at prediction time, or uninformative for the target post. To address these limitations, we propose TMRP-Net, a temporally aware multimodal retrieval framework for social media popularity prediction. TMRP-Net uses CLIP-aligned image-text features and task-specific temporal representations to capture both weekly periodicity and global temporal position. It retrieves only previously published posts and ranks them according to content-time relevance, ensuring that the retrieved context is both causally valid and temporally comparable. The retrieved candidates are further refined through contribution-aware selection, modeled by a lightweight target-conditioned relational graph, and fused with the target representation using time-guided weights for final prediction. Experiments on ICIP and SMPD show that TMRP-Net consistently outperforms competitive baselines.

papers.title: Knowing When to Escalate: Disagreement Patterns for Uncertainty-Aware Content Moderation
papers.abstract: Agentic content-moderation systems increasingly rely on collective judgments from LLM agents, while aggregation methods commonly treat inter-agent disagreement as a reliability problem to be removed through consensus or voting. This framing is inappropriate for value-laden tasks, where disagreement may reflect irreducible value pluralism - a distinction standard uncertainty decompositions cannot recover, since they operate on output distributions and discard the reasoning behind each judgment. We propose Reasoning Trace Divergence Analysis (RTDA), which embeds model-generated justifications from perspective-differentiated agents and classifies each case by justification similarity and conclusion agreement. The resulting four-state taxonomy isolates convergent disagreement, where agents reasoning similarly but concluding differently, as a candidate signature of value-laden conflict. On 1,000 items from the Measuring Hate Speech corpus, this structural signal predicts human annotator disagreement better than magnitude-only and output-only baselines. We contribute a design principle: condition human escalation on the structure of disagreement, not its magnitude alone, with RTDA serving as a post-processing layer for systems that already generate reasoning traces.

papers.title: Evidence-Aware Prompting for Causal Fact Verification with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into information retrieval pipelines to reason over retrieved textual evidence and produce final decisions in tasks such as fact verification. However, causal fact verification presents a more specialised challenge than conventional claim verification: models must aggregate multiple pieces of evidence and assess whether the evidence supports a claimed causal relation, rather than merely verifying factual consistency. This setting is captured by CHECKWHY, which, to the best of our knowledge, is currently the only publicly available benchmark specifically designed for causal “why” fact verification. Motivated by this specialised problem, we propose Evidence-Aware Prompting (EAP), an evidence-centric framework that separates evidence selection from decision generation to enhance LLM reasoning. EAP models query-conditioned evidence selection as an explicit intermediate step and aggregates decisions over selected evidence subsets, mitigating query-only shortcuts and reducing the influence of irrelevant context. Experiments on CHECKWHY across multiple closed-source LLMs show that EAP consistently outperforms strong prompting baselines and achieves more balanced and robust evidence-grounded decisions for causal fact verification.

papers.title: Dual-Granularity Text Guidance for Dyadic Motion Generation
affiliations: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.abstract: Generating realistic dyadic motions from text is challenging due to complex inter-individual dynamics. Existing works lack in-depth exploration of input textual descriptions, leading to insufficient text-motion alignment. To address this problem, we propose DualGuidance, a diffusion model for dyadic motion generation that leverages dual-granularity text guidance, built upon three key designs. Firstly, we employ cross-modal attention to refine dyadic text features with individual motion features, obtaining coarse-grained text features that retain individual-specific motion information. Secondly, we use an LLM to generate individual textual descriptions, extract text features, and compute matching scores with individual motion features to achieve identity-aware alignment, yielding fine-grained text features. Finally, the dual-granularity text features are fused via gating mechanism to form the control signal for motion generation. Experiments on the InterHuman benchmark demonstrate that DualGuidance achieves state-of-the-art result on semantic alignment while maintaining competitive performance on other metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness of dual-granularity text guidance for dyadic motion generation. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/Xiangxi-Liu/DualGuidance.

papers.title: When Visual Frames Flip Mental-State Answers: An Item-Level Audit of Multimodal Theory-of-Mind Reasoning
papers.abstract: Multimodal Theory-of-Mind (ToM) evaluation often assumes that visual frames provide useful evidence for answering questions about beliefs, goals, and intentions. We test this assumption with an item-level audit of MuMA-ToM, a benchmark of 900 multiple-choice questions about multi-agent household interactions. The audit compares six settings: question-and-answer only (QA-only), video frames only (Video-only), text only (Text-only), text paired with frames (Text+Frame), generic chain-of-thought prompting (CoT), and QLogic, a structured text-only prompt that makes the question logic explicit. Across GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, Video-only outperforms QA-only, showing that frames can be useful. However, Text+Frame does not outperform Text-only for any model, and GPT-4o shows a significant paired drop. We therefore analyze answer transitions rather than aggregate accuracy alone. The main transition is Vision-Induced ToM Degradation , defined operationally as an item that is correct under Text-only but wrong under Text+Frame. On GPT-4o degradation cases, generic CoT recovers 14 of 78 items, while QLogic recovers 62 of 78; an exact McNemar test confirms the paired recovery difference (p=2.92×10 -12 ). Ablations show that condition tracking and candidate comparison are the most informative QLogic components. The results support a narrow conclusion suited to short-form multimodal evaluation: added visual evidence should be audited for how it changes individual mental-state answers, not only for whether it improves average accuracy.

papers.title: Text-Conditioned Scene Graph Sequence Generation via Discrete Diffusion
papers.abstract: Scene graphs represent visual scenes as objects and their relationships. While considerable research has explored predicting scene graph sequences from images or videos, generating such sequences from text remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce a discrete diffusion framework for text-conditioned scene graph sequence generation, focusing on visual scenes centered on human--object interactions. The proposed framework represents each sequence as a fixed-slot discrete state, where each slot encodes the state of an object over time, and employs a Transformer-based denoiser to generate scene graph sequences aligned with the input text. The denoiser jointly leverages within-frame slot attention, cross-frame temporal attention, and text cross-attention to capture inter-object relationships, temporal dynamics, and text--graph correspondence. We compare the proposed framework with diverse baselines, including retrieval-based methods, scene graph parsers, large language models, sequence-to-sequence models, and non-diffusion generative models. Experimental results show that our framework improves both text--graph alignment and the accuracy of temporal dynamics represented in scene graph sequences, including object appearance, persistence, and disappearance.

papers.title: Active Learning for Human Pose Estimation via Submodular Optimization on Latent Hyper-Ellipsoids
papers.abstract: While deep neural networks have significantly advanced 2D Human Pose Estimation, their performance relies heavily on massive datasets with costly, dense skeletal annotations. In practical scenarios, while raw data is abundant, the high costs of manual annotation necessitate budget-constrained approaches. Active learning mitigates this annotation bottleneck, but traditional heuristics often struggle with structural overconfidence and batch redundancy when dealing with complex, articulated poses. To address this, we propose a novel, density-aware active learning framework designed to robustly explore unannotated pose distributions. By leveraging a variational auto-encoder, we map unlabeled images into a probabilistic latent space, conceptualizing instances as hyper-ellipsoids. This representation explicitly captures both local data density and epistemic uncertainty, enabling the computation of a directed Mahalanobis divergence. We then ensure diverse and highly informative batch selection by optimizing a submodular facility-location function, weighted by a "likely-miss" prediction score. Experimental results on standard Human Pose Estimation benchmarks demonstrate that our geometric approach significantly accelerates convergence, outperforming current state-of-the-art active learning methods with substantially fewer labeled samples.

papers.title: SUMO-SimQA: A Benchmark for LLM Cross-File Reasoning over Traffic Simulation Files
affiliations: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: SUMO (Simulation of Urban MObility) is a widely used open-source traffic simulator for urban mobility research, operations, and planning. While recent work has integrated SUMO with large language models (LLMs) to automate scenario generation and result interpretation, a fundamental question remains unanswered: can LLMs answer decision-relevant questions grounded in SUMO simulation files? This setting is uniquely challenging because most practitioner questions require integrating evidence across multiple files, and even a single log file can exceed the context window of current LLMs. To answer this question, we introduce SUMO-SimQA, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLM reasoning over SUMO simulation files. SUMO-SimQA comprises 480 questions that span five SUMO file types and three traffic networks, organized into three levels of reasoning complexity (retrieval, reasoning, and cross-file reasoning). We find that naive approaches fail substantially on cross-file reasoning tasks, revealing a critical gap in existing LLM-SUMO pipelines. To address this challenge, we propose Plan-Execute-Revise (PER), adapting planning and iterative revision to the large, cross-file setting of SUMO-based traffic QA. PER improves accuracy on the hardest cross-file reasoning tasks over ReAct-based approaches (56.0%?82.0%), demonstrating that structured reasoning strategies are essential for reliable performance on these tasks. Our benchmark and code are available on GitHub.

papers.title: Stitch the Fragments: One-Shot Hierarchical Federated Clustering
papers.abstract: Federated Clustering (FC) faces a critical bottleneck in real-world scenarios, i.e., global clusters are rarely intact, often fragmenting into incomplete, multi-granular unlabeled “clusterlets” distributed across Non-IID clients. Although hierarchical clustering is theoretically well-suited to model such nested distributions, its recursive nature strictly relies on multi-round communication, introducing prohibitive computational overhead and severe privacy vulnerabilities. This paper, therefore, proposes a novel one-shot hierarchical federated clustering framework designed to seamlessly “stitch” the fragmented local clusterlets into a holistic global distribution. Our approach enables clients to perform autonomous fine-grained distribution exploration, uploading prototype-level knowledge via a dynamic parameter-interleaving mechanism to scramble transmission trajectories, which effectively prevents the server from tracing individual client data distributions. Subsequently, a multi-granular learning mechanism at the server fuses these granularly inconsistent local clusterlets, reconstructing a coherent global hierarchy for ultimate clustering. Extensive experiments on real benchmark datasets illustrate the superiority of the proposed approach, which effectively bridges the granularity gap among heterogeneous clients while minimizing privacy exposure risks via anonymized informative one-shot communication.

papers.title: Beyond Naive Disparity: A Size-Matched Audit of Demographic Effects in User-Agnostic Ranking
affiliations: Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa
papers.abstract: User-agnostic ranking systems aggregate ratings into a single shared item ranking without consulting user attributes, motivated by privacy, manipulation resistance, and regulatory frameworks such as the EU AI Act. Prior work has reported demographic disparities in such systems using metrics that do not separate a genuine group effect from the sampling variance that small subpopulations inevitably exhibit. We propose a reusable audit combining a faithful implementation of rating-preservation disparity, a size-matched random-group null, and a stratified resampling robustness check. Applied to the UARS filter on MovieLens-100k, MovieLens-1M, and BookCrossing, the audit shows that absolute disparities are small (around 0.01 to 0.05), that ML-100k disparities largely vanish once group size is controlled, and that on the larger datasets only the youngest age groups exhibit disparity beyond what size alone produces.

papers.title: FAIR-PIVOT: Fairness-oriented Perspective-Inversion via Viewpoint-balanced Outline-then-generaTion for Mitigating Political Bias in Web Corpora
affiliations: Seoul National University of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Large-scale web corpora (e.g., C4) are severely imbalanced in terms of political perspective: on the death penalty issue, e.g., left-leaning documents outnumber right-leaning ones by more than 8-fold. Such imbalances can transfer to downstream large language models, reinforcing political bias. We propose Fairness-oriented Perspective-Inversion via Viewpoint-balanced Outline-then-generaTion (simply, FAIR-PIVOT), a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based two-level-agent framework that builds balanced perspective-inverted synthetic data for politically sensitive topics. After annotating web texts with multi-persona LLMs, FAIR-PIVOT retrieves documents from contrasting orientations and inverts their viewpoint, preserving authentic discourse structure rather than rephrasing the same-view text. Across nine topics, FAIR-PIVOT generates 13,954 instances and reduces the total variation distance, a measure of how far the orientation distribution deviates from uniform balance, by up to 83%, while improving linguistic fluency as measured by Perplexity (25.5→21.8). Fine-tuning small language models on the balanced corpus further shifts their downstream behavior toward the intended orientation (Gemma (L−R)% +48→+34, Qwen +55→+50), confirming that data-level balancing can yield fairer model responses. Code and scripts are available at https://github.com/bigbases/FAIR-PIVOT.

papers.title: Stability Analysis of Signed Graphs under Structural Perturbations
papers.abstract: Signed graph learning has emerged as a powerful framework for modeling networks with both positive and negative interactions. While graph-filter-based methods have achieved promising empirical performance on signed networks, their stability to edge perturbations remains poorly understood. Existing stability analyses primarily focus on unsigned graphs and do not account for sign-flip perturbations. In this paper, we study the stability of signed graph filters under edge additions, deletions, and sign flips. Our theoretical analysis reveals how signed edge perturbations and node feature correlations jointly determine the learned representation stability. Based on this analysis, we propose a theory-guided perturbation strategy that selects structurally influential signed-edge modifications. Experiments on synthetic and real signed graphs show that the proposed method consistently induces larger embedding drift, polarity change, and downstream link prediction degradation than baselines. These results highlight the importance of sign-aware and distribution-aware stability analysis for signed graph learning.

papers.title: Type-aware Prompting for Community Search over Heterogeneous Information Networks
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
papers.abstract: Community search over heterogeneous information networks (HINs) aims to identify a cohesive community of nodes sharing the same type as a given query node. Existing methods either rely on manually designed structural constraints that generalize poorly to unseen communities with diverse characteristics,or depend on query-specific supervision that is prone to overfitting under limited labels. In this paper, we study community search over HINs in an inductive learning setting, where test communities are disjoint from training ones and only a few labeled vertices are available per query. We propose HINT-CS, a type-aware prompt learning framework for community search over HINs. HINT-CS augments the original HIN with shared learnable virtual nodes: a primary virtual node that provides an explicit structural anchor to the query node and auxiliary virtual nodes that aggregate type-aware local context from heterogeneous neighbors. These prompts are inserted in a query-dependent manner and encoded by a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT), enabling the model to capture transferable community patterns. We further employ an alternating training strategy to jointly optimize the prompt nodes and the HGT encoder under limited supervision. Experiments on four real-world HIN datasets demonstrate that HINT-CS consistently outperforms five representative baselines, improving the average F1 score by 9.09% over the best baseline.

papers.title: Who Should Teach? Confidence-Aware Dual-Teacher Learning for Few-Shot Node Classification on Text-Attributed Graphs
papers.abstract: Text-Attributed Graphs (TAGs) integrate graph structures and node-associated textual attributes, and recent studies have increasingly leveraged Large Language Models (LLMs) to improve TAG learning in few-shot settings. However, existing approaches typically utilize LLM-derived information uniformly across all nodes, despite substantial variations in its reliability, while also incurring considerable monetary costs. We argue that the most appropriate source of supervision may differ across nodes, as Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and LLMs exhibit complementary strengths in exploiting structural and semantic information, respectively. To this end, we propose CoTeach, a Co nfidence-aware dual- teach er learning framework that dynamically selects the more reliable teacher for each node. Experimental results demonstrate that CoTeach consistently improves few-shot node classification performance while reducing unnecessary LLM utilization and associated monetary costs.

papers.title: Efficient Dynamic Node Classification via Target- and Memory-Free Cross-Attention
papers.abstract: Dynamic graph learning faces key trade-offs: self-attention suffers from quadratic computational scaling, while memory-based methods compress interaction histories into fixed vectors, losing fine-grained temporal patterns. Furthermore, existing link prediction models rely on destination nodes as attention anchors, making them inadequate for standalone node classification. We introduce DANCE, a memory-free framework using learnable embeddings or global tokens as self-contained queries to perform identity-aware trajectory matching via linear-time asymmetric cross-attention over raw neighbor histories. This eliminates the quadratic bottleneck while preserving full per-node expressive capacity. Enriched with multi-scale temporal features, DANCE achieves state-of-the-art AUC-ROC performance (up to 6.2% relative improvement over best baselines) with significantly lower training time and memory overhead. To handle cold-start settings, our two inductive variants substitute node-specific parameters with global tokens, ensuring robust generalization on unseen nodes. Code is available on GitHub (https://github.com/erfanmoshiri/DANCE).

papers.title: PairWatch: Pair-Aware Anomaly Transformer for Detecting Adversarial Rendezvous in Public Satellite Catalogs
papers.abstract: Documented adversarial rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) appear in the public TLE catalog, yet existing TLE-based maneuver detectors treat each satellite in isolation—mistaking routine station-keeping for adversarial behavior and missing RPO entirely when the target stays passive. We argue that the right unit is the satellite pair and the right inductive bias is the kinematic symmetry between approach and recede. We instantiate both with PairWatch, a pair-aware AnomalyTransformer whose attention prior is augmented with a sign-symmetric geometric similarity over relative-motion features, and release an open benchmark of 359 windows from public Space-Track data spanning 11 documented RPO events, 100 Clohessy–Wiltshire synthetic adversarial windows, and a five-class hard-negative set culminating in the TerraSAR-X / TanDEM-X helix formation. Under the deployment-relevant criterion of a single threshold separating real RPO from operational negatives—a necessary property for catalog-scale screening—PairWatch is the only model that succeeds, with the property holding in 100% of bootstrap resamples versus 0–19.5% for three neural baselines and under 0.1% for four physics-informed detectors. A per-source analysis exposes a shortcut-learning failure mode of single-number AUROC: simpler baselines attain higher overall AUROC by shortcutting a synthetic-vs-formation contrast with no operational meaning; removing this single cell flips the test ranking entirely (LSTM-AD), and these baselines fail the security-relevant task the benchmark was built to measure.

papers.title: SyDE-Net: Shapelet Synergy Discovery and Evidence Modeling for Multivariate Time Series Classification
affiliations: Competition Policy and Assessment Center of State Administration for Market Regulation
papers.abstract: Multivariate time series classification (MTSC) often depends on sparse but discriminative joint local evidence. Shapelet methods provide interpretable local evidence units and are appealing in limited-label settings. However, existing models often represent many shapelet or subsequence features as separate fine-grained evidence units and infer their class relevance through implicit interactions, which may mask sparse joint evidence among redundant or weakly relevant local features. We propose SyDE-Net, a Shapelet Synergy Discovery and Evidence Network for MTSC, which captures complementary class evidence from coordinated shapelets through explicit synergy discovery and hierarchical evidence modeling. SyDE-Net mines class-specific synergy priors with Rank-JIG and injects them into the Synergy-Class-Decision Evidence Bottleneck (SCD-EB), where shapelet features are progressively organized into compact synergy, class, and decision evidence. Specifically, global temporal context modulates the selection of class-relevant synergy evidence. Experiments on UEA and HAR datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of SyDE-Net, with the best average rank in the UEA main comparison and competitive performance under full-data and limited-training HAR settings.

papers.title: Candidate-Fate Accounting for Transparent Sensor Diagnostic Pipeline Search
papers.abstract: Industrial sensor diagnostics relies on preprocessing, representation, and classification pipelines, making automated pipeline search useful for reducing manual design cost. However, existing automated machine/deep learning (AutoML/AutoDL) reports typically retain only fitted trials, scores, and winners, omitting generated candidates that are invalid, pruned, skipped, cached, or unfitted. This omission limits reviewers' ability to check signal constraints, budget use, and unevaluated legal alternatives. To address this, we propose candidate-fate accounting, a candidate-level audit framework for diagnostic search traces. It records each observed candidate as auditable evidence: hashes merge repeated observations, legality checks flag invalid candidates, allocation rationales explain budget decisions, and a closed fate ledger assigns one terminal fate to each candidate. Experiments on three bearing-diagnostic datasets show that the framework detects invalid candidates and identifies 30–41 candidates omitted by fitted-trial-only reports, with closed fate records verifying complete candidate accounting while maintaining competitive diagnostic performance. The code is available at https://github.com/XXIE999/candidate-fate-accounting.

papers.title: Chi-Square Weighted k-Means for Fast and Interpretable Text Clustering
papers.abstract: Document-term matrices are sparse, imbalanced, and naturally interpreted through relative frequency profiles, yet many feature-weighted clustering methods still rely on Euclidean distance. We introduce CW-kmeans, a simple extension of k-means that combines the Chi-square distance with automatic feature weighting. The resulting objective preserves Lloyd-style updates, learns discriminative term weights, and remains efficient on high-dimensional sparse text. Across six standard text clustering benchmarks, CW-kmeans is competitive with or better than strong sparse baselines and compares favorably with sentence-embedding pipelines while retaining explicit term-level interpretability. Weight inspection further shows that the learned weights identify removable low-information terms and produce concise, specific cluster descriptors.

papers.title: CLARE: Cluster-Number-Independent Latent Representation Learning with Graph Autoencoders for Deep Clustering
papers.abstract: Deep clustering uncovers latent structure in the data, but the number of clusters K is rarely known in advance. Because the true K is unknown, data analysts cluster the data under many candidate values of K and compare the results to find the most reasonable clusters. Many recent deep clustering methods improve accuracy using self-supervised methods, such as pseudo-labeling, but K is defined in the training objective. Evaluating each candidate K requires retraining the model from scratch, making a complete sweep across all K values computationally expensive. We propose CLARE ( C luster-number-independent LA tent RE presentation learning), a representation learning framework that does not use K during training. CLARE builds an adaptive kNN graph that reflects the clustering objective and keeps an edge only when it is consistent with a node's local neighborhood. A graph autoencoder then learns a single embedding from this graph, and we can group the data into any number of clusters without retraining. We further introduce a cluster-number-independent clustering loss that sharpens the cluster structure by extending the global clustering coefficient to two-hop connections. Across eight text and three image benchmarks, CLARE reaches state-of-the-art accuracy on long-text and on two of the four short-text datasets, remains competitive on medium-text, and sets a new state of the art on fine-grained image clustering.

papers.title: Parameter-Space Incremental Drift Adaptation for Regression
papers.abstract: This paper addresses incremental drift adaptation, aiming at accurate online prediction using past data streams under incremental drift, i.e., temporal changes in mixing weights over fixed base parameters in the parameter space. Existing online updating and model-pool methods are largely drift-agnostic, while the few structure-aware approaches focus on data-space mixing rather than parameter-space incremental drift. In this paper, we propose IDA, an Incremental Drift Adaptation method, which explicitly exploits parameter-space structure. We first show that minimizing squared errors under incremental drift requires modeling both the conditional and marginal distributions. Based on this, IDA models these distributions with Gaussian, learns the base parameters offline, and adapts online by estimating mixing weights over time. Experiments on six real-world drifting datasets show that IDA achieves the best average rank against strong baselines, demonstrating the benefit of structure-aware drift adaptation for regression.

papers.title: Out-of-Distribution Detection with Anisotropic Cosine Similarity
papers.abstract: While cosine similarity is widely used in out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, its assumption of isotropy often leads to suboptimal detection boundaries in anisotropic embedding spaces. To account for this limitation, Mahalanobis++ attempted to extend feature dispersion modeling to the normalized feature space. However, it applied Mahalanobis distance under a Euclidean interpretation, even though the features reside on a hyperspherical manifold. This mismatch can introduce geometric distortion. To better respect the underlying geometry of normalized features, we propose anisotropic cosine similarity (ANCO) that rescales angular deviations based on direction-dependent in-distribution dispersion. By leveraging the Fr\'echet mean and tangent-space covariance, ANCO aims to incorporate anisotropic dispersion into cosine similarity while preserving the manifold geometry. Extensive evaluations on ImageNet-1K and CIFAR-100 indicate that both ANCO and its adaptations to NNGuide achieved state-of-the-art results. These findings suggest that ANCO provides a principled way to incorporate directional sensitivity into cosine similarity across a wide range of applications, including OOD detection.

papers.title: When Can Pre-Trained Policies Be Reused? Inference-Time Policy Composition from Fixed Policy Libraries
affiliations: National Technical University of Ukraine “Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute”
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) policies are typically trained for fixed objectives, making adaptation to new tasks expensive and often requiring retraining from scratch. We study inference-time policy reuse: given a fixed library of pre-trained policies and a new objective, can a high-quality policy be constructed entirely offline without additional environment interaction? We introduce MOSAIC, a framework for retrieving and composing policies from reusable policy libraries. Beyond the framework itself, we investigate a more fundamental question: under what conditions can policy reuse succeed? Experiments on GridWorld environments reveal two distinct regimes. When objectives can be solved by reusing previously observed behaviors, inference-time composition achieves performance close to training from scratch while substantially reducing computation cost. In contrast, performance degrades when solving new objectives requires long-horizon planning across behaviors that are not jointly represented in the library. Additional experiments show that reuse remains robust under moderate reductions in library coverage and that policy retrieval and ranking become increasingly important when exploration is limited. Overall, our findings provide insight into when reusable policy libraries can serve as a practical alternative to retraining.

papers.title: Predict to Generate: Enhancing Diffusion World Models with JEPA-based Latent Dynamics for Traffic Management
affiliations: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the cooperative control of connected and automated vehicles (CAVs) and traffic signals by introducing a Predict-to-Generate traffic management framework. The proposed method employs a diffusion-based world model to generate desired future traffic states, and a Scenario-Agnostic Head (SAH) to decode state-transition representations into signal phases and CAV speed recommendations. To overcome the limited ability of conventional diffusion models to explicitly learn action-conditioned traffic evolution, we augment the framework with a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) auxiliary task, which predicts future traffic representations in latent space under action conditioning, while SIGReg regularization prevents representation collapse. Extensive simulations on SUMO demonstrate that the proposed method achieves the lowest average delay in four scenarios and maintains competitive throughput across all tested settings. Ablation studies confirm the essential contributions of JEPA-based latent dynamics modeling and the SAH decoding mechanism to performance improvement.

papers.title: Beneath the Noise: Uncovering and Distilling the Encoding Bottleneck of Quantum Models
papers.abstract: Quantum machine learning (QML) has attracted growing interest for its potential to match large classical models with far fewer parameters. This derives from encoding classical data representations into a Hilbert space exponentially larger than the number of qubits. In practice, however, noise mitigation limits these models to few qubits and shallow parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs), shrinking the accessible Hilbert space. This avoids noise but exposes a deeper problem of information loss that varies across samples: encoding compression . We uncover this bottleneck with the Hilbert-space encoding margin ( HEM ), partitioning inputs into a collapsed-encoding (CE) region and a preserved-encoding (PE) region, and find baseline accuracy on CE lagging PE by 43–58 pp across six setups. We propose quantum region-aware distillation ( Q-RAD ), a dual-PQC architecture that distills knowledge from a classical teacher separately on CE and PE samples. Under oracle routing, Q-RAD improves overall accuracy by up to +8.9/+8.1 pp over single-PQC and parameter-matched depth-doubled baselines. These results show that the encoding bottleneck can be exploited via its sample-level structure and architectural separation. Our code is available at https://github.com/skwonbb/Q-RAD/.

papers.title: ConRAC-SE: Evidence-Agreement Routing for Cost-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Security Classification
papers.abstract: Enterprise document security-level classification must balance rare high-risk recall, precision, and inference cost. Static ML pipelines lose recall as sensitivity patterns drift, whereas retrieval-augmented classification (RAC) grounds predictions in auditable precedents but still struggles on boundary cases, and verifying every document with an LLM is expensive and can inject variance when the evidence already agrees. We introduce ConRAC-SE, a deterministic evidence-agreement routing controller for cost-aware RAC: it commits top-1/top-2 evidence-consensus cases without an LLM, verifies only non-consensus cases with a small LLM against a top-3 evidence vote, and escalates only verifier–evidence disagreements to a high-capacity LLM. On the WikiLeaks and DISC security corpora, RAG-style RAC always-LLM decoding helps when the retrieval backbone is weak but regresses when it is strong; under a limited call budget on the strong backbone, ConRAC-SE instead improves quality consistently while lowering average latency and LLM cost. LLMs are thus most useful here as residual adjudicators rather than always-LLM decoders, and the routing additionally surfaces the ambiguous tail for review.

papers.title: Decision-Focused Learning with Differentiable Micro-Demand Aggregation for Electricity Retail Procurement
papers.abstract: Retail procurement decisions are made by forecasting future demand and then optimizing procurement plans under time-varying unit procurement costs and operational constraints. In this predict-then-optimize pipeline, even the same magnitude of prediction error can induce different downstream procurement costs because prices vary over time, and operational constraints can make forecasted demand infeasible when used directly as a procurement plan. As a result, minimizing standard prediction losses, even with weighting schemes, does not necessarily minimize downstream procurement cost. This motivates Decision-Focused Learning (DFL), which trains predictors with respect to downstream decision objectives. Applying DFL to large numbers of consumers requires demand aggregation to smooth noisy individual demand, stabilize forecasts, and prevent downstream optimization from yielding noise-driven decisions while preserving heterogeneity relevant to procurement decisions. We propose a DFL framework with differentiable micro-demand aggregation that jointly trains consumer clustering, aggregate demand forecasting, and downstream procurement optimization in an end-to-end pipeline. In numerical experiments on demand forecasting and electricity retail procurement optimization, the proposed method reduced procurement regret, defined as the cost gap between prediction-based decisions and the full-information optimum, by 25.6% versus a k-means-based prediction-focused baseline and by 3.3% versus its DFL counterpart. Furthermore, this approach exhibits robustness to the number of clusters.

papers.title: Does AlphaFold Rediscover the Hydrophobic–Polar Model?
papers.abstract: AlphaFold predicts protein structure from sequence with remarkable accuracy, yet which physical principles are reflected in its predicted structures and internal representations remains opaque. We ask whether AlphaFold rediscovers the hydrophobic–polar (HP) model (the classical abstraction in which folding is driven by maximizing contacts between hydrophobic residues) using the HP model as an interpretability lens rather than a prediction target. Mining predicted structures from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database for the E. coli proteome, we reduce each sequence to a binary HP string under a standard hydrophobicity scale and test the central HP hypothesis with a label-permutation null model. AlphaFold structures robustly over-represent hydrophobic contacts (median ≈ 1.8× enrichment, >97% of proteins), an effect stable across hydrophobicity assignments and contact definitions; yet on short chains they fall short of the extremal compaction an HP optimum would demand, indicating a directional preference rather than an optimized objective. As a complementary probe, we show that AlphaFold's internal representation linearly encodes residue burial —the structural signature of the hydrophobic effect—well beyond amino-acid identity, and more sharply than a sequence-only language model. Together these analyses bridge a learned predictor and a classical combinatorial model, providing an interpretable account of how hydrophobic structural information is reflected in AlphaFold’s predictions and representations.

papers.title: CG-Probes: Recovering Guardrail Directions from Patient Query Embeddings
papers.abstract: Patient-facing AI assistants promise valuable support to patients, but incoming queries can pose medical risks. To create guardrails, we work with oncologists to define three ordinal risk axes: Medical Urgency, Psychological Urgency, and Topic Sensitivity. We propose Clinical Guardrail Probes (CG-Probes) to measure the risks from query embeddings. We probe for each axis in the normalized embedding space of frozen embedders via the difference-in-means method, treating each axis as a potential linear direction. To train the probes, we cluster 79,658 Czech oncology search queries with BERTopic and use these clusters to generate pairs of queries with contrastive risk levels via few-shot prompting. We evaluate the approach on 200 queries (90 real, 110 synthetic), each graded by two oncologists, against two open-weight LLMs and a frontier LLM. We find that urgency-based axes are recoverable as linear directions, and the probes are competitive with open-weight LLMs (no significant differences in quadratic-weighted ?) at a fraction of the latency. Each axis yields a scalar score that clinicians can inspect and use to set escalation thresholds. The pipeline requires only search logs, axis definitions, and black-box access to the embedding model, suggesting transferability across healthcare domains. Robust validation on new queries and axes remains future work.

papers.title: Ontology Concept Overlap as a Training Signal: Knowledge-Grounded Reinforcement Learning for Clinical Question Answering
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning post-training for language models relies on two reward designs: human preferences (RLHF, DPO) and binary verifiers (RLVR). Clinical question answering fits neither. Near-correct answers differ by a single substituted entity, and no executable check decides clinical correctness. We instantiate a soft verifier from a maintained controlled vocabulary: UMLS Concept Unique Identifier overlap (via scispaCy, set-level F1) gives a graded, externally specified reward computed without a model in the loop. We combine it inside GRPO with an entropy-normalised LLM judge, which covers the safety and evidence axes overlap cannot see, and a small consistency penalty on padding and repetition that keeps early-training samples scorable. This three-term composite improves over SFT on Phi-3-mini (3.8B) over MedQA by 2.9% on EM (0.700 vs 0.680) and 39% on Token-F1 (0.202 vs 0.145); on Llama-3.2-3B the corresponding gains are 14% on EM and 35% on Token-F1. We report Token-F1 as the primary metric because it credits partially-correct clinical content that EM discards at this open-generation scale. Main-table results are means over 3 seeds with standard deviations below 0.005. The method transfers to PubMedQA, where training on the PubMedQA train set with the same composite reward improves Token-F1 over SFT by 22% on Phi-3-mini and 17% on Llama-3.2-3B without retuning. A reward ablation on Phi-3, varying the judge-ontology split at a fixed consistency weight, attributes 3 EM points to the ontology term, the contribution that catches entity substitutions the judge cannot. Three negative findings constrain the design: DPO under random negatives underperforms SFT for strong-prior models but helps the weakest-prior one; PPO under a sparse neural reward diverges; GRPO with KL-in-loss collapses at 7B. The recipe is designed to transfer to any domain with a maintained controlled vocabulary, a generalisation we leave to future work.

papers.title: Reliability-Guided Video Token Learning for Contactless Vital Sign Estimation
papers.abstract: Contactless vital-sign estimation from video remains difficult because physiological cues are weak, spatially localized, and easily corrupted by illumination changes, motion artifacts, pose variation, and sensor noise. Existing methods typically learn deterministic mappings from video to physiological waveforms or rates, but they rarely model which visual evidence is reliable or when a prediction should be trusted. We propose a reliability-guided video token learning framework for uncertainty-aware physiological signal estimation. The framework learns to mine informative spatiotemporal tokens, suppress unreliable visual evidence, and infer structured physiological dynamics through masked video-token modeling, signal-guided alignment, and supervised vital-sign estimation. In addition to predicting physiological waveforms and rates, the model outputs an uncertainty score that reflects visual ambiguity and prediction reliability. We evaluate the framework across heterogeneous contactless sensing settings, including respiratory and rPPG benchmarks. In addition to standard accuracy metrics, we assess reliability using uncertainty separation, high-error detection, and risk--coverage analysis. Results show that explicit visual-evidence reliability modeling improves robustness across datasets and provides a practical confidence measure for contactless physiological monitoring.

papers.title: CAPA: Context-Aware Prototype Adaptation for Weakly Supervised Histopathology Segmentation
papers.abstract: Weakly supervised semantic segmentation (WSSS) reduces the need for costly pixel-level annotations in histopathological image analysis. However, CAM-based WSSS often suffers from ambiguous tissue boundaries, inter-class visual similarity, intra-class morphological variation, and a missing spatial context in patch-level processing. We propose CAPA, a Context-Aware Prototype Adaptation framework that improves CAM generation through two components: Neighbor Context Attention, which incorporates information from spatially adjacent patches, and Reliability-Aware Contrastive Loss, which adapts subclass prototypes while suppressing unreliable CAM-derived samples. By jointly modeling spatial tissue continuity and sample reliability, CAPA provides more discriminative and stable supervision for CAM generation. Experiments on BCSS-WSSS and LUAD-HistoSeg show that CAPA improves the mIoU by 6.4 and 4.2 pp over the previous best method, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining neighborhood context modeling with reliability-aware prototype adaptation for weakly supervised histopathological segmentation.

papers.title: Beyond Independent Predictions: Learning the Browsing Journey for Sequence-Level Re-ranking
papers.abstract: Re-ranking aims to present users with an ordered list that maximizes sequence-level utility. Industrial deployments widely adopt the Generator–Evaluator framework, where the generator proposes candidate sequences, and the evaluator scores them to select the best one for display. The fidelity of the evaluator's utility estimates thus directly governs recommendation quality. However, existing evaluators predominantly follow the Independent Behavior Modeling (IBM) paradigm, which simplifies the continuous user browsing journey into independent per-item predictions (e.g., CTR). This oversimplification ignores two physical realities: (i) a click can occur only after the item has been reached and impressed, and (ii) items compete for finite user attention. As a result, IBM produces systematically biased evaluations and suboptimal sequence selection. To address this, we propose a Joint Behavior Modeling (JBM) perspective that explicitly models the display → impression → click process to capture causal and competitive dependencies within a sequence. Building on JBM, we develop the Impression-Click Evaluator (ICE) , a plug-and-play framework that (i) predicts a browsing-depth distribution to estimate per-position impression probabilities, (ii) leverages predicted impressions to suppress spurious context from unexposed items during click modeling, and (iii) introduces a click distribution matching objective to capture intra-sequence dependencies. Extensive offline experiments across diverse backbones, together with a 14-day online A/B test in the Taobao App (+0.70% clicks, +3.67% revenue) and full-traffic deployment, validate the effectiveness and robustness of our approach.

papers.title: SARM: LLM-Augmented Semantic Anchor for End-to-End Live-Streaming Ranking
affiliations: Institute of Information Engineering, CAS; School of Cyber Security, University of CAS
papers.abstract: Large-scale live-streaming recommendation requires precise modeling of non-stationary content semantics under strict real-time serving constraints. In industrial deployment, two common approaches exhibit fundamental limitations: discrete semantic abstractions sacrifice descriptive precision through clustering, while dense multimodal embeddings are extracted independently and remain weakly aligned with ranking optimization, limiting fine-grained content-aware ranking.
